A real gem, but not for the faint of heart.  This game combines the quirky and "gross" visual style of Edmund McMillen (worked on Meatboy too) with roguelike and Zelda-esque procedural dungeon delving.  The game has hundreds of power-ups and rooms and dozens of bosses and enemies, many of which require unlocking through achievements, ensuring you'll never have the same playthrough twice.  It's a good thing, because the game itself is short even if you know how it works, and even shorter if you don't.  Gameovers are perma-death and require you to start over, but it really adds to the character and survival/horror aspects of the game.
As far as games go, look no further if you want a cheap roguelike that offers awesome variety, visuals, music, and tactful combat.  Try the online demo to see for yourself, as few games offer nearly as much fun in such a small package!

I'm delighted to find this hidden gem while perusing the games for a Meridian 4 bundle as it's been a while since I really enjoyed a platformer (the last would be Trine and Trine 2). There are many detailed reviews here and I agree with most so I will try to sum things up here:
(1) Storyline - man lost his son and tries to find him in a swamp. Meets a wisp that helps him to get deep into the swamp.
(2) Gameplay and difficulty - 12 levels (about 6+ hours I'd say for one playthrough, more if you want to get all achievements). You will obtain various powers (i.e. the 3 types of light) at various levels, first when you meet the wisp and then by defeating some of the later bosses.
The lights are the key to the enjoyable aspects of the game because at times you will need to solve puzzles by activating switches / platforms by using various combinations of lights. You can only activate 1 colour at any time with your character but there are many occasions when there are lanterns present which means you can have multiple colours so you need to figure out the combination of colours. Some of these are quite tricky even for someone like me who plays a lot of puzzle games and I needed to take a break for some of them to clear my head so if you enjoy some intellectual stimulation while platforming this is definitely for you but if not you can start looking at other games right now.
The platforming is also enjoyable because some of the jumps require switching colours (you press 1, 2, or 3 to activate each colour) so there are times where I will go, "ok, jump, 1, 2, jump, 1, 2, etc." because sometimes you need to remove a barrier by activating one light and create a platform by activating another light. However, while it may be fun for me, I think some found it too frustrating hence the reviews weren't as positive as I would expect it to be. Granted that there are sections where it can be tricky but there was none that took an overly long time and the reload checkpoints are fairly generous so usually after any section of 30 seconds to 1 minute of platforming you would hit the next checkpoint so that you don't have to go through all that again... Also, I don't think there was any unfair or unrealistic expectations. One review I saw mentioned about the problems when two lanterns are together but actually there is a consistent way the lights interact so you can predict what will happen. The game requires a fair bit of skill and reflexes but it is one that gives a great deal of satisfaction.
(3) Graphics + Sound - cool graphics and I liked the artwork. Voice-acting wise was ok for me and I'm usually not picky about this unless it's quite bad. I quite liked the wisp's voice but the man sounds a bit dead which given the circumstances sounds like it should but there was just something off about it. Music was quite appropriate at certain junctures and I especially liked the one in the "Speed of Life" level because that's the fastest paced level and I felt tense listening to the music hahaha.
Overall, I think it's a really good game especially at the price (about USD $7 currently) and deserves better ratings than just 80%.

I find this game a little pretentious. It is like the sort of writing you would expect from a high school kid. Someone who thinks that adding long winded explanations and if you don't use a word over five sylibles in every sentence it will be ignored. Kind of juvanile really.
The combat isn't up my street either really. I find that by focusing the torch on something directly in front of you the game sends in enemies from the flanks on purpose because it is trying to force you to move. But the fact you need to degrade enemies shields with light before you can kill them means the entire thing just ends up feeling cheap. You have such a limited amount of vision at the sides that enemies which have ranged attacks or that I don't see more often than not end up sledge hammering me in the back of the skull, before I've even had a chance of dodging.
Also the ability to evade enemies and run in this game is downright broken. The game actually advises that you sometimes evade enemies and run for the safety of light but normally the enemies are faster than you and will just slaughter you the second your back is turned. That coupled with the fact that the combat in some areas feels so limited that you just want to run away, you end up trapped between a rock and a hard place.
The game is very linear, and the gameplay is quite tedious. You just know that in every chapters sooner or later you are going to go tumbling down a cliff or get knocked out and end up in the dark, running through the woods trying to get from point A to point B. Running into a constant stream of enemies that sping up when you cross a threshold. It does break up the gameplay with the odd tweak like some vehicle driving and the fact you have to search for light sources and often this involved starting up generators using a small quick time mini-game type thing.
But negatives asside the game is very good. It has a fantastic atmosphere and a very intriguing story. I am a science nerd by nature so anything that pulls and messes around with space-time and the fabric of reality and multi-verses is right up my street. I like the fact that it has a good amount of twists and turns and it does break up the action using well placed radios to listen to about local events and the TV shows which mess around with physics ideas and weird sub-plot.
Also this game is very good at making you low on ammo. For the most part anyway there are some annoying areas where they will place an obscene amount of ammo in a massive box right where there is a boss, so you basically have unlimited ammo if you can get to it. Kind of pointless really but when you are out in the wilderness you do want to concerve your ammo because if you aren't careful you will run out.
There are a variety of weapons and picking up different types of torches as you go along is a nice twist.
The game is based around Alan Wake, a writer who's wife gets locked away in some unknown place and there is a woman who captures Wake and forces him to write a story. A story which when finished will allow the woman to regain her life. Somehow though Wake manages to write his own escape into said story at the same time and it is this escape that you are playing out. As you go along you pick up manuscript pages which give insite into the world and is a kind of progressive narrative. You find them as you move along and some searching is often needed though I have not deviated massively from the path and I have found the majority of them.
There is also a rather stupid addition of finding coffee thermos flasks at random around the place. Which kind of make sense if you find them in a cafe or in someone's kitchen but when you find them out in the middle of the woods on a rock or just happened to have been left on the tracks of a piece of lumberjack equipment it kind of seems idiotic.
But overall this game IS very great. Though I don't worship the virtual ground it is made on, I do see how people can like it. If you are a gamer looking for a great story, this is for you. Don't expect a top-top end performance overall but it is still a great adventure. If you aren't sure waiting for a sale might be the best option.

I don't even know where to start. The game itself isn't bad; I've had the disc version for years and I loved it. One lost install key and a hard drive crash later, though, and I was stuck with this.
Here's the SHORT list of everything wrong with this game:
-Dovetail gave it their signature laundry list of overpriced DLC. On games like TrainSim, you at least know you're paying for good stuff, but on this, it seems DT is just adding in a bunch of low-quality payware and even former-freeware addons at a ludicrous markup.
-To ensure their profits keep coming in, DT ensured that there would be enough tweaks to the game's code so that it rendered most third-party addons incompatible. (chief among which being VRS' TacPack)
-The multiplayer community is a shadow of its former self. While this isn't Dovetail's fault, they could certainly do a lot more to promote the multiplayer experience. There seem to be a lot of military groups; why not add an AWACS to their mile-long list of DLC?
To sum it up, I'd say that if you're already familiar with this game, go ahead and buy this. But if you're a first-timer, don't waste your money. Get something else, like X-Plane or even Prepar3D if you can spare the extra cash.

Alan Wake was one of the first things I bought on the Summer Steam Sale - I was a bit apprehensive as it was originally an Xbox Exclusive, and I'm predominatly a PlayStation player (Not a fanboy or Xbox hater fyi). I was never too keen on Xbox's exclusives, and the price tag always made me think Alan Wake was just a small arcade game. I was so wrong.
When I first played it, I was a bit confused - wasn't entirely sure what it was all about. The tutorial is rather strange, but as soon as you get used to it you'll love it.
The game is full of tense moments, jump scares and plot twists. One of my favourite aspects was the TV series style, which again I wasn't expecting. I absolutely loved the moment at the end of episode one where it ended like it's 24 or True Blood.
Definitely recommend!

Quick review so I can get back into it.
-Story is great, not award winning, but pretty damn good.
-Player choice is brilliant, certain decisions can make you miss levels or characters alltogether.
-A little short by comparison to other similar games,but if you go for 100% stealth (not all missions work though) it significantly draws out the play time, and is really rewarding.
- The debrief after each mission gives you a run down on the effects of each of your choices, which is an awesome addition I think.
- Gear customisation is decent, and looks pretty cool. Weapon customisation is meh, all attachments look the same which makes some guns look stupid (shotguns)
- Character customisation is limited to skin tone, hats, eyewear and some pretty horrible facial hair.
- Boss fights are laughably easy with the pistol skills, but tedious and annoying with other weapons.
- The different builds you can have greatly change how the gameplay feels
- Every choice has a consequence and it actually matters unlike many games that make the game claim.
Definitely worth picking up, I only wish Obsidian had more money when making this, but they made a pretty damn good product with what they had.

I don't know I'd call this a game as such. Sure you are navigating a character around a virtual world, but this feels to me like what holodecks will be like - a truly interactive experience where your choices actually matter and drive the narrative.
This isn't a game. It's an interactive story, and dear god it's an incredible one. I have never been so immersed in something like this before. I just finished this, and I actually have a bit of a tear in my eye from it. I cared about the characters, I agonised over choices, even knowing that I could make them again if I wanted.
I doubt I'll ever play this game again. I know I missed a lot of things on my way, but I don't want to go back and make those choices again. It's like one of those films, in the American Beauty, To Kill a Mockingbird, Last King of Scotland vein - it is so so so so so good, and something you are very glad you saw, but something you want to make a one-time thing, because you know that if you see it again, knowing how it ends, you wouldn't enjoy it so much. A famous film reviewer once said that if they had one wish, it would be to see their favourite film again for the first time. I feel that way about this game.
Anyone who plays this should be aware that it can be dark - very very dark - and deals with some pretty horrific events. But they should, more than anything, take it slowly. Wander round the levels, explore everything. There is so much in this game, but you won't want to come back, so you need to see everything the first time round. But there's joy in it, and the detail which has gone into it is magnificent.
You don't play this, you experience it. And you should definitely experience it.

Maybe the writers took the wrong lessons from what people liked about the first one (the game is dark and the ending was sad) and made the whole game overly maudlin and almost agressively bleak and depressing. Maybe the departure of some of the major creative talent from Telltale between the releases of seasons 1 and 2 means that same spark just isn't there.
Whatever the case, I want to stress that I did still like and would recommend this game, but it's a much more flawed experience.

This game looks simplistic at first glance but may be one of the best space/rocket simulators out there. Even though we're not launching real humans into space, the premise will grab your attention. Launch everything from simple rockets into orbit to landing onto other planets. A warning to the player though, this game is not easy when it comes to getting where you want to go. The game is fun but comes with a huge learning curve called orbital mechanics.
Kerbal Space Program is a rocket simulator. The objectives change as the player progresses through the game depending what game mode was chosen. There are 3 modes : science, career and sandbox. Career is the real challenge as reputation, contracts, money and research all play a crucial role in completing objectives and acquiring better technology to build better rockets. Science throws aside the funds and reputation but still respects research in which the player still needs to meet certain objectives. Sandbox lets the player run loose without any strings attached and even has some pre-loaded vessels ready to be launched. Do not be fooled though, this game isn't as easy as launching into the sky and flying to another planet. There are a lot of calculations involved and for me personally, a lot of youtube tutorial videos. Adding all the components you wish to isn't always easy, and definitely isn't easy to launch all that off the planet!
There are a few primary structures that start small and grow (visually) as the player progresses. These structures include a vehicle assembly building, launch pad, space plane hangar, runway, tracking station, and astronaut complex. The vehicle assembly building is where the rocket, ship or even lander can be assembled and saved/loaded. The Hangar is for planes that need to take off on the runway. The tracking station is for data, mission management and tracking statistics (such as where landed ships are). Lastly, the astronaut complex allows the player to recruit new units to fly into space. Each structure can be upgraded by clicking the right mouse button. Other structures include research and development (which is important to improving and discovering new parts), mission control used to obtain contracts and the administration building, I'm not too sure what it does.
Building in Kerbal Space Program is relative simple and easy to do. The challenge is finding something that works and doesn't blow up during launch. The trick is not only to be able to pilot it without it spinning out of control but also have enough fuel to land. The first part comes easy to me but the second part is actually quite difficult if take off isn't done properly. There are a tonne of parts that the word limit on this review won't let me name them all. Parts included are parachutes, cockpits, aerodynamic wings, de-couplers, rocket-fuel boosters, fuel canisters, biology bays, research attachments, and all sorts of other thrusters and boosters. To add more depth to the construction, frames can be added to the rocket so that the rocket doesn't need to stand on it's own boosters. Meaning, if you have a rocket that can't really stand on it's own due to it's odd shape, size and weight, there is a method to suspend the rocket in the air prior to launch. Releasing the rocket is relatively easy but ensure that you place everything in proper order. Order is especially important in this game and can be easily overlooked when constructing. If you don't put everything in sequential firing order, you just might fire the wrong rockets and cause an accident. Order (or stages) are everything! Double checking this will definitely save some headaches.
the game is basic but ensures details where necessary. The rocket parts are pretty detailed but the world itself sort of feels bland. I do feel they could have added a little bit more to the terrain (or added some cities) to make it more... decorative. What is cool is that they decided to include a camera on-board every shuttle. So whether you're flying one Kerbal or many, you can check their facial expressions at any time (which is a neat feature).
are basic and do provide the essentials but nothing extremely out of the ordinary. Crash effects are definitely included.
Overall, good game but with a big learning curve. Don't jump into this expecting to hit the moon right away. It will require some skill, observation and background. When you do succeed and understand how it works the game, everything becomes a lot easier to do (obviously)! It's just getting through the learning stage is what makes it difficult. For future updates or games, I would recommend trying to make an "easier" setting so regulars can simply jump in and play. Then again, the challenge is what attracted so many players.

When I bought this game, I got the Gold Edition for $70 bucks. As I haven't seen what the Season Pass will hold, I'm completely happy paying $70 for just the base game. Keeping it brief, here's what I think about Shadow Of War:
In my first steps back into Mordor, I found myself getting nostalgic from the original Shadow of Mordor. Everything that has happened in this game is either completely new or a part of the rebuilt systems from the first game. All of the things that are new were created extremely well, pandering to a better gameplay experience and making the game far better than its already incredible predecessor. All of the rebuilt parts put into Shadow Of War are brilliantly configured to perfectly complement the game as a whole. The entire Nemesis System was redone and improved to help you actually gain relationships and history with your new found "Friends" and perhaps future enemies.
I think the only downside that I've encountered 37 hours in, are some of the Orc's AI when they are in Pit Fights. I've watched my child Orc, that I've raised from Grunt to Captain, just stand around and taunt the other Captain while he was sliced and mauled to death. This isn't a problem that I've seen often, just on a few Orcs here and there. It's more of an inconvenience than anything else really, so I don't even count it as a con to the game. As to all of the people who view mircrotransactions as a negative, I see it as something extra that was added for us all to use, if we would like. It's not anything that is necessary for your to progress through the game, as far as I have seen. If you want to throw a few more dollars at SoW, more power to you!
Just having the chance to be lost again in the ruinous terrain of Mordor, was worth the cash in my opinion. All in all, if you enjoyed Shadow of Morder or have fallen in love with the world of Middle Earth as I have, Shadow of War is worth the purchase and certainly the time.

With a setting seemingly taken out of a book from Stephen King, this game is full of scary stuff.
...  Nah, really.  I couldn't count the amount of times that I physically JUMPED out of my chair.  This one has more frights than the latest Resident Evil game.
Released originally for the Xbox360 (2010), and ported to the PC (2012).  Yeah a port.
Taking the role of Alan Wake, a writer stuck on vacation.  Your wife goes missing, and its your mission to find out what happened to her after your concussion.
Dark forces are at work, and light is your only escape, and method into beating them.  Using a torch, you wear away their "shield", and once you've done that, you can shoot them with any regular means (guns...).  There is no knife, or melee weapon to fall back on.
Story is the real strongpoint to this whole game.  The player wants to learn what happened to the wife, and is sucked into the world with its great writing.  Writing?   Oh, and you find white paper on the way actually telling you what will happen next.  Confused?  Yeah, its a bit strange like that.
There are six episodes in the package.  Each a chapter to the story.
A few of the characters, Alan, Barry (comic relief), the police lady, Odin and Tor, that doctor guy, the freaky guy.  There are many in this story, but you'll only remember a handful.  Everyone else just gets the nickname "that xxxx guy".
Gameplay is pretty good.  Whilst I'd have liked to see slightly tighter controls, it plays very well.  Battles are quite exciting and you get a slight choice in weapons (there aren't many).  It plays similar to a crossbreed of Resident Evil 4 & Indigo Prophecy.  The battles, however are a bit hit and miss, as they seem to be a bit on the "lite" side.  Serious gamers will probably be bored with the same enemies by the second or third episode.
Graphics are very good.  Whilst textures at times are a little less than desirable (eg, Episode six, when you watch your TV), they help bring the player into the story.  I'd say comparable to the first Batman : Arkham game.
Sound?  Great.  No complaints at all.  Soundtrack fits.   Swizzle.
As this was first released on the Xbox360, it may have been released in parts.  But towards the middle of the game, there is a feeling of it being slightly rushed.  You will keep encountering the same enemies, yet the battles play out no different.  You defeat them in the same way.
The surroundings also feel like you're still in chapter one.  Night setting, full of trees...  Wood cutting tools...  For the length (six chapters, maybe 10-11 hours standard playtime), it feels like you are going around in circles just to watch the story continue.
Pros
+Great story
+Good graphics and sound, helps portray the story well
+EEP!  Jumped out of seat a few times
+Good controls
-Many characters I don't care about
-Copy and paste enemies and environment models.
-On, and on, and on (too long in comparison to substance)
Overall rating; 7/10
Last thought:  Feels like a spiritual sequel to Resident Evil 4.  I wouldn't re-play this title, but if you are a gamer that likes a strong "horror" type story- this game is worth a shot.  Might feel a little uh, "cheap" half way through though! ;-)

Republicans have plenty of talking points they could be repeating (however correct those points are) but instead they get stuck with answers that don't fit the candidate at all. Other areas they could have improved (but didn't) from the previous game include

- Radio: They've actually outright removed this. But didn't bother to replace it with anything so now you just have "the ground game" (very cheap with limited outreach) and TV.
- Internet/Social Media: There is no internet/social media component to the game. Even though this has played a huge part in this election.
Overall it seems like Stardock only put the absolute minimum amount of effort required into this release.

Be warned, based on the preview, this is not really so much as a "horror" game as it is an "existential dread" game. You are constantly feeling the alien experience, and it kind of weirds you out, but it's not a bunch of Lovecraftian monsters crawling out of every crevasse, as the preview might show you.
Overall, it was a fun experience, and I would still recommend giving it a shot if you enjoy Lovecraft or want something different from your horror game.

First off, I love this game.  I recomend it highly, it was worth my 60 dollars to play it in the early release it is definitely worth the 40 dollars it is now.   It has come a long way since the Early Access review that I did, so I am updating it now.
This game plays very much like Final Fantasy Tactics or Fallout Tactics (minus the real time option).  In it you will create 4 of your own Desert Rangers and then head out into the wastes and explore, and either clean up the wasteland or kill everyone and thing in your path.  Along the way you can recruit many extra characters to your cause, each with their own personality and traits, up to 3 may travel with you at any given time.
The difficulty of the game varies sharply depending on how you choose to play it.  Early on most enemies you fight will be much weaker than you are, however you are not forced to play the game in any linear fashion and as such you may wander into areas with much stronger enemies than you are prepared to face (not that you can't win but it can be brutal).
The ability to go where you want and do what you want flows throughout the entire game.  You can sweet talk people into giving you what you want, threaten them (with the proper skills) or if that fails shoot your way through.  Wall in your way?  Use a grenade.   Person make you mad?  Shoot him, or don't.  Raiders take over a town?  Negotiate or kill them it's all up to you and how you want to play.  Most choices have concequences further down the line, some amusing and some well down right destructive, even when you think you are making the right choices nothing is ever black and white.
You will collect all kinds of weapons and armor, and most weapons can be customized by stripping down others for base parts.  Everything from WW2 rifles to futuristic laser weapons are represented each with an optimal range, armor penetration and rates of fire.  In battle many of your enemies will show up with different kinds of weapons, often enough you can kill them an take it for yourself.  The various enemie types also force you to prioritize targets: Do you kill the big guy with the sword made out of the one way sign (yes, they really are swords made out of sign posts and one way signs) attacking your medic, or do you take out the guy who is still too far out to hit you but is charging with grenades that will hurt everyone?  Oh and friendly fire is a thing, don't try and use a shotgun from behind your own people.
Character progression is handled in an RPG like fashion with skill points gained at every level and ability points every 10.  You can be a generalst and do a bit of everything but nothing well or you can specialize each of your characters (highly reccomend you do) into different things.
I broke my basic team into:
a) Sniper / Lockpicks / submachine gun - gave me nice range and something when stuff got closer
b) Sniper / Perception / Kiss A** / Submachinegun - can see traps still shoot far and sweet talk
c) Heavy weapons / Safe Cracking / Assault Rifle - HMG to mow down eneies - rifle to consere ammo
d) Energy weapon / First Aid / Rifle / demolotions - can remove traps and is the field medic
Then I picked up and kept in my party a
e) A drunkard shotgun specialist whom I also turned into the groups weaponsmith (because drunks make the best weapons right?)
f) Lady scientist who can hack any computers and is handy with a pistol (and later rifles)
g) Young kid who's life I saved,  he started with brawling and ended with rifles pistols and the ability to talk to strange animals.
I built my team knowing that I would go to a specific place and pick up a particular npc.. how you create your team is entirely up to you and playing around with different builds is half the fun.
- Pros -
- Great turn based combat.
- Easy to understand mechanics
- Fun!
- Lots of humor built into the game
- So many different ways to resolve things in the game
- Ability to break your own missions through poor choices (and sometimes good ones) requiring some creative solutions to be used to move on.
- Solid strategies will win most fights.  Using cover, hitting clusters of enemies with a grenade etc.
- Ammo doesn't grow on trees, making conservation of rounds part of the strategy.
- All different kinds of weapons with all kinds of pros / cons built into them.
- Not all weapons are a straight forward upgrade, sometimes you just have to try them out.
- Each person can only carry so much weight, there is no way to be Rambo and run around with 1000's of rounds of ammo and infinite first aid kits.
- Cons -
- Did I really just wipe out an entire town on accident? Oops.
- Random battles can be major easy or completely overwhelming.  Luck plays a part.
- Bah stupid AI won't stop throwing grenades at my clustered people.
- Drunk bugger keeps going rogue on my party and getting himself shot to pieces.
- Some fights, more so early on can be extremely difficult to get through.  The first boss fight was really bad for me as my squad was almost dead and did not expect the guy to attack me since we were talking at first
- Ammo can be hard to come by in the early game, forcing you to either use weapons your team isn't skilled for or to spend all of your money on nothing but ammo instead of armor / weapon mods / first aid kits etc.

This review is based on the early access so I will try to be reasonable with how I feel about the game.
The game reminds me so much of Fallout 1 & 2 with support for higher resolution. The graphics are nothing spectacular but it doesnt have to be since the game focuses more on user experience and immersion. Yes immersion! I'm not a big fan of reading especially long dialogs but this game does it well by letting you visualize what's happening in the world via text (type writer) and npc barks. It totally allows you to use your imagination without even realizing it. Yes, there are a bunch of typos that I've noticed which affects my experience personally, but then again it's still on beta. I like the fact that the quest log system does not treat you like a dumb person, unlike Fallout 3 where it shows you on your compass where you need to go. Instead the log gives you details of what you've accomplished so far and what you need to do next. I'm playing the default difficulty (seasoned) which is very challenging and the loot system is well thought of. The scarcity of ammos and health pickups allow you to decide whether you should go back to citadel (home) by travelling which is by the way is very very dangerous, or just keep pursuing hoping that you'll maybe get lucky and find some loot or vendors along the way. There are also a lot of interesting items you may find such as sega genesis console, neogeo, and even a used condom. I think they are irrelevant to the game but it's defnitely entertaining. I probably won't sell them. It would really be awesome if the developers can go even further with it and allow you to give it to a person in citadel to place it in citadel collection room or something, to display your awesome finds.
The controls are pretty good, it's could be improved though. But I liked the fact that I can play it with just the mouse, so I don't have to hunch down in front of my keyboard. I can just sit back, relax, with one hand on the mouse. It accomodates old gamer like me who's retired and doesn't have to work and just allow the kid inside me to just enjoy what I've missed when I was growing up working too hard. No more stiff necks and sore elbows. But like I said it can be improved. Also, if I may add, I really like how the cursor system was in fallout 1& 2. I think it's actually one of my favorite and memorable to me that right-clicking changes the cursor behavior to walking or action command. I can't remember if it was double click the walk mode to run but that would be awesome option. instead of holding down shift key.
I like that they stayed away from static camera, but sometimes I wish there's an option to turn it back to static camera because the camera can get a little clunky sometimes. When you're tryign to find the travel zone it can get very frustrating, I think the way to solve this is by minimap (starcraft like)  which you can click on an area in the minimap and move the camera to that spot, which is currently not in the game. Speaking of map, I wish they have the option like in fallout 1 & 2 to have some kind of a town map that you recently visited to allow you to just go directly to a certain part of the town instead of walking all the way from the travel zone just to talk to one guy, then walking back all the way again to get out of the town. By the way the first time i took a ride at the crane elevator at highpool i was like, "Oh cool", but after doing that for about 10 times I'm like "Okay...", then I'd noticed one of my party member was left behind so i have to go through the cutscene again just to get my other team mate. I know it probably took some time and even effort for whoever designed this but it get's annoying especially when you're on the go. I'm not sure if there's vehicles in the game that you can ride like in fallout 2, and if there is it'll be awesome if you can customize it to add protection from radiation and and dehydration and allow a faster travel with options to attack random encounters using a higher outdoorsman skill. Also what's up with kick♥♥♥♥♥ smart♥♥♥♥♥ and hard♥♥♥♥♥ I mean, does it really need to have 3 separate skill for each one? I hope they make this into just one skill, I don't know like just Kick♥♥♥♥♥
I'm kinda glad that it's still in beta, which leaves a lot of room for improvements, I just hope that the deveopers are as open as they should be for suggestions and improvements. And I look forward for this awesome game to get even more awesome.
Bottom line is I'm totally recommending this game if you can tolerate grotesque, rude languages, violence, drugs, prostitution, and sad reality of the world to come after the apocalipse.

I backed this game on Kickstarter, and I would have got my money's worth following its development even if the finished product wasn't particularly good. Fortunately that hasn't happened, and Act 1 of Broken Age is the most fun I've had playing a game designed by Tim Shafer since the last one I played! It's a beautiful game in every respect, the art and animation is wonderful, the music is of the highest standard, and the voice acting is excellent without exception. Really, as a demonstration of what a modern adventure game can be, there's no finer example. It's mildly amusing throughout, with a couple of laugh out loud moments. The puzzles aren't particularly challenging, although I did get modestly stumped a couple of times, having to come back the next day before the solution presented itself. Frankly, that's about my speed, but I still hope Act 2 is a little more challenging. Even if it isn't I would have had a great time. Overall a great success then, as far as I'm concerned. Like any good two-parter, the story ended on a suitable cliffhanger with some burning questions remaining unanswered, hopefully Double Fine don't take too long completing it.

Even though released in 2006 and thus a bit dated, FSX is still one of the 3 most played flight simulators.
Flight Simulator X offers different grades of realism for differend kinds of players, newcomers and professionals alike. Luckily, the Steam Edition also includes the "Acceleration" Add-On, which added a bunch of content.
FSX is great to boot up and take a short flight or spend several hours with, although the default aircraft aren't as detailed, there is tons of Add-On content out there, both free and payware. With it's plug and play system for new content, FSX made it incredibly easy to develop more, and most importantly, realistic content for. From aircraft that couldn't get closer to reality, with detailed cockpits and every switch working as it does in real life, to amazingly detailed scenery and sounds. Latter is often found in payware content, though.
There is also a multiplayer mode, so you can fly with your friends or strangers and even have real people in charge of ATC. If you want it even more realistic, you can join VATSIM, a network dedicated to giving you the most realistic flight experience right at home.
A great game, unless it bugs out on you... which it might

Even with this easier than classic gameplay I'd strongly recommend this game to old and new gamers alike.
Also if you enjoy this I'd recommend checking out previous work by the Double Fine team and Tim Schafer!

Upon replaying this again (4th playthrough), I understand why some people hate it, but I think they don't GET it. Very strict RPGs with gunplay are always challenging because of unlearnable notions about action games. To compare, Mass Effect 2 is an ACTION RPG. And the core gameplay loop does not change much a la cover shooter with cool-downs and waist high cover arenas start-to-finish. Nothing wrong about that. But it is a poor RPG in comparison to AP which has a clear sense of character progression that has signifcant impact on gameplay. At the start you can't shoot with any amount of instant-gratification accuracy but by the end you can instantly head shot 6 dudes without leaving cover, or go invisible and knock out everyone in the room, etc.
That being said, this games dialog system and branching narrative is among the best in the business. The story can unfold in so many different and surprising ways depending on the intel discovered, choices you make, how you interact with the variest characters, the order you complete missions in, etc...Play it more than once and play differently each time and you'll find just how different the game can play out.

Well I find this a difficult game to review on its merits as I found the story, atmosphere and combat all highly enjoyable, but felt that, despite its attempts to present a new style of gameplay, it was little more than a linear game that borrowed heavily from HL2. Whilst the locations were beautifully represented, with plenty of atmosphere, I felt like I was replaying many of the levels and physics games from Valve's classic. Many of the timber yards were very reminiscent of Ravenholm, and there was even a level where you lit up the enemies with your flashlight whilst the female NPC sheriff accompanying you shot them. Ring any bells from HL2? All in all I was disappointed in the way that the game borrowed so heavily from other games, but the combat was spot on, using the torch to burn off the darkness from your enemies before you could pop them delivered tense fights when 4 or 5 enemies were approaching from all sides, meaning you were constantly having to check their position and hold them back with the torch before you could move in for the kill. However this led to some fights being heavily weighed in the enemies favour and I rage quit several times after constantly dying in some levels. In addition, some maps certainly overstayed their welcome and at times progression became laborious. I would recommend the game is worth playing for the story and atmosphere, and some of the locales up in the mountains are simply stunning and well worth visiting. But, ultimately, it is not an FPS, and it certainly wasn't a patch on RAGE!!!

- The jumps 'feel right' with respect to speed and height.

Simply stated, this game is a lot of fun, just don't go in expecting anything serious!

This game will frustrate you. It will make you want to tear your hair out. It’ll make you want to punch your computer. It’ll make you forget about everything outside of beating this one level. And it’s amazing. The gameplay is fast-paced, intense and graphic. It will make you think on your feet while at the same time have you plan your moves out ahead of you. As the levels progress, Hotline Miami increases in difficulty, but at a rate that feels natural and doesn’t seem to be too difficult. In one hit you die, and the most common action you’ll do will be ‘Press “R” to respawn”. Thankfully, the satisfaction you receive after killing everyone in the building makes all that frustration worth it.
As you play, you’ll unlock different masks that will have different effects that may or may not make the game easier. The story is dark and suspenseful and very confusing while at the same time able to keep you engaged. Hotline Miami is certainly replayable, and you might need to do exactly that to fully understand the story, unlock all of the masks, weapons and secret levels.
Hotline Miami has been acknowledged all over the internet as having one of the best soundtracks ever made. No matter how many times you die or how many hours you’ll play, the music will always feel fresh, exciting and motivational. I’d highly recommend buying the soundtrack as well, as you’ll probably want the songs on your phone.
The retro graphics are also well done. Hotline Miami has bright, bold, engaging and sometimes neon colours throughout the game that remind you of the 80’s, and the characters and levels have a lot of detail in them for an 8-bit graphical game.
Hotline Miami is a game that has done everything right. I’d highly recommend this game to everyone who likes fast-paced and graphic games, especially if you’re a fan of excellent music.

This game is 100% PURE Lovecraftian Goodness :D I have been waiting a long time for a new game to pay so much attention to detail and source material as this one does. If you are a fan of Lovecraft's Cthulhu Methos, or just "Out There" type Horror and Story Telling, then look no further, you have found your current destination.
I was very much prepared to start running and hiding as some due to the description given on the store page, but to be honest I used these mechanics very seldom. The game is more of a Walking (Run to speed things up)/Puzzle game. Normally I'm not a fan of puzzles, but these were presented in a way that worked very well, and was not to difficult after a moments reflection. Now, you CAN Die. There are a handful of parts were running is necessary (a very nasty area were you are being chased by multiple ... things, immediately comes to mind. I have read that most people had their only real progression issue with this area, and rightfully so. I was fortunate enough to get past it on the first go and didn't exactly realize how much I lucked out until reading discussions on this area after the fact. Pure Luck).
Honestly, I wish the running for your life parts (they are very few) were not in the game. Just the story, exploration and general visuals/hallucinations would have been more then enough to make this a solid experience with out the sudden "Oh, Lets run away now... no really its not a hallucination THIS time, Run!"
Overall, very fun and atmospheric game. I loved it.
Pros :
*Deep Lovecraftian Storytelling (Takes place a few years after "At the Mountains of Madness")
*A pretty tight narrative.
*ATMOSPHERE!
*Multiple Endings and Collectibles (Replay Value)
*Good Horror Elements not Dependent on Jump Scares
*Very Good Level Design
*Lovecraft done right, with respect to the source material. This in itself is a Major Plus.
Cons :
*Its kinda short.
*Maybe ... two or three times are you are in any real danger. You spend so long doing the puzzles and following the story that when you do eventually have to run, your a little stunned as to what to do. "Run away you say? What button was that, I haven't used it the last hour or so..."
*(This one is more of an opinion) No Native VR. If any Horror Game out there should have been in VR, its this one. The atmosphere is practically begging to be as immersive as possible, and it succeeds, largely. However, VR support would have made it sooo much more then what it is. I used VorpX drivers to play Non-VR games in VR. Its not a perfect solution but it does work.

The genre "walking simulator" is a plague and the games based on that genre have a lot of issues. Some of them get away with incredible story, some have great puzzles or maybe both. Conarium has neither. Its selling point is that its based on a Lovecraft novel. I'm sure the novel is good however the way the game tells the story is sadly the exact opposite. Throughout the 4 hours of gameplay I was almost entirely not invested in the lore/story as I'd hoped.
The presentation of the story does start ambiguous and interesting at first but then slowly starts to give you hints about how it will end or what it is about which is a bit sooner than you'd expect. At some point they even repeat the definition of Conarium, just in case you were too slow to "get it". The ending or at least the one I got was somehow uninterestingly anti-climactic and I'm guessing one of the good ones based on how I was expecting it with all the lizard people references.
Sound wise, it does an okay job. Dialogue isnt really bad nor good and the soundtrack, sound effects do a decent job at creating the atmosphere. Sadly the atmosphere after the first hour just drops completely into tedious cavern walking. The graphics alone while good, cant save the atmosphere either.
I have not played the developers previous games though I can see they are inproving and I do hope the next game will be better. For the time being however, Conarium is a passable experience unless you're in dire need for some atmospheric game or if the game is on sale.

TL;DR Choppy graphics (poor aliasing), poor performance, no guidance, frustrating physics, feels like an alpha
KSP is great for sandbox space exploration and realistic physics, but no in-game guidance, buggy playing, and poor performance that feels like an alpha game. If you want frustratingly detailed physics in a space exploration/engineering game that lacks guidance and punishes you for issues you can't forsee, this is a good purchase on sale.
The main issues are that the game:
- Provides very little support to teach you how to do anything,
- Has so many bugs that it feels like an alpha release, and
- Runs slow and flickers (i7, Radeon Pro Duo, 16GB RAM can run DOOM on ultra, but this game won't run well)
Only a few hours in after hearing what a great game it was and watching friends, I had to quit from frustration. Building rockets in career mode severely limits you until you have science points (similar to Civ where time and effort experimenting and doing small tasks give you points to spend). Those points are used to get new parts to build and upgrade, but it's not clear what you have to do, even in the side quest" tasks that give you science points. The tutorial tell you the purpose of each building, but not how or why to use each building or how to use the controls. The game doesn't flow well and there were many times when I wondered how the game could be released. For example, putting three rockets together using the triple tool makes the ship unstable and you can't place fins to properly balance without experimentation and the snap function doesn't help with stability (even multiple tries don't often work, which is just frustrating). The launch menu is difficult to use and until you try to launch your first rocket, you won't know you need to set the sections to fire manually. Finally, the game runs very choppy (aliasing issues) and slow, no matter what settings I set (I can run DOOM on ultra, but can't get a single nice screen beyond the main menu in KSP -- I have an i7, Radeon Pro Duo, 16gb RAM, and a Freesync monitor using Displayport for reference).
Overall, I was disappointed to play a game that felt too early access, but had huge potential based on the great physics.

Judgement:Apocalypse is an early-apocalypse settlement simulator in a world very similar to Hellgate:London. You were out camping, demons have spontaneously appeared through Hellgates and before you could make it back to the city it was on fire.
So far so good.
Whats my first goal? Build a log cabin and dig a well. Digging a well is a pain in the butt and you can technically only do it where there is ground water, but all right. Then I make myself a club or two. I'll then spend the next 30 or so game-days alternating between building buildings, repelling attacks and exploring for resources and new village members. Exploration consists o moving somewhere with a bad guy, fighting on a tactical mini-maps in realime, the collecting the loot and experience.
The game is enjoyable enough for the 30-or-so hours I put in it but around then I got the feeling one gets with games -- what's the point? Do I really care how this ends up or am I a monkey pressing a button for his nuts? Here are the issues with the game that get in the way of it becomming something special:
Issue #1: What's the Story?
The development plot makes no sense. At least in the US there are more guns than people. Apocalypse? Less people, about the same number of guns. Why when I sneak into a farmhouse and fight multiple demons I am doing it scraps and water and not a weapon makes no sense. In a world filled with guns, the successfull village doesnt scramble first to learn metallurgy so they can invent their own glock. They go pick up a few on the street. This is true of leather jackets and baseball bats.
If clubs and leather jackets armed by a few kids can beat off hordes of demons, why is everyone dead? They had the top end military equipment players aspire to.
The best defense against demons are sharp spikes on the ground. Even flying demons cant seem to fly over them. However you cant put a sharpened log into the ground directly. You need to plane it first. Work tables, luckily can be built directly out of logs.
If you want a multi-tier resource constraint and production system, spend some time to invent why you need to do it. Id rather hear that normal guns barely hurt a demon and need to research how to build Hellgate:London style weapns and search the mp for parts to build components.
Issue #2? There is no village management game
Build one well and now you have unlimited water as long as someone sits there to draw up water. Build three vegetable gardens and now you have unlimited food as long as you tend the food and chop it into salad. You can store an unlimited amount of resources which no one needs to carry in an invisible resou8rce bank account. Chop too much wood? Plant a tree and watch it grow within 4 days.
Its a time management game.
Thank god our campers landed somewhere with clay and metal deposits both within walking distance. These can get used up and, okay, you can use magic to make more but its magic so Im okay with that.
My humble request is this -- if you are going to take the time to make a game, have a world that makes sense. Differentiate yourself from the world of freemium games with their non-economies that are asking you to just spend time and make micro-transactions.
In the end, I feel in its current state Judgement: Apocalypse is leaning more towards a freemium game that you pay up front for than the good solid simulator that it could be.

NO SPOILERS
1) I loved the game, and I have gotten the true ending on normal difficulty without spending any extra money on the game after my purchase price, there was no need to.
2) you absolutely do not need to spend money on microtransactions to get the "true ending".
Im gonna break it down here, to get the "true" ending of the game (which in reality isn't necessarily a true ending in that it changes anything, its 100% something that when you get to the ending before the grind you already understand its going to happen, its a 25 second cut scene and a credit roll) You need to defend your bases in 10 stages against attacks increasing in difficulty. And basically, if you lose any orcs in the fight they are essentially gone forever. You can however replace these orcs through either A) dominating any attackers, B) getting loot boxes.
And here's where I have my issues, because this is definitely heavily blown out of the water. You have 3 levels of loot boxes, Silver, Gold, Mithril,(Silver having 2 items with one at least rare, gold having 4 items with at least one legendary, and mithril having 4 items all being legendary) and 2 types. One set of loot boxes gives you random orcs and the other set gives you gear,m all scaled to your level. Silver loot boxes are purchased through in game currency, gold and mithril boxes are purchased through premium currency "gold". As far as I understand, you are only allowed ever buying 3 mithril boxes, so if you're a wallet warrior you can not just buy a  bunch of mithril and have all legendaries.
People like to jump on bandwagons and complain about things, but here's the thing, Silver loot boxes can ONLY be bought with in game currency, which the game absolutely THROWS at you every step of the way. I got to the beginning of the farming section with over 100k of the currency and that was after spending some on loot boxes whenever i needed, and upgrading all of my gear. Some missions give over 10k of the in game currency, and the only thing that uses up your money is buying upgrades for your castle, which doing 2-3 missions is enough money to fully cover. A loot box costs about 1000 currency, and since the contents scale to your level its basically 2 free things that are very helpful that is just extra stuff.
There is NOTHING in the loot crates that you cant earn pretty easily in game through just playing, and its definitely false that any  types of orcs or items are locked behind a paywall. Legendary orcs spawn randomly, and you can recruit them same as any other orc while playing, you can also get legendary orcs during the fortress assaults which guarantee at least one spawns, and you CAN get the highest tier gear in loot crates that you buy with in game currency.
Honestly a lot of the problems people have with the loot crates is pretty foolish, and if anyone is going to tell me that the grind is any more "grindy" than the true ending of Batman Arkham Knight youre absolutely insane. Sure, having lootcrates COULD be bad in single player games, but in this game with how much♥♥♥♥♥♥is just given to you, i was absolutely never feeling like i needed to put any money in. The microtransactions did not take from the game in any way of the sort, if you loved Shadows of Mordor or you at least liked it, or the Batman games, youll love Shadows of War, it is absolutely one of the best games released this year, and is one of the few games I fully intend to do more than one playthrough trying out the hardest difficulty.

In short: No FOV slider... again!
The longer explanation is that FOV is hard-coded and outside player control. It changes depending on exploration, holding a weapon, sneaking, running, and so on. Ie, FOV is outside player control.
And! I! Dont! Like! That!
In addition to the loss of player-control, the 'toon is positioned so that the centerpoint of the screen is where is head is. The question becomes a simple "why!". All this leads to is make a large portion of the screen blocked, leaving only the upper 1/3 open to view the scenery. I dont get this setup. They had the same idiocy in Shadow of Mordor, and it had to be fixed by activating cheat-engine with associated graphical issues.
I cannot fathom the reason behind this issue. As stated, shadow of mordor had it. Mass effect Andromeda has it. The witcher 3 has it. Almost all games that have mods released to it has a camera mod that returns control to the player. Skyrim had a mod that also stopped the annoying as hell "cinematic kill-cam" ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Why is this even a thing?! All it serves to do is show off the frekkin boots of the 'toon.
It is like the guy designing the boots on modern games, is actually the son of some sith-like shadow-ceasar, so now games have to show off these boots or other devs will die to a bond-like crotch lazer for daring to hide the amazing foot-wear modelling.
FOV sliders are always requested in all games. But not all gamers require them to play. I know that I am in the minority that simply have had enough of this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. But that does not change my inability to play a game that makes me feel like I am trying to look over the shoulder of that impossible large dude on a concert.
I seriously dont understand why they cannot include it in the options. The engine allows it. The cheat-engine FOV fix proves this in all games that dont include them (the entire Mass Effect series of games, SoM, SoW, etc).
In the 90's and early 00's it was standard and mandatory for all games on PC. But since the "new game experience" has settled with console-first development. So I've played through the whole game until the end of act IV. And unlike most people, I'd say that the second act was the most boring out of the 4, just because it was nothing else but a Shadow of Mordor replica.
What is Shadow of War like? Shadow of Mordor, multiplied by 2 - you get all the old mechanics you had in SoM, plus the new ones, like Redefined Nemesis System, Fortress System, Combat Abilities etc. The play space got expanded tremendously and now includes 5 medium-sized maps of different environments, from Ash Mountains to Ephel Duath.
Two most considerable pillars of SoW are the actual combat and nemesis system. Combat, while is pretty primitive, makes up for it with an inconceivable amount of fun it delivers when slashing, incinerating, maiming and dishonouring the shadow forces. The good variety of omnifarious finishing moves, realistic sounds, and energetic flow can keep you entertained for hours, perhaps for dozens of hours. The other merit is the aforementioned Nemesis System, that now stores a huge amounts of different personalities and appearances that orcs can bear, along with their behaviours and habits. They somehow feel alive and can potentially become a great emotional attachment for the player.
The Storyline is decent, it's made so it can be sewn into the original LoTR narrative (even though it's rogue to it in most parts). It's nothing special and offers nothing of an actual interest respectively.
Graphics of SoW are one knitted tie away from its' precursor, Shadow of Mordor, even though now they miraculously eat up to 8200 Megabytes of your VRAM and 10 Gigabytes of RAM on ultra settings. 8,2 bloody Gigs of VRAM!
Visually, the game is OK, but in a just-just kind of barely for 2017 standarts.
Now, let me indicate my opinion on this incandescent steel-fashioned remonstrance of Lootboxes. I do think, that this is a formidable savagery for a dev to put microtransactions in a singleplayer game. Yes, a singleplayer game with no server-sided contents that couldn't be modified with a good old Cheat Engine prog or a game trainer. So why do you lose your heads over this, if it's not an actual problem to be reckoned with in order to have a good game experience? What's more is that while you're not pouring your money in, you don't sponsor this practice.
In conclusion I'd like to say that while Shadow of Mordor is a really good game to invest your time in for a wild time, it also is not of indigince with lots of conversial parts and frankly monotonous junctures.

It's kind of funny that Schein isn't the first puzzle platform game with a light gimmick that makes elements of the world appear and disappear that I've played. Fortunately, it's the best one of those that I've played, and a pretty good, if very challenging, platformer.
Your character awakens in an appropriately dismal swamp, seeking his son. He soon finds a chatty little wisp that casts a magic light that can make special platforms and obstacles appear. Like Closure and other games that came before it, Schein is built around using light sources to clear the path ahead. In addition to revealing platforms, the light can power certain devices and reveal hazards, as well. As if that wasn't enough, you'll find additional kinds of light further in, multiplying the complexity.
And boy howdy, is there complexity. Schein throws both puzzling and precision platforming at you, and does not hold back on either. There are twelve levels to traverse, and as early as the second or third you might run into puzzles that trip you up. They're a good kind of challenging, the sort that look impossible until you get your head in the right place, like the ones in Braid or P.B. Winterbottom. They only get harder, too, which makes Schein a good game to fill the gaps between other, less trying titles.
You'll need breaks from the platforming, because some of the timing and light-switching can get absolutely brutal. Never unfairly so, and there are generous checkpoints and instant respawns, but it goes far more difficult than the look of the game would suggest. It is a very pretty title, with the different light sources changing the look of the world in salient ways, and some lovely sound effects and minimal music to support. As long as you don't let frustration get to you, Schein will keep you engaged and busy for quite some time.

For People who plan on using their sims for serious matters:
Why I do NOT recommend it:
If you are one who wants to make their simming experience as realistic as possible, I would NOT recommend this "game". At least when it comes to the feel of it The reason for quoting it as a "game" is because people who are serious about flying, don't want a game, they want a Simulator. FSX (SE) has been long debated wether it is a true Simulator or just a game. Of course there are always people who want to defend what they are used to and so you'll have mixed reviews. Truly, the flight controls, no matter how much you tweak this game or purchase more add-ons, will always be less realistic. This game doesn't feel like flying a real plane. It's close, but not quite there. Also, the standalone aircraft are absolutely obsolete. there is no way of learning much about an aircrafts systems when flying these planes. If having the feel of flying and being more into a planes systems without purchasing 3rd party Add-Ons is important to you, I'd reccommend X-Plane 10. The wise choice is to not go for this game when taking things more suriously but I also do.
Why I recommend it:
FSX, because it is so old, has made a lot of progress. The game itself is already a fun experience but when truly taking things suriously, one can just purchase 3rd Party Add-ons. I will be honest, if one plans on purchasing them, this game is a must for you. There are highly realistic replicas to real aircaft to buy that are absolutely a great experience. Such as the famous PMDG developers or A2A, RealAir. Then others such as ASN, REX and FSUIPC. If you have this kind of money, this game is perfect for you because such complex simulations do exist, but for a price.
Summary:
Reasons not to buy:
- When wanting to get to know how flying a plane feels like
- When not wanting to spend more money to learn about an aircraft's system
Reasons why to buy:
- If you have the money, the best 3rd Part Add-ons exist and are great for learning a planes systems
such as: PMDG, A2A, RealAir
All factors can be important but overall, for what I look for in a sim, I'd recommend FSX (SE) more. The reason is because I find learning the systems before flying is more important. I do have the money to purchase 3rd Part add-ons and do. I own many nice Aircraft which have tought me great things. I also own X-Plane 10 and use it if wanting to practice Hands-on flying. Of course I also own 3rd Party add-ons for X-Plane. With about 6-7 years of simming in my life and 4800 hours of flying experience, I am happy to share my thoughts about this game.

You start playing thinking "okay, very neon, nice soundtrack." The music plinks and hisses, background throbbing, and you wonder who this man is and why there's a rubber♥♥♥♥♥♥mask on his head. The messages on his answering machine are bizarre, strangely mundane in the urban decay that surrounds him. A date. An appointment. Those naughty kids down the block.
You're pondering it the whole time--who is he? What's happening here? Why is he being confronted by a horse mask and a caustically sarcastic owl?
Then you realize you've stuck your thumbs in a man's eyeballs and popped them out like a particularly juicy zit, all while the throbbing soundtrack and neon light of the level surges like the hammering of your pulse.
Your character vomits, but you don't. You're too busy trying to figure out how to get to the pan of boiling water on the stove so you can surprise the guy in the next room with a shotgun. A quick succession of buttons, the screen bursting and crackling like fireworks with your score, and you've knocked him down with the door and boiled his head. Even having to restart each level more than ten times, you realize it has been worth it.
"A brutal game," you think, half-admiring and half-starting to worry what kind of person you both are, but it is swept away under the riptide of action. Some part of your brain is fizzing like a mouthful of Poprocks as the points keep adding up. It doesn't matter that the graphics are primitive--you're primitive. In fact, you're a savage. You and your character, together, blood like pretty cherry spray over the floors, the walls, everything pulsing and surging as your fingers twitch on the buttons.
"B+," you think at the end of a level, as it grades your performance. "How DARE you give me a B+! I can do so much more." You take a shaky breath as your fingers stab at your keyboard, taking you back out of the level. For a moment, the lettering on the screen seems mocking, and then you realize it's merely waiting for you, patient in the way only a machine can be patient.
It's waiting for you to come back with your lead pipe, and your katana, your baseball bat, and your assault rifle.
"Here," you whisper tenderly at the screen. "Let me show you what I can do."
What can I say, it is great. Anything that makes my cold heart feel emotions is a good thing.

TLDR: Conarium is a faithfully Lovecraftian adventure game with nearly perfect artwork, but a few annoying design flaws.
Review:
Overall this game holds up perfectly to even the best of Lovecraftian games. Visually it is flawless, fully utilizing its first-person view to add mystery and intrigue around every corner. At the beginning it seems pretty plain with a basic arctic facility which has a couple interesting items but mostly seems boring, but as you progress and see the actual crafts and architecture of the ancient Lovecraftian civilization it becomes much more interesting and is outrageously faithful to the source material. It all looks like it could really exist in our world, but with differences that give you the ominous feeling of other worldlyness that is always mentioned in HP Lovecraft's writings. All of this gives the game an excellent atmosphere and, while there is no fighting and only a brief moment of action involving running away, the game kept me interested for the entirety of its journey, the ending of which is interesting and satisfying.
The puzzles are very logical, and can be solved with reasoning or reading. This makes them exactly what they should be for a Lovecraftian game, since Lovecraft based everything off of the gathering of information.
Because I always like to mention the music: The soundtrack is passable, but nothing truly special. It sufficiently helps the atmosphere although it doesn't necessarily amplify it like it could.
On the negative side, there were some design flaws that made some of the puzzles frustrating. While the solutions were easily found -aside from one or two which seemed to be a little too obscure for me- the actual implementation of these solutions had some flaws. For example, there is one where you must draw a symbol on an alien device. If you explore and figure out earlier puzzles you can find the symbol which should make drawing it easy, but its not. I had to repeatedly draw the same symbol, connecting the appropriate dots on the device, over and over again until the game finally recognized that it was the required symbol. It wasn't overly bad but the game seemed to be too sensitive on how precise the symbol needed to be drawn.
Overall this is a definite recommend for adventure game players and Lovecraft fans alike. Lovecraft fans will appreciate the lack of fighting since it was never present in Lovecrafts writing -for very good reason- as well as the loads of lore and text that helps draw you into the Lovecraftian world, and adventure fans will love it for its solid adventure elements and overall good puzzle design.

The Walking Dead Season 1 was one of my first games I played with a mouse and keyboard, so when Season 2 came out, I was excited to walk back down memory lane with the series. Since Season 1, I had a handful more experiences with both the mouse and keyboard type games, as well as the Telltale-style. With this added experience, I think it better prepared me to enjoy this game in its full entirety.
You start this season as the much loved character from the previous season, Clementine. Based off of her experiences she encountered in Season 1, she has matured quickly for a girl of her age. Spoilers aside, Clementine was thrown into a few situations back in Season 1 that allowed her to become the what appears to be fearless warrior she is in Season 2. However, since this is a "pick your own adventure" game, your decisions will impact how fearless her character really becomes by the end of the 5 episodes.
If you are not familiar with the series, these games give you the ability to manipulate random objects you come across, interact (or refuse to interact) with a variety of characters in your group, and of course, fight zombies to guarantee your survival in the apocalypse.
Clementine has grown in many ways since we met her in Season 1 however she still is not as strong as some of her mentors were, which she sometimes forgets. She is desperate to survive and protect those around her, which plays into her strong motivation to get things done throughout the series. The new group(s) of survivors that she encounters on her journey provides her more opportunities to grow and mature through these 5 episodes. These relationships however can lead her down some challenging and life-threatening paths. You will develop your own connections with these characters, which will lead you to make dialogue choices in hopes that you can save the lives of the characters you care most about.
Being able to set up how your character will grow was one of the most interesting experiences I felt during playing these episodes. Sometimes the choices you make will not directly impact the final outcome, however it does mold how you feel about certain characters and situations you encounter. However, be prepared for the ending of episode 5, all your choices lead up to one final decision, and that decision is a tough one at that!
Enjoy your adventure; I know I did!

A wonderful tool to assist in playing tabletop-style RPGs over the internet. In today's world, it is hard to get a group together on a regular basis, and Fantasy Grounds helps to make it so that those of us who love pen and paper/table RPGs can play them. The program is regularly updated and has a wide variety of user-made custom rulesets, extensions, and themes.
This year, Fantasy Grounds became the only officially supported platform for D&D 5th edition online play. There are regular "online conventions" that allow free play for everyone, and the license and DLC structure is set so that only the DM needs to pay (I personally take donations from my players to help buy the content, and they each pitched in $15 for the ultimate license - cheaper for them than buying a full version).

After 30 hours of playing this game, finishing the story and experiencing alot of this game I'm ready to fully write a review for this game.
(I will try not to spoil anything)
FYI, I am not dissappointed in the games outcome, but I am also not fully satisfied. I waited years for this game to come out after playing the original mafia 2, which is one of my all time favorite games. I had high expectations for this game and was expecting alot more from it.
I'll start off with the Gameplay features first.
Combat:
I loved the combat aspect of the game, being able to sneak around and silently kill enemies if you had the right weapons. I also loved how guns work in the game and overall just how getting to shoot enemies felt good.
Overall rating: 9/10
Driving:
I loved the driving in the game, especially in Simulation mode. It feels like your driving an actual car, but I feel like if I were to play with a controller it would be better. But even on a mouse and keyboard it was great.
Overall rating: 8.5/10
NPCs:
Personally, I think the NPCs in the game could have been better. They are really oblivious to anything, sometimes you could just slit a guys throat right next to another guy and that dude wont notice anything unless he sees you. Also, when you aim guns at civillians some will say "Dont point that gun at me" and will keep walking, and some would just do nothing.
Also, dont get me started on how people always repeat the same lines and how alot of them look the same.
Overall rating: 6/10
Misc and Pastimes:
Now this is where the game shows a problem to me and many other people, like I said before I am not satisfied with the content in the game because it lacks alot of content and features which mafia 2 had and this game doesn't have.
The whole game itself is just story, theres no features that I know of where you can do other things besides missions such as:
-Changing Clothes
-Customizing Cars
-Visiting Stores to buy something with all the money you get
-Cant visit friends or have other people with you on missions, its all you.
-Cant sleep, drink, eat, shower, watch tv. Nothing.
These are key features which I think that if they were in the game, it would make this game be one of the greatest of all time. Lets hope that future DLC Updates can include some of these and more things to do.
Graphics:
In all honesty, I had no problems with the graphics besides some weird lighting in some places and the 30 fps cap that was a thing when the game was first out. I played the game on high but I tweaked a few settings to make the game look a little better and remove the blurryness and I really thought it looked nice. Probably not as good as a game like GTA V though.
Overall rating:
8/10
And finally,
Story.
In my opinion, the story was too short and broad. Comparing this to Mafia 2, this story lacks emotional scenes and filler scenes, and these made Mafia 2 a good game. Your purpose in this game is just to do one thing, and that is to get revenge on someone. At first the story is very interesting until after a certain point in the game which takes place in the bar, (if you passed this you know what im talking about) everything after that point is just not entertaining. The game gets repetitive asking you to do this, kill that person, steal this.
My rating of the story:
6.5/10
I really did enjoy the game for the most part, I love the combat and I love the overall gameplay. Driving feels great, shooting is great, just the whole movement aspect of the game is good. Its just that the game lacks alot of key aspects which made the previous game, Mafia 2, such a good game. I would still recommend this game, but I would honestly wait until they add some new DLC that fixes all the bugs, and adds new things to do. Honestly, I dont see a point in playing anymore now that I finished the story.
Hope my review helped you decide on this game, I tried to not spoil anything, my apologies if I gave anything away.

Most Immersive
Having used most virtual tabletops out there, I always found Fantasy Grounds to be the most immersive of them all. I'm not really sure why is that: perhaps a combination of elements, like the graphic user interface, the feeling of a real table, the dice, the character portraits, character sheets, visual handouts, it not being "map-centric" . . . The text chat capabilities of this VTT are awesome, which is a plus for my game mastering style.
It's very easy to use actually from the player's side, and that is true as well for the DM side if you are covered by a specific ruleset for your role playing game system. Currently it comes with a good bunch of them, from GURPS to D&D 5E, just included in the installation.
This virtual tabletop, being constantly updated, has a great range of features while keeping itself faithful to its basic framework. The learning curve is soft unless you want degrees of customization, but the community is very helpful and there is some official documentation and tutorials.

Disclaimer: Ignore the fact it says I only have a few minutes in this game.  I use a non-steam version and have used it for at least 8 hours every week  for the past 4 months.
I have a RPG group that meets every Saturday at my place.  A few months ago I bought a projector to use for showing maps and whatnot.  I started out using Roll20 but found it to be annoying at times.  I finally said screw it and tried out Fantasy Grounds, and I haven't looked back since.
The only thing Roll20 had that FG doesn't have is the dynamic lighting, but that's still able to be done yourself with the masking in FG.
The campaign management in FG is awesome, I love it.  It has most of the game systems you could want.  I'm currently using it for 5th Edition D&D, but will be trying it out for Shadowrun pretty soon, just for keeping notes and displaying maps, as I'll just be playing, not GM'ing.
While it is a bit pricey, it's worth the one time investment if you can swing it.  The monthly license are also quite affordable if you just want to check it out first.  I had the Ultimate license prior to buying the regular version while it was on sale during the Steam summer sale.
Unfortunatley, I do not have the 5th Editon PHB or Monster Manual data sets yet.  But as a DM, I find it quite easy to just put monsters in as I need them, and I don't really need the player details on my end, just the important stuff.
All in all, I cannot recomment this product enough.  Doesn't matter if yo'ure using it to game online, or for live games, it's an amazing tool.  And not that I use it myself, but there's the possibility to create your own rulesets as well.
