I don't think a lot of people don't see the value in Mountain, and when people do they tend to simply overcomplicate the game for what it is. It's not meant to be a 'game' exactly. The developers of the game purposefully say this originally: "Leave it open - it's designed to run in the periphery of your life. Only interact with it when you feel like it. You can play Mountain while playing other games. If you are not playing it, it will play itself. ". Again Mountain is just mean to be left open and you can return to it when you feel like it. You might not see the aspect of it originally but you can find it later… hopefully. But then again, what are the standards of a 'game'? Are we to simply segregate Mountain simply because it is possibly outside of the norm? On the contrary! Different experiences lead to different viewpoints which make you more open-minded. So can people truly state that Mountain is not a game but a screensaver? There are many ways to view Mountain and seeing it as a screensaver is one of the more popular demoralizing viewpoints to which many have so acquired. So one can only view Mountain as simply a standalone and not compare it to more contemporary issues. Or one can compare it but by doing so one loses the face value of the game itself. I think I've settled for now the dispute that this 'game' might be a screensaver or simply not a 'game' at all.

On another note, the developers stated this: "If you're having an annoying storm or boring night, play a melody (using your keyboard) and time will accelerate." Mountain is there for you when you decide to return to it and play it. I think that is a common misconception. It's not as much meant to be a 'game' but rather a subsidiary and supporting game next to you. Yet there are many ways to view Mountain as with any form of issue in life. But the Way Mountain was constructed, at times unappealing to the eye, allows it to show you a different path and possibly one you may not have seen before hand.

But you don't have to follow what the developers say. A 'game' is meant to be played whichever way you feel like it. If you feel like you've been cheated off by buying this game, then take two steps back and think about the aspects of this 'game' and the elements. Perhaps you begin to notice that wonderful ambient sound that plays amidst the night, or perhaps you fall in love with the way the streaks of the sun touch your Mountain. But you might not have to like all these things to truly enjoy the game. Perhaps you have all these games and you developed a love for the game. Or perhaps you try to ridicule the game but in turn you've actually Grown accustomed to the game. I for one cannot answer that question of whether a gamer should like this or not, but it is all up to the gamer who buys it, and whether he is willing to open up his heart and mind.
Now is the Mountain truly your Mountain and your own property? I think that is in the conception of the gamer alone for the gamer can make notion whether the Mountain truly is a self embodiment, or the player truly controls the Mountain. Does the Mountain not speak to us and tell us of its thoughts? Or is it conveying a hidden message to where we might be its own spawn and it is the master. Whichever way you see fit, there are quite a lot of ways to see Mountain, as with any game. Mountain might not have a storyline, no shooting, no love triangle (unless you begin to make one up between somehow the items, the Mountain, and the sky in which case you probably might have gone a bit too far), but Mountain contains a moment of solitude in which you might notice things in games that can be recurrent in Mountain. Perhaps Mountain might contain all these elements in which you create the story. Mountain can always be a storyline in which you, the gamer, is going along a path with the Mountain to a destination into your subconscious. There is much to do in Mountain and blocking your imagination and logic will only hinder it. But if you so choose to do so than you have not hurt no one but yourself in denying the possible powers in the 'game' itself. This review cannot display my neutrality toward the game but I only wish to explain to the gamer that Mountain can only be accentuated by only the gamer.
And another thing many question is the role of the keyboard in the game. Although at first it may seem like the keys simply advance time and increase it in a way the human eye can perceive, Mountain is inevitably omnipresent and time is of little importance to him. Binding ourselves to this thought, we can perceive the passing of time as not one full of dread and dreariness, not one full of change and a different scenery, but becoming part of the universe and its infinite realm of possibilities. What we perceive as a minute can seem as nothing more than what has occurred to the Mountain. What we perceive as the future is simply the happening in the Mountain. What we perceive as the past is imply seen as the done by the Mountain.
And another question still remains as to what is the value of the items that the Mountain contains and at times loses. Are those pieces of our memories or life lessons that we must cope to accept? Or are those as somewhat like to put it as simple items that simply 'fall' on the Mountain. No they are granted upon the Mountain and delivered first hand to the Mountain or possibly to you. And what is of this item leaving our grasp and floating off into space? Have we broken your heart, Mountain? Have we done some unforgivable act too which I've lost my pony? That alone can be answered only by the gamer and his affiliation with the mountain.

And what of this inevitable destruction that reaches the doorsteps of the Mountain ever so often. Are we to simply ponder over the oblivion of the Mountain or sputter key notes to protect the Mountain? TL;DR Choppy graphics (poor aliasing), poor performance, no guidance, frustrating physics, feels like an alpha
KSP is great for sandbox space exploration and realistic physics, but no in-game guidance, buggy playing, and poor performance that feels like an alpha game. If you want frustratingly detailed physics in a space exploration/engineering game that lacks guidance and punishes you for issues you can't forsee, this is a good purchase on sale.
The main issues are that the game:
- Provides very little support to teach you how to do anything,
- Has so many bugs that it feels like an alpha release, and
- Runs slow and flickers (i7, Radeon Pro Duo, 16GB RAM can run DOOM on ultra, but this game won't run well)
Only a few hours in after hearing what a great game it was and watching friends, I had to quit from frustration. Building rockets in career mode severely limits you until you have science points (similar to Civ where time and effort experimenting and doing small tasks give you points to spend). Those points are used to get new parts to build and upgrade, but it's not clear what you have to do, even in the side quest" tasks that give you science points. The tutorial tell you the purpose of each building, but not how or why to use each building or how to use the controls. The game doesn't flow well and there were many times when I wondered how the game could be released. For example, putting three rockets together using the triple tool makes the ship unstable and you can't place fins to properly balance without experimentation and the snap function doesn't help with stability (even multiple tries don't often work, which is just frustrating). The launch menu is difficult to use and until you try to launch your first rocket, you won't know you need to set the sections to fire manually. Finally, the game runs very choppy (aliasing issues) and slow, no matter what settings I set (I can run DOOM on ultra, but can't get a single nice screen beyond the main menu in KSP -- I have an i7, Radeon Pro Duo, 16gb RAM, and a Freesync monitor using Displayport for reference).
Overall, I was disappointed to play a game that felt too early access, but had huge potential based on the great physics.

Review/How I made the game a good experince
Flight Simulator X, for the price is a truly amazing simulator. When you account for its true age (10/2006) it makes it even more astonishing. While only being on steam for a short while most of the modding community have embraced it although I will go into detail with this later.
The unmodified experience is great, until you start getting into it more. For my first 100-120 hours I was playing with just the base game planes and free online mods and it was plenty of fun. But once you decide to really get into it, say hello to montly subscriptions, goodbye to $500+ in addons and much more!
Here is my summary though.
Air Traffic Control:
The Air Traffic Control in hine sight is terrible but I never knew at the time not with only being new to the community, now I am a member of Vatsim and a paying customer of PilotEdge to get online ATC which greatly improves your experience.
Planes:
After that is sorted you get into the issue of planes. If you are happy with the stock planes, I urge you to continue using them because once you decide to expand on your library and get premium planes you struggle to go back to the limited ones. When purchasing planes also dont go crazy on your first purchase, and buy adverage planes. My first payware plane was the Just Flight Boeing 737-200Adv. and it is alright but as I continued to advance I discovered the wonderful world of PMDG. They are from my understanding the best addon company for planes on the market. I started off with their flagship, the 777-200LR/F package, a truly fantastic plane and then advanced to purchase the BAe 41 Jetstream which is where I run into my first truly major con of Steam Edtion. I learnt the hard way that not every mod is compatable with Steam Edition, and I can not urge you enough to ensure that any mod you purchase clearly states that it is supported because spending $50 on a unsupported mod does not make you happy (There are work arounds but it is not perfect). I am now wanting to add few more planes to my fleet then will be happy with that department.
Scenary:
I am yet to purchase scenary mods because I personally like to fly all over the world so purchasing scenary is just not going to work for me yet. But the option is there and the built in stuff is terrible but changing it costs a lot. If you fly in one area and VFR a lot then I couldnt recommend anything better.
Gameplay Mods:
The final polish in my opinion is mods like GSX (Ground Services), FS2Crew (Co-Pilot/Voice control), FSIPanel (Training) and many others that just add so much to the overall experince. GSX was the first thing I added to my collection because it makes all the time you spend on the ground a little bit more fun and the I got FS2Crew with my 777 which makes the games fantastic. FSIPanel is new to my collection and I am still to really play around with it but it will help make me a much better pilot. I also have mods like FSPassengers which add a goal to the game, to run an airline but that didn't appeal to me much. It will make some people enjoy it a lot more though. These either mean a lot to you or just about nothing, but to me these are probably the most important.
Conclusion:
I get asked a lot how do you have so many hours in that game. I reply I dont know :P At first look it looks boring but once you really get into it and put the time into planning out what you are going to do, roleplay and do it it is really damn fun. It has cost me a lot to get it to where i have it and it was not easy, trail and error like anything I guess.
This game is not for everyone but I can not suggest it more to anyone that is really into planes.

The apocalypse has happened. You were out camping. Ned is dead, and the three of you are now struggling to survive in an old abandoned canyon outside of nowhere. You're all basically idiots, with a few interests based on your job.
You must find or grow food and resources, research new occult rituals and weapons, and fight off the evil curses that plague what remains of humanity. But try not to attract attention.
It's a top-down colony simulator with simple graphics, but it's a lot of fun. Not as complex as Rimworld. You set up basic production chains of crafting, but you've got to have the people to be able to do it. Eventually, you get equilibrium of inventory to use. You create squads of people to send out into the countryside for scavenging and rescue purposes. Combat is quick, cell-based, and strategic, as you level up survivors and weapons.
It's still in early access. I've got about 7 hours in since buying it on Wednesday. I am save scumming like crazy, because the Challenging difficulty is indeed. Researches, both occult and normal, are more important than they seem at first. Dedicate people if you can. Keep your awareness down, and the demons won't find you.

Alpha Protocol is a game you’ll either love or hate, and whether you’ll love it or hate it depends on what you’re looking for in a videogame.
The gameplay is not very interesting, but once you figure out the exploits (pistols are king) it’s relatively easy.
The minigames are another matter. This is a console port and the minigames are seriously frustrating without a controller. However, once you’re out of the tutorial you never have to do another minigame again, provided you have enough EMPs and one rank in “Sabotage.” Still, some people can’t even get through the hacking minigame in the tutorial; if you find you can’t you might wanna get a refund, unless you’ve got a friend who can do it for you.
There are also some glitches related to enemy spawnings at certain checkpoints. But I have never run into any gamebreaking bugs.
The story is mostly just a bunch of spy movie clichés. The game is self-aware about this however and doesn’t take itself very seriously. There are enough clever one-liners to keep me satisfied. The characters are okay, a couple are memorable for the humor they provide, even if you don’t get all that emotionally invested in  them.
The conversations in this game are timed, and I’d be lying if I said I was a fan of this. I often find myself reloading an earlier checkpoint just to try a different response. But then I often do this in games with traditional dialog trees as well, I’m just weird like that.
In spite of all its flaws I absolutely love this game. It does one thing exceptionally well, and this one thing is the main reason I still play videogames at my age.
The area where this game shines brighter than the dog star is the branching paths of the narrative. The freedom you have to affect the story with your choices is something beyond any other game I’ve played. The way you treat characters in conversation can lead to radically different result, each of them either interesting or amusing. I have played through this game about a dozen times and no two playthroughs have been identical.

So, I would recommend this game to anyone who is interested in the unique way a videogame can tell a story. You’ll just have to suffer through some uninspired gameplay and glitches to access it.

Alan Wake is a third person action/thriller game, which eases in the direction of horror without ever completely descending into it. Despite not being released in an episodic format, the game is laid out in a series of "episodes" complete with credits and an ending theme which I feel needs to be noted because each one is excellently chosen - I wish all the licensed music could have been on the soundtrack.
Combat controls aren't bad, but aren't great - they act to make the game a little more stilted than it otherwise would be, and definitely lends the combat to feel more like padding between cutscenes instead of something interesting into the gameplay itself.
The story is more "unsettling" than outright creepy/horror, but if you're easily scared it might be best to skip it.
Graphics hold up excellently, and the two DLC chapters which follow the original game are.....weird. Good, but weird.
All in all, the game is VERY solid, and the atmosphere of the game is incredible. Highly recommended, and I'd also give a nod toward getting the collector's edition so you get the soundtrack, as well. The soundtrack is dissimilar to many game soundtracks in that there are vocal tracks as well, and it's very, very good.
Heck, just buy the franchise pack - American Nightmare is even better than the original game (if a tad short), and the combat controls were tightened up to the point where the combat is quite fun.

I sort of can't believe the core development team at Zoetrope Interactive consists of like 3 people? Come on. Conarium sounds, looks, and plays like it was made by a dozen developers at least. Impressive? Like, very impressive. While it is a puzzle-lite walking sim where death is unlikely (though a "game over" can result after a few sequences where you run-n-hide from some Lovecraftian nightmares), the environments are heavy and oppressive, creating just enough anxiety to keep you inching carefully forward.
The story is properly strange and well voiced, and the collectable documents are superbly written. The use of lighting and color is spot-on (I even got a high quality Bioshock vibe here and there), and the mixture of bizarre and ancient technology brings some sci-fi to the horror table. (Can I use the word anachronistic here? Amongst the glowing crystals, weird alien statues of Elder Things, and revolving stone monoliths projecting lazers, I'm pretty sure I saw a dot matrix printer sitting on a pedastle...and this whole story takes place in the 1940's, so...yeah, perfect.)
Horror addicts take note: It's not a hold-yer-breath kind of terror a'la Outlast--but I would still put Conarium squarely inside the horror genre. Let's call it Story-Centric Horror. All in all, worth the full price, no question. If, though, you are a 13-year-old whose mama is finally letting you chainsaw monsters in your first horror game...just move on. There's nothing for you here. Instead, Conarium provides an odd, thoughtful narrative wrapped in some really impessive UE4 visuals...made by 3 people? Hmmm, I still think there's something wrong with that math...
PS: I played in ultrawide 3440x1440, using ini tweaks shared by others in the discussion thread. The game displays wonderfully at the ultrawide aspect ratio (highly recommended), and it ran smooth as glass for me at that resolution.

" The problem is, that they couldn't just rip the playmode from Mafia 1 and paste into Mafia 3 which i believe they very much did. Mafia 1 came out in 2002, and what worked back then doesn't hold up now.
The way you take over a district is by going after businesses in that area, like moonshiners, stripclubs and drug distribution. You do this by going in, destroying drugs/liquor or setting strippers held there against their will, free. This will damage the business' income by about 1/3 or 2/3 but the last part of the business is just walking around grabbing dolla' bills lying around.
All takeovers feel very much the same, and the gameplay quickly becomes repetitive. The first part of the game was very good when i first played it so i had high hopes, but that's because it was story centered at that point.
After that there isn't much besides go here, destroy this, or go there kill that guy so the more important guy will show.
They also liked to hammer in alot about stealth in this game, problem is with stealth is that in order to work you have to make your A.I dumb, and this is one of those games where the A.I is too dumb.
You can litterally stand at a doorway and switch sides from left to right by the door, moving in full view to anyone looking at the door inside and they will not spot you.
The game is also filled with lots of bugs, most notably with the game's bloom and abient lighting.
It's a shame to see this game go the way it did, had it gone on a more story heavy path like Mafia 2 did, i'm very sure this game could have done well. Lincoln Clay is an interesting character, though I'm having doubts about him being fitting for a Mafia game, he feels more suited in some other game with it's own world and stories rather than the Mafia universe.

Conarium is a love letter to Lovecraft.  Unfortunately, it's scribbled in crayon.
Pros
-(Mostly) pretty visuals.  The graphics are decent.  Each distinct area is interesting at first.
Cons
-Awkward writing
The characters' lines are unnatural and uninteresting.  Characters state the obvious and repeat themselves frequently, in more words than necessary without adding any clarity or flavor.  If you're looking for a good imitation of Lovecraft's writing style or convincing period dialogue, you'll be disappointed.  Half of the rambling musings you'll read in the notes scattered in random drawers are nearly incoherent, and not in a way that generates intrigue or dread.  Word choice is strange-- modern phrases are interspersed into the flowery prose that struggles to convey anything worth saying.  It's possible to be deliberately vague while still using precise, evocative language, but this game goes overboard in trying to create a sense of mystery and just ends up being incomprehensible.
-Poor voice acting
Cheesey from start to finish, and not in a deliberately campy way.  Granted, given the script they were working from, it would be pretty hard to make any of the lines sound natural, but there's nothing compelling here.  The belabored droning of Dr. Faust doesn't inspire apprehension or loathing, just impatience with his character, and the main character is equally bland.
-Rushed pacing and obtuse plot
Lovecraft's work generally followed a pattern: Ease the reader into the story with a believable, mundane setting, told from the perspective of an intelligent, credible, skeptical narrator, and then sustain the reader's suspension of disbelief by gradually hinting at the strange, horrible truth by degrees, finally culminating in a single mind-shattering glimpse at some nameless cosmic horror, at which point the narrator loses his mind and the story ends.
Conarium starts off mundane enough, and then dumps in aliens, the necronomicon and madness within the first 10 minutes.  It has nowhere to go from there.  There's very little building of tension or intrigue, and the interesting plot hooks introduced early on are mostly left unresolved.  It feels like a collection of Cthulhu mythos cameos rather than an attempt to mimic Lovecraft's storytelling style.
-Tedious gameplay
90% of the game is scouring every square inch of each room looking for items, which include the aforementioned scraps of journals and letters, keys, levers, and trophy items.  You'll spend a lot of time rifling through cabinets and drawers, for what feels like very little payoff.  The trophy items seem like they should be significant, but you only get a very basic description of the items, which is generally so bare-bones that simply looking at the object makes the description unnecessary.
There are a few puzzles, which are either as simple as "find the lever", or time-consuming but not difficult.  A few of the puzzles require you to copy something out of your notebook, which is a simple task made frustrating by the clunky inventory/journal/puzzle interface controls.
There are only 2 times you can die in the game.  One is from crashing your submarine into walls, which, in tandem with the ungainly sub controls, discourages you from exploring the environment.  The other is from a chase sequence that amounts to trial and error.
I finished this game with the bad ending, but was so tired of playing when it finished that I had no desire whatsoever to replay it and get the better one.
Should you buy this game?  Only if you really like searching through peoples drawers and reading really bad prose.

This game will frustrate you. It will make you want to tear your hair out. It’ll make you want to punch your computer. It’ll make you forget about everything outside of beating this one level. And it’s amazing. The gameplay is fast-paced, intense and graphic. It will make you think on your feet while at the same time have you plan your moves out ahead of you. As the levels progress, Hotline Miami increases in difficulty, but at a rate that feels natural and doesn’t seem to be too difficult. In one hit you die, and the most common action you’ll do will be ‘Press “R” to respawn”. Thankfully, the satisfaction you receive after killing everyone in the building makes all that frustration worth it.
As you play, you’ll unlock different masks that will have different effects that may or may not make the game easier. The story is dark and suspenseful and very confusing while at the same time able to keep you engaged. Hotline Miami is certainly replayable, and you might need to do exactly that to fully understand the story, unlock all of the masks, weapons and secret levels.
Hotline Miami has been acknowledged all over the internet as having one of the best soundtracks ever made. No matter how many times you die or how many hours you’ll play, the music will always feel fresh, exciting and motivational. I’d highly recommend buying the soundtrack as well, as you’ll probably want the songs on your phone.
The retro graphics are also well done. Hotline Miami has bright, bold, engaging and sometimes neon colours throughout the game that remind you of the 80’s, and the characters and levels have a lot of detail in them for an 8-bit graphical game.
Hotline Miami is a game that has done everything right. I’d highly recommend this game to everyone who likes fast-paced and graphic games, especially if you’re a fan of excellent music.

This is the most engaging story I have had the pleasure to witness in years of gaming. When I was young I could play games for hours without getting bored, or wondering when I would reach the end so I could go do something else. As I grew older, my attention span for gaming withered, which upset me as someone wanting to move into the industry. I was worried I was losing interest in the medium, and that I was making a mistake moving my entire life in the direction of something that doesn't engage me the same anymore. I thought the problem was me, that my child like interest was disappearing in favour for more grown up, mature, boring things.
Then I played this game. Every screen is a work of art, every character has so much personality, the art is whimsical and the sound direction is so very subtle yet powerful that I found myself compelled to continue until I reached the end of this act in a single sitting. I just could not put it down, and when I reached the end I was disappointed that I couldn't continue learning about these people, and this world. I realised that it wasn't me that was losing my childlike wonder and interest, but the games developers and what they have been releasing. The industry has lost its personality in support of annual releases and massive profits, but this game made me believe again. You don't need the very best photo realistic graphics with the most true to life smoke engine to tell an immersive story, you need character. This game has character in spades, and I cannot recommend it enough. This game has reminded me why I am going through university to learn to become a member of the industry, and if I can be a part of just one project that turns out like this, then I will be incredibly fulfilled.
Play this game, as soon as possible.

I don't normally write reviews, but there is a lot of controversy surrounding this game and the fact that it contains micro transactions. I will touch on it at the end of the review, but know that with micro transactions in mind,  I am still having a blast with this game. It was hard for me to make the purchase at full price, but I found it at a much lower price than steam's price and I am happy to say it was worth it.
This is one of those games you get lost in with the endless combinations and posibilites that are part of the experience. The nemesis system is refined and brings a lot of posibilites. For instance, I was fighting two captains at once and one of them i cut his arm off and he ran away. The other captain I killed. The one which had his arm removed later ambushed me and wanted me to suffer for what i did to him so I ended up killing him and cutting off his other arm. Thats not it though.
The guy comes back from the dead with two make shift arms and says something like "you can't kill me, Ive been alive on this earth longer than you, i wish to rest"
so i kill him again. Later he ambushes me again....and i once again killed him....
This is where I am now. I don't know if he is coming back, but this kind of stuff is awesome. The amount of unique dialogue the captains have is amazing. I have not heard the same dialogue twice. I  haven't progressed past the second zone  because of how fun the nemesis system is.
Give it a try.  I get it, lootboxes suck. If we purchase premium single player games that have micro transactions, we are telling the developers that its okay to include microtransactions in future games. Depending on how well the game does, other developers will take note and also do the same thing. So yeah, I don't like the micro transactions and loot boxes. It does not matter that they are not required to finish the game.
You can chose to not purchase the game based on the micro transactions, and I get it. I would not have purchased this game full price, instead I got a good deal and I am glad I bought it. Give it a try if you like spending countless hours with endless ways to kill orcs.

Holy crap, where do I start on this marvelous game?! Ok, this masterpiece came from the brilliant mind of Tim Schafer, the King of point-and-clicks, who hasn't made a point-and-click adventure game in over 16 years. But he still has it! Broken Age tells the story of two vastly different, yet eerily similar, young people, Vella and Shay. You can play whoevers story first and alternate between them, in case you are stuck on a puzzle, which I believe is a brilliant mechanic. The visual art style is absolutely gorgeous and the characters are well developed. The gameplay is, well, point-and-click and if you aren't a fan of this, the game won't change your opinion on it. However, absolutely everyone should play this game, it puts multimillion dollar "triple A" games to shame and I can't wait for the second part! (FYI the game is split into two parts, the first is out right now, but the second is coming out later this year as a free update)                                                              I'm giving this game a 9.7/10.

Since playing Flight Simulator 98 back in the early 00's on my first computer, I've been in love with Microsoft Flight Simulator.  Friends and family (including some pilots in my family) thought it was just a silly video game and nothing comparable to flying an actual aircraft.  That was until showing them Microsoft Flight Simulator X later on...and now, thankfully, the Steam Edition has worked out some kinks and it runs smooth on Windows 10.
This simulator is great for a first timer who thinks they may want to fly, an enthusiast, or even an experienced pilot.  It is an amazing teaching tool if you know what you're looking for.  There are many guides posted on Steam that inform you of the lingo and controls on certain aircraft.  This is how I have learned and applied this to finally taking pilot lessons.  Doing your first flight from loading passengers and taxing to the runway all the way to successfully landing and unloading passengers at a destination is something you will be proud of.  It's also extremely relaxing after a long day.
On a silly note, this simulator helped me win over my girlfriend's dad - an amazing pilot who has done unthinkable landings and maneuevers in large cargo jets.  10/10

I've had this program for a couple of months now, and I'd highly recommend the steam version of FSX. They've done an excellent job of updating and integrating a very old flight simulator. I've bought quite a few add-ons for the program, and I haven't had any significant issues getting them to work, even when installing them to another drive and pointing back to the Steam FSX folder. So far I've installed Orbx FTX Global Base, Vector Global, PNW and NCA and Australia scenery upgrades, several of the Orbx airports; PFE ATC program, MyTraffic 6 (a little bit of an odd install, but it works well), REX Cloud textures (though the full REX weather engine didn't seem to like FSX:SE very well), an unregistered version of FSUIPC, and finally, and my favorite by far, A2A's Cessna 172 Trainer. It's amazing and has worked nearly flawlessly with FSX: SE.
I tried X-Plane 10 (and reviewed it separately), but even with it being a much newer simulator, and over twice the cost on Steam, FSX to me does a much better job of conveying the realities of flying, at least as much as a simulator can. The A2A Cessna helps a lot with that as well. I'm currently about a third of the way on a virtual flight around the world in the 172, and loving nearly every minute of it (though an 8 hour flight over Siberia between runways was tedious at best).
I haven't run into any showstoppers so far, fingers crossed, and enjoying FSX:SE very much.

Quite possibly the best espionage action RPG, Alpha Protocol pulled me in and refused to let go for the entirety of the story.  It clearly draws inspiration from the juggernaut in the room, Mass Effect, but stands on its own with a drastically different story and game mechanics.  The stealth aspects of the game are absolutely phenomenal though the brute force combat could use some improvement.
The narrative of the game is full of twists and the choices that you are given have long-lasting effects on future events.  To delve any further into that particular aspect would spoil those who have not played yet so I will not continue down that path but I can say that I was pleasantly surprised by how often I saw the effects of my choices.  The fact that each mission had multiple ways to complete it and each map was a unique experience were the icing on the cake.
Mechanically, Alpha Protocol is a lot of fun as long as you play it as a stealth game.  The character that I created specialized in stealth, martial arts, and pistol, making him something of a modern ninja.  It was truly a thrill sneaking across the mission area, ducking and dodging out of the way of enemies as well as eliminating those that were a threat to me.  On the other hand, I wouldn't say that the shooting was terrible, but I would absolutely say that if they wanted to make all of the different character builds viable the developers should have put a bit more effort into it.
Alpha Protocol is a great game and one that you really should not miss out on if you enjoy stealth and/or narrative games with choices that matter.  If you're looking for a good game to blow off some steam by annihilating terrorists with your machine gun, you may want to keep looking.

Life is Strange has to be one of the best games I have ever played. It has a very deep story with great character development that makes you become emotionally attached to the main characters.
The rewind-time mechanic is very unique, unlike any other game I've played, and is paired perfectly with the choices and consequences mechanic, where each decision impacts the story in some way. The choices and consequences mechanic also provides an incentive to replay the game, make different choices, and see how it affects the storyline.
The game can be a bit movie-like at times, especially in the fifth chapter, but given the game mechanics, this is to be expected, and didn't take away from my overall enjoyment of the game.
Expect to be hit "right in the feels" on more than one occasion.

Alan Wake... Originally this game to me was one of the most stupid games in existence, until the day my friend and I played it. He had already beaten the game so we decided to play it in nightmare mode (the hardest difficulty). I then fell in love with the game but sadly I had no money and wasn't able to afford it at the time. Then steam came along and had a sale for it for five dollars. I bought the franchise package and can honestly say that it was one of the wisest choices I've ever made. If you're someone who's all about graphics, then you will have no complaint.
The story is about a writer named Alan Wake (obviously), who travels to a small town in the mountain side. His wife is worried about him because he sadly hasn't been able to write a word since his last book which was written 2 years ago. He finds out that the real reason they took a surprise "vacation" is because there is a "therapist" who says he can "help" Alan (when you play the game you'll findout why I put the quatations). They get into an argument and he steps out of the cabin that they rented. His wife is INSANELY afraid of the dark so she didn't follow. The darkness grabs his wife and drags her into the "lake" Alan jumps in.... And the rest you can findout for yourself.
This game so richly deserves a Five-out-of-Five Stars! This is one of the greatest games I've ever played if not the best.

Let me put it this way: it took 62 hours of playing before I decided to take a break from it, and I haven't had it but a couple of months. If you like old school turn based rpg stategy, such as Falloout 1 & 2, old X-Com, Jagged Alliance series, Balders Gate, Planescape: Torment (and somebody needs to gtf on with rebooting Torment, that game was !@#$ing GREAT!), you're going to want this in your collection. The story thus far is pretty damn good, in my opinion, voice acting is well done too. I think it looks great graphically, and I run a mid range gaming comp. Buy it now and help them make it great, or buy it on release, but get it. Seriously. Just understand it's a beta build and treat it as such and you will enjoy it if you like this kind of game, the bugs are not that bad, except for a couple I'll note below. .
The random encounter battles as you travel on the world map are a little small in area, which makes combat down and dirty and  fast, if you're playing anything but Rookie difficulty. That can be a pro or con, depending on what you like and your play style. Feels cramped to me on the majority random encounter maps. It takes away from the strategy aspect when you're pretty much at point blank range in most of your battles, which are pretty lethal to begin with. BUT, they are still fun and it's extremely satisfying when you win by the skin of your teeth. The big battles are hella fun!
Not so much a con and probably a bug, but DO NOT dismiss characters on the world map. At least not Angela, if you have her. I did and unless she's supposed to be gone, she's still out in the Wasteland where I left her. Hope I left her some water, I tkink it was close to a water source, or her and Ace are gonna be meeting again real soon....she's not in the Ranger Citadel either. If you take that kid you save from drowning into your party, and go back to the Citadel, leave him at the entrance or don't let him be with you when you go in, a conversation fires off between him and another member of your party when you go near the museum and you'll be stuck there, in the conversation, with no choice for a response and no other choice but to reload, and that's the only game breaking bug I've found so far. The UI could use some tweeking, status effects are hard to determine visually on quick glance; I had already played many many hours before I noticed the tiny consussion icon above the character portrait for the first time.
Other than those issues and some very minor stability issues that are probably more related to my rig than the game itself, any other bug I've come across, hasn't been anything major. I emphatically recommend this game, it has the potential to be one of the best titles of it's kind in a very, very long time.

Conarium is a first person horror adventure game that is based on the Cthulhu mythos. The story of the game is heavily inspired by the novella "At the mountains of madness" by H. P. Lovecraft. It's not a long game and can be finished within 5-6 hours. Note that this is not a walking simulator like Ethan Carter or Dear Ester.
I do not play a lot of horror adventure games but I was interested due to the connection to the Cthulhu mythos and I can say that it really paid it off at the end. The game very clearly understands what makes the Lovecraftian stories and novels gripping: the fear of the unknown, the feeling of despair due to the existence of cosmic entities and races and humanity's insignificance in the grand scale. The game doesn't try to frighten you with cheap jump scares, instead by the usage of the atmosphere, environment, and story the fear slowly grows in you (I strongly suggest playing the game during evenings).
Game has many references to the Cthulhu mythos. The game starts based on the ancient city in Antartica in "At the mountains of madness" and build upon that story by partly following the mythos and partly inventing new things.
Pros:
- Very gripping atmosphere and environments.
- Mostly, the regions in the game feels very different from one another in terms of aesthetics and visual assets.
- Good amount of puzzles which are neither too simple nor too difficult.
Cons:
- I understand that this is a Cthulhu game and "not able to understand everything" is part of the charm. But I guess some parts of the game could have been explained in a bit more detail.

Let me start this review off with saying that i had serious doubts in getting this game, as i am no fan of "Novel or puzzle games". But let me tell you boy do i regret waiting this long playing Conarium.
Conarium is a Puzzle Horror game based on the works of H.P. Lovecraft, famous for his story The Shadow over Insmouth and the Call of Cuthulhu. Actually Conarium's story is based on one of his other works called At the mountain of madness. Few video games tend to recreate a good adaption on the Lovecraftian story telling. But Conarium hits the sweet spot and had me with a constant unease that something was following or watching me. You are alone no human in sight and it will hit you with a certain sense of loneliness and horror. Your mind will start playing tricks on you, imagining things that are not there.
At its core Conarium is a Detective Puzzle game and the ambiance is pure cosmic horror. So for lovers of Lovecraftian story telling Conarium is a no brainer and should already be in your collection.

You start playing thinking "okay, very neon, nice soundtrack." The music plinks and hisses, background throbbing, and you wonder who this man is and why there's a rubber♥♥♥♥♥♥mask on his head. The messages on his answering machine are bizarre, strangely mundane in the urban decay that surrounds him. A date. An appointment. Those naughty kids down the block.
You're pondering it the whole time--who is he? What's happening here? Why is he being confronted by a horse mask and a caustically sarcastic owl?
Then you realize you've stuck your thumbs in a man's eyeballs and popped them out like a particularly juicy zit, all while the throbbing soundtrack and neon light of the level surges like the hammering of your pulse.
Your character vomits, but you don't. You're too busy trying to figure out how to get to the pan of boiling water on the stove so you can surprise the guy in the next room with a shotgun. A quick succession of buttons, the screen bursting and crackling like fireworks with your score, and you've knocked him down with the door and boiled his head. Even having to restart each level more than ten times, you realize it has been worth it.
"A brutal game," you think, half-admiring and half-starting to worry what kind of person you both are, but it is swept away under the riptide of action. Some part of your brain is fizzing like a mouthful of Poprocks as the points keep adding up. It doesn't matter that the graphics are primitive--you're primitive. In fact, you're a savage. You and your character, together, blood like pretty cherry spray over the floors, the walls, everything pulsing and surging as your fingers twitch on the buttons.
"B+," you think at the end of a level, as it grades your performance. "How DARE you give me a B+! I can do so much more." You take a shaky breath as your fingers stab at your keyboard, taking you back out of the level. For a moment, the lettering on the screen seems mocking, and then you realize it's merely waiting for you, patient in the way only a machine can be patient.
It's waiting for you to come back with your lead pipe, and your katana, your baseball bat, and your assault rifle.
"Here," you whisper tenderly at the screen. "Let me show you what I can do."

As an early access game, this review will be fairly short. I have put just under 10 hours into the game as of this review.
I would call the gameplay similar to that of RimWorld or Prison Architect, with a demonic evil threatening the world. You lay out building plans, set crafting queues, and can direct characters to perform tasks. Combat is simple, you can tell characters where to move, what to hide behind, what to engage, and some basic inventory management. Since this game is early access, I'm taking into account the lack of contant for that reason.
Pros
- Fairly simple gameplay. It didnt take too much to learn and the "missions" give decent guidance to the basic gameplay.
- Under-used theme (I was a Hellgate: London fan for this reason as well)
- Research is simple but vital to sucess
Cons
- Very taxing on decent systems. Mods that increase map sizes have noticable lag for even small increases. (Devs have addressed that issue specifically, so I expect to see improvement)
- Maps seem too small for my taste, also leading to the mods issue.
- Character customization is minimal, but ill write that off as an early access issue.
- Exploring and salvaging are currently tedious and minimally involved.
Overall, I remain cautiously optimistic as to what this game can become. At $17 USD ($20 USD when not on sale), I would still recomend this game to those who are a fan of the theme, but wouldnt call this game "a must have" yet. I will make best efforts to update as progress is noted.

I see this game get a lot of hate sometimes, but when you get down at the bottom of it, it does everything it promises: it's an ambient procedural mountain. It's a game that plays itself.
Draw some doodles. Watch the mountain get generated. Watch it get rained on. Watch it get snowed on. Watch it get annihilated by random cosmic activity. Play notes with your keyboard. Sit back and get hypnotized by it for a good 45 minutes. Simple as that.
You buy coffee on your way to class every morning? Skip it for just one day, save the ninety nine cents and try this one out. You'll enjoy it for far longer than an eigh-ounce coffee.

It seems to me that survival games are being created by game designers who never experienced a day of real hardship. The rule of thumb for deprivation is 3 minutes without oxygen, three days without water, and three weeks without food, individual mileage varies of course. As one who has been around the world and out in the rugged wilderness areas, I can personally attest you do not drop dead in a few hours without water, even under the most scorching sun in the hottest desert. I myself experienced periods of a few days when I had nothing to eat, other than an annoying rumbling in my tummy, I managed. I've encountered people going through famines who went more than a week without a single bite, and they looked it, but they still tried to eck food out of their land. My point is, we humans can endure a lot, far more than these survival games give credit for.
Judgment seems to be the worst of the genre, not only is it a major huge grindfest, but people in the game literally die in hours  - of game time not real world time - from no food or water. Other survival games are at varying degrees grindfests but at least the game rewards you for good decisions and planning which in turn makes them fun to play. This  game seemingly sets you up for failure from the beginning, your well is very limited, runs out in a couple days, you have  to construct a new well, you have to research woodworking and brickmaking, then make a sawmill and furnace, both very high in resource costs, then make enough bricks which for some strange reason requires stones in addition to clay (at least wood makes sense), before your well runs dry and your guys drop dead shortly from dehydration. I didn't play long enough but my guess is each well is short-lived, so, you rinse, repeat. It seems if you don't from the beginning direct your people to beeline in research and construction to being able to make wells, your game is doomed very quickly. Thank goodness we are not that weak in real life lol.
If these designers think people are this fragile, I feel really bad for them if we ever do enter a real apocalypse. I can't recommend this game at this time, it's frustration without the fun. There are much better done survival games out there, while with their own problems, at least they are fun to play.

For instance, I was fighting two captains at once and one of them i cut his arm off and he ran away. The other captain I killed. The one which had his arm removed later ambushed me and wanted me to suffer for what i did to him so I ended up killing him and cutting off his other arm. Thats not it though.

Beautiful game in terms of art, animation, sound design, music (orchestral score!), voice acting, and story. The animation especially is something that stands out as a modern change over the old 2-D affairs where a walk cycle was six frames or less. Some of the newer 3-D (or 2.5-D) adventure games have had good animation, but I can't currently think of another completely 2-D adventure game that has had animation up to this level. Of course, there haven't been many 2-D adventure games made in the last decade, so...
I do wish the puzzles were more challenging. I've been playing adventure games for a long time and didn't really find myself stumped for more than a few minutes at any point. However, from being a backer and watching the documentary, I believe the plan is to make Act 2 a bit tougher. So, it seems that Act 1 is meant to ease players into the world and its logic before a (hopefully) more challenging Act 2 hits. That would be very welcome.
I also didn't find it laugh-out-loud funny--though there are plenty of chuckles--but the stories are more subtle, personal and mature than, say, Day of The Tentacle, and that's totally fine with me.
When first released to backers, the mouse interface was very tablet-centric (tap and drag as opposed to click and click), but the game has since been updated with more reasonable mouse control (it's in the settings if yours is currently set to the old way).
Act 1 ends on a surprising cliffhanger (at least I was surprised, and delighted by the symmetry) and has left me wanting more, so I'm really looking forward to Act 2. I hope enough other people are as well. I think Double Fine deserve great success as a studio that births good things into the world.

I've ran into some serious performance problems with this game. First, the game crashes about 50% of the time when opening it. Second, the game suffers from some serious frame rate stuttering. This affects the control input, which causes me to fall and die frequently. Third, the sound has a strange echoing effect which seems as if it might be related to the frame rate issue. This issue even affects while you are navigating the menu while the game is paused. The problem does not get better or worse by changing the graphics settings. Seems to be a hardware optimization issue. I'd love to try it more, but can't play it until this is resolved.

This game is hard, but for all the wrong reasons. Lots of blind jumps, you can't see the obstacles from the "other world" until it's right in your face. Blind jumps are a thing that stopped existing after the 16 bit era because game designers realized it was bad level design, but this game has tons of blind jumps. The fact that I can only see things from the other world in this small orb around the player makes the rest of the screen completely useless. There are vines with thorns that instantly kill me, and can only be seen with that orb on. So I have to turn off the orb to get past them, but there's no indication as to when I'm past them since I can't see them. Overall it just has lots of really bad level design from the get go and it was too frustrating for me to continue. I'm fine with difficult games when they make me feel like it's my fault when I lose. This game, the majority of the time I lose, I feel like it's due to lack of information that the game is supposed to give to me.
Definitely recommending to everyone who likes sandbox games.

Charming little puzzler that does a lot of things right, but some wrong. In general the idea is that you manipulate light around you to reveal and mix different worlds so you can overcome obstacles. The concept works great and allows for some difficult brain twisters. The puzzles are challanging but also rewarding once you get past them.
Graphics are decent, nothing impressive to me, in fact if anything I would say the game feels bit unpolished there but given its an indie game I'm not taking that as a con. It didn't bother me. Couple of things that did bother me though:
- Unless you shed the appropriate light color you won't know whats there. This may not seem like a problem at first, but there will be many sequences where you have to navigate tight spaces switching lights and you will die many times because you switched the light too soon or too late and there is no way for you to know until you try (and die). Game that does this much better as an example is Fly'n where you have shadows of the other world.
- The game tries to do a decent job at introducing you to different things you can do, but doesn't hold your hand. This means if you are particularly resourceful you may overcome some obstacles in a non intended way and never learn what new mechanics you were supposed to pick up until you get stuck much later, because you never learned it. Other things you never tried or had to try until you are stuck 30min on the same puzzle and discover "Hey! This is possible?! That would have saved me hours had I just known!"
The story is non fairly shallow, not going to say more about it. Overall it was a nice journey and I would still recommend just be prepared for some (good) frustration. 7.5/10

I'm an Ultimate license holder and I've run a couple of adventures using D&D 3.5 and PF with a group of 4 players talking with Skype for over 2 years, long before this product was available on Steam.  I absolutely love working with Fantasy Grounds.  Having looked at other competing products, nothing came close to packaging everything for the particular ruleset I was using all in one PLUS still allowed me full free form editing when needed.  Being able to add in library modules of rules, including spells and equipment, that you can simply drag onto your character sheet and have it automatically populate the stats is so convenient!  A player doesn't have to remember how things work or worry about making sure the right saves / resists are applied, etc.  It's all automatic!
There have been continual improvements to the product since I began using it which greater and greater features added each time.  Full table support for designing random search and loot tables or anything else you want to roll randomly is such a help.  One of the best things is the combat tracker which can link to your "map" image that you are using for moving tokens around.  It keeps track of current initiative order, heath and conditions affecting each entity, quick look at weapons being used or saving throw values, and can be used for quick targetting for players wanting to drag attack dice directly onto the monster entry.  You can show/hide entries on the combat tracker which when linked to their token on the "map" image lets the DM setup surprise encounters that players can't see until you spring it.
There are so many things that make using Fantasy Grounds the closest thing to being around the physical table in my mind that it makes gaming feel like "the old days" again.  With the official D&D license from WotC, it has allowed Smiteworks to enhance their product by releasing official 5E products for use directly within Fantasy Grounds.  While none of these are needed to play a 5E game, you are always free to add data in by hand from your hard cover books, it does help streamline game play by saving you the time of entry letting you just drag and drop and the products are very well done.
Thank you Smiteworks for letting me recapture the passion for fantasy gaming that I grew up with!

***UPDATE***: Since the 1.2gb patch that was released just recently, the FPS limit can be set to 60, and even unlocked completely in the options menu. Some other of my issues have also been resolved (I've stricken the points that no longer apply). I will keep my negative review up because I still don't feel it is quite where it should be just yet, in terms of the port work. Expect a revised review with future patches.
***ORIGINAL***:
One of the laziest ports of a AAA-game I've seen in years.
So, the game seems pretty interesting. Likeable characters, great animations, fantastic soundtrack, okay graphics, etc. I haven't nearly played enough to review the gameplay or story yet.
What I AM able to say something about, is the PORT work. And boy is this one lazy. I'll jot my main issues down in points:
2. There's mouse acceleration or smoothing or something going on, because the mouse movement is irritatingly imprecise. You're unable to disable that, of course.
3. Graphics options are laughably vague. Anti Aliasing choices, for example, are either "Low", "Medium" or "High". How hard would it be to give us the exact numbers? What is High, exactly? Is x8? What type of Anti Aliasing is it? FXAA? MLAA? MSAA?
5. Further  control issues; You can't map the mouse thumb buttons for anything. That is a HUGE offense for me. I use my thumb buttons in every game, and not being able to in 2016 is just odd. I accepted it back in the mid-2000s when thumb buttons were still "new" and not everybody had them on their mice. Today, there's no excuse for it.
6. There's no way to disable UI elements like the compass/map, the 3D navigation and so on. Minor gripe, but worth noting if you like customizing how the HUD looks.
7. The auto-centering during driving snaps into action really fast, and it's not possible to disable it. So if you're the kind of person who likes to look around while you're driving, you're going to get annoyed fast; you'll be fighting the camera with your mouse constantly.
8. You can change your graphics options in the launch menu before you actually boot up the game. Except the changes don't apply so you have to change them all again once the game has started. "Luckily", there are only about five or so graphics options to choose between, ALL of which have the same choices; Low, Medium or High.
9. You have to adjust the edges of your screen when you launch the game for the first time. Why? Can't the game just detect that on its own? Another miniscule gripe, but it just adds to the whole feeling of lackluster interest for making a good port by the devs.
10. As mentioned lots of places already; the game does not support native 1920x1080 resolution. It's upscaled from what one would assume to be 800p (ie Xbox One standard). You can force it to look at least slightly sharper through the Nvidia control panel, but not nearly good enough to warrant that 30 FPS cap "for performance's sake". I haven't seen a big game not being able to run at native 1080p resolution in over a decade now. It is absolutely puzzling to me why they would do this.
So, there's my early impressions of the port of the game. It's not abysmal, it's not unplayable (I haven't had any crashes yet). But it's lazy, and you can tell that the developers (or publishers) threw this port together in a hurry to make a buck, rather than showing the PC version the respect it deserves.
There's a good game in here, it would seem. You just have to fight a lot of unnecessary battles to be able to enjoy it. And I wouldn't currently recommend it at full price on the PC. Let's see if they get that 30FPS lock fixed first.

Not so long ago, in a review for a game called At the Mountains of Madness, I bemoaned the distinct lack of quality Lovecraft adaptations/homages in the games industry. Time to swallow my words, methinks, as a bona fide good'un has finally graced us with its presence.
I haven't yet played Zoetrope Interactive's Darkness Within series, so all due apologies if THOSE games beat this one to the punch. I don't tend to leap at point-at-click adventures these days, but when I saw this was the same people doing a full-blown first person game, I couldn't resist. And, I'm pleased to say, I don't regret one cent of the twenty dollar price I paid for it.
Right off the bat, what this game reminded me of most were the Penumbra games, which all you true horror game buffs should know were the "spiritual predecessors" to the Amnesia series. Perhaps it was all the ice and snow, sure, but the slow-building style of gameplay was there too. It wasn't long, though, before I found a "trophy" item which gave another clue to this game's glorious origins: a book entitled "At the Mountains of Madness", written by none other than a fellow named H.P. Lovecraft! Well how about that, then. Maybe that book has influenced a noteworthy video game after all.
The early part of this game won't please those who don't like extensive exploration and a♥♥♥♥♥♥tonne of reading, with only the occasional hint of something more dangerous and supernatural lurking in the background. Believe me when I say you can search things pretty thoroughly in Conarium...though it can be oddly selective at times (i.e. you can look in the three drawers on this desk, but not the one next to it; and no, we won't let you open that particular book, despite the tantalising title which suggests you probably should). There's also a bit of puzzle-solving, which varies from easy-peasy to challenging enough that I felt quite chuffed with myself after single-handedly solving a morse code-related riddle (I'm generally pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥at puzzles, gimme a break).
It isn't TOO long, though, before the player is drawn into a time-and-space-twisting tale of cosmic horror worthy of Lovecraft himself. But wait: is there any danger, I hear you ask? Well...let's just say there's a little - you CAN most certainly die - but not a whole hell of a lot, no. Enter expecting a world of wonder as opposed to a constant bombardment of perilous events, and you may well find yourself as bedazzled as I was.
All in all, a crackingly good old-school adventure, told with spiffy new graphics, highly immersive sound and, well...passable enough voice acting. And please, whatever you do, don't listen to the people spouting the usual "this game isn't long enough" ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. It's more than long enough for what it is, and if we don't start acknowledging that indie developers don't have the same means of producing high quality 25+ hour games as AAA companies, we'll have no indie developers making awesome games like this any more. The megaplexes are already full of mindless dreck thanks to this mentality. Let's not see our beloved video games industry go down the same tedious ♥♥♥♥ing path.
Verdict: 9/10.
(PS to the devs: that first "chase" sequence adds nothing to the game. Lamely executed and incongruously difficult, Red Barrels have nothing to fear from you guys as of yet.)

Let me start by saying, that I couldn't wait to play Mafia 3. The game has a really strong start plotwise, but then the side quests kick in... And after that all you do is:
1. Pick up a mission.
2. Go to a few places, where you kill a bunch of goons and interrogate their leader to get information. Now you are being offered a choice to either spare him and add some money to your racket, or kill him and earn some cash straight away.
3. Go to a another place, that is, again filled with goons - Kill them all.
4. When you have done enough damage to lure out the racket boss, you will have to kill him and his goons.
After you've done all of this, the main story continues a bit and you get to see a cutscene. Then repeat, repeat, repeat and repeat.
The controls for the keyboard + mouse takes a little time to get used to. AI is also pretty dumb. For example, when I was interrogating a guy, another goon just stood there pointing a gun at my head, and waited for me to finish the conversation before he would react.. And when I entered a vehicle with hostile goons in it, the guys at the backseat started shooting at the driver, who I'd just thrown out of the car.  There's bugs here and there, but to some of those I just can't help but to laugh at.
Some positives though. The soundtrack is really kickass. When you fire up the game, you get to hear Jimi Hendrix + the game offers many hit songs from that era. Don't want to stop driving when I hear songs by Steppenwolf, Roy Orbison, Otis Redding etc.
I will continue to play this game, but I wouldn't recommend this to players who:
1. Don't like repetitive, grindy side missions.
2. Don't want to be forced to complete side missions in order to continue the main story.
That's my 2 cents folks!

Life is Strange is a powerful emotional experience and a well-made example of the puzzle-and-conversation adventure game.  If you like soft sci-fi stories in a modern setting and can tolerate the occasional cringe-worthy line or teenage cliche, you'll like this.  Really, though, as long as episode 1 is free you should certainly try it; it took me only an hour to make up my mind that I wanted the rest of the series, a decision I did not regret.
There are two things that I really like about this game: the time manipulation mechanic, and main character Max.  The time manipulation alone is the kind of thing that is so simple and yet does so much.  If
it did was allow you to try out the different conversation and action options, and find the one you like the most, I'd consider it worth mentioning.  How often have you been unhappy with your dialogue choices in other games, or worse, made the wrong choice because the options weren't clear?  That's never a problem here.
And yet, time manipulation so much more.  Many puzzles involve rewinding time, and those were the most satisfying ones to solve.  They did require some lateral thinking, but the solutions made sense once I figured them out.  It's certainly a far step from randomly clicking items on other items.  Max's time powers also drive significant parts of the plot, with characters openly discussing their origins, extent and limitation.  The only real weakness is that the ultimate explanation of their origin isn't really an explanation at all, and has ontological problems too.  But I personally can overlook that given how much it brought to the rest of the game.
Apart from time-related puzzles, the other main aspect of the gameplay is conversation and choices.  In both the main and side plots, much of how things develop depends on who you talk to and what you say.  Plus, periodically you'll get the standard dilemma, with two or more options neither of which is clearly better.  Despite the mundane setting, the stakes ramp up considerably as the story progresses, and the decisions can get quite hard.
Still, these options do have the usual problem that they don't change the main plot.  No matter what you do, you'll always end the second chapter in the office, the third at Chloe's house and the fourth in the junkyard.  You
change the side plots and how characters relate to you quite a lot.  But if you are the type of person who considers this only the illusion of choice, this game probably isn't for you.  Personally, having finished two playthroughs taking different options, I think the influence you have on the details is enough.
The other thing that really drew me in was Max.  I found it really easy to emphasise with her, no small feat as she's a teenage girl, photography nerd and self-identified hipster; I've only ever been one of those things, and that some years ago.  But this is one facet of a broader point, that the characters here are well-developed and believable.  Even the minor characters have
that takes them beyond cardboard cut-outs, while all the major characters have a sometimes surprising amount of depth.  And that characterisation is essential for the story, and for the emotional bonds you develop with the characters of Arcadia Bay.
Though, that characterisation can run both ways.  I found second main character Chloe to be really obnoxious till episode 4, which did interfere with my enjoyment.  Thankfully she did eventually grow on me, as I understood more of her background.
Life is Strange can, at times, be a bit too mellow and non-interactive.  These are minor complaints compared to clever puzzles, difficult choices, believable characters and emotionally powerful storytelling.  If you like interactive narratives you owe it to yourself to at least try the first episode.

Imagine the games Layers of Fear and Kholat would have a child. This child is Conarium, a game not so much about jump scares but rather about a dark and menacing atmosphere, based on the story Mountains of Madness, by the grandmaster of horror, H. P. Lovecraft.
And just like in my review for Kholat, I have to make it clear: This is
an
! If you expect a game like Outlast then you will probably be disappointed, unless you're a huge fan of Lovecraft's works, of course. In terms of action this game is rather comparable to Layers of Fear. You wake up in an expedition camp in the Antarctic, just to find the whole site left with no sign of anyone else, but a strange machine next to you. Now it's up to you to explore what's going on. There's no HUD in game, only the mouse pointer gives hints if you're looking at an interactive object, no shooting and no fighting.
- Is there much to do in this game?
-- This one is a rather short game. You might be able to finish it within 2 to 3 hours if you rush through, or if you play it a second time. You will definitely spend much more time in game if you take close looks at the enviroments, search for and read all the letters and reports you might find - or if you mess with solving the puzzles the way I did. To be honest, the puzzles aren't too complicated, usually like "find item A and put in in place X". But since there is no visual highlighting in the game, the puzzles and solutions are sometimes very hard to discover. I've been doing quite a lot of unnecessary back tracking because I simply overlooked something important quite close to the puzzle. Other than that there's a whole lot to discover if you're familiar with Lovecraft's works, but that's all I'm gonna spoil you.
- What about the story...
-- I've finished the game and I've unlocked all endings, and the story is almost as confusing as Kholat and Layers of Fear. It gives less space for interpretations since the Cthulhu myth gives a huge and well defined lore already. It isn't exactly The Mountains of Madness, but is very closely related to it and you will find a whole lot of reference that gives you the feeling of actually participating in the story. So, to enjoy this game in it's entirety, I absolutely recommend you to get familiar with The Mountains of Madness and maybe the other works by Lovecraft, too.
- ... and the atmosphere?
-- The atmosphere is astonishing and sometimes surreal and bizarre, the enviroments are beautiful and put you in the middle of the Lovecraftian horror. The game gives you the feeling of being lost in an abandoned expedition station, and sometimes even in nightmares. The voice actors are doing a great job bringing the story to life.
- Is this a Horror game after all?
-- Well, this game is set in the middle of a Lovecraft story. And is Lovecraft a horror author after all, or is he not? ;)
To cut it short: So far I haven't had many technical problems with the game, the controls feel quite good. A few times I got stuck in the ground, for no obvious reason, and the only way out was to crouch and move (the game doesn't offer jump mechanics though). Since I've been familiar with Lovecraft's stories already, I cannot tell how interesting this game is for someone who doesn't know them yet. But maybe it's a good start for those of you, so I recommend you give it a try.

Do you want to be creeped out, but not given a heart attack by cheap jump-scares and run-and-hide scenes? Then this is a game for you.
I am no expert on Lovecraftian games or books, but I do now see that it means "psychological horror" in a very specific way. This game nurtures that horror in such a gradual and confusing matter which is an excellent twist on the normal development of a plot. In most games you will begin very confused and then gradually become much more aware of what is going on. This game flips that narrative in a wonderfully terrifying manner. Leaving you with a sense of dread and confusion that feels corporeal in nature.
I will admit that I did not enjoy the couple of chase-sequences that the game threw at me, though not very challenging, they did feel a bit forced in comparison to the underlying horrors of the environment. The heart beat sound FX, the shaking screen, the slow following monsters? Bleh. I felt like a teenage girl in an 80s horror movie who had done something naughty in the previous scene.
Aside from that single and admitted feeble complaint, I greatly enjoyed what this game offered and ended up becoming. I did at one point have to pause and go pour a cup of whiskey to help ease the nerves, and that is exactly what I was looking for, tension that doesn't end up breaking you, though you may take a break or two to remind yourself that this is just a game.
Graphically it ran very well on my system with a solid 70-90 FPS at 3440x1440 Ultrawide without ever spinning up my CPU pump/fans since it is not a physics heavy game. The styling did not feel like a copy and paste of props or textures which is good, though they by no means attempt photo-realism.
TL;DR:
Its good. Play it. No jump scares. Much spooky.  Many Wow.

Conarium is the latest horror project from Darkness Within developer Zoetrope Interactive. Much like it's two predecessor, this tale of terror pulls plenty from the writings of H.P. Lovecraft to flesh out the disappearance of an Alaskan research base's crew. The primary inspiration from this tale is pretty evident, pulling from the famed tale At the Mountains of Madness with nods to elder ones from others stories qnd alkaloidal cults.
Even though the influences were more a science fiction meets horror, Conarium has some steampunk nods from time to time. Thankfully, this is just an underlying aspect (based on the amount of time I put in with the game at the time of writing this) behind the various mind games often played on. Whether ovious or minimal, There are a number of changes that slink in through natural gameplay that leave you scratcing your head as to whether or not you overlooked them prior.
However, a fair warning to those willing to dive in: This is a slow burn with most of the fear and tension lying in the documents you uncover. The more you read, the more the story unravels and begins to make sense, not to mention begin plaguing the sanity of your character. There have been a few jump scares so far, but they aren't cheap and actually wuit the narrative of the story, such as misinterprerting a shadow or seeing things that aren't really there.
Simply put: Conarium is Lovecrsftisn done right.I've sunk over an hour of time into this title, and it's only getting better the deeper in I get, If you'rre a fan of a slow build, as well as reading and discovering more background information to enhance the tale, Conarium is definitely one worth checking out.

- really dangerous game to have in your library - just sucks the hours from your life. I started playing around 10 pm, and by the time I glanced at the time, it was 5 am.... Hoooooly cow.
I mainly wanted to give the devs a thumbs up for making such an engrossing game, but I wound up writing too much. In short, I think it's a great game. The devs genuinely listen to player feedback, and are happy to make changes based on players' comments or concerns. I'm very happy I purchased it. Besides, gotta' love a world where you can buy a suit of Sacred Armor and a couple of Transmutation Guns with Spaghetti and Pickles.
Judgment's heavy on research, craft, scavenging, and battle. I've played a few games that are similar, but Judgment's the only one that makes me feel like I'm on the verge of fighting the long defeat. Still, it's hard to throw in the towel. I was ready to start over on day 16, yet here I am well past day 100 still kicking demon hiney.
By the time you think you're equipped well enough to start busting down some hell gates, demon hordes are regularly popping in unannounced, and keeping everyone alive starts to feel more and more difficult - and that's on the recommended setting. There are two tougher modes beyond that, but I won't be going anywhere near them anytime soon.
However, if you keep up with your research, design your base well, and survive a few calculated risks - before long you'll be able to weather even the toughest attacks. The demons who were once too difficult to take on become game, and the hunters become the hunted. That's pretty satisfying.
Even though it seems tough at times, the game is very retry friendly- to the point where not only can you reattempt a botched battle, but if you're on the campaign map, the game will generally spawn your group into a different map with enemies in a different position which is very useful since some maps offer more tactical choices than others. There's an auto resolve option as well which really simplifies things once you're running around with a fully leveled team equipped with optimal gear.
* * *
I just have to point out one of the more appalling errors I've read in a number of reviews. Anyone who claims melee is worthless in this game has obviously never seen a capable Fighter spec'd for melee - wearing Obsidian Armor and an Evil Ward - wading through a pack of Legions, Werewolves and Succubi to hack up some Fallen Angels or Caortharnack with her Sacred Sword. It's a sight to behold... One or two good melee Fighters are also really useful during Auto Resolve battles since they soak up the enemy's attacks leaving the rest of the party completely unscathed - often walking away with nary a scratch themselves. Having survivors take turns at melee allows the Taskforce to stay away from home for longer periods of time before they have to go back to heal.
Another repeated criticism is that the Enemy Awareness bar is inaccurate, and enemy attacks come too quickly or before the awareness reaches 100%. That's really only an issue in the very early game when enemies are weak and few in number, and you don't have any Lookout Posts built or survivors actively Patroling. At some point when your base is huge and crawling with survivors, Enemy Awareness reaches 100% every day, yet you can still go for days without an attack.
