Alpha Protocol is a polarizing game, and rightly so. It's janky, not quite balanced, and has some miserably bad voice acting. It's also one of my favorite games of all time. Have I gone crazy? Well...
To begin with, there are over a dozen different types of items to find, customize, and use in missions. Nearly everything in the game that you can equip can be upgraded, and all of the upgrading is optional. Importantly, there's no one item or item type that you must use to progress. You could finish the entire main storyline with your starting guns and punch the vast majority of hostiles with your fists, which can be upgraded. And your character's durability can be upgraded in much the same way, which is important if you want to start a bunch of boxing matches with armed gaurds. You can play stealthily, loudly, loudly like a fox (trick the guards into activating an alarm panel that's rigged up with a sticky grenade, for example), or any combination of approaches that suits your playstyle. The difficulty comes from the enemies and hazards directly, and not from the all too common "everything-proof shield" that most developers of action games lazily rely on.
The level design is excellent, for the most part. You'll rarely be completely lost, guard placement is optimal, items aren't too densely packed to be challenging, nor too sparse, and turrets and the like aren't common enough to be infuriating, but not so rare as to make a technology-focused build less powerful than the others. Your decisions in previous missions, and in the sequences between them, will even open some paths and block others, but it isn't overdone enough to become tedious. And it's quite rare to be without cover and alternate paths simultaneously.
The levelling system is quite good, for my tastes, but will certainly bother others. If you focus on putting all your points into a skill, your character will become quite overpowered in that skill by the end of the game. Stealth skill will eventually give you a cloak on a cooldown, pistols can be aimed in slow motion and fired cartoonishly rapidly, shotguns are eventually able to keep bosses almost permanently knocked down, and so on. On the one hand, this means that the skill points you spend are going somewhere useful, regadless of what you prefer to level up. On the other hand, if you're looking for something brutally difficult, or even realistically difficult to overcome, you won't be satisfied by Alpha Protocol. By the end of the game you're basically a superhero fighting large hordes of well-armed goons and the occasional supervillain. Or sneaking past the ones that aren't bosses... but still.
The characters in the main cast are boring, forgettable cliches. Their voice actors put forth as little effort as possible and the writers didn't try very hard with them, either. The secondary characters, though, are often very endearing and well-acted. James Hong makes a delightful cameo. Stephen Heck, Sie, Albatross, and too many more to mention are also greatly more entertaining characters than the main ones. It's fair to say that the more central a character is to the plot, the worse their writing and voice acting gets, with Mike Thorton (the main character) easily being the worst.
The main plot isn't a strong point. It's about secret agents trying to stop an evil CEO from starting a world war. Fortunately, though, it frequently takes a back seat to the secondary plot arcs and doesn't get much more than (jarringly frequent) lipservice throughout most of the game. You'll have to put up with some characters bringing up the main plot every chance they get, but it's mercifully rare for gameplay to be impacted by it.
The dialogue itself is of drastically varying quality (see above), but the user interface that directs your character's responses in conversation is an unmitigated disaster. If you've played Fallout 4 you know what to expect - you can push one of four buttons to make your character say something, but it's impossible to know what precisely you're making him say without prior knowledge. You get a vague indication of the tone and topic you're going to be responding with and a very limited time to peruse your options. And some characters will only like you if you mash the B button [(for example) (Xbox360 controller)], while others will hate you if you mash the B button, which is as dumb as it sounds.
So who do I recommend this game to? If you thoroughly enjoyed Deus Ex 1, bought a copy of Deus Ex: Human Revolution, and it made you facepalm so hard that it sounded like a gun went off, you'll find Alpha Protocol a much needed relief. If you're looking for a believable spy thriller in an original setting, you'll probably find this game painful to play. If you're the type that played Fallout: New Vegas as an angry, drugged-up whackjob that goes around starting fights with everything that moves (or did so at least once and enjoyed it), and want something that brings that catharsis back now that you've played F:NV to death, you'll be amply able to scratch that itch in Alpha Protocol. I'm a big simulation game person. It's all I've known, ever since my first game of SimAnt, or Rollercoaster tycoon. I also understand that they are non-linear games, and thus, programming non-linear games is a whole different beast than your FPS's and RPG's, where things can be easily scripted and predicted.
Recently, I've fallen in love with Rimworld, Prison Architect, and (especially) factorio. These are the big guys in the simulation world today, and at this time I take that into consideration when judging other games of this genre.
Judgement: Apocalypse has a good idea of what it wants to be. It wants to give the player options and freedom to play the game how they see fit. But to this idea, it is not executed in a good way. There are multiple branches of research, but with each limited by finding "research items", which are found randomly. By the time you generate enough points to research everything, you're just waiting to find that random find to continue. And the enemies scale horribly. I'm sure another reviewer can tell you what the scaling is based on, as I don't know. I just know that by the time you see multiple reapers and minor demons, you're barely still trying to get your people armed with♥♥♥♥♥♥tier weapons that won't leave a mark on them. You're left taking on impossible missions with♥♥♥♥♥♥gear, just waiting for those lucky drops that get you to the next tier of research. I've seen others claim that the game is brutal and unforgiving. They are right. But they are right in the wrong way. It is brutal, and from what I've seen, the key to success is very linear. You have to build everything the right way, and have luck on your side. It just doesn't leave much room for variation.
And as a simulation/sandbox game, it leaves very little room for customization. You start off being able to build little "cabins" that are either 2X2 or 3X2, where you fit your little objects in. It upgrades to stone, but there is no drag/customize features. Everything is static. You build a garden or you don't.
I suppose a lot of criticism comes from the fact that they stole from Rimworld with their "priorities" menu where you can sort the improtance of tasks for each person. This is a big mechanic in Judgement. Recently "Oxygen Not Included" did the same. I own that and I've played it, but it also leaves a bad taste in your mouth. Both of these games leave me feeling stale. Good ideas, but poor execution.
I didn't want to refund Judgement, because I think there is potential. Also, and mainly, because I encourage development of the genre. This is likely a first for many of their staff, and should be a learning experience. You guys had a good idea. Just work on it and polish it and you're good to go.

A turn-based tactical game where stealth and conflict-avoidance are the main focus. You sneak through corporate offices stealing everything that isn't nailed down while working on some objective such as stealing important files, or brain-hacking an executive. The world has a neat dystopian corporate-police-state vibe that serves as an excellent backdrop for all the sneaking and thievery you'll be doing.

Let me start by saying that if you're looking for a colony management sim, this is not the game for you.  That aspect of the game is exceedingly simple.  Keeping your survivors alive and happy generally amounts to no more than building enough beds, farms, and water wells.  Instead, the home base in this game is more of an R&D facility for developing and crafting better equipment in support of the other aspect of the game:  Combat.
Combat in this game will be frequent, as scavenging supplies from the demon infested outside world is a big part of expanding your power quickly enough to stay ahead of the ever increasing demon threat.  It can best be described as squad-based real time strategy with pause.  Success depends heavily on your gear and the placement of your fighters.  In terms of placement, cover is an important aspect of the combat field and will greatly improve your survivability against ranged enemies.  Also, flanking enemies will grant you bonuses both to accuracy and damage.
On the negative side, enemy diversity is stat-based only: Hp, damage, attack range, etc.  None of them have special attacks or intelligent attack scripts as of yet.  Your survivors can do a little better, gaining access to special abilities through their gear.  Overall combat can be repetitive, but the steady progress you make grinding through it can be satisfying.
My final word is that Judgement: Apocalypse is not the greatest of games, but hey.  It's only $15, and it will probably keep you entertained for a good long while.  I would recommend it to RPG/RTS fans who enjoy base-building features.

Damn, I remember playing all of the previous versions before it was recently released into Steam.
Be warned because this is NOT your typical HL Mod, is not very casual friendly (Currently) and it has it's system to learn.
In this mod, you have three classes to choose:
:  The most weak of all of the three but very powerful
: A very good supporting class with summoning Angels
: Another very good supporting class that can help your team to survive with HP / Ammo drops
When you enter, you can start with different weapons, depending on your class, and btw, every time you survive 10 waves, your perk / class saves.
In your HUD, you will notice you have HP (Duh), Mana, EXP for next level, and your current money. When you kill, restore barricades or kill the hardest alien In-game, you get money, which you can use to trade with allies, buy weapons, upgrade your inventory, items, etc
Another important thing, when you kill NPC's, there's a small chance you get Salvage or Souls, with those, you can upgrade your weapons with unique stats, which is something you WILL need, because those npcs will kick HARD in later waves!
About Exp, killing npcs gives you xp, or "getting lucky", with that xp, you can choose how to level up you character:
: Speed / Gravity Reduction / Maximum ammo
: Damage / Accuracy / Critical hit damage & chance
: Total HP / HP Regeneration / Damage Reduction
: Total Mana / Mana regeneration
*Special Items can give extra efectiveness to some of above!*
Playing multiplayer can be great fun, but check for your teammates and learn new stuff.
Playing Solo..WILL test how much knowledge & tactics you have (HL Itself and BDef) Enemies will deal a lot of damage and if you wanna fight IT, it will have a LOT of HP, and can end you VERY easily *More easily at extremely higher waves!* Take your time, Kite around, and it's worth it, because it can drop very valuable items to help you survive. And if you die..This is when Saves come in.
As I said before, every 10 waves, you save your progress (Stats, money and wave progress), but it's saved from the map, NOT generally. You can choose which save to continue, which can be very helpfull if you want to know your class.
This mod isn't very hard for newcomers, but it will test you a lot AND punish you if it wants!.
Highly recommended for Half-Life Fans.

An immensely satisfying story, atmosphere and setting seem almost completely wasted by questionable gameplay decisions. Levels are overly long and linear, leading to many repetetious combat segments barely broken up by any other mechanics. Alan Wake's main new mechanic, the use of light to make enemies vulnerable is overused and while there is some variety to it, these segments are often just as edious as they require you to take on larger waves of enemies. While the developers do such a splendid job weaving the story into the actual game portion of the game, creating rich ephermera in the form of Manuscript pages, radio programs and a Twilight Zone-esque TV show, these are often extremely far apart, as combat and walking are the main focus of the game. For such a story driven game, it seems a shame that the developer seems to pad the runtime out and not introduce more stry elements or cut scenes to make it feel fresher.

I want to start this off with this comment; the game is currently in beta. That said, I am sure you have read that multiple times now through the various posts. So, where to start?
PROS:
--Character customization and looks in game.
--Story is great thus far.
--Combat will be great once game is complete.
--Graphics / audio / and interface thus far are all great.
--Gameplay is sweet. I said it may not be for everyone because combat is tactical / turn. So, think back old school with X-Com. I love that part of it, personal opinion.
--Combat animations / effects are sweet.
--Choice and consequence are a part of this game. You save someone from drowning, his parents offer him to you as an added party member if you want. Plenty of characters to change up the party.
--Different skills are used for different things. Obviously, ha ha. Those chances to use the skills on a frequent basis are not persistent in other games. There are a lot of opportunity to use each skill you have in your party. I like that.
--A TON of interactions within the world. Be it digging stuff up, repairing gadgets, even down to repairing toasters, ha ha! (definitely have someone in your party that can repair them, because you never know what's stored in one!)
--Completed game will hands down be great.
CONS:
--Loading a save will often change the portrait of your character(s) if they are created from scratch. A minor annoyance, unless you get into combat, then you have to go by name. Or, if you made a guy and your portrait is now a gal.
--Combat, sometimes, can be a bit.. Interesting. You have a sniper, that has 0.0% chance of hitting a target. That same target now moves behind cover, and you now have an 80.00% chance to hit.
--Combat again, some enemies have ridiculous move / attacks. They will move across the screen, attack you twice, then move again... BETA, remember. It will frustrate / annoy you though, ha ha.
--Make sure you get a dedicated surgeon / healer. I roamed around for a bit trying to find someone that could heal my wounds, to no avail.
--There are times when walking around on the world map you are accosted by bandits, raiders, whatever, only to enter combat (if you choose) and find everything dead. Good for the free loot, bad because you never know what will really happen!
--The game crashes from time to time AFTER combat is completed.
--Some game choices have to be made on the spot, you do not have a lot of time to fart around and trying to figure the puzzle out. You take your time, (drowning boy for example,) he will die. Some people may not like that part.
--With no tutorial yet, character creation can be.. difficult.
--Finally; some characters you may spec for conversation bonus dialogues, sale prices, et-cetera. Once you enter dialogue, there is no way to change who is talking, so in cities, towns, you want to lead the party with the talker if that is your thing.
Fans of Fallout 1 and 2 need to play this game, awesome on so many levels! There's real consequences for your actions, believable dialogue, survival based resource alocation (water), and toasters!
What to say about this game, there really is nothing else to say but for you the reader to choose do you want that really nice mouse or keyboard or do you want a peice of history... An early look.
After finishing the intro and a few other missions.
Note; I am playing the game on an AMD FX-6300 and GTX 750 ti. I am by no means on a supercomputer. This is my experience at medium settings.
Pros:
-Gunplay is good.
The idea of making the game a half documentary style in cutscenes is very refreshing, very rarely see something like it these days. Well done boys.
-Story is looking really promising from the bit I've done.
-Character audio is well done. +1 to the voice actors of this game. Every character sounds amazing.
-Driving is very much like a Steve McQueen film like Bullitt. It's very fun, yet firm. Cars feel heavy, yet they move like they have power.
-The world design of New Bordeaux is fantastic. Each district does indeed capture a different vibe, all of which I appreciate. The suspense in the Bayou, the bright party feel of the french ward. It is all great.
-The one well expected thing of this game from the get go, the soundtrack is amazingly well put together. Every moment near a radio is a good one in this game.
The 60's was a time of joy, yet also displeasure. This game captures both of these feelings. Bringing up MLK, JFK and Malcolm X, with constant throwbacks to people talking about 'Nam, yet also seeing the bright lights during Mardi Gras. By far one of the best side by sides in a game.
Cons:
-The 30fps lock is obviously a mention. Not the biggest deal, don't let it stop you from looking at a great game. Its supposed to be fixed on the weekend of this review, heres hoping to that.
-Textures are iffy. Some people hate them, others, like myself, dont really mind.
-Also to do with textures, I've noticed some textures are slower to load than the most here and there, with quick yellow flashes here and there as I turn. Bit of a shame, but it only happened a few times.
-I have experienced one crash total, but I was also pushing my computer a bit further than I should with all the programs I had open, so it may have been my fault as well.
Some people will say the game is completely unfinished. It has bugs right now, especially on PC. But if it gets fixed within the next couple weeks, it could very well be the best AAA game this year. The actual game is amazing. If you want to wait until bugs get patched or at least some get fixed, I recommend you wait to avoid some displeasures. But looking past  the bugs, the actual game is fantastically good. Well done Hangar 13, I am not dissappointed.
Second note; I will write more as I experience more over the next couple weeks. Perhaps make edits or point out patches that fix problems.

I didn't play this game for very long, because I couldn't. I was bored by both the dated gameplay and the cliché and badly written storyline. Perhaps there's a big unpredictable twist at the end that makes everyone like this game but I can't really force myself to play it for any longer. If you've seen any horror film or read any horror book where the main character is a writer you've probably already seen something like this before.
So let me explain why the gameplay has aged horribly. Firstly, it's very clunky to control, aiming works well but movement is pretty stiff. Another reason is the collectibles, now there's nothing wrong with collectibles, don't get me wrong, they just don't work in this type of game. In a horror game you're not supposed to be thinking 'let's wander around this deserted forest to make sure I didn't leave behind any randomly placed insulated coffee mugs', you're supposed to be thinking 'I need to get through here quickly because I really don't want to run into the thing that's seemingly following me!' It could have worked but since the areas are very linear with an obvious direction to head (and made even more clear by the objective in the corner of the screen); you know you're just going to go the other way simply for a collectible so it completely breaks the immersion (if that's not already broken by the terrible lip sync and awful animations). If you didn't know where you were supposed to go, not only would it be scarier, it would also have been rewarding when you find collectibles. Lastly, there are puzzles, if you can call them that, placed around simply to add a little bit of variety. They are, however, as simple as just looking at them and finding a power generator and are very common ideas used in many games.
Now let's talk about the storyline and the writing: it's not very good. Why? They start the game off by saying horror is scarier when it is left unexplained, which I agree with, we are afraid of the unknown. However, Alan Wake feels the need to write a commentary on every little thing that's happeneing as well as explain to you what's already clearly shown through what you can see. If it was mystery they were going for, they really don't understand the concept as Alan Wake makes sure that you not only understand it instantly, but also that it is spelled out for you so not even the simplist of minds could feel unsure of what's happening around them. Any deep concepts or subtle messaging that could have been are ruined by Alan Wake's monologue. I should also mention the enemies, or should I say the enemy. The one guy with the axe that does exactly the same thing over and over, he has some of the most ridiculous quotes; I'm not sure if it's supposed to be funny or scary - because it's neither, it's cringe worthy. Best example I heard whilst playing it 'It's rabbit season!'
If anyone reads this, can you tell me if the storyline is actually surprising or interesting by the end? I might try to play it just for that and rewrite the review based on the full game if it is.

Liked it overall and most of the positives e.g. music and art (which is even better this time, some of the painted battlefields are masterpieces of detailed drawing) remain, but it was a bit worse than the first part although somewhat longer with more to do.
They made it even more “eventful” than the more "down to earth" "leading refugees away during massive invasion" of Part 1, but exaggerated it to "world is ending and giant beasts are tearing the entire world apart" level, at this rate you'll be fighting deities in Part 3. They even added some patented BioWare romance writing near the end of the game potentially foreshadowing said for the next part. The bit with the Ravens was a nice diversion from the main plot and a more fun / better part of the game.
They didn't change that much about the combat from the first part other than that cover exists now in a few cases and there’s some really annoying maps that are sizeist and discriminate against Varl, there’s also more enemy types and they introduced some imba abilities like “Cull the Weak” with which you can decimate the enemies in one turn or “Overwatch”, which with Strength Knockback or +3 talent items can keep the entire enemy half of the board in check. They also got rid of the “WARS!” that were popping up constantly in the first part in favor of single battles, although one of the hardest parts of the game combat-wise was still a two-staged boss event.
And the "Horseborn" after being foreshadowed as this interesting mysterious species in the first part turned out to be kind of a lame unimpressive fan-fiction/furry-tier race a lot less likeable than the Varl/Giants.
Still overall solid enough and looking forward to the third part and conclusion of the story, since they still left a lot of questions/mysteries about the World/Dredge/Darkness/Serpent/Menders/What-Juno-Did unanswered and story strands open. If people considered the ending of the first part open-ended, they likely didn't like the ending for the second too much.

It's powerful, suspenseful, and has enough story to fill a novel. Keep in mind, that's mostly what the game is - a cinematic experience. If it's not your cup of tea, then don't bother.
You are Alan Wake, a famous author on vacation who suddenly realizes the stories he wrote have come to life. These stories are no ordinary stories mind you, they are horror stories that want something in particular from Wake. That's when the game truly begins. It is a psychological horror, entirely story driven, that will have you questioning what's real and what's not. Alan Wake is very similar to any TV series - released in episodic content to keep you on the edge of your seat. There's 6 episodes totaling 2-3 hours each of playtime with 2 bonus DLC episodes (approximately 2 hours). Overall you are looking at nearly a 20 hour game. There's also a stand-alone follow-up called Alan Wake's American Nightmare.
The gameplay is fairly straightforward - you are equipped with a flashlight and pistol. The flashlight is used to hurt the enemies by shining light on them and the pistol is used to kill them for good. The enemies themselves are hard to describe without ruining the game - essentially they are a paranormal darkness that stalk Wake and members of the community. The game borrows its inspiration heavily from Stephen King novels, Alfred Hitchcock, and the 90s TV show Twin Peaks. Most of the game you'll find yourself running from enemies, battling them, or solving a minor puzzle. Everything is there to drive the story forward. It's more exploration and survival based as opposed to run n gun.
Overall, Remedy presented us with the definitive cinematic experience of psychological horrors. It's got an amazing atmosphere, a very fitting soundtrack and score, and the graphics are beautiful. As a game however, it loses points for being limited in what you do. The game gets a solid 7.5/10 from me.

TL:DR: Best investment I have ever made in both time and money with anything digital.
Dont get fooled by my time "played" I have had this program (yes PROGRAM, not GAME) since 2012.
I started playing Pnp RPG in the 80'ies and while it's always been a part of my life, I've had some slow periode of gaming. Mostly because my gaming buddies moved, got work and some of use got kids. It's difficult to find the time.
One day I stumbled upon Fantasy Grounds and checked the demo out. I did some extensive testing with the demo following the guides and the videos found on the official forum. It was like opening a door more and more. The possibilities opened up right before me!. I was sold.
I persuaded my friends to get FG. Then began my preperation for our first adventure in many years. I admit it was hard work, but also very fun. I normally use all the time I have to spare, playing games here on Steam, but I actually pushed that aside for 2-3 weeks and focused on preparing and getting better at using FG. I was ready for many session of gaming after that. And I was having a blast to! I do not use so long for preperation anymore though.
After I felt ready, we started. The first couple of sessions were slow as my players had to learn the program (not all of them bothered to invest much time getting to know FG, so I had to teach them). But after that, everything went smooth.
I now use FG both for my online sessions with my friends, where we play Rolemaster at the moment, but also when I play Pathfinder with my son and 4 of his friends. Actually it was my wife who said "Why not just use FG?" when I raged after I had been through so many other "RPG managers". It works well. A neat thing would be to start two FG up and show the player one, on a different screen than the GM side. But for our game the boys want to use all the cool miniatures I have painted in the past years ;).
The community behind FG is amazing. I have never joined a more mature (well we are kids in our heart of couse ;), but you know what I mean) and helpful community.

I own the full version of FG since shortly before the Steam Launch. I think it is very important to realize that Fantasy Grounds by itself is not a full game - it is a tool and might be better fitting for the Software Section of Steam rather than the Games section.
There is a high learning curve to the game for a Game Master. It takes a few hours to get used to the rules sets, the various tools provided and all the little things you need to consider. Once you do spend these hours to familiarize yourself you have a powerful tool to handle campaigns, battle maps and characters.
We started playing Savage Worlds in Fantasy Grounds and are having a blast. As an experienced pen & paper player, I have to say that gameplay is actually sped up by the tools provided, allowing us more time to actually roleplay and less time discussing rules, piece positioning or anything else.
If you are willing to tackle the initial learning curve and understand that FG is more a tool than it is a game, I can highly recommend it to you. If you are expecting a highly interactive video game however, you might want to direct your attention towards Divinity: Original Sin or something similiar.

Amazing game. Prior to playing Conarium, I never really cared about H.P. Lovecraft. I had heard of him like most people, but I never really knew anything about his works. So I played the game, and OMG, this game has made me fall in love with Lovecraft. I actually bought his entire collection and am now reading it. I want to start reading At the Mountain of Madness, which this game is based off of, then go back and play Conarium again. There seems to be a lot of hidden stories here that you won't understand if you haven't read the books.
I digress. This game is a very solid point and click puzzle/horror game. There's hardly any action, and most of the scares are not jump scares, but psychological ones, where you can't rationally explain what's happening. I'm not usually into point and click games, but this one held my attention the whole way.
Conarium is powered by UR4, and I have to say that it is one of the best looking games I've played in a long time. The atmosphere is so incredible, that it makes up for not having constant scares. If you're like me and have a powerful rig and can run it at max, the game has this constant fog which just adds to the creepiness. I'm not sure if this is disabled with lower settings, bc fog is usually a heavy performance strain, but it definitely added to the creep factor for me.
You can also tell that this game was made with love. Everything has so much detail and nothing seems like it was added just to be in there. The objects and puzzles in the game are very complex and everything adds to the lore. I'm also not usually into reading in-game documents, but I was reading every journal and item description I came across. Most of it wasn't earth shattering lore, but if you found all of them, it gives you more detail on what's happening.
Performance wise, I couldn't find any issues. This game ran a smooth 60fps the whole way through. I wish the settings menu would be a bit clearer, instead of just saying things like Post FX: Low-High; that doesn't explain what kind of Post FX it is, which can sometimes make the game look worse. But those are just small complaints.
If you're a fan of creepy games, I'd 100% recommend this game. Even if you aren't a Lovecraft fan like I was, you'll still find this game to be a solid 3-5 hour game.
The learning curve is pretty steep, but once you get through it, it's great.
Don't feel intimidated by it at first, because learning is the fun part. Trust me. Don't hesitate to buy this game; it's amazing.

What this game is:
110% Lovecraftian exploration and puzzle solving
What this game is not:
An outlast clone with fishpeople, nor is it a shooter
This is a BIG RECOMMEND if you enjoy the works of HP Lovecraft, and just the vibe of those works in general. It covers a lot of major themes, while also stepping occasionally into new territory, yet still completely consistant with the inherent nature of the Lovecraftian reality.
The developers should be very proud of their game, and the genuine love for the source material that is clearly established in the details.
CAVEAT: This game isn't a hide and seek or a killstreak game. Be very clear on that on the front end. If that is what you are looking for, then this excellent game is not it.
Beginner's tip: Search extremely hard if you want to find most of the notes and backstory, I'm talking wastebaskets, overturned boxes that are hard to access, opening crates, drawers, etc. I scoured hallways and offices, then went back and found 2 or 3 fragments more, even when I thought I had cleared everything.
TLDR: A must get if you enjoy anything Lovercraftian, and if you like to support smaller studios doing excellent work.

This is a game that I would truly like to give a positive/recommended review, however, in it's current state I'm finding that difficult to do. As a note: I am currently in stage 4 of act 4 and I'll be starting a new game, so I have yet to achieve the final cutscene. There are no story spoilers in this review.
Positive: If you enjoyed Shadow of Mordor for solely the gameplay, then you will get your monies worth. The gameplay is
a copy. Additionally, they've added many new additions to the nemesis system's traits.
Neutral: I wouldn't say the story is terrible. It has a bit more substance than Shadow of Mordor, however, this game's story is not something that can be seen as great. It's good at some points, bad at others, but mostly it's just average. Additionally, the microtransactions are not as pervasive as I'd thought they would be, however, it can be said they have no place in this game.
Negatives:
-Repetitiveness: The gameplay is fun for sure, however, after the second region I found myself simply not caring any longer. Instead I found myself simply going through the motions.
-Regions: The regions are NOT what was shown off in the initial trailer. There are about twice as many as Shadow of Mordor, but for some reason they feel smaller than Udon. Additionally, the maps for the regions seem almost poorly constructed.
-Bugs: The game in its current state is certainly buggy. I've found myself riding a drake that remains frozen in the air until archers finally killed it and I was able to move again. I've found myself trapped in the environment and unable to move. I've found that under Sieges the attacking Uruks/Ologs will simply die when a wall falls and you will be unable to revive them (if you spent time making some legendaries this will really♥♥♥♥♥♥you off). I've been deleveled, I've had silver being lost, I've had Orcs randomly deleveled.
-Pathfinding, AI: Okay so this is an issue of many open-world games. The AI will run in circles, get lost, sprint one way and then run back the other way, get trapped in the environment or simply stop working and stand there getting killed. Additionally, when you're fighting in Sieges it will become a large moshpit. You may be trying to attack an enemy, but find yourself targeting a friendly captain instead.
-Targeting: When you're fighting in Sieges it will become a large moshpit. You may be trying to attack an enemy, but find yourself targeting a friendly captain instead. This is a massive issue. If you attempt to stop, but you keep targeting the same ally they will eventually betray you and cause issues.
-Side content: This is in regards to the collectibles. They were a boring addition in Shadow of Mordor and they are just as bad if not worse in this game.
-Misleading information prior to release: I won't spoil anything, but trailers and content was misleading in terms of what you'll actually be getting.
-Abilities: Often times I find Talion weaker in this game than he was in Shadow of Mordor. Additionally, they've split up skills that in SoM you could use at the same time. It's not a big negative, but is irritating at best.
--------------------------------
TL;DR: In its current state it is not recommendable. If the bugs are fixed, gameplay, pathfinding, targeting and AI are tweaked then I can see myself changing my mind. Expansion updates like other developers have done would also be nice, but I'm not holding my breath and won't expect such a thing.

I've been a FG user for over 4 years.
(I see a lot of misconceptions in the reviews below)
This software allows you to play as a player or GM/DM a session over the Internet.
Session: An adventure created by the DM/GM that players connect to.
The DM/GM puts together his adventure by inserting images/descriptions/ideas into the interface.
The Interface can automate a lot of the math involved in hit/miss and damage totals.
The concept is to allow a group to enjoy playing a Pen & Paper style Roleplaying game over the Internet.
You will need your books or PDF's, although the rulesets in the interface includes a lot of this info.
The GM/DM will need to invest some time making an adventure, like he would with a real Pen & Paper Tabletop RPG session.
He will then need to insert all the images/maps notes into the session prior to hosting the game.
(You can also download/buy ready made adventures as well)
(You can pre-make adventures and save them... then activate them in the session as you need)
This is not a video game, it needs a GM/DM to set things up first, so the players can play.
Now that you have a better idea of what this software is...
Fantasy Grounds does an excellent job at automating a lot of your session, Once you watch some videos on how people put together their adventures, you will have the tools to recreate anything you made with Pen & Paper within FG.
I think we need to have more videos to explain this a bit more, but what it does, it does GREAT.
I've invested more time as both player and DM/GM than any video game I have.
I personly use Skype or Teamspeak so we can voice what our character actions are in the game.
It allows social interactivity and brain stimulation we so much miss in our computerized world.
I recommend trying the free DEMO and hooking up with a DM/GM with an "Ultimate" license (because they can let you connect to their game like the paid version).

Absolutely validates the ongoing resurgence of adventure gaming - while not the first to do so by any means, Broken Age will certainly be a standard bearer among current peers.
The picture book art motif is wonderfully executed. It supports the characters, world, and cheeky dialog perfectly. The narrative doesn't consistently hit the heights of levity present in the SCUMM adventure legacy, but it's damn close. The highs it does reach certainly recall those cherished experiences. The performances in key parts are a joy, too.
The puzzles are entertaining and largely logical. Though perhaps not as multi-layered as possible, they do allow the narrative pacing to be maintained. Without entering spoiler-ville, it would have been nice to see more content that connected our protagonists during this act. Even considering this as the first act, it felt as if things ended a little too soon, though that could be a testament to just how hooked I was. It never felt artificially padded, either - pacing here is near flawless.
Highly recommended. Can't wait for Act 2, and the future potential this game heralds.

A success in storytelling and choice/consequence. A missed opportunity in gameplay.
Alpha Protocol does a superb job in making your choices matter. Tackling the story missions in a different order leads to different reactions from the main character and other NPC's, alliances being made with different factions with enemies made from others, and significant impact on the endgame. Likewise conversation options, and how fast or slow you make dialogue choices, can impact the strength of your opponent or even skip a fight entirely. This game does a great job in enforcing the weight of your decisions and making you feel like a spy.
Alpha Protocol fails in the combat department. Shooting feels inprecise and melee combat (especially in 1 on 1 scenarios) is a simple test of mashing the attack button. AI is poor, even for the time this title was released.
I still recommend this game to fans of choice and consequence in games or fans of the action/spy genre. If the combat systems of a game like Mass Effect could synergize with the rest of this game, Alpha Protocol would have become much more than the overlooked title it has become.

This game really is a mixed bag.
To keep it short, this is a third-person shooter with RPG elements (conversations, relations, skills). The overarching story has to do with espionage and conspiracies and thriller stuff like that. You play the role of Michael Thorton, a new recruit in Alpha Protocol. You can pick different backstories that affect your starting skills as well as some conversations later down the line, a la Mass Effect 1.
To highlight the good points, I really enjoyed the conversation system in this game. It was very similar to Mass Effect, and the voice acting was solid for the respective roles of the characters. The story seemed interesting at times, and enough to keep me going.
However, that's where the good points end. This is an incredibly clunky game while in the shooting sections, and regularly glitched on my computer. It was nothing game-breaking, but very immersion-breaking. Also, the shooting mechanics seemed woefully half baked. You can improve your shooting skills, but your reticule never gets any smaller even when crouched and not moving, and its a big damn reticule which means this super secret agent f##king sucks at shooting.
Also, its VERY short for a single-player-only RPG; probably about 9-10 hours. Tripling that length wouldn't fix all this games issues, but i'd still press on because I wanted to see how Thorton's story ended.
I really wish I could give this game a recommendation. I really do like it, but this is disappointing coming from a studio as good as Obsidian. I'd definitely play a sequel if they made one, but they'd have to iron out the bugs and tighten up the story. I wanted to see deeper and more involved conversations and character development.
As it is though, I cannot give this game a recommendation unless its on sale for $2. I REALLY hope Obsidian makes a sequel, because I will definitely be first in line to buy it.

I didn't play this game for very long, because I couldn't. I was bored by both the dated gameplay and the cliché and badly written storyline. Perhaps there's a big unpredictable twist at the end that makes everyone like this game but I can't really force myself to play it for any longer. If you've seen any horror film or read any horror book where the main character is a writer you've probably already seen something like this before.
So let me explain why the gameplay has aged horribly. Firstly, it's very clunky to control, aiming works well but movement is pretty stiff. Another reason is the collectibles, now there's nothing wrong with collectibles, don't get me wrong, they just don't work in this type of game. In a horror game you're not supposed to be thinking 'let's wander around this deserted forest to make sure I didn't leave behind any randomly placed insulated coffee mugs', you're supposed to be thinking 'I need to get through here quickly because I really don't want to run into the thing that's seemingly following me!' It could have worked but since the areas are very linear with an obvious direction to head (and made even more clear by the objective in the corner of the screen); you know you're just going to go the other way simply for a collectible so it completely breaks the immersion (if that's not already broken by the terrible lip sync and awful animations). If you didn't know where you were supposed to go, not only would it be scarier, it would also have been rewarding when you find collectibles. Lastly, there are puzzles, if you can call them that, placed around simply to add a little bit of variety. They are, however, as simple as just looking at them and finding a power generator and are very common ideas used in many games.
Now let's talk about the storyline and the writing: it's not very good. Why? They start the game off by saying horror is scarier when it is left unexplained, which I agree with, we are afraid of the unknown. However, Alan Wake feels the need to write a commentary on every little thing that's happeneing as well as explain to you what's already clearly shown through what you can see. If it was mystery they were going for, they really don't understand the concept as Alan Wake makes sure that you not only understand it instantly, but also that it is spelled out for you so not even the simplist of minds could feel unsure of what's happening around them. Any deep concepts or subtle messaging that could have been are ruined by Alan Wake's monologue. I should also mention the enemies, or should I say the enemy. The one guy with the axe that does exactly the same thing over and over, he has some of the most ridiculous quotes; I'm not sure if it's supposed to be funny or scary - because it's neither, it's cringe worthy. Best example I heard whilst playing it 'It's rabbit season!'
If anyone reads this, can you tell me if the storyline is actually surprising or interesting by the end? I might try to play it just for that and rewrite the review based on the full game if it is.

It's powerful, suspenseful, and has enough story to fill a novel. Keep in mind, that's mostly what the game is - a cinematic experience. If it's not your cup of tea, then don't bother.
You are Alan Wake, a famous author on vacation who suddenly realizes the stories he wrote have come to life. These stories are no ordinary stories mind you, they are horror stories that want something in particular from Wake. That's when the game truly begins. It is a psychological horror, entirely story driven, that will have you questioning what's real and what's not. Alan Wake is very similar to any TV series - released in episodic content to keep you on the edge of your seat. There's 6 episodes totaling 2-3 hours each of playtime with 2 bonus DLC episodes (approximately 2 hours). Overall you are looking at nearly a 20 hour game. There's also a stand-alone follow-up called Alan Wake's American Nightmare.
The gameplay is fairly straightforward - you are equipped with a flashlight and pistol. The flashlight is used to hurt the enemies by shining light on them and the pistol is used to kill them for good. The enemies themselves are hard to describe without ruining the game - essentially they are a paranormal darkness that stalk Wake and members of the community. The game borrows its inspiration heavily from Stephen King novels, Alfred Hitchcock, and the 90s TV show Twin Peaks. Most of the game you'll find yourself running from enemies, battling them, or solving a minor puzzle. Everything is there to drive the story forward. It's more exploration and survival based as opposed to run n gun.
Overall, Remedy presented us with the definitive cinematic experience of psychological horrors. It's got an amazing atmosphere, a very fitting soundtrack and score, and the graphics are beautiful. As a game however, it loses points for being limited in what you do. The game gets a solid 7.5/10 from me.

What a tremendous disapointment. I loved the story, graphics and sound effects. I like the main characters too. When I first started playing I really liked everything about the game. I love the setting and the ambiance. The first few chapters are really engaging and I couldn't wait to see what happened next. But after the third chapter I realized that this game wasn't getting any better. It's nothing but a bland third person shooter masking itself as a story driven horror game. It is a little creepy at first, but after a while the game becomes incredibly stale. There is no variety to the gameplay whatsoever. It's just point your flashlight at an enemy until you can shoot it with a gun. Rinse and repeat and on and on and on.
I like shooting as much as the next person and the lack of variety in gameplay might have been forgivable, but there is no ending to the story. The game ends with absoutley no resolution to the story. Oh, wait. You have to buy the dlc to see how the story ends. Well the package I purchased came with the dlc, so I was open to forgiving the developer for this disgusting money grabbing oversight, but the dlc was even worse than the single player campaign.
And there is no better way of ruining the immersion than making you start every chapter with none of the equipment you earned in the previous chapters. There is a part where you get arrested and locked up in a police station and it makes sense that you would lose your equipment. But then you get the chance to get it back, but magically the storage where the police stashed your belongings contained weaker equipment. I guess the police decided to exchange my high powered flashlight for a weaker one, because as we all know high powered flashlights are illegal. Pathetic.
Remedy is a developer without a single orginal idea and they make the gamer pay for that. The only way they were able to ramp up the challenge was to add more enemies. The dlc was just more shooting and completely unfair due to being jumped on all sides by enemies constantly.
And then there are the camera issues. Throughout the game enemies spawn all around you, and the camera is supposed to give you a small birds eye view in slow motion to prepare you for the enemies. Well, enemies constantly spawn directly behind you making for an unfair and frusterating experience. Stacking the odds against the player is not a valid way to make the game more challenging. It just ruins the fun. On top of that, the dlc made this issue even more glaring, so I stopped in the middle of it. The dlc was just awful.
I wanted to like this game so bad, but I ended up hating it. It's obvious to me that the devleoper created this game with a single idea in mind, but lacked the creativity to do anything with that idea. And it's sad that they couldn't even come up with a proper ending and instead tried to sucker you into paying money only to disapoint you with an amatuer effort. The fact that this game got 9's and 10's on metacritic just shows that the only thing the average gamer really cares about is killing in beautiful HD. Beautiful graphics couldn't save this pathetic atrocity. 6/10

The pursuit of forbidden, ancient knowledge... the descent into madness in search of transcendence... these are staples of Lovecraftian horror. Those are present in the story and atomosphere of this game. You get the feeling throughout that the members of the expedition were in over their heads from the beginning, but didn't realize it until it was too late.
This is fundamentally a puzzle/adventure game. You unlock new areas to explore, each of which has a puzzle or two to solve in order to progress to the next area. There are some "pixel hunting" elements, where I would swear I searched an area back and forth a dozen times, only to discover that the item I was looking for was on a table in plain view the whole time. The environment is full of details and objects, and it's not clear which ones are interactable until you mouse over them while also being near enough.
The puzzles range from trivial to difficult. I did not personally find that they were necessarily harder as the game progressed -- the difficulty was almost random. Perhaps I personally found some puzzles easier or harder to solve than the developers expected. I completed the game in 7 hours, but I don't remember if I paused it and wandered off during that time (which I frequently do without realizing it) thus inflating the time.
Several times I scoured an area for the way to progress, and found what I thought was "the way" with a thrill of triumph -- only to discover I had merely uncovered a secret.
The only hint you need is that you rarely need to backtrack. Once a new area is unlocked, the tools you need to progress are all contained within the unlocked area itself. I spent a lot of time backtracking until I realized this.
I strongly recommend this game for anybody who is a fan of Lovecraft. The "feeling" of the story is spectacular. People unfamiliar with Lovecraft will doubtless be a bit confused, and consider Conarium to be a fairly middle-of-the-road puzzle game. The game shines when you are a fan and want the feeling of personally delving into an interactive Lovecraftian story.

For table top simulation, I have found Fantasy Grounds to be the very best. The automation makes combat flow more quickly, modules can be created and shared, features for maps, pooled resources, movement, area of effect, etc., all work quite well.
There are free options such as the RPTools suite, but such tools are clumsy, kludgy, prone to breaking, and lack a lot of features. Fantasy Grounds has everything you need in one single application.
There's only a few drawbacks:
1. The learning curve. You need to spend time with the software to understand how it works. For most people familiar with pen and paper RPGs, spending some time learning isn't a big deal.
2. No automated fog of war or light sources. Areas of the map must be revealed manually by the game master. MapTool from RPTools does this, and it would be a great additional feature for FG in the future.
3. The built-in rule sets (3.5, PathFinder, 4.0, etc.) work very well, but if you want to customize the rule set or, god forbid, build your own, expect to spend days and weeks mucking about undocumented blobs of XML and Lua. It's a MESS, and even trivial changes can be difficult to implement. I say this as a professional software developer! FG's documentation in this area is appalingly bad.
4. Like ANY computer software for running RPGs, GMs with a spontaneous style may feel a bit stifled and limited by the tools.
Overall though, Fantasy Grounds is the best of breed for this type of software. If your gaming group is spread far and wide you should definitely give this a try!
A hint: Buy your licenses in bulk from the official website. If Steam is ever down or dies or whatever, you can still download and run the software.

Its creator is also in the process of making a video tutorial series for it.  Through a combination of his first tutorial video, a read-through of the ruleset's functions on its forum page, and an afternoon of playing around and experimenting by myself, I was able to learn the entire system & host a short session today (bought it yesterday night after learning on the demo version).
Overall, it's VERY fun, very pretty, and the extensive amount of features designed to keep everything organised is exactly what I was looking for in a virtual tabletop for Star Wars. I'm absolutely satisfied with my personal copy~!

I found this game to be exceptionally impressive! Granted, I am a huge Lovecraft fan, so my objective opinion on this as a game might be a bit biased. However, the feeling of exploring an abandoned reasearch facility in the snowy mountains, is captured so well in this game. It was a great experience methodically going through the whole thing, and slowly figuring out the truth.
The puzzles are fairly simple, I didn't have to look a walkthrough, except for one case, where I had missed a fairly obvious item on my first walk through the facility. It still manages to make you feel accomplished when you solve them, and slightly anxious about what might come up next.
The story is pure Lovecraft goodness. If you've read "At The Mountains of Madness" this will NOT feel like a fan-fiction, but will be totally believeable, as being something Lovecraft himself would have made, had he been around to experience the medium of video games.
If you are NOT into Lovecraft, there is still a great horror/adventure game here. Obviously, you won't be as familiar with some of the terminology used, BUT, I think it is in a way, that will not as much confuse you, as much as it will make you interested in learning more about it.
A sure recommendation for any fans of horror, but a MUST-PLAY for connaisseurs of Lovecraftian media.

This is a pretty cool game but has a few pretty severe flaws that I cannot understand why they still exist.
It's basically a rocket science simulator and does a pretty good job of it.  The physics are all real (although the devs might have tweaked a few constants relating to mass/density/gravity and whatnot in order to make things play better and scale better).  You will learn alot about orbital mechanics from this game and have fun doing it.  Unfortunately, the game teaches you absolutely nothing about any of this.  It seems like it would be much more accessible, educational, and effective if there was some sort of tutorial that explains the relevant info or even helps you figure out why a rocket blew up or whatnot.
One of my biggest gripes with this game is that the time warp feature is utterly ♥♥♥♥ed.  It is supposed to allow you to speed up time during those substantial parts of missions where your rocket will just be coasting through space doing nothing.  The problem is that for some reason the time-warp feature alters the physics of the game.  A rocket that has no trouble breaking atmosphere on normal time will fly apart if you time-warp.  I can't understand how this game could have been out for almost two years and not have such a basic feature fixed or at least worked around.
My other main gripe with this game is that the way parts are put together to assemble rockets doesn't work very well.  Things don't snap correctly, or a part may clearly look like it's attached to a coupler or something only to find out on launch that it isn't.  Working with storage compartments such as service bays is a nightmare.  The default way many items snap into place often puts things in a position where you can't access it at all (they'll be upside-down or sticking through a wall or something, and you can't even click them), and the only way I've found to fix it is to delete the whole service bay and start over, snapping the items somewhere else entirely (NOT in the service bay), tediously rotate each item, then snap it back into the service bay.  This system could easily be GREATLY improved upon.
And there are some other pretty significant interface issues along with some pacing issues that are annoying or occasionally game-breaking.  For a game that has been out this long, it lacks a surprising amount of polish.  Hopefully the devs will work this stuff out in the future.
Having said all that, it's a fun game that you will find yourself obsessing over it for many hours - IF you look at it more as an amusing rocket simulator than a game.  It is certainly game-ish but lacks polish and other elements that would make it play better.

After an overwhelmingly successful Kickstarter campaign, Tim Schafer and his team at Double Fine have decided to return to their roots with their first point-and-click adventure game in over 15 years. Similar to their past projects like Grim Fandango and The Secret of Monkey Island, Broken Age features unforgettable characters, puzzles, unique themes, and plenty of humor.
The game centers around two characters each from a drastically different walk of life. One half of the narrative follows Vella, a girl who is to be offered as a sacrifice to an enormous monster known as Mog Chothra. While the other half of the story focuses on a boy named Shay who finds himself trapped on a spaceship under the watchful eye of an overly protective computer that holds him prisoner under the pretense of safety. Both of the characters yearn for change and freedom in their own way. While Vella is surrounded by overly zealous villagers that cling to tradition, Shay is completely isolated and patronized by an overbearing computer as he’s forced to endure the same routine day after day.
The puzzles are quite satisfying, they’re not overly complex but they still require some thinking which is a refreshing change from most recent games in the genre. They consist of scouring the environment for various items which can be combined with one another or given to certain characters. The amount of overall polish added to the dialogue is impressive, as you’ll most likely try to use the items in your inventory in clever ways to prompt humorous reactions and responses.
The art style is unique and really sets the game apart. While not being overly impressive on a technical level, Broken Age is brimming with personality and has an undeniable charm. The game feels like a children’s book come to life but the underlying themes and subtle humor make it appealing to players of all ages. The environments are varied and interesting to look at while the characters are all quite memorable.
Sporting an all-star cast, the voice acting is top notch which brings each of the characters to life with standout performances from Elijah Wood as Shay and Jennifer Hale best known for her work on Mass Effect (Femshep) as the megalomaniacal computer. The soundtrack is also well done, fitting the mood and atmosphere of the game perfectly.
Unfortunately, the game is quite linear and doesn’t really offer much in terms of re-playability. The different dialogue options add a bit of humor but have little to no impact on the story. For example: choosing to lie to certain characters won’t change the way they perceive you and will have the same effect as telling the truth.
Act one is also fairly short, lasting around 4 hours and it ends with a bit of a cliffhanger which will leave you anxiously waiting for Act two. Broken Age probably would have benefited from being released all at once but Act two is promised at no additional cost at a later date.
Overall, Broken Age is a charming game with a strong narrative, great humor and memorable characters. It’s proof that there is still room for creativity and innovation amidst the slew of modern action titles. Broken Age not only revives the point and click genre, it helps redefine it.
TLDR? This review is also available in video format:
Pros:
+ Strong Narrative
+ Solid Voice Acting
+ Great Sense of Humor
+ Reasonable Puzzles
+ Fantastic Art Direction
+ Charming and Unique
Cons:
- Cliffhanger Ending
- Short Length (3 - 4 hours long)
- Linear
- Dialogue Options have little influence on the story.

Oh my, yes. A deep space and flight simulator in which you, the titular kerbal, must design, build, accidentally destroy vehicles, and be responsible for the deaths of so many good kerbals. Did you insert them into that orbit on purpose? You know they're going to orbit the sun forever since you couldn't save them, right?
Or leave them on the Mun because you didn't get the return fuel correct.
The game never really punishes you for these mistakes if you play in sandbox mode, my preferred mode, because I like earning "science," the in-game currency which let's you research new parts to play with. I don't prefer career mode because you have to worry about money. I prefer the free money and science aspects of science sandbox mode.
But, in short, a very rewarding space and flight (and probe and space truck) simulator that puts you in charge of designing and flying these many vehicles in an effort to explore your local solar system. I love this game, as my nearly 200 hours of play time attests.
Highly recommended for: science nerds, simulationists, people who like firing rockets into space.
Not recommended for: people who don't like rockets, people who will give up when their rocket has exploded again and you don't want to try to figure out what you did.

Are you ready to set up satellite relays and mine asteroids?
I've spent hours and hours on this game and found it to be one of the most rewarding games I own.  When you set yourself a mission which is a complete success and the science motherlode jackpot you're like a kid in a sweet shop.
Essentially, you're the head of a space corporation on a (presumably) fictional planet called Kerbin.  You'll spend your time designing, building and operating rockets, shuttles and spaceplanes.  You can take it from a sandbox mode where you get all the toys with freedom do build and do as you please, to a full career mode where you earn new parts through science and contracts, with no take-backs if you make a mistake if you're a hardcore player.  For me, the career mode is where it's at, but I like the comfort of the take-backs for now.  :)
With every patch Squad put out, there are new features that usually make starting again worth considering.  Recently, the tech tree has seen an overhaul which means there's no wall you hit where the next tech level is nearly prohibited.  You still have to make smart choices.
There is so much to do in this game it's hard to explain where to begin.  The truth is, it's a fabulous game and well with the full price, let alone if you're lucky to get it on sale.

ACT I:
Broken Age is a Double Fine adventure game which promised at conception to be like the Lucasarts adventure games of olde. You might remember its conception. Big ol' deal. Raised multiple millions in dollars because everybody has been harboring a secret erection for Tim Schafer's dazzling beard. Any negative reviews you might read are the result of his removing said beard. What was I talking about.
So I guess the question here is, did it deliver on that promise? The answer is yeah basically.
Broken Age is... a liiiittle more focused on story and world than puzzles than in those adventures of yore. Things are not quite as ridiculously complicated, but there's certainly a respectable amount of puzzle solving to be done, and it is good puzzle solving at that. I've heard the grumbles in the crowd. There is discourse over the difficulty of the puzzles to be solved. In regards to that, I can personally say that, while I never needed to consult any outside help at any time, I feel like the puzzles weren't anywhere in the realm of TOO easy. They felt... well maybe slightly easier than just right, but they're fun enough to let that slide.
In screenshots, the art never took my fancy. But actually watching it in motion, and seeing the subtleties in animation and how the art style comes to life, it looks magical and pleasing to the eye. The soundtrack fits it nicely, and the voice actors display their talent proudly.
Which leaves us the story to worry about. And, you know, obviously THAT'S going to be stellar. Remember that whole thing about the story being more of a focus? I just said it. Right up there. You alternate between playing Shay and Vella, and helping them through their plights. It's been said that you should play Shay's story first, and I agree. It gives things a good flow. Although you can switch back and forth between the characters mid-story (or, at least, I'm assuming you can, judging by the Day of the Tentacle-style portrait in the corner of the characters' inventories), you probably won't. The stories are fairly short - running you somewhere in the vicinity of 1-3 hours each - and are unlikely to drive you from one's arms into the other's before it forces you there.
So far this is quite a nice story, and I'm anxious to see where it goes from here. It's going to be a long year, but I think more quality storytelling like this will be well worth the wait.

The people at Klei have impressed me with their games since I first got my hands on a demo of Eets. Invisible Inc lives up to the already high standards I had for them. Once again they marry gameplay and style into a really fun package.
This is a stealth game at its heart, but throws in elements of hacker technology. While there isn't much story to be found each level is based around reconnaissance, meeting objectives, and then getting out. If you can grab some other resources along the way for future missions, all the better.
The game takes place in both the real world and in cyberspace. Agents can move around the level, trying to avoid being captured by guards, while the security gets tighter the longer they're inside. There are firewalls guarding anything worth accessing, but can be disarmed by programs, which take power to use. There are multiple ways to traverse levels, depending on the agents. You can collect credits to buy programs to infiltrate security, or you can spend credits on tools to do that for you. There's enough variety that you can try a few different play styles.
Replayability is very high. Levels are proceduraly generated, and you learn to apply different tactics through trial and error. Playing more means you unlock more agents and programs, giving you more tools to get past tighter security. If you're a fan of stealth and turn based tactics, this game is a must.

Greetings, comrades! Alan Wake stands out (to me) as one of the "hidden gems" of the horror genre. It really feels as though you're playing a (albeit a little less graphic) Stephen King novel, as the psychological aspect of the story is thrilling and (for lack of a better term) dark, but in a way that hits very close to home (especially for those of us in a rural community). Anyway, here we go!
The Pros:
A great story-line that's told in an exciting yet believable way that makes you feel like you're really there. For such a far-out tale, it's told in a way that blur the lines between what is real and what is not.
A lot of people complain about the combat, but I rather enjoyed it. The controls are fluid and responsive, the enemies are unpredictable and surprising (often materializing right before your eyes), and the weapons do the job, but aren't so OP'd that the game isn't a challenge. BTW, all those things are aimed right at you, Resident Evil 4, may you burn in hell. (PS, It's a joke. Laugh. Please?)
The concept of "fighting with light" is so unique and so well done that I felt it needed its own segment. When an object like a street light or a road flare becomes a better weapon than a Remington 870/Mossberg 500 shotgun, you know you are dealing with a developer with a great imagination. It isn't just run and gun (as that will get you killed), it's about using the environment to your advantage, and the moments when you can't do that are the moments when you die the most.
The environment is very well done, creating a fully realized and spooky environment that is (more often that not) your real enemy. Crisp and clean lines make the slightest detail stand out, everything is very well done. Also, something that is very unique about this game is that it brings the environment to life, creating a living, breathing (literally) atmosphere that really feels, well, ethereal. I really can't describe it and do it justice, try it for yourself
The Cons:
The game lacks replayability, as once the story is completed, there's nothing really drawing you to come back. I found that on my second play through I focused more on getting from point A to point B instead of the journey there.
Some may feel that the world is too linear, and I really can't disagree with them, however I view it as a positive aspect of the game. For the sake of justice though, I'm including it among the Cons, because it is genuinely linear. You have been warned.
Another thing is that the ammo drops are frequent, and supplies are not really lacking unless you miss some caches, which is hard to do. That's why I don't consider the game a "survival-horror" game, and if you are looking for something like that, this isn't the place for you. Go play your laggy RE4. (Sorry, I couldn't resist!)
Anyway, that's that. I really can't recommend this game at full price unless the Pros above really grabbed you, but it goes on sale quite often, and there's no good reason to let this slip by you.
Thanks for reading and have an awesome day!
(Disclaimer: This review is based on personal opinion. If you don't like it, don't hate on me about it. Viewer discression is advised.)

A slightly re-vamped version of the 2006 classic.  Dovetail Games have agreed distribution rights with Microsoft for this flight-sim and released it on Steam late 2014.  Along with the distribution rights they have been permitted sufficient access to the code to allow them to adjust and optimise the sim to better suit todays PC.  That having been said, this is

32-bit application and even the most powerful of todays PC's struggle to attain "high" frame rates, especially when you start to include a few add-ons.
That brings me nicely on to the add-ons.  Due to the program being around since 2006 there is an unbelievable amount of DLC available for this sim, before you reach for your credit card though, make sure that the supplier specifies that it is compatible with FSX Steam Edition or the add-on is listed in the known compatible add-ons on the
There are some very good add-ons that are free, there are some exceptional add-ons that cost quite a bit of money (A2A Simulations, PMDG) and there are add-ons that are free for limited functionality or can cost for full functionality (FSUIPC). The key is research, have a look at
to get an idea of what is possible for nothing more than bandwidth. Alternatively you can very quickly rack up a £100 or more spend and still think there is room for improvement (REX, Orbx).
A final word about add-ons. FSX requires you to generally get your hands dirty when adding features, if you don’t know your “%appdata%” from “My Documents” make sure you have fully researched the product you intend to buy and ensure you are comfortable with the installation procedure before you cough up the dough for it. This isn’t the case for the DLC that can be purchased from Steam, though I have to admit, most of the Steam DLC doesn’t appeal (see edit at the bottom).
Regardless of whether you stay with the stock program or buy enhancements, the core sim can give hours of enjoyment if you have an interest in aviation. Users range from the complete novice that has only sat in row 14F of an A320 (me), to fully licensed pilots (so it must be OK).
Although not a requirement, a joystick is recommended as well as a bit of patience and a lot of reading. You can jump into a Cessna 172 and lark about, or you can plan a flight for the same plane and follow, as close as can be reasonably expected in a 2006 sim, required procedures and protocols.  If, for example, you buy a PMDG add-on you have to calculate the fuel for the plane based on the number of passengers and their luggage, then you have to program the flight management computer and select your route, waypoints, approach etc. It must take 20 minutes or more to get to a point where you can actually start the engines! Alternatively you can just jump into a micro-light and be flying over Friday Harbor in a trice, the choice is yours.
Edit 18/12/15: DTG are introducing a number of add-ons that don't deserve my original comment. Examples are FTX Trees HD, REX Texture Direct 4, RAAS Pro, Accu-Feel and a couple of the aircraft.

If you’re a fan of the H.P.Lovecraft mythos, or just of good dark storytelling, this game could be great for you.
The beautiful graphics and well-crafted narrative draw you into a strange, forbidden world. You’ll experience investigating ancient ruins built by long-forgotten, monstrous beings; mysterious events; and a worsening sense of dread – that you’re in a place no human should ever enter. The game does a fantastic job of world-creating. The alien constructions have a real feeling of tremendous age, size and power.
Don’t buy Conarium looking for jump-scares and action, however. This is a story-driven game: there are lots of documents to read to further the story; trophies to discover as rewards for exploring; and a range of puzzles to solve. It’s not a game your rush through, but one you enjoy at a slow pace. I bought Conarium looking to visit an age-old Lovecraftian city – as in At The Mountains Of Madness, which this game draws story elements from – and I got to thoroughly relish that experience.
On the negative side? Early puzzles are simpler and directly progress the story (such as restoring power to an Antarctic base). Later  puzzles, I thought, felt artificial as opposed to being obstacles I needed to overcome. They drew me away from Conarium being an absorbing experience to feeling like a puzzler game instead. A couple of the puzzles, I googled for answers because I didn’t find it fun and I wanted to get back to exploring. Other people, of course, might prefer the puzzles to the rest of the game!
I completed the game in 5-6 hours. I had no crashes or glitches at all.
Overall, I loved Conarium – the few annoying puzzles didn’t spoil it at all. Gorgeous graphics; a fantastic and authentic Lovecraftian atmosphere; smooth controls; a great soundtrack; and a dark mysterious narrative. If you want to step into a Lovecraft story and “be there”, Conarium is near-perfect.
