Conarium was a bit of a mixed bag for me. I enjoyed playing it, and it is by no means a "bad" game. At the same time though, I often kept thinking "this could have been done a bit better". Then again, when I consider that the entire game was created by three people (plus two voice actors and two text editors), the level of quality that was achieved here can only be described as impressive.
Let's go into the details. Conarium is first and foremost a narrative game, it tells the story of another expedition into the area described by H.P. Lovecraft in his novella "At the Mountains of Madness". This story is mostly told in retrospect, via text documents and "visions" of past events that you witness or play through. The writing and the atmosphere nail the "Lovecraftian Horror" genre like few other games do. The game has no jumpscares and no fights - the horror derives from the realization that you are just a small, fragile, vulnerable human being who is dabbling with things so alien and powerful that we are incapable of understanding them, and even just learning about them may spell our doom. Unfortunately though, while the atmosphere is excellent, all characters remain underdeveloped.
The game's texts, objects, and imagery contain many references to Lovecraft's work. This makes the game especially enjoyable for players with knowledge about these things, but can make the story a bit confusing for players without, since those won't have a bigger picture in their minds to connect the details to. That said, the game's story _can_ stand on its own, and a feeling of confusion is definitely not in contradiction to the type of horror that is being evoked here, so the game does definitely not
prior knowledge of the Cthulhu mythos in order to be enjoyable. I just think players will probably enjoy the game
if they have it.
Gameplay consists mostly of exploring areas to find the aforementioned details, and of solving puzzles. The puzzle design is varied, but sometimes it was not really clear what the game expected me to do. However, many puzzles can be brute-forced fairly easily, without having to understand them. The general difficulty is more on the easy side, I went through the entire game without ever truly getting stuck on a puzzle.
Another gameplay element are action scenes, where you run away from something, or try to navigate a submarine through an obstacle course. Personally I did not feel that they added much to the game, in fact I found them a bit annoying. They feel half-baked since the game barely has the mechanics to make them interesting. But there are only a few of them, so they don't have much impact either way.
The game's graphics are receiving much praise, but I found them rather hit-and-miss. Items that you can inspect are rendered in high detail and usually look very good. Other objects may do so as well, but there are also objects of lower quality (regarding both models and textures), which the developers apparently tried to mask by putting glaring colored light sources next to them. I generally did not like the lighting in this game. Most levels are very dark, and in order to see anything, you have to rely on your flashlight - which is blindingly bright in close-ups. This makes it hard to appreciate the environments, because it's either too dark or too bright to see the colors properly. I also felt that the art direction of the stone ruins and the large glowing plants did not mesh well, it did not look like the organic structure it was described as. That said, given how thrilled many people are about the art, perhaps it's just a matter of taste. What I really liked were the murals, which depicted scenes from the Cthulhu myth. Each mural is unique, and they enhance the atmosphere greatly.
The sound design is adequately creepy, but a bit too attention-grabbing in my opinion. Sounds and background music in an atmospheric, non-jumpscare horror game work best when you don't consciously realize that they are there, and in Conarium they push into the foreground a bit too often. For example, there is a "falling rocks" noise that is probably meant to give you the impression that something else might be skulking around in the caverns. But it's so loud that you always register it consciously, and then - because you put your attention towards it - you realize that there never _is_ something else moving around, so you quickly learn to ignore the noise. I believe sounds like these work better in a subdued way, building a creepy atmosphere on a more subconscious level.
Conarium is not a very long game, but the price reflects that appropriately. My playthrough took 6 hours, and I'm a slow player who likes to investigate every object, read every text, etc. A second playthrough is almost certainly required if you want to see all the secrets and get all achievements, as some are hard to find (partly due to the fact that the game gives no clear indication as to what you can interact with until you're very close and look straight at the object).
Keys are rebindable - the developers implemented this feature 3 days after it was requested, which is impressive, especially compared to the "We'll look into it" (and nothing is happening for months) treatment that I'm sometimes seeing from other teams. An FOV slider unfortunately does not exist and apparently is not planned, but the devs explained a way to change the FOV in the game files.
In short: I found Conarium to be a decent horror adventure with good atmosphere, an interesting story, and a few (mostly engaging) puzzles - recommendable especially for fans of the Lovecraftian brand of horror. Just keep in mind that it is the work of only three people, and don't expect the production values of more expensive games done by much bigger teams.

I replayed Act 1 and went on to beat Act 2. Everything I already said about Act 1 stays true in Act 2. Act 2 is about another 8 hours if you take the time to talk to everyone and try to do every combo of item with person/thing you can. The puzzles are a little more difficult which is good, but at the end of the game figuring out exactly what to do can be a little annoying what with the multiple possibilities of the "wire puzzle".
The answers to what is going on are basically answered, but not to the depth I (and I'm sure many others) would have preferred, especially given the implications of what it meant. If you're worried about a cliffhanger, there isn't one; it just feels like there could (and hopefully will) be more to the story when you beat it. Sequel perhaps? There easily could be one.
Overall I did enjoy this Act 2 and I feel it was very well done. One of the more memorable point n' click adventure games in a long time.
As of this writing only Act 1 is available but boy did I have a good time! Act 1 is only about 4 hours if you take your time, but what is there is so superb you're not likely to mind. The story is so well put together with truly excellent dialog voiced by professionals. If you didn't already know, this is a point and click adventure game with 2 main characters that have their own unique and separate, but ultimately converging, story. One story is of Shay, a lonely boy who is on a spaceship with only his AI "mother" and "father" for company, while all he gets to do is play boring child-like games. The other story is Vella who is in a pre-industrial civilization and must prepare for the Maiden's Feast. I can't say more without spoilers.
You may notice a lot of people complaining about the puzzles. What they are actually saying is that the puzzles in this game are all logical and usually have a clear goal given to you. Because of this the puzzles aren't convoluted and illogical like in so many adventure games prior. My only complaint is that the puzzles here aren't complicated at all, but this is only the first act and I expect they will get more challenging in Act 2.
I can't say much about the characters you will meet or places you will go without spoilers, so I'll just say that the people you meet and interact with are all imaginative and well done, no complaints. Although this game doesn't have an examine feature (or taste, touch, etc.) I do like all the different reactions from people as you use items on them. Some are fairly funny with a few adult-oriented jokes thrown in.
I saved the best for last: the ending. Oh man was this cliffhanger of an ending amazing! I seriously can't say more without possibly ruining it and that would be a travesty. For me at least the ending had me continuing to think about and examine the game hours after I had beaten it and even as I was trying to go to sleep. In the context of the game it is so thought provoking, bringing with it many more questions than it answers. I can say I haven't been looking forward to the conclusion in a game with this much anticipation and desire in a long time.
So is this game worth 25 bucks? Right now it only has Act 1 that is 4 incredible hours, with Act 2 to come in the future for all current and future owners. If you want the most bang for your buck
then you should probably wait for a sale or Act 2 to arrive. If you know you want this game but are thinking you'd rather wait until it's all done, don't! Part of the impact and effectiveness of the Act 1 ending is the fact you can't immediately proceed in the story to see the conclusion. Instead you are forced to think and mull it over, analyzing what it means and could mean. Conclusion: buy this game now or soon if you can and know you want it, otherwise be sure to get it later.

I have never seen a community as split as it is in this game. There are those that absolutely hate the game (blindly) for it putting microtransactions in a singleplayer game already worth 60$ base price, and then there are those, like me, who actually put faith in Monolith as developers and reserved their judgement for the game until they played it. If you're still on the fence and thinking of getting this game, I'll tell you not to worry, and here's why:
Microtransactions: Let's get the elephant out of the room and talk about MT first. As you have probably seen on most posts on reddit/any other forum, MTs don't impact the game at all, if you're looking for a SP experience and have minimal impact on the online aspects of the game. Everything in the game can be acquired with playing or just the ingame currency (which you'll have a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of anyway). The MTs are never shoved in your face or advertised AT ALL in the entire game, not once.
So if that was your only gripe with the game you have nothing to worry about, if you remain unconvinced, here's the rest:
Story (8/10): Although the story is this game's weakest point, I still think it deserves a score as good as 8. It does so many things right: it's easy to get into, but you might want to play Shadow of Mordor first if you haven't already, as the story follows up on that game (like any good sequel should), it's got infinite replayability due to the Nemesis system and it will keep you occupied for 30+ hours on it's own.
Online Modes (7/10): The online sieges are a great addition adding even more content to an already great experience. The vendetta missions are alright, they've stayed in the same shape they were in SoM. They could be better but it's nice that they're there at all. The addition of Online arena would be greatly appreciated once the AI gets fleshed out.
Graphics (9.5/10): The game looks pretty and runs great on my average-high performance PC. You easily get 60 fps and the load times are short. You really couldn't ask for more.
Sound (10/10): All the voice acting and sounds are top of the line, music is fitting and nice to listen to. There are a lot of different voice types for all the different orcs so the game stays fresh for a very long time.
Gameplay (9.5/10): The action and movement are great aside from minor hiccups here and there. Every movement feels fluid and nothing feels out of place. There are a lot of abilities and playstyles you can go for. You want to be a god in melee combat, you can do that, maybe want to snipe the enemies from afar while your followers hold them in place, go for it, have an army of beasts rip your enemies in pieces, here you go (but it's not the best).
Overall (9.5/10): Overall a great game and really close to a masterpiece, do not let your hate from MTs keep you from playing this treasure. It's clear that Monolith poured their heart and soul into the game and made it fantastic despite the greedy publisher's attempt at sabotage. Go play it.

It's an Obsidian developed Espionage RPG. It's a real "diamond in the rough" situation. It plays like a third person shooter, but doesn't handle like one. This turned off a lot of people who tried to play it like Splinter Cell and realized just aiming a headshot wasn't enough to actually hit if your skills weren't actually high enough.
The real star is the story and conversation system. You have a set timer on how to respond to conversations, keeping the flow natural and pushing you to role play on the fly, without a lot of time to judge your response.
It's also, like many Obsidian games, *very* buggy. Expect to reload saves from falling through the floor more than once. When I originally played this on Xbox 360, I only had a couple of crashes through my entire playthrough.
I really recommend the game if you're wanting something different from an RPG.

Ok, where to start?
Story: The game forgets your decisions, regularly, and ♥♥♥♥s you up during the final mission for it. If you want to do a through and through American agent playthrough and perform non-lethal attacks on every enemy through the whole game, at the very end you will be randomly accused of killing American agents and have the "'merica" ending locked out.
Also in the final mission, despite never interacting with a certain character who I had no intentions of harming through the entire game, I'm looking for the room where I can rescue them, then, bam! Checkpoint pops up, overrides my save, and informs me that I shot them. Not that someone else did, I am told by another character, that I was in a conversation with this person, and shot them. Locking me out of another ending...
Mechanics:
The ability UI is super clunky, pressing Z, X and C to bring up three different menu's for ammo types, abilities and equipment (Grenades, Sound generators etc.) However, when you bring up one of these menu's there's like a 2 second pause where you can't do anything (Dispite my high end computer), and once that's over you have to click the thing 7-8 times before you actually select it. Even worse, if you bring up the wrong menu, you can't just press the correct key and open the other menu, you either have to close the current menu and open a new one, or press these *TINY* little arrows that scroll though the menu's.
As for the weapons. Use the pistol. It has an ability that let's you instantly line up 6 headshots that automatically crit and usually kill any soldier you have LoS too. The assault rifle is the most innaccurate thing in the world unless you point it at the same spot for 4 seconds (1.5 seconds if you pump ALL your level-up points into it). The SMG's will never hit anything and the shotgun causes too much collateral and just doesn't seem to do much in the way of damage.
Saving. You literally can't. There's a checkpoint system, you can make it remember your checkpoints, but they're usually far-ish apart, and god forbid you make a bad decision in an important conversation, (Or a flatout the wrong one, sometimes you're given less then a second to make a choice) as after almost every single one is a checkpoint, and the game has an awful habit of putting important conversations up to half an hours of gameplay away from the last safehouse, or fifteen minutes if you force the game to remember EVERY checkpoint. (Perhaps intentionally, make you live with your decision? Sucks for player choise I guess...) I guess the game is simply trying to encourage replayability so you can play through to make the disicions you wish you made last time? But I dunno about everyone else, but I sat through a second 60 hours of Mass Effect so I could play a different character, not the same one with a little less schitzophrenia...

I think it's a mistake to talk about The Walking Dead Season 2 and say "well, compared to Season 1, it's...." because you really shouldn't be playing this game if you haven't played Season 1.  There are many decisions made in Season 1 that affect the plot of Season 2, and there are several returning characters in Season 2 whose characterization only works if you know of their involvement in Season 1 - so to talk about Season 2 in comparisson to Season 1 is, to me, a mistake because it suggests that you can also talk about it as a standalone game.  You really can't.  This game can only exist in comparrison to Season 1, it does not function otherwise.  Having said that,
I was very disappointed with Season 2.
I can count on one hand how many games I have CONSIDERED playing through twice - at the time of writing, I have played through The Walking Dead Season 1 four times.  I was absolutely biased in favor of Season 2 when I started, but I had a bad taste in my mouth before Episode 1 was finished.  It seems like the team that created Season 2 had no idea what made Season 1 so great, so they tried to cheat by copying some plot events without putting in the work to make those events impactful.  The end result is a game that has worse plot, characters, and even gameplay, than Season 1:
- Season 1 did a good job of making the post-apocalyptic world the antagonist to it's characters.  Lee and the group fight against hunger, they argue over what to do next, they struggle through disasterous days.  Season 2 doesn't know how to make the world the antagonist, so it creates a bad guy, and it does so in the laziest way.  Carver has no redeeming qualities, no tragic flaws, no aspect of his character the viewer to sympathize with.  He is just a BAD GUY.
How bad is he?
Look, he just killed like 3 of your friends!  What a bad guy!
Look, he hit a little girl!  Are you convinced yet?
He may have sexually assaulted someone.  Now that's really bad!
Look, now he's beating up a crippled person!  Wow so bad!
A villain that is 100% evil is not interesting or captivating, and no matter how many times Bonnie insists "he just cares about his people" it doesn't change the fact that he has 0 depth.  Worse still, the game has no idea what to do once Carver is removed from the plot, so again it takes the laziest approach and manufactures disagreements between characters that have no reason to oppose each other - often contradicting their established personalities.  Which brings us to:
- Season 2 begins with a character death in the first 10 minutes, followed by a "16 months later" screen, and then another character dies immediately after.  The rest of the game follows this pattern, and throws an absurd number of character deaths at you that end up having no impact or meaning.  In my review of Season 1, I talk about how I tried an "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" playthrough but the characters were so well-rounded and endearing that I couldn't bring myself to needlessly antagonize them.
5 minutes after meeting Clementine's new group, I had resolved to murder everybody.  Season 2's characters go out of their way to manufacture drama and conflict for the sake of drama and conflict.  They are irrational, and often blow things way out of proportions to make false equivalencies:
"Wait did you push a kid?  You're just as bad as the guy who tied up 3 people and shot them!"
"I'm sneaking out at night with all the ammo and medicine because
guy is going to tear the group apart"
What's worse is how horribly inconsistent they are.  Season 2's characters are so inconsistent,
about how inconsistent they are.
The end result is characters that did not inspire me to look out for them, that I could not relate to, that did not drive me to seek attachment to them.  My favorite part is when two characters fall through a frozen lake, and you are given the option of trying to save one.  The other dies and is literally never mentioned again for the rest of the game.
- even for this style of game, gameplay was very tedious.  While in Season 1, every input by the player feels important and impactful, Season 2 is full of decisions that have the same outcome regardless of what you pick, decisions where one outcome is objectively better than the other, and several instances of "Press a button to continue the story"...
By that I mean, parts where the game prompts you to press a button, you have no other possible action to take, there is no time limit - the game literally pauses and asks you to press a button to continue the story.  There were no instances of this in Season 1.  This is tedious.
- As I mentioned above, I do think the last 10 minutes are absolutely incredible - but I made choices that left me with a particular character when the game ended.  I don't know what the ending will be like if you make different choices, but despite having played through Season 1 four times, I have no desire to play through Season 2 a second time.

Nuclear Throne. Where to even start. It's simple in design, easy to learn, but impossible to master. I've got a few dozen hours of gameplay as of now, and I've still only managed to beat it once, and not even looping it because I didn't know how when I first got there. It's designed for you to reach the end within about 20 minutes if you play it right, yet after 40+ hours I've only done so once, which goes to show how hard it really is. It's addicting; I can't stop playing even though I must have rage-quit about 150 times already, only to pick it back up after about 20 minutes. There are definitely some flaws in the way the levels and enemies are arranged, allowing for situations where you are just ****ed, but plenty more are the mistakes you make yourself and scream ************!! You might string together profanities that you've never conceived of while playing this game and dying. Yet it keeps calling you back. For that, I'd tell my friends to try it out, but I would not recommend them to buy it if they like winning or have rage problems. It feels like there is something that could be added/fixed to make it more enjoyable than being slaughtered repeatedly. I wish I could make it to looping so I can actually try out the end game, but I've never gotten there and can only imagine there is no magic pixie that will suddenly allow me to reach it more than 2-3 times before I put the game down for good. On a 1-10 scale, I'd rate it a 6.5, simply because it is really fun, but you get so worn down by it's repetitive nature and constant failing (I'm so over the desert starting area). Sure, I get that it is designed to be that way, but it's more rewarding when the difficulty is something you can overcome, rather than being luck-based. Will I keep playing it? Surely, at least until I finally see a loop, but something tells me by the time that happens I'll be done with it for good.

OK...now this is the game. This is the successor to the grand father of cRPGs, the spiritual father of FALLOUT...This is Wasteland 2!
The game is still in beta (or early access, what ever you want to call it). It is also still suffering from optimization issues, bugs, and clunky game design.
HOWEVER, these things do not hinder the game. In its state, is is solid, and plays very well. It feels like a true port-apocalyptic game, and it can definitely stand up to FALLOUT of STALKER. The story telling is wonderful, combat works and feels great, the atmosphere is just perfect, there is a bit of humor and secrets, many new and unfamiliar enemies, andTONS of customization. You can tactically set up your team and develop them as they level up, or you can build your own character from the ground up. It is just overall a well done project.
It is still being developed, and new updates will be coming out for it. The UI will be fixed, it will be optimized, much more will be added...and in the end, this wonderful, promising stone will be polished to be one of the greatest cRPGs done.
I know, the price tag is a little steep. But, if you are willing to buy it, and if you are willing to put up with a (currently) incomplete game, and if you are going to commit yourself to giving back to the devs, then it will be a worthwhile purchase. Additionally, this is a great game if you loved FALLOUT (esp. the first 2 and tactics) and Wasteland.
Should you buy it? It depends, you might not want to, and you are certainly not being forced to. But if you do, know you are contributing to a constantly developing and promising sequel to a beloved game.

This game has great potential; I've never though of a dinosaur based survival game. On the other hand, there are some things that need tiny tweaks and major improvements. First of all, I'll be talking about things that need to drastically be changed.
1. The AI for the dinosaurs need some changes. All that the ground dinosaurs do is, if you're on the ground, bolt after you with no strategy and try to eat you. If you're somewhere they can't reach you, they'll either start randomly running around not knowing which path to take to get to you, or they'll go and destroy the generator. Also, if you shoot a dinosaur it does not affect its movement; it will keep in charging at you until you finally kill it.
2. Very frequently I've been kicked out of a match for no reason. The game doesn't tell me why I've been kicked which is a major drawback.
Those are two things that need major improvements on. Now I will list things that could slightly be improved on.
1. Animations for dinosaurs could be made more natural. Going along with the first thing I listed, If you shoot a dinosaur, they could flinch and/or stagger a little before continuing on with what they were doing.
2. Animations for the player have been a little buggy for me. If I reload my weapon, sometimes the magazine will fly into its place before the hand can move the mag into its place. If I equip a pistol, the pistol will be in its ready position without my hands and then my hands will come to hold the pistol.
I think all of these things should be changed, and I hope the developer of this game sees this and takes action. I've heard this game has made improvements, but once these are changed, I will be able to recommend this game.

Edit:
After few months I gave it another chance and fired it up.
Now the game itself is alright, more or the less. Depends if you like unlocking story scenes by an almost everlasting loop of -> Go talk with this person -> Go interrogate this guy -> Go break material value and kill lots of cloned plain stupid AIs -> Go to the same place again and do the same thing again just kill one more additional dude -> loop again.
Graphics:
>> Overall pretty nice. Perhaps the textures are reduced here and there, but considering the love for the detail of the entire city this can be understood.
>> Rainy days look very very good with all the reflections and so on
Sound:
>> Not that cool.
>> Really hard to tell where a character might be, since the AI usually talks all kinds of repetative stuff instead of sneaking around making it harder for you. (I am using SBX 5.1 with the headphones. The directional stuff works exceptionally well with other games, not with this one though)
>> Overall mixing is poor. Gunshots are far too quiet compared to everything else. They also sound pretty mashed potato
>> Environment is alright I guess, you can usually tell in which kind of district you are by the background noise.
Gameplay:
>> As said, very repetative.
>> Very easy (even on hard), since you get all sorts of indicators where enemies are and usually they are quite dull.
>> Weapons are not very different from eachother. Of course a sniper rifle has its advantage on the distance compared to a shotgun, but the rest inbetween is just boring after a while. You can basically do everything quite easy with the pistol, since its pretty accurate and HS will do the job with any firearm. Whilst it even takes 5-6 body hits with the "AK".
>> One usually fights the 5 same NPCs models over and over again, which combined with the very repetative tasks makes the game pretty darn boring on a medium run.
>> Driving the cars is somewhat alright. Though I believe there is no way to manual shift gears, which is a real bummer.
Story:
>> If you are up for some brainless driving around, doing the same task again and again, you can enjoy the cut scenes as a good movie.
All in all it feels to me that this trend it going through the industry, where games are forged for people with presumably having down syndrom (which of course is a nice thought by the vendor) or people just not capable of otherwise doing simple tasks. But if you are a friend of games that make your life not very easy and actually require the player to get better with the game by playing it, this game is not for you. It's just a simple (very simple) concept of run here, click that and do it again. No skill required at all.
I personally hope that this trend will shift again, back to demanding the players more, not just by making the player's damage less and the NPCs higher, but by game mechanics and default settings.
TL;DR:
>> Developers got lost in making a beautiful nice scenic city with love for detail, then quickly made a mission concept that lasts 10 minutes, copy-pasted the scheme between the cut-scenes and offered it as a game. Graphic ok, Sound not so, Story typical but good.

Conarium was inspired by "In the Mountains of Madness" by H.P. Lovecraft (the guy who wrote the Call of Cthulhu).
This simple line should tell you that the game features some tentacles...But not that much actually !
You play as Frank Gilman, a scientist studying the remnants of an ancient civilisation in Antartica. The game starts with this simple plot, and thickens as you progress into the game, by reading notes and journals.
And yes, you do have to read a lot if you want to fully experience this game, as it is all about the atmosphere and anticipation. There are very few enemies, and absolutely no fighting but there are some enigmas that aren't extremely challenging, unless you are like me ;)
If I had to compare the gameplay of this game to another, I'd say Amnesia or Penumbra (interaction with the environment, although not as much as in the latter ; Hiding when stalked ; resolving enigmas ; etc)
Overall I really loved this game, but it's way too short (I finished it 3 hours) but there are more than one ending, depending on your completion rate (I had 57%), so there is a form of replay value to it.
I think it's one of the best Lovecraft-inspired games ever made, and it looks great too (Unreal Engine 4 rules !).
Pros:
- Mesmerizing Lovecraftian atmosphere
- Beautiful Art Direction
- Excellent voice acting
Cons :
- Way too short
- Too damn short
- Gosh, I wish it was longer...
To anyone who is a Lovecraft reader, buy and play this game as you won't be disappointed !

I want to start this off with this comment; the game is currently in beta.  That said, I am sure you have read that multiple times now through the various posts.  So, where to start?
Straight up, this game will not be for everyone.  No, that does not mean it is a bad game.  Far from it, honestly.   I bought the deluxe edition on a whim.  Wanted to try something new.  I saw it was beta, so I started playing with that mindset.  That, so far, is the biggest thing.  It is not a complete game, so some things do not work, or work as expected.  Now, keeping that in mind, if you get this game, the end product in my opinion, will be phenomenal!
I am playing on max settings, looks and runs smooth, no issues.  I DO NOT have a top of the line machine.  Voices thus far are good, dialogue is great.  Combat mechanics are good.  Story so far seems great as well.
To make this easier, if you take the time to read this, I will break it down.  Again, keep in mind this is a BETA.  Not a beta you may be used to, more like end of the line alpha.  Point being, a WORK IN PROGRESS.
PROS:
--Character customization and looks in game.
--Story is great thus far.
--Combat will be great once game is complete.
--Graphics / audio / and interface thus far are all great.
--Gameplay is sweet.  I said it may not be for everyone because combat is tactical / turn.  So, think back old school with X-Com.  I love that part of it, personal opinion.
--Combat animations / effects are sweet.
--Choice and consequence are a part of this game.  You save someone from drowning, his parents offer him to you as an added party member if you want.  Plenty of characters to change up the party.
--Different skills are used for different things.  Obviously, ha ha.  Those chances to use the skills on a frequent basis are not persistent in other games.  There are a lot of opportunity to use each skill you have in your party.  I like that.
--A TON of interactions within the world.  Be it digging stuff up, repairing gadgets, even down to repairing toasters, ha ha!  (definitely have someone in your party that can repair them, because you never know what's stored in one!)
--Completed game will hands down be great.
CONS:
--Loading a save will often change the portrait of your character(s) if they are created from scratch.  A minor annoyance, unless you get into combat, then you have to go by name.  Or, if you made a guy and your portrait is now a gal.
--Combat, sometimes, can be a bit.. Interesting.  You have a sniper, that has 0.0% chance of hitting a target.  That same target now moves behind cover, and you now have an 80.00% chance to hit.
--Combat again, some enemies have ridiculous move / attacks.  They will move across the screen, attack you twice, then move again... BETA, remember.  It will frustrate / annoy you though, ha ha.
--Make sure you get a dedicated surgeon / healer.  I roamed around for a bit trying to find someone that could heal my wounds, to no avail.
--There are times when walking around on the world map you are accosted by bandits, raiders, whatever, only to enter combat (if you choose) and find everything dead.  Good for the free loot, bad because you never know what will really happen!
--The game crashes from time to time AFTER combat is completed.
--Some game choices have to be made on the spot, you do not have a lot of time to fart around and trying to figure the puzzle out.  You take your time, (drowning boy for example,) he will die.  Some people may not like that part.
--With no tutorial yet, character creation can be.. difficult.
--Finally;  some characters you may spec for conversation bonus dialogues, sale prices, et-cetera.  Once you enter dialogue, there is no way to change who is talking, so in cities, towns, you want to lead the party with the talker if that is your thing.
Again, it is a beta.  So far, overall, great.  Most of the cons I have listed will be fixed (I assume / hope) with end product.  If you can look over those things for now, you will not be disappointed.  ESPECIALLY if you like RPG, tactical combat, decision making, and crafting.

A hidden jewel for a game, even in beta.  I give my nod of approval.

Now that the situation concerning the game to only be playable at 30fps has finished, I can properly review the game.
Before the "problem" with not being able to play in over 30fps, I was enjoying this game. I agree that the graphics look slightly washed out, however this doesn't at all put me off the game. I occasionally crash while playing, however due to the auto save after every mission, I can reboot the game and carry on where I crashed.
MY PERFORMANCE PLAYING MAFIA III:
I see a lot of reviews slating the game as they don't get good performance in game... I have a R9 290 (4GB) and a AMD FX 8350 and I am currently having no problem playing this game at high settings 60 fps. Don't get put off this game by people complaining about their hardware related problems, if there is a problem with the game that is causing some people to not be able to play, then 2K will fix it, like they did within a couple of days of announcing that the game will only be playable in 30 fps.
Things I Like about the game:
- The stealth in this game is very good imo, the mechanics of sneaking around make it fun to complete a mission by not alerting everyone, and slowly picking everyone off.
- The driving mechanics I personally think fit the game perfectly, I can see a game like this being criticised heavily for its driving mechanics as it feels a bit like you are permanently attached to the ground, but a game like this with driving mechanics like GTA V would not work at all (imo) and would ruin driving for me.
- Calling in a car, weapon salesman and money handler (whatever she is called) is something that I really like in this game. The weapon salesman rolling up in his red van saves having to find a gun store, and likewise having to find a bank to store your money with the money handler.
- I don't personally know much about this time in history, however it feels like it would be realistic with the way the buildings look and the different cars and weaponry in the game.
Things I don't like about the game:
- Not being able to change your clothes is a little annoying, however I can kind of see why they left this feature out as it can take away from the realism of the game.
Conclusion:
I have personally not found much wrong with this game at all, I have been looking forward to this game for a while, and in my eyes it doesn't disappoint

Conarium is undoubtedly one of the most successful adaptations of Lovecraft's writing to a game. The game is crafted as something of a sequel to "At the Mountains of Madness", and Lovecraft fans will find a lot of familiar territory here. While the story itself is a bit confusing, the game succedes in building a sense of mystery and cosmic dread from the start. The visuals and sound design are beautiful and the environments succede in creating a sense of horrifying scale. The game is well optimized such that it ran at a decent frame rate and without glitches on my relatively outdated PC. The atmosphere is far and away the strongest aspect of Conarium. Even after finishing the game, I found myself replaying it almost immediately just to experience its haunting vistas again.
The gameplay relies mainly on exploration and puzzles. However, if you are primarily looking for a challenging puzzle game, look elsewhere. Fans of Zoetrope's earlier Darkness Within series might find the puzzles unsatisfying in comparison. I thought many of the puzzles were exceedingly easy, while others were unnecessarily obtruse, finicky, or required excessive backtracking. At times, the puzzles felt like unnecessary impediments to exploration of the environments.
While Conarium is on the shorter side, coming in at just 3-4 hours, the game is still a huge achievement for such a tiny studio. It is well-worth the price for the incredible visual and atmospheric experience it offers. This is a must play for fans of Lovecraft or cosmic horror in general.

Invisible, Inc. raises the bar for stealth games in a massive way. It is by far one of the best games I have played.
Without going into excessive detail, the biggest features that make it what it is:
- Depth: Many characters, game modes, user friendly settings for gameplay that  let you play what you want, how you want without punishing the player for doing so. You are free to approach the game with whatever strategy or "play style" you feel, and at no point does any tactic feel "not as intended" nor does the game too heavily favor or punish any of them. Any playstyle comes with stronger and weaker points for diffferent mission types or with different characters.
Unlike many titles with a variety of different characters to pick from, none of them are too similar, and none of them are too good, too bad, or not an asset to your team. One of the most fun things about the game, is figuring out how to use different characters together, to best make use of what they bring, and play to their individual strengths. The same (mostly) goes for the gear, upgrades, and other things you have in your arsenal as you play.
- Replayablity: So many "randomly generated procedural" games recently seem to be anything but. In efforts to make a game random, many end up being repetitive, bland, or (in the other direction) randomly punishing. Invisible, Inc. hits a very happy middle ground. Levels offer variety that is interesting without being unfairly random.
Different game modes give you more to do once you've learned (or mastered) the game's mechanics. Especially endless, time attack, and harder modes. As you increase difficulty or add more challenge, the difficulty is not artificial - simply adding more hazards, or reducing resources. New, dangerous mechanics are actually introduced; guards will start patrolling through multiple rooms instead of remaining inside of one, sight lines can be hidden until you actually see an observer, for example.
There are so many possibly combinations both in what you start a campaign with, and what you can find (or the strategy you use to win) that there is always more to do.
- Respect for players' time: With the number of games being created these days, more and more players seem to be buying games based largely on the question of "will I get my money's worth?" or "will my time spent playing this be wasted?" Invisible, Inc. is neither a grind, nor boring. It has a bit of a steep learning curve, which can make it difficult to start with, but it never wastes the player's time. In this sense, it is somewhat like a rogue-like game, in that trial and failure are part of the game, and failing is practically always a product of the player's choices, not unfair, punishing, or random elements. It always gives you the opportunity to make the most informed choices (or not to) and the consequences of them are what make each turn exciting.
-Style: The setting, story, visuals, and music all come together to make a fantastic and unified game. Surprisingly immersive for an isometric turn-based strategy game, great realisation of the cyberpunk setting.
My only regret is that I've finished it and moved on to new(er) things!

I want to start off saying that i typically hate stealth games. I have the patience and love the strategy that usually comes with titles that carry this genre but i tend to get bored with the concept quite quickly and it becomes a very unsatisfying style of repetiveness with constant waiting and alot of boring valuables for you to steal. Invisible Inc removes this problem while adding a slew of additional mechanics that keep it feeling fresh. It is fantastic at creating and keeping tension and forcing you to move at a good pace to ensure a better result. You have to move fast as the danger increases over a steady amount of time more and more. This creates the feel of actual risk with staying in a location too long and the fears of getting caught instead of finding a hidden location and being like "well no one patrols here, guess il setup a basecamp and come back if i ever get too scared, i might even make pancakes". Its also fantastic to see a lot more choice into what you decide to go after that really lets you make your team your own and control what type of thief you want to be.

Overall a fantastic stealth game that takes an interesting look at the genre and keeps you invested for hours.

I'm surprised I haven't written a review for this before.
If you've heard bad things about Alpha Protocol... let's be fair, there were MAJOR issues when the game originally launched.  The game was unstable as heck on PC, the framerates were terrible on ATI cards, and the load times were unbearable.  It was really terrible technical experience.
But even back when the game launch, I endured those technical problems and found quite possibly my favorite FPS/RPG hybrid.  This one ranks up there with the original Deus Ex, folks.  It's *really* good.
These days, it's much better.  Alpha Protocol has been patched up, any modern hardware is way more than powerful enough to run it smoothly.  So now you can pick it up and enjoy a fantastic FPS/RPG experience without the terrible technical issues.
Cutting straight to the heart of the matter, Alpha Protocol offers you absolutely
amounts of choice, and every single decision awards you with a different perk that provides buffs to certain playstyles.  And I do mean every single decision.
Did you complete the mission without doing side objectives?  Did you complete the mission doing only a specific one?  Did you complete the mission without: knocking anyone out, killing anyone, or even being seen?  There's different perks for each.
The most refreshing part of the dialogue system for AP is that it's both "in-depth" (classic ME-style drill downs) without the silly "top choice is good person, bottom choice is bad person, middle choice is neutral person" crap.  Intead, Good/Neutral/Bad are broken into Suave/Professional/Aggressive.  Effectively, choose your own spy action hero stereotype.  Are you the suave James Bond?  The professional Jason Borne?  Or the brutally effective anti-hero John Wick?
And based on that stereotype you get - you guessed it - different perks that provide different playstyle bonuses.  Even the personality type isn't purely for decoration.  Different characters like different personalities.  But what if you don't commit to a style?  Well, the game is paying attention to THAT, too.
And if you're picking responses to get people to like or hate you specifically, you must be bluffing to manipulate these folks - gasp, your character is a charismatic mastermind!  And there's a perk for that too!
Really, this is a legendary title that was very poorly received due to massive technical issues.  If you've overlooked it before, I can't recommend enough giving it a spin if you're a fan of "0451" games.

Well, this one is still good, but it's definitelly not better than the Season 1. There are many reasons to this:
- Child main protagonist. - As much as I liked Clementine in Season 1, as a main protagonist it's lacking in actions, emotions, possibilities. In this game you're facing a lot of hard choices, but as a child, why should your choices even matter? You're a child, you're hiding in a treehouse not so long ago and now you're making choices for whole group?
- Much less "puzzle" playstyle. Not that Waking Dead would be an advanture, but still in the first Season you had to solve some situations just by "unscrew this screw, move this box, dig a grave" sort of things. Here not, it's just a straight action with choices. Some people may like this more, but I don't.
- People dying even faster than in the first Season. Come on, I know the story is about surviving, but if you introduce new characters into the story just to let them die in less than 1 hour, you're not helping to build up the story at all (or the emotions). In both Season 1 and Season 2 you're going through 5? 6? groups? After some time I just stopped caring. "New people? Shoot them", "I can't shoot them? Ok, lets invite them, they will die anyway".
Well, I should point out some good things, becase this game *is* good. It just isn't that good as the Season 1.
- Playing an evil characters is easier. I like to play evil characters and do evil things (in games ;)), so playing a mean Clementine is much better and feel much more in-character than playing a mean convicted murderer (strange, isn't it?).
- I can drink alcohol and smoke. - Well, not freely, I just had few opportunities, but I really like I had the opportunity.
- Better Quick time event.
If you are into story telling games or just want a relaxing game, pick this one, it's really good. But don't expect much more than 8 hours or playtime.

Nuclear Throne is an extremely fast paced, randomly generated, top down shooter that is in the end, marketed to people that may enjoy a challenge. If you're looking for a fun experience under a pretty cheap price, I think that you will get that from this game, but be warned, Nuclear Throne is one of the hardest video games to master and conquer fully. If you're looking to play it casually, you probably won’t get too far without putting it down forever, as it does take a while to get the handle of if you're not an avid gamer and is extremely unforgiving to mistakes. To reiterate, it's not like the game can't be played casually, it's just that it probably won’t serve as a source of enjoyment for people that only want fun from a video game, as it is very centered around the challenges to overcome. Now that I've covered that, let's start with what I actually think of the game.
Nuclear Throne is essentially what could be described as a roguelike, similar to such experiences as Spelunky or The Binding of Isaac, but with an enhanced focus on the gameplay and less focus on the more methodical feel that the aforementioned games operate on. Nuclear Throne doesn’t have any items like you would find in either Spelunky or Isaac, but purely functions on a leveling system and random gun drops, all of which feature different abilities, and all of which are very fun to use and experiment with. The game is also very well known for its difficulty, and is in combination with its music and art style what make Nuclear Throne a unique experience from any other game. The amount of polish to make this game feel unique is very present, and the final product absolutely shows the amount of care that the developers put into making it.
I would not say that this game is not without its flaws, such as the late game still needing some huge overhauls and some final aspects being added to make for a smoother experience, but I think that it still serves as a good challenge and enjoyable experience in the long run. Considering it's as cheap as it is, I would consider picking it up if you like the type of genre that the game belongs to.

What the hell was that sound? Oh man I’m freaking out right now. These damn shadows seem to move and all I have is this small flashlight. To make things even worse I have some guy screaming "You take two pills in the morning.... and then you'll be nice and calm all day" in some demonic voice. Ya my nerves aren’t racked.
Alan Wake is a psychological survival horror that will scare you and amaze you at the same time. You play as Alan Wake an author who is on vacation with his wife to get some relaxation in or so he thinks. Once you arrive in the nice little town of Bright Falls things start getting a little weird when some old lady in black gives you keys to a cabin on Cauldron Lake. You arrive at the cabin and are trying to get settled in when your wife screams. You find the porch railing broken and an image of her drowning in the water, so you dive in after her only to wake up in your wrecked car with no clue how you got there. This is the beginning of your insanely scary story to find your wife Alice and the secrets behind Cauldron Lake.
The story through the game is fantastically written and is actually your book come to life. Voice acting is superb and fits each character well. The support characters are likable and funny and help bring more depth to the story. Barry, your manager, is probably one of the best sidekicks I’ve seen in a game with his humorous, pushy personality. Your fight is against the darkness which takes over people in town and makes them way scarier. The best though is the lines they spew at you when running around in the dark. Things like "Omega 3 fatty acids are good for your heart" and "There are 65 billion cows and pigs in the world!" will have you laughing and also wondering what the hell are they talking about.
There’s a total of 6 chapters that the game is broken up into and in-between each one is some great music to listen to. It may help you relax a bit before beginning another chapter of horror. In the beginning of each chapter they also give you a recap of the previous one in case you took a break and forgot some things. I found this really cool and thought it should be an option in many games. How many times have you not been able to get back to a game and then forgot what, when, and where.
Wake’s gameplay is some of the best mechanics of light and dark. You use a flashlight to find your way around in the dark and is also used to help fight the Taken. The Taken cannot be killed until blasted with light for a little bit, then you can shoot them with your gun to take them out. Inanimate objects can also be taken over but those only need to be blasted by light for some time. When shining your light on your enemies you will see a small halo that will shrink and then disappear when they are vulnerable to regular weapons. Other items to help you fight the darkness are your typical guns like a handgun, shotgun, or rifle. Then there are the light items like flares, flash grenades and a flare gun. The flash grenades and flare gun will actually destroy the Taken most of the time without need of your guns.
Many collectibles are scattered around the chapters for you to find. TV’s you switch on to watch a small episode of Night Springs similar to the great classic Twilight Zone and radios you can listen to and hear what may be going on in town. 100 coffee thermoses scattered all over the place to find and even manuscripts which are the actual story of the game. Some of the manuscripts can also only be found on the hardest difficulty nightmare which adds more replay value to the game. Then there are the secret stashes you can discover by finding glowing marks with the flashlight.
Alan Wake is a well put together game and feel it’s overlooked by many. It’s well written story, great voice acting, and challenging gameplay make this a must play game. I’d really love to see an actual sequel come out for this but those may be some high hopes. If are looking for something to pull you in then don’t hesitate to play Alan Wake.

Edit:
After few months I gave it another chance and fired it up.
Now the game itself is alright, more or the less. Depends if you like unlocking story scenes by an almost everlasting loop of -> Go talk with this person -> Go interrogate this guy -> Go break material value and kill lots of cloned plain stupid AIs -> Go to the same place again and do the same thing again just kill one more additional dude -> loop again.
Graphics:
>> Overall pretty nice. Perhaps the textures are reduced here and there, but considering the love for the detail of the entire city this can be understood.
>> Rainy days look very very good with all the reflections and so on
Sound:
>> Not that cool.
>> Really hard to tell where a character might be, since the AI usually talks all kinds of repetative stuff instead of sneaking around making it harder for you. (I am using SBX 5.1 with the headphones. The directional stuff works exceptionally well with other games, not with this one though)
>> Overall mixing is poor. Gunshots are far too quiet compared to everything else. They also sound pretty mashed potato
>> Environment is alright I guess, you can usually tell in which kind of district you are by the background noise.
Gameplay:
>> As said, very repetative.
>> Very easy (even on hard), since you get all sorts of indicators where enemies are and usually they are quite dull.
>> Weapons are not very different from eachother. Of course a sniper rifle has its advantage on the distance compared to a shotgun, but the rest inbetween is just boring after a while. You can basically do everything quite easy with the pistol, since its pretty accurate and HS will do the job with any firearm. Whilst it even takes 5-6 body hits with the "AK".
>> One usually fights the 5 same NPCs models over and over again, which combined with the very repetative tasks makes the game pretty darn boring on a medium run.
>> Driving the cars is somewhat alright. Though I believe there is no way to manual shift gears, which is a real bummer.
Story:
>> If you are up for some brainless driving around, doing the same task again and again, you can enjoy the cut scenes as a good movie.
All in all it feels to me that this trend it going through the industry, where games are forged for people with presumably having down syndrom (which of course is a nice thought by the vendor) or people just not capable of otherwise doing simple tasks. But if you are a friend of games that make your life not very easy and actually require the player to get better with the game by playing it, this game is not for you. It's just a simple (very simple) concept of run here, click that and do it again. No skill required at all.
I personally hope that this trend will shift again, back to demanding the players more, not just by making the player's damage less and the NPCs higher, but by game mechanics and default settings.
TL;DR:
>> Developers got lost in making a beautiful nice scenic city with love for detail, then quickly made a mission concept that lasts 10 minutes, copy-pasted the scheme between the cut-scenes and offered it as a game. Graphic ok, Sound not so, Story typical but good.

RNG is not a proper replacement for actual design.
Nuclear Throne has some good parts. It has good art design. It has good sound design. The weapons are decently varied. The RNG behind the drops doesn't seem actively malicious. The enemies are pretty varied.
But it's pretty much all sunk by the parts that have no actual design, or poor design, behind them.
For instance, mutations. You're given a choice of four at every level-up, but I think only ONCE so far I've actually felt like there was any choice. There's pretty much always one useful one, and three that are pointless or mediocre. With better design, I'd have been torn between the options every single time.
Secondly, the lack of invincibility frames. Which means that when a boss teleports or other enemy on top of you without warning, you'll take three or four hits in rapid succession, and die as close to instantly as it gets.
Thirdly, the various character "abilities." I occasionally completely forget what the button for using them is, because they're of such limited utility.
Lastly, the utter lack of any level design. Levels are 100% down to the RNG which means that some levels spawn you in a wide-open field full of enemies that instantly zero in on you, including the ones outside of sight range which will start opening fire on you(and no, enemies do not suffer from friendly fire, so you can't even harness that to get out of the situation. PS: If you want enemies to have a longer firing distance, give me a view range equal to it! It's not fun being gibbed by things I haven't even had a chance to spot yet.). In other cases, you get nothing but narrow corridors which pretty much trivialize all of the combat, since the enemy "AI" simply can't deal with them and there are plenty of weapons to help you "cheese" these situations.
I think that last bit pretty much encapsulates my experience playing Nuclear Throne. It's not about winning the game on a fair and even basis, it's about finding the broken parts of the game and exploiting them, because NOT exploiting the broken parts of the game(like some of the weapons and mutations which are BLATANTLY superior to the others, the bad AI/pathfinding, etc.) is just opening yourself up to random death, which just isn't fun.
It's not that I don't like roguelikes, it's not that I don't like randomness, but the developrs need to know how to use it correctly. Too many just don't.
Supposedly Nuclear Throne is up to some 98 updates so far. Maybe they'll actually address some of these issues, but I doubt it.

Now that the situation concerning the game to only be playable at 30fps has finished, I can properly review the game.
Before the "problem" with not being able to play in over 30fps, I was enjoying this game. I agree that the graphics look slightly washed out, however this doesn't at all put me off the game. I occasionally crash while playing, however due to the auto save after every mission, I can reboot the game and carry on where I crashed.
MY PERFORMANCE PLAYING MAFIA III:
I see a lot of reviews slating the game as they don't get good performance in game... I have a R9 290 (4GB) and a AMD FX 8350 and I am currently having no problem playing this game at high settings 60 fps. Don't get put off this game by people complaining about their hardware related problems, if there is a problem with the game that is causing some people to not be able to play, then 2K will fix it, like they did within a couple of days of announcing that the game will only be playable in 30 fps.
Things I Like about the game:
- The stealth in this game is very good imo, the mechanics of sneaking around make it fun to complete a mission by not alerting everyone, and slowly picking everyone off.
- The driving mechanics I personally think fit the game perfectly, I can see a game like this being criticised heavily for its driving mechanics as it feels a bit like you are permanently attached to the ground, but a game like this with driving mechanics like GTA V would not work at all (imo) and would ruin driving for me.
- Calling in a car, weapon salesman and money handler (whatever she is called) is something that I really like in this game. The weapon salesman rolling up in his red van saves having to find a gun store, and likewise having to find a bank to store your money with the money handler.
- I don't personally know much about this time in history, however it feels like it would be realistic with the way the buildings look and the different cars and weaponry in the game.
Things I don't like about the game:
- Not being able to change your clothes is a little annoying, however I can kind of see why they left this feature out as it can take away from the realism of the game.
Conclusion:
I have personally not found much wrong with this game at all, I have been looking forward to this game for a while, and in my eyes it doesn't disappoint

The atmosphere in this game is pretty impressive, especially considering the size of the team making it.  From a technical perspective, it's a solid game that uses the engine well.  I didn't encounter any glitches and it ran very smooth on my laptop.  Like you might expect from a small studio, there aren't many configuration options, which might bother some.  the only thing that I would've preferred is a FOV slider.
The story is very interesting and well paced.  If you're looking for a creature-based horror experience, or a shooter, this isn't your game.  It is story driven and has you utilizing tools that help examine your environment more than hide from creatures or fight enemies.  The main mechanic in the game is puzzles.  I'm not a big fan of puzzle-based story-driven games, but these weren't too frequent and didn't clash with the rest of the game.  There were a few moments where i felt the devs could've made it a bit clearer on what you were supposed to do, as i was looking for little details and still got stumped on progressing further.
The premise is rooted in Lovecraft, like the synopsis explains, so having an interest in lovecraft is very helpful and might disappoint some if you're not into that sort of style.  This game tackles that premise quite well and had me continually interested with what was going on and wondering what would happen next.  I appreciate that it was tasteful in how it took inspiration.
It is a fairly short experience; I was logged as finishing the story in 3 hours, 9 minutes; which is quite short, but i'm glad the game wasn't stretched longer than it was.  There is a lot of tension and this would've made the experience less fun most likely.  The price point is a big factor if you're worried about the length.  For $20 at full retail, you're getting a AAA-looking game that is well optimized and has moments of immersion-building that at times are as effective as a game like Bioshock.
Well worth the asking price if you don't mind a puzzle and story-driven experience.  I'll definitely be keeping an eye on the studio from now on.

Shadow of war review
I have given this game a negative review for two reasons: it looks more like an indie studio proof of concept with the great nemesis system, but poor implementation of most other elements and it was designed to push you into the oblivion of microtransactions although it is a premium priced game. Now let's get into details:
GOOD:
+ An excellent nemesis system bringing the world to life and adding depth to the enemies. There are numerous variations of orcs you will encounter.
+ Decent combat mechanics with enough depth due to different damage types and various enemy strengths and weaknesses.
+ Diverse bioms.
+ No significant bugs or crashes.
BAD:
- Too few innovations compared to the previous game. This is basically more of the same.
- Some mechanics are not explained well enough. I have finished the whole game, but still, don't know what some of the objects in orc camps do.
- Almost all characters seem uninteresting and cliche. They are so terribly plainly good or evil that Nazgul's mumbling about how many evil things they will do to me and how they are generally evil makes me want to just skip all of the cutscenes.
- Due to the lack of character depth and a simply boring story, there is almost nothing memorable in the game plot. Character motivation is lacking and interesting plot twists are extremely rare and quite predictable.
- Although it would seem that stealth is an integral part of the game, it is rarely present and poorly implemented. The only viable tactic is to hit and run otherwise you can be overrun by even much lower level grunts.
- Although there are more abilities and their variations in this game, about half of them seem completely useless and plainly uninteresting. Some of the game mechanics that are offered and clearly HAVE soon become repetitive and boring.
- Although bioms are diverse and the map does not seem small, but there is no feeling of a large and dynamic world like in other open world games.
- The movement system clearly copied from the first assassins creed games has stuck back in 2007. How many times have I stumbled in the wrong direction or tried to climb a wall when I wanted to run next to it. Assassins Creed games have come a long way since the first one and their movement mechanics have evolved greatly, Middle-earth developers should have copied a more recent game instead of the first on in the series.
UGLY:
* Microtransactions in a premium priced game! This is a cancer of game industry these days and we must vote with our money by not falling for them even though many game mechanics are built around forcing players to shell out some more money.
* The UI is painfully console-ish requiring dozens of extra button pushed where a simple drag and drop system HAS to be present and the same results could have been achieved with a single click. Plus the whole user interface system could use a lot more polish.
* Unskippable orc speeches!!! There are so many orcs and each one needs to say something when: (1) he arrives, (2) he starts fighting me, (3) usually before he dies. All of these cutscenes are UNSKIPPABLE(!!!) and uninformative. They would have been very nice if less frequent, but in this state are simply HORRIBLE.
* Around half of the game time is locked in its final fourth act. The ONLY thing you will be doing in it is defending your bases over and over and over and over and over again. In between, you can enhance your armies, but overall this whole act is one messy and boring grind of only ONE from the whole plethora of possible activities.
VERDICT:
A great proof of concept for a single idea: procedurally generated enemies can be fun. All of the rest is a poorly implemented action game that would fit a decent indie team on their first attempt but is clearly not a AAA project. Get it at a major discount and don't pay into microtransactions. The game can be boring and grindy at times and you may want to speed up things a bit, but on PC there are many other free ways of doing so ;-)

The Binding of Isaac is one of those weird games that don't really try or pretend to bring anything new, but manage to captivate nonetheless.
Binding of Isaac is, for lack of any better way to grossly simplify the whole game, what happens when a newground flash game is stretched out as much as humanly possible, with much more talent and competency than you'd usually find in those titles.
The gameplay for BoI is quite self-explanatory: it's a room-based action game where you cry on monsters to kill them. If that weirded you out, it only gets worse from there on.
The game's whole purpose is that of exponential progression. You start out a naked, crying boy in a basement who shoots tears at spiders, and you end up covered in items, shooting (literally) ungodly projectiles at increasingly large and powerful monsters. The initially simple projectile patterns turn a (also literal) bullet hell.
While its gameplay is solid and convincing enough on its own, what was for me the biggest appeal of Binding of Isaac was not so much its gameplay as its visuals. There isn't quite anything out there
like Edmund McMillen's style, and this is perhaps the one title where his grotesque, unsettling designs are exploited to their fullest extent, to an often legitimately troubling degree.
It doesn't mean that BOI is without problems, however. While it came out at a time where "procedural generation" was still somewhat fresh and not quite the indie gaming buzzword it has become, the randomness factor  can and will still be somewhat of a deal breaker for many. Binding of Isaac is a ridiculously hard game and a lot of that is purely due to its entirely unpredictable framework, something the game does wonderfully well in exploiting, but the mere concept may displease plenty. This is the type of game where mere muscle memory and understanding of the game mechanics won't save you, and you have to expect death on every run - because down the line, whether you get to the end is going to only be half skill, with the other half being getting the right items at the right time and not getting backstabbed by the random factor at the worst possible moments.
There's also an issue of performance that's innate to its engine - flash was not designed to handle anything quite this intensive, and the constant onslaught of projectiles and beautiful but complex effects means that this game will NOT stay at 60 fps, or even at 30, on any PC.

RNG is not a proper replacement for actual design.
Nuclear Throne has some good parts. It has good art design. It has good sound design. The weapons are decently varied. The RNG behind the drops doesn't seem actively malicious. The enemies are pretty varied.
But it's pretty much all sunk by the parts that have no actual design, or poor design, behind them.
For instance, mutations. You're given a choice of four at every level-up, but I think only ONCE so far I've actually felt like there was any choice. There's pretty much always one useful one, and three that are pointless or mediocre. With better design, I'd have been torn between the options every single time.
Secondly, the lack of invincibility frames. Which means that when a boss teleports or other enemy on top of you without warning, you'll take three or four hits in rapid succession, and die as close to instantly as it gets.
Thirdly, the various character "abilities." I occasionally completely forget what the button for using them is, because they're of such limited utility.
Lastly, the utter lack of any level design. Levels are 100% down to the RNG which means that some levels spawn you in a wide-open field full of enemies that instantly zero in on you, including the ones outside of sight range which will start opening fire on you(and no, enemies do not suffer from friendly fire, so you can't even harness that to get out of the situation. PS: If you want enemies to have a longer firing distance, give me a view range equal to it! It's not fun being gibbed by things I haven't even had a chance to spot yet.). In other cases, you get nothing but narrow corridors which pretty much trivialize all of the combat, since the enemy "AI" simply can't deal with them and there are plenty of weapons to help you "cheese" these situations.
I think that last bit pretty much encapsulates my experience playing Nuclear Throne. It's not about winning the game on a fair and even basis, it's about finding the broken parts of the game and exploiting them, because NOT exploiting the broken parts of the game(like some of the weapons and mutations which are BLATANTLY superior to the others, the bad AI/pathfinding, etc.) is just opening yourself up to random death, which just isn't fun.
It's not that I don't like roguelikes, it's not that I don't like randomness, but the developrs need to know how to use it correctly. Too many just don't.
Supposedly Nuclear Throne is up to some 98 updates so far. Maybe they'll actually address some of these issues, but I doubt it.

Invasion looked interesting for me since I like pixel art and I love Crimsonland. Sadly it was a big disappointment.
Let's start from the menu. It welcomes us with irritating techno music and tiles with 10 levels. The screen with next 10 levels can be reached by clicking an arrow. But the music is pinned to every screen separately, so every time the arrow is clicked it starts the annoying song from the very beginning. And after beating level 10 you have to click the arrow every time you want to reach higher levels.
The playable character is so big and the camera so close that it is almost impossible to see anything. Moreover the camera is not attached to player, but its movement depends on mouse position. It is okay idea, but not when field of view is heavily limited. The environment of bushes etc does not help but narrows it even more.
Beating one level doesn't mean the player can smoothly go to the next one, because their weapon is usually too weak. Therefore there is a shop in which new weapons and upgrades can be bought. But hey, the prices are so damn high and the amount of money monsters drop so little that you have to grind every level number of times to be able to buy anything.
So you die. And you die again. Or you don't die because you need money and play the level like 100th time.
Before you would be able to have some reasonable weapon, you probably will be dead anyway... due to a boredom.
The pixel art graphics is not bad, but as it is the only good point of this game, I am not going to recommend this game to anyone.
