You play as Alan Wake, a best-selling writer. After a few years, Alan is unable to write anything. His wife, hoping to help him with his thoughts, brings him to Bright Falls.
Once you drive to your cabin, Alan gets into an argument with his wife and storms out. Darkness consumes the cabin and Alan's wife disappear. He runs outside and sees his wife in the lake and jumps in. Afterward, he finds himself in his car with a head injury, with no memory of what happened after he dove in the lake.
The core story spans six episodes, each crafted like part of a TV miniseries. After the first episode's exposition each that follows ends with a cliffhanger, fades to a title screen and then transitions into a plot recap as the next begins.
To finish the game it takes a bit over 10 hours, the story may seem a bit short, but collectible items like hidden coffee thermoses and collectible manuscripts, which tell more and more about Alan Wake's story, offer some incentives to return to Bright Falls.
Alan Wake has stellar lighting effects and environmental design that creates an atmosphere to make the scares and thrills more affecting. The game is full of shadows and effects that put the mood of the game into good use.
The in-game music is atmospheric and totally in-tuned with the story. The moments of tension were always made better because of the music.
Alan Wake is truly a masterpiece. It proves that survival-horror can be very well done with an intelligent story. I can highly recommend this game to all.

Seriously one of the most enjoyable RPG games I have ever played. It is also the
RPG I have ever felt after seeing the ending that I've had a meaningful impact on the plot.
Positives
-Well-crafted, intricate plot you can influence. Reputation with characters serves as both flavor, and enables certain dialogue decisions.
-You can invest in varied skills, which will influence how your character plays.
-You can customize how your player character acts, and looks.
-If you stick to a tone(casual, professional, etc. There's four of them), you will eventually form a reputation. It serves to further validate who you play as.
-Cool boss fights(80's gangster, STRYKER APC, Helicopter)
-Not everything is as it seems(plot-wise). In other words, there are lies and intrigue that aren't frustrating, clunky, or immature.
-Rewards exploration. There are hidden goodies on levels.
-Varied minigames. There are hacking, lockpicking, and(though it is not presented as such) sniping minigames.
-Speedy and immersive dialogue system(sometimes it backfires and makes a choice you didn't want. It does more good in my opinion than bad)
-Cool Safe-Houses.
Negatives
-The character customization is very limited, and boils down to hair, facial hair, and what kind of eyewear you do(or don't) wear.
-Akimbo SMGs for players, but mooks have single SMGs.
-Minigames escalate in difficulty too much.
-Ridiculous camera swinging. It's easily the most annoying feature of the game, and will kill you at least once.
-Level of Detail rendering at distance will leave some cutscenes very.....lacking. This is a minor issue in a few cutscenes.
-An all-too-familiar almighty evil megacorp cliché and the accompanying evil CEO serve as the main antagonists for this game.
Loved the ending I got. Easily in the top 10 RPGs I've played(in terms of how much I've enjoyed them, not technical accomplishment). Don't get this game if you can't handle a clunky experience. I would like to note that I encountered a single minor plot bug throughout my playthrough.
......Though I did realize halfway through the game that I am playing as an agent disavowed by the U.S. government referred to as 'Mike' who wears casual clothing and sunglasses.
Glad there isn't a 'Miami' level.

As the description says, this is a Lovercraft-influenced adventure game set in some of the same locations as At The Mountains of Madness without actually being an adaptation of it.
It's a story-focused adventure game that takes between 3-4 hours to complete a first playthrough, depending on how hard a time players have with the five puzzles that appear in the game.
While there's fairly limited interaction (no combat, limited puzzles and item collection), the game tells its story extremely well, and manages to truly capture the spirit and feel of HP Lovercraft's mythology, even going so far as to have all of the characters speak and write in his trademark stilted and florid language.
Even though it's not drawn straight from one of his works, Conarium is one of the best Lovecraft games available, as the developers fully understand what makes the stories powerful, and have done a fantastic job of building a game around those strengths.
Also, there's a brief cameo by a Shoggoth, which is always a plus.

Having loved the Darkness Within games, I was very much looking forward to playing whatever else Zoetrope Interactive had in store, and so far, this game hasn't disappointed.
Inspired heavily by the story 'At The Mountains Of Madness' by H.P. Lovecraft, you will take control of a scientist attempting to discover the true limits of nature on an Antarctic base. Unfortunately however, you wake up with a strange device attached to your arm with little memory of what has happened to you and your crew. There's a distinct feeling of something being terribly wrong.
The gameplay seems quite similar to Darkness Within 2 in the way you'll wander around the antarctic base interacting with various items, whilst trying to understand what happened to everyone and where you fit into all of it. You have your inventory where you can use and examine items, as well as a journal to record important pieces of information and documents you collect.

Controls are intuitive, graphics are sharp and the audio brings an eerie ambience to your efforts.
Recommended to fans of the Darkness Within games and the stories of H.P. Lovecraft.
Be warned though, to fully appreciate this you'll need to read quite a hefty amount, which might not be your thing.

Satisfying combo of survival, defense and exploration. Most recent update made the game much more visually pleasing, especially during your "base time" which is most of the early game.
Favorite thing: Being able to shape your survivors skills in meaningful and branching ways. Makes you more invested in your group.
Least favorite thing: Tech tree progress stops and can be held up by chance. You have to find research materials to unlock certain branches, but In my 18 hrs on 4 or 5 different groups of survivors I have yet to see research materials.
Feature wishlist: Interactions between survivors. I know this can screw up time efficiency, but it can make for some pretty cool emergent gameplay. Won't name names, but on another game I had a survivor group go all to hell because one my people was a hussy. Everyone got mad at eachother and started abandoning one another during fire fights. While I'm certainly not looking for a promiscuous priest, it would be nice to see anything that adds to emergent gameplay.
It's cool for killing time.

or watch it here:
You play as one of the research scientists in a small team stationed in Antarctica. In attempts to push bounds of nature, events during the expedition take a turn for the worst. You wake up with no memories of what happened, or knowledge of where your team is, so you set on your own in search of answers. As you play, you experience bizarre memories that help make sense of what’s going on. The story is intriguing, and I like the idea of defying nature, but I found the endings somewhat anti-climatic. One ending was significantly better than the other, but overall, the story feels a bit dry.
The gameplay encourages you to explore and find lots of notes, clues, and audio files to learn more about the story. Some of the notes are lengthy, but they do help quite a bit in understanding the plot. Conarium also requires you to find items or solve puzzles in order to progress. Locating the necessary items isn’t too difficult, but you’ll need to be aware of your surroundings. As for the puzzles, there aren’t a lot of them throughout the game, but the ones there are are unique. The puzzles are decent, but solving them requires you to find clues in the environment to help you, so if you miss the hints or don’t understand them, then you might get stuck for a little while.
There is a small amount backtracking at times, but it’s not too much. You’ll be walking around for most of the game able to take your time and soak in the atmosphere. The atmosphere is suspenseful at times, but I’m a little disappointed that there are only a couple occasions where you actually encounter enemies and have to run for your life. I think more encounters would have been fun, but the game’s style is in line with Lovecraft’s focus on creating a chilling atmosphere rather than conflicts.
The game took me a little over 4.5 hours to complete. I played both endings and found most of the collectibles. I don’t see much in the way of replay value, but there were some collectibles and secrets that I missed along the way, so I do suggest thorough exploration.
Conarium does a good job with the atmosphere, but has a story and gameplay that is not going to satisfy everyone. I expect that those familiar with Lovecraft’s work will be more likely to enjoy the game, while others may find it uninteresting.

Without having played it to its end I cannot say much on its quality of play all the way through.
However for the time I have played I can say that it is a rather enjoyable survival sim.
The player does not face the harshness of the elements as in many other suvival sims, as there is other more pressing stuff going on without having to face a reality engine pushing winter in your face.
Instead, the player faces off against the hordes of hell, an obvious summation which of course resides in the title.
In its current phase I feel it could use a quicker player progression in terms of survivor output, as the player has to research in order to go up the tech tree, often having to scavenge for pieces the player cannot produce either at that time or at all, early players begin with little to no armour and weaponry and it takes a while to build an armoury, let alone a respectable armoury, leaving the player to up the aggro of external hordes as they fight for much needed skills to build bigger and better tech.
Enemy aggression is based on amount of research stations at the player base, number of survivors at the base, and raids on enemy bases, which makes it difficult to grow larger and stronger in every respect without having a large and/or well armed demon raid rain down upon the player base.
Suffice to say that enemy aggression could do with going much slower and having a method of managing their aggression by perhaps leaving them the hell alone for an hour or so.
The survivor's need for food and water is also a slowing factor to player progression, this can easily come in the way of gathering much needed resources for basic materials, which are in fact limited at the player base camp (guess who has to go a'raiding demons when you run out).
Yet another factor to all of this are events, periodically a player will find themselves dealing with Night Howls, Red Haze's, Blood Moon's, and other such hateful things, these events will raise enemy awareness (night howls mean one of your survivor's won't stop making a damn noise at the moon), they will make enemies 30% stronger, and even damage survivor morale enough that mining or research or random useful thing of your choice becomes a % slower ...
Events eventually go away, but they do their damage to time constrictions that are already slow enough, or give enemies strength that are already strong enough, and they happen far too often, usually occuring anywhere between 1 and 3 times in a single game day.
And just for perspective, I am playing on easy.
Custom Settings for beginning a game could also use a tweak, currently it stands at choosing which features the player desires to be on easy or difficult, whereas what I feel it also needs is to do with amounts, i.e "high deposits of clay/wood/stone" at the base ... If anyone has played Factorio at all I would suggest a similar set up to that.
Now ... Let's talk tech tree ... It's actually pretty cool, but a bit of a mess ... Hovering the mouse above advancement of choice, the player will be given a very rough idea of what it does and what is required to gain it, however it does not list skills required to build certain items, nor does it list damage or defense on weapon items, i.e "is the crossbow better than the handgun? I don't know!!!", which makes it very difficult to choose how the player advances, often wasting points by trial and error.
Some of these advancements do not make sense, one in particular allows for the making of a combat knife, directly following this is "swords", the only sword in this advancement is a katana ... Let's get this straight, a katana is a cutting weapon only, traditionally and even as a point of physics it is not for use in blocking a blade or chopping through a large variety of things, although I will admit they are used in enemy beheading ... Also, it is a far cry to go from a combat knife to a katana, one is simple machine pressed metal, the other is layers of folded steel and finely crafted. -
- Medieval weapons on the other hand ... If one has a forge and the patience to read a manual, pretty simple to craft.
I feel as though there is a lot to add, I don't see why survivor's cannot raid a garage and glean access to a simple sledgehammer, they already mine stone with picks I never made them, and a sledge really nasties up anyone's day, take that sucker to a demon's face and you're laughing, possibly maniacly.
Instead the player finds themselves crafting weapons that are either of high skill or already exist in the real world, which brings me to the point there is not nearly enough melee weapons, most of it is guns (which I am very thankful do not require the constant production of ammunition).
I would like to see the addition of searching and raiding houses, as raids consist of delving into demon infested neighbourhoods and wandering the streets for loot.
It has a way to go, but it is still in beta as I write this, and is subject to grow more awesome over time, so far I am quite enjoying it and appreciating its potential.

There's no intensity. None. Why would I panic about any of my fences breaking when I can easily outrun even the fastest zombie? I often found myself jumping over the barricades anyway, searching for stuff to kill that was actually taking forever to spawn.
Guns and ammo are far too cheap and some are gamebreaking. As soon as I got hold of the shotgun, it was essentially game over. Everything dies in one shot except the giants who die in three and move so painfully slowly that they're more of a threat to the other zombies by blocking their way than they are to me.
By contrast, the ranged weapons are practically pointless. Molotovs do nothing. Zombies just wander through the fire like its scotch mist. The tactical use of the mines and the one-shot kill of the knives are just as effective as a shotgun blast, except I don't have to craft shells for that in multiples of three. The grenades have a fuse delay so they're utterly useless against the runner zombies who are the only mild threat in the game. Which I shotgun. Because the shotgun is insane.
The first survivor's gun appears to do nothing. I've stood there watching him pour nearly a hundred M16 rounds into a standard undead just for it to carry on shambling towards me.
It's called DUCT tape. Not 'duck tape'. Although there is a brand of tape in the US called 'Duck' but I sincerely doubt that's what you meant.
I think that'll do for starters. Maybe after that we can talk about the sheer repetitiveness and emptiness of the scenery or the fact that the flashlight doesn't really do anything useful but honestly, I'll just be reposting some variant of this review on another zombie defence title next week so I'm pessimistic to say the least.

TL:DR Worth getting if you enjoyed the first game and the strong storytelling is continued in this sequel. It doesn't introduce many new features or ideas though.
The Banner Saga 2 picks up the story from the ending of the first game. You can actually import your save and continue on with the characters you had left from the first game. The gameplay is almost identical with the travelling caravan and needing to manage supplies and morale. The choose your own adventure style events that can occasionaly kill caravan followers or party members depending on your choices. And the tactical turn based combat also makes a return.
Banner Saga 2's story is its strong point and manages to keep the same feeling of tension and mystery that the first game had. There hasn't really been many improvements to the sequel though. The combat which I felt was the first games weak point is still a bit monotonous though there is more variety of enemies which at least is an improvement over fighting the Dredge constantly.
Overall I think Banner Saga 2 is worth getting if you enjoyed the first game. If you havent played the first game I'd strongly recommend playing that first as the story is dependant on knowing what has happened previously. If you didn't like the first game however this sequel won't change your mind.

I was one of the original kickstarter backers for this game back in March of 2012.  As I expected to happen, over the course of these 22 months my anticipation for this game steadily grew, ever so much more as its appetite was fed a diet of documentary episodes, game and art design updates, and an engaging dialogue with the reinventers of Adventure.  My fear was that this ravenous anticipation of mine would spawn an equally monstrous set of expectations that no game could hope to live up to; never have my tribulations been so firmly laid to rest.
Irrespective of which story, Shay's or Vella's, you start out with, you are immediately drawn into a beatifully imagined and fantastical world filled with well developed characters following a meticulously laid out story.  I would often find myself having to briefly pause in my play of the game when the humor left me laughing too hard to continue for several moments.  The most enjoyable moment of the entire game was how the ending of the first Act caught me completely by surprise and desperate to continue.  This very satisfied backer's only real disappointment is the delay in continuing my exploration of the world and story.  Double Fine did an excellent job resurrecting a nearly extinct genre and I am very much looking forward to finishing the game when Act II comes out.

A brief review:
The game is quite good, better than Shadow of Mordor (SoM). Its flaws generally don't fall in the boundaries of poor game design, but instead poor business practices.
Micro-transactions and day-1 DLC are abominations that deserve an immediate death. Both exist for this game. However, you can complete the game 100% without them.
In short, the game is SoM with better graphics, an expanded (like 50x better) Nemesis System, and more areas (4 as I recall) roughly the same size/larger than the 2 areas in SoM. If you liked SoM, as I did, you’ll like this game. If you didn’t play SoM, you’ll probably enjoy the Nemesis System as it’s a fairly unique mechanic and can make for some very interesting mini-bosses.
My major complaint, outside of micro-transactions, is that the story is bad up until the final few missions. Not much else to say, as the story in SoM was also a significant weak point. If you were expecting the writers to finally wake up and understand that they are working with Tolkien’s legacy, you will be disappointed as I was. Gameplay and the Nemesis System are what drives this game the most.
Overall: 8/10

In no other game have I found myself teetering on the brink of failure, toeing the line of how far I can go while still successfully completing the mission, and balancing greed versus risk while still remaining entirely in control.
Every infiltration starts off slow, exploring the area and learning guard patrol paths.  The threat level gradually amps up, and by the time you've reached the main objective it's turned into a full-on sprint for the exit.
The variety of items present leaves you with plenty of options when in a sticky situation, and the subtle but still notable differences between agents makes each playthrough unique.  Indeed, the game is designed to be played through multiple times, with new agents and programs unlocked after every successful or failed campaign.  Such replay value, with randomly generated levels and a range of difficulty levels (that actually change gameplay, rather than being the usual health/damage increase most games profess), is a large part of my recommendation.
Oh, and the music is awesome.  It gets more intense depending on what has happened; by the time your agents have entered combat and made their way to the exit, the calm ambiance has become fast-paced and beat-driven.
I bought it on sale but can say that it's certainly worth full price.

This game fits the same mold as other base-building survival games, like RimWorld or Dwarf Fortress. It's far more simplified than either of those two, but there's a similar feel to it. Right now it's a very limited state (it IS in alpha, so obviously it would be). I'll explain my main issues and what I'd like to see below (spoilers):
* There isn't much in the way of research and you can usually get all of your technologies fairly quickly if you know how to manage your resources enough. Despite that, there's no method to success when it comes to technology. If you wind up with a bunch of survivors who are great with hand-to-hand combat and not particularly great with ranged weapons or get a penalty with them, then you could hold off on researching firearms technologies in favor of base-building things. Despite that, I'd like to see technologies more fleshed out and maybe have a few more.
* There's a neat dichotomy between holy magic and dark magic in the game. They don't appear to have anything to do with what you do, though. I kind of expected there to be some consequences when I loaded up some demonic weapons on my scavenger crew considering we're fighting demons. It seems like that could be expanded into an almost alignment-based situation.
* I would like to see more buildings. As it stands, there's a lot of customizing you can do with your base, but you do eventually reach a cap where the only thing you need to keep building are outbuildings for beds for the survivors you rescue in late game.
* The class system is kinda meh.
* Combat is awesome. It's very difficult and requires you to be very tactical about how you approach fighting. Sometimes fights can only be won by splitting your scavenger group and having multiple lines of fire, or sacrificing a  weak melee character in favor of taking something down with more poweful firearms.
* I absolutely love the lore but wish the devs would expand on it, maybe drop books and tomes you can find occasionally that'll explain what happened to make the world get to this state.
All in all, this is a pretty awesome post-apocalyptic simulator/strategy game with RPG elements. It's worth the price and it's been a long while since I wound up losing a whole day to an early access game. I would highly recommend this.

This is a game that, if a friend who's trying to learn game design shows it to you as a work in progress, you begrudingly play around with it for a few minutes. I cannot think of a single nice thing to say about this game, other than that one of the synths in the grating, repetitive soundtrack made me think of Gary Numan, and Gary Numan's cool.  The different parts in the soundtrack go in and out of synch with each other as you play, by the way.  I feel like some coding ingenuity was probably involved in messing even that up, but I find myself unable to really appreciate it.
Hipix, you should be ashamed of yourselves, and may God have mercy on your souls.

There is a large variety of guns which I doubt I've done more than merely scratch the surface of. The core gameplay loop is very enjoyable and I will continue to put hours into this gem.
I do however have a few gripes with the video choices within the game. The framerate is capped at 30. I have heard that this is a problem with gamemaker studio, not necassarily the devs though. Apparently when you create a project you have to explicitly choose a framerate for it to run at and later on requires a tonne of work to change. Perhaps the blame may lie with the devs on that one but frankly it's not a big issue for me becuase of the existing graphical quality of the game and it's not in first person. Also the game is played in a 4:3 window within a 16:9 interface. I think this is an odd design choice but hey- It hasn't affected the gameplay for me. I would also love a story mode for this game, it doesn't have to be 30 hour campign or anything but I think it would enhance the experience for me. I will ot however hold this against the devs.

Like most Microsoft users I have to re-install quite frequently so my "Hours" played might not be accurately reflected...
PROS:
- Accurate Flight model
- Active Modding Community
- Active Multiplayer Community
- Active Sim Support despite over 10 years of development
- Exellent selection of aircraft to pilot

This is by far one of my favorite simulators of all time.  I remember playing this years ago with my buddy who got this to replace his 'Janes' simulator.  I can't talk well enough about this sim, it literally has everything, the whole planet, amazing aircraft, fantastic flight mechanics (STILL), an outstanding modding community ...
CONS:
- Dated Graphics
- Dated Current/Weather Models
- Empty World
- Airports!!!!
- Expensive Modding Community
As with any game more than 10 years old, things will start to look a little dated.  Some of the textures really need a reolution touch-up being they were made for old tube-style 240p televisions but hey - that's progress!  The airports are abysmal seriously, Dev's wanted to keep things light-weight rendering the whole world and all but still, abysmal.  The world while absolutely gorgeous feels somewhat empty even when you are online with DTG's FANTASTIC multiplayer addon.
I saved this part for last as in my opinion it is the most important and potentially the most controversial:  FSX:SE DOES still have a hyper-active modding community, but they don't come cheap.  There are a lot of free addons but for the most part, the supported and most widely used addons will cost TONS of money.  A single airport mod can run almost $40 or more and just ONE aircraft *addon* can run nearly the same figure (or upwards of $100).  For those of you on a fixed income like most of the world at present - You really need to pick and choose.
CONCLUSION:
For the newly initiated in the flight-sim community, FSX:SE is still one of the best sims in town despite the grey hair and crow's feet.  If you do just a little research, you can gussy this girl up to be the GPU/CPU Killer she was always meant to be (seriously be careful) and fly some of the best aircraft available today.
A special thank you to DTG for showing the love to the flight-sim community and bringing us back from the shadows and into the ... well .... streetlights at least.  Great Job I look forward to Microsoft Flight.  PLEASE!!!!!  If you are absolutely looking for the best flight-sims - stay tuned for my upcoming review on X-Plane 10!

Were you looking to bathe in blood and fury? You've come to the right place. Hotline Miami is a game where you can sweep out an entire building of people in about two minutes and get your rampage playstyle called "GENERIC".
The gameplay is vicious. It takes some getting used to; the reticle moves with your character, you will always aim at the same spot on the SCREEN, not the map. With time, you'll grow to get used to it. Before long, you'll be stringing together twelve kills in a row, blasting 6 people with your shotgun, throwing it at someone, punching their friend, stomp both their heads in, and then rushing around the corner to gun down two more, kick open a door, blast the guy farthest away, and then kill the last guy with the message of "GO TO CAR" your sign to calm the ♥♥♥♥ down, you bloodthirsty animal.
There's secrets aplenty to be found. Not only can you discover things such as aditional masks that are either purely for fun or offer different playstyles, but you find things such as newspaper clippings showing what the latest headlines are, and mysterious letters in the form of purple pellets on the ground that are used to solve the puzzle in the start menu. Collect them all and solve the scramble, and something happens... brilliant, right?
Here's the obligatory paragraph on how awesome the soundtrack is. I mean, holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ How does it even exist? If you've heard the soundtrack you know what I'm talking about, if you somehow haven't then actually don't listen it, just play the game and let it be the cheering crowd as you tear people to shreds because a guy on the answering machine told you to.
There's some glitches here and there, mostly relating to the dogs. It's amazing at everything it does. You might not like a level or two, but that will not stop you from having a 10/10 experience with any other level in the game.
The only excuses for not having this game are "I don't want to give money to Valve" and "I am waiting for the sale because I didn't have two dollars during the 2015 Summer Sale." This game is worth more than $15, but feel free to wait for a sale.

Battles now feel like you can actually win them, rather than just endure. The difficulty setting is not a minigame that you play to gamble on how much frustration you can take before you ragequit in return for more experience points. Character growth is no longer quite so aggressively capped. The story *really* starts to open up...
I could sing its praises for quite a while, because Banner Saga 2 also carries forward all the things BS 1 did *right*. Everything is beautiful. World information is portioned out very slowly, but all of it matters. Your choices have consequences and being a good leader isn't about saying things people want to hear, but things that make a difference in their heads.
The only dark spot on an otherwise immaculate game comes at the very end, with a rushed final chapter that lurches out of nowhere culminating in a boss battle against a character you've been building for half the game and using a character that you possibly haven't been building at all.
There's nothing to telegraph this fight, and while trying to savescum it (to deal with a character that regens 4A/4H every turn and then hits for 7A/13H) I accidentally died, advanced the story, and wiped the pre-fight autosave--thereby sticking me with the bad end.
I'll definitely play Banner Saga 3 when it comes out, as the series seems to be sticking fully to its guns on making its player choices count and keep counting, but I'm not relishing the possiblity of having to replay 2 if I somehow inexorably locked myself into bad ends forever.
Oh, and if you've read this far but haven't played BS1, it's sort of a pre-requisite for having fun with this game. It's hard as balls, and I recommend playing with a walkthrough tabbed and consulting it before every decision, but it's also quite pretty and has a really satisfying story.

I didn't cry because Im a boy and boys don't cry, but nonetheless I got that feeling that you get when you finally finish that show or that book series that you've been watching and or reading for years and now know it's ultimately over. I DO reccomend this game becuase I gotta say, even if extremely cheesy at times, the dialogue is actually brilliant. The art style is very pleasing (to me at least), and the characters are relatable although I will say, most are extremely shallow and sorta played out if you know what I mean. But one thing I will mention is how beautifully the studio played me for a fool and how great I felt finding out I was the fool, let me explain: there was a character I hated Episode 1, 2 and 3 and then episode 4 and 5 had me do a full 180 and I understood the nuance behind the character and it was like replaying the game all over again with fresh eyes. It was beautful and spectacular. Also I reccomend this game becuase Episodes 1 2 and 3, Im not gonna lie, were sorta really mediocre and borderline unintersting. The plot was drawn out and predictable, characters were shallow (as previously mentioned), and the gameplay was nothing special. Basically an animated visual novel, I wasn't a huge fan. I wasn't drawn in. But I powered through and then Episode 4 BAM, kicked that♥♥♥♥♥♥to 11, and the game and story became something I was extremely invested in. And then the ending... maybe you've had it spoiled for you (I'm sorry for your loss) maybe not but the ending really made it all worth it. It wasn't mind blowing but it was... moving.

But... there are a few things about this game that I'm not so hot about and I'll list a few here. First sometimes the protagonist is stuck between making two decisions that are neither ones I would wanna make. Like sometimes I want to take the middle path between two decisions given, but I can only make one or the other. In a way the story makes you sorta ♥♥♥♥ up on purpose which is sort of the point, but it's sort of annoying at times. Another thing is that the sometimes the rules of time travel within the game itself are contradictory and the game breaks previously established rules of time travel. It's not game breaking, but it's inconsistant. Also a few things go unresolved, but that's only because they get overshadowed by bigger plot points, but they sort of also should be touched upon for a more complete feel.

So now you're still stuck: buy the game, or not buy the game, that's your decision. But this is a game about making tough decisions, so I think at this point, this game might be exactly what you need. 9/10 Do Reccomend.

Alpha Protocol is one of the most responsive RPGs I have ever played. Even as the overall plot stays on course to take you through much the same set of levels, characters and circumstances react to your actions in ways you may not even appreciate without a second playthrough. Alpha Protocol's story isn't even that interesting from a wide perspective, honestly - what makes this game amazing is all the work Obsidian put into its execution, shaping a story whose interactivity blows so many other games out of the water.
Many of the mechanics are roughly executed or even just ill-conceived, for which Alpha Protocol has been deservedly criticized. Even at release it was not a very good shooter or a very good stealth game, and those parts have certainly not improved with age. But at the end of the day, solid execution on the narrative end keeps things interesting and helps make the game more than just the sum of its parts.
If you like branching narrative in your action RPGs, then you need to see what an amazing job this game does in both making its narrative threads reactive and in tying them all together. After playing Alpha Protocol, I always wish more games were like it.

I'm a huge fan of apocalypse games, and I think that Wasteland 2 is awesome. You need to be into the genre, and appreciate the history and work put into it, as well as enjoy the gameplay.
Graphics: The game was made in Unity, and it shows. The visuals are by no means top notche, neither should they be. I'd much rather inXile focus on good gameplay than good visuals (though good visuals don't hurt).
Gameplay: The game is turn based and that is a pretty specific type of game. There is strategy involved and heavy rpg elements that make this game slow, but fun if you enjoy that kind of thing.
Audio: The sounds in the game are good, gun shots sound powerful and voice acting is clear and easy to understand, though not the best voice acting in the history of gaming, i'm just glad that it's there.
The games start up menu can get a little obnoxious as far as audio is concerned because everytime you move the mouse a noise is made, and when you hover over a button a different noise. At times that can get a little tiresome.
The game crashes on a regular enough basis for it to be a problem, especially because of how slow the gameplay is.
Considering the price of $59.99, I recommend waiting until it goes on sale. The game is worth $30, not $60, especially considering that the OST and graphic novels that come promised with the game aren't actually available upon purchase. Though this is temporary, it's still a gimic to get folks to buy the game. And Wasteland 1 is not that fantastic of a game, especially 20 odd years down the road.
All in all, I'd give it a personal rating of 7/10, give it time and I'm sure they'll have some of the major game breaking bugs fixed, for now, it's an incomplete game. They've done a great job bringing back a fan favored game though, and I look forward to seeing what they do with this.

The Walking Dead Season 2 is a point and click adventure game which serves as the sequel to the original The Walking Dead. I’m going to preface this by saying that you should NOT be playing this game if you haven’t played the original game. It does not make any room for those that do not know what happened in the first game while making a whole lot of references to it indeed.
So assuming you have played the first walking dead, let’s start with reviewing what’s new in season 2. Well, quick time events are back. And in my review for the original game I mentioned them without really ranting about how much I hated them, how stupid they were, and how I wish they were gone. THIS time around though I want to say that The Walking Dead Season 2 took the horribly done quick time events from its predecessor and actually made them better. It’s hard to explain, but they don’t just pop up at stupid moments anymore or have the same premise each time. They actually work well now and I felt they helped add to the game experience far more than the last time around, but I still find them a little pointless, and if you are interested in this game you should know that yes, they are still here.
The graphics have seen an overhaul. In fact there’s one scene in the game that does a flashback to the original that copies the original graphics, you can actually see the difference quite evidently. The game didn’t sound as empty this time around so they definitely improved on their soundtracks and ambience. I never once lost immersion in this game. Not once.
The gameplay is very much exactly the same. A point and click adventure puzzle in between story segments. There isn’t much to tell or much to say got improved here. Fans of the point and click genre will love it, while those that are here only for the story will likely find themselves trying to find what they have to click to move the story along every time such a segment comes along.
This story is arguably even better than the first one now that the perspective has transferred to our lovely dear Clementine. You now get to play as the character you spent the entire first game protecting at all costs. It is a rush to survive in this zombie apocalypse, and this time you get to play as a child! This is a very unique way to play. Your small size makes you very useful in certain situations, but at the same time no one ever takes you seriously because you’re a child. Paired with this very interesting new perspective comes the return of a couple of characters from the first game. Every chapter of this story and the situations you find yourselves in are thrilling and probably overall just the perfect followup to the original walking dead. And this game can be a LOT more gruesome than the first one. If you’re queasy … then there’s a few scenes that will make this a game that isn’t quite for you.
HOWEVER. This game has the same exact problem as the first one. Your choices mean jack♥♥♥♥♥♥in just about every single instance. If a character is supposed to die then that character will die no matter what you do. If they’re supposed to live then they will no matter what you do. It’s the same garbage illusion of choice amidst a typical linear plotline as the first game. The quality of the story makes up for a lot of this for your first playthrough. But honestly, NEVER rewind and NEVER do a second playthrough with the intent of making different choices lest you find out just how shallow the choices in this game really are. Nothing you do matters for more than one sentence out of someone’s mouth.
Overall I think The Walking Dead Season 2 really did improve on what the original Walking Dead created. They also didn’t fix the biggest issue from the first game, but they did fix most of the smaller issues without introducing new ones. It gets an 8/10 from me. One point up from the original walking dead for providing a better game experience overall and for letting me play as my dearest little Clementine. However they still advertised this based on your choices affecting the story. And meanwhile your choices have literally no influence on the story whatsoever just like in the original game. I do recommend it, definitely for the story and point and click adventure aspects. Just do not buy this game if you’re looking for an interactive story where your choices will actually influence things, because that is NOT what this is.

That meloncholy pride of completing something you love with the sadness that it's over, maybe you know what I mean (I got this when I beat Legend of Zelda: Wind Waker the first time a billion years ago).

I DO reccomend this game becuase I gotta say, even if extremely cheesy at times, the dialogue is actually brilliant. The art style is very pleasing (to me at least), and the characters are relatable although I will say, most are extremely shallow and sorta played out if you know what I mean. But one thing I will mention is how beautifully the studio played me for a fool and how great I felt finding out I was the fool, let me explain: there was a character I hated Episode 1, 2 and 3 and then episode 4 and 5 had me do a full 180 and I understood the nuance behind the character and it was like replaying the game all over again with fresh eyes. It was beautful and spectacular. Also I reccomend this game becuase Episodes 1 2 and 3, Im not gonna lie, were sorta really mediocre and borderline unintersting. The plot was drawn out and predictable, characters were shallow (as previously mentioned), and the gameplay was nothing special. Basically an animated visual novel, I wasn't a huge fan. I wasn't drawn in. But I powered through and then Episode 4 BAM, kicked that♥♥♥♥♥♥to 11, and the game and story became something I was extremely invested in. And then the ending... maybe you've had it spoiled for you (I'm sorry for your loss) maybe not but the ending really made it all worth it. It wasn't mind blowing but it was... moving.

But... there are a few things about this game that I'm not so hot about and I'll list a few here. First sometimes the protagonist is stuck between making two decisions that are neither ones I would wanna make. Like sometimes I want to take the middle path between two decisions given, but I can only make one or the other. In a way the story makes you sorta ♥♥♥♥ up on purpose which is sort of the point, but it's sort of annoying at times. Another thing is that the sometimes the rules of time travel within the game itself are contradictory and the game breaks previously established rules of time travel. It's not game breaking, but it's inconsistant. Also a few things go unresolved, but that's only because they get overshadowed by bigger plot points, but they sort of also should be touched upon for a more complete feel.

So now you're still stuck: buy the game, or not buy the game, that's your decision. But this is a game about making tough decisions, so I think at this point, this game might be exactly what you need. 9/10 Do Reccomend.

This game is entertaining and fast paced, with a good clean chunk behind all your shots, but the sloppiness of its "random" mechanics far exceeds what makes sense for a game of this type. And the game itself is just generally low quality.
There are a few examples of this
-The game is flush with characters, but each character has relatively few unique upgrades.
-The map can generate specked monstrosities with one by one paths or vast expanses. Either trivializing gameplay or massively increasing difficulty in the face of certain enemies. While randomness and its influence on gameplay are to be expected in roguelikes, the patterns its leaning towards warp the game in a disgusting excess. From nongame baby-mode to spawning in a room with 5 snipers aimed at you and 3 men throwing cars that insta-wipe you.
-Each level ends when you kill the last enemy, spawning a black hole on his corpse and taking you to the next level.  Which would be a slick fast paced way of continuing the game, if it weren't that the black whole could cordon off a section of the crumbily generated map containing items you had yet to acquire. Replacing this with a button press activated ANYTHING would fix the problem, but alas this was never done.
-Instant kills exist, at all. These are haram for any roguelikes that involve character progression. Cars blowing up and killing you is a silly idea. Especially when enemies throw them beyond vision range. Dying should be the players fault, and should be avoidable by playing better.
-Melee weapons exist, but enemies that explode when killed also exist. And being out of ammo exists. And with their powers combined, you become captain planet. And by that I mean take damage unless you have a melee weapon of significant length.
I played a version of this game back when it was called wasteland kings, and assumed all the sloppiness and quality issues would be handled. But upon giving the fast paced romp the benefit of the doubt and buying the release, I was massively disappointed. It's just not a well made enough game for the price tag. This game as it stands is worth about five bucks.

Hotline Miami has managed to work its way into my top 3 favorite games. It's fast paced, the style of the game is really nice and colorful to look at, the music is the kind of stuff I would like to hear playing in fighting scenes of an action movie, and it constantly provides a challenge that gradually increases with each level. It's a short game, and I'm not gonna lie, the replayability is pretty low unless you're interested in the questions the story leaves you with. However, to fix this they threw in a secret ending. It's not much, but it's enough to get you to come back.
You don't usually expect a game based mostly on its gameplay to have that much of a story, but you certainly won't find yourself skipping over a bunch of cutscenes because you think they're boring. In fact, if you skip over them at all it's more likely that you're doing it to get to the real meat of the game.
The game isn't perfect, though. I personally could do without the hospital mission towards the end, as it really takes away how fast the game is being played. That's not to say I didn't enjoy it the first time, because it's an interesting way to get more involved with the plot, but most of the time I just want to get to the rampages.
This is a game I could play for hours on end without question, and it's easily one of my favorite games. With that said, this game is very violent. If you're sensitive to violence, or if you have kids around, you really shouldn't play this game.

Life is Strange is a great game. As a big fan of both RPGs and more linear narrative driven games, Life is Strange struck me as a happy medium between the two genres as the sole focus of the game is a well written plot that is heavily influenced by player choice.
Pros:
- The story is great! The plot and the characters are all very well written, and it's highly engaging from the get go. As you play through the game, you get to learn about all the characters (all of which are very interesting) and develop relationships with them, and as the plot advances these relationships develop differently based on player choice. The narrative itself is really interesting and its filled with wild twists and turns that are sure to keep you engaged and at the edge of your seat, and if you choose to interact with all the people and items throughout the game you get a ton more story that makes the main plot more enjoyable. One of my favorite things about Life is Strange is that no character or situation is black and white. Almost every player decision falls into a moral grey area, and after every conversation or decision I was left wondering how whatever I said or did was going to come into play later on down the line. There were times when I would make a decsion and then go back and change it, only to go back and change it again several times over. Additionally, the game is great at providing satisfying feedback and acknowledgement of player decisions.
- Although the levels or "episodes" are techinically linear, there is quite a bit of exploring you can do as well as opportunites to interact with people or items, all of which ties back into the plot in some way.
- There are a plethora of dialogue options and decisions, which adds a ton of replayability to the game.
- Throughout the game there are lots of cool puzzles that don't feel too difficult but are at the same time satisfying to solve.
- I absolutely love the art style and graphics in this game.
- The soundtrack is in my opinion amazing, although I'll admit its probably very hit or miss on person by person basis.
- The story is very easy to become emotionally invested in. It will probably make you laugh, and it will definitely make you tear up at times.
Cons:
- To my surprise, based on how good the rest of the game was, I was kind of disappointed by the ending. I don't want to spoil anything, but I felt like it was kind of abrupt, and my decisions throughout the game didn't have enough impact on the end IMO.
- Some situations were left unresolved and some questions were left unanswered.
- Occasionally I experienced an issue in which dialogue had no audio and there was only music.
All in all, I loved Life is Strange and I think any fans of narrative driven games and/or RPGs will thoroughly enjoy it.
TL;DR: Life is Strange is a great game with a beautiful story, unique and gorgeous art style and graphics, memorable sound track, good puzzles, and a satisfying system of morally ambiguous choice/consequence. 9/10

Life is Strange was a suprisingly refreshing piece of work for me to play. I choose to not directly call it a "game" because it is walking a thin line between a visual novel and a movie as well as a game. It comes with aspects of all of them but it mainly focuses on storytelling so you can not expect a real game when playing this.
The game puts you in the life of Maxine Caulfield, an 18 year old Artstudent at a private school. She is shy, introverted and thinks way too much about the people around her and her actions. Of course the game will focus around her development a lot. Let me just add a personal not here: This is the first time I wanted to actually hug a game character for what it has done. There, I said it.
You can wander around the scenes, examine objects, people and similar to hear Max's thoughts about those things and persons. This creates a suprisingly good working way to get the viewer to like Max or to understand her after a while as we can get commentary from her about everything we expierence.
Max finds out that she has the power to rewind time, very similiar to "The Butterfly Effect" Movies and "Spoiler Alert" the game is basically that: A Butterfly Effect Spinoff from start to finish.
She uses her power to save a not so random girl from getting shot only to realize it was her old friend Chloe and they both rekindle their friendship which the main plot develops around. Chloe's best friend Rachel got missing and they want to find a way to save her.
This is the basic story of the game. I will not tell you anything about what is going to happen only how it happens from here on.
So using her Rewind Power they both eventually uncover a mystery at the town they are in. It involves heartbreaking tragedies, murder, psychopaths, drugs and much more. In the later episodes we also throw a bit of Chaos Theory and Multiverse Theory into and an voila: You have a perfectly fine mind♥♥♥♥ with one of the most emotionally twists I have EVER come across in any game or movie.
So much about the story that you can expect. The game however has a few problems: Many of the happenings are literally just placed there to create drama. There is no reason for them to exist other than either to waste our time or to create artificial drama. This really bothered me in some sections. The main plot is basically held up because we have to find some stupid bottles at a junkyard or because our dumb friend Chloe did something so stupid not a single sane person would have ♥♥♥♥ed up that hard.
Some of the conversations and outcomes also feel very unnatural or even unrealistic. Some of the time rewinds that should actually affect the timeline simple do not do anything.
The game itself is completely inconsistent with Max's personality as she literally jumps around from being a pacifist to wishing someone to Quote: "Eat♥♥♥♥♥♥and die".
Writing just seems lazy at many places in this game.
Then there is the ending itself. This was the biggest let down for me as it was obvious to me after the second episode at least in one way or another to turn out like this. This ruined the emotional ending for me as I was expecting it to happen. The ending also wastes a lot of potential the game still had but nonetheless:
The Artstyle is probably what this game deserves the most points for. It looks like a comic game, websites, chatlogs, photographs are all drawn instead of created to look digitally. I really like that about the game. Many textures also look like they were made using brushes instead of being realistic. Amazing work there. I enjoyed almost everything I looked at.
The Soundtrack is also just about perfect for the game. Many acoustic tracks to capture the rural area of Arcadia Bay. Very calm tracks for the wilderness and almost serene enviroment. A perfect fit, easily 99/100.
It is basically a Visual Novel. It runs without a single framedrop. It should run on most older PCs as well, no worries.
This game is easily one of my most favorite stories of all time. I loved most of it and I can definetly recommand it to anyone that just wants to relax for a few hours and play a game that solely evolvs around story rather than action or intuitive gameplay. This is a story driven game after all. Explore the world, take everything in, take breaks between episodes to thing about the plot.
Oh and one last note: Make sure you are not working on the day after you finish Ep. 5. You won't get it out of your system that fast.

You can also purchase augments which attach triggered abilities to your agents, and programs for your AI companion. The AI is used to hack the devices within the level, such as switching off cameras so that your agents can't be spotted as they move through a room. At some point in development they added lower difficulty levels via a turn rewind feature, which I thought was an interesting way of reducing the diffuclty without compromising the core gameplay.

I've spent a bit of time (16 hours) on this game and feel like I can give a sufficient review. I've given the game a "no" with a provisional "yes"; at this point in time, because it needs work to make it feel worthy of purchasing for most. If you are like me and enjoy supporting/trying alpha indie games and you like the genre, yes it is worth a punt.
The survival element is pretty easy to pick up. The survior management system is upthere with the best, to make it pretty easy to avoid micromanaging and focusing on your overall plan. The skill and build trees need serious rebalancing though. As the ocassional hordes get more powerful, you start to feel like you fall behind the curve - not in the least because the higher & more expensive skills are not particularly useful (if they are activated at all).
Along with these elements, it feels more and more like a tower defence game once you get into the routine. The travel/quest feature is nice, but the rewards/resources don't seem to match the effort. It does get difficult to find the resource rewards you need for building up your survivors after a time, as the quest features are non-renewable (the periodic events don't really count).
An interesting experiment, but it definitely needs some work - I'm not particularly driven to play this again in its current state. Hopefully I will get the chance to update this review in the near future.

You like Rimworld do you?...
Yes this game is almost the same as the other. A colony simulation but this one is not focused in colony building, no inter character relationship or canibalism.
Summary:
This game focused on combating the devil apocalypse, devil spawns that roam the world looking for unfortunate human to be their meals, or something. Your objective is to find the cause of this apocalypse and put an end to it.
Started with only one base and a handful of survivor, you have to scavenge, harvest resources, planing your defense in order to protect your occultists as they are researching how to put an end to this demon scourge.
Upgrade your survivor, gear them up with the best equipment you can craft.
Gameplay & Design:
It's a survival simulator. You build your base, make improvements and then go scavenging. There's a world map with representative icons for its location. Schools, hospitals, factory, etc. You can send your survivors there but only 5 survivors could do that, stealthily gather the resources or just kill all the demons and get all the rewards, your choice. Some research breakthroughs need items that can only be obtained by scavenging.
The combat is simple, just like traditional RTS but the hitbox is too wide in my opinion and the animations are a no no. But for me, I really don't care. It's acceptable because it was overshadowed by the concept of the game. I'm not a graphic ♥♥♥♥♥ so it's okay.
Music:
The music is perfectly blend in with the atmosphere of the game, especially when you go scavenging or doing stealth mission. At first, when no enemies notice you, the music is calm and lil bit eeire, but when you see an enemy, but it didn't see you, the music started to play lil bit upbeating. But when an enemy spots you, the music will be very upbeating and it's like "Time for action!"
Graphic:
I dunno, it's 3D with some hand-drawn objects? I'm not quite sure, but it's look like a hand-drawn for me, especially those workbenches. Like I said before the animation is a no no, especially in combat. Walking and running animation is good though.
Enjoyment:
I'm having a blast playing this game, my playtime is only 4 hours when I write this review but I will be back for more. Having to take care of your survivors, improve them, prepare them for the upcoming battle, it's just my kind of game, and most importantly, they are randomly generated, you never know what combination of survivors you would have in your disposal. Final verdict, it's a 8/10, it's a good game.
You like Rimworld do you? You should try this one. It's in Early Access, but in the roadmap it'll be released in May 2017. Can't wait to see the finished products.
Edit: Now the release date changed into Q3 2017, they sure take their time to make it better.

As game developers have begun to deliver games for sale long before they're complete, I suspect there has been a relative increase in dissatisfaction and perhaps some disappointment.  Despite the caveats openly warning potential customers from buying a game in the early stages of its development, many people purchase the game (for a variety of reasons ranging from nostalgia - why I bought Wasteland 2 to pure childish impatience and excitement).

Utterly fantastic space simulation game. I cannot recommend this game enough, it has brought me hours of fun and has really managed to enable me to rediscover my personal passion for space exploration.
There are three main game modes: Career, Science, and Sandbox.
In Career mode you take control of your own space program and must manage administrative, financial, and logistical aspects of your space program. There is a detailed research system for unlocking new technologies to use in your spacecraft. You will take contracts from various organizations, earning money upon completion. These contracts will get progressively more challenging and rewarding as you advance your space program.
In Science mode you are free from the financial and administative burdens of career mode but are still faced with having to research technology for your spacecraft. You progress along the tech tree by performing various science experiments on your home planet and various other celestial bodies, with experiments performed in more distant and challenging environments granting more beneficial rewards.
In Sandbox mode you are free to build and explore whatever you like and are not limited by any tech tree or financial limits.
+In-dept and accurate space simulation with realistic physics and particularly noteworthy orbital mechanics.
+Very challenging and rewarding gameplay.
+Wide variety of celestial bodies to explore.
+Ability for player to choose from a selection of pre-built spacecraft or construct their own using a very intricate construction system featuring a large variety of parts to choose from.
+Features unmanned probes aswell as spacecraft piloted by Kerbals.
+Optional communications system for unmanned probes which require them to have a connection to mission control. This adds an additional layer or difficulty and realism to the unmanned space program, allowing for the construction of satellite communication networks around the star system.
+Excellent community.
+Large amounts of
mods available.
+Very large explosions.
+New features are still being added by the developers.
~Planets, although
large, are not realistically large.
~Celestial bodies are (somewhat accurately) extemely empty and desolate, with few surface features apart from a few rocks or trees
~Does not feature any real form of pre-made story (though the player is free to make their own).
~Does not feature any online functionality or multiplayer.
~Has a very steep learning curve, particularly for players with no previous knowledge of orbital mechanics or astrophysics, though a wide variety of
easily available.
~Unfortunatley lacks Steam Workshop support as of the time of writing.
-Not a particullarly good looking game. (Personally, I use a variety of mods which make the game look
.)
-Can have some performance issues when dealing with extremely large spacecraft. (significatly improved as of the 1.2 update)
-Some may consider the game to be a bit too expensive.
Overall, I would thoroughly recommend this game to anyone with an interest in space, adventure, or very large explosions. In my opinion, no other game can give you the same amazing feeling as when you first land kerbals on the moon (Mun). This game has brought me so much fun, and I simply love it.

I think The Banner Saga 2 will end up being regarded as the sophomore slump in the trilogy. The first game had such a unique style and spin on the traditional idea of a strategy RPG that it was always going to be difficult to follow up with something that felt new and inspired.
There are a few new playable characters, and a couple new enemy types. But it's so largely a copy-and-paste of the first game that it was hard to get excited for the combat the same way I did with its predecessor.
The meta-game management system was also extremely frustrating this time around. You have no idea what decision will lead to a positive or negative or neutral outcome, so you're largely just guessing with each encounter. The first game seemed to make more logical sense in this department and not be nearly so random.
The story did move things forward, but it had that middle-entry-in-a-trilogy feel: the characters are moving from point A to point B, but almost nothing noteworthy actually happens. I also wasn't nearly as invested in the characters this time around.
I played through number 1 a second time to make different decisions and get a repeat of the great experience I had playing. The biggest difference with 2 is that I had no desire to play any longer once I finished. The survival mode is the antithesis of what I wanted and a waste of development time: exploiting over-powered abilities and micro-managing the battle system, without a shred of story attached.
I'm still interested in seeing things through to their conclusion, because the story is fundamentally interesting, but I'm hoping for a more fun, epic saga next time.

TL;DR While the story is epic. The developers went too far down the indie rabbit hole trying to make a unique combat system which ultimately falls flat on its viking face.
If I were to rate this game I would give it a 4/10.
The artwork / story - Top notch! This would make an epic movie trilogy, or maybe even a mature cartoon series. A few days ago I read a review where the reviewer says that if there were an option to skip the combat and just play the story it would be ideal. I remember reading it and being puzzled.
"How can the combat be so bad you'd skip it entirely and essentially just read a visual novel?" I wondered.
Then I started to get into it. Man....there are some massive issues here that I can't believe the developers didn't take a step back and realize they created a system that just isn't fun.
For a "tactics" game the combat has very few moments to utilize real tactics. Every map you battle on is just an open space with a pretty background. There is no elevation, no obstacles, and the position your character is facing is irrelevant.
Top all that off with this straight up weird armour / strength dual health bar system. You have an armour health bar and a strength health bar, the less armour you have the more damage you take. Makes sense right? Right. Instead of an HP bar you have a strength bar. As the strength bar diminishes your character deals less and less damage, so a character who is down to 1 strength is useless and there is no system in the game to replenish your health pool (which is for some reason known as your strength pool instead).
The developer just wanted to think of ways to make their game unique, but to that I say you've already got a unique setting and an epic story. Why do you need to RUIN it with a straight up garbage combat system.
My other gripe is with the lack of minor quality of life things that are just standard to this style of game such as the ability to choose when you save, and restart a battle (yes, you can be 20 minutes into a battle and realize you ♥♥♥♥ed up and need to restart but the game forces you to play out a losing battle). I could go on and on about how much I loathe this combat system but I really don't want to write a long-winded review. Just be warned, it's really ♥♥♥♥en weird.
Thumbs up for story and a giant thumb down for combat.

You know, if there was a level editor provided, I could see giving CRYLINE a more positive rating because what few interesting ideas are here they do work and they are effective, but they are far towards the latter half of the game. Even when you factor its price, the first twenty-or-so levels are so rudimentary that they feel too bland or they introduce minor obstacles with no challenge. Later on, there are a few levels that feel unrefined due to their physics simply not cooperating with the idea behind the puzzle.
Compared to the other games from this developer, CRYLINE feels like the most barren of its unique ideas—which is a shame because I do enjoy various aspects of its mechanics, and I would enjoy more levels or the ability to create them to enjoy the sweeter parts of the experience.
CRYLINE is more of a return to what has been already refined in puzzle games, block movement obstacle courses, and adds a few interesting modifiers to make up for its simplicity. The objective behind every level is simple: collect all crystals to progress and don’t destroy all your boxes in the process either through your own fault or the level requiring you to sacrifice them. Within the first twenty or so levels, you learn about interactable objects like satchels, rotation circles, hazards and other small things, but the gameplay remains focused on simple block movement. It’s where the game begins to show some originality that it begins to shine.
Taking a page from the Double Cherry ability from Mario 3D World, there are certain levels that tax you with manipulating multiple boxes as one character to get through a puzzle, and it’s working around this mechanic that makes later stages compelling. In addition to this new ability, new items like C4 are introduced which sticks to blocks, making them able to destroy obstacles in your way, as well as modifiers like fire and frozen states to reset your control of your block army. Admittedly, these latter mechanics create their own problems, but the former do build on an interesting premise where you have to think about more than simply navigation but how to sacrifice pawns to win the game.
Every stage after these mechanics are introduced simply builds more and more puzzles around their challenge, some of which are the highlights of the whole game, yet a worse problem than starting too slow is abrupt difficulty spikes, and CRYLINE suffers from this problem
This isn’t intended to poke fun at the language barrier from the developer, but the physics can become so wonky that they break certain challenges from their behavior that I wouldn’t call them physics out of respect of the science. Fire and Ice rotation puzzles are the worst offenders because the particle effects are given hitboxes that seem too precise for these kinds of puzzles. Even with a level-editor, these physics need to be tweaked to be more clear or more responsive to guide players on the right path.
What may seem like a simple freeze and defrost challenge to guide another block to its destination leads to having to deal with precise particle effects versus the rigid controls. The fire-barrel modifier also suffers from this issue when you have to guess if the elemental effect will affect the explosive you need to use to remove a wall after defrosting a block. It’s never clear how close/far you have to be because of the visual feedback of the fire. This can lead to a lot of guess-work and game-over screens as a result of these effects, and it’s why I detest these puzzles so much when they really shouldn’t be so bad.
Some people might believe just because a game on Steam runs with Unity that any game is an asset flip when CRYLINE doesn’t feel like it. It may feel amateurish, yet it does feel like a game brimming with the ideas it wants to create yet not confident to simply make that the basis of its game. The only lesson to learn with a game like CRYLINE, the only real step forward, aside from tweaking the physics and adding a level editor to add more value, is to take the lessons learned into consideration when making another game with the same ideas at the forefront of its foundation.
Whether that is CRYLINE 2 or something completely different, if the game is going to be based around managing multiple characters and learning to sacrifice them, then put that emphasis from the beginning. You only need to look at The Swapper to see it in action; it manages to utilize that idea and every facet of its gameplay is about using copies to get through puzzles. Hazards, unique challenges, etc. should never detracted from the core gameplay but were additions to the foundation to give it more support. That is the direction that should be handled for whatever project comes next.

By far one of the best Telltale games out there. The only other that could rival such a masterpiece is Their Batman game. All Telltale games that I have seen, and played through like this one are just beautifully written. The Cinematic shots are absolutly amazing, and stunning.
*minor spoiler in case you haven't played it yet.*
in the fifth episode, Clementine is talking to Kenny from the group, and after their conversation, Clementine steps out of the truck. As she steps out, the camera zooms in to a close up, that shows Clem staring into the truck's left side mirror. (you can always check my screenshots if your curious, or google it.) The camera pans away, when you(Clementine) walk away.
Like all Telltale's story driven games, Your choices matter(to an extent), and with an adaptable story line, adds many ways to replay the game. You wanna be a goody two-shoes, who listens to everyone, and doesn't upset them? play that way! You want to be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and burn as many bridges as possible? DO IT! in my first playthrough I was primarily picking the options I feel Clementine would most likely say, and when she had the option to curse, I often chose it. In addition, at the end of every episode Telltale games has a bit of a survey, or stat board of all your significant choices you made that episode, and ranks them from .1% to 100%(generally something inbetween that) depending on what other players made the same choices as you. there are generally five MAJOR choices in the game that shift the narrative further, and you will fall in to one of three catigories: minority, Majority, and neutral. Also, in Telltale's games, each episode generally streches between 70-90 minutes, so if you plan on playing the game, I'd reccommend that you finish an episode in one sitting.
The Gameplay of this game, is similar to most of Telltale's other games like The Walking Dead(Season 1), The Wolf Among Us, Batman, and Tales from the borderlands. So you can expect to see a lot of walking around and exploring your surroundings, also expect a lot of quick time events, and cutscenes.
One of the best features of this game, is the multiple endings, I each with their own emotional impact to the player. The ending I chose had me in tears, much like the season finale of The Walking Dead(season 1).
Now as I said earlier, Your choices matter to a point. This is true, because what you say, generally provokes a unique respons from the characters. In a conversation you have four options to say the "good" or nice response, the "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" or conflicting response, the "neutral" response, and "..." or silence. You will also have a limited amount of time to answer each question or conversation point, sometimes ranging from a mere 5 seconds, to a thought provoking 30 seconds(these are all rough estamates), or the game will pick for you. Now depending on your response in the top left of the corner, the UI will say "XYZ will remember that." and later on in either that episode, or sometime down the road, they will bring up that choice you made. Now the downside of this is, after my playthrough, and watching other playthroughs of the game, what would feel like unique and branching paths, are actually very scripted. Hence which brings me to my next point: Illusion of choice. your first time playing through, feels genuine, but as you play it more, the paths become more clear. There will be cases when the character will say the same thing for every dialogue option, and there will be cases where when you say "X" the NPC's response will be "Y" followed up to the point where they say "Z," and there will be times when you say "Y" and the NPC's will take you right to "Z."
This is the best game I have ever played, and would hope you play it too.

As someone who has been a fan of Mighty Switch Force since the start, I am frankly disappointed in this game. When compared to MSF1/2, Mighty Switch Force Academy barely brings anything new to the table. MSF2 introduced the new gimmick of Patty being a firefighter (and all the bells and whistles of using water instead of a stun gun), and yet here we are again with generic MSF1 police Patty. Granted, the game does offer new gimmicks by way of "fall off the screen and reappear at the top", but that alone isn't much when compared to what MSF2 brought to the table. On top of this, the entire game feels like cheap filler. It doesn't have any of the pretty backgrounds, environments, or so on.
Also, as someone who has been around since day 1 of Early Access, I can say with much disappointment that WayForward never really communicated with their customers via the Steam discussion boards. They never seemingly took any sort of user input from us, and they seemed to simply just fix a couple of reported bugs, post an update log, and call it a day. They claimed that they would take our feedback about creating levels, but they never did. They also apparently deleted all the old forum posts about these discussions.
At the very least, I would have expected the following:
1.) Actual backgrounds. Having what looks like my old Windows 98 screensaver as the background isn't too pleasing to the eye, and the levels themselves are horribly bland in the visuals department. I thought this was a police academy, not a multicolored void of nothingness.
2.) Make the game actually feel like a police academy. That means having training dummy/training robot versions of the various enemies, Patty actually wearing an academy uniform (instead of a cheap reuse of her MSF1 sprites), using a training gun with rubber pellets, and so on.
3.) Online co-op. Local co-op on a PC exclusive game... really? I may have a friend or two to play with, but it's rather absurd that a game such as this would not feature online co-op. I'm not even sure I have enough USB ports on my computer for four controllers to begin with.
4.) A level creator/editor, or at least fully open in terms of mods. Neither of these are the case, and I find it rather irritating.
5.) More content. I blew through the entire game in Early Access in all of an hour, along with hitting the course par on quite a few of the levels without any sort of difficulty. Granted, there's about 5 new levels I have to go finish, but $10 for such a short game isn't very fair, especially when MSF1/2 are as low as $1.50 on 3DS.

Choices MATTER and actively mold the storyline.  The rest you should find out for yourself.
It engaged me from the beginning of play clear through to the end of the game.  I played it through a couple of more times just for the fun of it.  There are four different classes to choose from and a different conversation or choice during gameplay can DRAMATICALLY alter the storyline and player-relationships.
That is about it.  It is NOT the most polished game with fantastic performance or graphics, but in my estimation, a very enjoyable game.  I highly recommend it for anyone interested in the RPG/Spy Game genre and for that matter, anyone looking for something a little bit different.
