Hotline Miami has managed to work its way into my top 3 favorite games. It's fast paced, the style of the game is really nice and colorful to look at, the music is the kind of stuff I would like to hear playing in fighting scenes of an action movie, and it constantly provides a challenge that gradually increases with each level. It's a short game, and I'm not gonna lie, the replayability is pretty low unless you're interested in the questions the story leaves you with. However, to fix this they threw in a secret ending. It's not much, but it's enough to get you to come back.
You don't usually expect a game based mostly on its gameplay to have that much of a story, but you certainly won't find yourself skipping over a bunch of cutscenes because you think they're boring. In fact, if you skip over them at all it's more likely that you're doing it to get to the real meat of the game.
The game isn't perfect, though. I personally could do without the hospital mission towards the end, as it really takes away how fast the game is being played. That's not to say I didn't enjoy it the first time, because it's an interesting way to get more involved with the plot, but most of the time I just want to get to the rampages.
This is a game I could play for hours on end without question, and it's easily one of my favorite games. With that said, this game is very violent. If you're sensitive to violence, or if you have kids around, you really shouldn't play this game.

To spell it out: I do not recommend this game. After playing through the story of the game, I can see how some people can like it, but I personally was counting the seconds for this game to end. Mentioned by the title, you play as Alan Wake, a writer that decides to drive to a random town with his wife in order to relax and maybe work on a new novel. But then things go awry as it seems as his wife goes missing and he finds himself at a police station, and now it is up to Alan to figure out what is going on in this town and what happened to his wife. As far as the story goes, there is not much I can say about it. I was not a particular fan of it; a lot of suspense, references to Stephen King and a large use of light and dark imagery. But it served its purpose, and those who are a fan of Stephen King novels will probably like it.
The gameplay was boring to me. You equip a flash light and an assortment of guns (but you really only need to use the pistol) as you try to stun Alan's enemies with light sources and then shoot them for massive damage. That is about it: grab a light source, shine it upon an enemy until they become stunned, and then shoot then a few times with your pistol. Eventually in the game you find different guns and flash grenades, but the formula remains the same (flash and shoot). It was satisfying to dodge a few enemy attacks and then flash and stun them, but that got old every quickly. In addition, for tension whenever you move forward a few paces the camera would zoom in on some enemies in front of you or behind you, which actually ruined the suspenseful tension. Since killing the enemies provides no benefit, I found the most useful solution at times was to set off a flare and sprint to the next checkpoint; at least it made more sense than to stand your ground and try to shoot away the random axes you never see coming.
The final pin in the coffin however, is the fact that this game does not need you to be around in order to play it. Most of the time before the shine/shoot elements you are stuck walking around as one of the other characters is speaking. And this speaking is usually coupled with walking to a destination (by the way most of this game feels like an artificial corridor). You can move in advance to the destination, but the speaking will not stop until the NPC arrives to its destination, and at times this feels like forever.
So my final verdict is that this game was not fun to play. With the combination of repetitive gameplay and unskippable dialogue through corridor after corridor it really feels like this would have made a better movie than game, The atmosphere and the story and the numerous cut scenes seems to fit that mo.

While I wish the devs would add achievements to give me more incentive to play, there is no denying that every time I load this game up I have a blast trying (and failing) to complete missions in career mode.

Shonky camera, Wake will never run forward or backwards properly but slanted to one side. Controls are manageable and that's all that can be said. It's a real pity the developers didn't respect the PC fanbase enough to add crisp, precise controls instead of just adapting the floaty, unresponsive console controls to the keyboard + mouse. Control of Wake is frequently taken from the player to 'show' him that enemies are about to attack and for 'cinematic dodges', these are annoying since they frequently disorient you.
Combat in this game is the work of the Devil, it's hideously bad, uncreative and tedious - and there is a lot of it as the game is REALLY padded out between the cutscenes that advance the story. Enemies are the same and 'bosses' don't require any special tactics or learning. It's something that just has to be endured to get to the decent part, which is the story. Overall, good story, would have been MUCH better as an open world game and the many forest hiking levels needed to be 30% smaller and not filled with so much ♥♥♥♥♥♥ boring combat. Limited replayability. Maybe just watch an LP and save yourself the 10 hours of un-fun combat.

Utterly fantastic space simulation game. I cannot recommend this game enough, it has brought me hours of fun and has really managed to enable me to rediscover my personal passion for space exploration.
There are three main game modes: Career, Science, and Sandbox.
In Career mode you take control of your own space program and must manage administrative, financial, and logistical aspects of your space program. There is a detailed research system for unlocking new technologies to use in your spacecraft. You will take contracts from various organizations, earning money upon completion. These contracts will get progressively more challenging and rewarding as you advance your space program.
In Science mode you are free from the financial and administative burdens of career mode but are still faced with having to research technology for your spacecraft. You progress along the tech tree by performing various science experiments on your home planet and various other celestial bodies, with experiments performed in more distant and challenging environments granting more beneficial rewards.
In Sandbox mode you are free to build and explore whatever you like and are not limited by any tech tree or financial limits.
+In-dept and accurate space simulation with realistic physics and particularly noteworthy orbital mechanics.
+Very challenging and rewarding gameplay.
+Wide variety of celestial bodies to explore.
+Ability for player to choose from a selection of pre-built spacecraft or construct their own using a very intricate construction system featuring a large variety of parts to choose from.
+Features unmanned probes aswell as spacecraft piloted by Kerbals.
+Optional communications system for unmanned probes which require them to have a connection to mission control. This adds an additional layer or difficulty and realism to the unmanned space program, allowing for the construction of satellite communication networks around the star system.
+Excellent community.
+Large amounts of
mods available.
+Very large explosions.
+New features are still being added by the developers.
~Planets, although
large, are not realistically large.
~Celestial bodies are (somewhat accurately) extemely empty and desolate, with few surface features apart from a few rocks or trees
~Does not feature any real form of pre-made story (though the player is free to make their own).
~Does not feature any online functionality or multiplayer.
~Has a very steep learning curve, particularly for players with no previous knowledge of orbital mechanics or astrophysics, though a wide variety of
easily available.
~Unfortunatley lacks Steam Workshop support as of the time of writing.
-Not a particullarly good looking game. (Personally, I use a variety of mods which make the game look
.)
-Can have some performance issues when dealing with extremely large spacecraft. (significatly improved as of the 1.2 update)
-Some may consider the game to be a bit too expensive.
Overall, I would thoroughly recommend this game to anyone with an interest in space, adventure, or very large explosions. In my opinion, no other game can give you the same amazing feeling as when you first land kerbals on the moon (Mun). This game has brought me so much fun, and I simply love it.

The Banner Saga 2 is, in many ways, a definite improvement over the first game/first act of the story. But at the same time, as it's strengths are unchanged, so are the weaknesses. It still looks and sounds great, even if it's strangely locked to unchangeable and dynamically adapting to your desktop resolution setting. The story is expanding and growing in very interesting directions, never feeling like it's retreading the same steps and evolving the characters and the storyline as it goes. Although, the fact that it's just a second act of three feels even stronger here, this being the mid-point of the saga - there're too many hints and not enough answers by now and I'm hoping the developers can really unload all this build-up in the third part with grace.
But the battles are still the same boredom as before, despite new classes and types of enemies. I know, I'm not a fan of such games so it's clearly not for me, but I'm genuinely surprised that with the story as important as it is in this game, there's no "story-only" mode that just skips the battles or leaves them to the random element based on how your characters are developed, to skip past what people like me will find boring. As strange is the fact that none of the RPG stats still mean anything outside the battles and aren't actually used to define anything in the choices you can make in the story. Which ultimately makes me feel that while I can understand the financial reasons behind the 3 separate releases, so far I feel like this disjointed, separated by years, narrative doesn't really benefit the story at all and I hope there's some special "The Complete Banner Saga" in planning, which will address the issues and make the story feel complete.

Now I'm just keeping my fingers crossed that Double Fine can keep it together and manage their budget enough to actually finish the whole game.

It was sixteen years. Good things come to those who wait.
If you like adventure games in the style of Full Throttle or the later Monkey Island titles, this is one of the finest. The first act is thematic, and by that I mean that's rich. And not just with the money you're going to give it, oh no -- I mean with themes. It has so much themes that it has to have two protagonists to fit them all in. This isn't a gimmick, and it feels very natural. You can switch between the two at whim, which should you get stumped by a puzzle on one of them, you can sleep on it be resuming the other's storyline. Without spoiling too much, I will say that although the two characters initially seem to be inhabbiting different universes, well, you'll see for yourself.
If you don't like adventure titles, then I can't say for sure if you'd like Broken Age. It doesn't transcend the genre, but is an exceptionally good addition to it. And it should be noted that veterans of the genre have stated that the puzzles are on the easier side, so your own familiarity with adventure game design might color your experience. Finally, as the blurb says, only Act 1 is available at this time, but the second part comes with the first, so we'll be getting it automatically once it is complete. Don't think of it as getting half a game. Instead think of it as eating half a cake and then saving the other half for later. Possibly months later. But it's a kind of cake that gets BETTER with time instead of getting stale and then moldy.
So Broken Age is like a non-moldy cake. That's basically what I'm saying.

Invisible Inc turns turn based strategy into a tense stealth game where every single move can mean life and death. The hacking elements feel natural while enhancing the tension. The plot isn't that fleshed out, nor is the world, but it does have a very distinctive cyberpunk look. The characters aren't really involved in the storyline either, but each one is distinct and interesting. They get very few lines, I'm still waiting for Internationale to give me that lecture on the condition of the Global Proletariat, but through visuals and abilities they still feel nicely fleshed out. All this game needs to be one of my favourites is a multiplayer mode. Either co-operatively controlling different agents in one team, or competitively running different teams of agents after the same goal.

Let me preface by saying that although my playtime was limited with my home account, I can assure you all I've played a great deal of the game with my fiance, as well as on my own with a friend's account.
Now, to the review. Mighty Switch Force Academy proves to be one of the most promising titles delivered by wayforward, and with it's development promises (including the community-shaped patches and changes), it may, upon 1.0 release, become something bigger and better than both MSF and MSF 2 combined. The replay value for this title currently has its ups, as getting par time is always fun, and the incentivising music and quirky enemies will keep you playing for awhile. Admittedly, the music IS the same from previous titles, but that's not necessarily a bad thing. If they could get virt on some more tracks for this (which they probably will), I'd wager to say it'd make the experience loads better.
It should be noted, however, that this game may not seem as appealing to newcomers to the series, as it takes heavily from the first game, this time with a zoomed-out camera. This is perfect for those MSF fans who love to speedrun, since it's made easier to plan out moves much quicker.
Oh, and while we're on the topic of speedrunning, the game makes it pretty darn fun to do so. Learning the layouts and applying your skill with the Switch mechanic and the platforming really makes for an excellent experience. My hope is the game will eventually deliver an integrated Workshop for players to share their layouts. It'd be interesting to see an incentivised player course system where things like custom skins for Patty or equipable spritepacks can be rewarded to players who complete a course on the Workshop (these rewards would be created by the same author of the course). A man can dream.
All in all, if you haven't already played the Hyper Drive Edition of the first MSF, then you should probably get your feet wet with that one, since I can understand the apprehension behind purchasing an early access title. If you're already familiar with the series, get this game, and support it! It's got great local multiplayer, and a par-time counter just like previous installments. Its already a fun game where it stands now, and it'll only get better from this point on, so get in on this now if you want to have an effect on this project's early stages of development.

Season 2 ultimately suffers from some of the same problems season 1 has -

Walking Dead: Season 2 is an alright game that is let down by the things that made the first season good.
Season 2 suffers from the same problem as season 1, you're given the illusion of choice rather than making choices that actually matter or impact the story.  Let a character die?  Oh well.  Save a character?  They'll barely be visible until they're killed off later in the same episode or the next one.  Make someone hate you, doesn't really matter.  Make someone like you, doesn't really matter.  Take the middle road, doesn't really matter.  Hey, we have the option of doing A or B, what do you think Clementine?  Well, turns out it doesn't matter what you think because you're going to go wherever the game tells you to go, do whatever the game tells you to do, or watch events happen in pretty much the same way despite what you tried to do.  The only exception to this comes in the last 5-10 minutes of the 5th episode, where the choices you make during that 5-10 minutes alone determines your final ending.  Now while the lack of choice bothered me somewhat in season 1, I was able to get over it because season 1 had other strengths that made it good.  The problem with season 2 is that many of these strengths are much weaker this time around.
The biggest problems with season 2 are the plot and stories.  A good drama has a natural flow and has characters making decisions that for the most part make sense, but maybe they face opposition or some long term plan comes to fruition against them or something unexpected but still sensical happens.  A bad drama has a poor flow and usually involves characters making terrible decisions for the sole purpose of making terrible decisions or having nonsensical things occur to drive the drama or shock the viewer.  Season 2 is full of bad drama and the game makes this very clear in its opening scene of episode 1.  There is no reason that Clementine wouldn't have been in the same bathroom as the 2 other characters she's traveling with.  The only reason she goes into a separate bathroom is to drive the plot.  This kind of bad drama continues throughout the game.  You'll constantly be asking yourself questions about why these nonsensical events are occuring.  It probably hits its biggest bad drama moment when the group runs into a Russian gang at the end of episode 4.  Yes, a Russian gang.  All I could do was shake my head at how poorly written this part was.  The Russians have no clue the group is coming that way, yet they have an ambush set in the middle of nowhere for them.  Why was that Russian dude hiding medicine/drugs in a trashcan in the middle of nowhere all by himself?  Why are they a 3+ hour walk from the cabin that they stay in?  The best part is, no matter what “choices” you make throughout that entire ordeal, it doesn't matter.  I could go on and on about the bad drama, but then I'd be mentioning most of the game.
The game is also much shorter than the first one, which wouldn't bother me if the quality was still as high, but it's not.  Due to the much shorter length, characters often don't feel as well developed and fleshed out.  Some of the characters that are actually given face time are decently written and likable (Luke & Jane), but other characters are pretty much one dimensional and forgettable (Alvin and Carlos), or are killed off 10 minutes after meeting them.  Another problem is that most of the major characters will randomly go off on you for no real reason at some point, no matter how much they supposedly like you.  Almost all of them act out of character or irrationally at some point to drive the current story to where the creators want it to go.
The game still has parts that are decent.  Dialogue is written well enough in certain areas.  Making some conversational choices are still fun depending on how you want Clementine to react to people, even if it doesn't matter.  The game also took an interesting approach allowing you to play as an 11 year old.  Characters typically don't think much of you until you prove to them that you're fully capable of handling yourself.  This was an interesting way for the game to have it make sense that all these people want your help and input into situations.
The very best part of the game...........
WD S2 isn't terrible, but it's hard to get past the constant bad drama, the lack of real character development, and the fact that your choices still have no real meaning.  Also, Kenny is a ♥♥♥♥♥boy, never forget that.

Microsoft Flight Simulator X: Steam Edition:
Coming from the regular boxed edition of FSX the switch to Steam Editon was a little bumpy at first with some of my favourite addons such as PMDG, Ultimate Traffic 2 and many more not working out of the box. Over time DLC developers updated their software to work with the new steam edition. So anyone planning to purchase FSX:SE now I'd say go right ahead.
For me I feel like the only really noticable improvement is with the content management now that DLC can be bought through steam. As for actual in-game performance I haven't noticed much/ if any improvement at all. If you play Flight Simulators often then the chances are you've built a pretty good PC to run the simulator well and so an improvement of 4 or 5 frames per second on top of your usual 30 isn't an awful deal.
Saying that I do appreciate how the multiplayer servers are back online and thus allow virtual pilots to fly together, this was a really nice editon to the updated game.
All in all FSX is really a must buy for any flight or aviation enthusiast with thousands of DLC aircraft, scenery and scenarios to purchase from the steam store and online FSX is probably the most supported flight sim available.

tl;dr
Snail-paced VN with poor 3D models and animation, created to tear up teenagers. Go watch 'Butterfly effect' with Kutcher — it is practically the same thing, but 6 times shorter.
I still wonder how this game has received so many top reviews: it is completely unoriginal in plot and technologically sub-par.
===================================
The game is extremely disappointing. All the reviews go about how touching the story is, how much you bond with the characters and how your choices matter. It has taken me 13hrs to finish 'Life is Strange' and I deeply regret spending my weekend on it. Although I might have enjoyed it, had it been shorter.
Well, first of all, the story is a "Butterfly effect" ripoff. Not absolutely lame, it had one major twist, but overall uderwhelming.
As for the choices: they do not matter at all. In the end it all goes down to one big decision at the finale that cancels anything that you have achieved. Honestly, I was expecting a much wider decision tree with lots of bad endings, which would start branching at episode 3.
But I gotta admit, that there quite a few ways to get to episode 5 (that, I emphasize, holds only 2 endings) which may entertain you until you get bored by the plot.
The game will constantly tell you the choices matter but that is big fat lies. So feel free to choose whatever YOU want as there is no way to end up in a non-existing bad ending.
I didn't feel emotional in any parts of the game. That may indicate that only the most sensitive people get to finish this game and leave a positive review, while people more like me tend to drop it halfway. I considered dropping it at episode 3, but still was hoping to see more basic problems discussed in end episodes. But unfortunately. I get just a story about how you can't judge a book by its cover and how important friendship is.
The gameplay is the weakest part of 'Life is Strange'. You may like the story, but gameplay is what nobody can enjoy. Despite it being basically a VN , you can't fast forward or access text log, you constantly have to watch annoyingly long cut scenes with emo music and sometimes the game will throw boring tasks at you like 'collect five bottles'.
Also the movement speed has really gotten on my nerve. You may jog in the game, but there is virtually no difference between jogging and walking.
My overall impression of the gameplay that the developers have decreased the pace of 'Life is Strange' as much as they could on purpose, so they could publish it as a 13h 5-part game and not as a 4h short VN.
The replay value is extremely low. Firstly, you lose interest in replaying as soon as you learn there are only 2 endings. And secondly, you can't speed up the replay, which means you'll practically need to sit through all the scenes you have already seen to discover the new ones.

Darkness can be a frightening thing. It was certainly a factor for my childhood; anything beyond the crisp reaches of light was out of bounds, and I’d do everything in my power to stay in. Anything could be lurking in those shadows. What if there was only perpetual night, and there really were dark creatures out there? In the town of Bright Falls, that’s exactly what happens.

Alan Wake is a psychological thriller which draws the majority of its inspiration from darkness, and what happens when those with an active imagination are thrust into it.
The titular character - a famous horror writer – escapes with his wife to Bright Falls for a holiday, and to help write his next novel. Things turn south when his wife goes missing, and he is haunted by an evil supernatural presence. It goes from bad to worse when he then realises that he is now the protagonist of a horror novel he cannot remember writing.
My impressions after roughly halfway through the game were not positive. I had a massive break from the game, because when I left it, it just wasn’t engaging enough to return to. It felt like the creators got together in the back corner of a cinema lobby: “Hey, how many cliché horror references do you think we can get thrown into to one game?”
The swarms of crows, the axe through the door (here’s Johnny!), and the plot twists (was it all his imagination?) were all just collected from other sources, mainly Stephen King. Which they certainly don’t deny; in the very first monologue, his name is mentioned, and it isn’t the only time.
The gameplay mechanics, although initially fresh, began to feel repetitive as you run through the dark woods from generator to generator, hoping to step under that pool of light before the “Taken” reached you. Shining your torch on these Taken until they’re rendered vulnerable and shooting them is the only way to take them down. Flares and flashbangs were fun to get out of that sticky situation, too.
Anyway, this was before I left the game for a year. My recent impulsion to finish all those incomplete games brought me back, and I’m glad it did. The plot, although a little complicated and brandished with a few pot holes, did turn in the right direction. The challenges in the game did gradually increase (dang haunted bulldozers), and the game wasn’t afraid to have a little fun on the way, most notably when defending a music stage on an old farm, blasting the Taken while the rock plays on.
While the graphics weren’t pushing the boundaries when the game was released, the visual direction was excellent. Stalking through darkness only to have an old trawler boat land metres in front out of nowhere is hard to see coming.
It wasn’t Game of the Year material, but it was fun to escape into the Darkness.

It's one of the best games I have ever played. It beautifully merges the mechanics of a turn-based strategy title like XCOM or Jagged Alliance with something like Metal Gear Solid or Splinter Cell. Turn based stealth may seem to be a weird concept in theory, but it is executed wonderfully here.
One playthrough of the campaign will probably take you only a couple of hours, but here's the deal; every playthrough allows you to unlock new means (agents and programs) to tackle the increasingly difficult obstacles you are faced with.
Maps are randomly generated, so the game offers nigh-endless replayabilty and you are constantly left wanting for more (which is evidenced by the time I've spend playing this title).
What is more, different combinations of agents and programs you start with, force you to alter your strategy (i. e. while it is usually wiser to knock people out, some characters like Draco from the DLC might actually gain benefits if you rack up a lot of kills early on) so you can experiment with different playstyles as well.
The aesthetics of the game are gorgeous; the graphics and artsyle give a wonderful vibe, the music perfectly sets up the mood of the game (it starts slow, but gradually becomes more frantic as the situation grows more dire) and the voice acting is really good (although it is used rather sparingly).
I enjoy a challenge in games like this and I am happy to say I find the difficulty of the game to be great as well. You can choose from many difficulty levels, and it seems it is best to play through them all in order to get acquianted with all the mechanics of the game. You genuinely have to get better at the game to tackle the harder settings.
If at any point you'll find a single element of the gameplay is not to your liking, you can choose the 'custom' difficulty which gives you a lot of reedom to tweak the gameplay exactly as you want it (to make the game easier/harder as you see fit).
As a fan of both the new XCOM titles and stealth games I can confidently say this is the game I've always been waiting for and I can wholeheartedly recommend it.
Still, I understand this is not a title for everyone. Turn based stealth is a rather novel concept and it may not be to everyone's liking. However, If you found anything I wrote here even remotely appealing, you would be doing yourself a great disservice by not trying this game out.

My 2nd OVERDUE review of the game.
Now the game revolves around clementine who's turned 11. You would control her to do all the choosing and how the story would goes.
Comparing this to the first game where we used Lee to sort of protect her and what needed to be done to keep her alive is much more.. unemotional to me. Why? Because you are playing her.. You're not making the difficult decisions as an adult, you're what's best for her AKA yourself. It's all straight forward decisions so you can go super rude/selfish and so what? If you played Lee you know she is fragile and what you do, Clementine would see it and use it as a role model.
Besides that, the decision making in this game considering she is 11 years old(eventhough its a post apocalyptic world) are not that logic? I'll explain it in detail below the line.
Overall I would say (7.5 + 1)/10
Still recommends it even though you can sort of see *****spoiler***** it doesn't really matters what decision you made in the middle of the game it would just goes back to the original story. Like saving one guy and the next episode he wouldn't really have much impact of the story later on. Telltale.. I know it's difficult but you have to make it bigger and more significant.
+1 for an ending I didn't choose but it's wayyy more emotional than the one that I chose.
***Beyond this are the slight spoilers for the game. Do not read if you haven't finished the game***
I'm a logic person that has some give and take. Here's my thoughts.
The game ask you as the clementine to do alot of things. I wouldnt trust a 11 year old kid to turn off a wind turbine. Although you can argue with me that the other is "covering" her while she is figuring it out. It just not make sense to me that you would let a few years worth of education kid to figure out things.
Also I definitely don't trust her to be on the driver seat of the car. I would rather gave her the baby to hold on to (even with the bullet wound) than having her to drive the car in case of any emergency. It could be worst. All of them could die (although the game wont do that of course).
I'm fine with sneaky stuff though. It's just her speciallity. No one else could do it better than her. Or handling a gun(it's a zombie apocalype for god sake). So i'm good on those.
Yes she's grown up and has to be independent but if I'm there I wont let her do that stuff. I would rather teach her bit by bit. Not resting on what might possibly be life and death situation.
In the end. Whenever I heard Lee, I would have a flashback of what happened ( just like what you would get if you are falling.. your life flashes before you kind of thing ). I have never ever played a game that I'm so emotionally attached to and feel sad whenever I heard Lee. It's like you really are missing someone in your life. They have really
done it good.
Some of the choices got me good. I had to rethink the choices that I made, whether it was for the better or not. And some choices even affects me a few days in my real life. I kept thinking did I made the right choice and tried to convince myself that I'm right to make that choice.

This is why Steam needs a "meh" option. Combat and the tech tree are unbalanced as hell and clunky. But the story makes all your choices seem to matter. Even the order of doing missions seems to affect outcomes. Making me want to play through the game again. The dialog wheel works better than Fallout 4 or Mass effect, as the choices come down to "007", "Jack Bauer", "Archer". Meaning the entire tone of the game could change.
But that combat and unbalanced tech tree really hurt the game, as you can imagine it is a big part of the game....

Flight Simulator 10 is an odd duck of a game to be sure. I feel some days it is not as much a game but an operating system. The potential is one of the allures to the game, some days it feels like it is as close as you can get to real world flying and have fun doing it. I own X plane 7 and 9 do not want to argue about realism.  X plane is the cheapest wind tunnel you can buy it can simulate planes that do not exist yet and can do things by the numbers, It is technically better a better simulator, so why not just fly X plane?  I have never been able to completely switch over because Flight Simulator feels more fun.
X Plane uses a Blade element theory to figure out flight.  Lift is simulated by flowing virtual air over an approximation of a virtual wing. This is very good, the feeling of lift and interaction of lift and balance of a plane is well represented. If you design a new plane and want to sort of know if it works you can. It falls short where there are odd drag or flow interactions on a plane that make the perfect math model not match the real world.
Flight Simulator 10 uses Table lookup so the planes are more of a grab bag. They only can simulate the Data and are only as good as the Data in the table. Some mod planes all feel the same because they don't have the flight model they deserve. It is cheaper to calculate the plane this way computer wise.  It has fun multiplayer and with a good plane it is wonderful. If I were to start today I would buy FSX 10 and the A2A piper cub
and a Joystick, and have fun.
Flight Simulator is not a trouble free game; it is much better as the steam edition then the boxed version of the past. All problems are solvable with some reading, and people are usually nice and knowledgeable. I needed to install the Orbx Felts field and had an error of missing building tops  I needed to write into a forum to get an answer, and it has been patched, but sometimes things don’t always work as you would expect them. I have had good luck with windows 10 no real errors or crashes when flying. I found if when I am choosing a flight and click out of the game window and start looking stuff up on line or starting other programs it will get mad at me and crash. It is a far cry from the boxed edition when I would save on a schedule so I didn’t have to start the flight over from the beginning and crash at the same spot. As long as the crashes are just in the menu and only because I am trying to multitask I can live with that. I also hope with continued development we will see 64-bit version in the future.
If you want to shoot down stuff, have latest technology or have a very short attention span then this game is not for you. If you love learning new things, detail, tinkering, flying, messing with how computers and graphics work, moding, or honing a skill this could be the game for you.

I have to say, I really wanted to like this game.
There certainly are a lot of compelling, well done mechanics of the game, but they don't seem to flow together very well.
The combat is incredibly repetitve, the cover and aiming systems are occasionally finnicky and annoying. My biggest concern with combat is the viewport. The field of view makes it very difficult to scan the area and locate all of the enemies. Meanwhile, the all know your
location if there is an alarm going off. Part of a stealth game is the ability to have information about your environment and the enemy, and I can't tell you how many times I set off an alarm because I couldn't see a guard walking around a corner as I climbed some stairs.
The story was somewhat derivative, but the choices effects on the storyline were very well done. That said, the dialogue system feels a bit clunky. First of all, you usually have to make your decision before the other person has even finished talking, so it doesn't feel like you're responding, but rather choosing a stance before you know what's happening. There is also a perk you get for choosing one of each stance in a conversation. Interestingly, the left, top, and right choices seem to be hard coded to a type,  there are a few times where the three options are not related to a personality but are just collecting various intel about the upcoming mission, but you can still get the perk that way. There are also many characters who show up once and seem super important and then never have any effect on the story.
Lastly, the main character's writing/voiceacting is AWFUL. I can't stress enough how forced all of his lines were and how his tone failed to fit the moment. Very often I regretted some of my dialogue choices not because of what they were but because of how dull the character was saying them.

TL;DR Good gameplay and an engaging story allow the game to overcome some flaws/annoyances.
Overall, I really enjoyed my time with both this game and the first one in the series. Banner Saga 2 makes no changes or improvements to the game graphically or in terms of UI. In fact, it seems as if they simply made one really long game and broke it into three stages for release. However, it is strong enough to merit a full playthrough.
Pros:
- The battle system is strategic and deep enough that it is both challenging and rewarding. Also, losing battles changes the course of the game (in most cases) without requiring a reset.
- The story is very engaging, if very confusing at times.
- The choices you make seem to have a genuine impact on how the story plays out, even though there really is just one conclusion that is reached regardless of your choices.
- The art, sound effects, and music are both absolutely gorgeous.
Cons:
- There were two storylines to follow in this game. One (the Alette/Rook march) offered considerably more by way of items and party growth opportunities, which meant I always looked forward to those chapters more. The dichotomy was aggravating.
- It's really hard to tell what decisions are going to lead to what specific actions, so it's hard to judge which decisions will have impacts you like.
- The final battle (not including chapter 15) is very easy.
- The story did not really climax in this game. It's very clearly just setting up for the third game.
- Character development is pretty boring. If you're someone who really likes to develop characters along specific tracks that have heavy decision making portions, this is not the game for you. Each character has one or two decisions you can make for them (which special skills to learn, where to put the skill points) but since you'll only earn about 14 skill points per character in a playthrough, there are very few decisions to make.
- This game's decisions are easier and more impactful on the player if you played the first game more recently and remember certain characters and characteristics. One particular character's (Ludin's) story is significantly more interesting if you remember him from the first game. This isn't necessarily a fault of the game, but it did take away from my experience as I haven't played the first one in quite a while.
- The UI needs some work...also, why can't we undo move actions? Many other games in the genre allow it and it makes things more forgiving.
Verdict: 8/10

Well, them vikin boys are back at it again. Runnin around the entire world and whatnot. Really makes you think, huh? What we got here is a more refined Banner Saga 1.
First question: would you need to buy the Banner Saga 1 to understand what happens in the Banner Saga 2?
Answer: Yes, more or less. This is a direct sequel, and I'd expect the Banner Saga 3 to follow suit. This game takes some time to spell out things, and throw in some more flavor via character bios; but if you're looking for the whole picture of what's going on, I'd recommend buying and playing the first game.
Second question: what's different this time around?
Answer: The game feels a lot more cohesive this time. Things are a bit more fleshed out comparatively to the first game in the series; and overall things seem to be a bit more thought out. Its an improvement, but the basis of the game is largely unchanged.
So, things are really heating up in banner land and the end of the world is upon us. And no walls are gonna save you when the dredge come a knockin, so sir. It was like that in the first game, but this time things seem to be spiraling downwards more rapidly than before. Viking land is all but destroyed, and anybody left is angry and hungry. It is in this great time of crisis that you are asked to lead your people to safety.
In that respect, Banner Saga 2 is exactly the same as the first game. A series of events stand in your way to the promised land. Some of them are tricky. Some of them are predictable. Others are surprising for different reasons. Now, of course, these events are scripted; and like the first game, major story beats are exactly the same no matter who you're swinging battle axes at. But the biggest difference I can tell is that the enemies of tBS2 are far more varied than before. Previously, you were either fighting dredge or raiders. This time around, everyone's out to get you; much like what would happen in a more typical apocalyptic fantasy Viking adventure. The dredge are more varied. The raiders are far less common. Different animals and beasts show up to the battle to eat you and your people before lunch on any given day. This makes the game a lot more interesting, especially from a resource management perspective.
Your decisions actually have downsides, and I was second guessing myself sometimes as to what was the best way to do things. Wasting food, being careless with your heroes, trying to push with low morale; all of these things make the game significantly harder, which is interesting. I didn't find the game particularly hard, but I was definitely challenged by some of the battles. Some of them can be downright brutal, as this game really likes throwing waves of enemies at you. Expect to be consistently outnumbered in just about any fight. tBS2, does however reward bravery and the clever use of resources. Various bonuses can be earned throughout the game to make the game a lot less punishing.
Overall, I was pleased with this game. In my opinion, this game is standing head and shoulders above the prequel. There's a great deal more at play here, from the battles, to the heroes, to the mechanics and the choices. Everything comes together very nicely. One complaint I do have is that the game doesn't have an ending per se, being that it's part two of three. However, I am excited about what's to come, and I'd welcome an even more improved third part to send the trilogy off with.

As advertised, it really is a... mountain simulator. A really fun and thought-provoking one, at that.
All you have to do is start it up, leave it open, and go about your other business. Simply peek in from time to time or when you hear a ping announcing that your mountain has a thought to share. A few hours pass and you won't recognize your mountain anymore under piles of fun, but also meaningful stuff that drops onto it. Where are the things coming from? What is their purpose? Is the mountain aware of them? Seems like it is... just like it is aware of the weather, time of day, and its own existence.
It's obvious that Mountain is not a game for everyone. It is a peaceful, lazy, laid-back experience, with a touch of philosophy and a sprinkle of peculiar humor added to the mix. Recommended with all my heart.

The Walking Dead Season 2 picks up Clementine's story not long after the end of Season 1, and this  is definitely Clementine's show in much the same way that Season 1 was Lee's story. If you've played the previous game in this series or any other older or more current Telltale game, then you basically know what to expect from this one, and, frankly, you've probably already formed an opinion about it. People love or hate Telltale games, mostly because they're not really adventure games in any conventional sense except the narrowest possible one: they focus on relaying a narrative to the player. Telltale games are about watching cutscenes unfold with dialog choices that propel the story in one direction or another and occasionally too-frequent QTEs. Whether this constitutes the kind of game that you personally enjoy is a matter of taste; I do.
In Season 2, we see Clem lose old friends, gain new allies, fight new enemies, and, at the end, lose another old friend. In short, it's basically what you would expect from a tale set in this fictional world, but the story and characters are mostly well-written and compelling. You don't have the same sense of attachment to them as you did in the first series because there are so many groups in this one. However, I did find my eyes leaking fluid near the end. Damn you, Telltale, you did it again.
This game features Telltale's typical cell-shaded art style and high-quality voice acting. Highly recommended.

So I'm starting to go for early access a lot more often now, and for Judgment I'm happy to say it's worth the buy.
First, the systems are all simple and easy to access. You click survivors, you tell them what to do, you build your new colony. The farming, crafting, and research system are all easy to access for beginners, and for veteran strategy players the game is relatively effective in conveying the sense that your small band is rebuilding something from the end of the world. Of course things are simplified ("I just built a glock pistol!" "How, we're still learning how to fight basic infections!") but the general idea of how the game is supposed to function is there. And this is only after a few hours of gameplay, so I can only imagine what will happen later on.
My larger complaint comes from the story, or more accurately the lack thereof. Of course since the game is still in early access the developers are undoubtedly pursuing a good storyline to explore the apocalypse. However, I would like to see maybe a less expensive research tree. Maybe I'm supposed to build multiple research labs, but for now when you're trying to get started in the early game several of the food and crafting technologies seem a little too costly in terms of research and occult research points. Also, I don't feel like the world map quite gets you interested in going out in the world to explore. Maybe adding in random survivors to find, or various other obstacles and rewards to find in the game? I have mentioned this in the Discussion section, but I would also like to see various rival survivor groups involved in the game as well, just to add more dimension to the game. An in-game encyclopedia of world locations, demon entries, and just some in-character lore would be pretty immersive as well.
Overall, definitely a game to watch for the full release of. Get in on the ground floor now so you can see it grow and play it through.

I have to say, I really wanted to like this game.
There certainly are a lot of compelling, well done mechanics of the game, but they don't seem to flow together very well.
The combat is incredibly repetitve, the cover and aiming systems are occasionally finnicky and annoying. My biggest concern with combat is the viewport. The field of view makes it very difficult to scan the area and locate all of the enemies. Meanwhile, the all know your
location if there is an alarm going off. Part of a stealth game is the ability to have information about your environment and the enemy, and I can't tell you how many times I set off an alarm because I couldn't see a guard walking around a corner as I climbed some stairs.
The story was somewhat derivative, but the choices effects on the storyline were very well done. That said, the dialogue system feels a bit clunky. First of all, you usually have to make your decision before the other person has even finished talking, so it doesn't feel like you're responding, but rather choosing a stance before you know what's happening. There is also a perk you get for choosing one of each stance in a conversation. Interestingly, the left, top, and right choices seem to be hard coded to a type,  there are a few times where the three options are not related to a personality but are just collecting various intel about the upcoming mission, but you can still get the perk that way. There are also many characters who show up once and seem super important and then never have any effect on the story.
Lastly, the main character's writing/voiceacting is AWFUL. I can't stress enough how forced all of his lines were and how his tone failed to fit the moment. Very often I regretted some of my dialogue choices not because of what they were but because of how dull the character was saying them.

I love post apocalypse games, but most are either zombie apocalypse or nuclear apocalypse. This feels refreshing in that it's a demonic apocalypse. I've not played as many games with that setting and this one combines RPG aspects with settlement building/management and rescuing/upgrading survivors. I like that you can send multiple search parties out to scavenge multiple locations while some people stay back at the base and maintain/improve it. I'm up to 19 survivors now and haven't lost any despite the odd combat system. It's not bad, it just feels off and I think it can use some work. I like that you can pause combat and issue commands to your survivors, but the battles don't last long enough for some of the survivors to do something as simple as cross to the opposite side of an enemy to attack them from behind. Again, I haven't lost any survivors yet and I don't dislike the combat system-I'm not even sure what they could do to improve it, I just believe it frustrates many other players as much as it does me at times and I want to warn potential buyers in advance. On the base building side, it's incredibly useful to be able to reconfigure your survivors' priorities to individually manage what they're doing every minute of the day. It's important to optimize your colony by making survivors do what they're best at more than what they prefer to do. For example, one or 2 of my survivors prefer chopping trees and farming, but they suck at it and are really good at researching, so I don't let them farm or gather resources-they just research. The AI is still a little wonky, so sometimes they seem to completely ignore what i want them to do, but I think it has to do with how high the task you want them to do is in their list of priorites as well as whether you have the available crafting table to make the item AND how high that item is in the list of overall crafting priorities. (I often notice they're not making the item I want when I want it.)
Since it's currently still in early access, it's not quite a finished game and it's apparent in the research tree that is upfront with players that some of the final techs aren't implemented yet. I'm excited to see what alchemy and machines add to this game that already has magic rituals to make your survivors wanna eat less, your food grow faster, the rain to come, to summon enemies and to weaken them in combat. I love the many different locations that can be scavenged such as hospitals, schools, churches, supermarkets, military bases, etc. Each location tends to have loot geared towards what one would expect to find there-for example: rare research books in schools, or weapon parts in a military base. It's a nice little extra bit of realism and makes me more excited when I find a location I need for a new technology or demonic ritual. I don't know if you can eventually establish new colonies and slowly take back the map/world from the demonic invasion and rebuild civilization. I don't know if that's the direction they're heading with this game, but I'm excited to see however this game evolves until it's full release. In summation, I love this game and have definitely found a new favorite-I definitely recommend checking out this game.
Edit: I'm now 30 hours into the game and I have more than 23 survivors and still counting. I'm not sure if there's a limit to how many you can have, but at 38 game days, my survivors have looted all locations within a 7 block radius of my base and the fights are getting longer and my survivors are actually able to respond to/utilize my battle tactics during combat missions. My base also has enough survivors that I can constantly keep 3-4 squads out in the world scavenging new locations and continuously bringing in fresh supplies as I amass resources and slowly research the last few techs I need to take on this hellgate I see on the map that's guarded by more enemies than I've seen in one location before. It's going to be a tough fight and I'm certain I'll have some casualties, but I'm tense with anticipation for this upcoming fight that has the feel of the ending to the game-or at least as it stands in its current early access state.

The sequel to Banner Saga retains all the aspects that made that game great and set it apart. Think of it as having all of the moment-to-moment decision making weight of a game like XCOM while telling you a story that's much stranger and more personal (in an odd way). Gripping story with meaningful decisions and tense tactical combat make Banner Saga 2 punch in a much higher weight class.
Art design is unique and conveys the world's mystery/mythology and norse-like aesthetic sensibilities, while the writing is wonderfully concise, doing a really effective job of conveying character and plot in a way that's not only meaningful but clarifies the stakes in player decisions.
The turn-based tactical combat is, as well, tense with weighty decisions. Each upgrade or skill feels useful and unique, each movement an opportunity and risk. There's no dice rolling, just execution of your (good or bad) strategy - it's really marvelous.
Play this game!
Note - there is at least 1 more game coming, so the ending is a bit of a cliffhanger. That said, the resolution of this narrative arc is suitably 'complicated' for the player - I don't think it's a letdown at all, but rather (and in line with the overall narrative) keeps things from descenting into a black-and-white worldview.

Once you manage to survive one of those rounds, you go back to mopping up little dinosaurs.
The weapons are not bad, but aiming down the sights is pretty much useless, as I've experienced.  The AI is also pretty stupid, as the dinosaurs mindlessly run at you as soon as the game starts.  This is the sort of thing I'd expect from a game that was released ten years ago.  The game is obviously old fashioned; the graphics look like something from 2007 that got touched up a little with some motion blur.
Overall, there's very little to say about this game.  It's very forgettable, and once you've played it for ten minutes, you've seen it all.  Mann vs. Machine from Team Fortress 2 is better than this, and it's free.  My friend bought this game for me, but I still couldn't imagine spending $1 on this game, let alone $15.  If you have 99 cents burning a hole in your Steam funds, give this game a shot.  But once the sale ends, do not even think about shelling $15 dollars on this game.  It is simply not worth it.

This is a turn-based stealth game.
It's brilliant!
I don't like stealth, turn-based strategy and cyberpunk.
I love this game.
Here's why:
This game does everything right - variety, replayability, story, gameplay and graphics.
Perfection.
In other games, cyberpunk is gritty, depressing and outdated, in this game it feels fresh and exciting.
I don't like stealth games like Dishonoured because it forces me to do stealth when the non-stealth approach is faster and more fun.
In this game, stealth doesn't feel slow, and mistakes can be re-winded.
And you'll never fail because of platforming slip or just slower reaction.
Movement is more precise because it's tile-based, you can see everything - where enemies will move and what do they see.
Because everything is in turns, there's a lot of time to plan and enemies won't walk on you while you're thinking.
This game shows that turn-based strategy and stealth are made for each other.
Buy it when you can.

Broken Age is a simple, point & click adventure game that returns to its roots.  I love this game.
I find it difficult to pick out many faults in the game, yeah, people were disappointed with how people backed this project to 3 million dollars and got a 2D adventure game, as opposed to something greater, which I can understand.  But this turned out extremely well as both an adventure game and a nostalgia trip.  The thing with a lot of nostalgia trip games is, they focus more on the nostalgia value than something original, what this game did, was make something nostalgic, but original at the same time.
I remember when I was a child and I used to play the old Indiana Jones games on ScummVM, along with all the Monkey Island games, and this game almost succesfully brought me back to being a child, playing those classic games...but then there's the difficulty, which is one of the few problems I could scrape off from this game's proverbial barrel, the game felt too easy in its puzzles.
There was like, one puzzle that really stumped me, and that was this one part in Shay's story where you have to alter the Space Weaver's direction with the Crotchet Hook.  But other than that, I pretty much blasted through all the puzzles without much pause for thought.  Now, the differance between this and Tim Schafer's older adventure games from the '90s is the colossal change in difficulty in comparison.  Both the Monkey Island games and the Indiana Jones games stumped me a lot more than once as a child, and still does today!  But with this, it just feels a little dumbed down.
And the voice acting is great, not really much else to say, other than Jack Black's appearance amused me, it felt really unneccesary to the voice acting prosess and really felt like he was just there because he's Jack Black.  Whereas Elijah Wood fit the character Shay really well, and did a great job, typical of a Hollywood actor.  Jennifer Hale is great as the mother figure and makes the character feel almost geniune, for a computer. Masasa Moyo did a brilliant job as Vella, who is one of my favorite characters in the game. (my personal favorite being a mix of the vomiting tree and The Spoon).  And Pendleton Ward as Gus kind of woked, in a weird way, with that voice that feels like it's slowly slipping into an Lumpy Space Princess voice.  And everyone else did a good job!
Music felt a little all-over-the-place here, it didn't know if it wanted to be epic, or simple background music.  It's great, but it didn't feel like it sat very well with the game most of the time, except for the some of the background music.  The one piece of music I loved was the music that came in when Vella rode the bird into Cloud Town, it really made me want to slay a beast!
Art/graphics were really stylized and really nice to look at, which gave me an overpowering sense of childlike wonder, just like its storyline, it's almost like playing a children's story-book; surreal and wonderful.  It's just a pretty game to me overall.  And it also reminded me quite heavily of Psychonauts with its character designs and surreality, and the funny thing is that they actually got the original voice actor for Raz to voice character here!  And he also does well here!  I also have a love for great lighting in artwork.
The story is so simplistic, just like an oldschool point and click...but with a slightly modern twist!  It's a coming-of-age story, and the game's title makes alot of sense in that regard, and I don't tend to care much for coming-of-age stories but this is one that I could really latch on to.  The story is simplistic and surreal like a children's story, like I said before.  And I honestly believe this could work extremely well as a story-book for teens and children alike, Tim Schafer: Please make this happen!
And well, yeah! Can't wait for Act 2!  This was a really great game to play through and I'm glad I bought this, thank you Tim Schafer for making another great game, and a possible game of the year!  Thank you for reading this review!  Thank you, backers for making this game exist!  Thank you, Jack Black for being Jack Black!  Thank you, Double-Fine Studios for existing!  And thank you Jesus!  Good-night!

I know I'm supposed to write a review here, but I will not. Instead, I'll tell a tale. A tale of an Assassin, a tale of a Machine, a Tale of a Ruin. A tale of Borgu.
It all began when I was around level 12, minding my own business and killing some orcs along the way. During my adventure, I found this orc, Borgu, the Assassin. He looked just like every other orc, nothing special about him, so I thought I would just take him out like every other until then. Oh, what a mistake. He crushed me - He was fast, he had this annoying poisoned weapons, and, to make matters even worse, he had this No Chance ability. He killed me once. He killed me twice. And he just kept killing me. For gods sakes, he killed me 5 times!
But things were about to change. I was starting to build my own army and decided to use that against him. By then, he had already murdered his way to Warchief (which he achieved by killing one of my best Captains), so I thought I would infiltrate his army and kill him from inside. And so I did.
I had 3 spies ready to assassinate the Assassin, and I gave the order. We cornered him, and it was a bloodbath. When I broke him, I didn't even think about dominating him (which, I found out later, I wouldn't be able to do because his level was higher than mine) - So I cut him in half. And that was it for the Assassin.
After getting hid of him, things got sad - I missed my Nemesis more than I though I would. And I guess he missed me as well.
I was on this random mission, once again killing some orcs, and I heard this voice yelling at me. I looked and just couldn't believe what I just saw: his name was Borgu, The Machine. The Machine tribe found him and put him back together, piece by piece, until he became a new orc, ready to spread Progress by murdering everyone in the name of Machines. He looked different, he fought different, but everytime he mocked me when he was about to unleash his final blow, I could see that, deep inside, he was still the same Borgu I've met so long ago.
And so it went - everytime he killed me, he became stronger and I became thirstier for revenge. But this time, I didn't want more surprises. So I fought him with everything I had, broke him, shamed him so that, finally, I could dominate him and put him in my army. And he was the best overlord I ever had.
Time went on, I was way stronger now - level 32 - and decided to pass by that region so I could upgrade my fortress and train my orcs. But it didn't go quite as planned.
There were we, Borgu, another Bodyguard and I, ready to intervene on a fight between 3 captains. Things were supposed to go smooth, they were way weaker than us. But luck wasn't on our side that day. It was chaos - fire everywhere, my army crumbling to the ground, and there, at a distance, I saw it happening. One of our enemies struck Borgu from behind. I cringed while his lifeless body fell to the ground. He was, once more, dead, and, now, he wouldn't come back. Or so I thought.
I had my revenge on them, on all of them, only to be killed soon after that by a random grunt, who later became a crucial part on this tale.
I went on a vendetta mission against this ex-grunt who killed me - found him guarding a passage on a secondary fortress. They never saw me coming. It was all going well, until a poisoned spear hit me from the back, and I heard a voice, a voice I never thought I would hear again. There he was, Borgu the Machine, alive, stronger than ever, and ready to kill me for leaving him behind. But, that night, he didn't get to kill me, the ex-grunt managed to do it once more.
Eventually, I killed the ex-grunt (whose name I just can't remember anymore) and went to find Borgu - Our story had to have a closure. This time, I planned to kill him for good -  I wouldn't be able to dominate him again because his level was, again, higher than mine and because he acquired the Iron Will skill, and I just couldn't risk leaving him alive. And then we fought, only the two of us, while his men ran away in fear of morgflies. It was an epic fight, exactly as I thought our final duel had to be. Finally, there he was, on his knees, waiting for the final blow. But I couldn't do it. I decided to give him one more chance - to shame him, wishing that he would lose the Iron Will skill and that, then, I would be able to recruit him one final time.
Of course, it didn't go as planned. When I shamed him, he yelled "I can't go crazy! I can't!" and just ran away. Borgu, the Machine was dead. Borgu, the Ruined, was born.
It was, now, my mission to find him and help him - I turned him into that deranged beast, and, after everything we went through together, I couldn't just let him go like that.
I found him in a camp crying that he was crazy, that everything was crazy, and, once more, managed to recruit him to my army. This time, I promoted him to warchief so that he could have at least a little bit of luxury in his madness (I would promote him to Overlord, but I just didn't think it would be a good idea considering his mental health).
Now, he's there, watching over my fortress and my overlord, and everytime someone try to invade my territory, it will hear the Ruined's cry.
The end(?)

First things first - I've finally learned my lesson and will only review a game after completing AT LEAST 50% of it.
Why did I change my mind? Well, turns out I still think it's a pretty good game, after all, but, after completing the story (at least most of it - I ignored de endgame content because I just could'nt take those green humanoids coming back from the dead to annoy me), I've realized that it just doesn't pay off... I'll try to quickly break it down:
GAMEPLAY - It's amazing at first, with quick paced battles, lot's of heads popping around, and so on...  But it gets just SO REPETITIVE, really, the orcs are always the same (except for captains, of course, but even them get boring after a while), the fort battles get annoying and extremely easy after the first 2 forts, its only rinse and repeat,  and the game just expects you to have fun with that: its whole selling point is to raise an orc army to take over forts (if you stop to think about, most of the game's marketing was ONLY about that, they didn't even talk about story... Probably because it barely has one... Anyway, moving on), but they never mention that, outside the fact that there's snow in one place and lava in another, every territory it's excatly the same, and so are the forts and the enemies and the animals and pretty much everything...
STORY(?) - Ok, so here it gets weird... The story, in my opinion, is pretty much inexistent... It shows up once in a while and kinda just keeps you going through different places and taking over forts... But, even though I didn't like it, it was the only reason I was still playing the game... When it ends, you are tasked to keep doing everything you've already done thousands of times ad eternum, but this time without any kind of conversation or cutscene to push you forward (I actually liked Talion and Celebrimbor's chats), besides those that happens EVERYTIME A CAPTAIN SEES YOU and ALMOST EVERYTIME YOU'RE ABOUT TO KILL A CAPTAIN and SOMETIMES WHEN YOU HIT A CAPTAIN FOR THE FIRST TIME (and no, you can't skip any of those and it actually slowly drain your life away after some time)
Furthermore, it took me a LOT to find out that I had to select the secondary storylines via quest menu, otherwise they wouldn't show up on the global map, and after I found them, I was just disappointed - it was more of the same
Oh, and btw, sometimes, when a captain saw me or when I was trying to recruit an orc, instead of a dialogue, there was a bug that the Talion and the orc would just stare at it each other without saying anything, and that scene was EVEN LONGER than the captain's speechs...
P.S.: If you're wondering about Borgu, it turns out I found another orc EXACTLY LIKE HIM in a vendetta mission and just ruined it for me...

I have mixed feelings about this game. There is a small learning curve (which is to be expected) but really within an hour you should be able to understand the game. It's not as involved as a game like rimworld.  It is Alpha, so it's hard to beat up on it too much, and in that reguard it's a good Alpha.
The resource system and cratfting system is good but the pace is too slow in way of branching out because you need research books or kits to advance, which are really hard to find. I understand that's the point, but the catch is you have to send your survivors out to different locations to fight the evil baddies and loot the area, which is done for you once you kill the baddies.
There really isn't much to the combat, which is one of the downfalls for me. It lacks tactics besides perhaps send one person ahead and hope you don't run into a creature that has a long range attack and try to ambush them. You can't even set up a formation, even if you see a creature you generally dont have time to take cover or get your crew in the right spot. You can pause, but most of the battles are 4-5 seconds so it almost doesn't really fit.
Since basically 1/4th of the game at least is based on combat, I feel like a better battle style could have been used. A turn base would be too slow for all the places you have to visit, but I hope it gets improved. Something with the combat just feels off.
There are some issues such as the best person not doing the job you want them to even though you set it up so they would, but again it's alpha.
I wouldn't say stay away from the game, I'm actually going to keep playing it but I feel for the general public at the moment it doesn't work. The game just needs to be fleshed out a little more, such as the occult rituals aren't that interesting and some you prolly will never use.

Life is strange.
And so is this game.
The story of Max Caulfield, a time-travelling weirdo, and her punk companion Chloe who are on a quest to find Chloe's missing friend will absolutely charm you, but it will also devastate you without a second thought. Every choice you make matters. Be it seemingly meaningless friendships or saving actual lives, every decision you make will lead to a certain outcome.
You find yourself inside of a nightmare - a chilling vision of a tornado destroying Arcadia Bay, a town you moved back to a month ago. You wake up from the nightmare, finding yourself in the middle of a photography class. A chain of events follows and you realize you can control time. You're a living superhero! But why and for how long?
The gameplay relies on your ability to turn back time. Find out crucial information, spot important items, prevent fatal mistakes or even cheat death. Everything revolves around you and your ability to go back in time.
Visually, the game is very soothing. An artsy approach fits really well and a more realistic look would only make it seem more boring and less immersive.
On top of it all, Life is Strange carries an important message. Mental health is not a toy for others to play with and there is always someone willing to look after you, even if it's just one person. Additionally, a message just as important - your choices have consequences! No matter how small or meaningless they may seem.
I would very gladly recommend this game to anyone as it touched me on a very personal level and the price is ridiculously low.

***Welcome to Alpha Protocol Recruit!***
Disclaimer: This game is an espionage RPG, NOT a SHOOTER. So your hard-earned split second pixel hunting skills do not matter that much.
When I have noticed this game, at first I was sceptical due to multitude of bad reviews out there but the game itself proved me wrong over and over. Feeling masochistic I decided to set the difficulty to hard and chose Recruit background which essentially starts with no skill at all.
*Your Career As an Agent*
At the initial stages of the game you choose a background and decide about your skills which you shall develop and the amount of different skills provide a good deal of options to you. Whether you want to go in stealthily, guns blazing or with Bond-style techs, you can develop such abilities as the game progresses. Of course when you approach the game you should consider that this game is RPG which means for example when you use an Assault Rifle, investing in some mods to stabilize your weapon and supporting that with some Assault Rifle skills...you will have an easier time. Do not expect shooter style easy aiming. If you are inexperienced at a certain skill do not expect your gaming reflexes to save you. And similarly if you do not invest in Stealth abilities, you will have a hard time remaining unnoticed...but it is not impossible. Everything in this game tries to enhance your preferred gameplay style.
Now as an agent of Alpha Protocol you will be given an initial training and then they will send you to certain missions where everything you do or say will have a future consequence. Now that is where the game shines. Every person and organization within game contains a dossier where you can learn about them which can be to your advantage. A person might like aggressive and intimidating approach while another will try to remain professional or sneaky. In dialogues and actions if you reflect such things, then you get on their good sides. But you do not necessarily need to get on their good sides and sometimes antagonizing people could provide you different benefits on the long run. And let me tell you...you shall face several important decisions throughout the game, some doors will open for you some will close.
The killer side is the amount of memorable characters and lore the game has. Considering this is an Obsidian game, expect really good writing and indepth lore regarding the gameworld/characters whether it is about an arms dealer or a hierarchical corporation which has too many fingers in every pie across the globe along several side factions which you can encounter as allies or enemies depending on your actions.
*So You Want to Be a Hero?*
Unlike other games where you hoard countless gold/money/coin where you will never use...Alpha Protocol provides you several tempting options to spend your ill-gotten or hard-earned money throughout missions. You want some intel on a certain person? Maybe an armor fit for stealth? Perhaps we can interest you in some incendiary grenades? You pay up on Clearinghouse which is the online blackmarket ingame where you can buy/sell several weapons, armor, gadgets, ammunition, weapon/armor mods, intelligence regarding missions and support. For example, if you buy a sniper dead drop at a certain mission it might make your job easier or you can hire a surveillance service to provide you detailed map of an area or maybe one of your allies can provide assistance at a mission for a fee. As you can see aside from material stuff in Clearinghouse you can spend your money on things which will alter your missions for better.
Of course, there are some downsides to the game since we are in 2016 the graphics will seem a bit outdated but that is easier to get past. There are also minigames which are tolerable except hacking which can be extremely confusing at start but requires a bit getting used to abyssmal mouse control during it and good eyes to spot unchanging code segments. But it is recommended to avoid hacking most of the time if you are not patient and invested in technical abilities which makes the process easier and more palatable. Other minigames are fairly straightforward such as lockpicking and disabling alarms, you shall have no major issues with them. And one last issue could be the hard boss battles which requires tactical approach since they have no mercy. But as a recruit I never gave up, no matter Mike is blasted up with grenades, sub-machine gun'd to death or beaten by several sucker-punches from behind! But yeah boss fights can be hard if you are not properly equipped with some lethal means let it be martial, gunpower or gadgets.
Now on my experience there are moments when the game truly shines. On one of the missions I was quite cornered and decided to give up on stealthy-nice guy approach and threw some incendiary grenades to kill 5-6 enemies which then granted me the perk "Plan B: Kill It With Fire" which literally cracked me up. On another note, if you go in stealth suit to meet certain people they make fun of you whether you will sneak out after the conversation or not. Which reminds me that the game provides perks based on your actions, choices and playstyle. Even watching news can be helpful at times you know.
Also as a final note, Recruit background will have different cutscenes/dialogues/emails then Veteran which is unlocked by finishing the game on Recruit. So there is you NG+ if you are looking to try different things with a more experienced character. But as I initially said Recruit can be hard at start.
*Conclusion*
Alpha Protocol may have its shortcomings here and there, but if you can look past that you shall have great time with one-of-a-kind espionage RPGs. In my opinion this game is better then games such as Deus Ex: HR which while had excellent differing approaches to missions, they did not have emphasis on relation with other characters too much. In Alpha Protocol nothing is ever black and white. So if you are up for some espionage RPG, give Alpha Protocol a try.

This game is absolutely spectacular.  It is very difficult to get into so I would definitely recommend doing the tutorials and probably researching some guides online. There is also a very useful mechanic to make it so you can't ever get into a position of a game being unplayable where you can, after a crash etc. revert to the launchpad or the construction phase of the ship you built as if you never launched it in the first place.  Hooray for time travel making sure you don't lose all your money etc.
Although the sandbox mode is fun because you can build whatever you want and test infinitely, I think the actual campaign depth is marvelous and truly enjoy having to build a program up from the bottom.  You get to do research to gain more vehicle parts and abilities as well as actually manage your base, funding and much much more.  The fact that you manually have to perform actions during flight to gain more research etc. is a truly unique experience that is quite fun if not a little bit hard to get used to.
I would definitely recommend this game as a fabulous sim and I am only a mere 5 hours in.
