A game I can't recommend.   I'm a little shocked at this game, because on the surface it's everything I should want.  The game has a very innovative gameplay system, where conversations matter, and the game doesn't rely on a basic morality, but rather what you say and what you do.
On paper, this is an incredible game, and honestly I'd love to love it I just can't.
The problem with this game is essentially, I've tried to play it three times, and I've failed to get involved.  The first time I didn't give the game a real try, so we can forget about that.
The second one I played three levels, and I started the game as a "Recruit" putting my points into weapons skill to try to make weapons better.  It didn't so I gave up.  About a week after that I heard if you put the points into stealth the game becomes incredibly easy.  I tried that, and ran into a third problem.
The first thing to say is this game's dialog choices are incredible.  It reminds me of Catherine a little in that EVERY thing you do feels important and matters.  The difference from Catherine is instead of a morality system, there's just important dialogs everywhere.
The downside of this for the third playthrough is none of these dialogs are that different or skippable.  And there are some long dialogs in this game, and while there's a decision how the player will respond, most of the time, it only gives a "relationship" point and continues the same dry dialog with minimal acknowledgement.   Did I want to sit through 4 hours of hearing the same dialog a second time with no way to skip?  I chose no.  But it wasn't only that.
The other major problem with this game is the combat.  Dear god, that combat is SO bad.   I realize Obsidian was trying to make the combat weaker so stealth became a viable option but often I feel the player can't even aim a gun and can only get a solid firing reticule by standing around for solid minutes.  It's BAD.   Watch a video and you can see why.
I don't understand this design decision because it takes what is actually a really good game, down to the bad game territory.  There's a number of games that have figured this out.  Metal Gear Solid 5 heavily pushes stealth but when you make a mistake you can go in guns blazing and save your life most of the time, or hide again.  But a SINGLE mistake here, and you're either going guns blazing for the rest of the level (poorly) or you're reloading from the last checkpoint which is usually far away.
I can't really complain about the combat enough, because it's one of the core gameplay in the game, and it really ruined my love for the game.
There's one final issue that people have with this game and I agree with it.  The game is NOT made for PC.  It's a port and I'll accept that most of the time.  I get it.   However in this game, there's three mini games.  A game where you clip and trace paths works great.  A game where you lock pick is quite annoying but still can mostly work, especially if you have a gamepad.     But the game where you hack just seems almost unplayable on the computer, maybe it's always that bad but it's annoying as hell.
I gave this game a solid try, three solid tries in my opinion.  And I could never get far.  It's not the worst game in the world, but there's no way I can recommend it as the combat is just painful.
Here's the final thought.  Maybe in the future I'll try this game again and get through the entire game and love it.  That's possible, but I won't change my recommendation because NO game should take four attempts to get into.  No game should make loving it this hard.   I might turn around and say "I love you" to the game one day soon but that will be an abusive love.  And that's not ok!

Alpha Protocol made me think – what does a shoddy game have to do to get a free pass despite all of its flaws? Even the worst of the bunch sometimes have redeemable qualities, right?
Well, Alpha Protocol definitely has a cool premise going for it. It's inspired by futuristic superspy flicks, and if only it had slightly more personality and charm, I might say it's worth overlooking boring gameplay, throwaway RPG mechanics, linear level design and other issues that plague the game. But Alpha Protocol has no charm. Everything about it is plain, bland, lifeless and uninteresting. The writing is only "okay". The story is merely "passable". Same with voice acting. It's the definition of mediocrity, like a James Bond movie reenacted in a school theatre play (come to think of it, that might actually be a fun thing to watch).
I've played quite a few bad games that were enjoyable regardless, as I'm sure many people have. Deadly Premonition, for example, got away with terrible design largely because of its wild story and superb atmosphere. Games like Oblivion got away with questionable gameplay mechanics because of their deep and intricate world building.
This game has none of those qualities. It starts with a promising setup and never does anything meaningful with it. As you can see, I've only played it for 5 hours. Despite the fact that it's not even a double digit, I still consider it a long time and would happily get those hours back if it was possible. But it's not. So don't repeat my mistake. Play the old Deus Ex instead. Or Splinter Cell. Anything, but not this.
Oh, and whoever designed that hacking minigame deserves to have a stroboscope taped to their eyes.

From what I've played on the free weekend, I wouldn't buy this game, even for a dollar (I wonder if their Robocop reference was intentional). It may have been playable before this event, but now and probably later, given that it's $1 (and 1 whatever everywhere else, because devs can't work out exchange rates) the community will die.
The controls as a dinosaur are nuts and really hard to master, because it's 3rd person and has very lengthy attack animations. As a human, the controls and gameplay are simple class and perk/upgrade based sci-fi FPS, with jetpacks and healing guns and cloaks and all that stuff. The guns are pretty fun but don't FEEL very varied in their own class, one pistol is like another ect.
The powers are really fun to use, especially the jetpack, which got me out, and into, a lot of scrapes.
The game itself is pretty hard, and it makes sense to be like that. If you're up against raptors or whatever, you'll easily take them alone, like it were a zombie game. But if you're faced with anything bigger, it's VERY hard to solo them, and (on the server I played on) dinos were crazily unbalanced, most were going for T-Rex with a few as pterosaurs to provide aerial support. For some reason, even when I'd jetpacked up a mountain to hide from the T-Rex jaws, the two ganging up on me could still attack me, despite a large gap between myself and their faces.
The biggest issue here was the lack of teamwork. Like I said, most creatures are hard to take down above the size of a raptor. Here you NEED to work as a unit. This makes sense but the game itself isn't very conducive to teamwork, and what little support there is to rally your teammates goes ignored while they camp and fail the objective. Dinos don't have this limitation, though, because they can solo almost anything because they're ♥♥♥♥ing dinosaurs.
The human classes are cool, but the dino classes are dreadful, with little variation on the ground based dinosaurs, going only from small up to big.
All in all, this feels like Tribes, Halo, or some other sci-fi FPS, but then the devs threw in dinosaurs, because the dinos are really badly implemented.
If you want a dino game, I'd recommend the superior Primal Carnage (when it's on a sale, though, seeing as it's got a slow dev cycle and only has two game modes).

I've just barely scratched the surface of the beta, but so far I am incredibly enjoying myself, as many other  recommenders have stated it feels just like Fallout 1. The dark humor, the enemies, the world, the interface, the attributes, they all fill me with a sense of nostalgia and pleasure I haven't felt since exploring Fallout or Baldur's Gate for the first time. The world is meticulously fleshed out, even the edges of the map have a creative backstory. Wasteland 2 has it's share of bugs, but this is completely normal in a beta. I don't think there has ever been a beta without a bug but I could be wrong. Wasteland 2 is far from a Fallout 1 clone, a lot of elements will feel familiar, but that is more the developer's personal style than anything tied to Fallout in particular. It certainly pays due homage though, and I can safely say to anyone that wanted Van Buren to be a reality, well this is as close as you are ever going to get. The graphics are much nicer than I expected, with special attention to weather effects like billowing sand, and the scenery textures. It's nice to gawk at the many, varied, and unique enviroments. The sound is top-notch, with the musical score being immersive and exhillarating, the composer does a fine job. The story hooks you right from the first mission, with a deep foreboding that creeps into your bones as the clues add up of an unknown enemy threat. People who have played other Black Isle & Interplay games will know this feeling very well, it's one of their favorite themes to drive suspense and even though I should expect it by now, they pull it off masterfully so I don't know what to expect, or when to expect it. The world is kept equally enigmatic and alien, like navigating a cave with a torch, but the resourceful player is able to pry clues from helpful characters to slowly piece this brutal, damaged world together. All in all, I have to say job well done inXile! It's a little early to break out the champagne but I am very pleased with the direction of Wasteland 2 and look forward to watch it grow into a full release.
P.S. I haven't played Wasteland 1 so that is why there is no references to that in my review, it wouldn't be fair to pass along second-hand information that I can't verify myself but I am sure there are plenty who have played both.

Just a note that when I first tried to play this, importing my Banner Saga 1 save resulted in a game that was broken in the initial tutorial and wouldn't let me progress at all. I'm not sure why that was, but since it had been so long since playing BS1 I decided to play the whole of the first game again to get a fresh save, and the second time it worked. So beware.
Once I got past that, I found that this game is essentially identical to its predecessor in terms of mechanics. Combat is the same, with armor and strength pools being targeted separately, which can require smarter use of your attacks. The caravan mechanics are the same - you move through the world, trying to keep morale and supplies up by responding properly to random events, and occasionally encounter story beats or battles to be fought. It's a simple and engaging formula that still works in a second game - I'm actually glad they didn't change much of it.
In terms of story, I think it suffers a bit from the lull typical in mid-trilogy works - half of the story splits off to follow a separate caravan populated by almost entirely new characters, and it takes a while for them to get interesting (but they do, with some really interesting story stuff going on). Meanwhile, the main caravan seems to be a little conservative with developing the protagonist's story - little wonder, given who that protagonist is depends on the end of Banner Saga 1.
But there continues to be lots of unpleasant decisions, and the occasional unexpected death, and new and interesting lore gets revealed as the game goes on. The art and music are gorgeous as usual, and the ending feels like a suitable setup to an epic conclusion. I've backed the third game on Kickstarter, so now it's just a question of waiting it out to see what happens next!

I don't write many reviews, but this deserves one.  I've only played for a few days, but I'm seriously impressed with the balanced challenge (not too hard, not to easy), the variety of play styles supported (upgradeable gear, programs, weapons), and the way I've already had several very memorable missions where I was able to just barely escape from the clutches of security.  There is a great feeling of success when you can stealth your way past guards, steal victory from defeat, and sometimes hide practically in plain sight.
Of course, the 'rewind' ability helps, but the fact that you're limited to 5 rewinds per mission (and only one turn each) gives you enough leeway to recover from a mistake without turning the entire game into a cake-walk.  Looking forward to many play-throughs!  (Oh, and the fact that missions are procedurally generated means I'll have just as much fun the second time around)

The game's a blast. At first glance from screenshots or video on the store page, the game looks extremely bland and reminiscent of a standard online flash game. The truth however, is that its looks are deceiving. The music in it is amazing, as is generally the case with Danny Baranowsky, and while there is nothing graphically impressive about the game the look and style actually fit well together.
Each game is randomly generated, your end of the game appearance, abilities and experience are virtually unpredictable. The game has a great difficulty curve, which actively shifts depending on progression and completion count via unlocks and enemy shifts. The gameplay is both exceedingly simple, yet challenging and sometimes frustrating.
Overall this game is easily a 9/10. It's a blast to sit down to if you feel like listening to a podcast or some of your own music and just killing some time. Check it out, and if you can, pair it with its DLC (Wrath of the lamb).

That said, the style hits some good notes, and the roleplay elements are still pretty neat, being better and more complex than almost any of the competition even now. Which just makes the unforgivable control problems that much more tragic.

Alright, so first of all, I enjoyed this game! It was a fun little story about a person (pick your gender) who happens to be a half breed of the old gods from Lovecraftian lore that needs to amass an army to destroy Innsmouth. However this game does it in a Visual Novel type presentation that also happens to be an RPG, cause you have a few stats here and there that affect the game. Also there are multiple branching paths you can take depending on your choices throughout the game. You can tell a lot of time and thought was put into the design of the overall product and how it functions. Also the humor reminds me a lot of the sarcastic, trope ignoring, 4th wall breaking, pop culture referencing, snarky humor you'd find in a game like The Bard's Tale, and I enjoyed that quite a bit actually. It's what kept me playing to the end.
That being said, this game isn't going to appeal to everyone. The humor type alone may put off some people, while amusing others. Also you have to get past the art. The way it's presented is with photo backdrops with artistic renditions of the characters that are talking. The art and characters aren't bad though, you can just tell it's done with multiple artists with different art styles (which strangely works for the type of quirky game this is). This can be jarring at first but I was able to quickly look past it.
Overall I was looking for a fun story with Cthulhu/Old Gods type mythos in it, and I got it! Also the price point is cheap enough that even if it slightly piques your interest in it you should go for it!
TL;DR
Fun Visual Novel/RPG Hybrid game with qwirky Bard's Tale type humor which you may love or not that suggests multiple plays due to branching story paths. Also if you can get over the inconsistent art style and photo backgrounds and see the charm in it then you'll enjoy it. There are worse ways to spend $5.

Pros
-Music is awesome
-Simple controls that handle well
-Occasional upgrades to help tilt the odds
-Simple but appealing graphics
-Different characters with benefits and/or detriments
Cons
-Mostly only fun for masochists and those who just don't care if they win or not
-Cheap deaths: Since the levels have random enemy placement, you can go from full health to dead in under a second due to the misfortune of getting hit when multiple enemies fire at once or a single enemy with a shotgun-like attack (such as scorpions) hits you perfectly
-Occasional upgrades are randomly taken from a pool of upgrades, meaning you could just be screwed from the beginning of the game and not know it until it's too late
-No progress if you die aside from character unlocks: Love replaying the same tilesets over and over because you made a single split-second error or because the game's randomization made it virtually impossible for you to win?
-Melee weapons that suck: there might be good ones later, but in a game where a bad moment can make you start over from the beginning, you really want your melee weapons to kill in one hit, but don't count on it against a lot of early enemies, making melee weapons fairly useless, given how much ammo there is

Hotline Miami is very, very hard. Its top down, brutal and gory combat is fast-paced and suprisingly repsonsive for the mouse and keyboard. Having played it before on a Playstation 3 I was suprised to find the mouse and keyboard much better to play the game with.
You can be forgive for skipping the story in a agme like this, but it's your loss. Often in arcade-y games players just skip the plot to get into the action quicker. Hotline's story, however, should not be skipped. The story is told in little clues in the environment or dialogue and is actually really interesting. The setting and plot compliment eachother and after finishing the game, I was compelled to replay all the levels to collect all the masks (which provide perks or create interesting challenges to overcome) and find all the puzzle pieces to unlock the secret ending and have closure.
Gameplay can become frustrating (because you will die, a lot), but it's pleasurable and incredibly rewarding when you finally finish a level. It's responsive, quick and when you do die you know that it's your fault for taking a certain risk. Approaching a level carefullyand strategising is fun, but all the planning in the world will inevitably all go down the drain and you will end up standing in a hall way of blood and bodies with a shotgun. I guarantee it.
And that soundtrack. AWESOME. Just awesome. The reason I am leaving this review is because I was heading to Hotline's store page to purchase the soundtrack and got sidetrack by the 'review' pop up.
or you will regret it.
In short, Hotline Miami is old school - Hard to play, and even harder to master. (Having said that, by the time I finished this game I was speed running previous levels that took me ages beforehand.)
I give Hotline Miami 4/5 stars.

This is such a terrible game. I think it's a disgrace to the Painkiller franchise. Let's break it down:
+ There are a few levels which doesn't have an atrocious setting and design. I quite liked the Studios level.
And that's it, there is nothing else positive about this game.
- Almost half (maybe even more) of the monsters in the game are directly copied from Painkiller and Battle out of Hell. And those that are created specifically for this game suck big time. They have jerky animations, low-quality sound effects and most of their attacks don't even make sense. They don't even fit the environment they appear in. Clowns spawning in a power plant? Check. Nurses spawning inside a plane hangar? Check.
- The game blatantly uses an entire level from Battle out of Hell. Remember the Loony Park level? They used it here, with almost no damn change to it (they just cut the ride at the end and replaced it with a lame broadside battle between two grounded ships).
- The boss battles suck so much that words can't even begin to express it. One boss battle takes less than 50 seconds (it's even a Tarot card requirement to kill it before 3 minutes), one boss is just a bullet sponge with no stages at all, and the final boss is so artificially difficult that I had to use cheats (even though I was playing on Insomnia difficulty, which is like Medium).
- The game is very difficult, but not the good kind of difficult. I called the first season one of the most emotional games I've ever played. So, my standards for this one going in were extremely high. It was probably impossible to ever have met them.
But it's not just that season two isn't as good as the first one. It's not very good at all.
The problem I have with a lot of zombie fiction is how self-serious and forcibly edgy it can get. The Walking Dead show and comic suffer terribly from this at time, but the first season of the game managed to mostly avoid that. There was hope, there was humanity, but there was still that dark, ugly side that we all love the genre for. People died suddenly and terribly. It was sad. The characters were imperfect and divisive, but they felt human. Which made it all the harder to see them go.
But this time around, it just seems like much of the cast is only there to die. They get a single personality trait, and then development gets tossed aside in favour of counting down the minutes until another one of them is torn apart or whatever. I'm sitting here trying to remember anything about some of them aside from how they died.
There were plenty of shocking moments, but they came so often and without any weight to them that it hit that terrible, damning point overly bleak stuff like this can reach: I stopped caring. I was no longer worried about the cast (aside from Clem herself) and didn't care who lived or died anymore. There was no one to root for but her, and the plot seemed to be going absolutely nowhere aside from the group walking forward.
One major character seemed to be written to be intentionally divisive. You'll know who I mean once you meet them. But the way it's done feels clumsy and irritating. Which is a problem when a huge amount of the drama unfolding centres around this one person. I was just exhausted listening to them speak by the end.
That said, the season does have a really strong opening episode. It's harrowing and brutal and tense all throughout. Just like the rest of the season should have been. But after that, it becomes a parade of meaningless death without any real purpose. The first season had a goal, even if it wasn't a very good one, had a main character with a purpose, and it had a proper arc to the overall plot. But this one is just meandering for four episodes before they decide that's all, folks.
Also disappointing: most of the cast introduced in the 400 days add-on for the first season is absent or irrelevant. That DLC had a lot of cool mini-stories that I would have liked to see developed more. One character does return full-time, but the rest are forgotten.
I'm still a big fan of what Telltale is doing in their other stuff, and I don't have any technical or gameplay complaints to bring up. But I have to say they totally lost me here. It just felt like they didn't know where to go with things and the edge was just too strong to take this season seriously or invest myself emotionally. Which is probably good, because I don't think I could take being as devastated as last time all over again.

If you liked anything about the first game, this sequel improves on just about everything (though not in any real ground-breaking way). They added more interactions with the nemesis system, improved the combat here and there, added some loot interaction and skill challenges, and--most importantly--added a boatload more random orcs.
The story is thin and dumb, so if you're a LotR purist you'll be upset, but it's perfectly serviceable in its goal of motivating you to murder and dominate orcs. And boy howdy, if you want to murder and dominate just all the orcs, this is your game.
There's a lot of orcs, and they all have gimmicks. Imagine you are the first man into the WWE Royal Rumble, but every 2 minutes a new orc runs down the ramp instead of a sweaty wrestler. Chatty orcs. Screaming orcs. Sneaky orcs. Brutish orcs. Sometimes they have poison and sometimes they have armor, and sometimes they'll ambush you, or run away. Sometimes you'll capture one like a pokemon, and send him to the fighting pits to work his way into a position of power.
But you will eventually have to murder and dominate them all. Because they're orcs.
PS. The game also runs pretty well and looks pretty, and the DLC/microtransaction stuff seems way overblown by nerds.

The Walking Dead was a great game that made me fall in love with Clementine. In the first game, she practically transcends the video game and becomes your daughter in reality. Certainly, Telltale Games's great story and character development will lead you into emotions that make you feel that way. Everyone I have spoken to about this game will legitimately go through the emotional highs and lows of Clementine's story. You'll want nothing to do but protect her, and see to it that she's okay.
The Walking Dead: Season 2 lets you play AS Clementine this time, and while you see things from her viewpoint, the emotional rollercoaster you'll take with her is still strong, though I think comparably not as much as the first game. Still, a particularly agonizing scene wherein Clem has to sew up her own wound made me visibly emotional like a little schoolgirl. The daughter attachment to Clem the first game set up is still there in the second, and I'm very thankful for that. Few games bring out emotion in me, but this series is one of them.
The gameplay is more of the same. Nothing different, but nothing needed to be different. This game runs on its story and character emotion, both of which I feel can pull you through the slower-paced gameplay and QTE cinemas. At the time of writing this, the third season is out, but I have yet to play it. I suppose I will, but the ending I received for Season 2 felt so final and complete, I almost don't want to move forward with anything beyond it.
As I did with my Walking Dead Season 1 review, I should note that I do not like Kirkman's comic or the AMC TV show based on his franchise. I don't find many of the characters likeable. I think Telltale creating many of its own characters and melding them into Kirkman's IP is a great thing. They clearly understand stressful situations and how to bring out emotions towards their characters.
Play it. It's great.

Microsoft Flight Simulator X, now owned by Dovetail games have re-released the game onto the steam platform. There may be no actual new gameplay features, but a endless list of bug fixes to help support this classic, yet fantastic game onto newer computers makes the experience much better.
Back in the days before 2010 I would play the boxed editon, I would encounter endless crashes mid-flight for no apparent reason. I would be cruising at 35000ft directing to my next waypoint and all of a sudden, "Microsoft Flight Simulator X has stopped working." Then boom. Flight over. This use to drive me nuts. Thanks to Dovetail Games re-releasing the product to make it extremely stable with new computers, I can fly now without the stress and worry that the simulator would stop working.
If you have the boxed edition, getting the steam re-release is an absolute must.
If you don't have it, then I will still say the exact same thing, I have spent so many hours on this extremely versitile simulator. Whether I go for an IFR flight with a virtual airline whilst connecting to an online network with thousands of pilots and controllers or whether I go for VFR flight, I still get the same satisifaction.
Admittely though, if you are like me and wanting to take your simulation experience to the next level, you are going to have to purchase addons, to make especially IFR flights in commercial planes more realistic. As much as the default 737 -800 and A321 are ok to start off with, you become hungry to endevour in the replica aircraft, like the PMDG Boeing fleet that costs up to £40 or the Aerosoft fleet that usually is about £30. Then you want your home airports to look like the real thing and so on. You become to demand more.
This is game fantastic, But in my opinion, it is a very much a base package for what is an ever growing flight simulation world.
I still though totally recommend this. It could be your purchase of the year.

From starting the game and playing for a few hours I personally can say I like this game. This review is my opinion and all others are entitled to their opinion. Now then......The game itself is a continuation of the old wasteland classic and the original is considered the godfather of post-apocalyptic rpg games, that in itself is more or less true. A game to compare this to would be the original fallout games 1 and 2. Both of which were developed by Brian Fargo and his team, I considered them to be great games and more addicting than most of todays mediocre games. So far this game is in beta but from what I played it will hopefully continue to get better.
-Combat is pretty simple. Ammo and weapons as well as armor and abilities all play major factors in this game. If a party member runs out of ammo they dont auto-reload, reloading is done manually. Melee is pretty self-explanatory, just close range and knock the enemy down. As far as combat goes it is wise to put experience towards what your characters are proficient in as it can help out a lot but variety works too.
-The game world is just like the original fallouts and wasteland in which you move your party across a map to various locations while avoiding radiation hotspots and coming across random encounters. Water is important! Your party will need water to keep traveling otherwise they will die at some point.
-Dialogue is interesting and if you can deal with reading text it brings a lot of backstory into the game about your mysterious enemy.
-Sound effects and music are great. I found myself at one part cringing when a group of soldiers were panicking and screaming after they were attacked by an enemy with chainsaws.
-Art and environment are beautiful, and naturally in my opinion graphics dont make a game and with the increasing technology and race for better graphics I find most games nowadays to just be pretty light shows anymore.
-The price is steep for a beta yes, however.....this was done because of the amount of money some backers put up on kickstarter and in trying to not♥♥♥♥♥♥of those who already backed this game, that is why this game is $60. In my mind its understandable but a lot of other people would disagree.
-The only game breaking bug Ive found is when loading a save that none of my characters will move or do anything at all but yet other npcs and whatnot still move around and music and everything still play just fine. Ive come across no other issues so far.
Final Verdict: Overall Im enjoying this game alot. Im a fan of fallout 1 and 2 as well as the original wasteland. The price is steep but I can't include that in the final verdict. I found it comical the little prank played in the main menu about the dlc (there is no dlc by the way) which in itself was very clever since most companies now sell day 1 dlc. So without further ado aside from the game breaking bug I would say this game falls into about an 8/10 due to the bug and the fact this game is still in beta. Some might think this score is way too high but this is my opinion, for anyone interested in whether or not they'd like this game well they'll have to find that out themselves.

Grade : F D C B A
Main Pro: Rich variety of deliberate, to-the-point tactics
Main Con: Unrealized plot potential
Invisible Inc. is easily the best
turn-based strategy game I've ever played. Why, you ask? Let's get right to it: Invisible Inc. doesn't mess around much with fluff and neither will I!
Perhaps one of the most defining characteristics of this game is that it employs the use of heroes (aka agents) without using traditional RPG leveling. Instead, nearly everything (stat upgrades, skills, items) is purchased with money, and you can divy it up as you so choose. Efficiency and progression, then, is often defined by how well you complete a mission, not how much you utilized a particular hero.
Why am I bringing this up? By removing the need for confrontation--and by extension the experience it normally brings,--the depth of tactics you can effectively employ becomes massive. Want to be dodgy by using cloaks and hologram projectors? Do that. Want to run a power-hungry setup so you can hack all the computers and drones? Sure. Or maybe you really do want to punch every security guard you find square in the face? Absolutely! Invisible Inc. can be such a surprise at times, as I constantly discover new nuances and ways to navigate my way through sticky situations.
And believe me, things can get very sticky. Make no mistake: Invisible Inc. can get bonkers tough. Foes are predictable but lethal. An alarm tracker increases with each passing turn, periodically dropping new countermeasures on your squad. The procedural generation aspect of the game means you'll stay guessing... but that's actually another remarkable aspect of this game. As stealth can have an "information warfare" dimension to it, Invisible turns what can be a weakness of procedural generation into one of its greatest strengths. Suspense can run high, but threading the needle on a harrowing infiltration has almost no equal for me in the strategy genre. Watching a strategy you personally concocted "beat the odds" can make for some incredible moments.
If I had one major complaint to throw out there, its the story. Look, story isn't a focus of this game, and you should know that going in. Despite that, I was severely disappointed in how the game ended. The basic narrative that's set up is fairly compelling but the game is content to use a very cliche, punch-in-the-face kind of ending that comes out of nowhere (although the DLC story expansion does a better job of setting things up.) I despised it so much, I felt as if I would have rather not had an ending!
There are a couple of other thorns that could bother some people more than others. One of the few places the game does use RPG leveling is with starting loadout unlocks; this isn't a huge problem as you really should get one solid playthrough under your belt before you start havey-duty scheming, but I imagine some might find it frustrating. The story's endgame missions can have a sometimes startling difficulty spike, although some actually find that endearing.
Either way, these low points are more like speed bumps than walls. These things are a lot easier to forget when the core gameplay loop is so stupid fantastic. I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of turn-based strategy games. And... yeah. Its amazing. That's pretty much it. Buy it and join the face-kicking... though I don't make any guarantees over which side will be doing the face-kicking initially. ;)

You put a certain level of trust in a dev when you buy an early access game, and honestly, I thought that trust I put into Nuclear Throne and Vlambeer was well put with what they did. They communicated with the community, they did weekly dev streams and weekly updates. You really felt like you were part of the development. I have never seen any other devs do the entire early access thing this good, and to this date I hope for it to eventually be the standard.
Nearing the end of 2015, it all started to get downhill. Several issues addressed by a lot of players back then were said to be fixed "in the polishing phase" - right now, we had the "feature and content phase" - so balance, bugs, crashes etc. were to be fixed by then. The problem was that the so called "polishing phase" never really came alongside of other expectations raised by the dev, like full-seeding-support, or other things, like balance-overhauls of areas and other things. There was an insane amount of potential for Nuclear Throne, and the community reported and helped the devs more than enough to make the fullest out of that potential.
Not saying they didn't do anything, though,  there was a certain level of polish done, some bugs were fixed, some details like
ravens leaving feathers added. Major crashes, some people literally being unable to play the game and other bugs though? Completely ignored. I didn't mind back then, since the game was in early access - and its completely acceptable for a game in early access to have crashes and bugs, since you know.
An early access game can have bugs and crashes, since its unfinished. A released game however says that the game is
- little bugs and crashes are supposed to be there.
So, around the end of 2015, the devs further and further pushed to release, constantly threw the sentence "we are almost done guys!" - which was followed by an insane amount of negativity by the community. Understandably, since, as I already said, there were tons of bugs, crashes and balance issues still to be fixed. No way they'll release the game like that - that's atleast what I thought, since I still trusted Vlambeer in their decision.
Until the shocking date of the 5th December - around 5 months have passed since the release. Remember that number, it'll become relevant later. That is when they announced the release of the game for both the PC and consoles, and that is when people started loosing their♥♥♥♥♥♥ The extremely negative stigma and feeling of disappointment really got onto some people, understandably, since the game is in a broken state.
"uhh buddy, ya sure you didn't mean "back then" ? - I mean, 5 months have passed, s-surely they fi - "

This is one of those very rare computer games that realises that it is one thing before all: A game and a learning experience for the person playing it. It is also the rare product that does not need to try to be more than it is.
As such, it takes the player as seriously as it does itself, providing the beginner with the contrivance of a plot, and the more advanced with a tactical (and strategical) gameplay experience that is hard to match- and above all, does not get old, no matter how many times you face up against it. It makes doubly sure of that by giving you many ways to customise elements of the gameplay and providing you with many unlockable and surprising characters (who would probably feel somewhat at home in the Shadowrun or Deus Ex franchises) and procedurally generated maps.
For the past 40 hours or so, it has trounced me thoroughly and I have "enjoyed" it more than I should have- and those hours make the first completion so much sweeter than if it had been easy. The Kleis keep surprising me with their deep understanding of varying levels of audience expectation towards the games they produce. In this case, reviews had led me to expect a game I would like. Unexpectedly, the reduced, no-nonsense, high-quality approach applied to Invisible Inc has revealed a compact, shiny gem of a game that has strong potential to supplant XCOM as my go-to tactical fix.
This is recommended for almost anyone who values substantial gameplay and a well-designed experience.

While I am all for creative ideas in game design that are often bizarre, experimental or would only be executed by independent developers, Mountain is a clear cut example as to why not all ideas should have a price tag put on them.
I have spent almost four hours 'playing' Mountain, though that clocked time was mostly me doing something else while the game ran off to the side. That's because Mountain is an interactive screensaver. Nothing more, nothing less, even if the genres on its Steam store page incorrectly label it as a 'simulation' and 'RPG'. Mountain does attempt to foster actual interaction by allowing you to play musical notes on your keyboard which when a correct sequence is played (Hot Cross Buns, Twinkle Twinkle Little Star, etc), you can cause various effects to rain down on your mountain, like hearts, fireballs or in morbid manner, blood. These effects are only visual, unfortunately, and gameplay in Mountain doesn't improve from there. You can use your mouse to look around your mountain, spin it or zoom in and out for a closer and more distant look, and cleverly enough you can briskly shake your mountain to clear away clouds if you want a clear look at your personal piece of rock (despite the trees and other textures looking incredibly poor). Oh, random space debris will also fly in and crash into your mountain, like a traffic cone, a child's toy block, a futuristic sphere and other oddities that you can then move around or throw away. Why? Video games!
Mountain falls apart at the seams once you realize you've exhausted these gameplay elements (and I use that term loosely), since the only progression in the game is the passing of time, the weather and seasons in your little bubble of an atmosphere, since zooming out will reveal your mountain is floating in space for reasons I still can't figure out. Apparently your mountain has emotions and sentience, since every few minutes it will make an observation or statement about the current weather, time of day and how it feels, even if during the night it will claim to be nervous one minute, and then another claim it feels bold from the darkness. Another 'thought' your mountain can have is some kind of existential question or statement regarding its existence, why its out here in space, if the player is a voice inside its head, why is it alone, are there other mountains like it, etc. and so forth (you can also press period to force one of these thoughts if yo﻿u don't want to wait). Apparently this is what has attracted players and journalists to the game, supposedly eliciting emotions and 'feels' from your mountain having a crisis of its own sentience and having to cope and adapt with the bizarre circumstances it finds itself in while 'living' day by day, season by season.
﻿The glaring flaw in trying to stir thoughts in the player this way is that Mountain is still a screensaver. Nothing more, nothing less. I've tried to find something positive to say about Mountain, but excluding being able to shake your mountain to clear the clouds being clever, I have nothing. Mountain feels like it's trying to be something unique, but it ends up looking utterly ridiculous and full of itself in the process, and the fact that it carries a price tag doesn't help its case. Yes, ninety-nine cents is a piddly amount which could easily be raised by selling Steam cards, but charging money for screensaver under the guise of an 'ambient procedural mountain game' is an absolute joke, where the punch-line is on the consumer.
In no way can I recommend Mountain, even at the price of being a penny shy of a dollar. It is a waste of time, money and patience from the four hours I burned away on this game, trying to make sense of it and realize what the positive talk of it was about.﻿

I liked the first game.  The story was good, I felt empathy for my characters, and the ending of the game was a surprise.  The game's graphics are good for what it is, but the combat system in both 1 and 2 can become annoying.  I am an initiative type of guy when it comes to turn based games.  I absolutely dislike doubling up on enemy turns just because.  Anyways, I started playing this game and started to feel emotionally drained.  I also found myself genuinely hating the cast of characters all of a sudden.  This game pretty much picks up where the first left off.  Having played through the first game, twice, I just felt like I have seen enough of the same.
The battles, the walking around, I just got bored of it.  I just wanted to hit fast forward and get through the waiting around time.  Even skipping the story scenes because I legitimately didn't care.  Probably should have played through as Rook, but, the combat isn't that fun either.  The way the turn system is handled is just garbage.  Love the moves, the strategy, the animations, but the turn system ruins it.  Not turn based, don't get that confused with how the system was designed.  There are games where your sides take turns, games where initiative scores are taken into account, games where dice rolls are added on top of initiative, games where weight effects your initiative, and then this game.  You move 1, they move 1.  No matter what.  You have 10 guys, they have 2?  You move your warrior next to him.  He hits your warrior.  You move archer on the other side of the map, he kills your warrior.  You move dude close to him, he hits dude you just moved.  You move other archer on the other side of the map, he finishes off the guy he just hit.  See where this goes?
Overall, the music, sounds, artwork, and story are good.  Though, I just became uninterested in the story.  I also became uninterested in the combat, which became more annoying than it was challenging.  My friends won't touch games like this.  But if you like story games, and strange combat systems, then this game might be for you.

Released three years after the initial game, Painkiller: Overdose is the second expansion within the long standing FPS action-horror series. Leaving behind main antagonist Daniel Garner, this installment sees you playing as Belial; a half-angel, half-demon abomination who was tortured by Lucifer and the evil hell-hound Cerberus, and imprisoned by Sammael.
The events of Painkiller: Overdose are set just after Daniel slays Lucifer. Belial, knowing that the king of Hell is dead, sets out for revenge against Cerberus and Sammael. Much like its predecessors, the story to Overdose is told through a series of cutscenes that play at the beginning of each chapter; there are three in total, each containing 5-6 levels within. Along with a new protagonist, the game features reskinned weapons for many of the favorites from the original Painkiller, as well as all new maps; with the exception of a slightly reimagined Loony Park from the Battle out of Hell expansion.
Unlike its debut title and first expansion, the levels featured in this game are extremely linear. It's easy to simply just bunny hop from one checkpoint to the next without much challenge, with no vertical obstacles or platforming to traverse. Many of the demons are borrowed from the two prior releases, although there's a sizable amount of unique foes as well that include cow butchers, vikings, scorpions, scarabs, hazmat suit zombies, studio standees, and possessed trees. Overdose also has a lot of creative maps that are fun in aesthetics, although lacking in gameplay, such as a desert, nuclear plant, and an animal farm.
The gameplay stays the same, where you must defeat hordes of monsters between set checkpoints, collect coins to purchase Black Tarot cards after earning them through level challenges, and obtaining souls to transform into a demon. The weapons this time around take on a more steampunk appearance, save for the dismembered goblin head and Hellraiser looking cube; although all of these items function almost exactly the same as the arsenal from Painkiller itself. The music has also taken a weird turn, whereas before it was more metal inspired, the tracks featured in this release are level-suiting ambient types.
Painkiller: Overdose does come with a fair share of problems when it boils down to performance. While I was playing the second level of the first chapter, the game kept crashing in the exact same spot. I eventually was able to bypass it by waiting longer to kill enemies. I then experienced repeated crashing throughout the level, and only this level in particular. The rest of the game, save for loading the final boss battle which became stuck at the loading screen, functioned fine. In one of the later levels of the last chapter, the audio sounded as though it had been recorded through blown-out speakers, and it kept cutting in and out. The rest of the music and sound effects were perfectly arranged, so I am unsure as to what caused this anomaly.
Much of Painkiller: Overdose is simple reskinning to make the designs within look fresh, all the while having you control a character whose witty quips make him seem like a Serious Sam wannabe. The story is uninspired, and the cutscenes in comparison to the first Painkiller are just laggard. Unfortunately THQ missed the opportunity to build on to the game, and rather provided a filler expansion that ultimately caused a lapse in recognition to the series. While the levels are enjoyable aesthetically, they become boring due to how straightforward they are. It's sad to say that the game is terribly average, and the ending scene is hardly worth spending 3 hours to get to. Suggested only to those who wish to experience Painkiller in its fullest, and for the visual design of the maps. If you couldn't care less, I'd suggest a pass.

Overall, this game is a pretty fun experience, it is a very good game at its core, but is let down by the fourth act of the game, which involves defending 20 forts, in successive "stages", this part of the game does not feel fun, it feels like a slow boring grind in order to get the true ending, which honestly, is not worth it in the end, this act it devoid of all interesting narrative and feels like it was designed simply to coerce the player into spending money on their lootboxes which offer better orc followers and gear. However, not playing this part of the game means you get no real resolution to the story, the end of the third act leaves a lot to be desired, it feels quite rushed compared to acts one and two. The first few fort battles are very fun, choosing how you're going to attack the fort and how to counter their defenses and vice versa is fun the first few times, however you quickly realise that mechanically, it's fairly shallow, going from point A-D, capturing them, killing some captains along the way (or have them joining you if you made them infiltrate the enemy ranks beforehand) and then facing an overlord who is only thematically different can get a bit boring after 5 or so times and certainly wears thin after 20.
Despite this, there is a lot to like about this game, the nemesis system feels a lot more fleshed out than the first game and the emergent gameplay it offers is certainly the main selling point of this series, if what you're looking for is more of the nemesis system then this game is totally for you. Your orc followers all have a tribe and a class which influence their individual abilites and personality, this time around they can have rivalries with other orcs, they can have blood brothers who will protect them with their lives, they can betray you and join the enemy once again; it creates a lot of fun moments in the game, as well as a lot of good stories. The combat, while still being a simple arkham-style combat system, feels fun and fluid for the most part, with a lot of interesting skills available in the skill tree to help you augment your playstyle. It is made more interesting by a larger variety of enemies and orc captains with certain immunites which force you to mix up your tactics. The side quests are fun and interesting for the most part and add a good amount of playtime to the game, with one quest even allowing you to take on a balrog. The main story is fine for what it is, it's far from the most lore friendly story, but I don't think that was the focus of this game, the story serves its purpose and is interesting at times, but certainly is not the focus for this game, this game might not be for you if you're big into LOTR lore, especially when the first few minutes of the game involve crafting a new ring of power and shelob transforming into a sexy woman for some reason.
The lootboxes in this game are a very contentious issue, but I never spent any money at all on the premium currency to buy gold lootboxes which guarentee legendary orcs and gear, nor do you have to. You can buy silver lootboxes in the marketplace for orcs and gear with in-game currency which cannot be bought and is readily available from missions and drops from certain orcs, this currency is also used to upgrade your forts and gear.
Recommendation: Buy the game, enjoy acts 1-3, watch the true ending on youtube. (Unless you're really into the fort battles)

Note: This is an early access review, the game still has a long way to go. To be fair: it  has some great ideas, especially the setting is exactly what I'd be interested in (apocalypse, survivor settlement management, scavenge missions, tactical combat,). A game like this, properly done, could wreck my life for months.
Pros:
-The task system (in base management) is really good and probably exactly how such a game should be designed, not sure if any other game has it yet like this.
- The general idea of managing your base, pursuing a storyline and going out on various missions is really good and executed in a solid fashion.
- The Demon/occult setting is also a refreshing change, though I personally prefer a classic Zombie apocalypse.
- Interesting Research tree, though still a bit unbalanced. It'd be much nicer if weapons could be customized/upgraded (see Jagged Alliance, Breach&Clear). Good idea with the occultistic techs.
- sound is ok, though proper fx still scarce, especially in combat
- Base-GUI isn't bad. Thoughtful general design.
Cons:
- The combat system isn't good. It is intransparent, clunky and unfair (rather fighting the engine than the enemies). Why not make it turn based (configurable maybe)? And what about grids? It is very hard to understand who stands where, who goes where and who can go where. It is almost impossible to execute a proper fixing/flanking plan, especially in bigger fights (5 vs 5 or so). Being able to pause in combat is good though.
- Who's shooting at what What is the effect? Who killed the last enemy? Which effect do weapons have? There is no real info and never really a feeling of who does what except to lure an enemy into a prepared kill zone and hope for the best.
- Game economics is one of the hardest thing to get right and judgment just isn't there yet. Some things are supposed to be hard but are easy to get (like food) while others are a constant problem and would never be "in the real world", like wood. It takes 30 trees to create one single wooden shield , that's more than ridiculous, it's an immersion breaker. Wood is probably the only thing that wouldn't be scarce in an apocalyptic scenario and a harvested tree should probably give at least 30 wood, even more.
- Some of the animations are the worst I've seen in a long time, especially in combat (some death animations are ok). Reminds me of "Friday the 13th"on Amiga. Unbelievable.
- Many weird and amateurish graphics, (in base and combat, mainly characters) while the event-screen artwork, research tree, demon portraits are quite good. I guess the graphic designer came on board at a later stage? Anyway, Factorio, Minecraft and various mobile titles have shown that a game can be great with a low-tech look, but some of the graphical game-elements (of the game engine, not the event-artwork etc) of Judgement are pure eye cancer, mainly in combat.
- some bugs (it is alpha, so forgiven)
- Serious performance issues if too many survivors
- some minor nuisances (weird resource costs of some items etc etc )
Feature ideas:
- filter for loot on the world map
- lockable gates
- traps (mines, tripwires, spike pit etc)
- alert states (maybe a "findable" schoolbell? Alert= noone leaves a certain area, so far away miners aren't too far off the barricades when pulling imps for example)
- electricity, running water, windmill?
- dogs ("Chopper, sic balls!")
- medical skill
- horses/cars
- morale attribute
- shoot from windows/bar doors
- spawn areas on map border should be marked and blocked for building
- there should be a faster way of deconstructing fortifications (like a row of sandbags)
- imp-pulling should have a warning period like regular base attacks
- distributing tasks to a task leader, who'd then have people assigned to him (leadership trait?). Give him goals with priorites like "prio1: always have at least 20 wood", prio 2 "always have at least 1000 water" etc..)
I would love to see where the game goes, but don't think many people would enjoy it very much in the current state. Kudos though for the general idea, seriously.

Okay this review gets an up-front disclaimer from me.  This game is well made.  Very well done.  But it is a comedy set in the Cthulhu Mythos.  I realize that there is a lot of fatigue going around for those right now.  This game had an extended development time, so I am not going to be holding that against it.  Games like Cthulhu Saves the World weren't out when the writing on this game was started, so I am not going to sling mud about the concept.  I am evaluating the game on its own merits not as an entry in a crowded field.
The good:  Great humor, seriously laugh-out-loud at times.  The humor ranges from broad to very sophsiticated, from generally funny to pop-culture referential and frequently stretches into the surreal.
The combat "system" involves arguing with enemies and their weaknesses force you to try to figure out what answers are likely to stymie them, either by patterns in their dialogue or knowing their personality.  These refer from triva contests ranging from 80s television to shakesperian insults to classic riddles to your knowledge of tabletop gaming.  A tremendous amount of content for the price, including a DLC that has a decently long campaign.  Creative story that coasts about the Lovecraft Mythos without ever getting too serious.  Also manages to do Lovecraft without accidentally importing Lovecraft's endemic racism, which can be hard to excise from his works.  The battle system offers plenty of allies with skills that can help out if you just can't figure out what the enemy wants you to say to beat them, which lowers what might otherwise be a high difficulty bar without encyclopedic knowledge.
Fully voice acted, with some great VO work for an indy game, seriously good.  Nice variety of VAs too, which avoids the "wait which one is Chigara again?!" syndrome some visual novel VOs suffer from where it's hard to tell people apart.
The bad:  I feel almost bad writing a bad section, because they're all forgivable especially in light of the price point here and the fact it's an indy developer.  Some combats are difficult to figure out the pattern of answers the enemy is looking for, some tip you off with their dialogue, some do not.  Some of the combat takes seriously broad cultural knowledge from 70s sitcoms to Shakespere to tabletop roleplaying games.  This is made easier with ally abilities that give you hints or lessen the penalty for wrong answers.
The Ugly:  If a bug-free game release eludes AAA devs like Bethesda and Bioware, what chance does an indy have? especially when they're pushing the boundries of what their engine can do?  I did have bugs but the developer was very responsive in fixing them.  So I'm not taking off points here, I forgave Skyrim, I forgave Fallout: New Vegas and I sure as hell can forgive an indy dev.
Buy this if:  If you enjoy fourth wall breaks, if you enjoy parody.  If your favorite part of Mystery Science Theater 3,000 was when you got an obscure theater reference they made ("don't talk about our son, Martha!") and feeling really clever about it.  If you enjoy visual novels with a light strategy game coating to keep things interesting.  If you're not SURE if you like games like this, then pick up a copy and see, it's worth the price and a good representative of the better parody games.
Don't bother if:  If you think Cthulhu Mythos has jumped the shark beyond the point parodies are funny.  If you were expecting a tentacle hentai, this one is PG-13 at worst.

EDIT: This review was originally a thumbs down.  To see my original post, read below.
I originally didn't recommend the EARLY ACCESS version of Wasteland 2 for several reasons but the main point was it being nearly unplayable.  The argument against this was that it's in "beta."  I don't disagree with that statement, but to ask $60 to test a product that can barely be tested makes me not want to recommend it.  I felt there were features missing and a general lack of polish that shouldn't exist in a product that was in development for over a year and then released for PUBLIC testing.  "That's the point of a beta" some say, and I don't disagree.  But when you sell a product, you must justify why the customer should buy it.
I Kickstarted the game so my money was already spent but I didn't recommend someone with no personal connection to the game suddenly drop money just for beta access. Some people thought this meant I hated the game which is far from the truth.  I like Wasteland 2.  I like how it's shaping up.  NOT RECOMMENDED doesn't necessarily mean "bad game" it means "hold your money for now."
So why did I change my opinion?  Because a recent glut of updates has brought the game to a pretty polished state.  The UI, which was once a buggy mess that often refused to work, is now workable.  Combat no longer favors fast, strong blitzing attackers.  Some tweaks to the beginning of the game help lessen the impact of practically going out naked.  Your party will now do stuff as a group such as reloading.  There's a huge list of updates and changes I could go into but bottom line is that Wasteland 2 is now looking like a commercial product whereas the original beta release was somehow less playable than the leaked Van Buren alpha from a decade ago.
I still have a hard time recommend dropping $60 simply because you're paying as much as a Kickstarter backer while recieving fewer rewards.  And that's just an unfortunate side effect of how Kickstarter works but if you really want to get into the game and seriously test it out, now's a good time.  Better yet, as of typing this there's a limited window for Kickstarter backers who didn't buy into the beta to get it for a flat $10.  I can recommend that.
Wasteland 2 is looking like the Fallout 3/Van Buren we were promised years ago and I'm excited to see the finished product.
--ORIGINAL POST--
Before you drop 60 bones to get early access, understand something: This is a beta.  An ACTUAL beta, not the feature-complete-a-week-from-going-gold betas that most big companies sling around.  The game is unoptimized, a quarter of the skills are either not implemented or don't work correctly, there are bugs galore, the UI is a wreck, and it's only a small chunk of the final game.  I have a mid-range PC and get 18-40 frames at max but people with beefier rigs get maybe half that.
That's not to say I don't enjoy the game or the testing process, because I do.  I backed this game and was looking forward to testing it and I'm not disappointed.  I love the game's aesthetic and design.  I see there's a good game buried here.  I'm not warning you away from the game itself, I'm warning you that unlike 90% of the games on Steam early access you are actually buying into a beta that's being actively worked on by the community, not a near finished stable product.

The game starts off easy, the first mission is not difficult at all so you continue playing. For me - the next couple of levels were still fun and kind of easy, but later on in the tier 4 levels i hit the point where the game becomes unforgiving. Positioning is everything, managing alarm levels becomes harder and harder, money to spend becomes harder to find so you are not prepared for the next level or even the next room. Stealth becomes pretty much impossible with the amount of drones and guards, and in the last missions I was struggling to keep my items off cooldown just because there is so much that you have to do but so little you CAN do.
I managed to beat the campaign of my first try but it was not easy.
The game's replayability comes from its "EXP" system. Every time you die or win you gain xp, gaining  new characters and abilities for incognita.
It's not as replayable as The binding of isaac for example, but it is a lot harder, and much more fun. With every playtrough, with every death you feel like you are getting better and better. Just the thing you want from a strategy heavy game.

No, no, no, no, no. This game is so badly designed, where do I even begin. By far the worst feature is a sort of "soft difficulty level" that they impose that seems to be based solely on your level. The effect of this is that you can never actually get good at any of the puzzles in the game - because as you invest in your character, the puzzles get harder at a much faster rate. Particularly if you are playing the game with a gamepad (which this style of game is well suited to, normally), at level 14 or so you will simply not physically be able to solve some of the puzzles in time.
This wouldn't be a deal-breaker by itself, but combined with how much of the game's content (in the form of intel) is behind these puzzles, and how many of them in a row you have to pass before your next checkpoint, the game eventually becomes a nightmare for anyone who actually wants to experience the content.
Also, there is way too much mandatory combat for a game that let's you invest almost exclusively in stealth.
Also, the writing is like a male adolescent sex fantasy.
There are some interesting bits - the intel system and the dialog system have potential, but they are utterly wasted in a game that becomes unplayable the more you play it in a certain play style.

+Strategic and fun due to great combination of stealth and turn-based.
+Beautiful art atyle.
+No RNG in combat.
+Procedurally generated levels.
+Vast array of weapons/gadgets and characters who have unique special abilities .

+Decent story.
Cons:
I can't think of any (but I am not a professional reviewer either). To be honest, once I like a game, I fail to see its shortcomings.

I spent at least 20 of my hours watching other orcs fight each other and playing another game on my phone.  I got to act 4 in the game and I'm having trouble forcing myself to keep playing the game.  Graphics are good, music fits what you are doing usually.  Jumping seems bugged, tired of hitting invisible walls in random spots, or not being able to make a jump that I have done twice the distance on multiple times.
Orcs are interesting, story is good.  Content is low.  Like, really really low.  Side quests and main quests don't justify the price.  Act 4 soft pay wall to make you spend money on boxes, don't care what any of you think, the only reason for such a ridiculous grind is to make you pay for things in a single player game.  The phone app I played while watching orcs fight had less of a paywall, and kept me interested at least.
If the price was $30 I would say yeah, its worth it, but at $60 to $100, it just isn't worth it unless you just have to fight orcs.
Also, as for the combat, everything gets repetitive.  You are pretty much fighting the same enemies over and over again (or watching them fight so they can level) for 60 plus hours just so they can defend your fortress from other players or NPCs.  Fighting gets annoying as what you are aiming for isn't usually what you are going to hit, and because of that you get moved into a spot that an orc is attacking for like no reason at all.   Or he can see the future.
Microtransactions aren't necessary, but you can buy a box instead of watching your orc pokemon fight, saving you roughly 2-3 hours in the process.  Of course, you can't buy the good boxes with in game currency (which they will probably change down the line seeing all the negative reviews, but the price will just be ridiculously high) so if you buy a box you still have a chance of getting some dimwit that will just die anyway.
Sieges (both offensive and defensive) are boring.  Avenging players is pretty lame since you usually end up fighting like 3 or 4 enemy generals (at least in my experience).  I just can't recommend this game.  It feels more decent expansion to the first game, and not like a stand alone game to me.

The idea of "Nothing will be forgotten" really doesn't apply to this game from what I've seen. The nemesis system from the last game was great because you could develop these long and detailed stories based on what captains you kill/which come back. But in this game the armies are totally different based on which region you're in and there's seemingly no crossover, so the minute you leave a region your history with that army stays. This forces you to have much shorter, less interesting stories with the orc captains and you never really feel in any way connected to any of them (aside from the story required ones).
The gameplay is the same as the first but a bit more expanded on and detailed, and the microtransactions (despite what everyone seems to be saying) are not required at all to complete the game. They help, but they're not required. Still sort of a sketchy business practice and clearly a way to take more money from your consumers, but not the end of the world like what people want you to think.

Cons:
- Battle animations are not interesting, plus it seems like damage doesn't necessarily coincide with an actual strike
- Music doesn't help immersion
- Scavenging (outside of camp) is just a battle and you "win" the supplies/loot

I like that because usually it's ONLY scavenging so it's an interesting twist - at lest for me. I like the idea of being raided as well as going on rescue and scavenge missions.

Invisible, Inc, is a turn-based strategy game developed by Klei Entertainment and released May 12, 2015.
As it seems to be the trend with Klei games, they appear simple enough to pick up and start playing withing minutes... but take many many hours to master.
You are part of a covert team of operatives who exist in a bureaucratic-controlled-world; Corporations are in charge of the world.
Invisible inc. is the name of the intelligence agency. When the game starts your agency has been compromised and all of the agents have been lost except for two. It's your job to help the agency recover by plugging the agency's AI ' incognita" into a super computer, you have '72 hours' emergency power.
I highly suggest you play the beginning tutorial to explain the movement and use of cover. I don't think I can articulate how the game works well enough. I would encourage you to watch my video at the bottom of this review to get a better idea how the game works.
The basic idea is you are moving your agents around in turn-based-combat form. You always want to look around corns, and peer through doors before opening them.
The game rewards stealth and patience... but you can't be too patient, because each turn a clock will tick and as the security level increases, so too does the complexity. The first few security levels will just increase fire walls and security cameras... but this will quickly escalate to summoning additional guards and ARMORED guards.
You won't be able to fight your way through armored guards until you have specific gear, and even then you'll better off just trying to sneak your way around or distract them away to create openings.
There is an overwhelming amount of things to consider when first learning how to play invisible, Inc.
I haven't even touched on incognita's hacking, viruses, upgrades, augments, the types of missions... Honestly invisible, Inc. Will appeal to people who love complexity and difficulty within their games. And It's a Klei Game... so you know it's going to be stylish as heck!

Lethal vs no Lethal takedowns create their own problems.
I leave you with this advice...
1.  You have Action Points (AP) and Power (PWR).  (Don’t run out of either at the wrong time)
Get Lvl 2 Anarchy on every agent.  (Stealing is necessary).
2.  Always have a Hacker in your Squad.  (PWR is a resource and hacker can get you’re the most).
3.  Acquire AP weapons sooner rather than later.  (Over time guards have better armor)
4.  The Teleport Beacon is great (in DLC addon)!!!  (You can transport yourself plus whoever you are Dragging which is great for escapes. I usually find the teleport pad and toss it down then when you get into trouble trying to finish that last objective or hack the safe you can teleport back.  It’s great for rescue missions and retrieving downed agents)
5.  Close doors behind you when you enter and leave rooms.  (A few bullets to the back will remind you should you forget)

I don't know how to communicate the quality of this game. Everything about it feels just right. The balancing, the mechanics, the abilities, and the difficulty are all perfect. The game's level generation feels fair but still presents a challenge. You can't just fly through your turns and/or kill everything either. They really emphasized stealth in the gameplay and it is very refreshing. You have to think about every square and the effect it will have on the rest of the mission.
