RELEASE VERSION UPDATE: Initial beta/backers review found after.
This is it. This is the big one. For many people, this is one of the most anticipated games of the year - the great inspiration for Fallout, the driver of classic RPGs, the callback to a genre slowly reviving. One of the first big huge Kickstarted games. After two years in development, how does it hold up? Spoilers: it holds up damn well.
Wasteland 2 is a classic RPG in the style of Fallout 1, 2, and Tactics. In fact, the original Wasteland was the inspiration for the Fallout universe, and shares many similarities and concepts with Wasteland. You take control of four fresh-faced Ranger recruits, sent out on a task to make yourselves worthy of your badges. What ends up happening is a journey across Arizona, and then some.
The game starts off with character creation. You can choose to create your own Ranger from scratch, or pick a pre-made Ranger from a list. The pre-made characters are alright, but for most people, you'll want to make your own customized Rangers. You can distribute attribute and skillpoints as you see fit, change your Ranger's physical appearance, and even stick in his/her own little bio and a custom portrait.
After setting yourself up, you end up in the Arizona wasteland, right outside Ranger Citadel. You are greeted by General Vargas, a veteran Ranger and an old character from Wasteland.  Another Ranger vet, Ace, has just died in action, and you and your team are sent out to investigate his murder and finish his mission as a trial. Succeed, and you all become official Rangers.
At first glance, one can immediately note the biggest downside to the game - graphical fidelity. While I personally feel that the graphics do not detract from the game, and in fact works to further the atmosphere it sets about creating, it is easy to see that the game is not about the shinies. Its easily trumped by Divinity: Original Sin in terms of fidelity, but that is not to say the game looks bad. It is simply objectively dated, even for a Unity-based game. Performance also leaves something to be desired - on a GTX 765M, the game hovers at about 40-50fps, sometimes dipping below to 30. Whilst expected for a new release, it certainly does not look like it should be choking up a moderately good mobile GPU as far as it is.  However, the graphical style the game takes is very immersive - you have varying environs, from lush greens to barren browns, and everything in between. The wasteland feels desolate and real.
Wasteland 2 is set in an isometric, top-down view. You control your Rangers overhead, order them around by clicking in the world. There are two world types - the main world, showing you Arizona and the rest of the area, where you go around between smaller local maps, looking for oases for water, and avoiding rad clouds, then the local maps, which is where you explore, do missions, talk to people, shoot people, all that good stuff. Combat is turn based, engaging when you run into hostiles or turn other people hostile by shooting at them/having a negative interaction. Characters take turns in commiting actions, with each action costing certain Action Points to do. Your characters can use a slew of weapons, from going in fisticuffs, to heavy armanents such as bazookas and heavy MGs, all of which can be skilled up. Positioning is key, with certain weapons being effective at certain ranges, and cover helping you avoid damage. Damaged Rangers can only be healed up with medkits, pain pills, and trauma kits if they bleed out. There is no idle healing, which means every fight has to be planned, and you have to have enough supplies to last.
Overall, I feel that Wasteland 2 offers a refreshing jump back into cRPGs, bringing the spirit of post-apocalyptic games from the past well into the 21st century. If you love turn based games, old RPGs, post-apocalypse settings, then you'll love (or absolutely hate - in a good way!) Wasteland 2. Give it a try.
_________________________________________________________________________________
Wasteland 2: One of the first gigantic projects on Kickstarter, the revival of an era, the granddaddy of Fallout, the great leap back for inXile.
Is it any good (so far?) The short answer:  yes, yes it is.
Wasteland 2 is one of the biggest, most high profile projects funded through Kickstarter – indeed, funding for the game came after Double Fine Adventure’s own successful Kickstarter. The game raised roughly 3,000,000USD, well exceeding its goal of 900,000USD.
The game follows up on Wasteland, which was the basis for many elements in the Fallout series. Many elements seen in Fallout can be seen here – radioactive wasteland, Rangers building up a civilized society, raiders, tech-fanatics, militant religious fanatics are all present in the game, clearly showing how much it influenced other games later on.
Gameplay is very much Fallout like as well. You explore the world with your party, with the world map being just that – a map that you navigate your party blimp through. Movement is dependent upon your water supply – you lose water, you die. Thankfully, there are hidden oases all over the map, giving enough opportunities to refill water to quench one’s wanderlust. In local areas, one goes about with the whole party, with your selected member doing the interactions. Conversations follow a keyword system – anything you observe in the environment might pop up as a keyword for characters in the locale, while some words in conversations can lead to further inquiries as well. Some conversation options require certain skills to be at a certain level, and can lead to clearing certain obstacles in a peaceful manner. Combat is turn based, following an AP system similar to, again, Fallout. On this, I cannot say much – I’ve only played less than two hours, and so far, the early mobs were easy enough to wipe without having to worry about cover and positioning. Even then, I did take a noteable amount of damage, and would probably lose my party members if I continued to do so.
Wasteland 2 runs on Unity – so far, in this current beta build, there are no graphical options to speak of, besides resolution and an overall graphics preset. Setting it to Fantastic with an i7-4700MQ and GTX 765M, the game looks fantastic – it pushes Unity to the edge. However, this being a beta, performance is not spectacular – fully zoomed out, FRAPS was showing around 24fps to a max of 30fps, which is barely passable. Dropping presets down to standard did not help performance, so I am assuming this is a “beta is beta” issue, and will be patched before the actual launch.
Is Wasteland 2 worth your time right now for 60USD? I would say, yes – if you can get past the beta-ness of it (you’ll have to download and print the reference sheet as there isn’t much of a tutorial in game), it is a good sign of the return of cRPGs and TBS games with rich narrative and an open approach to quests. While it wouldn’t hurt to wait, if you’ve been on the fence on it and can’t wait, it’s a solid game beta.

A finely-crafted psychological thriller from Remedy Entertainment, where you play as the titular protagonist Alan Wake as he tries to solve the mystery surrounding his wife's disappearance, while on holiday in the sleepy town of Bright Falls.
Gameplay is well-balanced. Oppressive nighttime sequences are punctuated by the serene daytime sequences, allowing the player a release of tension before having to jump again into the insidious dark. The setpieces are beautiful and are further enhanced by the cinematic approach the game takes to showcase them.
Thematically, Alan Wake draws predominantly from the works of Stephen King, from notable stories such as "Misery", "The Shining", "The Dark Half", and "Secret Window, Secret Garden" all of which feature writers as protagonists coming to terms with themselves and their creations. Other stylistic influences include Hitchcock's "Birds" and "Psycho", David Lynch's "Twin Peaks", Rod Serling's "The Twilight Zone", and "The X-Files". Further and perhaps unintended allusions to Neil Gaiman's "American Gods" can also be seen.
Alan Wake is not horror, but a self-aware and reverent pastiche of the horror, suspense, psychological thriller, paranormal fiction, and fantasy genres. In that regard it is wholly unique, and few other games are able to do what it does, as well as it does.
Highly recommended.

This isn't pac-man, it's some weird parody of the original. The maze litterally never ends (there's just one infinite level). You don't clear all the dots (you just get rewarded for chaining together as many in a row as possible). And you don't even get multiple lives (just one, die and start over).
After an hour of playing I'm not sure what the point is. You seem to unlock things after each death, but the gameplay doesn't really change. You get loot boxes full of coins that don't seem to have a purpose.
I'd call it a nostalgia trip but it kind of isn't.
I got this as part of a humble bundle and it's OK. It's probably worth $1 or $2, I think $5 (the regular non sale price) might be a bit steep for how shallow the game is.
I will say it's cheaper than feeding quarters into the original. And the ability to reskin the map into various abstract themes is a cute addition (that adds nothing to the actual gameplay, just appearance change).
If you are looking at the screenshots thinking "hey there's a bunch of different games/maps/mazes", no, there isn't. It's the same infinite map. You pick a theme when you start, it's just a skin change.
It was neat for about an hour, and whoever made this has a serious grasp on how to make addictive sound effects. But I'm not sure I'll ever put much more time into it than that.
If you need some vague parody of a modern pac-man game, this is it.
Great game. It's well worth this price.

Let's start with the fact that Middle Earth: Shadow of War is technically a good game, and nothing can take that away.
BUT (and this is a big one), the microtransactions, with the lootbox mechanics are so terrible and insidious, that it's on the same level of badness, as the game is good without it. You can disagree with me, but this is how I feel, this is the biggest flaw of the game. Lootboxes. They're really hard to avoid, and have a serious effect on the game in my opinion, and it'd be more grindy without it than it'd be acceptable for me. The greediness of WB is absolutely apparent in this case. This mechanic is just as bad in my opinion, as that other popular movie-based game that has lootboxes in it.
There are plenty of examples for the good parts of the game. I absolutely love the upgraded Nemesis system, the generated Orcs look awesome, and have great, often funny personalities, and your actions affect these personalities (as usual), but with more variations, and event triggers. The loot system would be cool on it's own (although I don't really like looking at the basic armor during cinematics), the items look really nice as well. I didn't finish the game yet, but I've spent quite a bit of time with it, and I like the story so far, tied in with the fortress conquering sections.
Overall, I'd give this game an 8 or 9/10, but the microtransactions drive it down for me pretty much, so I have to give it a 6/10, and I still can't recommend it because of these BS business practices.

Got all the way up to act 4 without spending anything beyong the initial sixty bucks and 50 hours of my time. The overarching story is driving and amazing, the combat is smooth with only a few problems like mis-targeting orcs for "Execution" (F on the keyboard), or clinging to walls when I don't want it to (But that's because I tend to hold Spacebar, and I'm bad at aiming Talion, so it's my fault). I hated the Celebrimbor flashback missions the most, they felt unnecessary, but as a completionist I felt obligated. And, a lot of times, the audio would desync from animations.... why? Those are the only things I found annoying or wrong with the game. I never encountered any other problems or bugs (though, I thought I did on one quest, but I was just blind).
Yup, there are microtransactions. Nope you don't need to Pay2Win. The game throws in-game currency at you in-droves, you can buy loot boxes just by playing the game. Get a few really strong Captains, and hit the pits... I know one pit will give you 5k per win, that's 3 loot boxes per win. Maybe some others will give you more? -it experiences the same problems that Overwatch had; allowing duplicate heroes. this creates pretty unfun scenarios that break the game
- some characters have disproportionate rate of fire and dps, specifically Ruckus. He also seems to have no damage fall off with range, which allows him to do too much damage at long range
- Some characters don't do enough or are irrelevant
- Hit boxes seem to be very inconsistent especially with headshots on moving targets
The maps are generally too simple in their design and do not have well thought out flanking routes and choke points
Every character seems to have an escape ability of some kind, which makes the game a little less exciting and makes poking a more viable strategy than diving. This is not my personal pref but whatevs
Characters and their abilities are not described clearly enough or the description are not obvious enough.
Overall, it isn't even close to Overwatch in terms of depth, balance or quality. it is an interesting iteration in the genre and worth a look as it is quite fun

NOTE: I have also played about 25-50 hours of the PS4 version of NT. so here is my review
Nuclear throne is a Top-down shooter Rogue-lite where you take control of a mutated creature in a post apocalyptic world where humanity has fallen. Your only means of survival is guns, lots of guns.
The Visual style is similar to many JRPG's like Suikoden with the camera angle being slightly tilted backwards slightly looking downwards and the action.  however the actual art, sprites, and color pallettes are very reminescent of 16 bit arcade shoot-em-ups.  The game is in a 4:3 aspect ratio which is said to be intentional for the atmosphere of the arcade like visual style. Due to engine limitations however the game is locked at 30 FPS with no fix in sight. That being said, Nuclear Throne still runs smoothly with very few hick-ups in the framerate.
The Music in Nuclear throne some of the best music I have heard in games in recent memory. Everything from the boss music, to the background guitars during the wasteland stages, and even a little rap in one area. the sound effects sound are strong and crisp with every gun sounding different and distinct whilst still sounding like guns (Black ops III could learn something from NT)
The gameplay is what I love most about Nuclear throne. The top down shooter nature of the action make the moments and peaks amazingly adrenaline pumping and fun. Even the slow parts of collecting the last of the guns for the next levels can't be too boring due to those parts being very short. The fast pace of Nuclear Throne makes the gameplay more inticing than even Binding of Isaac at some points. Not only does the rogue-lite influences in Nuclear throne make it a joy to play but, it also makes for nearly Infinite replay value and lasting appeal. however the game does crash on occasion, but it is thankfully rare.
THE VERDICT: Nuclear throne is one of the best rogue-lites currently available and makes a statement on how to correctly approach difficulty, fun and shoot-em-up action in new ways. Nuclear throne is also one of the most refreshing games I have played in the last 5 years. So the final score for Nuclear throne will be a 9/10

I haven't played the regular game at all because I remember the first Banner Saga's strange interpretation of "turn order". While innovative, it's also counter-intuitive, with generally the best strategy being to maim everything in sight but not finish off any particular opponent. I'm not crazy about constructing a barrier out of crippled foes while I plink away at their health back ranks, but thankfully, the second iteration of this game very nearly scratches my squad-tactics itch. My main interest is the (mostly) deterministic turn-based combat. It's really refreshing to play a game with deep tactics that doesn't rely on chance to provide a dynamic challenge. The armor/strength system is simple but brilliant and rewards careful planning and execution. So yes, full disclosure: I've bascially only played survival mode, but I've played a lot of it. If you like turn-based tactics, and don't like random-number-generated tension, I'd have to recommend this one, because it's about the only thing like it. (Incidentally, if you're reading this review and know of another game like this, particularly one that doesn't have the problem mentioned below, leave a comment and you'll have my deep gratitude.)
So I've got only one gripe, but it's a pretty significant one: The game is turn-based, but there is a turn-timer, and there is no way to pause. It's also single-player only, by the way. On top of that, the interface is a bit clunky; meaning that assessing the potential movement of an enemy takes several seconds, and if there are several enemies, it's pretty easy to run out of time and completely miss a character's turn. Don't try to wait to the last second assessing your options because any action requires several clicks to choose and confirm. It is frustrating to warrant the negative review in my opinion, although, as previously mentioned, if you're having trouble finding a game that throws that stupid d20 in the trash where it mostly belongs, try this one, you might have a different opinion.
I think the timer is motivated by the notion of "leaderboards". For what it's worth, I'm one of those people who couldn't give a frog's fart for how I stack up against other people in a turn-based tactical game. Well... I guess that's not completely true: I also play a lot of internet chess on FICS and pay some attention to my rating, so yeah... But still, I'd be elated if only there were a "hardcore" mode with ticking turn-timers and the like, but also a "sissy" mode for folks like me who enjoy turn-based tactics because of it's player-defined pacing.
Anyways, if that silly timer could be disabled (it can't and this game doesn't support mods), I would give this game a REALLY enthusiastic thumbs up, solely on the basis of the survival minigame. I'm sure the main game is lovely too, if you're into that story, character development and meaningful decisions sort of thing. I kind of leave that stuff for books, movies, and the cereal aisle, but hey, whatever floats your boat.

I really loved this game and it scratched my itch for a proper RPG style tale in a computer format. To get the most out of it I recommend playing it with a role-playing mindset, that is what made it a great experience for me, trying to get under the skin of the character you are playing and make choices based on what that person would do, not what you think would get most XP for. Min-maxing party membership and other stuff is important to many people and they get their chance to enjoy their thing, but it is not required to complete the game fully.
+ The setting, the story: Great stuff, some innovative storytelling right there. Trying to survive during Ragnarok is good material for dramatic tension.
+ Animation: I for one love the animation on the battlefield, the little manuevers the characters perform, the little dances, the gestures. I think the animation was top-notch and a important part of the game.
+ The sound: From soundtrack to voiceacting it was really well done and suited the atmosphere of the game.
+ The different perspective: Playing as the Ravens was a nice touch and the different approaches between a somewhat naive Alette and a cynical Borkverk was great fun to play out.
+ Artstyle: The characters, the backgrounds, the fallen gods, you name it.
The battle mechanics are serviceable but not great, the animations made me enjoy them a lot even so and I had more fun fighting in this game than in Banner Saga 1 wich has the same mechanics.
Overall I give this game a 9/10, though keep in mind I came for the roleplaying and the story, and I got exactly what I wanted.

text: A new and fresh take on the arcade shooter genre, Nuclear Throne steps it up to a whole new level. The addicting, yet difficult mission of conquering each and every level by slaughtering everything in your way with a vast array of weapons and multiple characters provides hours of fun for anyone. The character-specific abilities and varying mutations provide a mechanic in which the player chooses their own destiny, being a conservative health-garnering attacker, or an all-out assault type of character who harvests ammunition and greater damage. You can mix these sets equally if you choose, best suiting your character for their journey to the final boss. The game, personally, was very frustrating and hard to replay after dying with a good set of weapons and mutations. However, after a few hours, the game will gradually draw you back into playing it and going on another run for the throne. This doesn't happen for every player, as many will take secret shortcuts to further parts of the game. The game provides an excellent soundtrack, colorful maps and characters, and an all around fun feeling that's been missing from the current era of gaming. It's nice to see something so simple be made into a fun game, along with all of it's specialites and new additions. It never ends, and it only gets more difficult. This game does not hold your hand. Truly a game worth it's price, especially since you can play it without an internet connection and enjoy destroying enemies and looping the game. 9/10

I described this game to a friend as the love child of early Max Payne games and movie The Ring. While that's too simplistic of a characterization, it should nevertheless give you a basic idea of how everything plays out. From the outstanding design of the characters, each of which you will develop a connection with, to the simultaneously serene and terrifying portrayal of the Pacific Northwest, this is arguably Remedy's best cinematic gaming experience to date. The only gripe some might have is the combat system, which does take a while to get used to and might frustrate some players in the earlier levels. Stick with it though, as you become more proficient with the controls it will make every hostile encounter and progression through the varied levels an anxiety inducing ordeal in which every bullet, flashlight battery, and any other necessity must be used sparingly to ensure your survival. I have never felt the magnitude of relief and satisfaction this game provides in successfully moving forward in any other title. Follow the light (hah!) and get this game. Quick edit: By the way, this game has the best use of licensed music I've ever seen. Some of the song choices will leave a serious impression on you. So good.

As a preface, I've gotta say that Alpha Protocol is one of those games that does a hell of a lot of things. But then it does a hell of a lot of those things really badly. It's like a 2:1 ratio of good features to bad features.
For those of you who like RPGs, and making a character from the ground up, Alpha Protocol offers that pretty well. There's plenty of perks and a full set of skill trees to invest in as you level up, allowing you to make completely different characters each time.
BUT. You can easily make your character overpowered by investing all your points into select abilities that make you excel at your playstyle. About halfway through the game, playing as a stealth/tech guy, I had an ability that let me sprint around completely invisible for 25 seconds, with a 90 second cooldown. During that period, I could knock out anyone without getting spotted. This meant literally every stealth section of the game became as simple as using that ability. Also, the ability that lets you line up critical hits from cover meant I could just take down an entire room of enemies without even aiming a weapon.
Then there's the dialogue system. It's ♥♥♥♥ing phenomonal. No other game really gives you such a feeling of choice, and entire missions can be locked behind certain dialogue options. You never know what you're missing out on or what you've just gotten yourself into. For example, at one point in the game, I spared this one assassin, who shall not be named. I didn't have to do that at all, but when I did, it gave me good rep with a faction I didn't even know existed, access to some extra black market goods, a new handler and some extra support for later missions. Quite a lot just for one seemingly meaningless choice. Then again, I could have denied this other faction if I didn't trust them and I would skip all those other benefits entirely. The dialogue system is surprisingly extensive and you actually do make some meaningful decisions with it.
BUT. It's like Fallout 4. i.e. You pick the option "Dismissive", and suddenly your character has made some really condescending remark, while you were expecting him to say something completely different. On more than one occasion I've ♥♥♥♥ed up dialogue choices purely because I had no idea what my character was to say. A real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ It should be done Deus Ex style, where you can see a brief sentence of each option before picking it, because as is, there are plenty of important decisions you can ♥♥♥♥ up by just not knowing what your character is going to say.
I do like that the game has a full fledged reputation system for each character, and depending on what you say or do, each character will gain a different view of you. Depending on if someone hates you or likes you, they'll alter what happens later on.
BUT. The game really likes to drive home this whole "Reputation" system. On more than one occasion, the game will face you with a pretty laughable decision. "This person will be killed, but this other person can be stopped. You can only do one of them, but not both, for reasons. Why have I even given you the opportunity to only do one of these things? Well, err..." The game really likes to remind you that this system is in place and really drive home the "moral decisions" narrative.
The stealth gameplay in Alpha Protocol is pretty nice. It's very Splinter Cell-ish, but also gives you a lot more versatility. I found that I just levelled Martial Arts right up very high. That was enough for me to just beat my way through every area. Hell, it was even effective against bosses.
BUT. It's really unpolished. Enemies will spot you through cover in certain places. Maybe because the cover isn't adequate and they can still see you over it or something like that. The game doesn't really give you any indication of when you're in effective cover or not. Cover that doesn't seem to be effective, like hiding behind a chair, suddenly works like a charm. The alert phase is messed up as well. Enemies will head straight to full alert after seeing you for less than a second. There's no real period of grace or timeout. Once they see you, you're spotted. Luckily, this is counterbalanced by the "Evasion" ability, which makes you invisible for a certain amount of time after being spotted. To add to all that, distractions barely work. You're given a distraction device, but whenever you use it, the enemy will seemingly sprint right towards you anyway, even if they don't know you're there.
In terms of story, it's actually pretty good. I expected it to be another Splinter Cell type of story where "Jamal Rafiq Bumbaclot the Second" does something that violates national security so a bunch of spec op guys find him and realize he's actually just working for someone else, and it was all a ruse. Then the game introduces a different twist that turns the game more into Deus Ex. Now Jamal Rafiq Bumbaclot is still there. He's just been Deus Ex'd a little. I quite liked it, even if the ending was very simplistic.
On another note, the game is horrendously unbalanced. Just investing in a few different skills will suddenly make you overpowered af tbh fam. This one ability, when upgraded fully and used in a creative way, can be used to kill pretty much every boss in the game in less than 3 hits. Even the final boss, with his body armor and everything, was reduced to half health from one blast of this ability.
Also, the game's got a fair few weapons you can kit yourself out with, and a lot of interesting minigames, such as hacking and lockpicking.
All in all, it's a very Deus Ex-like game, story-wise and gameplay-wise. Alpha Protocol is definitely unique, but despite its flaws, I really enjoyed it.

I poured hours into this game (this does not show on my steam account because of reasons). Literally days, and this is where it all went wrong for me.
I live in a house with my Mother, Father and Two dogs. Sadly, while playing this game and excitedly trying out all the different keys I could use to play the piano, I failed to hear my Mother shout as she fell down the stairs. She broke both of her legs and stayed there all day. When my Dad returned home, he tripped over her unconcious body and also broke his legs. At this point I was mastering Beethoven's Moonlight Sonata, having finished all of his other symphonies. I did not hear them shouting for help.
The days came and went, the mail piled up on my doormat and the milk went bad outside the door. Eventually, after two months my neighbour came around to check on us, and roused me from my waking coma. I stepped downstairs and found that sadly my dogs had gone without food and taken to eating my parents. They had developed a taste for human flesh, and had already killed my neighbour, and had begun feasting on her.
I left them to it, as I'd been out for a few minutes and missed playing Mountain, and continued playing for a few more weeks until my electricity was shut off. I then went downstairs, fought off my dogs with a toaster and made some soup and am now waiting to die. I am typing this with 19% battery left on my phone, as I could not find a laptop with enough charge to play more Mountain.
Overall, I'd give this game a solid 11/10 for gameplay, however owing to it's addictive qualities which led to the early demise of both my parents, our concerned neighbour and my two beloved Dogs, I have had to lower this figure to a more conservative 8/10.

The hugely expanded Nemesis System in particular deserves praise, even after completing the story (which was okay-ish, very predictable but better than the fist game, it did keep me intrigued) I'm still encountering new Orcs constantly!
Now, I think other reviewers have discussed the game as a whole better than I can so I won't, so i'll just offer my quick thoughts on the 2 main "controversies" surrounding the game, namely the final Act (Shadow Wars) and the issue of microtransactions.
The end-game does get grindy, yes, but I feel people who talk about this have been missing the point of it. It's designed for people who have finished the story, and wish to continue defending their fortresses in the Shadow Wars, and killing/recruiting better and better Orcs. Essentially it's for people who love the game and its concept. I feel Act III does bring the story to its conclusion in a logical way, and everything on top of that is extra. I do wonder though why people complain after playing the game for 30+ hours, supposedly enjoying it and then all of a sudden it turns into something awful? Are those hours after the 30+ you spent worse than the ones you spent to get to that point? I don't get it but that's just me. Personally, I love the Shadow Wars.
Finally, on the lootboxes. In short, it's a complete non-issue that people blew up way too much. In my time with the game I have not bought a SINGLE Gold lootbox, nor has the game eve gated my progression at all. Actually, you can even earn Gold currency by doing community challenges. I have bought a handful of regular lootboxes with in-game currency - that is handed out in vast amounts by the way - and noticed that they make absolutely no difference, actually some of the Orcs I have gotten are worse than the ones in the open world. Does that mean I like microtransactions or support them? No, but in this particular case they have effected my time with the game...not at all actually.
All this said I will gladly support the game and recommend it for anyone who enjoyed the first one or wishes to jump in to the expanded (and much more difficult) experience with the Nemesis System for the first time. Don't expect the story to be anything mind-blowing, and enjoy the Nemesis System by letting your defeats and victories turn into unique stories, and I'm sure you'll enjoy the game overall.

A strong freeware add-on presence is also available for this game to cater towards more fruga simmers.
This simulation remains the industry standard for simulators for 10 years running. This sim gets a firm reccomendation. Banner Saga 2 feels and plays almost exactly like the first installment of the series, which is both a good and a bad thing. On the plus side, it is still an amazingly beautiful game; on the negative side, it still suffers from an incredibly stupid battle system.
To give a quick recap, in the world of the Banner Saga a characters' hit points is also equal to the amount of damage they can dish out. An uncommon yet interesting concept - which is completely ruined by one major flaw: your party and the enemies will always alternate turns.
If an enemy is killed, the next in line will simply take their position; this means that the optimal strategy to win is usually to beat down each enemy to its health minimum and then move on to the next opponent until the battlefield is filled with cripples. Conversely, this means that saving your own injured characters is a tactical disadvantage.
It also results in the absurd fact that battles are generally the easier the bigger the enemy army, as they will waste turns moving with far away characters while you can maim everything next to your guys with no resistance. As an unfortunate side-effect this drains atmosphere from the story, as the approaching giant army of Dredge hardly seems like a menace.
Granted, the developer has apparently realized how stupid their system is, and introduced a number of new talents and features which punish not killing enemies, allow for turn order manipulation, or outright alter/replace the combat system. Is it enough to save Banner Saga 2's merit as a strategy game? No. Which is sad, because it is a great narrative experience.
That said, there's a few other things about the game I found annoying, but also a few improvements compared to its predecessor:
Positive:
- more detailed and varied battlefields
- battlefields which are just squares are less common
- finally a decent variety of enemies
Negative:
- The ending. It is weak from a story standpoint, but gameplay-wise it plain sucks. None of the last few battles are challenging, and the final one is just a dumb gimmick involving no strategy
- Choices are oftentimes mundane, and choosing anything that involves your lead character almost always nets the best result without any danger
- You still made a bad choice and lost clansmen? Hard to care since they're little more but numbers on the top of the screen, serving even less purpose than before
- Inconsistent character sprites. One can clearly distinguish old and new character models (the old ones have a more grey outline, while the newer ones are black); some such as Rook have some animation frames with both, and it looks really patchy once you have noticed it for the first time
- RNG is a bigger factor due to numerous new talents which have a % chance to do something
- The game does a lot of "tell" but little "show". An epic confrontation between Eyvind and the world-eating Serpent just happened? Here, enjoy this still image of guys standing around and talking about how amazing it was.
Conclusion:
A bit better than the first installment, but Banner Saga 2 is another pass. Sadly.

text: A new and fresh take on the arcade shooter genre, Nuclear Throne steps it up to a whole new level. The addicting, yet difficult mission of conquering each and every level by slaughtering everything in your way with a vast array of weapons and multiple characters provides hours of fun for anyone. The character-specific abilities and varying mutations provide a mechanic in which the player chooses their own destiny, being a conservative health-garnering attacker, or an all-out assault type of character who harvests ammunition and greater damage. You can mix these sets equally if you choose, best suiting your character for their journey to the final boss. The game, personally, was very frustrating and hard to replay after dying with a good set of weapons and mutations. However, after a few hours, the game will gradually draw you back into playing it and going on another run for the throne. This doesn't happen for every player, as many will take secret shortcuts to further parts of the game. The game provides an excellent soundtrack, colorful maps and characters, and an all around fun feeling that's been missing from the current era of gaming. It's nice to see something so simple be made into a fun game, along with all of it's specialites and new additions. It never ends, and it only gets more difficult. This game does not hold your hand. Truly a game worth it's price, especially since you can play it without an internet connection and enjoy destroying enemies and looping the game. 9/10

The Banner Saga 2 is the second game in the Banner Saga trilogy (the third part being currently in development), and is basically more of the same, but with several improvements. It tells the tale of a few human and Varl, trying desperately to survive in a norse mythology based world on the brink of total collapse. The story follows two separate, but intertwined routes. One is a clan leader, trying to lead a caravan of his clansmen to the relative safety of the human capital, Arberrang. The second is Bolverk, a ruthless Varl mercenary on a quest from one of the mysterious Valka (sort of a human wizard). Both will face hard choices en route, and both will suffer the consequences. Essentialy, the gameplay comes down to three things. First is managing your caravan, making sure your clansmen are safe, happy and have enough to eat. This involves dealing with various events along the way, which is the second part of the fun. Every situation you encounter comes with a choice. It is sometimes difficult to tell what is the best course of action, and consequences can be dire - including the death of key characters. Third part of the gameplay are the tactical battles. So, here is a breakdown on what is done right and what needs some rework.
The Good:
+ The atmosphere of this game is incredible. Both the music and the gorgeous, hand drawn graphics make you feel engrossed in the game and the desperate struggle for survival of its heroes
+ Battles are improved compared to the first game. The enemies are much more varied this time around instead of the endless sea of Dredge in the first game. The battle maps are also much more interesting, since they now have destructible obstacles and choke points.
+ Added survival mode is loads of fun if you like the combat system. With the whole roster of characters available to choose from for your party, there are a lot of possible ways of approaching the combat. I recommend targeting some of the achievements for an additional challenge.
+ Saves carry over from the previous edition. Because of this, you can play as two different main characters, depending on the choices from the first game.
+ Choices have real consequences. Sometimes, they are really difficult to predict, so you feel just as lost as the main character, trying to do the right thing and often failing.
The Mediocre:
~ Sometimes, the options presented to the player are very similar, which makes it frustrating when you feel you have chosen the option slightly better suited to the character, yet get punished for it.
~ We're at the second game, and there are still more questions than answers. I am beginning to fear that the third game will not have enough time to resolve everything in a satisfactory manner. Hopefully that will not be the case.
~The interface is a bit clunky. This is especially true in the character screen. I get that this was done deliberately so that the game could work on touch screens and consoles, but come on, some streamlining for PC cannot be all that hard.
The Bad:
- Renown, the rather scarce main resource of the game, is tied to steam achievements. Each time you finish an achievement, you receive a certain amount of renown. I have two problems with this. First of all, it is easy to screw up. Hard. So, you'd probably want to load... and thus lose the renown for, say, killing 3 enemies with a certain character, which you managed to do just before loading. I get that this is done to encourage playing the game to the end without using saves and maybe trying another playthrough with other choices. This leads me to number two. If you are planning on a second playthrough, you are basically hindered from the start, since you will NOT gain any more renown from the achievements. And it is a significant amount - you could probably level a character from 5 to 10 for it, which is huge.
- Still no 'Undo move' in combat. This is incredibly frustrating. Many times I have moved a character only to find out I was out of range for an attack by one square or had to reload the whole battle due to a simple misclick.
TL;DR - Great game with an incredible atmosphere, consequence heavy choices and interesting combat. A must have if you played the first part. If you did not like Banner Saga 1, do not bother with this one either.

Did you like Banner Saga?
Yes?
Good. Banner Saga 2 is as much a direct sequel as can be expected. A few improvements here and there, though a notable absence of improvements the first game sorely needed (such as being able to undo your movements in tactical combat). It imports your save game directly from Banner Saga 1 and picks up where it left off. This results in you possibly starting out with wildly different parties, Renown (XP) and item layouts.
The overarching story is just as obtuse as the first game's, if not more, though what matters is the journey, the Oregon Trail-like traversing of beautiful landscapes and the challenges you find along the way, rather than the obscure main plot. The characters are dry and straightforward, and yet, I don't know how they do it, they manage to give surprising depth to many characters that barely have five spoken lines in the entire game. It's rather heartening.
As with the first game, Banner Saga 2 ends on a cliffhanger and rather obvious sequel hook. I have little to complain about this stupendous game. The art is beautiful, the music is stirring, the combat is tactical and fun, the worldbuilding is fascinating. You can be sure I'll grab the third one when it comes out.

XCOM, but without the randomness.
Like XCOM, you play a series of turn based tactical missions on randomised maps, with a world map and team progression that ties them together.  Missions take 1-2 hour, maps are procedurally generated, there's one main objective that gives you something useful (a super loot container, a super shop terminal, an agent to rescue, etc.), loads of other things to loot on the way, threats to avoid, and one teleporter you escape through.  There's a lot of variety to keep each mission interesting.
Big difference 1)  Once you're in a mission there's no randomness. Guards follow fixed patterns; they don't teleport around until you spot them; your shots never miss (neither do theirs...), you can normally spot every surprise before it happens (peeking through doors and around corners, peeking at guard to see where they move next).  It can be challenging but it's always fair and it feels like every mission is doable if you play it right and you don't get greedy (which is really impressive given that it's procedurally generated).
Big Difference 2)  Semi-ironman with the Rewind mechanic.  If you make a mistake (or just missclick, I did that a lot), you can rewind back to the start of your previous turn.  You only have limited uses per mission (3 on normal, 1 on hard, you can set it to 0), so it's not a free ticket (it's a very expensive ticket) and you can't use it to cheat RNG because there is no RNG.  I think it's a great for people like me without the time or patience for real ironman modes but do like have decisions matter.
Oh, and the 2D art and animation looks beautiful.
Edit: I recommend the UI Tweaks mod
, doesn't break achievements but does fix a few things.

The first half-hour or so of playing this game I just couldn't believe how beautiful it is. I had seen the trailers of course but they just don't do playing this game on a nice big screen any justice. It really goes to show what we lost the moment somewhere in the early 2000s when we had convinced ourselves that 2D graphics were outdated and had to be confined to flash games, low-bugdet indie productions and side-scrollers. I really think the visuals of this game are ground-breaking. Breaking new ground also means that the graphics aren't perfect. You will occasionally still see pixels at certain zoom levels, a problem that just does not exist in this form for 3D games or games that don't zoom.
Music and voice acting are also great. Elijah Wood is not just a big name to sell more copies, he's just genuinely great for the role and incredibly nuanced. It's fun just listening to his voice.
There are a lot of interesting characters and I found the storylines compelling and quite surprising.
The thing that's criticized the most is the linearity and puzzle difficulty. Well, is this game as complex as Day of the Tentacle or does its world feel as grand as that of Monkey Island? No, surely not. If that's what you're looking for then you should at least wait for Act 2 to come out. Act 1 is meant to be a warm-up for Act 2 but we'll of course have to wait and see how this turns out. I can't say any of these criticisms occured to me personally while playing. I had hoped for more character interaction but the two plots are very much separated throughout Act 1. I quickly forgot that while playing though but I do still hope that we will see more DotT style interaction between the main characters in Act 2.
So in summary, if you're after some serious brain teasing, you'll have to find it somewhere else. If you can enjoy a good story, beautifully told in every way and garnished with some puzzles along the way to keep you invested, then this is definitely a game for you.

Hello everybody, I have to say that I was very impressed with everything I've seen with FSX so far, I've flown a Cessna out of Groton-New London Airport in Connecticut while taking flight lessons so naturally this was the first airport I had to check out. And I was really surprised to see it was basically the same right down to the office building I use to do my PTI in front of before going up. The physics of the aircraft felt and behaved the same as if I was flying the real deal, Oh sure, a few of the switches and knobs were there for looks but I was really impressed with the number of switches that did work and even though a lot of the terrain is only 2 dimensional like what you find on Google earth, I was really pleased to see how much of the buildings and such was actually in 3D. I took a flight in a DC3 over the mountains in Alaska and from 9000 feet they were realistic enough that I was glad I was flying in good weather. The only real issue I had was every time I ended a flight or training mission or anything I would hit Esc like it instructed and all I would get is a black screen and that wouldn't take the program back to the menu board like I expected but just stay black until I hit the widows key and completely close it out at which time I would have to go back to the steam menu and hit play and start over again. This I believe to be more of a compatibility issue with Windows 10 and not one of the FSX program and look forward to getting it resolved very soon, even with all that said I'd say it was still worth the $13 I paid for it and am not worried this issue can't be resolved because the enjoyment I get out of running this program still out weighs any problem I have encountered thus far.  Personally I have to say that I can't fly or even drive to far anymore as a back injury put an abrupt end to all that a long time ago, and maybe that's why I am so grateful to have this program because even though it's called a "Simulation Game" it's a good way for me to get out and explore the world and see all the places I use to see and a few thousand more I haven't  all from the confines of my little apartment. I really have to hand it to the young people at Microsoft that put this together and continue to work hard everyday to make it even better and I have no doubt they will.
If your the type of gamer that loves the feel of open world games and more realistic adventure then check this out, It's not perfect, then what is these days? I believe FSX has enough to do and see to keep anybody from getting board for as long,long time. The reviews and comments I have read that say the add-ons suck and some of the other aspects of this  or that aren't good enough, well all I can say to those people is just wait. It wasn't that long ago we were trying to hit a square ball with a short flat line to another short flat line on the other side of a dark green or black TV screen, Now one can fly one of many types of aircraft to thousands of destinations all over the world and talk with other people from around the world while you do it. Maybe FSX might have a few bugs but I think it's a really cool way to bring a world of people together instead of looking for a way to rip it apart.
Just one last thought,  the next time you go to see an air show and see a really cool plane parked in the hot sun but can't climb up inside to take a look because of the line of people with screaming kids got there way ahead of you, maybe you'll wish you spent the money on the simulated experience of flying it instead as long as you want without the long lines or the terrible parking or the cost of admission or gas to be there.
Y'all take care and Maybe will CU one FSX, as usual, I'll be the one with my head in the clouds, bye-bye :)

I played this in a 4 player group for the first time and was pleasantly surprised by the multiplayer mode. It's not totally co-op, because you are battling for points, but you also resurrect each other and share power-ups: when one player grabs a laser, everyone gets to use it. By watching each other's backs and co-operating, you can make much more progress.
True it's repetitive, and lacks depth, but compare that to original arcade Pac-Man and there's plenty of fun to be had. Plus, lots of unlockables and missions to keep you coming back for more.
Pro-Tip: each colour of ghost has a different type of move. Some have a set route, some will constantly chase you, and others have their own patterns. Learn to predict where they'll go.

Go Home - Rage incoming is accurate in title but I don't believe in intent. It's supposed to be this very hard timing oriented game that I assume is supposed to irritate you into rage because you keep making mistakes. However, for me the real challenge was the aspects of the game design itself. I didn't try multiplayer, so that mode isn't being evaluated in this review.
The goal is to get your square to the home location, and on some levels it's required that you pick up tokens. Other levels require you to finish the level within a certain amount of time. Sometimes the timer kicks in once you get to a certain part of the level. Overall the idea is not very complicated.
Sound: No idea, I had it muted while I watched Netflix.
Graphics: This was one of the areas I believe that was unintentional rage. If you're slightly red-green colorblind like a good portion of men, playing the game is more difficult because of the issues with color choice. There is no color blind mode. Further, you NEED to play on the highest graphic setting for level 25. What is the only change that occurs between fastest and this setting? You can see wall shadows which is extremely useful. So, if yoiu want a harder challenge, play on the fastest graphic settings. Other than that, the game has extremely simple graphics which is all it needs. Don't expect a masterpiece.
Controls: This was one of the irritating aspects of the game. If you were pushing against a wall in a diagnol direction, you would push into it and then stop. So this could cause problems as you needed precise manuvering. Another issue was if you use the analog stick to control your character, clicking it will activate the level reset. This was my major rage issue. I'd be going along the level just fine, and then accidentally press too hard on the analog stick and it'd reset. Joy2Key would not override this setting either.
Rage incoming? Sure due to control issues and graphical issues. The actual gauntlets weren't that hard. They were quite fun, until the combination of all the issues together.
Overall: 4/10 unless you get it on a discount... and even then, it better be cheap. Forget that, wait for a bundle. If you get it that way, then it's worth the time and effort, but $5 as the base pricing is way too high. 25 levels, easy to complete, and honestly not really any replay value at least in single player. Still probably better to skip it: not really satisfying.

XCOM, but without the randomness.
Like XCOM, you play a series of turn based tactical missions on randomised maps, with a world map and team progression that ties them together.  Missions take 1-2 hour, maps are procedurally generated, there's one main objective that gives you something useful (a super loot container, a super shop terminal, an agent to rescue, etc.), loads of other things to loot on the way, threats to avoid, and one teleporter you escape through.  There's a lot of variety to keep each mission interesting.
Big difference 1)  Once you're in a mission there's no randomness. Guards follow fixed patterns; they don't teleport around until you spot them; your shots never miss (neither do theirs...), you can normally spot every surprise before it happens (peeking through doors and around corners, peeking at guard to see where they move next).  It can be challenging but it's always fair and it feels like every mission is doable if you play it right and you don't get greedy (which is really impressive given that it's procedurally generated).
Big Difference 2)  Semi-ironman with the Rewind mechanic.  If you make a mistake (or just missclick, I did that a lot), you can rewind back to the start of your previous turn.  You only have limited uses per mission (3 on normal, 1 on hard, you can set it to 0), so it's not a free ticket (it's a very expensive ticket) and you can't use it to cheat RNG because there is no RNG.  I think it's a great for people like me without the time or patience for real ironman modes but do like have decisions matter.
Oh, and the 2D art and animation looks beautiful.

, doesn't break achievements but does fix a few things.

An amazing game and a huge improvement over the first game, definitely worth the price in my opinion. The hugely expanded Nemesis System in particular deserves praise, even after completing the story (which was okay-ish, very predictable but better than the fist game, it did keep me intrigued) I'm still encountering new Orcs constantly!
Now, I think other reviewers have discussed the game as a whole better than I can so I won't, so i'll just offer my quick thoughts on the 2 main "controversies" surrounding the game, namely the final Act (Shadow Wars) and the issue of microtransactions.
The end-game does get grindy, yes, but I feel people who talk about this have been missing the point of it. It's designed for people who have finished the story, and wish to continue defending their fortresses in the Shadow Wars, and killing/recruiting better and better Orcs. Essentially it's for people who love the game and its concept. I feel Act III does bring the story to its conclusion in a logical way, and everything on top of that is extra. I do wonder though why people complain after playing the game for 30+ hours, supposedly enjoying it and then all of a sudden it turns into something awful? Are those hours after the 30+ you spent worse than the ones you spent to get to that point? I don't get it but that's just me. Personally, I love the Shadow Wars.
Finally, on the lootboxes. In short, it's a complete non-issue that people blew up way too much. In my time with the game I have not bought a SINGLE Gold lootbox, nor has the game eve gated my progression at all. Actually, you can even earn Gold currency by doing community challenges. I have bought a handful of regular lootboxes with in-game currency - that is handed out in vast amounts by the way - and noticed that they make absolutely no difference, actually some of the Orcs I have gotten are worse than the ones in the open world. Does that mean I like microtransactions or support them? No, but in this particular case they have effected my time with the game...not at all actually.
All this said I will gladly support the game and recommend it for anyone who enjoyed the first one or wishes to jump in to the expanded (and much more difficult) experience with the Nemesis System for the first time. Don't expect the story to be anything mind-blowing, and enjoy the Nemesis System by letting your defeats and victories turn into unique stories, and I'm sure you'll enjoy the game overall.

8BitBoy is a fun little platformer that pays homage to Mario, but plays more similary to "Super Mario Land" on the original Gameboy. It's fun for a few minutes at a time, but eventually grinds on your nerves with it's lack of overall polish. It's sprites and tiles are as drab and boring as it's forgetful grating chiptunes soundtrack; it simply lacks polish that other games in it's genre offer. What 8BitBoy does have going for it is it's skillfully executed level design which simply keeps the game together as a whole. Overall, you're getting all the polish in the game that the dollar you payed with offers.
There were things I both liked and disliked about 8BitBoy that you should take into consideration before buying:
+ Collecting 100 coins gives you a roulette that cycles through all the powerups in the game. You can hold this item and use it when desired, similar to holding an item in "Super Mario World".
+ Branching paths in the level design often reveal hidden secrets which reward you for exploration, some of which allow you to “warp” to other worlds, skipping entire parts of the game.
+ Can jump on enemies to kill them!
- Powerups consist of a fireball, or fireball, or another fireball.
- Has a single cutscene that's shown before the start of a new game; albeit, not animated and is told via a wall-of-text in slides.
- Has a tutorial that's you're forced to play.
- Pausing the game forces awkward navigation. Instead of navigating up and down with arrow keys or joysticks, you must navigate manually moving the mouse cursor to select the option you want, regardless of using a mouse.
- You lose ALL your powerups you've carefully been saving if you take a single hit, or die.
- A lot of the game's level design is made up of non-modular tiles which stack on top of one another, it takes away from the game's overall level of polish. Some levels do sport modular tiles, like ground tiles; however, others such as dungeons simply don't and are mostly made up of spammed tile placement.
- Enemies are mostly re-used and lack diversity.
This game has a gentle, sweet brilliance that's worth experiencing for yourself. Funny, warm, beautiful.

In Judgment, you constantly manage tasks in order to make sure your people have adequate food, water, and crafting supplies. This entails chopping wood, visiting the water well, and farming. These activities take place on a local 'town' map.
But eventually you will need more than you can initially supply so will then visit the world map and send teams to forage for food, medicine, and other supplies. When you visit various locations you can only secure the loot after successfully defeating all the enemies at that location. So this means you must forge weapons and armor.
The game additionally has an already extensive tech tree. In all, Judgment has a good flow of the usual gather, craft, survive loop that has become so common in games. What makes it interesting here are two things: 1) the town mangement makes you really feel like you are overseeing the well-being of your community. 2) much more interestingly,  Judgment's backdrop is occult as compared the to the now standard zombie fare. You will eventually research occult tech in order to unlock mystical weapons, etc.
In all, Judgment is making a stellar first impression. i will update this review as I plug in the many more hours I know the gmae will draw out of me.

If you haven't played The Walking Dead Season 1, definitely go play that first before considering this game. You have to know some characters and events from it to fully understand/appreciate this story.
That being said, I do wish some of the lessons Lee gives Clementine in Season 1 based on your choices there carried over to Season 2. But since you're controlling Clementine in this game, it's really up to you whether those lessons manifest in your choices as her here. Otherwise they won't show up in cutscenes or anything.
Compared to Season 1, I don't know which was the better game. Both of them had difficult decisions to make, and both centered a lot around your relationships with the other characters. However I did feel more tense with this game since there seemed to be less uplifting events compared to Season 1, and there was a lot of physical abuse shown that wasn't against zombies. There was also some talk about intercourse if that makes any difference to you. But Season 2's story still had twists and turns, jaw-dropping moments, and a teary ending that made it worth playing/watching.
Pretty much the same game mechanics as Season 1 except two new actions that deal with moving the left analog stick, one of which requires you to also simultaneously hold A (xbox). Unfortunately it doesn't look like you can remap buttons if you have a disability that makes these controls difficult. But I do think the game improved fight scenes, in that if you're using a controller, moving the cursor in the general direction of the enemy now locks it onto the target vs requiring the more precise positioning as with Season 1.
Overall, if you enjoyed the first game, I think you would definitely enjoy this one too. This game's a couple hours shorter but I think still worth a playthrough.

Early Access Watcher Reviews Judgment: Apocalypse Survival Simulator
Update Version: Alpha 5 v2
Disclosure: This game copy was purchased by the reviewer.
A long time ago, in a gaming era free from the wars of political correctness and full of worried mothers over virtual violence, demons were the go to enemy of choice. Now with the standard PMC and terrorist checklist clogging mainstream gaming like a bad case of constipation, demons have wandered back into their burrows waiting for a chance to rise again. With the release of Judgment: Apocalypse Survival Simulation into the Early Access market, they have a chance to invade the surface again. Will this be enough to overcome the shortcoming of development or force the surviving party into exile?
Survival simulators are a clear dime in a dozen with Early Access and right off the bat the game separates itself by being a overhead base builder. You start with three randomly generated characters with plus/minus stats to gather, build, craft, research, farm and fight your way through the story. The story is pretty simple at the moment and acts more like a "what to do next" prompt than an actual story. It is secondary compared to the base building which includes everything from houses to guard towers and of course crafting tables (workbench, furnace, stove). Most of these cannot be built until they researched, which is done by using a survivor to either use science or the occult to progress further into the tier trees. About half of these tiers are still in development (coming soon), but it gives you an idea of what to expect. Thankfully, the game is highly replay-able with randomly generated maps to start in.
Building is only possible though if you have the right materials to get the job done. While the base map has what you need to start, some materials cannot be gathered without having it first. This is done through the scavenging system, which involves using the overlay map to go to another area and fight demons for listed items. This same overlay map is used to rescue other survivors that pop up every once in awhile. This process of scavenging and survivor rescue is crucial in order to stand a chance against the demons that randomly attack your base in increasing difficulty. Food, water and sleep are also factors, so combined with everything else you can expect to be busy while building up to take the fight to the demons. This micro management is what keeps the game flowing though and is quite addictive in a "I cannot wait to unlock and make this" sort of way. There are some periods of downtime, but thankfully there is a enhancement tool to increase the speed of the game.
Base management is quite enjoyable, but what about the combat? The system used is similar to a real time tactical approach where you place your survivors and let them auto-attack against the demons. Based on combat skill and weapon type, the chance to hit increases, so a bit of luck is involved considering the demons really just charge in without thought. The base attacks are the same, but with the use of guard towers and blockades you can at least create choke points to make things interesting. It could really use some work to feel more fluid, but it works in the least. Hopefully the scavenging mission maps can be more diverse (about three to four maps used).
Generally, discussing performance and technical aspects of a game leads into a dark rant about optimization, but this time around the game works surprisingly well. I have not run into any real slowdown or frame rate drops, but that could be due to the simple (yet refreshing) game aesthetic. That doesn't mean the game is without it's bugs. On some occasions when a survivor left a gathering or research task, the display would still show the gathering icon as if you were gaining the material. Enemy units would not move even if standing a couple of tiles from a survivor and some actions require multiple button attempts to register (survivors in the retreat box not retreating when hitting the button for example). The AI used for determining the hierarchy of duties can also overlook when say trees need to be chopped, but the survivor quarries clay instead (even though chopping trees is a higher priority). It could be a hell of a lot worse though.
Edit #1:
The length of the game can be questionable with the relative lack of a story. The game has no general end without the difficulty ending it for you. Once the hell gate is discovered and dealt with, there is no real point of going on except to experience items you have yet to unlock. Until the story gets extended and new content is added, the time spent on a single play through is cut short by the lack of perspective and objective. It is certainly lacking content at this point, but it functions rather well for what is offered.
Pros
- Base building is simple and enjoyable
- Challenging micromanagement (staying up to par against increasing demon strength)
- Refreshing aesthetic (not pixelated thankfully)
Cons
- Some random bugs
- Combat could use some fine tuning
- Lack of general content and objective

30 FPS ASIDE, the game is fantastic! At 30 FPS, I'm not seeing any drops in frame rate, so its a steady 30 FPS right now, which is great.
STORYLINE is fast paced and flows nicely. It's a little hard to follow at the very beginning, but then everything starts to make more sense as its kind of shown in flash backs. Definitely has that action movie vibe, but also a serious tone. The writing is amazing and the characters are memorable.
GAMEPLAY and Gunplay is great and exciting. Shooting weapons feels good, its fast and fluid. Different weapons feel like they have power to them, and are each different with strengths and weaknesses. Motion capture is slick, and you can definitely move around from cover to cover no problem. Stealth is simple, and easy to apprehend. It's awesome watching different takedowns. Driving feels realistic, and simulation mode is ever more so. You can really use the e-brake to slide around corners, which is so cool to watch.
AI is pretty good. Cops flank you, and hunt you down. Enemies will use cover effectively, flank you, and use molotov cocktails effectively. They get a little stupid when they don't know where you are and just run out in the open looking for you.
GRAPHICS are pretty good. Almost really good! In the cutscenes, they are amazing because you can see all the facial features of the characters, but other scenes the graphics can be a little bland especially when driving down certain parts of the city. Although I'm really happy with the art direction. Night time looks stellar and the interior of buildings like pro-sti-tute rings are nice looking!
AUDIO is fabulous. All the tracks you'd expect to hear during that time are on, radio stations and radio shows. It definitely gives you the right time setting vibe.
Overall, the game is a really fun open world game that I'm enjoying every second of. 60 FPS will make this an amazing experience!

In all seriousness, the game is quite a simple concept, but at the same time, highly enjoyable. It will take around 2 hours to complete the game, based on your skill level. Unfortunately, both the spikes and the enemies are based on cycles - once you know how to avoid them, the same tactic will always work. Therefore the game has no replay-ability. The graphics are simplistic, making the game load very fast and play very fast. However, the harsh hitbox detection (and limited camera angles) make it very easy to get stuck around corners or bump into enemies.
Overall, Go Home - Rage Incoming is a very fun way to kill a few hours. However, I can't say the game warrants such a high price, as many other similarly-priced games contain hundreds of hours of gameplay, with much better graphics. If you can get the game on a good special or as part of a bundle, it's a fun one to pick up.

A mountain is a large landform that stretches above the surrounding land in a limited area, usually in the form of a peak. A mountain is generally steeper than a hill. Mountains are formed through tectonic forces or volcanism. These forces can locally raise the surface of the earth. Mountains erode slowly through the action of rivers, weather conditions, and glaciers. A few mountains are isolated summits, but most occur in huge mountain ranges.
High elevations on mountains produce colder climates than at sea level. These colder climates strongly affect the ecosystem of mountains: different elevations have different plants and animals. Because of the less hospitable terrain and climate, mountains tend to be used less for agriculture and more for resource extraction and recreation, such as mountain climbing.
The highest mountain on Earth is Mount Everest in the Himalayas of Asia, whose summit is 8,849.868 m (29,035 ft) above mean sea level. The highest known mountain on any planet in the Solar System is Olympus Mons on Mars at 21,171 m (69,459 ft).

That being said, lemme just go over what I think are the PROs and CONs of this game.
Pros:
+The feeling of satisfaction after trumping an iron wall standing before you is great with this game.

-Developers have an unstable edition on PS Vita and PS3, to which they have reported that they were "working on it", yet has been 3+ months with no fixes in sight. Purchase this edition of NT, as it's the optimal experience.
-Game breaking crashes still exist on the PC, most having solutions.
-Bosses can rarely spawn/get caught out of bounds, which they will then suffocate and promptly die immediately.
-No cursor lock for windowed

"Invisible, Inc." is a one-of-a-kind and an instant classic. As a turn-based strategy game, it requires a high level of planning and strategy to succeed. This is compounded by the "rouguelike" aspect of the game, meaning that you are not allowed to reload a previous save if you screw up. Depending on the difficulty level you choose, you may either have the ability to retry the level, use a limited number of "rewinds" which bring you back to the beginning of the previous turn, or, on "ironman mode," have no safety net at all, meaning if you lose your team it is time to start a new game.
This unforgiving style is compounded by the seemingly unfairness of the fight. You are outnumbered and outgunned, infiltrating unknown enemy territory (levels are randomly generated), and you must rely on your stealth and cunning to make it through. Still, there are a number of tools at your disposal: distraction techniques, lethal and non-lethal attacks, a wide variety of powers and gadgets that range from traps to cloaking devices, and a hacking system that targets the various devices found in the level allowing you to access, disable, or remotely command them.
While there are some random elements to the game that vary the way each run plays out (such as which types of missions are available, the layouts of each level, and items/powers you find on the way), the rest of the game is very deterministic. If you are very careful and diligent, you can play the enemy like a fiddle, pulling them this way and that so that your other agents can reach the mission objective (and/or rob the corporations blind). However, screw-ups do happen, and when they do, the situation can plunge from "astounding success" to "catastrophic failure" very quickly. There is no HP meter for your agents. If they are shot, they are permanently downed until another agent either drags them to the exit (leaving them vulnerable in the process) or revives them with Med Gel (which you may have inconveintly left behind to make room for that fantastic new gadget). It is possible to go on without them, but later missions are only going to be harder and it may be next-to-impossible to succeed with an under-manned team.
Hacking is a vital part of the game in order to get past cameras and drones - and to access the various "shops" that come in the form of firewalled terminals found inside the levels. The hacking system is, in some ways, a game within a game. You can switch between the "real world" and the "virtual world" of your A.I., Incognita. Everything she does requires power. Power can be generated by programs within Incognita, or through the actions of your agents (such as using their cybernetic augments or ordering them to hack consoles). This adds yet another layer of complexity to the game. If you are being hunted by guards and barely staying afloat, the last thing you want is to run out of power and get spotted on camera because you couldn't hack it. It leads to situations where you are running risky maneuvers in order to get to consoles, just so you can proceed unhindered through the rest of the level. The number of hazards, and their respective firewall levels, is increased each turn, so careful planning and efficient power usage is essential.
In the end, the beauty of "Invisible, Inc." is its balance and the choices it forces you to make. It is both ruthlessly hard and extremely satisfying when you make it through a level without a hitch. You must choose between dodging past enemies, knocking them out for a couple turns, or killing them, each of which has its own concequences. You have to choose between that awesome gadget or a new hacking program that will help you with the increasingly difficult firewalls. You may have to choose to end your campaign or limp along with an under-manned team because your agent was seperated from the rest of the team and shot. This, and the huge variety of strategies available, make it a wildly satisifying experience. I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys strategy games.

Banner Saga 1 & 2 & 3(probably) have filled a large hole in my heart that was left by Final Fantasy Tactics no longer continuing their series after Grimoire. Wonderful art, cool music (great for hiking in the winter/fall), fun tactics, and interesting decisions that reward and punish you in ways unexpected.
A great deal of games boast decision making being a big part of the game fail to do so. Typically they give you just 3 options; one obviously good, one obviously bad, and one neutral and the ending they present is just shows you made the world a better or worse place. In this game you can make a good guy decision and it pays off wonderfully like a new unit or something game changing resource, or nothing at all. Sometimes doing what you think is right ends up with one of your key characters getting his throat slit and never being able to play him again.
I have played both Banner Sagas many times in many different ways and it is always rewarding. If you like myth, morals, viking aged warriors, and a game that really pulls you in I highly recommend this and the first one.
There is even an online pvp version of this game that for whatever reason isn't publicized as much called Banner Saga Factions. It was released with the first game and hopefully they will update with Bannersaga 2 and 3 mechanics. It's alright but it is free to play.

Well damn.  I guess that "the best things in life" aren't always "free"...
Once upon a time, there was a developer who thought he'd make a game trailer showing fly-overs of his colorful world to hide the god awful controls and gameplay.  Once upon a time, he figured this would be a great idea to advertise a future installment of his game.
Sadly, we can see quickly why this game is "free"...  Don't let the fly-overs of the game in the trailer fool you.  The controls are horrible and awfully frustrating, and in a game like this where precision is important because interactable items require pixel perfect spotting of your avatar.  Yes, you can hold SHIFT to walk instead of the default run, but it still plays and feels sloppy at best.
When a game frustrates you in the first ten minutes, that's NOT a 'good thing".  While it's a valiant attempt at making the next "Uncharted", it needs a LOT of work, and when the price tag is zero, I have my doubts that the developer will ever devote the time needed to make this a game worthy of playing.  There's just too many "good games" with responsive and controls which feel good to spend time fighting the game every step of the way in this.
Add to this, the game completlely fails to ever load a saved game, always getting stuck forever at 90%, forcing you to start the game over completely adds to the frustrations.
Noble attempt like I say, but I can't recommend this, even with a free price tag.  Twiddling your thumbs would be as exciting and way less frustating.
