More greatness from Obsidian but this time in the form of a third person spy rpg and I must say there's so much right about this game with just a few minor technicalities. Firstly, the story was very well done and I liked how it went full circle from start to finish with a few non-linear points in the game that leaves you asking questions of how your actions affect the future and the repercussions they have.
Speaking of actions, the dialogue and choice system in this game was one of the best i've witnessed personally and I've seen a few people complain about the timer on the choices but I really didn't mind it and I felt it added to the realism of Alpha Protocol. The choices definitely have consequences and carry weight and I felt guilty at times in the game when I felt that I made the wrong decision and it actually made me want to go back and settle the score.
My main gripe with Alpha Protocol is the combat as it felt messy and bareboned at first, I could tell that Obsidian modelled the combat system and upgrade system after Mass Effect as it bore a striking resemblance but it wasn't as good i'm afraid. However, towards the middle of the game the combat picked up a little and I genuinely enjoyed the upgrade system and rpg elements that were present.
Overall, I would certainly reccomend Alpha Protocol to fans of the Mass Effect series and just rpg shooters in general and I just loved the clever, political writing like a corporation starting wars just to make massive profit by selling weapons to both sides.

Alpha Protocol is an espionage role-playing game through and through. Coming into this expecting a shooter will disappoint you, but if you are willing to see the game for all it has to offer you may be pleasantly surprised by what you get as a whole.
The game begins straightforward enough; you assume the role of Mike Thorton, a new recruit with an agency that is totally off the books, and begin taking on missions that may be as covert or as brutal as you please. As Thorton, you have full discretion to go into any situation with guns blazing, stealth, or even chatting your way through armed guards if the opportunity arises. There are no wrong choices only results, this is said right at the beginning and is a very accurate way of looking at this game.
Dialogue is a huge part of how this game plays, your ability to choose whether to be Aggressive, Suave, or Professional will affect how people respond to you. Other options depend on how you decide to start the game; Rookie dialogue or Veteran may be unlocked, and in some cases finding dossier intel can be used to your advantage or disadvantage. Want to know if a person likes an aggressive attitude rather than flattery? Check out their dossier. It is a great way to get some back story and learn what makes a character tick. Or don't read up on them and speak as you like, again there are no wrong choices, only results. Not everyone is out to be friends, but then even a friend on bad terms has his/her perks. It's an interesting system that allows the player to be as free as they want and do as they please.
Many of the skills at Thorton's disposal allow him to pick locks, disable security systems, or even steal secret information that can give an edge during dialogue or be used for profit to purchase weapons, upgrades, and gadgets. Some of the mini-games involved with things like bypassing and lock-picking are tricky, but even these can be adjusted by allocating earned stat points into specific areas to either reduce the challenge, or these can be bypassed by shorting the circuit with a gadget. Fail and trip an alarm, there's a gadget and a skill to deactivate those too.
One of the really great things about this game is that the way it plays out, from character interactions to mission objectives, even the ending, can all vary so much depending on the player's choices. Make and enemy, he'll double-cross you. Make an ally, you can double-cross them. Your friends and enemies will determine a lot of how things turn out in any given area, and with multiple possible outcomes that will offer a different kind of story experience base on what you say and do.

There are 17 maps in 3 chapters (or so) with a couple bosses and tons of unique and creative enemies. You have a lot of weapons to use, and some hidden secrets and pickups in the maps. You will find some weapons work better on enemies than others as you play which is quite satisfying.

Another new spin on Pac-Man that is really clever, and one of those ideas that I wonder why this hadn't been done already.
Pac-Man, as usual, is about mazes, dots, and ghosts. The formula is so perfect that for generations it has just worked as a pure arcade experience. It has been toyed with to varying degrees of success, but my favorites to this day had always only been Ms. Pac-Man, Pac-Mania, and Pac-Man Championship Edition.
Then along comes PAC-MAN 256, and I have myself another favorite game in the series.
PAC-MAN 256 is about outrunning the ever-encroaching glitch; a series of scrambled characters crawling up from the bottom end of the maze. To do this you must chomp dots, avoid ghosts, and race through an endless randomly generated maze that goes on forever. I've never gotten too far into the maze, but as far as I know it doesn't end.
A really cool feature is that the maze isn't the same experience twice, and it will take skill more than memorization to endure. Along the way you have a plethora of power-ups, and skillful players are rewarded with a maze-clearing 256 bonus.
Procedurally generated Pac-Man was a stroke of genius. Totally worth your time!

Don't get impression things go wrong all the time - instead - look at it this way - there are so many neat things you can add and enhance flight sim - well - sometimes these things don't play nice with each other - this is highly experimental - and usually not a problem - but every so often it's just easier to start fresh. (nice way of saying - i messed it up myself - its broke - it wont run - I killed - it but - .... never mind - its my fault) LOL

On fence X-Plane or FSX-SE ? GET BOTH! Each have TONS to offer - different flight models, add-ons, aircraft.... GET

I mean..  for me - this ... - LOG OUT (Don't shut down)
- Log back in
- Turn Rift On
Still Being Stubborn?

It's always interesting when people refer to "roguelike" and "shooter" in the same sentence.  Nuclear Throne is one of those games that pulls it off masterfully.
In terms of "roguelike," it has perma-death, random level layout generation, linear stage progression, and item pickups and upgrades galore.  In terms of "shooter," well, it has a great combination of strategy and all-out mayhem.
And it's hard.  Probably you figured as much.  You have a tiny life bar and no temporary invincibility after you are hit.  You will die, and die, and die...and somehow it never stops being super fun.
The only negative that I see with this game is that the graphics are thrown together.  They aren't bad, but there is a cheapness to them that can wear on your eyes if you aren't used to the low-resolution pixelation.  The default screen shake setting is also game-breaking, so I highly recommend reducing it.
Cheap graphics are complemented by some of the cleverest sound design I've heard in a video game in a long time.  There are tons of sound effects, an awesome musical score, and a surprisingly rich array of voice acting, even if the voices are all silly and incomprehensible alien/monster tongues.
The game is very rewarding to players who keep trying to get better--there are secrets to find, weapon combinations to exploit, and special character abilities and upgrades to unlock.  Pay whatever price Vlambeer demands--it will be worth your while.

I may have only scratched the surface of what Invisible, Inc. has to offer but I'm oh-so-pleased with it. It left me wanting more and even feeling a little cheated at the lack of a sequel.
There's wonderful, stylised graphics and animation that wouldn't look out of place in a game like Transistor. There's engaging and challenging turn-based-strategy that actually manages to pull off stealth (or repeatedly tasering your enemies in the face, whatever floats your boat) in a really satisfying way. There's a selection of playable characters, each equipped with very specific features that end up directly affecting your in-game strategy. Throw in a few well-implemented elements of -oh, that dreaded word!- ~randomisation~ and Invisible, Inc somehow manages to make each playthrough feel like a significant enough departure from the last.
That being said, its greatest achievement is making me genuinely care about all those characters in the face of a relatively simple plot. I was hooked from the opening animation sequence, fully invested & getting some strong 2007 Mirror's Edge-like vibes.
All in all, completing this game involved a strange balance of intuitive in-the-moment decisions and a several-steps-ahead kind of planning. Don't worry if you find yourself making mistakes -it's the only way to figure out what works sometimes.

Invisible Inc is a turn-based isometric stealth game.  It's great strength is how tactical the game plays.  Vision is clearly defined, any given attack or ability will work if it says it will, no miss-chance, no reduced damage, either you can do a thing, or you can't, there is no in-between.
The corps have found you, and you need to get your AI to a computer capable of hosting her, allowing her to protect you once again and resume keeping the corps in check.
The story is not a core focus of the game, but it is there, and the ending, when you first complete a full run, leaves you uncertain as to the future.  I believe that a sequel is planned to eventually take place, and I hope it does.
The basic gameplay is simple, sneak around, get money, get equipment, get out alive.  Vision cones are clearly defined, even when their source is still unseen.  The difficulty is good, a well thought out and lucky run is peaceful, but tense, running around recklessly will quickly turn into a nightmare, a botched run results in franticly attempting damage control as the situation worsens around you.
If you like sneaky tactical games, I highly recommend this.

In short, Nuclear Throne is a roguelite 2D top-down bullet hell dungeon crawler shooter.
It takes many elements from the great pioneers of all of these (sub)genres, violently mashes them together and adds some more difficulty to the surprisingly well-smelling mess.
You start off in the wasteland with... well, nothing but a bad gun with a bit of ammo really.
As you kill all enemies to progress to the next randomly generated stage, you'll try to loot dead enemies and chests for better guns (that all play differently and are all better in certain situations), more ammo for those guns and rads (which give you the ability to mutate between stages) in a desperate attempt to not die horribly.
As you git gud, you will also unlock: new characters which encourage different playstyles, a  variety of improved golden weapons to start with in future runs to make delving down to the throne less hard, skins that don't do sh♥t, and challenging crowns to add even more spice to the pili-pili.
Once you reach and kill the throne, the game will 'loop', throwing you back in the first stage with a lot more and harder enemies to kill (you). This process will repeat itself.
I have not played a whole lot of this game, but i'll be adding more to this review as i play and discover more.

Better in so many ways than it’s parent, The Banner Saga 2 is a gripping, tense and inspiring experience.
I must have taken screenshots every 5 minutes – the art is fantastic. Every landscape is a wonder to behold and this beautiful world is a great backdrop to the terrifying, cruel and desperate things unfolding in it.
Playing the game felt like Star Wars without a guaranteed happy ending, with death-defying odds, plot twists, tough decisions, soul-gripping soundtrack and engaging writing. Be ready to sweat and worry, as you try to keep your characters alive, no joke.
If the tough combat gets too challenging and you’re not a fan of deep strategy or tactics – no worries. Change the difficulty to Easy and enjoy the game – you don’t need to be a chess master to play this.
Taking in to consideration all of the above, I’d say that The Banner Saga 2 has something for everyone. I highly recommend it – give this experience a try and you’ll be surprised how easily it will grow on you.

BS 2 is the direct sequel to Banner Saga, who would have thought. The game continues seemlessly where you left off after Act 1. Depending on your final choice and how you skilled and equipped your heroes, the game starts you off with 1 of 2 protagonists. Items and level stay the same and can now be increased further up to level 10. The core gameplay remains 100% the same, so it's a waste of time to be talking about that again. Instead I'll give you the changes and improvements:
- THREE branching storylines instead of TWO, depending on who leads the caravan: Rook or Alette (though this is only relevant in 4 chapters or so and does not change the overall story, just the individual's, i.e. different dialogue and different reactions/outcomes)
- The battlefield now features barricades, rocks, etc. and not just a plain field
- Renown is still the only resource, but levelling up a character is a lot cheaper compared to BS1
- At level 6 characters get to choose a second ability
- There are a ton more abilities in the game now
- After you max out a stat you can now invest points into "unique talents" like 20% chance to crit, etc. These talents are the same for every hero though
- Clansmen will now forage for food. If you train them to become fighters they can no longer do that
- Almost no more actual battles with your army involved
- Enemy and hero variety has been dramatically increased. You will not only fight humans, but also feral humans, Varl, Dredge, undead Dredge and Horseborn, which varies up the battles
- Battles sometimes also have different objectives, like clearing obstruction or killing a specific enemy, etc.
- The background art has become even better and more varied: river journey on ship, travelling through cave systems, a spooky forest, etc.
- A few more cutscenes and even voice over
Generally speaking it's a great game with an interesting story and an all too familiar problem: ♥♥♥♥ing huge cliff hanger at the end, and basically the game ending too soon and you feel like something is missing. Better wait for BS 3 then...in 2018!!!! *sigh*. In the mean time, maybe you can play the story again with the other character. I'll wait for that until BS 3 arrives. The devs listened to some feedback without changing the game completely, so in the end I'd give it a 9/10.
Edit: Just played through with Rook as well. Not much difference. Generally not much difference to the story apart from some key moments, but the end will always be the same.

Man, this game has so much negativity pointed towards it. Was it perhaps not fulfilling enough for everyone? Not enough violence or shooting, nothing to kill?
I know I am being a bit broad and speaking in absolutes here, but honestly, not all gaming has to involve action. This diseased idea that games always have to have action is incorrect, same goes with movies. We all seem to have this tendancy to love violence, but why? People claim it to be relieving, but ambient games can do just the same. With 6 hours in the game as of now, and I very pleased with this.
Let me tell you something, this is not a game, that is right. This is a work of art, nothing is more acceptable as an accurate description than that. O' Reilly managed to capture the beauty of nature, the vastness and curiosity involved with space, and time. Not to mention it is quite satirical regarding the mountains occasional "thoughts". What's even greater is the thoughts are affected by what is perpetuation in the environment around it. It mocks society in a couple of ways, with some thoughts asking, "Am I fat?" and so on. It has emotion, and depth, and only can truly be appreciated by someone who can look past graphics, the lack of action, the absence of story, and typical games and gameplay. I have massive respect for O'Reilly, he's created some incredible things before, all being animations and short films. He is truly a mastermind, a modern legend in the world of art. He has a very recognizable style and is entirely original. Remember, nothing will change until someone is brave enough to come out and innovate. The reason we have action was the bold idea of an individual to break the normal arcade style and go for the violent side of gaming. Now it dominates the gaming industry, and something new needed to come along, and it has. Games can take off from this, we could have something relative to this, but maybe more to it, more of a story and purpose.
That aside, it's incredibly relaxing, and messing around with the piano can be quite fun. This game doesn't require you to play it much at all, just leave it running, check in on it. If you feel stressed and need a moment, boot up mountain. I, for one, am very impressed with this, and will definitely "play" it often.
So look past the idea that it isn't too much of a game, but something you own, a work of art. This truly is unlike anything else we've ever seen, correct? I reccomend it, 1 dollar will not hurt you for this incredible piece.

This trope from TVTropes says it best.
The Devs tried to think of almost anything, it's hardly possible to chose an action that hasn't been foreseen and consequences been implemented.
This doesn't mean you have a lot of ways to die and end the game (that too, though), but that anything you do WILL impact the game. Good, bad? Feh, it's how you work it.
Be good friends with your handler? Great, his/her support gives you a bonus to certain abilities.
Hate each others guts? All the more reason to show him/her you're better than they think, certain (other) abilities get a bonus.
Be nice to the informant, talk about his health? He appreciates it, and makes sure you stay healthy by giving a discount on armor.
Kick him around, be hostile? If it keeps you off his back, he'll give you a discount on weapons.
That is strewn throughout the game. Add in lots and lots of dialog options, each affecting the game and the way characters treat you, and you have a brilliant game which main flaw is that you can't experience it all without replaying it.
(Fortunately, there is a special replay mode, "Veteran", which is unlocked only after the first playthrough - it gives you more options from the start.)
After the initial mission it's basically an open world - you have three hubs to finish, but you don't have to do them in any order or at once - you can start at one, go to the next, and so on.
It probably is even better if you do - soak up the information, make contacts, etc... - it's a small world, who knows where you meet someone again you just met?
There is bad stuff, though. The combat takes a bit getting used to, the camera movement (third person) is not always good, and (IMO) they make it perhaps a bit too hard not to kill anyone. (Stark contrast to Deus Ex HR, where they made it too easy not to kill anyone after the intro.)
Since the game uses a checkpoint system, it's not easy to actually save the game - you can only save checkpoints, and everything done AFTER the checkpoint was reached is lost if you quit.
Still, make sure to save at every checkpoint - otherwise you only have the automatically saved ones. I just had to redo the final mission from start because I opened the wrong door and the auto-saved checkpoint was from before the beginning...
Still, all in all, one of the best games I've ever played. It has it's flaws, but story and voice acting are not among them.
(The main flaw no doubt is the hacking minigame. Computer hacking is horrible, and IMO conceptually wrong - even if you spot everything at once, there is not always enough time to reach it. Make sure to always carry a few EMP charges with you!)

Great game. It plays like an endless runner, but still feels 100% Pac Man. Your goal is to flee from an unstoppable glitch wall, but the maze of dots has ghosts, fruit and powerups littered around to keep things interesting. Powerups allow you to customise your playstyle slightly (some are great for clearing ghosts, and others like stealth are useful for making distance quickly since you can essentially ignore the ghosts altogether for the duration). You only have three slots but there are a ton to choose from, and after hitting total-dots-eaten milestones more will become available. It'll take a while to get everything opened up. Thankfully there are no microtransactions or ads to sit through to unlock anything, just play and they'll roll in. I love how each colour of ghost has their own behaviour, and will react reliably. There's very little down to chance, so with enough practice you can reliably get big scores. If you like Pac Man it's easy to spend a lot of time trying to beat your personal best.

Painkiller Overdose was released in 2007, three years after release of original Painkiller. It's a single-player "old-school" FPS with Deathmatch multiplayer. And a sequel or stand-alone second expansion pack for Painkiller. It started out as a mod, being made by fans effort, and then was made official.
So, technical side of thing. Game is supposed to still work on newest systems. It even supports wide-screen resolutions, even though HUD will be stretched. So it all should be cool.
Oh, and game is as bugged as it always was. It will crash on you. Randomly. Or in some cases always in same situations. Like, when you are trying to equip tarot card after beating some level and having some amount of gold. Nope, no idea what causes it, but you will relaunch game few times while beating it for sure.
AND loooooong level loading times. I have no idea what changed, but these take few times more than in original Painkiller. It's painful enough to make you wish that this game had either "rewind time" or more console-like checkpoint system. Or just anything that doesn't require you to reload level after death. Like, lower difficulty to die less to. Yea, it's bad even today.
Oh. And don't be surprised if ragdoll of defeated demon decides to kick you up to moon. Ragdolls don't feel done properly here.
As for multiplayer? Well, it was mostly competive one like Deathmatch. And well, I don't think it was played like Painkiller was. And with GameSpy shut down, you can still connect, but Internet Browser will not work. So it will be hard to find servers with people. Community is probably dead there.
Story follow Belial, child of demon and angel, who proved to be too powerful and chaotic-neutral in war between Heaven and Hell. Who was then imprisoned by Cerberus from Hell side, while being overseen by Samael from Heaven side. And now, after Lucifer death, he was freed and out for revenge. While travelling absolutely random locations.
So, it adds whole new campaign made of 16 levels or so. On theory it's great. It has great variety, as you will travel between such locations as fantasy land, space station, egypt, riot in modern city, zombie town and it has such interesting and amazing stages as Demon Farm and B-Film Studios. And borefest of green radiation like Power Plant, yes. And not only that, but each level is filled with at least some unique monsters, scarabs at Desert or living cardboards of B-Film monsters.
And yet all this random variety gives this game a cartoonish feel. What Hell? What Nightmare? Travelling around globe and time and dimension, it seems. It doesn't help that most monsters seem to be take off the wall, stereotype, futher contributing to this feel. Not that it's a bad thing.
It also lost some feel due to different music, which is weaker. There are some interesting parts of fight music for some levels, but it's all errr "bland epic", so to say. Ambient part is weak too. Just nothing truly memoriable, so good bye awesome metal too.
It'a also nice how few enemies, including old ones, gained a special death animations. Even though they are so slow at times, you may not notice that enemy is technically dead.
But hey, the game has 8 weapons. Freaking eight. And knowing how seven of them has two alternative fire modes, which use serapate unqiue ammo, and seeing how weapon switching is instant, that pretty much means that you got 17 different fire modes that you have to remember and think about! It pretty much creates a "having bunch of toys" feeling. Sure, you have many different ways to kill demons. It's probably fun for most. But you see, since functionality and effectiveness pretty much always overlaps with few of them, you actually will be lost what to use. They all do fine job and nothing is absolutely more effective in each situation, so you don't really have to think on which weapon to choose. Which is one of the things that keeps old FPS interesting, having to decide on weapon use. Well, aside from running out from ammo for some.
You will spend time scrolling around weapons to find the one with some ammo left. That's quite a lot. And game doesn't always provide you with enough ammo. Sometimes there is too much, other times it tries to give you only for some weapons and sometimes there is just plain crisis. Power Plant level comes to mind. It shows that this game started as a mod, as sometimes it feels amateurish with difficulty jump.
And I don't understand the use of acid flame thrower.
And yes, what I said, there is difficulty jumps. Some encounters will prove to be harder than others. And it's not always at the end of the levels. Like, it uses same Monks enemies in Ragnarog level. But this time, they didn't place any laying corpses around for them to be busy throwing, instead they will keep telekinetically shove player, doing hitscan damage on him from few miles away.
And then you got easy-easy bosses. Who got weak points. At least they aren't the worst of Painkiller.
And then there is a hero who tries to be baadass and Duke Nukem like, throwing one-liners regulary. Same ones. Not too clever. So get ready to hear "taste like chicken" a lot. He only rarely drops something more interesting like "did that demon just revive another one?".
And sadly, despite having big themes variety, it just ends up being monotonous. Original game was avoiding that, it had few surprises. It had more specialized weapons, more varied monsters. It wasn't too chaotic in themes. It just had flow. While in Overdose it just feels like you kill things and then repeat, not really mattering what kills and how you kill. Or at least not enough mattering. I don't really understand, on theory it's awesome, but on practise it's not so fun. Levels also feel sometimes on dragged side. Weaker music don't help.
And I wish weapons didn't gib everything just because.
Getting Tarot Cards is still not so fun, by the way. Just like in original game.
So, Overdose isn't a bad game. It's not good FPS either. It has variety in level themes, but it's too repetitive in gameplay. It's the kind of game that you will have fun with, but will have to force yourself with "I should beat this game fully because I want to beat games", otherwise you will abandon it in a half way.

In all seriousness though, there's a steep learning curve with this one. It's rough to figure out just how much food you need to generate to support your colony. It wouldn't be a problem if farms weren't so resource intensive and resourses were such a pain to gather. This is the basic run down of my first settlements:
1: Oh no, I'm not generating enough food!
2: Oh no, I don't have enough trees to build another farm!
3: Oh no, I have to grow more trees, wait for them to grow, chop them down, build another farm, wait for the veggies to grow and hope some one is still alive to harvest them!
4: Oh no, I'm out of water and my basecamp didn't spawn with a well! I need to research woodworking so I can make a furnace so I can make bricks so I can build a well!
5: Oh no, I need more trees to make a saw mill to make boards to make bricks so I can build a well and I chopped all the trees down so I could build more farms so my people don't starve! I need to plant more trees so I can maybe save someone!
6: Oh no, Everyone is dead.
this wouldn't be as big of an issue if it weren't for the fact that it takes so long to figure out that you're doing it wrong and the first thing you have to do is plant trees right there next to your base because the AI for the tasks system is rudimentary and can't handle the size of the base map in the beginning. Get ready to watch your survivor start to walk over to a pile of clay, get 3/4 of the way there, realize he's hungry, turn back to gets something to eat, finish eating and start heading back to the clay, get half way there, realize he's tired, then go wait for the only bed to open up.
The combat system could stand a bit of tweaking as well.
I get what they're trying to accomplish with the cover system, but it comes off a little cumbersome. It's wierd to watch a guy crouching by a barrel while an imp is wailing away at him 2 feet away. The tutorial makes a big deal about "flanking" but the enemy AI just bum rushes you every time they see you. Maybe I didn't get far enough into the game play to see the more advanced enemies, but over all the combat came off as tedious to me.
All that being said, The bones are there. I can see this being a good time sponge. I know as soon as I post this review I'm going to start the game up again and start over. I know that it's a work in progess and I can't wait for it to be done, but I think most people SHOULD wait. I cannot reccomend that my friends buy it now because I can see the potential for them being infuriated by it, but once it's been tweaked I would be more than happy to change my oppinion.

Overall, I liked The Walking Dead: Season 2. I have my criticisms, of course, but Telltale's main thing to boast is with their stories and the characters in them. In the second game of Telltale's take of The Walking Dead universe, you play as Clementine, the little girl who grew attached to Lee in the first game.
Taking place some time after the events of the first game, you're with Christa and Omid, who are still alive. That changes soon, of course, or at well, 16 months later after the incident in the bathroom. You end up with a new crew after running away from a group of attackers. The new crew live in a secluded cabin and aren't sure about you. There's immediate trust and mistrust. But you become attached to these characters as events unfold. You learn about their lives and why they're out there. My favorite of these characters was Luke, whom I'm sure most people agree was the central character and could be the next Lee.
Unfortunately, reality kicks in and you're forced to flee with the group. Basically, they're on the run from Michael Madsen. You eventually reach a lodge after some other unfortunate events and here's where you reunite with Kenny. This is where the heart of the story starts to take place. Clem and Kenny go back a long ways and you have to pick sides. Kenny seems unstable, but Clem is usually able to calm him down. You also have to see things from his point of view, he's a protector and he's caring, and he's selfless. He butts heads with a few other characters further into the game, of which I won't get into for the sake of spoilers. But he still has a big heart in the treacherous world. The other major character that you get to know is Jane. She's introduced after the events at the lodge, but she comes off as the big sister type. But she's also a loner and a bit manipulative. I really liked both Kenny and Jane in this game, so trying to ease tension between them was tough and it does affect a lot of the dialog.
But here's where my criticisms start. While the dialog can be affected, it doesn't change the outcome of most of the scenarios. Telltale's one boast that choices matter, well they don't. Choices ultimately don't matter. The story will still unfold with the same arc. It's just a matter of whether or not a character will die a certain way or how people react to Clem, or how Clem reacts to certain characters. The only major outcome is the final two choices. But if you've gotten to season 3, you'll see that the final two choices also don't really matter. The only thing that matters is if you feel satisfied with your interpretation of the story.
My other criticisms are typical of Telltale. For starters, their engine sucks. For producing licensed products and publishing the games themselves, you'd think they'd be able to spend more money developing a better engine with a better lighting system. I don't mind some of the stylistic choices in order to preserve the comic book feel, but at least give an attempt to make a realistic beard or mustache that isn't just a painted texture. Like Kenny's mustache, it's not great. The animation, while some of the cutscenes are pretty good, a chunk of it is just bad. Like, worse than some stuff I've done. Watching how some of the characters rotate to turn and face someone, or walk, or breathe, you can tell they rushed the animation and didn't bother with polishing it up. It's just so clunky. The fighting and QTE system is fine though.
But yeah, great story, all the feels. Excellent music and voice acting too.

In short, Nuclear Throne is a roguelite 2D top-down bullet hell dungeon crawler shooter.
It takes many elements from the great pioneers of all of these (sub)genres, violently mashes them together and adds some more difficulty to the surprisingly well-smelling mess.
You start off in the wasteland with... well, nothing but a bad gun with a bit of ammo really.
As you kill all enemies to progress to the next randomly generated stage, you'll try to loot dead enemies and chests for better guns (that all play differently and are all better in certain situations), more ammo for those guns and rads (which give you the ability to mutate between stages) in a desperate attempt to not die horribly.
As you git gud, you will also unlock: new characters which encourage different playstyles, a  variety of improved golden weapons to start with in future runs to make delving down to the throne less hard, skins that don't do sh♥t, and challenging crowns to add even more spice to the pili-pili.
Once you reach and kill the throne, the game will 'loop', throwing you back in the first stage with a lot more and harder enemies to kill (you). This process will repeat itself.
I have not played a whole lot of this game, but i'll be adding more to this review as i play and discover more.

Hey you!  Yeah, you!  Ever wanted to know what it's like to go on an acid-dropping, techno music listening, 80's Florida exploring, russian mob-killing, bat-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, serial killer rampage?  Well now you can, with the "Kill everyone in sight" Simulator 2012, or as the fans call it, "DAMNIT HE CAME OUT OF NOWHERE" Simulator 2012.
Hotline Miami is a top-down strategy shoot-em-up, which felt somehow (surprisingly) like an old Zelda game, except way more fast paced and with gratuitous violence, and with a lot less puzzles and exploring.  Or maybe with more puzzles.  In some ways, the entire game is a puzzle, since you have to figure out how to not die and kill everyone at the same time, which, especially in the later levels, is incredibly challenging.  Luckily for us, the restart button works instantly and with almost no load time.  I used it a lot.
Long story short, graphics are great, music is great, gameplay is great (if infuriating), and, most amazing of all, the story is great.  I didn't expect much story from a game that sells itself as what is basically a Russian mob massacre simulator (2012!), but what I got was thought-provoking and deep.  I've found that the intense gore in this game serves dual purposes; to attract pubescent teens and eagle-eyed indie gamers AND propel the story and deeper themes.
TL;DR: &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥ boy, game good.  10/10 would play again."  -My brother.

TL;DR: The game's strongest point is its characters. The plot was good overall but left at least one minor loose end. The ending could have been better, but the game was still fun. I did experience a few game-breaking bugs that a reinstall fixed. Play with an Xbox controller if you have one. I recommend this game so long as you know that you may be dissappointed at the end.
TIME
It took me 21 hours to finish one playthrough, but as a completionist I tend to take my time.
CHARACTERS
The characters have depth and were engaging. Occaissionally they did things that felt out of character (minor spoiler:
STORY
The story itself is fantastic. Nothing bad to say about it. The choices, however, left something to be desired. There are negative reviews with spoilers detailing what I mean: Some of the games 'important' choices either don't actually influence the plot, or render other choices moot. Additionally, it felt like I thought of at several possible consequences that the writers did not think of. That was frustrating and made me feel like I had to guess what the writers were thinking in order to progress how I wanted. And a minor loose end:
The worldbuilding felt a bit incomplete as a result.
BUGS/PROGRAMMING
I did encounter a few game-breaking bugs. Sometimes a cut scene wouldn't end properly and I was in free-move mode with the other characters frozen. If I fast-forwarded through dialogue I saw before, I would get stuck in the game state that happend when Max rewinds into the middle of a conversation.Using Steam to "verify installation" caught nothing. I used an Xbox controller after doing Ep. 1 with the mouse as the mouse interface is clunky (but passable).
CONCLUSION
A truly realistic choice & consequence is a high ambition to reach for because of the myriad of consequences that come from out words and actions, and while this game does a lot of things well, I think they did not reach that ambition. But I enjoyed the game overall, so I'll still recommend it.

Man, this game has so much negativity pointed towards it. Was it perhaps not fulfilling enough for everyone? Not enough violence or shooting, nothing to kill?
I know I am being a bit broad and speaking in absolutes here, but honestly, not all gaming has to involve action. This diseased idea that games always have to have action is incorrect, same goes with movies. We all seem to have this tendancy to love violence, but why? People claim it to be relieving, but ambient games can do just the same. With 6 hours in the game as of now, and I very pleased with this.
Let me tell you something, this is not a game, that is right. This is a work of art, nothing is more acceptable as an accurate description than that. O' Reilly managed to capture the beauty of nature, the vastness and curiosity involved with space, and time. Not to mention it is quite satirical regarding the mountains occasional "thoughts". What's even greater is the thoughts are affected by what is perpetuation in the environment around it. It mocks society in a couple of ways, with some thoughts asking, "Am I fat?" and so on. It has emotion, and depth, and only can truly be appreciated by someone who can look past graphics, the lack of action, the absence of story, and typical games and gameplay. I have massive respect for O'Reilly, he's created some incredible things before, all being animations and short films. He is truly a mastermind, a modern legend in the world of art. He has a very recognizable style and is entirely original. Remember, nothing will change until someone is brave enough to come out and innovate. The reason we have action was the bold idea of an individual to break the normal arcade style and go for the violent side of gaming. Now it dominates the gaming industry, and something new needed to come along, and it has. Games can take off from this, we could have something relative to this, but maybe more to it, more of a story and purpose.
That aside, it's incredibly relaxing, and messing around with the piano can be quite fun. This game doesn't require you to play it much at all, just leave it running, check in on it. If you feel stressed and need a moment, boot up mountain. I, for one, am very impressed with this, and will definitely "play" it often.
So look past the idea that it isn't too much of a game, but something you own, a work of art. This truly is unlike anything else we've ever seen, correct? I reccomend it, 1 dollar will not hurt you for this incredible piece.

Wow... this game is really fun.  There is so much to say... where to begin.  So, Invisible Inc. is very much in the vain of XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Within.  It is very tactical and strategic in your decisions. You really have to think everything through in order to proceed through the game.  The game does a really good job at building tension and making your choices matter in as far as which agents live/die/succeed/fail.
You control a team of agents that are part of a shadow organization that are trying to take down the corporations that have greedily taken over the world.  The game starts off by a break in of the shadow organization by the corporations, and your hacking AI pal is taken mobile.  This sets up the plot where the AI needs to be recharged after 72 hours (3 days).  Through out this in game time you build your team back up to its former glory for a final raid.  This has you breaking into detention facilities, stealing vault keys, and even enhancing your agents with cyborg type of modifications.

The game plays very well, it is not too hand holdy and lets you make some mistakes.  On the beginner level of difficulty it allows you to rewind, which is great for starting to understand how all the mechanics work without a huge long multilevel tutorial, don't get me wrong there is a very basic tutorial at the start but it doesn't prepare you like a whole first play-through does.  It is also one of those games that unlocks things as you play through it much like a roguelike, think how you unlock different characters in Binding of Issac. I feel as though this is one of those games that I can just sink a ton of hours into it if I am not careful. To add to this the game doesn't take itself too seriously and has a good sense of humor about it.
So... what are the cons to the game?  Well, I feel as though there a bunch of small little things that end up hurting the gameplay enough to knock it down a bit. The first thing is the controls and UI, most of the time they are fine but on occasion I found them clumsy.  For instance, in the previous image/video I was tabbing through my agents and thought I had Decker selected.  But in reality I had Dr. Xu selected and made a huge mistake of a move that I ended up rewinding.  The other thing	that normally doesn't get me is video game logic.  In the following video, you can see Decker taking out a guard right in front of another guard.  The second guard then gets alerted and dumbly follows suit in the next turn. First off the first guard should have seen a guy right next to him and not been taken down that easily, and then the second shouldn't have just followed blindly through the door on the next turn.  There are of ton of other instances of this fuzzy game logic, from doors magically opening to terrible patrol patterns that put a guard literally in a corner.  But this may have been more of the level of difficulty I was playing at but it still bugged me enough to mention it here.
In conclusion, I absolutely love this game.  It is right up my alley, the stealth is in a way I can digest it and process it.  The game really feels like a spiritual successor of sorts to XCOM.  I know it is exactly what they were going for, however, the bunch of mini issues brings this down to a 4/5 in my opinion.  If I were to change my scale I would even put it up there at a 9/10 or 4.5/5, it is a great game and I highly recommend it to anyone that likes turn based strategy games. I am looking forward to playing more of this in the future.

This is literally one of the best tactics/strategy games ever made.
It solves many of the issues with x-com, has near perfect balance and it brings a new brand of tactics gameplay focused on stealth instead of brute force.
Additionally, the game has NO RANDOM ROLLS. You cannot miss, you cannot be punished for making the right choice, and can only fail if you make a mistake. Very rare for a tactics game, because it is very hard to balance such a system but Klei has nailed it PERFECTLY.
When you go up from normal difficulty' to the harder levels the game completely changes. It doesn't just 'get harder', they don't just add more enemies, or give them more HP... they fundamentally change the balance of the game by making KOing a guard raise the alert level.
This one tiny change forces the player to completely alter their strategy and approach to every encounter, forcing players to focus on 'ghosting' enemies by tailing right behind them, ducking behind corners... getting the goods without them ever even knowing you were there... when it goes right, it's like an amazing spy movie. (Going up to these difficulties changes the game from 'good' to 'FREAKING AMAZING', although it is not for the faint of heart.)
Or maybe the right thing to do is actually direct one of your agents to deliberately trip a camera, bringing attention to your cause but distracting enough guards to do what you need to do and get out of there.
As you gain experience, the strategy space grows and expands with you, there are a LOT of toys to play with and a ton of strategies to experiment with. The skill cap on this title is extremely high.

Kerbal Space program is my 2nd most favourite game of all time. I always have loved building things. I love realism and I love the idea of space travel. It covers all these aspects and more! Better yet, you can mod the game to make it even more amazing. There is many hundreds of hours of gameplay to be had here. The Kerbal Space Program (KSP) game community is massive. With so many mods available, the game can easily be surpassed with more gameplay experiences such as Mechjeb or FAR (Ferram Aerospace). So when game updates, it can break your ship builds if the mod isn't updated. Some mods are not updated for months. That's about the only downer really. I would have liked multiplayer as a feature but it may be added in the future. Only time will tell.
Pros:
>> Building your own space ships.
>> Realistic stock physics. Can be upgraded with a mod called FAR
>> Exploration. Game can be played in sandbox mode a bit like minecraft.
>> Game actually teaches you orbital mechanics. NASA use this game to teach people about space.
>> Uses a recent build of the Unity engine so graphics are pretty decent.
>> Sound track is good for an indie game.
>> Many many hours of gameplay to be had.
>> Flight controls are good once you get accustomed to them. You can use joystics too.
>> Interface is useful, ie navball, fast forward, setting waypoints etc...
>> The KSP Forums are helpful where people share designs and talk about mods etc...
Cons:
>> Saving and loading is a bit confusing.
>> Could use a better navigation system. Ie hard to locate runway when landing or locating a waypoint on the map.
>> Takes away a lot of your real life time. You could spend 8 hours on this game and not even realise the time had gone by.
>> Some mods are so damn awesome that you become dependent on them.
Recommended mods:
B9 Aerospace parts pack.
B9 Procedural wings
Engineer Redux (To show you more info as to what's going on)
Ferram Aerospace Research (Adds advanced simulated flight physics)
Mechjeb

What do you get when you take painkillers, chop out some parts, put some new parts in, reskin a few things in here and there and add a dash of Pop Culture References?
You get an Overdose, Painkiller: Overdose to be exact.
Released in 2007 by Czech Company "Mindware Studios," Overdose was originally an Expansion Pack of Painkiller, where isntead of a random dude shooting demonic forces, you play as half angel, half demon, all snarky nephilim named Belial, where he's freed from his imprisonment after thousands of years. And yet somehow, despite living in a cage, he knows movie references.
I have nary an idea, so let's move on.
If you thought the original Painkiller was tough with it's hordes of enemies and some puzzle bosses, you'll be happy to know that there's not as much enemies to deal with and puzzle bosses aren't as frequent, and much easier to work with. The core principle of PK: OD is the same.
Blast they demon asses and kill the main bad dude at the end, this time being Sammael.
Belial's got some good firepower, like the Bone Shotgun from the original game, the crossbow/bomb launcher from Battle out of Hell, the Minigun/Rocket Launcher from the first game... yeah, there's a lot of returning weapons with reskins, but there are new weapons to work with like the Demon Head you get in the beginning of the gaqme that shoots lasers, Demon Eggs that work like remote sticky bombs, A dagger that can be shot out and float in place and eviscerate enemies.
Sadly, there's no weapon that shoots shurikens and lightning, for shame. :(
Along the way, Belial will face many enemies, some new like preachers that resurrect dead foes, Ladies with propellors for arms, plus some returning foes like the kids on fire from Battle out of hell, the puppets from battle out of hell...
I'm beginning to notice a theme here... things being reused from the first Painkiller and it's expansion pack. Hell, even the theme park level is ripped from Battle out of hell, just with a different final part. Laziness is a sin.
And like in the last Painkiller, if you want to get the tarot cards, prepare to deal with some BS requirements along the way, like not picking up souls, so you can't transform into a demon. Or collecting all the souls in a level, only for an enemy to be glitched out, leaving you one soul shy. :P
However, despite all the issues, I will still heartily recommend Painkiller Overdose. It may not be the prettiest girl on the dance floor and she might have some issues, but if you have patience and are willing to see what Painkiller's like without any puzzle bosses, then give Overdose a chance. It's not much on Steam and it's pretty short.

Disclaimer: I backed the original Kickstarter.
As a genre, "Point-and-Click" Adventure games have been largely pushed out of public view. Indies carry the torch. And now ex-Lucasarts auteur Tim Schafer has returned with the independently-made, independently-published, crowd-funded Broken Age.
Broken Age is, frankly, pretty damn gorgeous. It's unapologetically 2D. The "Bagel" art style has always been unique and it adds, in my opinion, to the charm and character of the game. Sound Design is solid and appropriate and the voice acting is top notch. The music is gorgeous -- you want the soundtrack. Just trust me on that.
Gameplay is buttery, and while I've grown up playing point-and-clicks, I often had a guide or walkthrough of some kind nearby. I purposely didn't have that for Broken Age, and only got hung up on two puzzles. The story, half-finished as it might be at this point, is compelling and the ending of Act 1 definitely leaves me curious to see how Act 2 will continue.
The original Kickstarter goal was $400,000 USD but ended at some $3.5 million. The fact the devs have essentially blown through that money and have publically delivered a half-finished game makes me extremely curious what Double Fine had in mind for the title when they started their initial crowd-funding campaign.
That said, the game is half-finished, with the second half expected (and promised) to arrive later this year.
Broken Age is a solid bit of adventure. It doesn't rely on nostalgia.
A classic (still) in the making.

The game is divided into chapter, which one comprises of a series of missions to investigate an international security issue. Well done. The safehouse concept was very well implemented in which you can buy/sell weapons, gadgets, and key intel to unlock additional side missions (investigations) related to chapter's story mission.
After completing the first chapter, you can choose from 5 professional styles which of them with unique abilities and gadgets. I can relate spy, soldier, engineer, etc.  I chose spy...it is a stealth game, guys. But fell free to choose a different one to go assaulting everywhere. There is always that game. The game most people know is good, but never played. Alpha Protocol can definitively be put in that category for a lot of people.
For the others, who actually played it, ask them what is the best spy game they played, and a lot of them will probably mention Alpha Protocol. Alpha Protocol is a lot less known than franchises suchs as MGS or Splinter Cell, which spawned multiple games, but it does a lot of things rights all while maintining a pretty realist setting.
You see, Alpha Protocol isn't just your random stealth game. In its story telling and character developpement, it's a lot closer to a RPG. The story follows the main protagonist as he gets recruited into an secret agency working for the US goverment. After training and a few missions, for some reasons I won't explain, he is forced to go rogue, and work on unraveling the conspiracy which put him in that situation all while avoiding being hunted by his former colleagues. On the way he will meet numerous allies and ennemies, and take part in a lot operations in various countries until the thrilling conclusion of the story.
But you see, even if I wasn't willingly leaving the details of the story vague, Alpha Protocol is a game where your decisions really matters. Who you will befriend, the ennemies you make, who gets to live or die, is all up to you via the decisions of your character. Dialogues often leave you a limited time to answer when you are talked to. So you need to respond in a pretty quick and instinctive manner. While some people may complain it's a bad idea, especially without a way to savescum easyly, I personnally find it gives the story a more organic feel. It does help the whole cast of character is really well done. Most of them have some pretty complex stories behind them, and their own psychology. Psychology, as such, is important when dealing with others. You need to understand the kind of person you're talking to and act accordingly. The character of Frank Heck, in particular, has become a fan favorite.
The game has multiple endings, some being pretty amazing, like joining forces with the "bad" guy(s), and even betraying them just afterward to take over. Something which isn't seen pretty often in games.
As for the gameplay, the stealth as well as the gunplay is pretty solid. And it's an other strength of the game, really. While you can go around relying on stealth on most mission(not all mind you), and/or diplomacy, you can also take a more direct approach, or being a tech wizard relying on gadgets to get the work done, there is even a hand to hand combat specialist path, depending on how you wish to build your character. Out of stat gains via missions completed, you  also get rewarded with passive bonus depending of your playstyle and your choices. Taking a lot of damage will grant you extra resistance, using a weapon a lot will make you better with it, going non lethal will make you better with non lethal weapons, etc etc. The good thing with such a system is, no matter how you play, you will get something out of it to suit your general playstyle, which is pretty good and clever.
The only flaw I could find is the fact some weapons were a bit poorly balanced, to the point the best guns are actually the pistols, and everything else is kinda bad(which is mostly due to one pistol skill being really brutal).
Some things are done via minigames, such as lockpicking, hacking and rewiring. A lot of people don't like the hacking minigame, but personnally I never had any problem with it.
Overall, if you want a spy game with a good setting, a really good story, interesting characters and enjoyable gameplay, you can't go wrong with this game. Chances are, seeing it's getting old now, you will get it for a low price, even more during a sale, so by all means, get that game. You won't regret it.

The Walking Dead: Season 2 is a significant improvement from the first game. First up, graphics. The graphics themselves are okay, there are better looking games and better looking cel-shaded games out there, but I have no real issue with the graphics here, they get the job done and everything generally is pretty detailed. Animations are also improved from the first game, but it's obvious Telltale Games needs to put more time into them.
Sound and voice acting is pretty well done. Besides a few individuals, everyone does a great job here.
Gameplay here is somewhat lacking, compared to your average game, but this is a visual novel more than anything. Story here reigns supreme more than anything else in this game. The game picks up a few months after the end of The Walking Dead (season 1), and you play as Clementine. TWDS2 has much tougher decisions than the first game, and more of them. One of my issues with the first game was that many decisions were black and white. Kill this man or save everyone, etc, etc. I won't go into much detail, as to not spoil you, but much of the decisions in this game have, and will continue to, divide the community.
I would HIGHLY recommend you play The Walking Dead (season 1) before playing this one, but it's not required. You can, more or less, pick some of the decisions from the first game as you play through this one, but understand that many of them will also be randomly generated, and you may not like what you get. Beyond that, this game is solid, has a great story, and can jerk a tear and pull on the ol' heartstrings more than once.

This is RimWorld-Lite with a pretty good tech tree. The upgrades can be difficult to get, and the system is somewhat obscure. In order to get the upgrade you want to make something, you need to HAVE some of that stuff already! To be able to mine, for example, to get metal, you have to first have some metal to unlock mining! It's like that for a number of upgrades.
To get the stuff for unlocks, you need to travel to a location and scavange what you need. Combat will take place there, and you get the items if you kill the enemies. Then you automatically go back to base and if you have the right ingreedients, you can then upgrade.
Combat is the weakest part of the game right now. It's pretty watery, with no options apart from movement and a base attack. Hopefully the combat will be upgraded in the future.
Some of the tech tree isn't ready yet, no worries, you get a good idea of what's coming.
As well as crafting upgrades, there is magic. So far the magic that I've unlocked just lets me make it rain, grow trees and get other mundane resorces. There is a spell I've just unlocked that apparently lets you find survivors, but I haven't seen any options to be able to use that so far.
Your base will get invaded with increasing frequency by creatures of increasing difficulty. If you don't keep up by training your peeps and giving them better weapons, plus getting other survivors to join, you *will* die. This IMHO could do with toning down, but Early Access.
I would say keep an eye on it and see how it goes. They have a great framework here, and it is very playable so far, but if you already have Rimworld then there really isn't much here right now to differentiate this game from that.

The 30fps cap isn't the biggest problem of this game.
Let me put this first: I am a Mafia franchise fan. Always have been. I bought Mafia on it's release in English and German. I preordered Mafia II. I bought every single DLC for Mafia II and I played them all. I have more than 100 hours of playtime in Mafia II according to Steam. I preordered Mafia III and was looking forward to it and it's new setting.
However, Mafia III isn't closely as good as it's predecessors.
I won't give you a final rating of the story or setting of Mafia III. Some people didn't appreciante that they moved from an Italian Mafia background to a black gang background. I was (and still am in a way) open-minded towards it and a bit apprehensive. I haven't played much of the story yet but so far it seems alright, even though I got the feeling that I might already know where things are going.
The conversations and cutcenes are still of high quality. IMO the cutcenes are at least on a Mafia II level, maybe even better.
So that's fine. What's the problem? Primarily the game's technology. I won't even mention the 30fps problem this game has but it has bad graphics, bad controlls, bad sound and bad physics.
As long as your on foot these problems aren't that noticeable. Shooting and the cover system are similar to that of Mafia II. There are some developer decisions that I have to critizise in this regard though: Your health will regenerate really fast. You also have the option to take a medkit in order to regenerate it instantly. Enemies are very passive during shootouts. You can easily kill them from cover even on highest difficulty. The protagonist seems kinda overpowered.
This becomes even more apparent when you take a look at melee fights: When you approach an enemy from behind you can instantly kill him / knock him out. But even when you run towards him you can knock him out with one or two hits (unarmed people on the street get knockt out after one single hit). There is no advanced melee fighting system like in Mafia I or II.
Most of the technlogical problems this game has only become visible once you get in a car and drive around a bit.
Driving itself is very underwhelming to begin with. You can still select "Simulation" driving mode in the menu but even if you do so the handling is very easy. You can drive at full throttle all the time without any problems. You can "drift" on a straight street. The whole driving model is very basic, unrealstic and easy. I don't think I can find any open world game with a comparable driving model in the last ~10 years.
You will also notice several other problems while driving through the streets:
-Mafia III's world might be bigger than that of Mafia II or Mafia I but it feels empty and lacks details.
-The car's motor sounds are bad. They don't change when you accelerate or make a burnout. The Thunderbird has the sound of a sewing machine.
-When you hit another other car with high speed it will barely slow you down but fly through the air like it was hit by a NASA rocket
-All static objects other than traffic signs are undestroyable and will stop you instantly if you crash into them though. Even some(!) phone booths.
-When you drive into a pedestrian they will be stand in front of your car while beeing pushed around. They will drop dead as soon as you stop. I have seen better solutions in open world games of the pre-GTAIV-era!
-Volumetric smoke? Nope!
-All in all bad effects
-Aggressivee LOD
-Bad textures
-Low draw distance
-Fog
-In the first daylight missions the weather will change within seconds from super light sunny with massive bloom effects to dark clouded and back. Quite annoying.
-All in all very bad lighting in the first daylight missions (bug?).
-Ugly, low detailed car models! Really. There are cars that look like they are out of the 50's. Some have a strong 	resemblance with cars that where in Mafia II. But they didn't take the models from Mafia II. They created new, similar looking models that look worse on closer inspectation. Makes me wonder why. Did they just buy the name and not the rights to use previous content?
-The damage models of the cars are worse than in Mafia II
-Sometimes shadows are casted to different directions
There are also bugs where certain items fly in the air because furniture isn't displayed or instances where the player falls through the floor of the map.
Mafia III feels like the first attempt on creating an open world game of a small studio that has no experience whatsoever. It feels unfinished. And it is. Even with a release half a year later it wouldn't reach the AAA game level of it's predecessors.
However, you can still have some fun with this one. But I recommend you wait til it is on sale.

As a writer and a gamer, I can recommend Alan Wake as the crème de la crème of both worlds. The story's quality is that of a blockbuster movie narrated by Alan Wake himself, divided into several chapters. Gameplay-wise this game plays with light like few other horror games do. Revolvers and shotguns sure are handy, but your best friend and best weapon in this game is any lightsource you can find. The Taken are surrounded by a shield of darkness that deflects bullets, and only a concentrated beam of light can break their defenses. Focus your flashlight's lightcone on your enemies and finish them off with a couple of shots to see them explode and burst into little sparks. It may not offer tons of replayability, apart from collecting all the collectables and achievements, but it's a thrilling ride any lover of great storytelling should go through at least once.

The rave reviews lead me to buying this game. My initial reaction was unimpressed, and i suppose it's much to do with the super simplified game play. But once i was moving through the levels, i was hooked.
It's a game that allows you to either kamikaze with guns blazing (although that will only get you so far), or advance through stealth, or a combination of both. Eliminating your targets can be methodical given the various setups of each stage. Oftentimes when enemies come at you, you're left to think and react fast since lengthy hesitations will cost you.
There is a slight frustration factor where the guns don't kill your intended targets all the time, especially when you feel like you're aiming directly. When the enemies are right in your face or sort of on top of you so to speak, sometimes firing at them seem futile as the bullets go right through.
As a whole, the game is fun and challenging.

You have to shoot your way through dungeons/maps that find ways of confusing you, so it's advised that you don't rush them. If you want a game that is packed full of challenges for your hand-eye co-ordination and reflexes, then I definetly believe you should play it.
How it manages to tie such a simple genre into an interesting story is quite unique and makes you want to keep going back to play it, just so you can finally say you reached that Nuclear Throne! - 85/100.

TL/DR: A decent online Co-Op FPS with a seemingly undeserved bad reputation that's at least worth a look.
Now, I never played the first incarnation of this game, so I don't know what it was like and thus can't comment on any changes and/or improvments that have been made. Hell, I only picked it up because it was $1 at the time, but from everything I've seen this game isn't bad. Not great, but worth it if you can pick it up on sale.
Graphics are OK. Not the best, but still good. Gameplay is straightforward; shoot dinos, gets credits, buy bigger guns, repeat. The problem here is there's no tutorial, so you're on your own when it comes to figuring out a lot of things. Example; I was into Wave 10 of my first game before I realised "Hey, the Weapons Store sells upgrades for reload speed, clip size and damage, too!" Yes, the tap said Upgrade, but I'd missed it the first few times I'd gone to get new weapons. Same goes for buying more ammo. Now there's no real plot or story here (so far) so the game doesn't need a huge intro, just something like in Natural Selection 2, a quick walkthrough of the most basic features of the game before you jump into an active game.
The controls are what I normally see in FPS games and it took some tweaking to get the mouse sensativity just right, but I expect that. But the default controls don't seem to make use of the middle mouse button, which seems strange now a days.
Overall this game is worth at least a quick look, and from what I've seen the devs are fairly active in responding to questions on the forums and well as with updates. Right now there do appear to be a few balance issues with weapon damage (tiny bugger of a dino taking to point blank shotgun blasts to kill, etc.) but it's balanced enough to play well.
Also, there's an achievement for killing a dev in-game. How can you not like that?

Highly polished, but lacks gameplay depth.
UI, sound effects, and art are solid, the animations are superb. Strongest element is the combat system, which manages to create complex tactical situations and cinematic moments without the use of either hitpoints or randomness.
Main problem is the repetitive feel. All the missions are "get in, find the target, get out" while trying to accumulate as many resources as possible. All missions are stealth focused where your party are 'underdogs', and after a while, they all start feeling like slight variations of each other. Games with high replay value alternate different mindsets of play, rather than having each encounter be the same sort of methodical stealth grind. There's a good explanation of encounter building and varied mindsets at

. Some games lack this mindset variation, but make up for it in tactical decision making (ie chess). Invisible Inc. is partway there. Interesting situations do come up, but most of the action is just moving around the map. Usually, you get 1-2 interesting puzzles per level, and fewer if you play efficiently and don't get yourself into tight spots.
That being said, the game is a joy to learn, and absolutely worth the investment of a dozen hours.
Overall, Invisible Inc. is worth $8-9 dollars, maybe more if you like game design.

I grew up with the classic X-COM games (on DOS, not the remakes) and Invisible, Inc. manages to recreate at least two aspects:

You can't develop your own weapons, though, but have to work with what is available in/between the missions. This adds to the complexity of the game. On "Experienced" difficulty and onward, you are being punished for exploring and looting: while the game is turn-based, there is a timer in the form of an "alarm level". The longer you take, the harder it is for you to go about unnoticed. So it's better to focus on the mission, even if there is a shiny corporate safe just a little detour away...
There is a bit of luck involved, just like in Roguelikes. The quality of your gear largely depends on what you are able to loot.
If you like turn-based isometric tactic games with an espionage/cyberpunk setting, definitely give it a go.

Invisible, Inc. takes the old school hi-tech international super spy routine that Archer loves to parody and turns it into a riveting and deep turn-based strategy game.
What to expect:
-A world map with a selection of missions that must all be completed within seventy-two hours of in-game time.
-Mission goals can involve securing loads of money, weapons, system upgrades or new party members
-Mission maps are facility interiors divided into Fire Emblem-style squares. Your units (minimum of two and maximum of four) have a set number of actions in one turn, consumed by moving, peeking around corners, attacking enemies and more.
-A cast of super spies with unique abilities and stats. As you progress, money that you steal can be used to upgrade them, buy them weapons, install augmentations into them or buy them tools.
-Also under your control is a computer system called Incognita. This system can hack into the various consoles during missions to unlock money, weapons, upgrades, as well as disable security cameras, robots and more. Resources for Incognita hacking are limited, so be careful with your points.
-Several difficulty levels and many options to customize a campaign. One campaign may involve six or seven missions before the finale.
-Plot and story and characters are paper-thin. Honestly, that's just the window-dressing. Just focus on the really, in-depth strategy elements, alright?
-Music consists of moody, dark spy themes that blend in with the technology and hacking theme of the game.
-Art style depicts our characters and world in jagged, pointed shapes illuminated by bright colors just like computer monitors. I don't think anyone smiles once during this game. While the tone isn't unicorns-and-rainbows, it really isn't miserable and drained of life like a Zack Snyder film.
In conclusion, Invisible, Inc. is a solid purchase for any strategy fan. There's a lot of depth and complexity, which is how I like my games. Prepare to spend a lot of mental energy into grasping and utilizing these mechanics to your advantage. I recommend trying out a few campaigns in the Easy mode first.

Fantastic visuals, thoughtful writing, incredible voice acting and uplifting music from one of the greatest studios that use all of their creative talents to bring you one of the most heartwarming adventure games I have ever played.

So WB Games did their best to put me off with a tiered release, pre-order bonuses and sodding microtransactions in a single player game. It’s hard to overlook and I wouldn’t blame anyone for boycotting the title, although it would be a shame in my opinion, especially if you enjoyed the first. Check out my in depth first impressions video for my thoughts on the game and those loot boxes.
Shadow of War does what a good sequel should do, by fixing the things that didn’t work and improving on those that did. One of my biggest issues with Shadow of Mordor was in the lacklustre environments and SoW improves this no end by creating more interesting and varied locations to run, climb, jump and stab in. The wonderful nemesis system has also been enhanced with the orcs given more character and variation in abilities, making fighting them even more fun. There are also a number of scripted orcs and the new conquest system which is fun and adds more depth.
There are a few problems other than the loot boxes, one being the usual map full of side missions that can start to grate (an arkham-creed staple) and another being the surprisingly narrow fov that can make fighting in close quarters difficult. I’m also not too enamoured with the two ‘token’ good characters but the story is entertaining enough and other than that it’s just nit-picks. I’m not at the end game yet so have no idea if the rumours of grind are true, but I wouldn’t be surprised because so far I have had no compulsion to purchase a loot box.

This feels poorly designed just looking at the infinite runner aspect of the gameplay and ignoring that Pac Man has been slapped into it.
Though the game is visually appealing(for, you know, a mobile port that originally wasn’t supposed to keep your attention for more than 5 minutes), there are a few game play elements that are hard to dissect in a quick, life/death situation.  The glitchy teleport effect is shared between randomly placed coins and glitched ghosts.  Both will show up randomly, but coins are a semi-frequent pickup that are crucial to progression when starting out, where as ghosts will of course kill you if you try and run through their teleport assuming it was a coin about to pop up.  The only difference I could see between their visual effect is that ghosts took about half a second longer to make the transition.  You already don’t get much time to judge what it is because of the corridor hallways the map is made out of and the 256 wall doesn’t allow for too much back tracking should you need to find a better path.
Power ups are horribly designed/balanced.  I should point out that if not all your power ups are lethal(as in a weapon of some sort), you will guarantee your death in multiple situations early in a run.  Not even pickups that give you non-lethal invincibility are useful. They can leave you trapped when they wear off and won’t earn you any extra points anyway.
While achievement hunting, I discovered that after awhile, the hallway setups and ghost placements become exceedingly predictable.  Its when I noticed that power ups are usually placed in areas in later parts of a run where they are absolutely necessary to progress through an area.  If you choose anything other than an all lethal loadout, you will either die within the area or not progress fast enough and screw yourself in the near future.
Many unlockable pick ups have straight upgrades with the only nerfs being less points for using them and less time given when picking them up.  This becomes entirely trivial when the better form of the same pick up is significantly more useful and will extend your game much further than using the longer lasting/better scoring pick up.  A grand example of this is the beam/laser pick up, with the Beam pick up reflecting off corners and being able to clear out large groups of ghosts without being anywhere near them.  The score/time bonus for using the inferior laser doesn’t even come close to being relevant, as it can’t kill ghosts without direct line of sight and is still vulnerable in many situations that the beam is not.
The periodic missions that give you coins as a reward for completing them often pressure players into doing things that would probably get them killed, so to progress and level up powers, you will have to sacrifice trying to play towards an actual score like you would expect in an arcade game, or even an infinite runner.  The coin rewards are also random and have nothing to do with what the mission objective was.  Though the objectives can take anywhere from the first 3 minutes of a run collecting a small amount of pellets to multiple runs searching for 6 of the exact same fruit, you can get anywhere between 128 and 1024 coins for doing them.  From my experience, it went more towards the low end of rewards more often than not.
All of this is just bad gameplay.  THEN you add the fact that it has a Pac Man theme, a game series with deep roots to classic, skill based arcade experiences, and that this started out as F2P mobile game… yeah its a pretty big slap to the face.  I would like to give them credit for making a solid port but honestly I don’t think many people would play something like this on PC, its really unnecessary.  I wouldn’t play this on mobile either, despite having mobile games ranging from both casual and a bit more in depth.  Pac Man 256 is just a bad game in general, and a pointless addition to anyone’s Steam library.

One thing to understand is that Banner Saga 2 is not a separate game—this is the second chapter of the same story which will make no sense if you haven't played the original. Also, unlike the first one, where the story felt a bit unsatisfying due to you only beating a small boss (rather than getting to the bottom of the whole plight), here the game ends in a blatant cliffhanger. More important events happen outside the camera's eye, left unexplained. Honestly, it all makes me feel that it may be smarter to wait for Banner Saga 3 before picking this up.
As a continuation of Banner Saga, however, this one offers no surprises and no disappointments; it's basically the same game. Still gorgeous visuals, still wonky voiceovers, still simple but fun and challenging fights. (On the highest levels there is now actually some RNG present in them, but it works well.)
The useful part about sequels like BS2 is that they offer no decision-making to you as a buyer. If you liked the first game, this one is a must. If you didn't (or haven't played it), there's no reason to buy it. It's as simple as that.
