I finished the game playing as stealth character and a little bit of shooting.
I do not recommend the game that much.
Here is a summary of what I think of the game:
The positives:
+ Does have variety of environments.
+ Interesting dialoug system and very similar to Mass Effect's. The only difference between this game and mass effect is that your response is timed. Pressing X usually gives a charming/sarcastic response, Y for more agrressive and angry, and B for Profoessional and calm.
Meh:
* Has various "mini-games" such as picking locks and hacking. They do get repititve and they feel unrewarding to do.
* There is ingame cash in which you could pay for weapons, upgrades, armors, and missions intel. However, since combat is bad (I will get to that) then having tons of guns doesn't really help.
* Character is customizable but the customization are kind of limited.
The negatives:
- Combat is very annoying especially when starting off the game. It takes from early Ghost Recon games where you have to stand still and aim at your target until the cursor circle gets smaller. This is not suitable for this game at all especially when you are caught with too many guards and they are close to you. It also make boss fights frustrating.
- A.I. with stealth is very very basic. If a guard get the sight of you, alert mode starts right away. This gets very annoying because sometimes they can see you even when you are behind a wall or a cover. Unlike games like Tenchu or MGS, the guard has no "Hmmm?" window. If he sees you expect swarm of guards coming at you.
- The game is not clear on the benefit of killing humans or knock them out since bodies simply disappear after 10 seconds. True that killing humans might trigger some conversations with NPCs later on, but this has no noticeable gameplay factor at all.
- Camera is a bit annoying and feels a bit stiff. Reminds you of some PS2 titles.
- Movement is not as fluid sometimes. For example, when you reload, the character stops moving.
- Stealth moves are very limited. For example, you can only jump on certain locations and others you can't. You can never move above any obstacle.
How good is the story?
The story did not really get me interested. It is very similar to Splinter Cell games. Voice acting is good. Didn't like most of the writing. Romance is very very very awkward and tasteless.
Overall
The idea behind the game got potential. At first instance, it seems like it can be a Mass Effect meets Metal Gear. However the game is simply not up to expectations and much of its elements are outdated.

Alpha Protocol is a 3rd person RPG game made by Obsidian Entertainment. You play as Michael Thorton, an agent with a top secret branch of the CIA.
I can not speak highly enough about this game. Yes it does have some issues which I will get to in a bit but overal this game is amazing and very much worth your time if you are interested in the RPG genre. Lets start off with the pro's for this game.
Gameplay: You have 3 options for how to play the game right out of the gate. You can play as either a complete stealth style never being noticed by anyone. A middle of the road style where you use stealth to take out your enemys. Also an FPS style in which you go in guns blazing with no regard for stealth at all. This alone opens up many hours of replayability and is something I personally have not seen very often.
Customization: Just about everything about your character, except general looks, can be customized. Your weapons, what gear you take with you, and your armor or lack there of are all fully customizable giving you a plethora of options for each misson you go on.
Dialogue: The dialogue system is top notch giving you multiple options for how you want to respond, some of which are very entertaining. This also leads into a reputation and romance system that is very well developed for characters that actually make you care about them on some level.
Impact: This is probably the most important part, at least for me. The decisions you make in game, who you talk to, how you handle each situation, all matter a great deal in this game. Your choices have consequences and you have to carefully consider what you want to say, how to say it, and what to do at any given moment.
Now  lets touch on the negatives for this game, and yes, sadly there are a few.
AI: The enemies in Alpha Protocol are not the best out there. The can be rather predictable at times and glitch out. That being said it is not game breaking in any way and personally it didn't bother me all that much.
Combat: Alpha Protocol is first and foremost a console game. It was ported over to the PC and as such has a combat system that at times can feel clunky and drive you nuts. Once you get used to it though you can get through the game just fine.
Hacking: There really is no other way to say it, the hacking minigame in Alpha Protocol is absolutly terrible. It really could have used an overhaul but it sadly never came.
Bugs: There are a few other bugs in the game some of which can be quite annoying but I personally never experienced anything to dramatic or game  breaking.
Graphics: This was a console game that is pretty old at this point and was ported over to the PC. The graphics are not top tier yet at the same time I have seen a LOT worse out there.
TLDR: Alpha Protocol  is a great game very much worth the asking price and even more so if you can get it on sale. 7/10

Like TBS, TBS2 is a great story game with a terrible strategy game attached to it. The turn-based combat is a drawn-out slog where the best strategy is to delay every fight as long as possible to setup a full team kill, so that weakened enemies waste turns in the meantime. The game also poorly explains many of the new mechanics and skills, and fails to give proper guidance on many missions, forcing you to fail to actually figure out what the win conditions are.
The story or "Oregon Trail Lite" would be acceptable if you weren't arbitrarily punished by your decisions. There are no difficult decisions to make about what to do, because every choice is either right or wrong. You either pick the right choice and get a bonus, or you pick the wrong choice and a crucial party member is killed or half your caravan is destroyed.
---
What I originally wrote was just supposed to be a short review, so let me clarify some points. Admittedly I was melodramatic about the game destroying half your caravan and party for a bad choice. That only happens once.
Now what makes a good game? Choice.
What makes a good story game? Making you feel like your choices had meaning.
How does a story game do this? Giving the choices you didn't make, a real impact to the plot.
This is why I consider TBS + TBS2 good story games. They have several key decisions that have a major impact on the plot and give your choices real heft. Unfortunately TBS2 is still a good story game with a worse strategy game attached to it.
It's important to understand that there are two distinct parts of your strategy in TBS. The turn-based combat part, and the "Oregon Trail" part where you basically play a choose your own adventure book. The problem is that the choose your own adventure book only has a few pages where you make a meaningful decision. The other hundred or so pages are just you being rewarded or punished for a choice, and then the story continues.
Why is this a problem? When you replay a good story game, trying out the choices you didn't make the first time is rewarding. When you play a bad story game, you realize that the other choices didn't matter or just led to game over screens. TBS doesn't end the game, but it does punish you. That little plus or minus of morale or clansmen is a sign that the choice you made was either wrong or right. And if the only real choice you have is to make the right choice or the wrong choice? Your choice becomes meaningless. The game hides this of course with text, but it doesn't change the binary nature of most of the choices you make, and it muddies the key decisions that really do matter in TBS. If TBS was just a story game this could be ignored, especially because you don't get hit by a game over screen, but unfortunately TBS is also a strategy game.
What makes a good strategy game? Being able to implement clever tactics against a clever enemy. Being able to make calculated decisions to win against the adversary.
What makes a bad strategy game? Having no real indication of how your choices will affect you. Having a single correct choice instead of multiple.
Now TBS2 actually has a solution to the problems I see in it, but before that I'll get to the turn-based combat. Now if you agree with what I said about what makes a good strategy game, you might not understand why I dislike the strategy in TBS2.
I actually liked it. In short bites. I had fun on hard until i got halfway and decided to switch to easy and just bruteforce the fights.
The problem with the combat is that the campaign rewards cautious behavior too much. Much like in the first TBS, maiming enemies to the point of uselessness and forcing them to waste turns is still the best way to play. Now you have some more options to waste time admittedly. You have more crowd control to play "keep away" and lock down dangerous enemies until you can whittle them down into nothing, but the best strategy is still basically slow erosion broken up by a few mass cullings. The highlight of the combat is when you can basically slaughter a half dozen enemies in one go and ride out to victory. And I mean, it's great. It feels like a great way to end a fight, but when the best way to end every fight is doing that? It loses its charm along the way. Real people could be different, but the AI's only real plan is rush you until you die, which is what makes the strategy so effective in the first place.
What could fix all of this? For "Oregon Trail", if instead of being punished or rewarded for the random events, you instead had to choose how you took the hit/ gain. I.E. choose whether to save fighters or clansmen while your ships are sinking, gather extra supplies while you have time or scout ahead to avoid a battle. TBS2 has a few choices that actually adhere to this (most of them being the key ones I mentioned earlier), which makes it mind boggling to me why it wasn't just used as a format for all of them. Likewise TBS2 also fixes my problem with the turn-based combat in its survival mode, removing enemies from the turn order when they die, and giving you a double turn that allows for much more aggressive tactics and flexibility in your playstyle. Again, why wasn't that just the default, or at least an option.
Still going to buy TBS3 probably.

While this game does a lot right, even going above and beyond in its predecessor's combat mechanics and building off its engaging universe, it doesn't offer a satisfying experience due to its abrupt ending, poor pacing, and rather simplistic gameplay.
Pros:
- It may require a refresher from the first game, but BS2 has a rich world to learn about with many unique and memorable characters.
- Great artwork and soundtrack
- Generally fun combat
- Engaging plot
Cons:
- Pacing. Throughout the game it's unclear how much food you'll need, when you'll need to spend/save renown, when heros will split and where you are in the story. It's not satisfying to suddenly save people, train fighters or buy food, etc. when there's little to form expectations. The sudden ending was extremely unsatisfying.
- Unused game mechanics. The playable partsof the game primarily consist of an Oregon Trail dynamic, dialogue options and combat. What are my unused heroes doing? Why do I need clansmen/fights other then to scavenge? Clearly things may make a difference in the next game if you decide to continue your game, but BS2 by itself doesn't offer much beyond combat scenes and journey dialogue.
- The game really depends on players carrying over knowledge, connections to characters, etc. from the first game. For this reason alone it's hard to recommend this game to anyone but people who have played the first one. While with this isn't exactly a ton to ask for an indie developer to ask for, there's the reality that this game isn't a complete whole on it's own from start to finish.
Just a few thoughts, but I'd recommend waiting for a sale or waiting until the next game comes out to really reap the benefits of playing this game.

The 30fps cap isn't the biggest problem of this game.
Let me put this first: I am a Mafia franchise fan. Always have been. I bought Mafia on it's release in English and German. I preordered Mafia II. I bought every single DLC for Mafia II and I played them all. I have more than 100 hours of playtime in Mafia II according to Steam. I preordered Mafia III and was looking forward to it and it's new setting.
However, Mafia III isn't closely as good as it's predecessors.
I won't give you a final rating of the story or setting of Mafia III. Some people didn't appreciante that they moved from an Italian Mafia background to a black gang background. I was (and still am in a way) open-minded towards it and a bit apprehensive. I haven't played much of the story yet but so far it seems alright, even though I got the feeling that I might already know where things are going.
The conversations and cutcenes are still of high quality. IMO the cutcenes are at least on a Mafia II level, maybe even better.
So that's fine. What's the problem? Primarily the game's technology. I won't even mention the 30fps problem this game has but it has bad graphics, bad controlls, bad sound and bad physics.
As long as your on foot these problems aren't that noticeable. Shooting and the cover system are similar to that of Mafia II. There are some developer decisions that I have to critizise in this regard though: Your health will regenerate really fast. You also have the option to take a medkit in order to regenerate it instantly. Enemies are very passive during shootouts. You can easily kill them from cover even on highest difficulty. The protagonist seems kinda overpowered.
This becomes even more apparent when you take a look at melee fights: When you approach an enemy from behind you can instantly kill him / knock him out. But even when you run towards him you can knock him out with one or two hits (unarmed people on the street get knockt out after one single hit). There is no advanced melee fighting system like in Mafia I or II.
Most of the technlogical problems this game has only become visible once you get in a car and drive around a bit.
Driving itself is very underwhelming to begin with. You can still select "Simulation" driving mode in the menu but even if you do so the handling is very easy. You can drive at full throttle all the time without any problems. You can "drift" on a straight street. The whole driving model is very basic, unrealstic and easy. I don't think I can find any open world game with a comparable driving model in the last ~10 years.
You will also notice several other problems while driving through the streets:
-Mafia III's world might be bigger than that of Mafia II or Mafia I but it feels empty and lacks details.
-The car's motor sounds are bad. They don't change when you accelerate or make a burnout. The Thunderbird has the sound of a sewing machine.
-When you hit another other car with high speed it will barely slow you down but fly through the air like it was hit by a NASA rocket
-All static objects other than traffic signs are undestroyable and will stop you instantly if you crash into them though. Even some(!) phone booths.
-When you drive into a pedestrian they will be stand in front of your car while beeing pushed around. They will drop dead as soon as you stop. I have seen better solutions in open world games of the pre-GTAIV-era!
-Volumetric smoke? Nope!
-All in all bad effects
-Aggressivee LOD
-Bad textures
-Low draw distance
-Fog
-In the first daylight missions the weather will change within seconds from super light sunny with massive bloom effects to dark clouded and back. Quite annoying.
-All in all very bad lighting in the first daylight missions (bug?).
-Ugly, low detailed car models! Really. There are cars that look like they are out of the 50's. Some have a strong 	resemblance with cars that where in Mafia II. But they didn't take the models from Mafia II. They created new, similar looking models that look worse on closer inspectation. Makes me wonder why. Did they just buy the name and not the rights to use previous content?
-The damage models of the cars are worse than in Mafia II
-Sometimes shadows are casted to different directions
There are also bugs where certain items fly in the air because furniture isn't displayed or instances where the player falls through the floor of the map.
Mafia III feels like the first attempt on creating an open world game of a small studio that has no experience whatsoever. It feels unfinished. And it is. Even with a release half a year later it wouldn't reach the AAA game level of it's predecessors.
However, you can still have some fun with this one. But I recommend you wait til it is on sale.

I don't write reviews. At all. But exceptions have to be made for what is hauntingly amazing.  I loved the first one, but TBS 2 is on another level.
Gameplay wise, it's fairly simple to play, but in my experience very difficult to master (I still struggle with *fully completing* one particular boss fight in the game on the hardest difficulty.) Despite the simplicty and challenge, playing the story battles over and over again is always fresh because of the individual heroes' abilities - the mixing and matching of their skillsets and having to give kills to heroes to level them (some need more help than others, of course) brought me closer to the characters, and weren't just pieces I was moving around on a board. And it's inevitable that some heroes will by much more frequently utilised than others, some less, but I have enjoyed TBS 2 to a greater degree by putting myself through the struggle of attempting to use weaker characters - mixing and matching squads of shieldbanger varl with archers, only having human characters armed with shields to form a defensive line and buff stats while restricting movement, or playing with more support characters than slayers.
I'm not one to complain or praise visuals because art more often than not is a *different strokes for different folks* thing in my opinion, but the art of TBS 2... I didn't want the game to end when it did, and one of the main reasons why is its visuals. Absolutely stunning by all accounts. While there are few animated scenes with characters moving about, the still depictions of the characters with their written dialogue below are just so fantastically vivid that the words come to life. Bolverk's character is truly out of the screen, for one. The silent moments between Rook and Iver. The chilling stills of Juno. Even simple details like Hakon's speech just fits the way he's so humongously built and towering over even other varl as a slayer in combat. The game can in that regard be enjoyed if played slowly, and the interactions made animate with one's mind.
The story. People liken it to Tolkien's universe, or at least from what I've seen in the other reviews. I'd beg to differ to an extent. It is after all based on Norse mythology to my knowledge, especially with the serpent's presence. So, take the carnage of Ragnarok with a Tolkien-esque twist, multiple narrative perspectives from two different caravans (including some ambiguity), and top it off with a tenderness in the moments less tense, very much made possible by the visuals. The moments when the caravan stops to rest, or has simply has to stop because they're too tired to continue. Watching the caravan make its way across the vast lands is a remarkable view and story to be told in itself. Coming across empty houses, battle-scarred villages, forgotten mine shafts, caverns, or even a death march across barren snowlands for a final stand at a ford... this is the story of TBS 2.
I bought TBS 1 on a whim just to try out an indie game that looked somewhat promising. The promise that it's delivered is far beyond expectations. It really is a world one can dive into and continuously appreciate if the time is taken or the eye is in awe of. Just get this game for god's sake it really is a bomb it's just wowza.

What impressed me about Alan Wake is the story line and how the game is set up. You're playing as a writer, and the game is played as if you were reading a book, or listening to an audio book. The game has a lot of potential and is fun to play, but it's clear the developers are completly incompetent. It's astonishing how clueless they're about their own game, the direction the game is taking, and how obviously they shut their ears to issue.
Anti-cheat protection is provided by "easy anti cheat", but is in reality actually fairly useless. You'll encounter cheaters, sometimes obvious, sometimes less so in particular in competitive. The sad thing about this is the game requires you to level 12 campions to 4 before entering competitive, but yet the hackers still manage to reach that point and then also play a few hundred rounds before getting banned; for a game that's trying to be "competitive" this is completly unacceptable.
Speaking of getting banned, if you're not the obvious "RAGE" hacker that doesn't even try to hide it, you won't be. Don't worry, people in competitive (some of which even play in leagues), have been using triggered/restricted aimbots and wallhacks for ages, reporting them is fairly useless because the reports most likely don't get looked at, and if they do whoever is looking at them is clearly clueless about cheats.
Matchmaking in this game is also absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. It's not surprising, matchmaking is hard to get right, but over multiple patches there haven't been any attempts to improve it. The issue here is that matchmaking often puts teams together with some people that -clearly- are out of their league; either they get put on a team of good players, eventually causing that team to loose, or some good players get put on a team that is essentially clueless.
It's probably their "attempt" at balancing matches, but unlike other games where it can work out due to characters being mostly identical this game is class based and there are roles that are need to be filled. If you got someone who can't play their role the game is already over.
As a last fun thing with this is that at a higher rating you'll get more hackers because naturally their hacks boost them to higher rating.
As related topic, they have a competitive rating for characters and for your account. Both function roughly the same, in that it's mostly based on how much you win/lose. This kinda works out for account rating, but since there are a lot of champions and they dont get played as much, it doesn't work out for it. So there are leaderborders, and they are mostly filled with players that primarily won most of their matches without playing any significant number of matches, often as little as 5:0.
Additionally if you actually play the champion for longer the system penalizes loosing in a ridicious manner; most of the time you only gain low two digits (like 10-20), and when you loose you loose over a hundred rating. Suppodestly the game tries to make your winrate 50:50, so if you want any "legitimate" rating you're pretty much screwed.
The road to a "world class" player here is to simply make an alt account or to get a few wins when you first play the champion in competive. Viola! You're in the top 100, now never play the champion again so you can keep your place.
So overall, champion rating is absolutly meaningless.
The developers also run a public test version of the upcoming patches. You'd think that is a great move and allow people to catch issues with those patches beforehand. And it would be case if the developers actually cared about anything the players say. They simply choose to ingore player feedback and put it on the live version anyway, regardless of the bugs reported.
Take the recent OB44 disaster as an example, there've been a number of bugs reported that made it into the game anyway, the balance of the new essence system was catastrophic and so were some of the hero changes, but it made into the game anway. After MASSIVE outleash on all social media outlets they're hotfixing it. Crysis could have been avoided by a developer who'd actually use their brain and player feedback.
It's also apprent they don't even know how their own systems work or how to treat their playerbase. With OB44 old players were to retroactively be granted chests for reaching specific champion levels. Instead only some players actually got them, they promised to hotfix the issue, but didn't actually fix the issue; the people who didn't get anything will now get some essence as compensation, but it isn't actually a compenstation since the chests can unlock things the essence can not. Great move to shaft a significant portion of your player base.
The worst part about this is that apprently the chests caused performance issues, if they'd known their own systems they should have known that in the first place and been more careful about this. But instead of doing a rollback or so and having an even playing field for everyone they just shaft a part of the playerbase.

This game has pretty simple controls, though it relies on tension and story telling rather than fighting or shooting it still feels a bit like your standard action game(ala Resident Evil 4, over the shoulder action) however, I have to stay the necessity of the flashlight, and the mechanics included, are a great twist on a style of gameplay that should be conidered standard if not a bit stale.
In the end this is a fun game but I will admit most of the fun actually comes from the story and the mistery you unfold rather than the gameplay mechanics or visuals(which are very decent).   I'm the kind of person who can look past graphics and gameplay if the game has a great story to deliver and Alan Wake(along with it's DLCs and addons) does not disappoint.

10/10 Square Enix delivers their masterful story-telling through the mind of an 18-year old art student, Max Caulfield, at her high school Blackwell Academy in Arcadia Bay, Oregon. Max wants to be a great photographer, but one day she discovers her power to reverse time. As you play as Max, you make important role-play decisions that will alter events during the game; you can still reverse a recent decision with your power which makes the game more flexible if you feel you have made the wrong choice. This game is one of the best RPGs I have ever played as all of the characters have a fleshed out personality and background.

If the epic explosions and guns of Serious Sam and the artstyle/gameplay of Risk of Rain had a baby and that baby was exposed to Hiroshima's Radiation, then that baby would be dubbed Nuclear Throne. Nuclear Throne is a Bullet-Hell/Roguelike game that features many interesting characters, with different abilities, weapons, level and enemies that help/distract you from reaching the "Nuclear Throne" at the end of every game.
You have to shoot your way through dungeons/maps that find ways of confusing you, so it's advised that you don't rush them. If you want a game that is packed full of challenges for your hand-eye co-ordination and reflexes, then I definetly believe you should play it.
How it manages to tie such a simple genre into an interesting story is quite unique and makes you want to keep going back to play it, just so you can finally say you reached that Nuclear Throne! - 85/100.

Same sort of progression/unlock system as crossy roads.  I never really liked crossy roads, but Pac Man 256 I do.
The board isn't a normal Pac Man board, you have to move up the board, it then scrolls down as you move up, if you don't then you'll eventually be swallowed up by a bunch of numbers and letters, the numbers and letters are like that for a reason.
In the original Pac man if you reached the 256th board you'd have encountered the famous 256 bug,  Players who reached the 256th board in the original Arcade Pac Man caused a buffer overflow, causinng the data in other areas to be overwritten, and thus you couldn't finish it.
There's various power-ups in Pac Man 256, you can choose 3 at the start of game, others will unlock over time.  It tracks some best stats as you play and tells you when you've just beaten one.

It's OK. When taken on its own and not held to any of its predecessors.
The problem there is, I've already seen what a modern Pac-Man game could be with CEDX+. When held up to that candle, this game falls short in just about every measure.
The various power ups start out interesting, and then either become obsolete (what is the use of choosing or upgrading Laser/Bomb/Freeze/Tornado/Fire/Magnet, when you have Optics/Boom/Shatter/Twinado/Pyro/Regen, which are respectively similar but more powerful versions?), or are pretty useless (Sonar) or unwieldy (Radar) compared to other power ups.
The incentive to actually get a high score is lacking. The game quickly becomes a grind about collecting coins to boost power-ups, and even with that, you will get far more coins from completing missions or just as free drops between games than you will actually playing the game.
Speaking of missions, in part these seem to be used as a crutch to make sure that you give every powerup, no matter how useless, fair air time. Because, eventually, you WILL get missions for things like "collect 5 Sonar power ups", and the only way to do that is to equip the power up so that it appears in the game, consuming one of your precious 3 slots. Ugh.
The game also breaks several traditional Pac-Man conventions. Forget about the tight, ghost-escaping cornering that you may have relied upon SINCE 1980, because the ghosts in this game will catch you every time. You will absolutely need to unlearn that to do any good at this game.  The fruit progression is not even correct, even among the paltry 5 fruits they included in the game, causing me to instinctually overvalue some fruits and undervalue others.
I'm a little under halfway through the grind to max out all power-ups (at 9h), and frankly, I'm not sure I'll find the motivation to continue to completion.  This seemed like it might be a good 100%'er, but that hope is fading fast.
If you want a good, modern Pac-Man game, get CEDX+.  If you already have CEDX+, play it some more.  It's more exciting, more authentic to the original, and just MORE in general than this game is.  I'm not saying that this game NEEDED to be just as good as CEDX+, but it certainly could learn a couple of things from CEDX+ in order to actually be good.

A few words: Jolly good fun!!!
Where to start??? A lot of choices, a lot of characters, a cool (if kinda campy) espionage story, what's not to like???
The way they handle choices is very brilliant. It's up to you whether you want to be a suave spy a la James bond or cold combat pragmatist a la Jason Bourne who punch the hell out of anyone dare to deter you from your objective. Choices matter. Some characters may like you, some may hate you. But what I like it isn't about good or bad choices. All choices have its own advantages and disadvantages. By threatening some informant you may get discount on weapons but he will alert the local government, blackmailing a local triad boss may get you a large sums of money but you lost his support, etc. There're also a lot of small details, such as dialog change based on where you start your mission first. Love this small care to details.
There are also a lot of characters, some of them become your handler (your mission intel guy) and give you passive bonus, such as lowering the chance for your enemy to detect you or increasing your endurance. Sadly most of the time you'll be guided by Mina (your default handler) with few option to change handler in several missions. The problem with a lot of character is most of the character aren't really fleshed out. Some of them are really interesting but their story end up abruptly without closure about who's this guy really is or who the hell they work for, etc. Such a shame, really.
And the story!!! Hell yeah it's your typical espionage story, about deception, betrayal, and controversial topic. What's make this game special is the way the story handled. A lot of your choices will affect the story. The story is immensely branching, many of your choices will create a completely different way the even unfolds and how the game will end. It's up to you whether you want to play a game about revenge, about patriotic spirit, or maybe you can gain something from all the conflicts? Who knows, eh? So what are you waiting for??? Play this game!!!

The game has some beautiful level aesthetics and monster designs, which is almost a shame, because everything about the actual gameplay is so bad that these great assets are just wasted.
Even on normal difficulty, you'll find yourself running out of ammo for not just your favorite weapon, but for all half dozen separate weapons extremely frequently - including secondary ammo!  You are simply not given enough bullets to work with, turning what should be tense or exciting fights against dozens of enemies into pure frustration as you run around looking for what few ammo pickups have been hidden across the large expanses.
While being forced to make the best of it with your infinite ammo starter weapon, you'll have to slog your way through countless bullet spongey enemies, many of which spawn adjacent to you, teleport or use incredibly hard to see projectiles.  Unfortunately, your character, who seems defined primarily by his ability to recycle the same three or four unpleasantly dull one liners throughout the whole game, is not nearly tanky enough to deal with these battles very well.
Finally, even the weapons are merely recycled clones of Painkiller Black's arsenal, making them not so much new as modded.
The not too shabby presentation of this game is let down by almost everything else about it, but especially by the total lack of respect for the player given in the design of enemy encounters.  Mixing and matching the strict ammo rationing of a Silent Hill game with the relentless hordes of a Serious Sam makes for a poor FPS experience, whether you're oldschool or new school.

Better than the first game definitely, this game continues last games story (which I highly recommend) but features a longer seeming story (which is nice). Combat will come naturally to veterans but might need some practice if you're new to this series. The story has some awesome twists and and secrets (some mind nukes are dropped), though the effect will be most acute for previous players. Overall I'd say this game is a good 9/10 in my book, perhaps a little expensive for those without income but well worth the investment if you enjoyed the last game. This game also features a survival mode which was a bit more dissapointing for me but is still engaging for people who loved the combat side of this game. It features a combat challenge with time limits and ever more difficult battles. It's effectively a minigame to measure how hardcore your skills are with this combat system.
Clan Improvements in BannerSaga 2:
Foraging: Villagers now forage food, if you balance fighters with clansmen just right you'll never starve.
Training challenges: The camp now gives you challenges to complete (ex: kill the spear men but only with specific attacks) which you can be rewarded for completeing.
Conscription: You can turn clansmen into soldiers! Soldiers wont forage well and eat more food, but will even the odds in war. This effect is not reversable.
Suggestions for the future of Banner Saga:
I'd personally love a scenario/sandbox mode (possibly multiplayer) where you survive as a clan that you make feeding your soldiers, training people, dealing with randomized events, and facing ever growing assaults by dredge. I understand this would be difficult but if combined with the steam modmaking community players could create some EPIC user generated settings and plots. Such a scenario mode (perhaps with some scenario creation tools) could create really interesting fan stories.
Alternatively a charachter creation tool would also be interesting if it could be implimented, so players can put themselves in the story with individual charchter designes. This suggestion I'd argue is the easier of my two suggestions to impliment in future Banner Saga games and would still create further player engagement.

(I'm going to assume that you know what Pac Man is. If not, watch a Youtube video or something! Pac Man is undeniably one of the most important and iconic video games in history.)
Pac Man 256 is a very well done, procedurally generated, dot eating maze game. The level scrolls infinititely upward, and the entire time you are chased by a slow-moving kill wall that forces your continuous ascent.
Unlike the old Pac Man games, the objective isn't to eat ALL the dots you see... There's simply not enough time to do that, and you'll get killed pretty quickly. Rather, you now simply have to eat as many dots (and classic power pellets) as you can as you keep going up, all while avoiding ghosts and collecting fruit (which are now multipliers) along the way.
In addition to the standard dots/ghosts/fruit, there are powerups and coins scattered throughout the maze. Collecting a powerup gives Pac Man a temporary power, such as the ability to slow ghosts down, or kill them from a distance in various ways. The coins serve as an ingame currency, which you can use to permanently upgrade your powerups between games. Powerups are unlocked simply by eating dots over your career, and you're allowed to pick 3 of them at a time to randomly appear throughout the maze. I've only unlocked a few of the powerups so far, but they all seem to work well with the game, and it's been fun to see what new power the game will throw at me next.
Just like the Championship Edition, this game is a great modern take on a classic game. It's sleek, it's polished, and it gets frenetic. It changes enough to be a new and exciting experience, but it still retains the classic features and basic gameplay that make it distinctly Pac Man. There's still that age old arcade-y drive to play again and beat your high score, while the progression system and powerup leveling mean that even short bursts of this game are enjoyable.
On top of that, this game is super cheap, even at regular price. Highly recommended.

8BitBoy a game made for those people who fell in love with super Mario in their prepubescent years. With its art style and sound bites, taken directly from the aforementioned super Mario, it does just that, it taps into the child that is still in there somewhere.
Graphics - Simplistic and beautiful, stays true to the grandfathers of its genre, without striving too far from its roots, but still trying some new elements. If you love the old 8 bit feeling of games, then you will love this. 8/10
Music - Wide variety, from the intro screen to the point where you are playing, it keeps the old feeling. 8/10
Cinematics - None
Story - You are brought into the game that you were playing, to finish what you started, but this time on the other side of things. A pretty simplistic idea, but well executed. 7/10
Content - Enormous, 5 whole worlds with 10 levels each, the level of toughness goes up all the time, but not like from a 1 to 10, little by little, but you can feel it surely. Whole range of powers, each has its own time and place to be used. The only minus here is that there is no permadeath, when you run out of lives (and you will, at least the first time playing it), you just click restart, and you begin again from the start. That really takes away from the old feeling you guys were striving for, you don't need to have for the main game, but have it for example an optional tab, where you can turn it on.
8/10
Controls - 4-5 buttons used through the whole games. Nothing too hard-core to remember. *Bonus Note* Be wary when you use Shift. 6/10
Gameplay - Well paced, the rate of when newer and newer elements are being introduced is well paced. Furthermore, do not expect that if you can pass 1 level from 1'st world that you are going to pass them all with such ease. 8/10
To wrap things up, 8Bit Boy is a really well made game which keeps to its roots, better than most of its genre. There are some points in the game where it is just unfair, but that is the point, it is supposed to be hard. It is made from some pretty passionate people, who made a game from their deep love for the old-school.
Final Score: 7.5/10

Pre-refund review, please take with a grain of salt.
Graphics-wise, it feels completely unfinished.
- Lots of blurriness or flat out ugly textures (even at 4600x1600 res).
- Recurring visual glitches, such as a massive shadow on the ground approaching you when switching from overcast to clear day (and it swung back and forth between the two 4-5 times).
- Car parked in garage before a cutscene got fused into the ground, turning it into scrap metal.
- Sunlight bloom (or, well, not proper bloom, just a huge bright spot) clips through all objects, literally couldn't see the road in front of me because of it despite that it cut through a wall and a tree.
- Graphics options are lacking, cant even turn off AA.
Gameplay-wise, your painfully average console game mechanics all the way.
- AI is typical, either stands and just shoots or runs to cover and peeks out to easily be killed, nothing worth mentioning.
- Difficulty level doesn't mean much, since you're never pushed up on by the AI it's just a matter of hiding and waiting for the goddamn health regen.
- One-button takedowns all the way, because apparently it's all about showing off animations rather than trying.
- Melee is pretty much just running up and spamming one button.
- Stealth is about as unimaginative as usual. Sneak up, takedown. Sneak up, whistle, takedown. Yawn.
- Good point is that the enemies at least don't take 30 bullets each to kill. So at hard difficulty you can at least pretend that it's somewhat realistic.
- Driving physics are fairly good at simulation mode. Crashing still seems to have no effect, with the other car often being pushed aside while you keep on driving like nothing happened.
- Cops are surprisingly effective, they managed to pop two tyres and ram me into a river, nice stuff. Stopped chasing the moment I started swimming though, so meh.
None of this touches on the storyline, which I reckon is the game's strong point, because with max 2 hours I wanted to test as much as possible before 'playing for real' the next time around. However, there seems to be extremely few moral choices, so it appears that we're just along for the ride.

I absolutely loved this game!  The storyline is intriguing and the gameplay is wonderful.  I also really liked the design of the characters and the animations - it reminded me a lot of Mark of the Ninja (surprise surprise)
I only played the beginner level and that was pretty challenging!  I very quickly learnt that patience was key, and sprinting everywhere was not a good idea!  I've ended up with 10 guards in one room and a couple of my guys just hiding behind a bed before because of this - that was bad planning!
This is a turn based game where you'll have 1-4 agents in the field.  Each agent gets a number of actions (starting off with something like 8 but can be more depending on upgrades) which you can use to move, hack, knock out etc
Simply knocking out the enemy can be fairly limited (they wake up after a number of turns or raise the alarm if killed) meaning that this game is very reliant on actually sneaking around guards as opposed to being able to knock everyone out on the way.  This makes the game way more challenging and fun.
You can observe guards though which enables you to see where they are heading, and this allows you to plan out your next move accordingly.
You can find new agents, upgrade their stats, install cybernetic implants, buy items for them to use, upgrade incognito (the system that lets you hack into other devices)
You can hack into their system to take down cameras, turrets, lasers, you can even hack into their robots and control them for a little while!
The moment I picked up this game I was addicted and I had to keep playing.  I would definitely recommend anyone to pick this up if you like stealth and strategy.

This is the best game on Steam I have ever encountered.
It was given to me as a gift and I can honestly say that I have always wanted to be a mountain. Experiencing the weather, the atmospheric pressure, the random items falling on me and getting stuck in my earthy complexion... it's just all so great. I just adore the structure of the game and the simplicity of it. There's so much you can do yet it's all so easy to get around! I love the feeling when it's raining and the clouds rushing through my grassy top. It just makes you feel so free as you're rotating on your very own axis. The scenery is breathtaking. I just love the random objects that fall and make their home on my mountainside. I feel like we're all a family and we get closer every day. The occasional rainbows are very intriguing and awesome to witness. I love the warm and fuzzy feeling I get in my soil after it rains and the sun comes out, it's just such a unique feeling. The snow brings many challenges but it's also very beautiful. When it's snowing, I have trouble breathing, on account of the snow covering every inch of me. But after... when the sun comes back out and greets me... I just get this rush of an icy-hot sensation as the snow melts. I feel rejuvenated! I feel fresh and clean. Overall, this game is the best I've experienced in my entire 8 years of being on Steam.

I really enjoyed Invisible Inc. It is an interesting turn-based stealth game where you must infiltrate buildings, fulfill varying objectives, and escape. I preferred a mostly stealth strategy: knocking people out and only using lethal force when necessary; but there are definitely many different ways to complete levels. What stood out to me the most, was the double-layered sneaking and hacking system. You have to balance advancing with your agents and hacking the cameras, barriers, and robots guarding the path.
The story was average in my opinion, but the procedurally generated gameplay was very enjoyable and holds plenty of replay value.

Many other people have already reviewed this game, much better than I could ever hope to. I just want to add a very simple "thumbs up" and recommendation here as well. It does not quite live up to SEASON ONE, but not many games will. My rating for THE WALKING DEAD: SEASON TWO: 9 out of 10.

Very cool tactics strategy game with tons of style. The art direction is really, really on point...the character designs are soooo good. I want to see Genndy Tartakovsky turn this into a series for Adult Swim. As for the gameplay itself, it reminded me a lot of Commandos, XCOM, and other PC strategy games from the 90s, with an extra dash of polish and flavor. It's pretty difficult at times and can be kind of maddening, especially in those stages where you have to find one specific item. The only problem is that things can get a little repetitive. There aren't many mission types, so you end up doing the same thing over and over. You'll get bored kind of quickly. I hope that you like shutting down security cams and knocking out guards, because that's going to happen a lot. The Contingency Plan DLC adds in some twists and a few new agents, but it doesn't drastically change things.
Despite the game's repetitive nature, I'm still going to recommend it. The core gameplay is just classic, and it brought back great memories of gaming in the 90s. The art style is fantastic and it's really nice to look at (the cinemas are also excellent, and the voice acting is flawless). Just realize that it gets repetitive pretty quickly and is also kind of short for the price. Buy it on sale and you'll be happy. I picked this up last Black Friday for 10 bucks, the DLC included, and that seemed fair to me.

So WB Games did their best to put me off with a tiered release, pre-order bonuses and sodding microtransactions in a single player game. It’s hard to overlook and I wouldn’t blame anyone for boycotting the title, although it would be a shame in my opinion, especially if you enjoyed the first. Check out my in depth first impressions video for my thoughts on the game and those loot boxes.
Shadow of War does what a good sequel should do, by fixing the things that didn’t work and improving on those that did. One of my biggest issues with Shadow of Mordor was in the lacklustre environments and SoW improves this no end by creating more interesting and varied locations to run, climb, jump and stab in. The wonderful nemesis system has also been enhanced with the orcs given more character and variation in abilities, making fighting them even more fun. There are also a number of scripted orcs and the new conquest system which is fun and adds more depth.
There are a few problems other than the loot boxes, one being the usual map full of side missions that can start to grate (an arkham-creed staple) and another being the surprisingly narrow fov that can make fighting in close quarters difficult. I’m also not too enamoured with the two ‘token’ good characters but the story is entertaining enough and other than that it’s just nit-picks. I’m not at the end game yet so have no idea if the rumours of grind are true, but I wouldn’t be surprised because so far I have had no compulsion to purchase a loot box.

The game has some beautiful level aesthetics and monster designs, which is almost a shame, because everything about the actual gameplay is so bad that these great assets are just wasted.
Even on normal difficulty, you'll find yourself running out of ammo for not just your favorite weapon, but for all half dozen separate weapons extremely frequently - including secondary ammo!  You are simply not given enough bullets to work with, turning what should be tense or exciting fights against dozens of enemies into pure frustration as you run around looking for what few ammo pickups have been hidden across the large expanses.
While being forced to make the best of it with your infinite ammo starter weapon, you'll have to slog your way through countless bullet spongey enemies, many of which spawn adjacent to you, teleport or use incredibly hard to see projectiles.  Unfortunately, your character, who seems defined primarily by his ability to recycle the same three or four unpleasantly dull one liners throughout the whole game, is not nearly tanky enough to deal with these battles very well.
Finally, even the weapons are merely recycled clones of Painkiller Black's arsenal, making them not so much new as modded.
The not too shabby presentation of this game is let down by almost everything else about it, but especially by the total lack of respect for the player given in the design of enemy encounters.  Mixing and matching the strict ammo rationing of a Silent Hill game with the relentless hordes of a Serious Sam makes for a poor FPS experience, whether you're oldschool or new school.

I went in expecting little and was not surprised.
Gameplay:  One-sided.  Humans are often spawn-camped because the dinosaurs can 3-shot you.  The only class worth half a breath is the recon, where you can use stealth to confuse your enemy.  Otherwise, consider the dino's kits (8 or more classes compared to 3) more useful.  Though, you can count on the dinosaurs to handle like a tennis ball coated in Elmer's glue.  Even the raptors turn like a buick.  Also, no built-in auto-balancing for teams.  It would make sense if, say, 5 humans vs 3 dinos, but there's no regulator.
Interface:  Okay, I guess.  Everything can be found somewhere.  Not amazing, not terrible.  Works, though.  But it should... it's technically a "release"... right?
Graphics & Sound:  I read somewhere on another review that the guns sounded like shrill shreeky something somethings.  Yeah, they're kind of obnoxious.  I had "hit marker" sounds turned on and I couldn't even tell when they were going off.  Really felt kind of low-grade from the sound quality.  Graphics?  Nothing to shake a stick at.  Environment is "arena-esque", but plenty of foliage.  Sprinting "depth of field" is horribly proportioned. and overall, smaller things can get lost in the background "haze".
Multiplayer:  Imbalanced, clunky, and unpolished.  Lack of damage feedback or immediate training/descriptions left me more to explore and see how horribly ineffective anything was, rather than go in with at least a baseline understanding of strengths/weaknesses.
Stability:  Yeah, servers are crashing randomly (don't know if it just means the host left or something) and I tried to play solo play and immediately crashed.  I decided at that point that it wasn't worth my time.
[[Would not recommend.]]  May be worth looking back at when it gets patched a few times, but I don't believe in supporting game companies that ask their player base for a high amount of coping with shortcomings at release and then making up for it later.  There's no need to play with an emotional investment as well as a financial one.

Nuclear throne is one of those games where you WILL have a love/hate relationship.
Love it for its characters, setting, fantastic soundtrack, bosses and butt-ton of weapons,
and hate it for its brutal difficulty and the occasional area where good runs go to die (im looking at you crystal caves).
So, lets get into it shall we?
Nuclear throne is a roguelike shooter set in a post-apocalyptic world filled with mutants, freaks and everything inbetween. You play as a rhag-tag band of mutants, all filled with character and personality. These mutants dream of placing their mutant butts on the nuclear throne, a myth thats believed by these guys. These mutants are special, because as soon as they die, they get teleported back by these mystical portals popping up across the wasteland.
The story is simple, you choose a mutant, and you travel across the many lands filled with a variety of freaks, bandits and  floating ♥♥♥♥ing crystals. In every main area (Badlands, scrapyard Etc) you'll encounter a boss that you must slay in order to go to the sub areas (Not the official name, but something I call them). These are areas that are inbetween the ordinary, 3 level areas. These are 1 level areas that are completely different in setting to other areas and hold special enemies and loot.
After doing all of this (Trust me, its a long task) and doing specific things related to things I cant say due to spoilers, you can loop. This means going aaaaaall the way back to the start, but this time its harder, much, much harder. The enemies are tougher and theres a whole new cast of bosses to slay, each one harder than the last. The loot is better, but the risk is bigger.
The way collectibles go, there are B-skins for every playable mutant, unlockable by doing specific things, some hard, some are very easy. There are also crowns to unlock through playing, this is essentially run modifiers that you can aquire mid way through the run or at the beginning. They add an extra challenge for the seasoned veteran. There are also golden guns that replace some of the original guns. These special versions are found in a certain area(s) and increase certain stats of the weapon or doing specific things. Also, it shines ingame and can replace the starting pistol if you finish the area its found in.
The soundtrack is one of the best ive heard ever. And ive played quite a few games in my time. Each boss has its own song to go in the backround and each area has its own song too. Its so good that I listen to the songs in my spare time.
So, to break it down, heres a simpler form of what I just said for the challenged reader:
Pros:
Fantastic sountrack
Vibrant characters (That talk in their own made up language)
Simple yet enjoyable story
interesting lore (read that♥♥♥♥♥♥ its brilliant)
colourful and marvelously designed areas
beautiful character and enemy design
A lot of variety in enemy types and looks
Bosses are amazing yet challenging if not prepared
Brutally hard- Keeps you on your toes at all times, even if you are just fighting a few bandits
Artwork is brilliant
Devs that listen to the community and are gamers themselves
Cons:
Some areas are more unbalanced than others (Crystal caves again...)
Bugs are uncommon, but come in small sizes
Often times you wonder "What the hell just killed me"
Thank you for reading, this game is my favorite roguelike, and I love it, even though my hours say otherwise.
Would I reccommend this game? Without a doubt. Are there things that could be improved? Of course, but every game is like that. Its 8.99 for endless fun, anger and stupidity with the amount of loot, weapons and collectables to be collected.
Thank you again for reading.

Alpha Protocol is a game that I really wanted to like. I tried to look past the flaws that this game had, but I honestly couldn't. The best thing I can say about Alpha Protocol is that it at least tried to be something different, but even if you try to do something different, it doesn't mean that it will always be good.
Alpha Protocol has a unique concept, an espionage RPG. I was surprised to see that this sort of idea, hadn't been done that often in gaming and that is one thing that I respect this game for doing. The main problem with this however is that in my opinion, Alpha Protocol doesn't really use any of the unique ideas it brings to the table that well and the basic stuff that are required to make a good game (like gameplay, playability and graphics) aren't really focused on as they put most of their thought, time and care into trying to implement these ideas to try and live up to it's name "an espionage RPG."
One of the biggest problems Alpha Protocol has is in it's gameplay. Nearly everything in the gameplay falls flat. While the training section at the beginning of the game, does show off some great ideas for an espionage RPG like sneaking mechanics, combat and gadgets, I didn't feel like I was having any fun playing this or doing any of these ideas for gameplay because in the end, that's what I was thinking they were, just some ideas. I felt like these ideas were only half executed. The ideas are there, but they just stopped after that. Sneaking is basically useless because the AI is really bad. Gun combat feels restricted an the sensitivity never feels right no matter what you set it to. Melee combat, while it's better than gun combat, feels slippery for the majority of the time, but at least it was more controllable than the gun Gadgets are basically useless in combat because you can't really tell where they'll land. There's no targeting ridicule for them so you just need to predict where they'll land.
Graphics are for the most part good however there are several flaws with them. There is quite a lot of slow loading textures from time to time and the longer I played, the more frequently these occurred. There is also a bit of pop in going on quite a bit. Apart from that there isn't much to say about the graphics. They're decent but they could have gotten more polish before release like the rest of the game.
The sound seemed to repeatedly cutting out randomly for some reason throughout my play time as well. However, this didn't affect my overall feeling towards the game in any way and I easily ignored it as it wasn't too big of a deal.
In this review, it might come off like I hate Alpha Protocol and even though that's true, there's still some good ideas that are put into Alpha Protocol, which might have been good if they developed these ideas further. The stuff that is common to see and expect in an RPG is present in Alpha Protocol but these things we have seen done a bunch of times are exactly that. Alpha Protocol does nothing to change the styles that are common in RPGs except for the dialogue options, which is one of the best I've seen.
Overall, Alpha Protocol is buggy and generic. It barely does anything to stand out from the crowd and when it tries to do this, it usually falls flat. However, it still uses some ideas which I hope to see in RPGs in a future and if the developers of this game were to make a sequel, maybe tweaking the game a bit, I would definitely buy the sequel to see if these ideas are developed more.
Pros
+ Some good ideas
+ Great concept
+ Good mechanics
+ OK graphics
Cons
- Underdeveloped ideas
- Terrible AI
- Restricted/slippery combat
- Slow loading textures
Final verdict: 3/10

After playing Broken Age for ten hours (finished two times) I can easily say that Act 1 is a masterpiece of art.
The game sets new standards for the visual presentation of adventure games. There are animations all over the screen, like tons of birds in the cloud colony. The cutscenes look fantastic and the overall musical score is monumental.
All supported by brilliant voice acting done by e.g. Jennifer Hale, Eliah Wood and Jack Black.
The two stories (Vella & Shay) seem to stand for themselves but lead to a masterfully written and stunning cliffhanger; keep in mind: Act II will be for free later this year.
The puzzles in Act 1 are pretty easy, though Tim Schafer (designer and writer of the game) already stated Act II will be harder. This reminds me a lot of Full Throttle (another Tim Schafer game) where the first half was also not very hard to master, but the second became a great challange.
I hope Double Fine can live up to the promise, because we would have a great balanced finished game in the end.
But as far as I can tell this is the best piece of adventure I have seen in a long time so far. The loveable, weird characters and the very interesting story of two teenagers trying to grow out of their surroundings make this a special treat for me.
This is (will be) a game that not everyone will be into; It's like it is with all art after all. But if you love a good story being told, well...

Pacman 256 is an endless arcade maze game.
+ Very polished
+ Very addicting
+ Calm sound design
+ Many interesting power ups
+ Many themes
The first thing you will notice is that this is not the original Pacman. The game is a endless maze where you must avoid ghosts and the glitch tsunami. Interestingly the glitch tsunami is based on the original Pacman map 256 glitch: the screen gets split into two with the right side turning into a soup of numbers and letters. It's impossible to beat and occurs due to the level number being stored as an 8-bit number, meaning the highest number it can store is 255 (2^8 - 1 = 255). It's also the origin of this game name. Being an arcade game the objective is to reach the maximum score. To get points you eat pellets, fruits or kill ghosts when you get power ups
There about 18 power ups available but you must unlock the power ups with points and you can only choose which three will be guaranteed to show up in each game. A random power up may show up from time to time a 256 glitch, which is usually the power up you're unlocking next. There's also the standard power pill that turns the ghosts blue so you can eat them which shows up in every game. Some examples are giant, fire, lava, laser, magnet and so on. As you progress the power ups get more interesting. You can also level up your power ups with the virtual currency you get in the game which will usually increase the duration of the power up.
This game is very polished. I didn't find any bug or complication whatsover. It's an easy enough game to just start playing. There's a lot of attention to detail. For example the game tells you how many pellets you ate non stop both with a small non distracting number on the side of pacman and with a faster eating sound the more pellets you get. You also get a score for that particular feat. You also have a very useful bar on top of the screen that tells you how long until your power up ends. You also have missions in each game to help you get currency to level up your power ups and keep you interested. The current mission shows up at the start of each level.
The color of the ghosts tell you which way they'll try to get you. Blue ghosts will just circle around, the orange ghosts just randomly travel through the maze, pink ghosts will ram against if he detects you, the black ghosts are sleeping until you get close and follow until you get far enough for the ghost go to sleep again and the red ghosts will follow you indefinitely. There are also lines of ghosts. The green line just goes from one side to the other and the purple ghosts follow which side you're on. You need to know these patterns to get an high score.
There are many themes in this game. You can choose one for every game and that's fine if you want to be used to one particular theme but I find it more interesting to just let the game chose one randomly each game. The colors and icons were designed so that you understand what's going on even if you have random themes.
Overall this is a very addicting and easy to play game, just like early arcade games, with a touch of modern games. If you like arcade games this one is definitely a keeper.

Just to get it out of the way:
Yes, this is not the best PC port a game has ever seen.
And yes, the game doesn't currently run above 60fps, no matter what rig you have.
Be aware that Hangar13 has already confirmed that there will be a patch in the next few days that will add pc options and improve the framerate. So if you do consider this a major issue, don't buy the game yet.
However I can at least currently say that the game runs solidly at 30fps without any major issues, besides a bit of texture glitching and one crash that I encountered so far. For those who are interested I run this game with a custom 1070, i5 6600k and 16GB RAM.
Also it has to be said - if it is not obvious - that Mafia 3 doesn't share the same production values a GTA game or a Ubisoft open world game like Watch Dogs have. It's just not as polished, especially concerning character animation and AI routines.
What is very strong in this game however are the gunplay, the narrative and the late 60's atmosphere.
If the trailers for the game interested you, it's probably still a must buy.
I'll update the review once I have played more and the pc patch has been published.

It's a semi-sentient mountain, of which you are mreely an observer. It's pretty much a digital pet rock that asks psuedo-philosophical questions about it's exsistence, and comments on it's current mood, based on the time of day, season, and / or weather.
Sure, it starts with "You Are God. You Are The Mountain". But that's not correct, not really. At least, not to me. But that's not a bad thing, either.
IF you go into this, looking at it as an art piece that is designed to run forever in the background (on my second monitor wilst I'm not actively using it to scoop up deals on Steam) - and you realise that there are no "controls" in this game, then what is there to complain about? It's exactly what it says it is on the tin: you know what you are getting, so WHY are you complaining?
The play through begins with it suggesting some themes, and asking you to draw something based on those emotive words. I gather it uses these couple of sketches for it's World generation. Then, the Mountain is 'born', populated with tress, and set spinning for you to watch it.
You can move the camera with the mouse, controls most gamers / CAD designers already find instinctive; (click + drag to rotate in any direction, Mouse scroll to zoom). you can play Music to your mountain, using A-through-K and Z-through-< {less than} to represent notes on a piano. I believe playing melodies speeds up time, and I actually think my mountain sang back to me once "beeboobeebupboop".
When the Mountain has something to say, He'll chime at you, then type it out across the top of his screen.
as previously mentioned, It uses sketches that you provide to generate your mountain.There is a full gamut of weather here, sun, rain, storms, fog. I haven't seen tornados or the like yet. There is also Seasonal differences... You mountain gets covered in snow, trees lose their leaves in autumn. An entire year cycle seems only to take a few minutes, and days are no more than 1 minute, so you get a wide variety of things going on very quickly.
Trees, I've observed 3 distinct types thus far. They grow and die. New ones seed and sprout. I like that as a feature. There are some little touches, too - like evergreens don't lose their leaves, and thus get a full covering of snow.
Things spawn periodically, and crash into your mountain, becoming part of it's landscape. Party hats, Electric fans, Dice, and I have no idea what else yet. My first item spawned inside 5 minutes though. This mechanic provides some variety to what would otherwise be a very serene experience.
The only kind of Fauna I have seen so far is fireflies... merely a flickering light near the trees, at night, during summer.
Clouds. wow, they look great, they really do... now get them out of my way so I can see my mountain! The other thing I don't really like is your zoom options. Zoom out too far and everything gets hazy, like looking through a mist or fog at something from a distance... which youy are... but you lose a part of the joy, I feel, that could e had by observing your Mountain from afar. Also, I'd like to be able to Zoom In more. I'd love to get up and close with those mushrooms.
I don't normally mention this, but I will this time, as I think it's relevant, for a 'game' that's supposed to sit on your desktop for most of it's life. It's idling at 250mb RAM (this is fine) and 65% of my CPU. That's more than BIOSHOCK INFINITE Stressed my computer. This interested me enough for me to install it on my old game rig, and when the game puts Mountain in the rain, it lags. (1gb ddr3 gpx card... I said 'old'). This doesn't bother me, unless I'm planning on running a few of my VM's at once, or want to play a game fullscreen (Mountain will let you run another game next to it, unlike most Steam games So in this respect it's more like a tool than a game).
I'd really love to see fauna here - I'd prefer it to random Traffic-cone-Asteroids making my pristine Mountain look like someone tipped out a public rubbish bin all over my lawn****. I'd love to see animals, with varied animations - feeding, grazing, grooming, wandering.... The young getting old and dying? It would be awesome if you could folllow one around and watch it's lifespan over a few minutes, or maybe as much as an hour. This, plus the improved Zoom functionality I mentioned would make this game... better. The Author wants you to connect with Mountain, I think. He wants you to feel that you ARE the mountain. having some kind of life to observe in the game would certainly help with that. I'm thinking fairly in depth, too. I'd love to be able to see opossoms in the trees, deer on the slopes, bears coming out of hibernation... "and fish in the stream"... hint hint. (Author; you would need a stream!)
Buy it if you want something to take your attention every few minutes, so you can see how it's changed. That's its' beauty - an ever-changing semi-interactive painting on your desktop.
Don't buy it if you want something to grab your attention and hold you for hours. - And don't drop bad reviews on something just because it's exactly what it claims to be!

This game offers a very similar experience to the Slither.io in many respects. However, I am not going to rate it down based upon its obvious similarities to Slither. Many of the negative reviews I’ve seen rate the game poorly, simply based upon its similarity to Slither. This logic is frankly, cofounding. Yes, Worm.Is is practically a clone of Slither, however invitation to a good idea is not a reason to belittle it. Under that logic, you should never say or think anything that has been said or thought by anyone else before you, or you’re copying them.
To degrade a game, based upon the logic, “It looks like something I have seen before,” without offering any actual solid reasons for why you did or did not enjoy the game itself, is well, confounding and small minded. Think, form ideas, conceptualize. Is the game a rip off, yes, does that make it bad, absolutely not. Almost everything is a rip off of something else. “Good artists copy. Great artists steal.”
That being said, I don’t mind that the game is obviously a rip off. The game incorporates different ideas and greater complexity, allowing for many features not currently available in Slither.io. Some of these features include, team battles, the ability to add and play with your friends, actual objectives which make the game feel meaningful, purchasable skins via collection of in game currency, many more game modes and an overall improved complexity. I have played Slither, and personally enjoy the features that this game offers over that of Slither in its current state. It simply has more to offer.
Some of the cons are: The detection hit boxes are very wanky and at times unpredictable, the graphics style could use some improvement, there are still many optimization issues with lag, changes need to be made to the inviting players system, the maps could use increased complexity, as well as many other bugs and glitches that those of you who play are certainly aware of.
Overall, it's an enjoyable experience, and it's free...If you don't like it, then don't play it.

I tried to like this game, I really did. While my friends were calling it garbage, I defended it. The truth is, however, that they were right. I never played Dino Beatdown, and I didn't bother with the Metacritic score; going off of some brief gameplay videos I figured that while the animations looked clunky it could at least be one of those games that is fun to play with friends. Those videos don't quite prepare you for Dino Horde, and I can safely say that even at the price of $1.00, I would not recommend buying this game.
The animations are bad, and in fact very laughable. Running looks like you've got a stick up your♥♥♥♥♥and when you're in first person in a car you can often watch in horror as your weapons wiggle around. However, these animations are typically situational - no, most of what you'll see of the animaiton quality is in the dinosaurs themselves who often come off as cartoonish, rigid or downright broken in their movements.
The gunplay is very unsatisfying. Everything kind of just haphazardly squirts blood when you shoot them. You'd expect such a loud game to at least have some great, satisfying sounds to accompany each shot, but they don't. Every enemy is a bullet sponge and each weapon is unpleasant to use.
However, the most frustrating failings of Dino Horde is in the fact that when buying upgrades in Survival, dying will cause you to lose them. Additionally, despite boasting a large number of game modes, many are just not fun. The worst was where you're forced to play Support and just stand around as raptors spawn out of the air on top of you, trying to last as long as possible.
The only positive points I can truthfully give this game was that the vehicles were at first very fun and interesting. If you're forced or tempted to play this game, jump into a vehicle as soon as possible. The only difficulty you'll really find with vehicles is how their tires are somehow incapable of running over small dinosaurs. However, even they were not enough to save Dino Horde for me. I will not be reinstalling this. If you want a dinosaur game get Natural Selection 2 or Primal Carnage, a lot of ORION's assets were ripped off from those games, anyways.

If you're looking for a challenging, fast paced old school FPS with cool weapons, tonnes of enemies to kill and a great art design, Painkiller Overdose is the game for you. There are lots of collectables to find along the way, rewarding players for exploring the maps. This keeps the pacing of the gameplay steady and allows you to take a few deep breaths after murdering countless demons and trust me, you'll need to. Enemy ai isn't the best but they will team up to ko you. Some enemies have tricks up their sleeve to be careful of. Plus there are many environmental hazards to look out for such as lava, swinging maces etc. There are also tarot cards to collect which give you special powers when activated once per level. These cards are permenant and you can unlock them by satisfying certain conditions at the end of a level. The weapons are cooler than ever, you will get some really creative ones to try as well as your conventional shotgun. Levels are well designed and have lots of hidden ammo/secrets and tonnes of enemies to kill.
Another thing to note is that the protagonist, Belial who just happeneds to be a demon/angel hybrid is a far more entertaining character than Daniel and has the tendancy to deliver one liners every now and again, particularly after consuming his favourite food, evil souls and he makes this very clear.
The only downsides are the framerate drop which often occurs when enemies spawn into the map. This can be annoying and can break you away from the action sometimes. Plus the enemy ai can be pretty stupid when it comes to pathing, something you'll find in most painkiller titles, enemies will lose track of you easily. Also be careful with your saves. always delete the ones you don't need as the game has the tendancy to corrupt data and crash the game when too many sames are accumilated. One level in particular, Animal Farm has an awful save glitch which can corrupt data randomly on that level, basically you're required to beat it all in one sitting with no deaths as i guarrentee 80% of the time, the checkpoint autosaves will get corrupted, if you want to get the tarot card on that level, i strongly reccommend playing it on daydream to save yourself the frustration of dying and having to return to the beginning of the level.
Other than that, this game is worth picking up if you are looking for a cheap old school shooter with a twist. Pick up the black edition too.

Since I grew up with 8-bit NES, I am a big fan of retro 2D platforms.
However, I'm starting to leave negative reviews for the games that fail to properly emulate the old style masterpieces.
One of such games is "8BitBoy". There is simply one reason why I'm leaving a negative review; the game would be perfectly done except for one thing: the threshold between "challenging" and "frustrating".
In few words (and IMHO) a good game ceases to be challenging when it becomes repetitive; it's ok to die several times and having to get back and repeat the stage from some checkpoint, but this game has no such thing and the lives count is useless; wheather you die with 10 or 1 life left, you have to get back and start from the same (save) point, which is exclusively at the beginning of every stage. Games like this are made to accumulate a dozen hours of gameplay in expense of the fun. I've played 2-hours worth of gameplay titles who gave me so much enjoyment and satisfaction thus had no need to be any longer to beat.
My advice: add some more freaking save points middle stage for once, and then make the player start from the beginning of the stage once there are no lives left.
Broken age has the Heart and Art of Gaming that the rest of the industry has lost.
