It's Super Alex Kidd Brothers in Adventure Islands!
Yes, this game delivers a fairly good approximation of many classic 8-bit games in a simple to understand homage to the mascot platformers of the 80s.
What I like about this particular retro-styled game is that it borrows and blends several classic franchises, without copying any single one completely to create it's own experience. Most notably, you'll feel elements of Super Mario Bros., Alex Kidd, and Hudson's Avdenture Island show up throughout the game.
So overall, I'd say I very much appreciate the game. Here are some of the reasons why:
- The controls are pretty solid, and controller support was hassle free with an Xbox360 controller.
- Secrets and hidden stuff everywhere
- Levels are long enough to be a challenge, but not too long that they become tedious
- Music and sound effects fit very well with the 8-bit style
- Pays respect to the games of yesteryear without directly trying to clone any one single franchise
I'd reccomend this game on or off sale, but for less then a dollar during the Holiday sale, I feel I got a great deal.

I would actually say in a pinch, that it might be a little better than GTA V driving model.....its feels and handles more realistic.  And the little touches are so nice......little wheel squeals when ou pull away and stop, and the headlights even get a little brighter when sitting stationary and revving the engine....nice touch!
Someone complained about cover controls.....they are there, although a little clunky, BUT you CAN cover move around corners AND swop from cover to cover....what more do you want!
As for content and stuff to do, I've only brushed the surface so far, and haven't even left the starting neighbourhood, but its quite full from what I can see.
Yes ,the graphics are a little fuzzy and dated, but its fine really!
Ignore those saying its the next No Mans Sky, lie filled game.....it's really not!  Overall, I'm glad I pre-ordered this one....not disappointed!

Alan wake is an survival horror game. It isn't really a game it's more of an interactive movie. The gameplay parts are just tedious parts added on too call it a game, instead of the movie it wants to be. The gameplay is completely build around the mechanic that you need to shine light on enemies so you can shoot them after it. While it's a nice concept, but it get repetitive after a while. The gameplay parts are just disrupting the story. Non of your actions has any influences on the game world.
The story of the game is fine. They have set a great creepy atmosphere. Too bad they made the gameplay not scary. Your always armed to the teeth. If enemies spawn behind you they show them with a cinematic. So you are never surprised by enemies. You also find pages of a manuscript that foretells events. It's like they wanted to make a scary game, but not to scary so it would scare some players away. The scariest part of the game is probably Alan's wife. I'd like to start off by saying: I was very excited when the first game was announced, and the very same hype came back for when this game was announced.
There were some hiccups with this game though, mainly the doubt that beset most of us on the arrival of microtransactions.
However, I remained hopeful, and this is my review thus far, on 25.5 hours spent, playing on nothing but Nemesis difficulty the entire time.
The game met my expectations and then some!
Just the "tutorial" phase of the game was nice, because it was less of a tutorial and more of an entire introduction. During this introduction I got enough skill points to unlock EVERY skill available, which there are plenty of, but not that many "perks" in those skills as most of them have a high level-cap you have to exceed, which is fine.
You get a nice backstory to the beginning city, mostly non-canon for all you lore-buffs, which is kind of the theme for the entire game: This isn't canon. Nearly none of it.
It doesn't mean you can't enjoy it. Just that it means you cannot rely on much of what this story tells you.
But onto my next point, difficulty.
Difficulty has been increased exponentially from the last game. I cannot speak for the lower difficulties, but on Nemesis it was a huge struggle in the start, partly because I had lost all my "Shadow of"- skills. Then it was also because I lacked abilities in-game and also lacked gear.
In the now 25.5 hour playthrough I have, I've fixed this issue of not having abilities, and also gear. Gear isn't difficult to come by, I have slotted full legendaries with a few legendary backups. I haven't even done any microtransactions yet.
Still, the game is very hard. I often find myself depending on my bodyguard Uruk to help me deal with captains, although I can regularly solo them now, but I die a lot.
I have died in the game world at least 20 times, and in missions where death means restart and not retry, I'd estimate about 50 more deaths on top of the 20 world deaths. The game is hard, you're on your toes the entire time, you can easily fail and die to caragors if you're not careful.
Once I had died to a captain, respawned, found a captain close to my respawn tower, so I shadow striked him, he immediately did an unblockable smack for over half my health, I did a light attack, he blocked and instantly countered with another unblockable attack, I was downed and wouldn't you know it, he gave me No Chance.
Dead again, with an interval of about 30 seconds from the last death. And right there I was about level 25 so it's not exactly the opening of the game either.
Missions then. Missions are honestly better than expected. You can completely decide what missions you wanna do, and at about 90-100% completion on each questgiver branch, you gain a new skill which you cannot unlock by levelling up.
Naturally, I did all Cárnan quests because I wanted to be able to summon my own tamed Drake at will, something I'd recommend others to do as well. Missions are hard, the final quest in each branch seems to have a theme of having you face off against enemies 5-15 levels higher than you without giving you much or any aid at all.
I fail AT LEAST 5 times before succeeding.
There's about a good 8-12 quests on each branch I'll estimate, with about 6 branches, which is a good amount I'd say, and I'll come back to that in some final thoughts coming right up.
Fort assaults, quite great honestly, not nearly as cinematic as how it looked when first announced, which was to be expected, but it's really fun and very hard. At first I didn't believe them when the developers said that the assaults would be hard without any Uruks on your own, and let me tell you, I can't disprove them.
Even when I did call in 4 Uruks I still failed regularly, to the point where I typically have 2 Uruks infiltrate the city and remove layers of defense. Only then I find it manageable.
All in all, I really like this game, it was well worth the wait, it was well worth its hype. Microtransactions really aren't something you'll pay any attention to, you'll barely think about it while playing, so don't let it hinder you. I still haven't used the market, but I will sooner or later.
Game is substantial, and even with me picking all collectibles and doing full completionist run, I'd say I'm halfway through the game at my 25.5 hours. Let's compare that to the previous game, where I actually had 100% completion and 100% achievements at 23 hours, before the arrival of their DLC's.
They HAVE pumped up this game, and it feels richer and smoother than the first one. I have some issues with a few strung up prisoners animations going wrong, and sometimes some animations play without any sound, but these issues fixes themselves and aren't major problems, it's just goofy or feels strange when you start breathing fire with your drake but there's no sound of your roaring flames.
Game is huge on your harddrive as well, taking up 67 gigs for me, but it is well worth it as even though my computer is starting to be dated, this obviously must work wonders as I've never dipped below 60 FPS.
Call me a fan boy or whatever, but in my opinion this has been a 10/10 game, a huge upgrade from the previous one, so I'm a lot less salty about the albeit huge price this game demands. Play with a controller if you have one, I don't even dare trying the PC controls because it just feels like it'd be really awkward. Only problem with the controller is how inefficient you are with the bow.

Alpha Protocol combines an enthralling storyline with a functioning role playing core and the highest grade of replayability in years! + An astounding variety of ethical decisions that affect how the story unfolds

Invisible, Inc. is one of the best tactics games ever devised -- certainly the best I have ever played. This is why:
Turn-based stealth that actually works, with a number of interesting twists (hacking, character progression, a very interesting item system where each item has a tactical niche and an array of enemies, all of which have their own tactical niche as well). It's apparently very modular in how it's coded, too, meaning easy moddability, and even though there aren't an enormous number of mods (this game does have a fairly small audience compared to other Klei games) the mods that do exist are quite high-qualify, serving to enhance an already-fantastic game rather than being necessary to make the game enjoyable as can sometimes happen with games built around moddability.
In addition to the impressive campaign, which has you doing missions within a limited timeframe (which you can set in campaign generation, by the way, for a longer or shorter campaign) before a final confrontation, there is an Endless mode where difficulty will ramp up over the days just as in the campaign, except that the difficulty limit is much higher because, well, it's endless.
I also love the way in which randomness is used here. Levels are procedurally generated -- which, by extension, means that guard placements and loot are also procedurally generated. But that's about it. This game is often compared to X-COM, and there are some similarities, but the fact that there is no "chance-to-hit" is an extremely important difference. If your agent has been spotted by a guard, you need to either break line of sight (without moving the spotted agent more than 1 tile; if they move from a watched tile to another watched tile they will be shot instantly) or neutralize (stun or kill) the alerted guard. All of this is governed by tightly designed rules, rather than the dice.
Also, you can customize the difficulty settings.
This is a very big deal. All of the factors that go into determining how hard the game is, you can change them individually instead of being frustrated that "Experienced is too easy but Expert is too hard" or something. Seriously, this is a fantastic way to approach difficulty scaling and more games need to implement it.
If you like turn-based games, or stealth games, or both, give this one a try. It's an amalgam of game concepts which seems like it shouldn't work, but in fact does so beautifully. In my opinion this is the most well-designed tactics computer game ever -- it creates uncertainty through random level generation, but without the game's mechanics being subject to randomness as is the case with too many other tactics games.

Obsidian is one of the few developers who have earned my trust enough for me to be willing to buy their games without hesitating. I can't think of a game by them that ever disappointed me, but I can think of plenty that became some of my favorites, and Alpha Protocol is one of them.
In terms of the core gameplay, the game is only slightly above average. It's framed as a stealth game, but there are plenty of character options to let you play as loud or quiet as you want, or even dump all your points into Martial Arts and become a kung fu spy if you want. The AI can be a bit finnicky sometimes, and the camera mouse controls sometimes have issues, but for the most part it's functional, and fun to play. The real distinguishing factor of the game is in the dialogue, and other choices. An average playthrough may only last 10 to 15 hours or so, but it has enough replayability to easily make it worth playing several times. Everything from the order you take on missions in to the people you ally with likely has an effect on future events, and there are enough ways that events can play out differently to continue to surprise you even after 3 or 4 playthroughs. The game features a full Bond-like cast of memorable characters, each of whom have their own likes and dislikes that can influence your results throughout the game. It really puts up the illusion that this is a real world of espionage, and it's easy to find yourself invested in the character and story because of it.
The one place where the game does falter is the dialogue interface itself. The game uses a Mass Effect-style one-word-choice system, where most dialogue choices fall into three categories - Suave, Aggressive, and Professional. It's not as simplistic as it may seem, and it is somewhat necessary to shorten the lines since unlike other similar games Alpha Protocol is fairly aggressive with its timed dialogues and often may not even give you more time than it takes for a character to finish their sentence to make a decision, but it does occasionally end with you misreading the prompt's intention and leading to the main character saying something you didn't want. This ties in with the fact that the main character's voice actor isn't all that great at times, and he doesn't do a very good job of actually sounding particularly suave when you pick those options. Alpha Protocol is the one game where I don't completely hate the use of the dialogue wheel, but I still wouldn't mind it being gone.
If you're into Bond movies or just spy fiction in general, Alpha Protocol is a pretty easy pick. Almost every Obsidian game has their faults due to both publishers rushing them and Obsidian themselves not being that great at managing their time, but like most of their games the faults aren't enough to bring down what ends up being another really great RPG to add to their list.

Summary:
A somewhat middling but overall satisfying "poor man's Deus Ex," with a good balance of choice, consequence, stealth, and action.
+High replayability, provided you enjoy what's on offer to begin with
+Lots of choice with respect to what order you do missions in, and which locales you visit first
+Satisfyingly diverging consequences for those choices, as well as for dialogue options
+Decent, if superficial, catering to different playstyles
+Equally viable stealth and action
+Pacifist options, although difficult to pull off throughout the entire game
+An affinity system that really does impact which characters accompany you, and how the story plays out... how you interact is the greatest source of player agency here. Think before you speak.
+Unlockable "Veteran" mode which adds additional funny scenes, options, and choices
+Intuitive controller support (I played with a wired 360 gamepad.)
-Quite dated graphics
-The occasional non-game-breaking glitch (prompts not showing up but interaction still possible so not a disaster, a mission not advancing thus requiring reload of a very recent checkpoint which doesn't cost you much progress, etc.)
-Despite playstyle differentiation being adequete, the levels themselves are quite linear. Most do not offer multuple paths
-Reused map/level assets and even entire buildings complete with the same object placement, despite being ostensibly entirely different locations
-A few choices don't seem to be reflected in cut scenes (though to be fair, most are)
-If you don't specialize in one of two extremes, it's possible to encounter drastic difficulty spikes, especially towards the end
-Not as deep, labyrinthine, atmospheric, or polished as Deus Ex or Human Revolution, both of which it is clearly homaging
-Locking to cover is extremely hit or miss (sometimes it works, other times it looks like it should but doesn't, which can screw up an attempted stealth run or get you killed)
-Instead of full dialogue options, you choose "stances" (E.g. aggressive, suave, professional, etc.)
-No female player character
-Limited character customization
-No true New Game Plus, in a game which cries out for it in my opinion
Despite the list of cons being greater than the list of pros, I absolutely fell in love with this game. It's definitely a middle of the road kind of game, and whether you enjoy it personally will depend upon whether it clicks with you as an individual and your tastes. If it does, you may find as I did that it's far more than the sum of its parts. I'm four playthroughs deep and still enjoying it immensely.
But it's definitely flawed and lacks polish and depth in some respects. Deus Ex this ain't. Still, I recommend it. Especially for the price.

If you liked the first episode, you will love the second.
The basics of the gameplay are unchanged. You are the leader of a caravan of survivors. Your job is to make tough choices during the way and to control the best fighters of the caravan during important battles. You can bring your heroes up to level 10 this time, unlocking new skills and new tiers of previous skills. The variety of both units and enemies is noticeably improved, and each battle is an interesting tactical challenge.
Sadly, the same can't be said about the "tough choices". While there ARE several interesting choices where each option is reasonable and no option is perfect, and you'll really have to reflect on what's more important to you, almost all of the small choices you'll find along the way are random "gotcha" moments, where you'll be punished for not having read into the developers' minds. There are no interesting tradeoffs or moral ambiguities there, just arbitrarily right choices and arbitrarily wrong choices.
Despite the annoying arbitrariety in the results, though, these small events work very well as a way to immerse you in the story and make you feel like the main character feels, a leader who hasn't chosen to be one and who is learning the job as he or she goes along.
It's very difficult to talk about the story without making spoilers, so I'll just say that it's good. There are new characters, several climatic moments and towards the end you even begin to get a few parts of the answers to the big misteries that have been looming in the background since the first episode started. The third and last episode will make or break the story, but this second episode does a great job of building up towards a great climax.

Nuclear Throne is a procedurally generated run and gun with rogue-lite features.  You play as one of several mutants hoping to find the eponymous Nuclear Throne for various reasons.  Standing in their way is a hoard of various enemies across various dimensions.  Sadly while I would like to recommend this game, at this I cannot do to a number of serious balance issues that currently exist within the game.
Characters: Each of the playable mutants has both an active and a passive ability.  These range from being able to eat weapons for HP and ammo to increased speed to summoning allies with HP.  This helps every character to feel unique with their own special playstyles and preferred powerups.
Weapons:  Weapons are divived into ammo types (with the exception of melee weapons, some of which actually use an ammo type).  The ammo types are bullets (pistols, rifles), slugs (shotguns), bolts (crossbows, disc guns), explosives (grenade launchers, bazookas), and energy (lasers, various plasma weapons, etc).  Weapons range from the strictly utilitarian like the default pistol to the downright insane like the double minigun/  Part of the fun of the game is definitely seeing what kind of ridiculous weapons you can find and the sheer level of destruction you can achieve with them.
Powerups: Nuclear Throne has a level up system in which experience is represented by green rods dropped by enemies and canisters called rads.  Upon leveling up most characters will be able to choose from one of four randomly chosen mutations with a character specific set of "ultra mutations" available at level 10.  These can range from extra health,  to Throne Butt which upgrades the character's active ability in some way.  There are a number of interesting combinations though due to the random nature of the options players may not be able to set up many effective synergies on some runs.
Pros
- Large cast of playable characters that all look and play differently due to their unique abilities.
- Large set of weapons to work with.
- Diverse enemy and level types each presenting their own unique challenges.
- Ability to loop through the game with increased difficulty, new weapons, and new enemies.
Cons
The game is sadly saddled with a number of serious issues.  The first is health and enemy damage.  Most characters start with 8 health and a normal red bullet will take away 3 health.  Most melee attacks take out 5 health.  As you can see there isn't much margin for error and it's made worse when you realize there are a number of instant death attacks and ridiculously lethal attacks such as the crystals in 4-1 which can instant kill you with a touch and fire a multi-laser barrage that can take a character from full health to dead in seconds.
There's also the enemy A.I. which I can only describe as schizophrenic.  Sometimes an enemy will fire once in a while and other times the enemy will seemingly freak out and spew bullets one after another.  Most enemies do not have tells meaning it is hard to tell if you are throwing yourself into an unacceptably dangerous situation at times and this can make for cheap deaths when a bandit decides to suddenly hammer you in the face with a rapid fire three bullet burst.
Both of above issues are compounded by the procedural level design.  It is common to see the game set up a level where not only do multiples of some of the most obnoxious enemies cover one another constantly, but I've seen countless instances where damage is effectively unavoidable due to a combination of the level design and the types of enemies you are facing.  Few things are as frustrating as popping into a level only to be wiped out in seconds because you were instantly cornered at the start or faced a hail of unavoidable bullets.  Special mention goes to 5-3 where level design and the boss within combine to make for a nightmare situation that can easily lead to unavoidable death.
These issues are compounded by a number of changes and design decisions Vlambeer has done throughout the development cycle to the mutations, weapons, and enemies.  The general trend of many of these changes have been nerfs for the weapons and mutations and buffs to the enemies such that any combination or situation that may be beneficial to the player gets minimized and some enemies have been made so hyper aggressive and random as to make it almost impossible to come up with a good strategy for tackling them.
The sad thing is there is a great game underneath all of this disfunction.  One or two of these issues alone wouldn't be enough to be worried about but with all of them happening constantly all at once it leads to an unacceptably frustrating experience.  While difficulty is nothing new to run and guns there is a definite difference between a fair difficulty curve and seemingly punishing the player to the point where skill and experience simply don't matter anymore.

8BitBoy™ is a retro 8-bit styled classic platformer. It's very similar to Mario, with a lot of elements taken directly from that game.
- 8BitBoy™ is an 8bit classic styled platformer. The graphics are retro styled, but they do feel very bland and generic, like something you could find online as a royalty free sprite pack. I think the visuals of this game are fairly unimpressive.
- The music in this game does not appeal to me at all. I loved Sonic, and adored it's music. But this game's music just annoys me. The sound effects are irritating and not appealing in the slightest. I could hardly bare the audio in this game unfortunately.
- The gameplay is nearly identical to that of Mario. You move and jump, and can jump up to hit blocks above you to make them reveal a coin or something. You can jump on top of enemies to kill them. Perhaps the only unique gameplay feature is the ability to shoot, but it's near useless because the trajectory of the shots is just facepalm-worthy. Some of the platforming is decent, but I can't say much due to only playing 13 minutes (I couldn't stand any more for reasons I will come to later).
- The story is that you are a boy, who one day is mysteriously driven to put an old cartridge in a console, and then he's suddenly in a game.
- This is where the game really falls apart and why I had to call it quits after only 13 minutes. The functionality of 8BitBoy™ is absolutely atrocious. For starters, the key used to fire projectiles is bind to the same key used to sprint. WHAT!? Did the developer run out of keys on the keyboard or something? Luckily it can be reassigned in some ugly key binding menu system. The movement controls of the game feel awkward, the acceleration of the character just feel off, like they haven't been tested and polished enough. And the worst part, the jumping. Half the time pressing the jump key did not initiate a jump. I can NOT play this game when it won't let me jump! OK, the jumping usually works fine, it only stops working if you're standing still. And that makes it near impossible to hit the floating blocks.
If you're looking for a retro platformer reminiscent of Mario, then I highly suggest you steer clear away from this amateurish imitation. Even if the game plays perfectly fine for you, I still wouldn't recommend it because how dull this game is. Want a good platformer? Play an original one like Mario or Sonic or something. This game failed to deliver.

Yup, because you will die, again, and again, and again, and never make any progress. And after months of playing this, I can honestly say it's one of the most frustrating games I've ever played because I can't get any better at it. Perhaps this is a personal problem, but I can't think it's purely a personal problem. I've never made it past level 5-3. I've seen crowns once. So, if you're looking for a sense of achievement, this isn't your game. Nuclear Throne does have funky retro graphics, addicting gameplay, decent music, and a great sense of immersion. For casual gamers, it's worth the money. Just don't expect it to be something it's not.

A very fun game when it goes reasonably well, but the randomization can get frustrating even by roguelike standards.
Pros:
The guns feel good, the enemy design feels good, the mutations can cause you to adapt to different playstyles you might otherwise overlook, the character powers are interesting (with one or two exceptions that are not very fun or interesting), and the bosses are mostly well-designed.
Cons:
The enemy placement has soul-crushingly bad randomization, even for a roguelike.
Once you're moderately competent at the game, your success is largely a function of rolling dice a dozen times hoping you never roll a 1. The problem is that the randomization makes the variance in difficulty too high. You'll relatively quickly get to the point where you can reliably beat a given level almost every time, but then 5% of the time that level will spawn you in the center of five rapid-fire enemies who immediately start shooting, three snipers, and a monster who spews AoE flames. Is it possible to survive those spawns? Sure - you can go on Youtube and watch people do it. But the discrepancy in skill required to be able to reliably beat the level in almost all cases and to be able to reliably beat the level when you get unlucky is just too massive.
It creates a very ugly long-term difficulty curve where there's a long period of time that you're good enough at the game to make it to the end except when you get unlucky - and every run for hours and hours will be predicated on whether you get unlucky or not.
The other big con is the third boss. The internet is full of complaints about this boss. Watch Youtube videos of the best players and the commentary will frequently suggest that they're still afraid of this boss. And that same commentary will reveal the problem: it isn't that the boss is too hard, it's that the boss showcases the randomization problems more acutely than anything else in the game. You can end up spawned in a position where it's functionally impossible to survive. You can be spawned in the open with thirty enemies and not nearly enough time to clear them out before the boss spawns. You can be spawned in corridor so long and narrow that it's impossible to avoid his bouncing attacks.
It's a shame because that boss is otherwise the best boss in the game. The attack patterns are fun, if you're in a decent spawn he's hard but manageable, and you can quickly come up with clear strategies to deal with him. But the decision to have you fight him in a totally random map with random enemy placements turns a fun boss into a source of frustration.
Finally, the boss also has an incredibly stupid gimmick - when you get to him, he'll start powering up, then an instant-death beam will cut straight down the middle of the screen with no warning (and there's no aperature or any reason to expect something to come out there).
It's a cheap shot that all but guarantees new players will die once. It feels like the developers added it to play into the idea that the game is hard, but it isn't hard - it's just a cheap shot that will leave you angry that you finally got to the last boss and the developers played what amounts to a practical joke on you and told you to go do it again. It feels incredibly out of place compared to the rest of the enemy design in the game and the game is worse for it.
Overall:
All in all, a very fun game hampered mostly by its questionable enemy and level randomization. If you're prone to feeling frustration when you feel like there's nothing you could have done to prevent your death (and having to start all over), I'd give this one a pass. If you think you can put up with it, I'd say the gameplay just barely makes up for it, edging it ever so slightly into recommented territory.

Many fans were skeptical of the micro-transactions in Monolith studios brand new game "Middle-earth™: Shadow of War™". I too was a skeptical fan, but after playing the prolouge (Act I) which took me an astounding 11 hours (On Nemesis difficulty) i did not once see any push for micro-transactions.
They implemented it so you could always see the micro-transactions on the pause screen. But there was no huge display to show them off, just a little side show of in the corner showing you the options they had, and weekly community challenges.
With that big issue out of the way, how is the gameplay? If you have played Monolith's first instalment to the series "Middle-earth™: Shadow of Mordor™", you know exactly what to expect becasue most of the core mechanics stayed the same; Just fleshed out a bit more.
The thing that has changed the most from the first installment is the story, you can tell from just the first act that they are putting a lot more effort into the story; making it more RPG than just a hack and slash. Also in the fashion of a more RPG-styled stance they added different weaponry and equipment; instead of Runes, defeated enemys drop Gear, of a progressive scale of rarity, which can be upgraded further by completing a challenge associated with the weapon.
Overall they did god (So far), i'm enjoying almost every minute of it except when i get a Nemesis enemy with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ traits and is impossible to kill but hey that's half the fun. I hope this has been educational enough to people who are thinking about purchasing this game, and i'll update this after i beat the game.

A turn-based stealth game with a LOT of great ideas that is unfortunately pretty much ruined by some ill-considered mechanics. Specifically, some enemies have "Armor" and in many run-throughs of the game, you will simply not be given access to any items which allow you to ignore Armor, meaning you often encounter literally unstoppable enemies and just have to shrug your shoulders and reset.
It also suffers from "roguelike" syndrome, which is where a lazy developer declines to provide balance to a system and then chalks it up to "it's a roguelike". You might get a team of 4 awesome hackers and thousands of credits worth of equipment in your first two missions. OR, you might get a bunch of "intel" missions, which just tell you about other missions, giving you zero opportunity for advancement. If that situation comes up on your first day or two, you can just restart. If it comes up when you're 75% done with the game, oh well - sucks to be you! "It's a roguelike".
I'd really like to give this a thumbs-up, the theme is awesome, the art is just gorgeous and fits the cyberpunk world perfectly, the voice acting is top notch, and there are a lot of great gameplay ideas that unfortunately just don't come together, due to a couple of bad mechanics.
Keep an eye on this if you're into turn-based, and try it if it goes on sale really cheap, or they ever fix the balance problems.

Wakka wakka wa67aka wa6767 w27890 3780278u&^&* is basically the idea for his game. Basically, how many people know about the kill screen in Pac-Man? A lot. Basically, when you get to level 256, the game freaks out and half the board is missing. That is how this game was born. It started as an iOS game, then it was ported to Steam, PS4, and maybe XBOX ONE. Since this was made by Hipster Whale, the guys behind the "Smashy" series, they took Pac-Man (with permission of course, as this was published by Bandai Namco) and sprinkled their magic to update the game. This version of Pac-Man has more than just the Power Pellets, since here, you have fire, giantness, and even LAZERS!! The game is also no longer a goal to eat all the Pac-Dots, as the game is now an endless run upward. You use said powerups to defeat ghosts as you go up, as like in normal Pac-Man. After all, in Pac-Man, the ghosts always do one thing: "Pac-Man, WELCOME TO DIE!!!" The game is super fun this way with the ability to upgrade your powerups for more points and longer lasts. The game also has a lot of fanservice (the good kind with all the references and what not. Not the... other kind) as you can choose many styles from the classic Pac-Man all the way to CE DX+. There is also a style that is based on Hipster Whale's iOS classics. To make it better for the ports Hipster Whale removed all microtransactions (as the iOS version probably has them) and added multiplayer. Sadly, there is no online. Just local, and that is my main flaw. My other flaw is that runs can usually end abruptly since ghosts can corner you at bad times and unlike the original Pac-Man, you have no lives. However, in multiplayer, you can be revived. I recommend this game to Pac-Man fans, players of Pac-Man who want a spin on the old formula, and people who want to just have a good hour to spend, as this can get addicting, especially to get the 256 Pac-Dot chain to screen nuke everything. The game is also only 5 bucks, so it's cheap enough so you can use leftover funds for other things. Like food, or something I dunno. PAC-MAN 256 is a interesting spin on the classic Pac-Man formula, introducing an endless scrolling maze, fun power-ups and local multiplayer. Power-ups can be purchased and upgraded with currency found in the maze during gameplay, and optional quests can speed up the process of getting that currency. On top of all of this, there's also a wide selection of themes that change the graphical appearance of the game.
With all of these features, however, the most important thing is that the gameplay is solid, and the game itself is actually fun to play. It certainly kept me coming back for "one more time" to see how much farther I can push my high score or to unlock the next power-up.
In summary, this is a well-designed spin on an arcade classic, and is a good pick for anyone who would enjoy classic gameplay with a modern twist.

For those of you expecting a return to the old-school point 'n click adventure games, you won't find it here. It's the genre reimagined for these modern times. This means the UI is optimised for tablets. No menu's, only one interaction prompt and drag & drop inventory. The level of interactivity is very poor as well, only essential objects can be highlighted. All really unintuïtive, so it'll take some time getting used to.
Once and if you get over these modernisations the game will present itself as a charming adventure game. The artstyle is amazing, voice-acting superb and the music hits all the right notes. Though very enjoyable there's no crude humor like you'd expect from Tim Shafer, the whole thing seems rather harmless compared to the old days.
Part 1 will only take about 3-4 hours to complete, because the puzzles aren't hard. You'll breeze through it, but at least that keeps the pacing going. It sets up part 2 to have some intruiging plot development and I'm excited to see where they take it.
Pick it up if you havn't yet, this is one adventure you don't want to miss out on.

Named after the famous level 256 glitch, Pac-Man 256 brings back the best things from the game that changed an entire generation back in the 80s and combines them with new ideas that make this game just as addictive as it was in the arcades decades ago. Played from a 2.5D perspective, the biggest feature of this installment is the 256 bit glitch that will constantly follow you from the bottom of the screen, making time an important element of the game, as you can no longer dance around the same spot for too long and must constantly be on the move to avoid the glitch catching up with you. Unfortunately there are only 2 game modes, a single player mode, and a multiplayer mode for up to 4 players via local play, but even with that in mind, Pac-Man's addictive nature will make the hours pass without even realizing, especially when playing with friends.
As much as I loved playing alone and collect more coins to upgrade my power-ups, the real fun begins when up to 3 other friends join you for a local multiplayer session, something that few games in this age even consider, and Pac-Man 256 does that so well. As the glitch will constantly follow you, sticking around for too long is not an option, which means that players cannot be too far apart, making multiplayer on a single screen feel natural and the movement fluid. There is no split-screen needed and all you need to do is pass another controller to a friend and you're playing together on one single large screen; fast forward one hour later and you will still be there trying to beat the high score.
This is still Pac-Man in every possible way, but the new features, power-ups and tweaks to the formula make it feel like a fresh experience, and thanks to 21 different power-ups there is a lot to play around with. Each power-up can be upgraded with coins in order to increase duration and finding the best combination to suit your play style is the key to success, as you can only equip 3 power-ups at a time, which means that once inside the match only the selected power-ups will spawn, in addition to the famous Power Pellet.
Even if at its core multiplayer mode is still the same thing, the fact that you can respawn other downed players makes matches much longer, and once you and your friends get that perfect combination of momentum and power-ups, you will constantly push for a bigger high score, which is pretty much all you have going on since there are no additional modes, but do not underestimate the power of leaderboards, as the desire to make it to the top feels just as genuine now as it did back in the 80s.
In terms of enemies you will still have to face Blinky, Inky, Pinky, and Clyde, in addition to their new friend Glitchy, each one of them having a unique AI pattern that you must learn first in order to succeed. Even though there is no tutorial to teach you which ghost follows which pattern if you aren't familiar with Pac-Man already, just playing a few matches should teach you that in a matter of minutes. Same thing applies to power-ups and trying them all before deciding on the three that best fit your play style is just as important, as players who prefer avoiding the ghosts might find the Freeze power-up more useful than the Laser for example, which is aimed towards the players that aim to eliminate every single ghosts in their path.
Even if the resolution and design quality are obviously better than they were back in the arcades, Pac-Man 256 still has an 8 bit style, but with a large number of skins inspired by previous installments in the Pac-Man franchise, you can choose the one that catches your eye and just go with that. However, skins don't change the overall layout of the map or the play style in any way, and are made purely for aspect purposes.
Sound is just as your remember it, with a better quality of course, but all the death sounds and pac munches are still the same, which definitely helps with the nostalgia element this game wants to pass along to the player. There are obviously new sounds made for the power-ups, and they fit nicely with the rest of the sounds that probably any kid who grew up playing Pac-Man could recognize in an instant.
Sadly, whether you choose to play alone or with friends locally, that one mode is all you get, however playing with power-ups and collecting coins to max out each one of them and unlock all of the achievements can keep you busy for 20 hours at least. Skins are a nice addition, but apart from changing the aspect, they don't change anything to the gameplay itself.
Pac-man 256 is a pleasant throwback to the times when video games used to be much more simple, yet still entertaining at the same time and reminds us why Pacman is still one of the most influential video games of all time, decades later still managing to be as addictive and fun as it was when it first came out.

A very fun game when it goes reasonably well, but the randomization can get frustrating even by roguelike standards.
Pros:
The guns feel good, the enemy design feels good, the mutations can cause you to adapt to different playstyles you might otherwise overlook, the character powers are interesting (with one or two exceptions that are not very fun or interesting), and the bosses are mostly well-designed.
Cons:
The enemy placement has soul-crushingly bad randomization, even for a roguelike.
Once you're moderately competent at the game, your success is largely a function of rolling dice a dozen times hoping you never roll a 1. The problem is that the randomization makes the variance in difficulty too high. You'll relatively quickly get to the point where you can reliably beat a given level almost every time, but then 5% of the time that level will spawn you in the center of five rapid-fire enemies who immediately start shooting, three snipers, and a monster who spews AoE flames. Is it possible to survive those spawns? Sure - you can go on Youtube and watch people do it. But the discrepancy in skill required to be able to reliably beat the level in almost all cases and to be able to reliably beat the level when you get unlucky is just too massive.
It creates a very ugly long-term difficulty curve where there's a long period of time that you're good enough at the game to make it to the end except when you get unlucky - and every run for hours and hours will be predicated on whether you get unlucky or not.
The other big con is the third boss. The internet is full of complaints about this boss. Watch Youtube videos of the best players and the commentary will frequently suggest that they're still afraid of this boss. And that same commentary will reveal the problem: it isn't that the boss is too hard, it's that the boss showcases the randomization problems more acutely than anything else in the game. You can end up spawned in a position where it's functionally impossible to survive. You can be spawned in the open with thirty enemies and not nearly enough time to clear them out before the boss spawns. You can be spawned in corridor so long and narrow that it's impossible to avoid his bouncing attacks.
It's a shame because that boss is otherwise the best boss in the game. The attack patterns are fun, if you're in a decent spawn he's hard but manageable, and you can quickly come up with clear strategies to deal with him. But the decision to have you fight him in a totally random map with random enemy placements turns a fun boss into a source of frustration.
Finally, the boss also has an incredibly stupid gimmick - when you get to him, he'll start powering up, then an instant-death beam will cut straight down the middle of the screen with no warning (and there's no aperature or any reason to expect something to come out there).
It's a cheap shot that all but guarantees new players will die once. It feels like the developers added it to play into the idea that the game is hard, but it isn't hard - it's just a cheap shot that will leave you angry that you finally got to the last boss and the developers played what amounts to a practical joke on you and told you to go do it again. It feels incredibly out of place compared to the rest of the enemy design in the game and the game is worse for it.
Overall:
All in all, a very fun game hampered mostly by its questionable enemy and level randomization. If you're prone to feeling frustration when you feel like there's nothing you could have done to prevent your death (and having to start all over), I'd give this one a pass. If you think you can put up with it, I'd say the gameplay just barely makes up for it, edging it ever so slightly into recommented territory.

So, after much of a huge wait we are given Mafia 3, made by the same people who made Mafia 2, but did not make Mafia 1.
Graphics: So the graphics do not look like the gameplay video's we've all been seeing.  I loaded up, maxed them out and running smooth on 1080p maxed and yet the graphics look like an updated Mafia 2, barely anything amazing about them like what we seen in the tons of video's posted online.
Audio: The audio of the game is spot on amazing.  The radio stations are pure amazing to listen to that time frame, the cars sound amazing, the setting and landscapped sounds are spot on too.  It really is indepth and thought through.
Controls: The controls in Mafia have always been simple and easy to get used too.  They are a little big changed from Mafia 2, but not much and you get used to them in seconds of playing the game!  - Also changing the keys is slighly annoying and not all binds are saving or working, so I have resorted to using an XB1 controller which works perfectly.
Game/ features: So, Mafia one is and always will be the best one.  Then the game changed hands with Mafia 2 and quiet a few features where removed from the game that made it good, which is where Mafia 2 fell short.  Now we are given Mafia 3, with the same people and again, they have removed certain features, like the gas tank, you now cannot fill it up and it does not add the feeling of realism to the game. One thing I noticed too though, is when speeding past the police in ANY other Mafia game, they chased you and gave you a speeding ticket.  In Mafia 3, I could not get them to do this, no matter how fast and crazy I drove... So another feature removed! Walking around with a gun in Mafia 1 (and I think 2) then you became wanted if the police spotted you... This again was removed from Mafia 3.  When going into a shootout now the police only call if a suspect see's it, so you can shoot everyone and not care about the police, which is a silly flaw in the game and needs to be corrected.
They have brought back freeride which is good.  They've removed the good stuff and given us little stuff.
The story so far seems on point and good fun, as I am only a little bit into the game.  I am unaware if it is actually any good but no matter the outcome of each mission, it all ends the same is what I noticed.  Run in guns blasing, sneaking around or whatever the end is the same result.  Also, I noticed the game seems to be playing a past story, like your apart of the story but the events have already happened... Kinda not appealing to me playing a story that has happened is abit meh!
So above they have removed many features that made the game great.  Yet again these Devs removing things that should be kept.  Sad times but still there are other aspects of the game that draw you in and offer a great fun experience.
The takedowns in the game are pretty brutal.  They give the game a nice feeling, the same as the out right brutal racism in the game, which is fitting because it has not been toned down, from an eara of this sort of behaviour!
The cars handle totally weird I found and actually take some time to learn how to control them all!
The racism aspect of the game is hugely based on the time the game is set and it is done so very well!
So far though I am entertained in the game.  I am a huge Mafia fan and this is a good game, it's not amazing wow take my breathe away like Mafia 1 amazing, but it's a good enough game to the franchise.  I just wish they would give the game back to the original creators and let them work on it.
Each DLC to the game they added is about 45minutes tops! You can power through in a lot less or take your time and go exploring the new zones but otherwise, if you done the story quests ONLY and nothing else, it's less than 30mins... for the price at this time £11.99, ontop of your original price etc... Unless you get the season pass (Which has never been apart of a Mafia series but now it is everywhere)
There are many elements of the game they've just copied from Mafia 2 (Which they made) like towards the middle of Mafia 2 in jail, you had to box... Well in Mafia 3 about the same time you have to do boxing.  It's like their just copying pieces of the previous versions but adding a new story and newer features.
Overal the game is enjoyable and there is a lot of positive to a franchise I love, but then there are a few wrongs I do not like either.
Would I recommend? Yes but only if you enjoy the Mafia series.  It's a bran new story and setting with some updated visuals and style. Steam doesn't record my playtime for Painkiller Black Edition, so consider this both a review of that and this expansion.
Awful enemy design. Compare it to games like Serious Sam or Duke Nukem, who both had enemies that were distinctly different from each other and easily displayed what sort of attacks they had. Instead, the obsession with having unique enemies for practically every level leads to boring and indistinct variations of "brown and grey spoopy thing" that often have attacks that aren't readily apparent. Also, most of the enemies with guns are hitscan. Combine this with level design that often borderlines on claustrophobic and you've got a game that falls flat on its face as a horde shooter.
The main game is slightly better than the expansion; some of the levels are actually nicely designed, and you aren't being peppered with the same 5 one-liners every 2 minutes, but it still suffers from the awful enemy design. If you do get any Painkiller game, get Black Edition and stop there.

Here is why I cannot recommend it:  According to the community dicussions here, the devs of the game, purposely made the hit box of the characters big. That means, it can appear that someone someone is aimbotting(which I thought and many others thought that, that was the problem), but they actually aren't, it's just that the hix box of your character is so wide, that shooting 1-2 inches, just in the area around your character, means that you will get hit. To make this simpler to understand: Let's say you're playing Street Fighter and you're facing Ryu. Ryu fires a Hadouken (not a huge one) and you jump in the air to dodge so it passes beneath you. Although you jump in the air to dodge, you still get hit.
The apparent reason is that the dev's said they want to make the game easier for new comers so its a design choice. If this is the case, the game is fun, but if you're looking for something serious, I cannot recommend this game. If you're just playing of fun and don't care about the hitboxes, then yes, I can recommend it. If there was a vote symbol that had a flat symboling "not bad not good" I would use that.

Well it's a bumpy ride to say the least. microtransactions in a single player game and all. That aside this game for me was great. I run a 1050 Ti with 4GB so maybe thats why i had no graphical issues like others complained about besides some crashing but that was due to my GPU overclocking and not the game itself.
The game's story is pretty good. Acting was good, uruks were good, and the graphics were pretty solid and overall optimization was better than expected.
Now for the key reason i got the game. The nemisis system. It is so much better. numerous changes to the combat mechanics ballance the game so that you are no longer overpowered yet they still managed to provide you with at least 20 new ways to kill captains so while i cant just hack and slash mindlessly anymore i can poison, curse, shoot them in the face while flying in the air, summon mounts, and have lethal counters. To me this is the cake of the game. The fact that the nemisis system has been compounded on and works alot better. I used to regularly slaughter 6 captain bodyguards and their warchief in the old game but now i get worried when there are 2 and i actively evade combat for 4 captains and up because they are much more agressive, almost all the captains are a threat now, and their ability to adapt to conventional combat makes frontal assault pretty much only a last option or a finishing blow. I play on the highest dificulty and have died 3 times, twice the captain had the "no chance" perk that prevents me from getting a second wind. I dont think i have been able to go toe to toe with a single captain because every skill only works 2-3 times before they adapt and then it is useless. The main skills i have actually seen adaptations on include vaulting over a captain, wraith stun/freeze, throwing knives, and one even adapted to stealth after a 4th attempt.
Worth noting that decapitating pesky captains is pretty much required as the return rate is insane. Almost a 3rd of my kills have returned and they seem to return anywhere based on a trigger (like low health or killing an enemy a certain way. even had one sneak up on me after i poisoned some grog and he told me i used to much poison.....) so you can have a captain or 2 ambush you while your trying to deal with a captain already anyway. At least they seriously buffed your mobility skills to near god-like levels (you can leap several floors vertically up a wall to climb a large tower in maybe 5-8 seconds.).

Well, apart from the sheer fanboyism, lets get serious, because this game deserves it. I have been playing this since the early builds before getting it on Steam, so i calculate i have well over 3000 hours logged total.  And if you expect flight action, or fancy cutscenes and effects, or a more casual game based on surreal spaceship propulsion systems, this game is not for you. Really. This game requires you to actually use your brain and learn things. It is disguised graphically as a cute little sandbox with them kerbals and fun explosions, but the truth is that this is a realflight rocket, spaceship, plane, and orbital simulator. Which means you will need to LEARN in a relatively DIFFICULT way things like orbital mechanics, manouvers, how to rendezvous and dock ships in orbit manually, and that kind of things. Expect a HIGH learning curve. Which in my humble opinion is worth its weight in diamonds in this world of stupid games we live in, but i digress. The game makes you learn things about space, spaceships, real propulsion systems, aerodinamics, and in general how things are done in real life with rockets and satellites, spaceplanes and such.... really i have no words that make it justice.
If your are an all things space aficionado, or always wanted to be, this game is a no brainer great choice for you. Plus Squad are great guys that are always improving the game in giant steps, like the recent comms net and satellite signal system, and you can always expect improvements. And also the communitiy is great, the mod scene is greatly supported... It's all good! Go get it!!
My only little grudge with it is that it still has no real habitat and life support simulation, appart from G force or heat exposure, but everything will eventually come, as always  :)

Invisible, Inc. is a game developed and published by Klei Entertainment, the same people behind Mark of the Ninja. Invisible, Inc. is simply one of the best single-player games I've ever played
The theme is evoked well and the mechanisms of play are finely tuned. The real genius though, lies in how the game handles mistakes. In many games failure just costs time, or you are forced to reload whenever you make a mistake
Invisible, Inc. also allows this, but it really shines when you set up a game without rewinds or reloads. Then you get to experience how good a game can really be
The perfectly executed stealthy infiltration can quickly become a deadly game of cat and mouse, and successfully pulling unconscious agents out of a botched operation is way more satisfying than a reload could ever be
Points of reference could be XCOM or the best roguelikes, but I think Invisible, Inc. outclasses them all
My only criticism lies with how certain equipment can make core elements of the game trivial to overcome. It's not so fun when you have a "super agent" able to avoid or overcome all opposition
The relatively short campaign time-frame and random item availability prevents this from becoming a significant problem though

tl;dr - 10/10 Awesome game if you even remotely enjoy Pac-Man, pick this up and play with some friends. Trust me. I'm a Doctor.
Having grown up with Pac-Man and always loving the challenge of beating your previous best, this is a perfect game that takes you to the roots of Pac-Man while adding new features.
The powerups that are able to kill ghosts or simply raise your score are a nice touch, and the ability to change the 'gameboard' prevents any sense of staleness that might creep up on you while playing a game like this. The time that it takes to not only unlock all the powerups but then also fully upgrade the ones you use will take some time, adding more fun if you are someone like me who enjoys 100% completion of games.
Sitting down with friends and all plugging into the same computer to play multiplayer gives it an almost nostalgic, classic feeling of the couch co-ops I grew up with, all of you fighting for the highscore amongst yourselves but also working together to get as many points as possible. The ability to revive each other when you drop allows you to continue playing with friends for long periods of time, even having ones drop out and back in by death.

Huge Tim Schafer fan. Monkey Island is by far my fav. point and click adventure game and overall love all his work.
I got this game through the kickstarter which got me extremely excited when I heard he is making a new adventure game, especially since he has 100% full creative control, no publishers.. AWESOME!
That being said, this is a good game... It's slightly below my expectations, I don't consider it to be AMAZING, however I do think it's fairly good.

The game has small problems here and there like various depth issues when it comes to certain animations, and also the game was dropping frames for me when I was using an item to interact with something. All those problems don't affect the experience, however I don't feel like the experience comes anywhere close to Monkey Island or Grim Fandango. That's probably just me being nostalgic.. or playing too many games and being desensitized.

A seriously charming piece of storytelling (even if it is only half a story) that shows that Tim Schafer and the Double Fine team still has the writing skills to make a point and click adventure (which, let's face it is pretty much the genre that time-forgot) both memorable and thought-provoking. The humor made me smile more than laugh-out-loud, but the voice acting is top-notch and the visual style is breathtaking, there’s hardly a screen in the game that wouldn’t make a suitable illustration for a press release or desktop background.
Of course, being a backer I’m clearly the intended audience for an experience like this; those who don’t have patience for dialog trees would do well to look elsewhere, as should anyone who is looking for a serious mental workout to scratch the itch that Myst left behind. Seasoned adventure gamers are really going to blow through this in next to no time (the overall difficulty level makes  the ‘easy’ mode in the Monkey-Island series look like Kings Quest V). This is really one to play for the story, characters and (at this stage) the anticipation of what will come next in chapter 2. Well worth the time for anyone looking to remember the great charms of a genre that is really overdue for a renaissance.

One thing that the publishers did that is common with this type of game is to release it as five episodes over a year rather than the entire game at one. The episodes are:
Episode 1: Chrysalis – January 30th, 2015
Episode 2: Out of Time – March 24th, 2015
Episode 3: Chaos Theory – May 19th, 2015
Episode 4: Dark Room – July 28th, 2015
Episode 5: Polarized – October 20th, 2015
And, in a way, it does feel like a serialized television series. Considering that Dontnod Entertainment is a small studio, that’s understandable. The fifth and final episode, without giving too much away, is very surreal. It took me 14-15 hours to complete the game, with each episode taking two-three hours to complete. Yes, I had to look for a little bit of help during episode 4.
The graphics are outstanding, but I have to point out that there have been some technical issues with certain parts of the game. Lip sync issues have been noted by other reviewers of this game, and at one point during the fifth episode, we hear Max talking, but her lips… aren’t… moving. Is she transmitting what she is saying by thought?  😆
Considering that this is a well-reviewed game, episode one is free, and the entire series is just $20, I encourage you to give this game a try.

I looooooooooove this game.
It's very similar to Telltale games, in that you're mostly walking around, clicking on things, and moving forward to unlock the next cutscene or decision.  Your choices matter, and the story you get unfolds in a way of your choosing.  The use of the 'Rewind' power that the main character gets is also kind of neat, meaning if you don't like the way something turned out, you can go back a few minutes and pick a different option.
The ending is binary, you get Option A or Option B, with a few variances depending on previous choices, but those are all you will ever get.  I was fine with that.  Some people were upset, but not every game can have 20+ endings.
The story is pretty great, if you like that 'slice of life' kind of tale, as well as geek culture references, art hipsters, and homosexual references.  If any of these things offend you, steer clear.
I adored most of the characters (Except for Kate.  Screw you, Kate.), but this does not seem to be universal.  Some people love them and some hate them, I see very few people 'meh' about them.  Ultimately I think how much you enjoy this game will depend entirely on how well you jive with the characters, because this is a game completely about them and what they go through.  If you will cringe when the main character, Max, puts a quarter in a vending machine and says 'Release the Kra-CAN!', then this probably isn't the game for  you.  If that'd make you laugh, then step on inside!  One of my favorite parts of the game was when the main character and another character are just laying in bed, having woken up, and neither is moving or saying anything (until you move Max out of bed).  It wasn't romantic, they hadn't 'done it' or anything.  It just felt peaceful, with that indie hipster cuddle rock playing in the background, like a moment the characters would never want to end, so they don't have to get up and face the real world.
Life is Strange is full of these moments, about the emotional rollercoaster of trying to reconnect and recapture your past, while also trying to move forward to where you want to be.
The game brought real emotions out of me, especially the ending I chose.  I was depressed and excited all at the same time, and I spent the next two days in my spare time day-dreaming about what the aftermath of my decision might be like.  It's very rare for me to feel very much past the first few minutes of a game's ending.  I haven't even played it again because I loved the story I made too much to want to taint it with my foul fore-knowledge.
The indie soundtrack was almost always appropriate, cool, and thematic to the moment, and some of it is stuck in my head until this very day!  Looking at YOU, Obstacles by Syd Matters.
If you play games for stories, and you like the kind of stories that come up when an art hipster girl gets time-bending powers, then I would highly recommend you try out Episode 1 for free, and purchase the rest of the game if you like it.
If you're even curious, well the first episode is free.  Why not try it?  It costs you nothing to hit the 'uninstall' button if you hate it.
UPDATE:  Forgot to mention that the voice acting in this thing is AMAZEBALLS!  You can feel the emotions they're experiencing through their voices.  Especially Chloe and Max.

It's a solid mobile port and a good reimagination of a Pac-Man game. PAC-MAN 256 offers just enough change from the original classic that it comes across as a fresh interpretation without renouncing its core mechanic.
The idea is to turn the 256 glitch of the original game into an ever looming threat that creeps up from the bottom of the screen, chasing the player and thus transforming this iteration of the classic into an infinite runner. It's a great game to play for a few minutes or a means to occupy your hands while listening to music or podcasts as it doesn't feature any background music. The familiar "waka waka" along with other retro sound effects are still there though.
The game draws from a pool of premade level sections where the paths and placement of the ghosts are set. Learning the level sets, ghost placements and most notably the ghost movement patterns gives the player the opportunity to improve and make decisions based on empirical knowledge. Countering the possible repetitiveness, new power ups can be unlocked and different themes activated.
PAC-MAN 256 doesn't reinvent the wheel but offers a short and fun arcade session close to the original.

Level design is good, but can be confusing at times. Just the right amount of props and nice attention to detail.
Monster design is flawless, and impressively creative for a title of this age.

Weapons are interesting and well balanced, and their handling feels superb.
The engine itself is a genuine masterpiece, and runs without any hickups whatsoever.
There are a few things I'm not a fan of though;
- You're forced to kill all enemies in a level, before being able to progress. Now, this wouldn't be that big of a deal, if monsters didn't sometimes hide in places they should never have been able to reach in the first place.
- The concept of soul collecting, because it forces you to wait around dead bodies for a handful of seconds, before they fizzle away and turn into souls that can be picked up.
- Coins/treasures/Tarrot cards - To this day, I still have not been able to figure out exactly what they're for.
You're fine ignoring them completely, and enjoying the game as a pure shooter anyway.
- The save/load menu is a frustrating thing to use, no matter how much experience you have with it.
The list of autosaves quickly reaches a length where maintaining an overview of your progress is impossible (just delete what you don't use at the end of each chapter).
That being said, I thoroughly enjoyed the game from beginning to end, and it managed to keep me entertained the whole time, which is a tall order these days.
The above applies to the first game of the series as well, which for some reason I cannot review.

This game is an acid trip with a touch of violence.
Hotline Miami brings a unique top down "dual stick" shooter and beat em up to a whole new level. There are a variety of weapons at your disposal as well as masks the player can choose at the start of each level- These can either buff or handicap you, so you have to change up your playstyle depending on which one you choose to don.
You can choose to be sneaky and take out the baddies one at a time, but the game rewards you with recklessness. To get a high score and rating; you must chain together combos, and use different weapons every so often.
YOU WILL DIE A LOT in this game but it's as easy as pressing "R" each time and the game immediately puts you at the beginning. No loadtimes after death so you can jump right back into the action and change up your strategies.
Now to the music, well... it's amazing, it pumps you up and is a mash up of dance and electronic music. Along with the trippy visuals the music ties in well with the game.
The Story is not uniform but random and obscure, it makes the game interesting. Each chapter has multiple stages and they always begin with the protagonist in his apartment, reading a message on his answering machine about the mission, and him driving to the stage.
I recommend this game, it has a lot of secrets and unlocks so there is replay value, and to my knowledge this is the only game that has this kind of flare.

So, I never thought I would write a review about this game, but I just have to after what I read from others...
This game really took me by surprise. I came out of Season One thinking that there will never be a better one. And I was right... to a point.
The game starts off soon after the ending of the first one. You are put into the shoes of Clementine, who is definitely a familiar character to anyone who played season one. This time you get to see what it's like to see the apocalypse from the eyes of an eleven year old girl. Telltale doesn't hesitate, and shows you its reality in the first ten minutes of the first episode. The mechanics of the game are also greatly improved giving the player an easier way to pick dialogue by finally giving us a mouse. This allows us to have more control and not accidentally pick the wrong answer like I did a couple of times in season one.
The gameplay itself gets a lot more interactive and it isn't all about point and click anymore. There is a lot of mouse control and keyboard play but of course not a crazy whole amount because we have to remember; this is a story rich game which mainly includes dialogue.
Just like Lee, Clementine is a character that we see change and develop through the game. Reactions and characteristics that make Clementine a character are always there, but clementine can be changed quite a lot. There are many moral choices you make that only have an affect on you in the end. Like choosing whether Clementine should smoke a cigarette or drink some alcohol. these choices won't affect the game, but it will make Clementine different in YOUR eyes.
When it comes to other characters, I was once again taken by surprise at how much I cared about some of them, whereas at the same time, I absolutely hated other characters. There was a certain character that I hated in the beginning, but as I went through the game, my opinion changed. It was a pleasant change as Season One never really did. Sure there were times I thought a character I liked did the wrong thing, But I never changed opinions completely like I did here.
As for the game's length, It was good. Exactly 10 hours to wrap the game up which is a bit longer than I should have finished, but I was delayed due to some very hard decisions, which I regretted straight away. Yes, I know it's basically cheating to go back and change my choices but I re-winded just a couple seconds after the picking my choice, mostly because I felt differently straight after I chose the answer. Take that however you want.
The ending of the game, once again came to me as a big surprise. To a point where I had to close my eyes after choosing what to do. Then I just sat in my chair and stared at the screen waiting to see the heart-breaking consequences.
Overall, The Walking Dead Season Two is a masterpiece. Its story meets the level of the first season and it did not leave me disappointed. If anything, it left me empty... As if my life was over. And it made me want more, exactly like Season One did. So in the end... Season Two was not better than Season One, if that's what your looking for, then unfortuneatly you're doomed to replay season one again and again because you will never get such a good story with such great characters. But Season Two definitely meets the level of its predecessor. Especially with how it concludes. Like it or not but no matter what your choices are through Season One, in the end you get the same ending. Whereas here, your choices take a big part when it comes to the end of the game. So like I did, choose wisely. Even if you need to rewind. As long as it doesn't ruin the game for you.
The Walking Dead Season 2 is definitely one of the best games I ever played and I would recommend it to anyone who completed the first one.

Invisible, Inc. is a game developed and published by Klei Entertainment, the same people behind Mark of the Ninja. Invisible, Inc. is simply one of the best single-player games I've ever played
The theme is evoked well and the mechanisms of play are finely tuned. The real genius though, lies in how the game handles mistakes. In many games failure just costs time, or you are forced to reload whenever you make a mistake
Invisible, Inc. also allows this, but it really shines when you set up a game without rewinds or reloads. Then you get to experience how good a game can really be
The perfectly executed stealthy infiltration can quickly become a deadly game of cat and mouse, and successfully pulling unconscious agents out of a botched operation is way more satisfying than a reload could ever be
Points of reference could be XCOM or the best roguelikes, but I think Invisible, Inc. outclasses them all
My only criticism lies with how certain equipment can make core elements of the game trivial to overcome. It's not so fun when you have a "super agent" able to avoid or overcome all opposition
The relatively short campaign time-frame and random item availability prevents this from becoming a significant problem though
