I'd like to start off by saying: I was very excited when the first game was announced, and the very same hype came back for when this game was announced.
There were some hiccups with this game though, mainly the doubt that beset most of us on the arrival of microtransactions.
However, I remained hopeful, and this is my review thus far, on 25.5 hours spent, playing on nothing but Nemesis difficulty the entire time.
The game met my expectations and then some!
Just the "tutorial" phase of the game was nice, because it was less of a tutorial and more of an entire introduction. During this introduction I got enough skill points to unlock EVERY skill available, which there are plenty of, but not that many "perks" in those skills as most of them have a high level-cap you have to exceed, which is fine.
You get a nice backstory to the beginning city, mostly non-canon for all you lore-buffs, which is kind of the theme for the entire game: This isn't canon. Nearly none of it.
It doesn't mean you can't enjoy it. Just that it means you cannot rely on much of what this story tells you.
But onto my next point, difficulty.
Difficulty has been increased exponentially from the last game. I cannot speak for the lower difficulties, but on Nemesis it was a huge struggle in the start, partly because I had lost all my "Shadow of"- skills. Then it was also because I lacked abilities in-game and also lacked gear.
In the now 25.5 hour playthrough I have, I've fixed this issue of not having abilities, and also gear. Gear isn't difficult to come by, I have slotted full legendaries with a few legendary backups. I haven't even done any microtransactions yet.
Still, the game is very hard. I often find myself depending on my bodyguard Uruk to help me deal with captains, although I can regularly solo them now, but I die a lot.
I have died in the game world at least 20 times, and in missions where death means restart and not retry, I'd estimate about 50 more deaths on top of the 20 world deaths. The game is hard, you're on your toes the entire time, you can easily fail and die to caragors if you're not careful.
Once I had died to a captain, respawned, found a captain close to my respawn tower, so I shadow striked him, he immediately did an unblockable smack for over half my health, I did a light attack, he blocked and instantly countered with another unblockable attack, I was downed and wouldn't you know it, he gave me No Chance.
Dead again, with an interval of about 30 seconds from the last death. And right there I was about level 25 so it's not exactly the opening of the game either.
Missions then. Missions are honestly better than expected. You can completely decide what missions you wanna do, and at about 90-100% completion on each questgiver branch, you gain a new skill which you cannot unlock by levelling up.
Naturally, I did all Cárnan quests because I wanted to be able to summon my own tamed Drake at will, something I'd recommend others to do as well. Missions are hard, the final quest in each branch seems to have a theme of having you face off against enemies 5-15 levels higher than you without giving you much or any aid at all.
I fail AT LEAST 5 times before succeeding.
There's about a good 8-12 quests on each branch I'll estimate, with about 6 branches, which is a good amount I'd say, and I'll come back to that in some final thoughts coming right up.
Fort assaults, quite great honestly, not nearly as cinematic as how it looked when first announced, which was to be expected, but it's really fun and very hard. At first I didn't believe them when the developers said that the assaults would be hard without any Uruks on your own, and let me tell you, I can't disprove them.
Even when I did call in 4 Uruks I still failed regularly, to the point where I typically have 2 Uruks infiltrate the city and remove layers of defense. Only then I find it manageable.
All in all, I really like this game, it was well worth the wait, it was well worth its hype. Microtransactions really aren't something you'll pay any attention to, you'll barely think about it while playing, so don't let it hinder you. I still haven't used the market, but I will sooner or later.
Game is substantial, and even with me picking all collectibles and doing full completionist run, I'd say I'm halfway through the game at my 25.5 hours. Let's compare that to the previous game, where I actually had 100% completion and 100% achievements at 23 hours, before the arrival of their DLC's.
They HAVE pumped up this game, and it feels richer and smoother than the first one. I have some issues with a few strung up prisoners animations going wrong, and sometimes some animations play without any sound, but these issues fixes themselves and aren't major problems, it's just goofy or feels strange when you start breathing fire with your drake but there's no sound of your roaring flames.
Game is huge on your harddrive as well, taking up 67 gigs for me, but it is well worth it as even though my computer is starting to be dated, this obviously must work wonders as I've never dipped below 60 FPS.
Call me a fan boy or whatever, but in my opinion this has been a 10/10 game, a huge upgrade from the previous one, so I'm a lot less salty about the albeit huge price this game demands. The premise of the game - a spy-themed action RPG - is pretty great, but the execution is so janky that it falls apart.
All of the RPG elements work. The skill system is pretty unique and keeps characters focused, meaning you don't run into that problem in a lot of newer action RPGs where your character is great at everything by the end of the game. The dialogue system is simple, but the timed responses give it a good pace. The characters are pretty archetypal for the espionage genre, but they're entertaining and well-rounded enough that I don't mind.
Where the game fails is in the actual action part. The stealth, the shooting, even just the movement all feels so sloppy and disconnected that the game is rendered basically unplayable. The camera is incredibly buggy - it sometimes jumps around for no reason when passing through doorways, climbing up ladders, etc.
It's really too bad. I wanted to keep playing to see how everything came together, but it quickly became so frustrating that I had to stop.

Great game. The game benefits from repeated plays and the numerous game modes such as ENDLESS where you try your darnest to avoid FRACTAL 2.0 as long as possible.  In a way, this game does rogue-like better than XCOM or Darkest Dungeon given that you always have a time limit - the main story you have 72 hours to do what you need to do; Endless has the ever-increasing difficulty where you will get HOSED if you are not prepared for the long haul by Day Six or so. You are always under time pressure and money pressure.
Expect a great game with wonderful mechanics and enough items/agents/augments to keep you playing and trying new things. The DLC is also great, namely for the story missions (The Research Lab, the Forge). The Steam Workshop has a few dedicated modders who provide great stuff (the 4 extra agents added so much replayability to this game when I was starting to wonder if I had any reason to run something other than Internationale/Nika every game.)
Lastly, yes, this is a stealth game. BUT. You owe it to yourself to embrace the lethal weapons and fire bullets when you need to. The game tells you that lethal weapons are rare. It tells you that reloads are expensive. It has the alarm level rise a ton on deaths. Buy a Flurry Gun. Give it to Nika. Disable enemy heart monitors. Enjoy the carnage.

Pac man is back with added variety and some fun twists; the game doesn't stray too far away from the original pac man experience.
You get to collect dots and evade ghosts as usual, but this time around the game comes in one big endless level that gets harder as you move foreward. Behind you, a glitch is eating up the world at a moderate pace, so you need to keep moving. You play with a different viewing angle than the original pac man, and the game rewards you for collecting dots in long un-interrupted chains.
As you play, you will unlock some power ups, and can and upgrade them with coins that you find, or get from completing some objectives.
The true hero of the game is the multiplayer, which supports up to 4 players on the same pc, and this adds a lot of replayability. The game also allows you to choose from different background designs, and different shapes for your pac-man. Without multiplayer expect to play around 10 hours if you want to experience everything the game has to offer, and collect all acheivements.
I haven't encountered any bugs or game slow downs as I played, and the game size is very light on the hard disk (just under 100mb).
___________________
What I think could have been improved is how the acheivements are structured, not much thought was put into the acheivements, and there are many missed oportunities.
To illustrate this, one of the achievements requires you to fully upgrade all power ups, it is not very hard to do but it requires lots of grinding, you will most probably complete all other acheivements way before this one, and it can possibly be your only remaining motive to play, most players just quit, as this acheivement only has about a 1.5% completion rate at the time of this writting.
Instead, this objective could have been lowered to upgrade all power ups to level 7, with additional acheivements for fully upgrading some of the powerups, or for using a specific combo of powerups in a single game and acheiving a high score, or for maintaining a powerup's active time for an elongated period of time, or for completing some of the objectives in a single game.

While I didn't expect much going into this game, with the documentary making the studio look like a bunch of naive hippies, I should have known better than to make any assumptions based on a documentary, because this game is awesome!  It is very well written, and I laughed at quite a few of the things that happened.  Plus, it isn't overly violent or inappropriate, so my daughter watched as I played.  She really enjoyed it, so much that she came over from her own game that she was totally addicted to (Sims 3) and just watched me play until I beat it.  I also liked that all the puzzles are intuitive enough that I was easily able to figure out the solution without looking for a walkthrough.  Nothing annoys me more about adventure games than when they put in a puzzle that makes no logical sense, and luckily that never happened in this game.
That brings me to the bad part, the game is very short.  I completed the act in maybe 4 hours.  While I don't mind short games (I actually prefer short games like this), I know some will be put off by the length of the game.  Also, there is no instructions on how to use items.  While the method of using them is simple (you drag them to the place you want to use them), there was no help menu that actually told you that.  I actually had to start the game twice before I figured that part out.  Beyond that, the user interface is simple and easy to understand.  You need nothing but your mouse to play.

I have to admit, I was a bit worried for a while. Kickstarter seemed to bring more poor quality content for a while and some projects were complete failures. I even got worried about Broken Age, given that Double Fine ran out of money. Now, they're not out of the woods yet but having finished the first part made me hopeful to say the least.
Tim Schafer is still the master of point-and-click adventure games, as proven by this game. The difficulty is significantly lowered compared to the stuff he used to make but I'm guessing that's an intentional change made to keep more players playing until the end instead of giving up completely. People who used to play these games are likely to have much less free time nowadays so I think it's for the better.
Speaking as someone who played LucasArts adventure games ever since Mainac Mansion, I kind of miss the parsers they used to have because it meant you get some witty humour from looking at certain objects or attempting something that might not advance the story but at least you'd get a laugh from attempting something silly.
Since only part 1 is out at this point the game is also very short. It took me roughly four hours to finish. I'm peronally okay with the length though. It's a very enjoyable four hours. I enjoy the detail put in the scenery and the characters. Voice acting is great (yay for Jack Black!), good pacing. Slightly buggy interface though, sometimes the drag-and-drop doesn't work and sometimes some objects are drawn in front of others that shouldn't be. Also, Broken Age needs more humour. I like the jokes that are there but they're not nearly as frequent as back in the day.
Overall, I really enjoyed the game and the ending of part 1 made me eager to see how the story concludes.

Well it's a bumpy ride to say the least. microtransactions in a single player game and all. That aside this game for me was great. I run a 1050 Ti with 4GB so maybe thats why i had no graphical issues like others complained about besides some crashing but that was due to my GPU overclocking and not the game itself.

Now for the key reason i got the game. The nemisis system. It is so much better. numerous changes to the combat mechanics ballance the game so that you are no longer overpowered yet they still managed to provide you with at least 20 new ways to kill captains so while i cant just hack and slash mindlessly anymore i can poison, curse, shoot them in the face while flying in the air, summon mounts, and have lethal counters. To me this is the cake of the game. The fact that the nemisis system has been compounded on and works alot better. I used to regularly slaughter 6 captain bodyguards and their warchief in the old game but now i get worried when there are 2 and i actively evade combat for 4 captains and up because they are much more agressive, almost all the captains are a threat now, and their ability to adapt to conventional combat makes frontal assault pretty much only a last option or a finishing blow. I play on the highest dificulty and have died 3 times, twice the captain had the "no chance" perk that prevents me from getting a second wind. I dont think i have been able to go toe to toe with a single captain because every skill only works 2-3 times before they adapt and then it is useless. The main skills i have actually seen adaptations on include vaulting over a captain, wraith stun/freeze, throwing knives, and one even adapted to stealth after a 4th attempt.

It's not a simple Mario clone as some other newly-made deliberate old-school platformers set out to be. Instead you'll recognize many nods to various games of yore. Sure, you bump against blocks and collect coins like in SMB, but e.g. the fireball bounces around similar to Super Mario Land, when frozen in the beginning of a stage the protagonist resembles Master Higgins aka Takahashi Meijin from Adventure Island, the glowing eye of the final boss resembles the Chozo statues from Super Metroid, occasionally you'll feel like in an Alex Kidd game or one of the later Wonderboy games on Master System. And the intro of the game even alludes to the Master System. Overall, though, the visual style mostly resembles Atari or DOS platformers, which is in no way meant negatively. It's great to see somebody use aesthetics somewhere between 8- and 16-bit to not ape NES games, but do something a bit different.
Gameplay-wise, I was about to give up on the game rather quickly. Jumping while running feels slippery, some platforms and enemies have been placed in a way developers of old (from the real 16-bit days) wouldn't have (or at least the good ones of yore wouldn't have), conveyor belts work in a stupid way (only the most outward one allows for high jumps, for no discernable reason) and so on.
There are tons of little nuisances, biggest of which is probably how the game cannot decide whether it wants to reward or discourage exploration. Each and every of the 45 stages (plus 5 boss fights) is loaded with hidden stashes, but only the one hiding each stage's bonus coin is really worth going out of your way for. Otherwise you risk losing a life for nothing but coins (100 give an extra life) or upgrades that can't shield your from one of the MANY abysses, spiky pits, streams of lava, etc., making them just worth much of an extra risk to take.
After a while, though, you get a grip on the slightly wonky physics and start hunting down the 50 bonus coins necessary for the true (and depressing) ending. Here is where 8BitBoy truly shines as most secrets are hidden rather cleverly. Sure, you'll have to endure the occasional leap of faith and the occasional invisible passageway right in your path, but as time goes on you learn how the developer thinks and you learn the rules of the game and what tricks it might have up its sleeve. By this point you watch the level structure closely for possible hints and test out theories, often to be rewarded with one of the elusive bonus coins.
In the end it was a close-call whether I'd recommend this game or not, seeing there are so many other platformers out there attempting to harken back to the good old days. Plus, there obviously still are tons of platformers from the 90s you probably haven't even played yet! Wonderful Euro platformers like this such as Gods, R.O.B., Plok, Jazz Jack Rabbit and so on. But still, for the small asking price and due to the addictive and cleverly designed hunt for the bonus coins, I give it a thumb up. Also, kudos to the developer for the fireball mechanics: You either shoot fireballs forwards in mostly a straight line, or by pressing down you aim them diagonally up, which is a simply and ingenuitive way of giving you more control over your projectiles.

Honestly, I want to finish this game, and I probably will. But the 8 to 12 hours of gameplay might be more because the physics are awful. I am already more than halfway through in what is currently a 2 hour playthrough. The hit boxes seem to either be pixel perfect or a square around the player, but it switches randomly and usually not in your favor. You slide on surfaces that you shouldn't slide on, making more of your movements overcorrections than actual movements. I have died so many frustrating times simply because the physics do not match the surfaces I am running on.
The graphics are cool and the asthetic are super retro and definitely fit the genre. I love that about this game. But honestly, this is more of a rage platformer than a game like Mario, simply because you do not die of your own misaction most of the time. Usually it is from sliding off something you shouldn't be able to slide off of, or because the collision detection changes randomly and decides that a bird can clip through a wall and shoot you, yet the first pixel they collide with you is an instant death without any powerups.
Which brings me another point. Powerups should be more plentiful because they are lost so easily and often. Sure, this may add challenge and difficulty to some who are looking for it. But when you die mostly cheap deaths and you lose your power ups so easily, there should be more scattered in the map.
Finally, this game encourages exploration. That is great. The problem is that many areas have spiky or open floors, so you die a lot trying to figure out whether something is hidden down below or not because the game is not consistent with "death areas". A few of them are marked with skull signs to say "Hey, you will die if you fall here". But most are not, and again, many deaths will come from the fact that you cannot tell which is which.
Because of these factors, I will finish the game, but I am not looking to try to find all the secrets or anything like that. It is too frustrating and unforgiving to truly encourage exploration like it wants. Not all is bad about the game. Unfortunately, what is bad is more central to the game itself, and thus strips the shine away from some of the other elements. As much as I love these kinds of games and have forever, I would not recommend this game unless the physics get a reworking.

Absolutely incredible game with great replay value. To illustrate, here are some highlights from my playthrough history (I wrote them all down because I was so excited to try new combinations of agents and programs after my first few runs) (warning: SPOILERS for unlockable agents and programs):
1. Beginner, Decker + Internationale, Power Drip + Lockpick 1.0: Victory!
2. Experienced, Shalem 11 + Banks, Fusion + Parasite: Defeat!
4. Experienced, Internationale + Central, Faust + Brimstone: Victory!
6. Expert, Archive Dr. Xu + Prism, Dynamo + Rapier: Victory!
11. Expert Ironman, Decker + Archive Shalem 11, Fusion + Lockpick 1.0: Victory!
12: Expert Plus with DLC, Archive Decker + Draco, Seed + Golem: Victory!
13. Time Attack, Archive Banks + Dr. Xu, Power Drip + Parasite: Victory!
15. Endless Plus with DLC, Archive Prism + Derek, Fusion + Parasite: survived over 20 days
The main reason I could play the game so many times is that the main campaign is relatively short (maybe 6-8 hours? x1.5 with the DLC enabled). This to me was actually part of the game's charm: because there are many ways your playthrough can go (which missions are offered, which agents you can rescue, which items you can buy; all of which are limited in a single playthrough), each playthrough really feels like you are making the most of what's presented to you to build up your team. And it is NOT the case that you will reach a point where you are definitively "ready for the final mission." The final mission will happen when it happens, and sometimes you will go into thinking you're not prepared because you botched a couple earlier missions, but you will actually manage to succeed. This happened to me more than once, and along with other aspects of the game leads me to believe the game is very well balanced. I like as a design choice that you can mess up along the way but still recover.
Not to mention the mods that the community has created. I just finished my 16th playthrough overall, but the first with a mod enabled (Shogal's Rescuable Archive Agents mod), and about to start my 17th, ready now to enable several mods at once, allowing for new agents, programs, items and enemies. The game's mechanics are easy to understand but hard to master. I'm excited to take what I've learned and apply them to a new challenge.
TL;DR: One of my all-time favourite (turn-based strategy/tactics) games; think XCOM: Enemy Unknown but shorter/with a greater focus on replayability, and less RNG/more procedurally-generated challenges. No manual saving allowed, but 1-5 "undos" per mission depending on difficulty keeps tension high without being overly punishing. DLC adds flavour but the base game is definitely already complete without it.

Pac-Man 256 is a Pac-Man reboot that does not wander as far away from the original as Pac-Man Championship Edition did. The view has been tilted weirdly (as if you were looking over the shoulder of someone playing the original Pac-Man), a ton of skins and powerups (which are unlocked and upgraded via coins collected in-game) have been introduced and the game forces you to move on constantly by destroying the level behind you as time goes by. Apart from those tweaks, it is very much a classic Pac-Man game.
The weird name is probably a reference to the weird obsession with the powers of 2 in the progress system. You need 2, then 4, then 8 and all the way up to 2048 coins to upgrade a power fully. Unless of course it really is the 256th opus in the franchise... Could be, for all I know.
If you loved the classic Pac-Man and played it a lot, chances are you'll have a good time on this game. You'll surely find what you enjoyed in the old classic, with just enough tweaks to discover new things and to have to rethink old strategies and rewire old reflexes.
If you never enjoyed Pac-Man or only its frantic Championship Edition flavor, stay away from this game.

PAC-MAN 256 is a great take on the series that's also quite addictive. Unlike the original game, you make progress by continually moving up the screen rather than trying to clear all of the dots in a given area. The goal is to reach the highest score possible, and you'll do that by eating ghosts, collecting power-ups and making combos of up to 256 dots. Getting a 256 combo can be quite challenging; ghosts (many of which behave in different ways) will try to stop your progress, and like in the original game you'll have to either avoid them or eat them with power pellets.
The game works well with either a keyboard or a controller. There are also different level skins unlocked from the get go, which include ones themed after previous Pac-man games, such as the Championship Edition series. There's also Steam leaderboard support for both highest score and number of 256 combos. Unlocking and upgrading the various power ups will serve as incentive to keep playing, but I found chasing higher scores was more than enough of a reason to return.
PAC-MAN 256 is well worth checking out!

Before you read further, note that my entire childhood was defined by these point and click adventure games, so my expectations are extremely high. I really wanted to enjoy this game. When I first fired it up, I was expecting something along the lines of what I remembered from the later Lucas Arts games such as Grim Fandango and Monkey Island 3. What I got was a very small, very simple game, with some seriously lacking dialog, gameplay and design.
There really is a lack of gameplay across the board with this one. The whole first part of the boys sequence is on rails, and after that, the area he is in (the spaceship) is lacklustre at best with very little to do but explore the on-rails areas you were in at the start, which are very small boring areas with not a lot of stuff to interact with. In fact, there really are no areas in the game with a lot of interaction, nothing like the point and click games of the past or even the present.
The girls sequence is a little more open, but you are still put on a linear sequence of events which are always the same.
The NPCs in the world merely act as a tool to guide the player through the linear sequence of events, which is normally fine, but with NPC dialog being not a lot more than 5 or so questions directed at them about the world and a walk away line, it feels pretty dry and boring. Only a couple of characters are actually interesting throughout the experience. It just feels like the NPCs are waiting for the player to interact with them, instead of acting like real people with questions of their own, not to mention none of them ever move away from their original positions, as if they are glued to the world.
Now onto the other important aspect of a good point and click adventure, the puzzles. They are so simple I didn’t actually have to think about them, with several of them solving themselves on their own. I remember the days when I used to spend a couple game sessions solving a specific puzzle, but this game really offers nothing that isn’t obvious. However, it might be a good starting point for a young child (even though I would suggest Spyfox or Freddie Fish over this any day).
I am not one of those people who gets their kicks from art style so I will just say from what I saw it was pretty good. The music tracks however just weren’t memorable. Usually with games like these there are a couple music pieces which are memorable, but really, I can’t remember any of the music. Nothing like Stan’s themes from the Monkey Island series, or the awesome tracks from Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis.
To finish I will just say this game is forgettable, and it is sad too. I was really hoping they would pull something incredible off which would bring back the genre with a bang, but this game isn’t going to do that for us. I really hope they aren’t going with the (swapping places) idea for part 2, I don’t care to see those old areas again, but heres hoping they make part 2 at least trickier with more interaction and more depthly dialog.

The only motivation is to collect dots to unlock new powerups and coins to upgrade the powerups. The required amount of dots and coins to upgrade and unlock all the power-ups are insanely high and you are required to grind through the game alot of times in order to use new power-ups or the upgraded version of them.
However, the game is still fun in small doses, but I believe there are still better games out there to spent your time on. I would recommend this game to Pac-Man fans as it is still a good game but the grinding element is really a turn off for me. If I were to rate this game, I would give it a 6/10!

Let me begin here - Don't read if you haven't finished the game : If you do you'll most likely ruin one of the best expierences  that you could ever have in a game. And, I mean that.
So I have to admit that I knew that LIS existed long before I played it, from the sound of the title and what friends said it sounded like just another game about some stupidly oversensitive teen girl who faces a world of problems - boring. I couldn't have been more wrong. Jesus... Well, I decided to get the game for free (episode 1) and booted it up to play it alongside a friend in a skype call to check how bad it could be? - 2 minutes into the game I ended the call and went "do not disturb" as the game already initially hooked me - even the music in the corridor when you first leave the class. No matter what people say, this game is beautifully made, I bought the entire season for full price after the bathroom incident when you find out about your power! It sounds stupid saying this, but I truly believe that this is one of if not the greatest game ever made. The art style, the soundtrack, the characters - They're quirky and wierd but they're very believable and you really start to form some sort of pseudo-emotional bond with a bunch of pixels on your screen, and MAXINE -damn, I was so into character when playing I forgot that I'm a guy!
The choices in the story could make larger differences, but at the same time its what keeps the game interesting. You want to know what happens next, but you're able to tailor the game/characters to the way you'd like them. Some might say that the time travel thing is daft, but really. It gives such an amazing factor to the game, something that TaleTale games lack. And talking of story, it is a bit cliche but what really gets you are as I already siadthe characters, for example Warren - starting off as some side and ending as someone I would be as sad loosing as chloe (probably becasue of my choices). Also, the simple features like the photos, or the diary and texts- thats what I spend an easy 20% of my time doing, it really helps you get deeper into the universe - and if you pay enough attention you even notice that your diary gets burned when Jefferson burns it, and in your nightmare you get texts form Rachel Amber and Pompidou XD The ending choice seemed so simple - save arcadia bay?? Or to some save chloe? But, even though it was expected lets be real, it made me cry like a baby with explosive diarrhoea, idk if that metaphor makes any sence but still. The emotional rollercoaster that you ride within this game is just something else, something a book or film just cant represent. I felt like I actually was the character, unlike any other game I've played and really couldn't stop myself from playing the game even if I tried. I don't think the game should get a sequel , but with "before the storm" coming we shall have another hopefully fantastic game to play.

It's all fun and games at first: you fire a few shots from your revolver, kill some lumpy desert mummies, dodge a bullet here and there, probably reach the area boss and feel generally good about yourself. Then you die and start over. And over. And over. Because that's what it's all about - dedication and persistence. So by the time you reach the third area, you'll probably have unlocked some characters and played around with quite a few weapons (occasionally blowing yourself up in the process). You feel more confident now. Familiar with your surroundings. You keep pressing on, fine-tuning your strategies and eventually approaching the ultimate goal, the titular Nuclear Throne, one step at a time.
And it's great. The game has very solid combat mechanics, the weapons all feel "just right". It's enjoyable, it's very challenging, and the constant flow of adrenaline it provides is enough to keep you going for a long time.
Until eventually you hit a wall and stop.
All of a sudden this jolly old rogue-fest turns into a groundhog day simulator. You realize that the levels are always the same. The layouts are randomly generated, of course, but their contents are quite similar every time. Things stop unlocking sooner or later, too, mostly because you're just not good enough. And you could keep practicing and honing your skills, of course, but at that point constantly repeating the easier areas becomes a torturous grind. There's just not enough variety in items and abilities to work for. The challenge is still there, but the reward is gone, and you probably didn't even notice, did you?
I suppose there are two ways to go from there. You either carry on out of dedication or spite for over 900 hours (there are leaderboards and everytrhing), or you simply stop playing, relish what good moments you had with the game and reflect on just how much you value your time.
Try this game either way. It's good.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing

It's not a Mario clone... It's what the developer says: an homage to retro platformers. Tight controls, creative level design, and a nice level of challenge. It took me a little while to really get into it and a lot my early frustrations were a simple matter of needing to "get gud" but this title ultimately stands out to me as a success.
My only criticisms of the game are the lack of achievements/trading cards and the Casual/Retro difficulties. Imo, the only difficulty should be Retro, wherein it saves when you find the secret hidden coins. When playing Retro you can tell the game was designed such that it's meant to be played that way, and the difficulty of certain parts is tuned such that it expects you to have either just saved or that you're just about to save. Conversely, on Casual, where you save at the start of every level, the difficulty sometimes seems lopsided and sporadic.
If you buy this game I strongly encourage playing on Retro and taking the time to explore and find the secret coins, which you need in order to see the real ending anyways.

This is one of those platforming games that aim to be retro and challenging which it accomplishes in a sense, but in a rather bland sense.
For some reason the world has been overrun by a reign of birds and your goal I assume is to take it back. Although the world offers a good number of scenery, the same can't be said for the enemies. As the previous sentence states, the enemies only consist of birds. They fire projectiles in which you're supposed to dodge (for obvious reasons) but that's about it. There's no different sprites, just chirpy chirps, even the bosses are birds. Your projectile is also flawed beyond belief. When you obtain your projectile, you can finally give those feathered ♥♥♥♥faces a taste of their own medicine, but there's one trade-off. If you've already watched the video above, you can clearly see that the projectile fires at a slight upwards slant. Um... why? Why does the projectile fire slightly upwards? I don't see a reason for this and in the obscure Nintendo game "Milon's Secret Castle", proves ineffective and ultimately causes even more frustration when playing.
Game controls are a bit slippery and jumping can be unpredictable at times, jumping on an enemy can send you flying or in other cases bouncing off as if you hit a speed bump. Best thing that can be described is that this game is more hard to play than anything. The game does require you to have some form of precision platforming skills but aside from that the levels are more trial than error if anything. There are many blocks that crumble when you land on them causing you to slightly bounce thus sending you into the pit of the unknown. There are no indications that they are fragile hence "trial and error".
The secrets like the game states is plentiful, but you have so little time to find them that there just isn't anything there to motivate you to do so. I have found some if not most of the secrets by surprise and it's really is nothing special, just a few extra coins or a weapon upgrade but other than that it's nothing. The description says it begs exploring, but you'll be begging for the time to explore it.
All this being said though, the game is I guess worth the price even at original. It is about 10 hours at least worth of gameplay if you play it like normal and even more if you try finding all those secrets. When you buy it on sale on the other hand, it's well under a dollar and if you're into platformers than by all means grab it.

Many fans were skeptical of the micro-transactions in Monolith studios brand new game "Middle-earth™: Shadow of War™". I too was a skeptical fan, but after playing the prolouge (Act I) which took me an astounding 11 hours (On Nemesis difficulty) i did not once see any push for micro-transactions.
They implemented it so you could always see the micro-transactions on the pause screen. But there was no huge display to show them off, just a little side show of in the corner showing you the options they had, and weekly community challenges.
With that big issue out of the way, how is the gameplay? If you have played Monolith's first instalment to the series "Middle-earth™: Shadow of Mordor™", you know exactly what to expect becasue most of the core mechanics stayed the same; Just fleshed out a bit more.
The thing that has changed the most from the first installment is the story, you can tell from just the first act that they are putting a lot more effort into the story; making it more RPG than just a hack and slash. Also in the fashion of a more RPG-styled stance they added different weaponry and equipment; instead of Runes, defeated enemys drop Gear, of a progressive scale of rarity, which can be upgraded further by completing a challenge associated with the weapon.
Overall they did god (So far), i'm enjoying almost every minute of it except when i get a Nemesis enemy with ♥♥♥♥♥♥ traits and is impossible to kill but hey that's half the fun. I hope this has been educational enough to people who are thinking about purchasing this game, and i'll update this after i beat the game.

This game has given me more than 80 hours of joy (with many more to come), and it's time for me to give back.
I would like to preface by saying I got this game on sale during the last Winter sale. Was it worth $7 including DLC? Absolutely. Is it worth $24 with said DLC? Debateable, depending on how much you're sold on this game before buyinig it. Invisible Inc. is an amalgamation of many different things that I love in video games. It's a procedurally-generated, turn-based stealth game with a cyberpunk aesthetic.
You start each campaign with two agents, and it's up to you to direct them through the sprawling, massive levels to accomplish the objectives, whatever they may be. There are four different corporations for you to infiltrate, with locations all around the world. They each have their own strengths and unique units to make life harder for your agents. But the agents are unique too. While you initially only start out being able to choose 2 at the beginning of the  campaign, you unlock many more by gaining XP at the end of each playthrough, whether you succeed or not. Each agent has unique starting skills and abilities, but you can re-spec them throughout a campaign to suit your own, unique playstle. You also gradually unlock new starting programs, which are used for the hacking mechanic. All of Invisible Inc's missions contain hackable items. You can hack a camera and make their eyes into your own, or you can hack into a safe and uncover credits or items. Hacking costs PWR, which is very limited, so it isn't the solution to everything.
Concerning the campaigns, every playthrough is unique. While they begin and end with the same mission types, the level layout and location are always different. Now, the campaign itself is quite short, taking place over the course of just 72 hours, or 120 if you get the DLC. This can be a problem for some people, as you may simply not get the right missions in order to be prepared for the brutal final assault at the end. I personally, don't get mad when I have to start over, because it just means I get to play more Invisible Inc.
The missions (you'll have time for about 5-7 of them in a 72 hour campaign), are thrilling high-risk, high-reward endeavors that provide a lot of memorable moments. There are many different mission types, such as robbing corporate vaults or accessing a server farm. They each present their own unique challenges; crack that vault open, and enforcer units will arrive to investigate the location. Universally, though, all missions have a turn limit of sorts. Even if your agents remain completely undetected, without disturbing any sentries, the alarm level gradually ramps up each turn. When the alarm stage increases, the mission becomes more difficult. Additional cameras activate, more guards arrive, and they eventually pinpoint your location. You spend the entire time stalked by this turn counter, so every move counts. In addition to main objectives, you may stumble across a side-mission that unlocks additional awards if completed. They're rather limited in the base game, but the DLC adds many more.
The story is rather minimal, which I found disappointing just because of the interesting universe that is implied by the parts we do see. The dev team was pretty small, and only three characters receive voice acting. For a team this small, I'm glad they focused on the gameplay, but your mileage may vary.
Overall, Invisible Inc is an absolutely thrilling experience that I recommend to anyone who enjoys turn-based tactics, stealth, or just cyberpunk in general. If you're interested but not fully convinced, then just wait for it to go on sale. I, for one, am happy to give Klei my money so they can hopefully make games like this, and perhaps, one day, a sequel.

I really wanted to write a funny review, but this game, second in a trilogy, is pretty serious. So, The Banner Saga 2. Damn, what a game. It picks up immediately after the end of the original with the clan continuing on to try and reach Arberrang, the capital of the humans. Of course, the Choices Matter approach is implemented, and your choices do affect the caravan's welfare. Most of the choices may have small aftereffects, but some can seriously come back to haunt you. You will have to sometimes fight for your caravan's good morale, particularly under the caravan of Rook/Alette (which one depends on the choices you made in the first game), which brings me to my next point.
You can start this game off without playing the first Banner Saga, but I highly recommend playing it beforehand for a multitude of reasons. The biggest reason is obviously that you will understand this game much, much better with the help of the first games story, the secondary reason is that the first game is freaking brilliant. If you play the first game beforehand, you can import your save game and continue onwards. This being said, there is an option to start a new game completely from scratch, and you can choose to lead as either Alette or Rook. On the home screen, there is also access to a recap of what happened in the first game. I found this to be useful even as a returning player.
At the end of Chapter 2, the caravan splits, and the mercenaries hired in Boersgard, the Ravens, split with Rook/Alette. Bolverk, the leader of the Ravens, is one of the most well thought out and developed characters in any game I've ever played. The story does feel a little bit like a middle-story, but this is ignorable with the addition of Bolverk as a main character. I think the game really makes Bolverk out as the main character, and I cannot wait to see what awaits Bolverk in the third and final game in this magnificent trilogy. Rook's caravan, meanwhile, goes south and encounters the horseborn. These centaur-like creatures are one of the many added combat bonuses in the second game.
I have played through both games on Normal Difficulty, and I have actually found the first game to be much more difficult, battle-wise. The AI in the second game is not quite as well programmed, but it is more varied and enjoyable which makes the poor programming negligible. Despite the AI, the combat is much better, and sufficiently challenging. I greatly enjoyed the turn-based battles.
A new game-mode has been added, and I have found it to be very enjoyable. Survival Mode has all the characters that you can fight with in story-mode, but once you pick your initial 6 characters, you don't have access to the others unless you recruit them with renown you earn through battle. You then proceed to fight in 40 battles that occured throughout the game. I have found this gamemode to be enjoyable, but also very challenging and PUNISHING. When a character dies, they aren't injured, as in story-mode, but they are DEAD. This is devastating if you have been promoting this character. This causes you to want to recruit a new character after the character is killed. This sufficiently detracts from your renown because for your character to be useful, you must promote them, and they are recruited at level 3. All in all, Survival Mode is a huge added bonus to a game that is already beyond stellar and well worth it's full price.
The art style of the characters and environment is absolutely freaking beautiful. When the credits rolled, despite the absolute mind-freak (yep, there's a cliffhanger!) I just kind of sat there and listened to the music, which was simply beautiful. Every piece of music and art in the game nearly took my breath away, particularly when Bolverk and the Ravens take the underground tunnels to escape from the mountains. Similarly to the first game, you come across many godstones in the game which are still just as beautiful. If you are playing as Rook, you may even find a pleasant surprise awaits you at one of the final Godstones.
Overall, the game is freaking brilliant. I highly recommend it to anyone new or returning to the series. Quick piece of advice, though. If playing on Survival Mode, do not use an item that draws aggro. I made the mistake of doing this and quickly lost my key tank.

Overall: 9.75/10

Free to Play:
No, you can't pay to win, to be honest you can play this game without every spending a dime. You can unlock all the champions with very little grinding, if you even call just playing the game grinding.
Comparing to Overwatch:
Those people who compare this to Overwatch and call it a cheap knock off have not played this game at all. This is no where near Overwatch there are so many key fundemental differences. Mac can run this, and by run I mean you would get 30FPS+ on mostly low settings 720p on a MacBook Air, which lets all be honest should not even be able to run Solitaire on Ultra Low settings.

Sound:

Now for the key reason i got the game. The nemisis system. It is so much better. numerous changes to the combat mechanics ballance the game so that you are no longer overpowered yet they still managed to provide you with at least 20 new ways to kill captains so while i cant just hack and slash mindlessly anymore i can poison, curse, shoot them in the face while flying in the air, summon mounts, and have lethal counters. To me this is the cake of the game. The fact that the nemisis system has been compounded on and works alot better. I used to regularly slaughter 6 captain bodyguards and their warchief in the old game but now i get worried when there are 2 and i actively evade combat for 4 captains and up because they are much more agressive, almost all the captains are a threat now, and their ability to adapt to conventional combat makes frontal assault pretty much only a last option or a finishing blow. I play on the highest dificulty and have died 3 times, twice the captain had the "no chance" perk that prevents me from getting a second wind. I dont think i have been able to go toe to toe with a single captain because every skill only works 2-3 times before they adapt and then it is useless. The main skills i have actually seen adaptations on include vaulting over a captain, wraith stun/freeze, throwing knives, and one even adapted to stealth after a 4th attempt.
Worth noting that decapitating pesky captains is pretty much required as the return rate is insane. Almost a 3rd of my kills have returned and they seem to return anywhere based on a trigger (like low health or killing an enemy a certain way. even had one sneak up on me after i poisoned some grog and he told me i used to much poison.....) so you can have a captain or 2 ambush you while your trying to deal with a captain already anyway. At least they seriously buffed your mobility skills to near god-like levels (you can leap several floors vertically up a wall to climb a large tower in maybe 5-8 seconds.).

Let me begin here - Don't read if you haven't finished the game : If you do you'll most likely ruin one of the best expierences  that you could ever have in a game. And, I mean that.
So I have to admit that I knew that LIS existed long before I played it, from the sound of the title and what friends said it sounded like just another game about some stupidly oversensitive teen girl who faces a world of problems - boring. I couldn't have been more wrong. Jesus... Well, I decided to get the game for free (episode 1) and booted it up to play it alongside a friend in a skype call to check how bad it could be? - 2 minutes into the game I ended the call and went "do not disturb" as the game already initially hooked me - even the music in the corridor when you first leave the class. No matter what people say, this game is beautifully made, I bought the entire season for full price after the bathroom incident when you find out about your power! It sounds stupid saying this, but I truly believe that this is one of if not the greatest game ever made. The art style, the soundtrack, the characters - They're quirky and wierd but they're very believable and you really start to form some sort of pseudo-emotional bond with a bunch of pixels on your screen, and MAXINE -damn, I was so into character when playing I forgot that I'm a guy!
The choices in the story could make larger differences, but at the same time its what keeps the game interesting. You want to know what happens next, but you're able to tailor the game/characters to the way you'd like them. Some might say that the time travel thing is daft, but really. It gives such an amazing factor to the game, something that TaleTale games lack. And talking of story, it is a bit cliche but what really gets you are as I already siadthe characters, for example Warren - starting off as some side and ending as someone I would be as sad loosing as chloe (probably becasue of my choices). Also, the simple features like the photos, or the diary and texts- thats what I spend an easy 20% of my time doing, it really helps you get deeper into the universe - and if you pay enough attention you even notice that your diary gets burned when Jefferson burns it, and in your nightmare you get texts form Rachel Amber and Pompidou XD The ending choice seemed so simple - save arcadia bay?? Or to some save chloe? But, even though it was expected lets be real, it made me cry like a baby with explosive diarrhoea, idk if that metaphor makes any sence but still. The emotional rollercoaster that you ride within this game is just something else, something a book or film just cant represent. I felt like I actually was the character, unlike any other game I've played and really couldn't stop myself from playing the game even if I tried. I don't think the game should get a sequel , but with "before the storm" coming we shall have another hopefully fantastic game to play.

I wanted more Championship Edition, but what I got was child's edition.
It's mobile-game style endless Pac-Man, which means grinding one randomized, endless level for coins to buy upgrades to use in that level, rinse and repeat. But even compared to other rubbish mobile games, Pac-Man 256 is boring. At least in Jetpack Joyride the upgrades make the game feel different, and the scenery changes.
I would rather play Pac-Man 1 for a few reasons:
- It had levels, so something to aim for, something to discover.
- It had lives, and as that supply dwindled, and you risked getting kicked back to the start, the game got more intense. In 256 one hit kills you, and you are supposed to die at some point anyway, so you can deposit your bloody coins, which takes quite a bit of the excitement of progressing out of it.
- The maps didn't go on forever, so it wasn't just about dodging a ghost once, but what you did after that, and after that. Sometimes you had to exploit the ghost's AI to escape, such as scaring away Clyde or confusing Pinky. That's what Pac-Man was all about, for me, so this game doesn't even get nostalgia points because it ♥♥♥♥s it up.
So after 255 sequels this series has actually gotten worse.
There is one cool mechanic in 256, actually, which is how as you eat pellets in an unbroken chain, and your combo increases, the sound effect frequency increases, until, after a minute or so, the beat is out of control and it climaxes in a satisfying screen-wiping explosion. It's kind of addictive. But not worth installing the game again.

Take the classic formula of Pac-Man chowing down on those little white dots and power pellets and turn it into an endless runner. Inspired by the infamous level 256 where due to memory limitations half of the level would glitch out this game has the bottom portion of the screen constantly being eaten up by a glitch forcing you to run away and continue upwards.
This game retains the awesome mechanics of the original... Eat, eat, eat and run from ghosts. The original ghosts are all back as well as the addition of a new ghost glitchy. This port from the original does have some changes. They have removed all the microtransactions which is a welcome feature and have added the option to play multiplayer! Co-op play in this is a blast. It gets very tense and if you die your team mate will have the opportunity to revive you. You can work together to unlock new power ups and continue to improve your score.
The graphics are off the hook! you have never seen such cutting edge pixels in your life! it will make your eyes bleed! In all seriousness this is a great presentation. It keeps the feel of the old while updating it and making it feel like something fresh and new. There are several different themes that you can choose from including the developers previous title crossy road.
All together I think one of the freshest takes on Pac-Man in recent years, and possibly even since its inception. A lot of fun to play in short bursts and true to its source material. I definitely recommend to people looking for a challenge or something as a quick burst of fun that you will keep coming back to.
This is not just a game. It is an experience which cannot be described in words.

I find the original Pac-Man arcade game no fun, but Pac-Man 256 is LOADS of fun!
Pac-Man 256 builds its maze procedurally as you nom through the pellets and power-ups, avoiding ghosts and eating them, in alternating phases. What's better is that each type (color) of ghost has a special behavior, so you know what they'll try to do as you approach. If you can swerve accordingly, gaining points, power-ups, etc, I imagine the maze is infinite.
The power-ups are fun, though some are definitely better than others. You can pick up coins in the maze, and earn bonus coins for completing missions (and earn random coin "gift" boxes) that you can spend on leveling up your power-ups. The power-ups have a limited time that can be extended by eating other power-up pellets, in order to chain your power-up to make it last as long as possible. Though the easiest to "chain" is the original Power-Pellet because you also gain extra time for eating ghosts (whereas the other power-ups "kill" them).
I can't recommend this game enough. It's definitely one that will stay installed on my computer for whenever I have downtime or want to unwind.

Broken Age is the game that launched a thousand Kickstarters... well, not really as Kickstarter existed 3 years prior to but I digress.  The original Double Fine Adventure arguably brought Kickstarter into the mainstream light.  After suffering a series of delays and controversial pre-production images that questioned the infamous "3.3 million dollar" funding, how does the final product hold up?
Very well.  Broken Age is a game of unrequited vision: a product designed by visionaries for a very specific audience.  The title of the game represents  adolescents, the titular "Broken Age" being the lives of the two protagonists who are caught in the pains of growing up.  Vella was groomed to be sacrificed to a monster and Shay lives his life aboard a ship run by a coddling AI.  Through a series of events the two characters break free from routine and challenge their place in life.  The result is a game that looks like a Little Golden Book and contains writing that's both light hearted and darkly comedic.
People expecting a puzzle heavy logic adventure like the classic LucasArts days will be disappointed.  There's little challenge here and nothing is really taxing on the mind.  But like Telltale's recent titles, Broken Age's strength lies in its presentation.  It is all style, little substance, but the style is more than entertaining to make up for its shortcomings.

Ok, if you've played this game, you already know it's a Mario clone, so naturally you'd have the expectation of that type of gameplay experience going into it, just as I did.  What I didn't realize is that playing SMB as a kid and playing this now are vastly different.  In other words, I'm old now and this game is F'ING HARD!  It's hard to time my jumps, and also keep from dying or losing my shield or gun when I try to kill those blue birds that speed up and don't die the first time you hit them.  The disintegrating platforms cause me to die often, too.  On the rising "lava" level, when I'm trying to jump up from blocks and they turn into stupid coins when there's already a blue bird there trying to kill me, that causes me to die repetitively.  That part is very cheap in my opinion, but it is what it is.  The only real complaint I have outside of the difficulty at this point (I warped to level 2-9, I think) is that the responsiveness of the jumps is a bit sluggish when you're trying to jump repeatedly to get the max # of coins from one of those blocks with multiple coins in them.  In SMB (back in my day) you could get a fast rythm going and Mario would jump again just as soon as his feet hit the ground.  8bitBoy won't--there is a slight delay before you can jump again so it throws off the repetitive jump rythm.  Aside from that, I haven't seen anything yet regarding the game mechanics that pisses me off.  In summary, if you got an NES as a kid, and you want to revisit it and relive the magic with a new game, be forewarned, it may be a lot harder than it was back then, on top of the fact that this is a brand new non-Mario game so it's not a well-worn, many times rehearsed path that you'll take.  I've quit in frustration for the 3rd time today, and I've only played for 36 minutes if that tell you anything.  I'd say it was worth the 2 bux I paid, but I don't know if I will finish it, if it gets progressively harder.  It's already hard enough for me as it is.

Nuclear Throne is a perfect example of what fast paced bullet hell-esque big gun shoot em' up indie games aspire to be. The humor may not be visible at first but is actually witty and silly and the messages between levels help piece together the lore of this game (because as of now there isn't a lore tab in the game) and it is enjoyable to learn tidbits about your favorite characters. The guns are fun and great and ridiculous at times. Double minigun anyone? The enemies are varied and the design and models of them are colourful and visually appealing. The mutations (when you level up you get an upgrade that lasts for your whole run) are fun and creating crazy builds really adds to the whole experience of the game. The characters themselves are pretty wild because hey it's a post-apocalyptic wasteland and everything is all irradiated and crazy. The game is hard but the challenge is fair and add to the whole experience. Every loss you get is all wiped away when you get to finally fight the throne, because of course you have to fight a throne. The background music is perfect and some of the tracks can be upbeat and some can send chills down your spine.
I personally rate the overall game 8.6/10

This is a classic Obsidian game. Many things feel unpolished, but because the writing, reactivity, and character building are done well, Alpha Protocol is unique experience.
Unlike other games released released in the same period, dialogue and choices aren't just broken into two camps (evil and good) and instead are given a range of responses, representing the personality of Mike. The player is also not given unlimited time to choose their responses either so one has to prepared, i.e. reading dossiers, when talking to npcs. Even better, characters actually respond differently depending on your choices. If they respond postively to your choices in the present, they may act differently in future encounters. They may help you in later missions or give you access to certain upgrades.  Sometimes causing one character to dislike you will cause another to like you more. This kind of reactivity is not found in most games on the market today.
Yes, the game is short, the controls are clunky, and the combat is not really that great. But one is missing the core of this is game if they are focusing on those things instead of the reactivity . IMHO, it's better have a game that does a few things great than one that is a blob of mediocrity.

The game plays like an objective-shooter. There are 2 main game types: Siege and Payload. in Payload a cart full of explosives spawns on a track and your team has to stand next to it to push the cart forward while fending off the enemy team. At the end of the time limit the teams switch sides and the defenders are now taksed with pushing the payload as far as they can. At the end, whatever team got the furthest with their payload will win. I'm not sure what happens if there is a tie. I haven't seen one yet :-p
In Siege a neutral "hill" spawns in the middle of the map and both teams compete to try and take the hill to earn the point. The team that takes a hill then spawns a payload to try and push down the other half of the map for another point while the other team defends. The first team to 4 points wins the game. The one thing that I find odd is that the team that loses the hill (and therefore defends against the payload) actually earn a point for a successful payload defense. And after capturing the hill the capturing team is only given 2 minutes to push the payload, so the defenders usually win. As a result 90% of Siege games come down to the last round of King of the Hill.
I would like to see some improvements be made to the UI in general, as well as some shop tweaks and possibly a rehaul on the scoring system in Siege (though I do love the game mode overall)

The plot and writing are well done. I cannot say that I don't love Life is Strange. It's definitely one of the most engaging and well written games I've played recently. It also has replay value - I'm trying to play through it again so I can see the different choices and how they adjust things.
What got me to buy the game at first, however, was the possibility of leaning Chloe and Max towards a queer relationship. Not to say I wasn't interested before, because I definitely wanted to know more about the plot, but before the final episode came out I decided to spend $20 on the full game purely because I was a gay kid desperate for more representation. I could have found out about the ending through let's plays, but I wanted to experience it for myself.
And as a gay kid, the endings really let me down. I pored over my choices for a long time... and I got the most heartbreaking choice I've ever needed to make in a video game. I won't spoil it - but I'll say one ending employs an awful trope, and the other is quite the letdown.
I do really love Life is Strange and I can tell that a lot of care was put into it. I've seen videos of the voice actors and writers talking about how much they love the characters, and I can believe them just by looking at it. The cheesiness of some of the lines is even endearing. I recommend it, but just to people who are more interested in the plot than in Pricefield.

Great game, fun for old school RPG, replay without question to see other endings and other choices, This game reminded me of KOTOR 2, with a modern twist. At the price it was being sold at it's worth it.

With all of the rave reviews, and the first episode being free, I was excited to check this game out. Oh my god, do I hate it already. What a letdown. It's promising enough until you wake up in the classroom, and then it rapidly goes downhill. The controls to interact with objects in the room are rip-your-hair-out annoying, particularly if you're on a laptop and have a trackpad to work with. *wave* It's not that the controls are buggy, it's just that they're far more complicated than they need to be. Click and hold  to produce a popup menu, and then drag in the direction of the interaction of your choice - simple enough to say it, but is highly annoying in practice, particularly when you'd like to rapidly explore an area instead of moving at a snail's pace.
My other complaint is all of the cussing. I swear myself, and am not offended by swearing, but the amount of cussing in this game just comes across as over-the-top and pathetic. And the swear words are so poorly placed it seems like it was written by a 10 year old who was gleefully employing "naughty words" for the first time ever. Ugh. Just distractingly immature, making it difficult to take the game seriously. If you're going to use swear words, do it right or don't do it at all. I should not be face-palming every ten seconds of dialogue. The developers should dial up the refinement just ever so slightly to correct this unfortunate effect.
I'll continue playing (unless I reach a point where the game makes me want to throw my laptop across the room - which seems possible at this point), and hope episode 1 will redeem itself, but I foresee an insipid experience at best. Sure hope I'm wrong. At this point, I feel it my duty to preserve the serenity of my fellow gamers by not recommending this game. If this review doesn't get updated to anything more positive, well, you'll know why.

A fantastic spin on the classic that stays true to classic Pac-Man while being supremely addictive. Basically it's an infinite Pac-Man maze where you have to survive as long as possible, and you get bonus points if you manage to eat 256 consecutive dots. To keep things fresh, you basically play to unlock further power-ups which make you more and more powerful. It's a good progression that makes you really want to play one more game to get the next powerup, but doesn't feel like a grind. Each round gives a great sense of progress and I topped out the final power-up after about 10 hours of play, which felt like good value and even now I find myself still playing just to top my old scores. Pac-Man 256 isn't quite as flashy or over-the-top as the also-excellent Championship games, but I feel like there's more room for strategizing with how you can pick what powerups you want, and there's a great sense of split-second decision making: Do I go for the powerup or try to keep the dot chain going? Can I keep this going, or should I escape the ghosts? Stuff like that makes the game fun and exciting and it feels like no two rounds are ever quite the same. Great game!

Drawing inspiration from kill screen from the classic game, getting to level 256 will result in a glitch that ends the game.  Using that as the inspiration, this game involves trying to get away from that glitch by making it into an endless runner.  By changing the formula, does it result in a better game?
Being made by the same people that made the mobile game
, the game has the same look and feel of that game.  The graphics shared the same block look of that game.  One thing that is good about this is that for those that prefer a different look, the game offers multiple styles to customize it to the player's taste.  From the Namco's
and
to Hipster Whale's
and even a few surreal styles like an office, a garden, and inside a computer, the variety makes it that there is something for everybody.  There is even an option to randomize it to make each game feel different every time.
Just like classic
, the player has to go through mazes while eating dots, power ups, and bonus items while avoiding the ghosts.  Since it was also made by the same company that made
, the game also involves constant forward movement to avoid the glitch—the thing where the title's 256 came from.  Besides the classic power pellets, new power ups like lasers and fire and new ways to attack the ghost or protect the player—all of which are upgradable through coins collected through gameplay.  Additionally, the game keeps tracks of not only your own score, but the scores of your friends as well.  This makes that the player has incentive keep playing to beat their friend's score.
Even with these updates, there is one big problem with the game.  Unlike the classic games, the game involves constantly moving forward instead of clearing each maze.  This makes it that the player has to move forward constantly instead of going after every dot.  Since each pattern will pass in just a few seconds, the maze will start repeating after only a couple of minutes.  Even with the extra looks mentioned before, it does not change the fact that it is the same few maze patterns looping around.  Despite the new features, it does not take long before the game feels like a big case of déjà vu.
One thing that brings the gameplay above its mobile roots is that up to four players can play at the same time.  Each player selects their look, and they work with (or against) each other to fight the ghosts.  The combined scored will be on the top just like the singleplayer mode.  As for the individual scores, they appear on the side where the friend scores normally appear.  Unlike the single player, it does not necessarily mean game over when an enemy catches you.  Once something catches a player, a spinning Pac-Man item will appear.  Grabbing it will bring the dead player back.  This is one way that the game allows players choose to work with or against each.  If they want help, grabbing it means more ways to attack the ghosts.  However, if treating the game like a versus game, players can leave it alone to boost their own score.  This makes that you will even question what kind of game you are in once you are waiting to see if the other players will bring you back or not.  With this level of unpredictability, the multiplayer is much better overall experience than the single player game.
Whether this game is worth playing depends on how people will play with it.  As a single player game, it will get old fast.  However, by adding multiplayer, the game has enough life to justify continuous play.  Make sure that you plan to play with other players.  Without them, there is not content to warrant a purchase.

Will you reach the nuclear throne?
I hope so cuz I sure haven’t! This is a rather hard one where you will die and die often. It gives me that unending feel of determination where every failure you learn something new and you always make it just a little farther then you did last time. It’s cut from the same cloth as Binding of Isaac so if you like that you’ll probably enjoy this.
Notably enjoyable differences however are a smaller pool of upgrades but with the trade-off of the upgrades being really good and game change in a lot of respects, especially when synergized with other upgrades. You also get to choose from a list of 4 every time and let me tell you, it’s rarely ever easy when it comes which one to grab. Enemies have a lot of complexity to them and analyzing how they move, when and how they attack and their own personal quarks leads to a rather fully realized environment. Characters are radically different and gear toward drastically varying playstyles.  even doing the beginning of the game over and over again never feels too easy and there is always enough danger to keep you alert and on guard.
There are a few issues here and there. some enemies have frustrating abilities that can be tricky to remember in the heat of constant action, unlocking hidden characters requires some backward moon logic to discover (I looked it up and I recommend you do too) and every character, even the ones with more health feel like they got glass for bones and certain hazards can instantly kill you no matter how much health you got!
The whole game feels like a literal wasteland. The worlds gone to hell and it’s up to you to attempt to navigate a cruel and uncaring world. If that sings to you then give this a shot. See if you dare reach the throne!
PS. there is a character that makes air horn sounds and he’s the best for that single reason

Middle Earth Shadow of War is my idea of a succesful sequel. It fixes almost all of Mordor's Weaknesses, and adds a grand amount of content on a massive scale. The story is better, the world is bigger, and i've couldn't have been happier about the way the game itself turned out.
Graphics: The base game's graphics are not substantially better looking than Shadow of Mordor, but that isnt a bad thing. Shadow of Mordor was a fantastic looking game, and this game is no different. Absolutely gorgeous graphics. The devs released a day 1 free dlc  to make the game look even better and let me say it does its job. Graphics get a 9/10
Sound: Soundtrack does an ok job at playing the appropriate track for the situation, sometimes I'll get the battle music when in stealth mode, which gets you a bit riled up even though you havent even been seen, but it happens quite rarely. The music itself is great. The menu and pause screen music is freaking awesome and it hypes me up every time I launch the game. The cutscenes are improved immensely and the overall game feels more cinematic with a good soundtrack and thery absolutely nailed it here. another 9/10
World: From what i've seen this game has a massive world. Stretching through mordor and parts of Gondor, including some of the most recognizable places in the LOTR universe. I love the addition of areas outside mordor, as in the first game the mordor scene got kind of old really quick. The combat was fun, but it didnt feel like a game in middle earth. This  improves the game greatly, and it finally feels like a middle earth game. 7/10
Story: The story is written pretty generically, just a continuation of the first so far, but the cutscene cinematics are on point and the voice acting is on another level for the videogame industry. These large AAA games are getting to be more and more cinematic and I like this trend. I haven't Finished every quest yet, but so far the game has me hooked, and I'll come back and edit this for sure. 8/10
Mechanics/Port: Day 1 bugs are already fixed and the game runs great on my PC. I am currently running a mid to high end system (gtx 1070, intel i7), and I can crank the settings all the way up and still get a constant 60 with no tearing. The requirements speak for themselves. The mechanics are similar to the first game, the game does add quite a few new moves, and it feels really fresh and innovative. Mounting a Troll and stabbing his back repeatedly, mounting a drake and breathing fire on everyone below, things like this add so much to the game and make it that much cooler.
Other: Of course the micro transaxtions are here and im not factoring it in to the review. Im just ignoring them for now and ive gotten along fine without them. All of those people review bombing are just missiong out on a really good game. What a shame.
Overall this is a great sequel to a good game. It adds so much to the first , and as a huge LOTR fan I can say this was worth $60. 8/10

I gave this gem a miss when it first came out, AFAICR because the reviews were quite off-putting. Having finally played it, I can't think why.
This is a game in the spirit of Deus Ex, and for the most part, it pulls it off.
- no fundamentally different / unique aproaches to mission (you can sneak, go in guns blazing or mix & match)
- no adventure-style missions, where you just walk around in your civvies and talk to people, maybe solve a puzzle or two. There are a few talking-only missions (and one exception from the rule).
+ dialogue, reputation and dossier system works really well, even though you only get a few choices at each juncture.
+ lots of meaningful choices, some with more impact, some with less, some more obvious, others less so. The story tree must be enormous, yet the game never gives you a line that doesn't fit what you did three missions back. This thing is really well written.
+ replayability looking good, though I've only done one run.
+ console roots are unmistakable, but it works fine on Windows.
It's not Deus Ex (not sure if one can surpass that), and it's not Human Revolution either (didn't have the budget), but it isn't Invisible War either. Recommended.
