PAC-MAN 256 is another variant of the famous PAC-MAN formula.
The basic Pac-Man gameplay is more or less intact but the game adds infinite random levels and upgradable powerups to the mix. Unfortunately neither of these additions really improves the base game.
The random levels are a decent idea, but they cause some problems too. Most importantly, they do make the gameplay rather unfair too. Even in the original PAC-MAN you sometimes end up in unwinnable situations, but in PAC-MAN 256 this is a far too common occurance as you can only see a small section of the (infinite) level around you.
The loadout system on the other hand feels like a pointless addition and the only justification for its existance seems to be the microtransactions in the original mobile release. The microtransactions are thankfully gone in the Steam version, but that doesn't make the rather grindy unlocks any more exciting or meaningful.
Overall I didn't feel that PAC-MAN 256 adds much to the original game, you are much better off playing the far superior PAC-MAN Championship Edition instead.
The good:
- The core Pac-Man gameplay still holds up well
The bad:
- The upgrade system feels extremely grindy and pointless
- The random levels lead to too many unfair situations

PAC-MAN 256 is a variant on the venerable game of PAC-MAN. It is an endless arcade game where you, controlling PAC-MAN, navigate your way through a maze, collecting dots along the way. Unlike the traditional PAC-MAN game, however, the maze is endless in the vertical direction. Using procedural generation, you must navigate your way upwards, while being pursued by the glitch – a wave of numbers, garbage characters, and darkness which gradually eats up the maze from below.
The title of this game – and the wave of darkness that pursues you – are references to a glitch in the original PAC-MAN game, where the 256th level created a bunch of garbage on the screen, generating an impassible kill-screen.
The game itself is very reminiscient of PAC-MAN, but is somewhat more sophisticated; there’s about twice as many ghost types, each of which have their own behavioral pattern. If PAC-MAN touches any ghost or the wall of glitches at the bottom of the screen, it is game over.
Orange ghosts try to go to the bottom of the screen, choosing to turn towards the horizontal side of the screen that PAC-MAN is on, but always turning down when able.
Red ghosts pursue PAC-MAN endlessly.
Pink Ghosts will remain dormant until PAC-MAN comes into a straight line with them, at which point the ghost will fly towards PAC-MAN at a speed faster than PAC-MAN’s own.
Grey ghosts will sleep until PAC-MAN approaches, then pursue PAC-MAN via the shortest route.
Teal ghosts will circle endlessly around a certain portion of the map, generally a single wall; this can sometimes lead to unexpected behavior, though, as they can also circle the OUTSIDE of the map, which can make them somewhat unpredictable when first spotted.
Green Ghosts always appear in groups of 3-4, and move a bit slower than PAC-MAN in a horizontal back-and-forth manner.
Purple Ghosts are similar to Green Ghosts, but move back and forth much more slowly, but will track PAC-MAN’s horizontal movement; you must move around them reasonably quickly (or use a power-up) to get past them.
Glitch ghosts constantly change color, and occasionally teleport around the battlefield; they pursue the player somewhat slowly.
All of this combines to make the core gameplay a bit different from normal PAC-MAN, but still familiar in many ways.
There are power-ups that you can pick up over the course of the game to kill ghosts with or to do other things. In addition to the basic power pills which turn ghosts blue, slowing them down and allowing you to eat them by running over them (and scoring ever more points by doing so), there are 21 powerups with various other effects. About half of them are variations on the power pill, but with added powers – one leaves a firey trail behind you, another shoots a laser beam in front of PAC-MAN, a third turns all ghosts in a radius around PAC-MAN into cherries, fruit which also appear naturally and give you extra points and a point multiplier.
The other half of the abilities are stranger. There are a couple of abilities that create roving entities that home in on ghosts and kill them for you, but don’t make PAC-MAN himself invincible. There are some abilities which simply slow down ghosts, which are pretty bad abilities, but one of them also gives you the ability to score a bunch of extra points (generally inferior to just killing ghosts, though). One creates static traps around the map to kill ghosts, and a couple allow PAC-MAN to gather dots, power-ups, and fruits in a wider radius.
You may select up to three of these abilities before you start each game, and the abilities are gradually unlocked by eating dots. The abilities can also be levelled-up by spending in-game currency on them, found via random loot drops after games, as well as by completing various tasks that the game gives you (such as eating five apples, or killing 20 ghosts with the tornado power-ups).
While all of this combines to make the game feel like it has a bit more of a point than a standard PAC-MAN game, in the end the game here is very simple, and it starts to get pretty samey after a while. While adding the unlockable power-ups makes the game a bit more interesting, and the various quests add a slight spin on things, the reality is that the game itself is very samey – there is a multiplayer mode and a single-player mode, but both are just endlessly running down a maze which, in the end, doesn’t have all that many variations on it.
It is a kind of mindless game, and it isn’t bad for what it is. But what it is isn’t exactly aiming for the stars; it is an extremely simplistic game, and most people will likely get bored with it pretty quickly. It is ultimately a bit of a time-waster, and probably better suited for mobile gaming than sitting down and playing it at a PC – it is just not a very sophisticated game. As such, it is difficult for me to recommend it.

Like the 1st game, BS2 is built upon a solid gameplay formula and fascinating worldsetting. Unfortunately, the execution falls apart. Stoic Studio behaves like that spiteful, arrogant artsy kid, bragging about the genius of their work but simultaneously mocks you for playing their game.
If you're new to the turn-base strategy genre, the game is going to feel utterly alienating. And Stoic really doens't bother to hold your hand. You're thrown into the thick of battle to fend yourselves. You're going to make mistakes and you're going to feel it. Not in a satisfying "everytime I retry I get a little better" kind of way. But in a "I'm hours into this playthrough and I just realized I don't have enough high level characters to get through this battle and now I must start all over" kind of way.
If you're a perfectionist then you're going to hate this game. The game doesn't allow you to make saves. You frequently find yourself having to replay entire chapters of the game to reverse a bad decision. Even that is frequently marred by the devs' sadistic, spiteful attempts at making life difficult for you. You want to get a power save to import into the next game in the franchise? We'll make it that the point of import is hours before the end of the game. So you'll have to replay hours of the game and watch unskippable cutscenese over and over again if you want that perfect save files.
Some games feel like a labor of love. Both Banner Saga games feel like labor of spite. Spite towards Stoic's own fanbase. As you play the game you never feel appreciate. You feel like a sucker sticking out throughout the deliberate abuse the devs hurl your way. Because they want to be "different".
Play the game game only because you want a genuine challenge, or if you really like viking mythologies; don't play the game because you want to support indie gaming. Stoic won't thank you for it. And it showed.

I just do not understand the love for this game. I really want to enjoy it and experience what other people are saying about the game, but reading people's reviews, I feel like I'm playing something else entirely... like an early alpha build compared to what they're playing. I've put quite a lot of time into trying to get things to make sense or work as everybody else describes (over 26 hours), and it's simply not enjoyable. I have heard some people saying it was all better before the v1.2 updates, but I didn't play the game back then so I have no idea.
The space physics are fun to play with, when you can actually get into space, since I did go through the tutorials (except that docking one which I never could finish). Getting to stable orbit in career mode is a challenge, but I am far, far more challenged by flaws in the game's physics and controls than in the actual concepts of rocket science.
This game is very heavily physics based, but has so many problems with rudimentary things. Every time I want to do a launch, I have to restart over and over before it actually functions anything like expected. I can't imagine playing without being able to revert the flight, if only for the first 30 seconds of each flight!
Like any time I try to build anything out horizontally, my craft will constantly shift and bounce like it's only held together by rubber bands. It doesn't help that the rockets and planes always spawn off of the ground. Just the mere act of putting my rocket on the launch pad is enough to cause excessive jiggling. Then there's the wait for the jiggling to stop, and then you try to launch and look... it wasn't quite done jiggling, so now your rocket flies over and blows up the administration building. Well, there's a stabilizer you can add, so I try using that, and it holds the rocket in the air so when I release it, it jiggles for the foot or so before bumping the ground, and since it's jiggling, the rocket promptly falls over and explodes. It only took about 30 tries to get the rocket to go straight up when starting the launch with the stabilizer... This is all with a less than 30 parts rocket.
Then there's the airplanes. How does anybody ever meaningfully do anything with airplanes? First off, I have to upgrade the air strip to remove the excessive bumps on it to even be able to get started on trying. Then, good luck getting your aircraft to go straight, regardless of how everything was meticulously placed with mirror mode and the different weight and thrust values were checked. When you finally DO get it to kinda go straight down the run way, then it hits a seam in the run way and starts bouncing around, the parts start jiggling, a wing barely scrapes the ground and explodes, then it all catastrophically fails. Having to try 40+ times every time you want to launch a very simplistic plane because the physics engine is so buggy is simply not fun...
And when you DO finally get a launch to go off properly, the janky controls make any sort of precision or proper control over the craft very difficult. This is ESPECIALLY true with planes, and coming from playing a number of flight and space simulators (yes, they're playable with a mouse and keyboard), it is incredibly frustrating.
There are sliders for the pitch, yaw and roll, but I can't figure out how to be able to actually use them as sliders aside from rapidly pressing the button so it jumps up and down and averages out about where I want the target to be. Trying something as simple as maintaining altitude with a plane requires so much up and down flopping, that my aircraft looks like it's waving at the horizon. Having a pilot "stabilize" the aircraft doesn't help much either, since there's no way to gradually go to a stable altitude... you just have to give up and live with slightly gaining altitude for a while, then slightly losing, to get much of anywhere. And this doesn't say anything about trying to turn the plane, which is an arduous task at almost any speed. Trying to roll and pitch to turn sort of works, except this generally results in quite a loss of speed and/or altitude. Using yaw is just awful, as your plane will start bouncing back and forth as you try to turn. Trying to land is quite an exercise, though I found that just plopping down in the water seems to work far better.
Controlling rockets is marginally better since you don't really expect or generally need a great degree of accuracy, thankfully. Also, the pilot can actually point you towards specific targets once you get into space, such as prograde and normal, so you don't have to use the wonky controls to try to manually do things.
I'll probably be trying some more, because under these flaws it looks like there is an interesting game to play... I just hate having to work so hard to try to get into it at all.

As a huge fan of the Mafia franchise I have to sadly say that I'm really disappointed by this game. And not only because of the PC port, but because of a lot of flaws in the story and the freedom. The story is extremely generic, its basically a vendetta, and a really boring one at that. The previous protagonists became part of organized crime for complete different reasons, which are definitly not revenge. It doesn't feel like a Mafia game because all you do is killing and killing, all you can spend your money on is weapons and upgrades related to combat. The freeroaming is EXTREMELY limited, worse than it was in the previous games, because in the previous ones you were able to customize your characters outfit, car, buy food and other stuff. Some small but extremely important aspects to the game, lacking it is critical. Stuff like that shouldn't be added as an update after the game is released. It should've been in the game already. When the developers said they were aiming for a same experience as the Witcher 3 I was pretty excited, since I played the whole Witcher franchise I can simply say they failed to remake that experience, it was nothing special.
Mafia 3 had so much potential, but most of it went to waste, most of the time you go around and kill people to destroy the income of that district, once you did it you are able to play the story missions that were really good, if most of the 30 hours were not grinding but doing story missions like that the game would've been much better for me. And bad optimization is a big minus for the game too.
What I personally really disliked was the open ending, since the previous games didn't have an open ending.
Shortly summed up: If you like shooting people 24/7 then this game is for you. If you want a more unique game with a lot of possibilities in freeroaming and a breathtaking story, then its simple = don't get it.

The best way I can explain this game is Halo meets call of duty Zombies, with dinosaurs. That said, the game is . . . simply made. Sometimes, the animation of the dinosaurs or people look a little silly (the flying dinosaurs, in particular, stiffly glide around and dive unrealistically, although I have to admit it is hilarious), and the bigger predators can get a little buggy trying to grab you from ontop of a rock or against a cliffside. But none of this is game breaking in the least, and what you get is one hell of a fun game. There are quite a few gametypes, all of which play differently and have their own unique maps. Survival is probably what you think of most when viewing this game, which consists of you (and other players or friends, though it has an option for solo) fighting off ten waves of dinosaurs/capturing objectives, earning credits (much like Call of Duty Zombies) to buy different guns, mods, etc. There are other gametypes but I haven't even delved into half of them (I would like to specially mention Rampage, though, which pits humans vs dinos, which is awesome).
The biggest drawback to the game, though, has to be the fact that there are in-game purchases for real money. All of it is cosmetic (and not terribly good cosmetic stuff either - would you like a♥♥♥♥♥♥green T-rex? Or a whiches hat?), but it is a little frustrating, especially when you color customization on your guy/guns consists of ugly baby blue, bright purple, or the darkest black ever. The shop is, however, incredibly cheap (for the most part), so it isn't a terrible thing. Even then, none of this will interfere with your playing.
I think I've said all I have to say this game, and I would highly recommend it, especially with friends. It's one of those games you can always depend on to be a good time.

This game is a shameless, blatant knockoff of slither.io. Don't get me wrong, there's nothing wrong with getting ideas from something else and basing your ideas on it, but at least add some new mechanics. They added some mechanics and new elements to the table, but, unfortunately, they're pretty bad.

The game is buggy as can be, with the hitboxes for the heads being miniscule, hitting things when you know that you weren't even touching, and sometimes being able to phase through other worms completely. One mechanic that is completely unacceptable is the fact that there is a limit on how big you can get. On a game about becoming huge, this is practically a sin.
There are some small things that make this game particularly unenjoyable. For example, when you first start the game, it prompts you to leave a good rating for the game to get 100 coins. That's a stupid way to get positive reviews for such a watered down game. Another small thing is the music. While I know you can just turn it off in the settings and play some stuff from your computer, I just have to complain about this. When you start up, you're blasted with sh-tty dubstep. You also have to make an account for this game (no, you can't connect to your Steam account like a normal game, you actually have to make a screen name and password), so that's pretty bad.

I'm sure my sentiments will be echoed across the internet, but I love this game.The visuals are a mix of artistic styles that are  by turns childish, childlike, wondrous, and serene but each scene has edge to it that belies the games darker undertones. The surface is placid, but there are things stirring underneath. The voice acting is fantastic as well. There's a panoply of famous names, and I'm sure you'll know them when you hear them. Honestly I was surprised by Jack Black in what had to be his tamest performance yet. The first time I heard his character speak I was honestly put in mind of the character Arthur from the Journeyman project games, a character whom I love. I eventually realized it was Jack Black and for once, I didn't groan. Well done. The characters are diverse in temperament there was something similarly off about most of them. Not to ruin the story but a person who obstinately remains calm in the midst of mind wrenching horror is one of the scariest things I can think of. The banality of horror is truly chilling. Not to say this is a horror game, ho no! But keep in mind this is Tim Schaefer. He don't make games what don't have twisted sentiments. Gameplay was your standard Point und Klick Adventurwerks we all grew up on, but the inclusion of the drag and drop rather than clicks to use items really threw me for a while. I am very much used to the "classic" controls-- ok the "Non-textual input classic" controls-- I see you over there hipster gamer with your second-hand copy of Zork. Shut up before you attract a grue. I guess this was decided because they felt it more fit with The Tablet Set who are more used to drag and drop. The story is difficult to describe without spoiling it. Suffice to say it's great. I highly recommend it and I eagerly await its sequel.

Be prepared to read the words "You did not reach the nuclear throne" a lot.  Be prepared to accidently kill yourself when your disk gun shot richocets off a wall and back at you.  Be prepared for an adrenaline rush every time you face Lil' Hunter.
In this game, you will die a lot.  It's bullet hell and you have 8 measly hit points.  Seems like it's not a problem right? Well, most shots in the game will take down half that and more.  There's no invincibility frames after getting hit, some enemies shoot powerful enough weapons that they will kill you in one shot.
And yet you keep playing.
There's a beautiful feel to the game.  The gunfire sounds are audibly pleasing, Every hit on an enemy is satisfying.  As you progress further, the game only gets more fun.  After looping, you begin to feel unstoppable, but eventually you get claimed and the struggle continues.  You always die in this game, but you die a little less frequently as you progress.
Do yourself a favor and pick this gem up.  You won't regret it.
One small note, the developers have stopped working on the game, so if you see any bugs, it's unlikely you'll get a fix for it for a long time.

I previously play FS2004 on my laptop, with many add-ons installed (REX, AI Traffic, etc) and it runs at 50-60 fps, Later when I tried to switch to FSX it lags really bad, without any add-ons I was running at around 15-20 fps. I tried many optimization guide on the web and none works for me. My laptop isn't very powerful as it only got a AMD A10-5750m CPU, and Radeon 8670m GPU. At the time, I gave up on FSX, and sticks to FS 2004, as I thought my system isn't powerful enough for FSX. Couple of months later, FSX:SE was launched and I read many reviews on the web stating that it really improved stabilty and FPS (not by a very large margin, the reviewers said). At first i'm not really interested in acquiring the Steam Edition, since I thought my laptop isn't powerful enough for FSX, but then FSX:SE goes on sale for around $2-$3, and I decided to give it a shot. I launched the game for the first time, and surprisingly, none of the lag issue I encountered before was gone. I got a good 50 fps, without any add-ons, and even after installing many add-ons such as ORBX, REX, and AI Traffics I still get around 40 fps, with occasional drop to 20 fps, when i'm flying near third party airport, with many AI Traffics. The only optimization I did was changing the Affinity Mask on fsx.cfg. I'm really happy that FSX Steam Edition works well for me.

Not recommendedEven though I thought this game sounded quite promising, and I really wanted to like it, I don't. It seems as if there was a lot of potential regarding what they wanted to do, but I don't think it was done well.
Graphics
Yes, the game is from 2010, so keep that in mind. However, I think that, even for 2010, the graphics aren't that good. Character editing (glasses, hat, hair) looks terrible, same for the movement in combat etc.
Gameplay
I usually LIKE stealth games, but this one, I didn't. I am not sure whether it's just a higher difficulty or badly done game mechanics. Trying to sneak up on an enemy to take him out often ends up in frustration, as he notices you. However, it feels like the mechanics are just clunky, it's not some overly high AI or bad playing... I have played several stealth games and usually do ok, but here, I tried to sneak up on an enemy, and sometimes, the silent takedown works, sometimes he suddenly alerts everyone around him.
AI
Terrible. On one hand, the second the alarm is raised, they know EXACTLY where you are and shoot at you, which I find HIGHLY unrealistic. I wouldn't mind if they had a general idea quickly and then search for you there, but the second an alarm is raised, it's like they have a hive intelligence and know where you are.
At the same time, I have seen some moonwalking, and you can just run towards them and take them down with melee
Combat
Terrible as well. If there are two obstacles, and you aim between them and aim PERFECTLY at the head of an enemy, you won't hit him. Let me get this straight - two obstacles, you aim between them (yes, there is room between them), and you won't hit him.
Even when in range, and the dot in your targeting circle is aligned with someones head, you often miss. Having to shoot someone in the head (they wear a mask, or sometimes just a bandana, apparently these items generate a bullet proof forcefield) isn't exactly that realistic either.
Minigames
There is lockpicking, disabling alarms and hacking. The first two are... ok. The first one is even fun sometimes (balancing the cylinders of the lock, then releasing your lockpick, with a time limit). The second one is ok. The third one is horrible. Not going into details, the other commenters have commented on how terrible that one is many times.
Characters
I didn't like the whole intro, the conversations, the character design. Apart from simply looking odd, I just didn't care for any character, and I didn't like the main character either, who looks like a mix between Shepherd from Mass Effect and some kind of cyborg.
Overall
So much potential. I'd have liked to explore the game more and find all the things that those who liked the game praised... the decision-making, the email conversations or whatever.
However, the intro went on for too long and didn't grab me at all, and the two missions I tried were simply not fun at all. It's not the very outdated (even for a 2010-game!) look, it's the clunky mechanics, bad AI, horrible sneaking mechanics (MGS V and even Sniper Elite 2 and 3 do this SO much better), bad animation, horrible combat/aiming and the minigames.
It's sad, because I was looking forward to trying this, I was very much willing to give it a chance, but I have no interest at all to continue after these two missions.
If you can get it on sale (I got it for like 3 or 4 bucks), maybe try it out, but unfortunately, I simply can't recommend it.

I find it difficult to recommend this game too highly.  While it's very linear and could be longer, what is here is extremely well written, well acted, and well designed.  The early and often references to Stephen King are extremely apt given the game's subject matter, and fans of King's will notice references from works as popular and famous as The Shining to works as little known as Rage or The Dark Half, and there's even veiled references to Misery.
If you find yourself with spare cash burning a hole in your pocket, by all means pick this game up.  You will not be disappointed if you are a fan King's work.  If you enjoyed Silent Hill you'll enjoy the themes in this game, although it's much heavier on combat that most Silent Hill works.  Fortunately the combat where it exists is fluid.  If you can, play this game with a controller rather than a keyboard, as it's occasionally awkward with a keyboard.

I was playing this on the tv and it looked great.  In regards to the controls I really can't complain about them.  I think the few times where I thought I shouldn't have died slipping off an edge is because well I am terrible at games.  Now as for negatives I didn't see a death counter.  I think a game like this where you can continue over and over and over again should have one.  There also should be a scoreboard online and just local that shows how many deaths you had to clear the game but also how many deaths you had to clear each level and sub level.  Still without this I have to say this is a very fun game.  Oh and as for presentation it was neat seeing the kid sucked into the world after he decided to dust off his old console and play a game.  He got much more than he wished for or hey maybe not.  Anyway if you like Super Mario type games then you will like this.  Last but not least this works perfectly with an Xbox 360 controller in Windows 7 64 bit.  I can't speak for any other operating systems and versions of them.  So in finishing this review I will say it is a 9 out of 10 with the only complaint being I just wished they would add stat tracking that I mentioned earlier in this review of the game.

Like Mark of the Ninja and Don't Starve, this is another outstanding game by Klei Entertainment. It takes elements of stealth games, XCOM, Shadowrun and rogue-likes and merges them together to create a tense strategy game about a secret agency that infiltrates companies in a dystopian future.
While there is an enjoyable main plot in the campaign, the main focus of the game lies in it's gameplay. Its rogue-like nature, its random elements and the fact that the campaign is not too long (without the DLC at least) let's you enjoy the game multiple times even after you have beaten it the first time. IF you have beaten it. I say that because the game can be really brutal at times (in a really enjoyable way). Unlike many rogue-likes, the game is very accessible and not too complex but the depth it achieves by combining all its elements is great. While permadeath and limited ways to undo mistakes appeal to rogue-like fans, the game is highly customizable and you can enable retries and rewinds to make the game easier for you if you like.
Apart from the good gameplay and the clean UI, the music is amazing and adds to the tension. Starting out relatively quite it ramps up and when everything goes down in flames on the screen, the music let's you know. And everything will go down in flames. Every game. Even if you think you have everything under control, something will happen. Part of the fun is getting out of these situations unharmed.
If you dig strategic games, rogue-lites, and stealth games you should definitely check out Invisible Inc. I did not think I would enjoy the game as much as I do, but I tried it anyways because I liked Klei's previous games and was not disappointed. It does a lot of things right and checks enough boxes for me to let me do "just one more mission".

The Banner Saga 2 is a better game, if a worse story, than the first game. The combat encounters are much improved and become a joy to play. The Oregon Trail sections still seem beautiful, a series of interesting choices, but inconsequential, as there's little incentive to keep your people alive. The plot becomes a bit off this go-round. Much is built around a mystery that's not really resolved in the course of the game. As a bridge to plot in later chapters of this saga, it makes this a less compelling narrative than the steady build up of the first game. But that game becomes unplayable with this one bringing a lot more game to the table. Perhaps the biggest issue is that the character development for the swollen cast of possible fighters is a bit underbaked. The Banner Saga should be a bit more aggressive about killing off some characters, or invest more time in developing the cast out a bit more. Or both, so that you care when one dies, like in the first game.

There is a lot of RPG out there but this one is quite different.
Right now it is the only one Espionage RPG in the world.
Critics from all over the world weren't impressed by this game and gave it mixed rating.
But I really enjoyed this game. The whole concept of several secret agencies and how they fight with each other is unique and, more importantly, very interesting.
The game has several distinct traits which differ her from other RPG:
1.	During the game you will have a chance to meet many different people who can become your curator. Curators in this game do not participate in the missions but they help you providing information and bonuses. The better your relationship with your curator the larger bonuses you get. You can affect your relationships with curators during the missions.
2.	Before a mission you have a chance to buy some useful information about the mission or even affect it somehow (for example, you can hire a person to drop a sniper rifle on the roof or poison a boss, which will make him weaker)
3.	The conversations in the game often time-limited. The game doesn’t give your time to think carefully about your answers because, you know, when you are being interrogated you don’t have a chance to think about possible outcomes of your answer.
The game has some flaws but I loved it, I loved the setting, the RPG system, the characters and the story.
I recommend it to anyone who likes RPG.

Oh my god. What the hell happend to PAC-MAN? I realise that this is a Free-2-Play mobile game, which makes it an extra kick in the teeth that I bought this, but this is pretty bad.
This game was made soley to sink time into. There is no fun anywhere in this. Just die and restart. It follows the model of games like Flappy Bird or Temple Run where you see how far you can get and try and beat your high score. I know that the original Pac-Man was pretty basic but atleast that had levels. That had extra lifes. That was a fun and progressively challenging game that you could master by putting time into it. You could figure out the patterns of each of the Ghosts and use that knowledge to trick them and get past them. This game trys that but just fails miserably. How the hell am I meant to figure out how to dodge a teleporting enemy? Whats the point in trying to get the highscore? You don't progress. There is no end game.

It gives you a false sense of progression. After you die and complete challenges you get coins. The amount of coins is so little that you have to play the game for hours on end to actually fully upgrade your loadout. This is just a facade to make you think that you are playing a game wqith actual substance. Plus, why have about 20 different weapons when there are only like 3 good ones? And about 5 of the weapons are just better versions of earlier ones. So why upgrade the earlier weapons? Whats the point if its gonna get replaced by a better version of itself?

When I was in the 10th grade or so, my best friend and I had bonded over a shared love of jets and military stuff. Plus we were both generally nerds in every sense of the word. He used to come over to my house and I'd load this up on my old 386. He wasn't very good at flying with a joystick, and since this game has so many keyboard commands (seriously, download and print out a keyboard guide off the net if you want to play this), he'd run tactical/nav with the keyboard and I'd pilot.
We got fairly good, where we were playing on Veteren difficulty. We'd racked up a few medals, earned some ranks, and since we thought we were superheroes, we decided to go for the highest score possible. We loaded up with the best missiles we could find and set out. Our goal was to not only destroy the primary and secondary objectives, but take out any targets of opportunity we came across.
We did, we spent every single missile and every single bullet, taking out tanks, convoys, bridges, SAM sites, enemy fighters, airports, you name it. By the time we were done we were completely out of fuel and ammo. We had to coast in for a landing, but we made it! Then the debriefing screen, then the ranks and medals. We got at least 4 or 5 medals on that mission, including the Congressional Medal of Honor! We were screaming, we thought that was the coolest thing ever. And still, 25 years later, we talk about that epic mission.
Well, I'm happy to report that this game still works perfectly. I have a Logitech Extreme 3D Pro, it got picked up and works fine. I downloaded a keyboard shortcut sheet off the internet and sent my friend a picture of it, said "Hey, I have a working copy of this, wanna play?" 10 minutes later he's at the house with a few beers, we fired the game up, and, well... it wasn't quite just like riding a bike. But a few missions later and we were stomping heads just like old times, it was great!
This game has a full damage model, with various info screens you can switch to. You can get a camera view of your target, or you can look at your fuel/waypoints, you can check damage, look at mission objectives, and that's all on the right screen. The left screen lets you switch between a nav map and a radar. In the middle is your radar signature. The filled area at the bottom is how much signature you're giving off, then you can see radar pings coming down from the top. Red bars are ground radar and blue bars are air radar.
The goal is to stay low and slow enough to keep your signature down, sneak in, take out the targets, and sneak out. It's very tense and satisfying. Maybe there's a SAM site pinging hard, and it's causing a lot of problems for you. There's nothing quite like taking out that monster with a sneak attack before it sees you. If someone does get a ping on you, you'll start getting notifications like "F-5 taking off from such and such airbase" as they scramble jets to look for you. Watch out for the F-4's, they have mean radar capabilities.
So yeah, pick this up. They don't make games like this any more. Horrific graphics aside, this is still one of the best flight sims ever made!

I got this in a bundle, I guess?  I just know this is not the sort of game I would have intentionally purchased.  And I would have been missing out!  Listen, I'm old, my earliest memories of videogames are of feeding quarters into Pac-Man and Marble Madness at the local pizza joint.  And it's not like video game designers don't spend a lot of time trying to capitalize on nostalgia for the old coin-op days, but they almost never nail it like this.
So, like, you're playing Pac-Man.  The mechanics are sort of like you might remember.  But it's an endless level, constantly growing in one direction while killscreen-style glitches eat it from the other side.  And it's isometric instead of straight-up top-down, there are more ghosts than you might be used to, and a wider variety of powerups, but for the most part everything still has that old Pac-Man feel to it.  Everything's congruent with that old Buckner & Garcia vibe.  It's just better, more suited to casual play, more leaning toward diverse gameplay than the old memorize-the-Ninth-Key-Pattern cabinet game.
This is a fantastic game, and I'm glad to have lucked into it.

This game is fun and charming! The musical soundtrack is fantastic (Melbourne Symphony Orchestra!), the art style is appealing.
The interesting story element of this game is - you play as two different people from two totally different universes, and you wonder how on earth they can fit together and make one cohesive story.  It's a fun device.  It gives some Day-of-the-Tentacle-like freedom to switch around and try another character when you get stuck.
The controls are quite simple, and to me this is a good thing.  There are no verbs to select from, you can either left click on a thing/person to interact with it, and you can drag things from your inventory onto things/people, and that's it - no trying "use thing, nope, push thing, nope, look at thing, nope, talk to thing, nope, pull thing...ah-ha!".  The interactable things on the screen have a large clickable area, and the cursor changes to a big ball-thing, so there is no pixel hunting - just run your mouse around once quickly, you find everything interactable very easily.
The puzzles gradually get more difficult, and Act 2 has some particularly good brain teasers.  Now that both acts are released, the game length feels just right.
This game is also suitable for children.
Oh, and don't pay attention to all the downvotes on these reviews, I think they're mostly from some sad internet hate group who got upset about a joke Tim Schafer made, so this is how they get their revenge.  Pretty sad way to spend time eh?

Broken Age has the same charm that I've come to expect from Schafer's games, like Psychonauts, Costume Quest and Stacking.  The characters are interesting though admittedly one-dimensional (just like most point and click adventure games) and the conversations are mostly quite entertaining.  I think the voice acting is superb as well, especially with the two main characters and the Computer ("Mom").  The animation and visuals prove that a game does not need super high def SSAO bloom TressFX etc etc to set the atmosphere of a game in the right direction.  The overall aesthetic (visuals, music, ambience) elicit zero complaints from me.

Unfortunately, the same cannot be said of the gameplay.  I'm not sure what I was expecting, but I found the item hunting a bit tiring at times.  I wish there was a way to speed up conversations, as I generally read much faster than people speak (pressing space will skip the entire conversation, not just the current dialogue with subtitles) and though there are some areas where your character can run, most of the time you walk at a very slow clip.  I'm glad that there isn't much hand holding, but when certain areas open up, it can be a bit annoying to walk back and forth between screens looking for an item I missed.

Still, it's not like I did not enjoy the gameplay at all.  I think the clever dialogue (and even off hand remarks as I look at items or walk past characters) cracked me up, and that makes a ton of difference in adventure games.  I had an idea of where the story was heading at first, but now I'm not so sure.  All I know is that Act 2 cannot come soon enough.

F19 Stealth Fighter is a gem from Microprose of late 1980s.
Early Microprose released several fight simulators which gradually became better and better, especially from gameplay perspective. F19 is the top Microprose game before Civilization and it has the last Sid Meier's flight simulator gameplay, the endpoint of Sid's flight evolution if you will.
F19's gameplay is a brilliant mixture of flight simulator and stealth. To my knowledge, currently it is still unique. In other words, you will not find a similar gameplay in modern games.
The core idea is the following. You, as a pilot of a stealth plane, go into the night far behind enemy front lines to hit special targets. The sky is full of patrolling MiG's, a lot of SAM's keep watch, and any clue or radar blip can alarm and the enemy will start to intensively search you. To be stealthy, you need to use landscape, watch the radar's and plane's activities, and, the most important, understand doppler and impulse radars and make relatively flight according to them (skim the manual due to it is a core feature).
Beware, the controls is tricky and you have to read the manual to take off and use weapons.
The game is realistic and not very hardcore, but deep and replayable. There are three types of bombs (among >20 weapons) with different way of using (bombing), more then ten types of targets (bunkers, ships, SAM, ...). Enemy units are randomly generated and you will have to think how to sneak through the enemy, hit target/take photo, and safely back home.
If you prefer better graphic you can look at the game "F-117A Nighthawk Stealth Fighter 2.0". It has the same gameplay, but more pixels and more scenarios.

Isaac possesses charm wrapped in a very twisted story. Originally I thought it was a very primitive top view shooter, but after spending more time with it and understanding some simple tricks, I found it's actually quite complex offering a mild strategy that can be frustratingly addictive. Permadeath really adds an element of player alertness making you try harder not to take damage.
Although the game is extremely short, there is a surprising amount of replay value due to its randomly generated maps, monster combinations, and item drops. You really never know how you are going to fair on any given playthrough which keeps it from feeling repetitive. With practice and persistence, you will unlock new items that make the game somewhat easier, but also more fun. Experimenting with item combinations is a treat, plus it's hard not to break a smile from some of the crazy power ups as well.
For a $1 game, Isaac holds priceless value.

The Walking Dead: Season 2 is a masterpiece, and a worthy sequel to the first game. It takes what was good about the first game, builds on it, and for the most part improves it. As far as gameplay is concerned, it is the same as the first game. It's a point and click adventure, with dialogue choices and quick time events. However, there are also some quick time events that require you to click and drag your mouse in a certain direction. These did not work so well, as my mouse would not always  register that I was dragging it, and I would have to reset it. It was annoying, but there are only about 5 instances of this in the whole game, so it's not too bad. Also, some combat scenes now require dodging, which is a fun addition. As far as the story is concerned, it's just as good as the first. The story is a lot darker than the first game (which was dark too), and it focuses on the mental stability on the group, and how people can lose their mind during the apocolypse. It's a gripping story, and I loved it. However, it is worse than the first game in some ways and better in others. For example, the villan in this game is amazing, and one of my favorite video game villans. He is played by Michael Madsen (Reservoir Dogs, The H8teful Eight), and he does an incredible job. The villan in the first game was ok, but not too menacing. This guy is the eqivalant to The Governor/Negan, and he is great. However, I did not feel the same connection to the group in this game like I did in the first season. In this game you play as Clemintine, and after some events that I won't spoil you join a new group. In the last game, you meet everybody over time, and learn backstory/character traits when you initally meet them. Here, you meet most of your group members at once, and you hear their stories rather than experience them first hand. They are good characters but I didn't bond with most of them as well as the first game. There are some exceptions, but I won't say who I liked better. As far as graphics go, it's about the same as the first game. It runs on Telltale's older engine but some of the textures do look a bit nicer in some areas. I did have some crashes however I am running this on an Intel graphics cars, which is clearly stated to be "not reccomended". I also played this with a friend on his computer (no Intel graphics) and there were no glitches of any kind. If you have Intel like me you might be able to run it, but with minor problems. In conclusion, this game is a worthy sequel and a must-play for fans of the first. It does some things better, some a bit worse but overall I love this game. I think it is worth buying at full price, but it can be very cheap during sales, if you are close to one. Either way, you should definately play this game.

This is a reasonably solid game overall, although there's some room for improvement. If you like tactics games or stealth games, you'll probably get a few hours of enjoyment out of Invisible, Inc. Maybe more if you like both.
The game really makes you plan out your moves 2, 3, 4 turns in advance which makes for a good challenge. In higher difficulties you feel like you're hanging on by the skin of your teeth, which is great.
The story is pretty thin, and I personally didn't care for the artwork which makes the cutscenes reminiscent of an extended Esurance commercial - of course that's just one person's opinion. The biggest gripe I have with the game is how little variety there is in the content. Levels all look pretty much the same, and although there are a multitude of items and weapons, I found myself relying on the starting melee weapon almost exclusively because finding ammo for the other weapons is such a chore. A little more balance would be nice to make changing up tactics more viable.
Overall, it's still a fun game although it's currently overpriced. I'd price it closer to $8 or $10 for the value I got out of it.

Seriously underrated game.  This is an RPG game, not a purely action game, so you need to level up and work on advancing your skills and customizing your character.  If you expect traditional action gameplay, you'll be disappointed.  But as an RPG, it's a lot of fun, and the espionage settting is a fun change of pace from the usual sword-and-board Tolkien cut-and-pasted drivel that most game makers seem to think we want in our role playing games.
The game is very ambitious, though you do have to be tolerant of some of relatively rough production values.  OK, very rough production values.  I guess that's why most people hate the game.  But if you are the kind of player who wants a game where your decisions really do impact the gameplay, the story, and the future missions, this is a great game because it delivers in that department.  Mass Effect has more polish, and better gameplay, but really, at the end of the day, all your decisions do is change a few seconds worth of cut scene at the end.   The Telltale Walking Dead games love to tease you with the choice between saving one character or another.  But then, no matter who you save, they end up dying a few minutes later.  Your decisions simply don't matter in most games.  But in Alpha Protocol, the story can change dramatically from one playthrough to the next in a way that most games still can't compete with.
And, sadly, it's still one of the only non-sci-fi, non-fantasy RPGs out there.

But good news, many of these games quicks can be house ruled. So you can configure the game to your taste. On your first game, I recommend using the 72 hours length with no expansion elements. I did the error of doing the 120 hour + 48 hours from the expansion which made the game way too long.

Overall very good game, I recommend it to everybody. The complexity of the game is not that high so it should be fairly accessible to anybody.

If you've ever wanted to be a secret agent like 007 or Jason Borne then Alpha Protocol might just be what you're looking for!
The good:
+The story feels like a fun mix between James Bond and the Borne Identity movies.
+The dialogue and writing is snappy, funny and delivered fairly well by voice actors throughout.
+The gameplay feels akin to Deus Ex in that you customize your own character and play as you please.
+The levels encourage exploration as you can find hidden stashes of cash, dossiers or even upgrades.
+The game is fairly short, but encourages multiple playthroughs with different approaches in both gameplay and story decisions.
The bad:
-Animations tend to be stiff and robotic.
-The camera zooms in too close and can be clunky to work with.
-The combat is poorly executed and you should at least max one weapon skill to keep up.
-Plays awful with a mouse and keybord, get a controller and enable it in the options menu in-game.
-Bugs, bugs, bugs! It just wouldn't be an Obsidian game without them.
-The final mission feels rushed and is more bugged than the rest of the game.
Bottom Line:
Alpha Protocol is a rough gem that will leave you frustrated at times, but satisfied by the end. If you're unsure I would suggest you pick the game up during a sale.

I keep seeing developers and reviewers alike describe it as an "Xcom stealth game"...only as an afterthought mentioning the Syndicate overtones; personally the Syndicate vibe hit me way more strongly, even though in terms of gameplay it probably does lean towards Xcom more than Syndicate (Syndicate wasn't turn-based).
I hated this game at first, mostly because it almost punishes you for exploring; but, that's not really what this game is about. In comparison to most stealth-oriented games, where exploring the environment, and figuring out how to use it to your advantage or make progress, is half of the game, this game doesn't work like that; you are effectively timed in each mission, the escalating alarms serving as a disincentive to open up the entire map of the level (think Spelunky), merely complete your objectives and gtfo, if you're an explorer or a completionist you're going to have to come to terms with this. The exception to this rule is endless mode, where eventually you will have to unlock pretty much every safe in a level to find an exit key, which I found aggravating as all hell but that's kind of the point.
Once I got past that though I really enjoyed it, the RNG can be unfair sometimes but that's generally when you break out the lethal weapons in a run, rather than knock-outs (at which point, it really does start to feel like Xcom). And really, once you're done achievement-whoring you can set up the campaign options however you like, even moreso if you download and install a couple mods, to the point of allowing you to control the frequency of random difficulty occuring mid-mission.
I have everything Klei's made besides Shank and the stuff precluding it in my Steam library...I still haven't played Don't Starve or its DLC but between this and Mark of the Ninja (the best Batman game ever made, by the by), and their upcoming Sims in Space game that I want so goddamn bad called "Oxygen Not Included", I'll have to at least look at whatever they release, even if it looks stupid; these guys do solid work, and their games are often either outside the box (and good), or its something that's already been done before, but now done like you always kinda wanted it to be.
Did I mention mods? Steam workshop, yessss.  At first it was just for new languages, there's actual mods there now.

I got this in a bundle, I guess?  I just know this is not the sort of game I would have intentionally purchased.  And I would have been missing out!  Listen, I'm old, my earliest memories of videogames are of feeding quarters into Pac-Man and Marble Madness at the local pizza joint.  And it's not like video game designers don't spend a lot of time trying to capitalize on nostalgia for the old coin-op days, but they almost never nail it like this.
So, like, you're playing Pac-Man.  The mechanics are sort of like you might remember.  But it's an endless level, constantly growing in one direction while killscreen-style glitches eat it from the other side.  And it's isometric instead of straight-up top-down, there are more ghosts than you might be used to, and a wider variety of powerups, but for the most part everything still has that old Pac-Man feel to it.  Everything's congruent with that old Buckner & Garcia vibe.  It's just better, more suited to casual play, more leaning toward diverse gameplay than the old memorize-the-Ninth-Key-Pattern cabinet game.

PRO TIPS FROM THE PROS:
- Tired of hearing the engine whine? alt + v will let you cycle through different levels of sound. All but the highest leave out engine noises.
- On a long boring stretch of flying back to your landing site, with nothing to do in the meantime? Alternate hitting shift + z and shift + x every couple of seconds. Shift + z speeds up time, but only seems to work for a few seconds. shift + x puts you back into normal mode.
- The way to earn the big points is on Cold War, not Conventional War. You make more points for flying around unseen than you ever could from blowing stuff up
- If your game is running really choppily and your controls suck, it's not the game. What you're experiencing is lag. "Lag? This game? On my modern machine? How could that be?" Well, DOSBox isn't emulating a modern machine. Throw some more cycles it's way with ctrl f12. Somewhere in the 15000 cycles range will cure all your problems (default is 3000)

Night Dive Studios has been able to get the rights to F-19 Stealth Fighter and make it available again commercially like this, which is great.
You won't see a lot of playtime on this game on my account yet as of when I'm writing this review, but that's because I played this game bunches as a kid and as of this writing just launched this version to be sure it was working etc.
This was a fun game I enjoyed. It's a simulation in that there's a lot of things to keep track of (how you first successfully take off by actually getting the momentum and then getting yourself to lift off the ground, how you deploy chaff when being targeted, how you go after mission objectives and try not to be captured, etc.). I'm actually super happy it's available again like this.
That said, I recommend reading the game instructional material linked to from the game page. Back in the day, even I as a veteran player would sometimes forget which key would push the throttle to max or get the brakes to quit so that I started moving forward, and referring to at least jotting down some keys common to my play was useful since the game is spending visual space on your cockpit and not on what keys interact with that cockpit.
Also, recommend saying YES to playing with a joystick when you launch the game. The game is really played with a joystick with the keyboard having some supplemental actions on it that were too excessive for the two (at the time) joystick buttons. The way Night Dive has packaged this with DOSBox means current gamepads will work as your joystick if you wake them up before launching the game - whatever counts as the first two buttons on the gamepad or flightstick or whatever you have will be the two buttons that the game listens to.

---Part 1 review originally written Jan 2014---
I may be a victim of my own overblown expectations on this one, but I came away from Broken Age (part 1) fairly disappointed.  The one thing that I expect from Tim Schafer is great characters and humor.  Small doses of the latter are still present, but the characters, I found I could care less about them.  Neither of the main characters has a standout personality.  The girl, Vella, is much better in this respect than the boy, and her section of the game is better too; but ultimately the game never comes close to approaching the excellence of Full Throttle or Grim Fandango.
The puzzles stay away from the sometimes ridiculous leaps of logic of 90s adventure games - but almost too far.  The game is much too easy, with options being limited and solutions being almost insultingly obvious.  The game is about as close to "click button for more story" as an adventure game can get.  So the gameplay is certainly not it's own reward, which is ok in an adventure game because ultimately the point *is* the story, but in this case the narrative and characters aren't much of a reward either.
---Part 2 review written Jun 2015---
Well, I guess they took the criticisms about the game being too easy to heart...and then went way too far in the opposite direction.  Some of the leaps of logic required in part 2 make 90s adventure games look sensible in comparison.  On top of that, there's incessant back and forth travel between several backgrounds that are recycled from part 1.  Whereas part 1 was just very bland, with part 2 I became actively annoyed with the game.  Given the choice between the boredom of part 1 and the vexation of part 2, I think I'd have to choose the former.
The story gets a bit more interesting in that it explores more than the immediate tasks set before the characters, but then suffers from a ridiculous amount of world building backstory (and basically the reveal to what the entire game was about) being crammed into the last few minutes of the game with no time to properly explore its ramifications.  I still also couldn't bring myself to particularly care about the characters who, being motivated primarily by a very specific list of video game like tasks set out for them, never really seem like actual people so much as puzzle solving drones.  Once again, Vella is still better than Shay, but neither is even close to having the personality or charm of the characters from Schafer's classic games.

You are a team of half-machine secret agent ninjas teleporting into buildings and stealing everyone's stuff without being seen. This is what all stealth games should be.
A bold move by Klei, the king of bold moves in videogames, this is an isometric turn-based PvE cyberspy simulator, and it goes much better than you'd think. It's 2074 and government has been replaced by evil supercorporations, so your targets are one of four of them who own all the credits and shiny plasma guns.
Gameplay consists of ninja-ing around buildings, predicting guard patrols, stealing items, hacking mainframe devices to use to your advantage, and trying not to get annihilated by the constant barrage of unforseen threats. A lot of this game's fun lies in getting ♥♥♥♥ed over halfway through a mission and having to dig yourself out, i.e., getting spotted by an unnoticed guard and alerting the whole building, security daemons that give you negative status effects, or just being an idiot and having no way to undo your mistake (You get 1-5 rewinds depending on difficulty). Invisible Inc. does not forgive, and I'm glad it doesn't, because then the missions wouldn't be mind-shatteringly tense to play, and incredibly rewarding to beat.
As per Klei, the art direction is beautiful. The bloom from glowing hallways, the stylised futuristic theme, and the subtle screen effects, like distortion when activating Incognita (Hacker mode) make for an incredibly nice game to look at, admire, admire too hard, die, and admire the game over screen. The game over screen is also beautiful, because it along with the mission report gives you a plethora of information on how you were the most unprofessional spy agency on the planet. Another lovely thing about the levels is the tantalising prospect of the perfect run: nobody sees you, you loot every safe, hack every camera, complete the objective, and leave before anyone even realises you were there. This is a rare occurrence, but when it happens, it's like thunderous applause from every human being on Earth.
The soundtrack... the soundtrack. It's exquisite. It's everything I could've ever asked for from this theme. The music ramps up gradually as security tightens, going from foreboding background strings to "Everything is insanity and red flashing alarms and on fire". It adds SO much to the game. Just - just listen to it. Go and look it up. It's masterful.
£15 to be a cyberninja. Yes, Klei, that will do.

If it wasn't for the gameplay that doesn't know what genre it wants to be, and if it wasn't for the fact that said gameplay doesn't really do well compared to most other games nowadays, this would be a stellar game.
PROS
- Voice acting is superb
- The graphics are good for 2010
- Conversations are done in real time. Not like Mass Effect, where Shepard awkwardly pauses while thinking of what to say. It's a bit like The Walking Dead game by Telltale.
- The generic RPG morality system has been replaced with a reputation system. Each character in the story likes specific things, and if you get their reputation high enough, you'll get bonuses and they'll treat you better.
CONS
- Like I said before, the gameplay doesn't know what it wants to be. If you're going to go soldier or tech, it's basically a shooter, and it's slightly below average at that. If you're going to go with stealth... oh boy. The stealth is not very good. Sometimes enemies don't see you when they should, sometimes they see you when they shouldn't. It's been a while since I last really played the game, so I don't remember it that much, but I do remember that I stopped because of the gameplay.

Note: I've generally liked every Obsidian game I've played despite problems with gameplay mechanics and general bugginess.
After three playthrough and multiple different approaches to this game, I can say that I would recommend it to someone in the mood for something different. Espionage is commonly seen in the gameplay of Splinter Cell and other action shooters with a stealth component. This is an RPG centered around espionage where you basically play as Jason-Bourne, Jack Bauer, James Bond, or some combination of the three.
Conversations are very well scripted and the characters are interesting, but the choice mechanic is nondescript (Aggressive, Suave, Professional). This is crucial because some conversations have a timed component. Based on the conversations and actions during the mission the storyline or flavor text will change slightly depending on which path you choose or who you befriend during the course of the game.  Final ending left a bit to be desired as it still had many loose ends to tie up and seemed to be setting up a franchise before Sega pulled the plug.
Gameplay is very uninspired and based off the 3rd person cover shooter model. Feels like Splinter Cell or Hitman without the flexibility in combat and stealth that those games provide. There is also a problem with the stealth mechanic being buggy at some of the higher levels of difficulty. If you try to play without alerting anything, save early and often.
This is not an open world RPG. It is a linear storyline driven RPG much in the same vein as KOTOR.
Note: I have enjoyed every Obsidian game that I have played and I liked their predecessor, Black Isle Studios. Obsidian games absolutely set the tone of the world and the adventure.

There is a reason why 3D physics engines should not be used for 2D sidescrollers and this is no exception. The physics engine can not handle slopes, causing staggering and making it hard to jump while in decline. There's also the matter of the character sliding off the very end of ledges causing further issues with jumping on time. As
is such an unforgiving game, having sloppily programmed controls is unacceptable. There is a fair amount of trial and error with the RNG that can make some areas near impossible to traverse under the wrong conditions. The final level is also filled with areas that alter the gravity with no indication that this will happen.
Tight controls are the backbone of a game like this but with how they've been handled, along with its physics,
may as well be classified as an invertebrate.

Originally an Xbox 360 game, this action RPG takes you straight into the world of spies and espionage (after selecting the type of agent you want to be), and you wake up in a lab, spending the “tutorial” of the game breaking out. It helps to use your common sense factor as well as the game mechanics of rolling around shuffle sneaking with a funny walk and hitting people. And possibly shooting everyone too. I didn't make my character too sneaky. And I think I set off the alarm by failing to pick the lock. I also accidentally shot someone when figuring how to sneak and be aware, so instead of being covert and suitably spy like, I ended up just shooting everything. ♥♥♥♥♥es got nothing. Who needs stealth? Ha!
Not that I'm defining my playstyle or anything. Let me just make my character look incognito by giving him big black glasses and a beret. No one will suspect anything.
The storyline balances well with the action given, it's enjoyable to follow, from your orientation/induction teaching you the different weapons and methods of succeeding, to the life challenging missions upsetting criminal organisations around the globe. It's pretty much like a James Bond movie in game form. The voice acting is good.
I like how I can have the options to be sarcastic, professional, indifferent or defiant, so I can create my own personality within the game.The music is appropiately slueth like, giving the feel you're sneaking around against the clock. It helps to set the mood.
The types of puzzles in this game vary, though most of them centre around time limits. For example you need to pick a lock in a certain amount of time, or clip circuits in order, or hack a computer by finding the embedded code on a screen of randomly generating numbers – though that took me quite a few tries to figure out since the instruction wasn't so clear.
The graphics are good, the environments are well defined and it's visually easy to follow your progress through a mission, along with promptings when you reach the right spot. It's high end Xbox 360 graphics so you can expect some prettiness.
The Ai mechanics focus on brute force, deceit/sneaking and picking and choosing targets, and explosions. I used sound generators to lure people into traps ... then punched them out myself.
There will be points where you can't get away with the reckless playing, because the alarm system will pull everything in the vicinity to take you down. It's a shame you can't scroll through to find the weapon of your choice, you need to go into a menu and select them. For me I have to press G in order to start looking in the menu. I would prefer it being more fast paced by being able to quickly scroll through weapons.
Recommended. It could even be worth more, so I'm happy to get it for the price I got it at. You can choose to be stealthy or not. You have the option to play it out how you want. And that for me makes it fun.

PAC-MAN Championship Edition raised the bar too high.
PAC-MAN 256 is a roguelike take on PAC-MAN, where it randomly generates an infinite map and you only have one life. It has multiple powerups which you unlock in addition to the standard power pellets. A slow wave of corruption destroys the map behind you and keeps a forward momentum.
Unfortunately, this exists in a universe where PAC-MAN Championship Edition exists, which was a lightning-fast modernization. Comparatively, PAC-MAN 256 feels slow and awkward. The new power-ups are cute but mostly just add randomness. And the randomness is part of the problem - sometimes you can have a smooth ride, but sooner or later you'll get into a no-win situation. Now, no-win corners are nothing new to PAC-MAN, but Championship Edition at least makes them predictable enough to avoid most of the time. Because PAC-MAN 256 is random, you can get randomly f-ed. Worst of all, it's a PAC-MAN game with grinding. Grinding! Yes! That's what PAC-MAN was missing! You can pick up coins to increase the duration or radius or whatever of some of the random power-ups. It's an attempt to add replay value to the game, but... it just kind of showcases how shallow the gameplay can be.
It's not the worst way to spend your time, but Championship Edition is a much better way. In a world where CE didn't exist, it'd probably be a welcome update. In a world where CE does exist, all PAC-MAN 256 does is bow to modern trends (endless! grinding! random!) to the game's general detriment.

Overall, I can’t really objectively recommend Alpha Protocol. It has a wonderful premise that works well in some places, but ultimately fails in a lot more. If you value story over gameplay and you’re in the mood for a good espionage story, then buy this game on sale and breeze through it on easy to avoid frustration. If you’re looking for a good overall stealth action experience, then you won’t really find one here. Here’s hoping Obsidian actually get the time and resources to try a game like this again with a lot more polish.
Mike Thorton is the newest recruit in for the top secret US government agency known as Alpha Protocol. His first assignment for the agency seems to be stopping a standard terrorist plot, which rapidly evolves into a globe-trotting conspiracy hunt.
This review is written from the perspective of a fan of stealth action games with an emphasis on multiple approaches. Also a fan of story driven RPGs.
Alpha Protocol’s gameplay is not its best asset. The level designs are largely linear stealth action arenas that don’t offer a lot of room for natural exploration or experimentation. There sometimes are hidden rooms that offer loot or alternate routes, but they are few and far between. If you want accurate expectations, you need to dismiss the notion that Alpha Protocol can be played as a pure stealth game from start to finish. Despite the tagline “the espionage RPG”, there are missions clearly designed for stealth, combat and mixtures of the two. If you try to employ combat in a stealth section or stealth in a combat section you’re just going to get frustrated. The problem is that game doesn’t exactly make clear what’s coming, requiring the player to employ some forethought, versatility and adaptability. It sounds neat, but can get frustrating when you show up in full combat gear to a stealth mission or vice versa.
The combat and stealth mechanics are a mixed bag. It employs are variation on Deus Ex 1s gunplay, where you basically can’t aim at all until you put enough points into that guns skill. It’s sounds cool, but at the end you basically end up with these horribly over-powered cooldown based weapon abilities that can 1 or 2 shot bosses. The bosses are another negative point for the game. A few of them can be beaten with stealth, but most of them are bullet sponges that you have to take on directly. It reminds me of a similar frustration I had in Deus Ex: Human Revolution, where you would manage your inventory and skills for one playstyle, only to run into a boss that demands another. These inconsistent difficulty spikes are irritatingly prevalent throughout the whole game. Sometimes it seems like the AI has a field of view of 45 degrees in front of them and sometimes it’s like they have eyes on the backs of their heads. The obstacles that enemies can and can’t see through are also inconsistent. The combat AI is smart enough, taking cover and using grenades etc. The stealth AI is less so. They like to stick to predictable paths, can’t hear anything and bodies can’t be moved so they hardly ever spot them.
The character progression system is very Mass Effect 1-esque. There are skills that are weapon based and the rest help with other aspects of the game (stealth, hacking etc.). Points can award you with passive abilities and active abilities. The progression starts pretty steady, but as mentioned before, by the end if you specialised correctly you can run around invisible, one shotting everything. Not an exaggeration.
The story and the way Alpha Protocol handles conversations is easily my favourite aspect of it. The conversation options are timed and almost always boil down to 3 responses. You can be a James Bond style suave guy; an Agent 47 professional guy; or just an all-out aggressive♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥nozzle. Different characters will respond to different tones accordingly and this can affect how much they like or dislike you. You can use this to your advantage, making your handlers and potential assets like you for information and perks and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off enemies to make them easier to beat. The game provides loads of dossiers with two distinct categories: individuals and organisations. Organisation dossiers are pretty straight forward, and are mostly used to give you a rundown of opposition tactics. Individual dossiers are more interesting, as you can exploit the information in them to find out what sort of responses people would like/dislike and times use secret facts in a conversation which have varying special results. For example, you can actually use dossier information in conversations to make two bosses turn on each other later making the fight a breeze. Of course, these options only appear if you actually read the dossiers, which feels pretty damn cool for a spy game.
The story itself is structured pretty similarly to your standard Deus Ex game. You have a straightforward prologue that introduces you to the world and then spans into a globetrotting conspiracy hunt. The game does a good job of conveying the feeling of unravelling the plot as you progress, discovering (or even predicting) plot twists as they are thrown at you. There are plenty of choices in the game that are all very morally ambiguous and open-ended in true Obsidian fashion. The factions you side with and♥♥♥♥♥♥off can have fairly significant effects on the rest of the game both during gameplay and in the story. You can try to be good or evil, but most choices boil down to picking between two awful things, which is great.
The actual voice acting in this game is surprisingly not half bad for the most part. This is surprising, considering the rough patches the rest of the game has. Aside from a few specific moments, the voice acting holds up for the most part.
Alpha Protocol is a rough looking game, even for its time (2010). The character models and animations are pretty terrible, texture work is very mediocre, and relying on lighting and shadow effects to stay hidden will almost always backfire. The animations in general are pretty laughable. This especially stands out when patrolling enemies freak out for a second when changing direction. The martial arts moves look pretty janky as well. A very average looking game, not dated enough to deter me, but not exactly anything to marvel at either.
Performance-wise, Alpha Protocol is an Obsidian game. What this usually means, is there are a lot of bugs, cut content and a few performance hitches. Alpha Protocol is not a stranger to any of these issues. As mentioned before, the AI is horribly inconsistent, a lot of missions like to bug out when reloading checkpoints (which are designed terribly, no manual saves), and you get punished for breaking stealth or rules of engagement when you know you didn’t. The bugs and technical problems combined with the poor gameplay mechanics make a very frustrating pile of game to get through the gems for the story content, which is a damn shame because those gems can be brilliant at times.

Middle Earth Shadow of War is my idea of a succesful sequel. It fixes almost all of Mordor's Weaknesses, and adds a grand amount of content on a massive scale. The story is better, the world is bigger, and i've couldn't have been happier about the way the game itself turned out.
Graphics: The base game's graphics are not substantially better looking than Shadow of Mordor, but that isnt a bad thing. Shadow of Mordor was a fantastic looking game, and this game is no different. Absolutely gorgeous graphics. The devs released a day 1 free dlc  to make the game look even better and let me say it does its job. Graphics get a 9/10
Sound: Soundtrack does an ok job at playing the appropriate track for the situation, sometimes I'll get the battle music when in stealth mode, which gets you a bit riled up even though you havent even been seen, but it happens quite rarely. The music itself is great. The menu and pause screen music is freaking awesome and it hypes me up every time I launch the game. The cutscenes are improved immensely and the overall game feels more cinematic with a good soundtrack and thery absolutely nailed it here. another 9/10
World: From what i've seen this game has a massive world. Stretching through mordor and parts of Gondor, including some of the most recognizable places in the LOTR universe. I love the addition of areas outside mordor, as in the first game the mordor scene got kind of old really quick. The combat was fun, but it didnt feel like a game in middle earth. This  improves the game greatly, and it finally feels like a middle earth game. 7/10
Story: The story is written pretty generically, just a continuation of the first so far, but the cutscene cinematics are on point and the voice acting is on another level for the videogame industry. These large AAA games are getting to be more and more cinematic and I like this trend. I haven't Finished every quest yet, but so far the game has me hooked, and I'll come back and edit this for sure. 8/10
Mechanics/Port: Day 1 bugs are already fixed and the game runs great on my PC. I am currently running a mid to high end system (gtx 1070, intel i7), and I can crank the settings all the way up and still get a constant 60 with no tearing. The requirements speak for themselves. The mechanics are similar to the first game, the game does add quite a few new moves, and it feels really fresh and innovative. Mounting a Troll and stabbing his back repeatedly, mounting a drake and breathing fire on everyone below, things like this add so much to the game and make it that much cooler.
Other: Of course the micro transaxtions are here and im not factoring it in to the review. Im just ignoring them for now and ive gotten along fine without them. All of those people review bombing are just missiong out on a really good game. What a shame.
Overall this is a great sequel to a good game. It adds so much to the first , and as a huge LOTR fan I can say this was worth $60. 8/10
