I found this to be an obnoxious little platformer in the ♥♥♥♥♥♥move' vein of games in which cheap shots and "gotcha!" moments make the rules (think 1001 Spikes). At only 5 levels in length, which will probably average to about a 30 minute play for most players, you wouldn't think it would have time to get on my nerves, but it did so very well. For the record, I enjoy short games and don't include the play time in my list of complaints, but that is a very valid issue for a lot of people. 30 minutes, an hour if you want to get both achievements - one for beating the game using continues, one for doing so without. I don't want to play it again.
The gameplay consists entirely of moving left, right, and jumping and platforming around all manner of things that will kill you instantly. I'm fine with that in principle, but this game shows its I-will-betray-and-trick-you cards right off the bat, and you won't trust a pixel in it from there on. It's not impossible nor terribly enjoyable.
Oh, I suppose you can pause, as well. Yeah.
I thought I had no expectations on what "troof" was awaiting, but it yet somehow managed to be disappointingly empty, so I guess it proved me wrong on that minor point. It plainly falls into a thickly clogged vein of similar "stories" and "endings", replete with something I'll uselessly call gamer/internet humor. Not a chuckle from me. Let me lay it all out.
Various NPCs hint vaguely about the "troof", you get to a level that would appear to be a spaceship, collect some pyramids, color happens, your potato stands and waits while making a few facial expressions, and then it lies down to be sucked into the most boring of color/pattern space void trips in what would appear to be some reference to 2001: A Space Oddyssey's still mysterious ending. After that, you reappear in the initial screen as a potato, able to roll around and bounce gently, but blocked entirely by the screen edge to one side and a cactus to the other. How blithe.
Graphics and sound I'll give a No Child Left Behind sort of pass.

Well, the bad news first: There's absolutely nothing different about Banner Saga 2 compared to its predecessor.
The good news: It is the same Game!
That's how I feel anyways, new chapters to the same game. And considering how great the first one was, this is as high as praise goes. We have the same story revolving around a caravan of people trying to survive a nordic fantasy endtime scenario. We have the same turn-based chess style combat RPG and the effects your outside decisions have in fights. We have the same, lovely graphics that often seem like a hand drawn backdrop from old school disney films. Everything that made the Banner Saga great is still present and expanded upon.
If there's one point of critisism, then that, with strong, imported heroes, the game is almost a little too easy. Bellower was a tough fight in part 1, Eyeless, the Sundr in this one, was nothing special if you can deal her damage in turn 1.
But it really is everything the first one was with about 20 hours of a new campaign and high replay value. I highly recommend it to any RPG fan.

8BitBoy is a 'retro' style game created to pay homage to the old 8bit platformers of yester-century.  Sound good? There are quite a few problems I have with this game:
- By all means, pay homage to your childhood games. However, there's a line where paying homage turns into gameplay plagiarism/copying. And sadly. 8BitBoy crossed that line. The similarities to Mario are just way too much for this game to be enjoyable. Every level in this game made me feel like I've played it before - and I have.. on a better game.

- 8BitBoy promises to bring nostalgia galore from the NES era with an 8Bit classic game. Oh wait... is it 8Bit? Hell no, the graphics more resemble a 16 video game and the colour palette is definitely not something out of the NES. It would really help to make your game 8 Bit if your game is called '8BitBoy'!.
- The music is... okay. It does a decent job on providing a 16 bit (cough, cough) experience to the game. However, the sound effects are nothing short but painful. If you intent to play this, do not play with headphones unless you happen to like the smell of blood dropping out of your eyes.
- The game.. well it lacks 'fun'. The controls are awkward, mapping the run button to the fire button was NOT a good idea. The hitboxes are off and the game leaves you wanted a better made, finished game rather than an uninspired mess.    I do not enjoy playing this game - it doesn't entertain me. That is not a good recipe for a video game.
So what then? What do I play, may you ask?
That's called Shovel Knight. It's a homage to old NES era platformers while bringing something inspiring and new to the table. I think Polygon put it best.
"Shovel Knight is so much more than a love letter to the genre — it is, in fact, the kind of game people write love letters about." - Polygon
And that's what 8BitBoy isn't. 8BitBoy is an unfinished love letter with terrible grammar - with classic lines as 'I wuv you' - and includes terrible references to other famous love letters but gets the references wrong every single time.
I think that's how I'll leave this game. It's a 'terrible love letter' to retro gaming.

Broken Age is a point-and-click adventure game, featuring two separate characters controlled by the player interchangeably. Vella and Shay, two teenagers living very different lives, find their worlds thrown into chaos as their fates are intertwined.
The graphics in this game are gorgeous. Not in the “Wow that looks so real” sense, but the “Such a beautiful work of art” sense. Every visual asset in the game appears to be produced by hand, leading to a stunning experience.
The nice thing about Broken Age, compared to some other point-and-click adventure games I have played, is the interaction points do not immediately stand out. You know how sometimes an object in a 2D game that is intended to move just looks different? This game does not do that.
So, Broken Age was originally released as just Act 1. Double Fine have since updated the game, and it now contains both Act 1 and Act 2. And I have to say, I almost liked it better when it was just Act 1.
Act 1 was definitely focused on the character development, and fleshing out the game world. Act 2, on the other hand, was far more puzzle-orientated, and not what I was expecting after going through Act 1.
Cutting this review short here, as I have less to say about this game than normal. The puzzles, especially at the end, became very frustrating. I may not be that great at puzzles in general, but some of these just seemed entirely counter-intuitive.
If you are a fan of the genre, this game is definitely a good one. If you are new to point-and-click adventures, this may not be the right place to start. It is a little… unique.

This game could have been amazing. The graphics are nice, the levels are well designed, it feels like a retro game, all should be great! The problem is the controls, they ruined any enjoyment I got from the game at first. The maps require preciscion platforming a lot of the time, problem is jumping is extremely floaty and movement is stiff. There also seems to be an input lag, I'm using a wired Xbox 360 controller which works fine on every other game, especially on jumping. The bosses are lazy, the first three are the same boss with a different color pallet and play mostly the same but with a small twist, the fourth boss was more uniquely designed but is still just a big bird, last boss is another big bird but is the most creative and fun to fight of all. To see the true ending of the game you have to collect all of the coins which is where I'm at right now, some of them are easy to find others are not which I have no problem with. My issue here is with the map, you select a level and play it but if you run out of lives you have to return to the map and reselect a map. This can be annoying if you're stuck with having one life due to a level you're struggling with, especially when hunting for coins where you may be dying more. Lastly the hit boxes are just odd, yours is bigger than your character and you can take damage by landing on the edge, I mean top of the head but near the edge of it, of some enemies heads. Overall  it's a good game ruined by bad controls along with lazy boss design and a few bad design choices. 5/10 It's too bad there's no neutral option.
EDIT: As I continue to play this game I found two bugs that keep popping up that are worth mentioning. First of all when you gather 100 coins you gain a spare item, it's hard to explain but basically you see the icon of the item in the bottom right of the screen and when you press Y (on a controller) you use the item, if it's a power up you gain that powerup, but the problem is it works when it wants to. So many times I'd lose my powerup and try to use my spare only for it to disappear from the bottom right of my screen and me not gain the effect of the item. Next up is conveyer belts, if you happen to run into one while sprinting sometimes you use the belt as normal, other times you just move forward at walking speed, unable to turn around, across them then if you try to jump you just give a normal jump forward.
EDIT: There is one more issue I forgot to bring up, the springs. They are attrocious, the hitboxes are dead center on the spring and only a couple of pixels, which makes then a pain to use, these should be made larger in a future update, otherwise it's hard to judge exactly where I am about to be launched into the air which just makes it easy to misjudge a jump from one spring to the next, which happens many times in this game, unless you somehow have a perfect landing technique.

There's a few things I really like about Armed Seven, not least the concept. Armed Seven is a side on, old-school, doujin shoot-em-up, where you play as a mech defending Earth from the alien hordes laying waste, before leading Earth's armies on the counter attack. It's all set to some bombastic Metal Slug esque music, it's a very assured game.
While Armed Seven isn't a great looking game what's there is well done. The backgrounds remind me of old Mega Drive games like Streets of Rage, all blurred skyscrapers and distant fires. There's touches of flourish happening in the distance, companions being shot down, an upcoming boss wiping out a few city blocks. Said bosses are creative and themed, the way bosses used to be, they split and change, again harking back to the 16bit era without feeling like yet another indie retro game.
Gameplay wise Armed Seven isn't quite a bullet hell shooter, nor is it particularly gimmick laden, it's something in between. Your hit box is tiny, particularly in comparison to the size of your mech, and there's certainly something approaching a swarm of bullets on screen at any one time, but it's not that frenetic. The gimmicks come on the form of selectable weapons, before the game starts you get to kit out your ship as you see fit (to a point). I never found much to suit me beyond the defaults, but I do like the homing missiles as a special. The reason to switch and try new things is because you can alter your aim, not unlike Zero Gunner. You can tilt, lock yourself in to shooting upwards or downwards, and if you don't want to deal with that pick a build that does it for you.
While we might not be talking Dodonpachi levels of bullets there's certainly enough that you'll be pleased your hit box is so small. That said I still took hits from bullets I couldn't see, lost in the background, my outgoing fire and exploding war ships. The health system is interesting. There's pickups to increase your weapon damage and shield, lose all your shield and you'll lose a life, which drops your weapon damage down. It means that your first life can last quite a long time, but staying alive after that requires all the concentration you can muster
On my first at easy mode I completed Armed Seven on a single credit. It’s not insultingly easy, but it’s certainly eminently doable, especially if you play shooters on a regular basis. The step up to normal is certainly more of a challenge, all of a sudden you’ll be put on the back foot, using everything you’ve got to wrestle back control. It’s where my lack of proficiency at the genre makes me doubt things. I can’t go in to any great detail about the scoring because I simply don’t understand the minutia of it, I can’t comprehend it. It makes me wonder about the game’s difficulty too, is the step up in difficulty evidence of a flaw, something not quite right in the high end of the game, something that is nigh on impossible to get right. Or maybe that I hit a wall with the game on the harder settings less about any tightness of control and refinement and more my lack of ability.
Whatever the answer I do know that I like Armed Seven, Without being overbearing it reminds me of my 16bit childhood in the Sega camp. It’s a fun game, with good ideas, some interesting enemy patterns, and memorable bosses. It lacks something though, a (vague) tightness, something to really mark it out. It’s fun though, and cheap, and considering it’s heritage as a doujin game it’s very well done

Recommended, but with some caveat.
If you have liked games from the Assassin's Creed, Batman-Arkham, or the Mass Effect series, chances are high you will like this infiltration/action/social interaction game (important: this is not a pure FPS game).
That being said, this game would be second choice. I don't regret buying it, but I will very likely get tired of it before finishing it.
On the pros side:
The developers went out of their way to make the player feels that his choices have repercussions, be it from a tactical standpoint (rushing in all guns blazing is rarely a good choice, at least for my style of play, except when this is the better choice) or during the dialogues with other NPCs. More importantly, there is no real "good" choice. They have all potentially good or bad consequences, and you will have to live with them.
The skill point system is somewhat unforgiving: in order to succeed at something, from hacking a computer to simply shooting a gun, the more points you have in the related skill, the better. So you have better to specialize. Except that sometimes, the needed action is not the action you specialized into. So you will have to reach a balance between specialization and versatility, with the few skill points you get awarded when your character level-up. This makes the game harder, but it helps with the immersion.
There is a system of perks given as a reward for doing the same thing correctly many times (e.g. 20 hackings), or for having tried different things (e.g. answered someone in all 3 styles), or for having created a good relationship with your mission handler (or a bad relationship - it works, too). Each perk is either a one-time reward (100 XP, 1 skill point), or a permanent small benefit (5% discount on the black market), and even if each perk is a minor reward, by their quick accumulation it's making the game more enjoyable. It feels very rewarding, because the game is basically telling you, you are doing something right.
This is a game where it is theoritically possible to do a "pacifist run", albeit that could be a wee bit challenging at time. The game is compiling two helpful values to judge your agressiveness: hospital bills (for non-lethal neutralisations) and number of orphans (yep, for hard kills). Feel free to maximize whichever value you prefer. Choices and consequences, as I said.
There is a definite gritty aspect in the atmosphere of the game. You are playing an operativegood at manipulating others (the "manipulating" is right there in your dossier, said your boss) in a "the end justifies the means" shadow agency, and your allies are certainly no angels (from coldly practical to downright sadists). For many players who are looking for a "realistic" spy/infiltration game, this has a strong appeal.
Which brings me to the cons side.
The occasional sadistic choices will sometimes leave me with a very bad feeling; if you prefer to play goodie characters, this game may not be for you.
An extreme example is when you catch an arm dealer in the first chapter. You can either kill him on the spot, arrest him, or let him bribe you and escape. With the first two, you lose access to some weapons and mods on the black market until the next chapter (and apparently, the baddies as well, so it's not that bad). If you let him go, you get a discount on the local black market, but the baddies are better equiped and the TV news will hammer you with the body count of a terrorist attack on a local US army base. But, eh, choices and consequences, deal with it. So far, so good.
That got under my skin in this instance is that happened when I decided to arrest him (in a first game, I let him go). My choice decreased the local terrorist activities, my operative got congratulations from his handlers and I got a "Due process" perk as a reward. And then the game told me repeatedly, in no uncertain terms, that the poor sod I arrested was headed for the torture chamber. And this godamnit operative I have been guiding for a few hours to sneak in and minimize casualties was totally unapolegetic about it. Quite cheerful about it, he was, actually. It thrashed my good feelings over an otherwise successful mission. And talk about "due process". The expression "bitter ashes of victory" comes to mind.
Storywise, it is a good reminder of the context and the "game" being played. As I said, gritty atmosphere and hard choices, the spy business is no job for the meek. One damning point is that, still storywise, this bout of torture is totally un-necessary: you get the info you need and around $15,000 in cash with whichever choice you made. If making the player aware of all of the amoral/immoral subtext in the spy business was the objective of the developers, I should commend them on this.
Gamewise, my point is that this sort of situation may result in divorcing you from your character. If you want to play a somewhat moral character trying to do a clean job, forget it. It's a messy job about to get messier, and he is a jerk in a world of jerks.
Another big default of this game is the aphazard mouse control. Regularly, when combat starts, I found myself aiming at the sky or the opposite direction because the mouse overreacted to my frantic attempts at aiming. Similarly, during hacking minigames, the code I'm busy slotting in a precise spot will go sideway when I click it home, often trigering the alarm. Conversely, in the lockpicking minigame, I will spend a good 10 s (out of the 15-20 alloted) pushing the mouse up again and again until the first part of the lock deigns to move up in the right position.
Part of these controlling issues may actually be a designed part of the game, as my mouse control gets better as I pour more skill points in the relevant skill (see the skill point section above); and in this case having no point in a skill is harshly punitive indeed. And part of these issues may just be me being me, a player of average skill and motor control. Still, I feel that the mouse sensitivity could have been better adjusted between the different parts of the game.
My difficulties at controlling the mouse during gunfight is actually one big reason why I prefer the silent, close-combat approach.
If you enjoy this type of game, there is no reason not to buy it. If you don't, it's a waste of $12. You're better off buying 3 or 4 coffees. They'd have the same effect on you.

A solid indie shoot-'em-up by Astro Port, makers of fine mecha games such as Supercharged Robot Vulkaiser, Gigantic Army, Steel Strider, and this. They also made Satazius, which... *cough*
Anyway, Armed Seven takes a lot of visual cues from Assault Suits Valken, which was released here as Cybernator for the SNES. However, it's a horizontally scrolling shoot-'em-up instead of a run-and-gun shooter. Unusually enough for a Japanese shooter, you have a "life bar", but it replenishes very slowly and gives a fairly long invincibility period after you're hit, making it essentially a retheme of the one-hit-and-you're-dead mechanics found in much of the genre. As with most shooters, it's fairly short at 7 stages long, but it's fairly difficult and very replayable.
Probably the biggest point of difference this game has from the rest of the genre is the ability to choose your weapons from a choice of four main guns, four subweapons that fire along with your main gun, and one special weapon that requires charging. "Better" main weapons cause the special weapon to take longer to charge, so you have to choose whether you want a more effective normal shot or to be able to use your special weapon more often. The major problem I have with this is that many of the weapons seem fairly useless to me, and I generally just end up using the submachinegun as a main weapon, either the rockets or the cluster shot as a subweapon, and either the beam cannon or the guided missile launcher as a special weapon. This isn't quite so bad for normal gameplay, but several of the achievements require you to beat each difficulty mode repeatedly using each of the 12 weapons at least once, so be warned if you care about that.
All in all, it'd be hard for an Astro Port game that isn't Satazius to not earn my recommendation, so Armed Seven gets a thumbs up from me.
(Note: I originally owned this game on Direct2Drive when it was released by Curious Factory, so my total playtime is somewhat longer than my Steam playtime.)

I first heard about this game from a list that was titled, "Best games you've (probably) never played". So naturally, I came into this game with mixed expectations. That said Alpha protocol has pleasantly surprised me.
This is a stealth infiltration game. It's not a shooter, it's not even a traditional rpg per se. If you come expecting a shooter with great shooting mechanics or a deep RPG you will be dissapointed. On the other hand if you want a game that lets you play out your fantasies of being a modern day ninja, with a branching "choose your own adventure" style story. This game is right up your alley. It's core gameplay revolves around stealth, with minigames that involve keypad splicing, cracking safes, hacking pc terminals for various secret agenty reasons (gain intel, shut off surveillance cameras etc). I liked it so much that I played it twice, back to back (I wanted to see how the story branches).
If you've played everything else and are looking for something a little different. I highly recommend this gem.

Confession: I don't really like Pac-Man very much.
I mean, I like other maze games, and I've played every version I stumbled upon Pac-Man since the early 1980s - both in arcades and home console (Atari 2600 Pac-Man is so embedded in my brain I immediately recognised its death sound used in Superman III which I watched the other day). I played the board game where a plastic Pac-Man physically chomps white marbles. I played Ms Pac-Man and Baby Pac-Man in arcades. I played Pac-Mania in arcades (I liked that one; you can jump!). I really like the 2D platformer Pac-Land (until you get to the bit with several springboards in succession). I played Pac-Man Pinball on the GBA (<3). I watched Pac-Man and the Ghostly Adventures on TV. I think Pac-Man in Smash Bros on the Wii U is a hoot.
I really like Pac-Man, as a character.
But... to be honest, I don't like the original base game of Pac-Man very much. It inspires a strange combination of boredom and fear. At the time, back in those early days, I always felt like... "but Mr Do does the same thing but better!"
And I don't really get along that well with Pac-Man Championship Edition, or Pac-Man Battle Royale.
But I like this game. It's a short format, it's different every time, the enemies feel more distinct and their patterns easy to read, the dot combo mechanic and its sound effects are pretty intense, and there's a real feeling of progression every time you play as you unlock new power-ups. And I like the concept of it; that it's based on the level 256 glitch weirdness.
I got this game in a Humble Bundle for $1. Very happy with it. Also - I've never played the mobile version.
All these years of putting myself through so many Pac-Man maze games I didn't *really* like, and it paid off in the end!

With all its different agents, augments, skills, and items there is a lot to explore. Tons of replay value, as every mission is procuderally generated so you never get the same map twice.
I'm also loving the alarm system. Each turn, the counter increases, so that every five turns the alarm level is raised and a new security feature is implemented. It forces you to be faster; you have to know when to leave and decide if looting that last safe over there is /really/ worth it.
If you don't like that though, you can just turn it off. There is a great amount of customization options so for anyone who is failing Experienced difficulty like me - don't worry, you can simply get rid of the thing that causes you to fail. Put more power stations into each level, make the maps smaller, disable the automatically increasing alarm, place more safes to loot. Whatever it is that frustrates you; you can get rid of it with one click.
10/10 would absolutely recommend if you like strategy games.
edit: No longer failing Experienced difficulty, I beat the game in Experienced, Expert, and Time Attack mode now, all of which once seemed impossible to even survive one level in. Which, nice, but also a reminder that you really do get better once you find what strategy works for you.

I really like Invisible Ink, which is for me the elegent version of X-com two. There is less content, less graphics, less super-powers, but the ones that exists have intersting interaction, and therefore the gameplay is funnier than the one in the X-com series.
- first randomness is correctly managed. No unlucky shots, or bad luck when performing and action. Everything you do will work, but the enemy reaction and the level layout are randoms. This is definitively a good decision as it create the illusion that the enemy has a plan, and it makes exploration crucial.
- then, exploration is fun, as it's a poker game : the more you explore, the better decision you'll take and the more loot you will gain, but the more time you will loose. And time (in fact turns) are a precious ressource : as time passes, the enemy gets stronger and you'll have more gards, more enemy programs and harder hacking to handle.
- then the game is more readable : this is simple 2D, with simple cover, and simple actions. You don't have to try everything 10 times to understand how it works. Things just do what's written in the description, that's intuitive and cool. Difficulties comes from poker and interaction, not from hard to understand interface.
So if you like strategy, you'll like this game.
Here comes the usual paragraph about music and graphics. In fe words, they do the job. Graphics are cool, with a style that fits perfectly well in a High-tech spy game and easy to read. There is no anoying stuff (like bad rotating camera, useless details, anoying particles, fog or whatever graphics cards sellers likes, but gamers hate), and no creative or awsome things. And the music is the same way : minimal ambiant.
And now, here is the paragraph about the invisible pink unicorn. She's in the game, but you cannot see her, as she's as invisible as the ink. But as she's pink, we're pretty sure that the invisible ink is pink.

So first off i want to say that if you played Shadow of Mordor and you liked it, then you should definitely get this game. I view it as pretty much the same game as Shadow of Mordor but with a few upgrades. The new fortress system, the new story that left me in shock, new talent/perk system, and much, MUCH, harder enemies, and the "microtransactions".
1. Fortress: pretty much you attack captains and capture points, then you face the overlord and if you win, you now control that fortress. You are able to upgrade the defenses and put your best captains in it to defend from real people  and the missions. This requires you to save A LOT of Miran.
Fortress Con: the only bad thing I have experienced with the fortress conquest is the online play. I have done a few off them and I have had 1-2 captains die right as they reached the wall. So if you do have this game I would suggest holding off on doing online conquest for now.
2. Story: the story in this game in phenomenal, from having funny ologs to fighting off hordes of uruks. I am about 95% done with the game, and some parts I just did not see coming. Don't want to spoil anything but the story is very good, and highly recommed fans of Shadow of Mordor buying this game.
3. Talent/Perk System: At first I wasn't too into the new system. It wasn't until i got further and further into the game that i realize it makes sense. You are only able to choose 1 upgrade from each perk so choose wisely. I like how it forces the player to choose between 2 different upgrade, for example: fire, frost or poison damage. You might end up getting all 3 and switching them out depending on what captian you are fighting. Really well done system.
4. Difficulty: Back in Shadow of Mordor I would just counter people, and build up my eleven rage and then execute every with the unlimited might you were given. The nemeis' you had only came back a few times and weren't too much harder than before. Now in this game, I have had 2 different nemesis' come back 5+ times, each time stronger than before. I have ambushed a captain and then got ambushed by 3 other captains twice. This game actually requires some strategy and skill to do well in. You cant just walk around hitting F and executing every enemy like in the previous game. You have to constantly have your camera on a swivel looking for the pop-up.
5. MC: The MC's in this game dont do you any favors they really don't. DO NOT spend money on them because you will be wasting youre money. The loot chests go based off of your level so buying them early is just stupid. Towards the end of the game you have to do a certain mission and you are given the oppurtunity to dominate captains that are very high level and very good. So just play through the game and get to that point before spending any money.
All in all i give this game an 8/10. It isnt a 10 because some of the cut scenes aren't rendered around your world. So someone who is fleeing could run through a wall and hes gone. A wall could block the view of the captain who is giving his whole speech to you, and sometimes animations just don't sync up. Also check if your PC can handle running this game before buying it. People are saying they are freezing and lagging but i have never froze of lagged a single time.

Right from the start, 8BitBoy feels like a Super Mario clone. You jump over enemies to kill them, hit blocks with your hand (not your head!) to get power ups; there's even warp zones! Now, is this really a bad thing? Well, I'd say that it's more of a homage than a rip off. Sure, the similarities are there, and are pretty obvious, but I think that's the point of the game; to bring us back to that magical time in our childhood, in which simple graphics and simple gameplay were wonders.
Now, even though it has similarities to Super Mario, it also feels quite unique. Rather than having a single fireball as a weapon, you can get up to two berries (what a great difference, you might be thinking, while rolling your eyes), well, in this game, you have two firing modes: forward, and upwards (diagonally). This can add a bit of an advantage for dealing with enemies. There's also many secret areas in each level, some providing alternate routes, and I'd add that it has pretty good level design, some of them can be quite challenging, but, once again, they remind me of the "old days" in which games felt challenging in a special way, requiring me to learn the quirks of the different levels and execute them perfectly in order to beat them.
When it comes to story, it isn't very complex. You play as this depressed guy who misses the "good old days", and while messing around with his old 8-bit console, he gets transported into a mysterious game. I'd say that, in this game, story isn't important, just like it wasn't important in games like Super Mario; we rescued the princess because that's what we were told to do (and, in fact, we weren't even told that we were looking for a princess until we beat the first world). It does add some background information, but, as I said, it's not really necessary for a game of this type. As for the soundtrack, it's pretty simple, since it keeps the 8-bit theme this game follows. Even then, it's pleasing to the ears, nothing too annoying or anything like that.
Well, to conclude, I'd say that I recommend this game, especially to those of you who enjoyed platforming games like Super Mario Bros in your childhood.

TL;DR: Game doesn't cost a lot at all, which partly justifies it's length, but if you want the whole story — you'd better off waiting for the trequel. This chapter blatantly cuts off game's story with a by-the-book cliffhanger as if it was some TV-series.
Also, consider that I do not reccomend this game mostly because there is no "mixed" button for reviews, but the game has a bit too high review score at the moment.
Pros:
+ More animated story scenes and attempts to present cutscenes\storytelling in new ways, which is commendable, considering what devs have on hands in terms of game engine and resources;
+ Brand new heroes with brand new abilities, who bring new strategies into the game. They feel fairly balanced and do not seem like some checklist addition;
+ Survival mode with it's own achivements and therefore challenges and tactics.
Cons:
- Obnoxious training challenges, that force you to play in one way and require to meet all winning conditions. Randomness of opponent's type and their starting position add nothing to these challenges, and just force you to fish for better starting conditions by restarting training. One can say that it's an optional content, but you get substantional amounts of Renown for completing these challenges, and if you want to have enough supplies and leveled up heroes to get a lot of achivements — you're left with no other option other than farming these challenges;
- Game divides your heroes into two different campaigns after certain point, but you have no control on who ends up in what camp. Depending on your playstyle and preferences, you will feel like one camp has much better heroes than other. You can say that such approach encourages usage of different playstyles which in turn keeps game more entertaining and fresh, but considering that unique challenges for each camp are never seen outside one-two story battles and training challenges — this is not true.
- Some moments in story feel underwhelming
and unlike first game, BS 2 ends with dumbed-down "boss" fight, which feels like a cutscene, and then cuts off story without resolving
storylines presented in this chapter.

OK! Tim Schafer's Double Fine Adventure game, Broken Age (act 1) has finally landed! After being successfully funded on Mar 13, 2012. It landed today. And I have to say... holy crap that was bad.
That was three hours of semi humorous adventure point-and-click game play. It was not particularly exciting or hilarious or anything I expected from it considering who was making it and how much money they had to make it with (asked for $400k, received $3.33 million).
The art, and sound, and voice acting, and just about everything that individually make up a great game were pretty much all amazing.  That said... The pinnacle of the game was a hipster lumberjack woodworker making a comment after he makes a stool for you that you can have it because he likes to spread his samples around.
I'm not kidding. The height of the game was a poop joke.
Every individual piece was put together nicely, but they combined to make a rather lackluster and incredibly short game.  I understand this is only act 1, and act 2 will come out, oh, sometime, eventually, but even knowing there's going to be a sequel, the ending to this game is a giant middle finger to everyone who's been waiting for two years to play it.
As it took me maybe three hours of actual gameplay to finish this without looking anything up (it says I've had it open for 4.1 total at time of writing), I cannot recommend this in its current state. Wait until act 2 is available and play it straight through (assuming act 2 actually ends up with a decent ending).

The Binding of Isaac is a neat little bullet hell game. It's pretty difficult but with the amusing yet simple story and catchy soundtrack by Danny Baranowsky leads players into an uncompromising Robotron-esque game.
Have I mentioned this game is hard? Even worse is that with each playthrough the game gets more difficult. While it may sound like a bad thing, it's actually quite nice to have such a difficult challenge.
One of the downsides of The Binding of Isaac is that it doesn't play nicely with gamepads. The game specifically references the use of JoytoKey in order to emulate controller input. Unfortunately that doesn't translate well as Isaac can only shoot in four directions with the angle changed only based on movement when shot.
Being a simplistic game that is hard to master is a great achievement. It's fun to improve espcially as you fight the increasing difficulty curve with each success and failure.

Initially the art design lost me and I don't like how a lot of the "animation" is basically a still picture with a moving mouth (think Scooby-Doo), but the story kept me playing and by the end I had fallen in love with the art style and wanted more. The game's puzzles are too easy, but you become so involved in the world you won't have time to complain. The humor is great and more than lives up to the Grim Fandangos and Full Thottles of yesteryear. Being able to switch between the two main characters is a great feature that really helps mix things up -- especially during those rare moments where you're actually stuck on a puzzle in one character's world.
I would very much recommend this game. After completing the first act, I found myself wondering what's going to happen next and actually thinking on these characters and where the story could take them (I do hope each character's story has a decent resolution -- even the supporting players). I would love for the puzzles to be a little more complex and brain-teasing in the second half and for the animation to be a bit more fluid; but even if neither happens I would still feel comfortable giving this a very solid recommendation.
Now, as a backer, all that's left is figuring out where I get the soundtrack that was supposed to come with the game. That's ONE puzzle I've had trouble solving. The music in this game is great.

A fantastically challenging roguelite with a frantic pace & very uniqute gameplay experiences between characters. Every weapon, character & upgrade you choose feels significant in some way -- there is very little in this game that feels insignificant to whether or not a run will be completed.
And that's the thing -- completion of runs is a very unsure thing in Nuclear Throne. The player is afforded very little room for mistakes, and makes up for this strict difficulty with the potential for your gameplay strengths to just become absolutely crazy. Players who find themselves at endgame-level "loop" runs will find themselves with a fantastically overpowered character in their hands, and the game responds in kind with even more jacked-up difficulty.
For 12 dollars, this game gives you a seemingly simple experience with a lot to learn. I highly recommend you give it a go.

Have you ever wanted to control your own units in RTS games? Like jumping right into that assault tank you just built? You can do that in Executive Assault.
The RTS/FPS gimmick is the strongest point of this game. There are already other similar games that attempted to do this, like
and
. But they are FPS game in nature, that have RTS elements (FPS/RTS). Executive Assault by nature is an RTS game, but with FPS elements. If all this time you've been itching for taking control your units directly, Executive Assault will help scratch that itch.
The switch between RTS mode and FPS mode is smooth. You actually control the CEO of your private military company, so unlike most RTS where you're a general in the sky giving commands to your army, in Executive Assault you have a physical presence within the game. As a consequence, the opposing forces can sneak into your HQ and assasssinate you.
Actually, that's the only way to win the game: destroying all enemy units and bombarding their bases are not enough, you need to assassinate the CEO. This makes the FPS experience not just a mere gimmick. To assassinate the CEO, you need to get past traps and mazes that your opponent have built in their base to make your assassination attempt harder (and you can make your own too).
This is the part where Executive Assault feels a bit challenging to play though. AI in this game is extremely ruthless, even in the easiest difficulty. You have a very limited space for building, so you have to plan well - and plan fast, otherwise the AI will smack you down in an instant. Executive Assault basically rests on "arms race" principle: who build the fastest, got to be the strongest. If you're already outwitted in the first few minutes, you better start over or prepare to face hell.
Unfortunately, while the challenge is interesting - and can be extremely satisfying when you've outgunned your opponents - this is also the game's downside. After you've reached a certain point in development, you can easily make the game as simple as zerg rush. It becomes less strategizing and more spamming units. Once you've managed to take a hold of missile launcher, you can just build 8 of them and bombard the enemy base to prevent them from mobilizing their units.
In this regard, varieties of maps could help in overcoming the problems of zerg rushing. However, maps in this game is quite limited. Once you master the map and you've reached the sweet spot of development, you can just use the missile bombardment and zerg rush tactics to wipe your opponent. Online multiplayer seems to be a bit too empty, so if you want to play this game with someone else, you better have friends.
Nevertheless, I still recommend this game. Executive Assault is one among few of its kind. It's more impressive that the game is made by one-man developer. If this game is successful, I hope more games like this could follow through.

The game has a ton of potential. It provides an interesting alternative to the stealth genre. That being said, it is a buggy mess. Grenades don't throw, the reticle ups and disappears, you glitch into walls and get stuck. It'd be one thing if this happened a few times throughout the single playthrough; this happens a few times in any given mission.
I'm disappointed in the lack of polish more than anything. This game has a lot going for it, but then the bugs and wonky combat go and rear their ugly heads. I get that it's an "RPG" and not exactly an action game, but that doesn't forgive the lack of control customization. Anyone remember Secret of Mana? Great game, right? Remember how often you spent cycling through your rotary menu during a boss fight? Almost 90% of the fight was just rotary menus and spamming spells.
Similar thing here, except unlike SoM, the bugs and lack of polish make the menu swapping far more annoying. It doesn't quite get the RPG playstyle aspect down - a tactical RPG would have been better for it. It tricks you into thinking it's Deus Ex or even a Splinter Cell stealth-action game, and then you remember the mechanics are blurry and it only emulates stealth action, it doesn't simulate it at all. Combat is just cover shooting, but it isn't smooth; sometimes I go to peak out and the camera swings every which way it feels like. Other times my reticle just disappears altogether.
All that said, it still has its charms, and for the die-hard stealth addict who likes that element of Mass Effect of influencing people and their decisions affecting your game, this definitely has it. I have to give it a thumbs down, though; there are way better games to throw money at that will fulfill your stealth/cover shooter needs if you haven't exhausted those options yet. If you can get it for a $3 on a sale, go for it, you'll definitely get your money's worth; anything over $5 is pushing its value, though.

Rather than just being the same old Mikey all the time, you can change your angle of approaching different people, by sometimes pis**** them off with the aggressive style often associated to Jack Bauer or you can just keep them doing favors for you because of the suave style of James Bond you chose to use. The thing is, you need to learn to adapt yourself to the ever changing environment.
When it comes to the action, you can choose to upgrade your skills to match those of Rambo's or put all your efforts on sneaking, depending on which one is more to your liking as a gaming style. Of course, it's not once or twice you can avoid being beaten up by a giant boxer if you choose the correct phrases. Just be sure to create good relations with the people you meet, and you will find yourself being helped by different organisations if the price is right.
Now, I beat Alpha Protocol twice on PS3 system soon after the game was released, and decided to buy it also for my laptop because of the glorious moments I had with it while playing it on PS3 years ago. To this date I have played this game through six times on my laptop, once with every background, and not until now can I say I know just about every twist this game has to offer.
Do I need to say anything more? Alpha Protocol has offered me good gaming experiences and memories in the form of a modern espionage RPG. If you are a gamer who dares to look beneath the surface of this highly underrated piece of art, I have no doubt you find yourself being comfortable with it. Just don't forget to turn up the radio guys!

If you liked the Banner Saga, you won't be unhappy with the sequel.  I'd give the original Banner Saga a 95/100 and the sequel a 90.  There are many holdover characters and a good number of new ones.  The most important new feature introduced is new abilities which become available once a character has toped out in a stat.  There are two new abilities tied to each stat, so the character progression isn't scripted.  Characters gain a new skill on reaching 6th level, often a choice of advancements.  Most of the new abilites fit in well with the old.
Another feature to note is that a player may start a new game, playing his choice of Alette or Rook.  Optionally, you may import an end state from the first Banner Saga and continue your story with your successes and failures carrying over.
As in the first Banner Saga, the story line splits early on and the player has two separate caravans.  Again, the story is linear and there is no possibility of going off course.  Avoiding spoilers, there were a few story events I didn't like and a few that made me laugh.  It's a decent story.  I've now played the game through three times and there are still things I haven't tried.  This game has a mederate replay value, in that there a quite a few characters to try.  I guess that I'll have seen all the events in about five playings.
The training tent feture is expanded.  You can still try out tactics against assorted opponents, but there is a training feature in which you arre to use specific character abilities,  Some of these are challenging while others are routine to players of the first game.
Combat is still chesslike, with sides alternating until one side is down to a single figure.  I have never played a game which operated in this way.  This has a lot of novelty value for me.
I heartily recommend this game, but suggest a new player start with the original.
I have recently received an update which includes something called The Survival Game.  This consists of a series of combats using the same maps and oppont types as the main game.  This version used a timer, instead of giving the player time to think.  I have played this only a little.  I had trouble controlling the characters and found it frustrating to know what move to make and yet not always being able to make it.  I had never had any mouse problems with either the first game or the main body of the second game.  Let's hope that there's an update that allows the player to reduce the sensitivity of the mouse.  It's a free upgrade, so how can anyone complain.
I have enjoyed both these games and plan to try the finale when it is released.

The second game in the Banner Saga Series, but no less beautiful or original. The story take more than one surprising turn, and you meet interesting new characters as well as races.
Pros:
+ I didn't think it was possible, but the visuals are even more elaborate in BS2, with short but high end animations. No lazy re-use of old character bases or backgrounds, originality also here up to par with the first game.
+ I appreciated that clansmen are now able to collect food, since supplies always were a problem for me in the first game and the clansmen were pretty much dead-weight. Also, I haven't run into any bugs so I'm guessing the devs really learned from the feedback they got first time around.
+ Again, the story is still super interesting, now with even more aspects and point of views. It's a fascinating way of story-telling, even though sometimes I did just want to stick to Rook's/Alette's group.
Cons:
- Some things in the plot did seem forced or out of character. But it isn't a major issue.
- I was once again surprised by how short the game was. I was done with my first playthtough after only 12h. This is probably the only issue I have with the game series. I was pretty dissapointed and at this point I'm bound to buy the third game. It's a good marketing staregy, I guess.
For people who haven't played BS1, there is a pretty self explanatory introduction, so you could start playing the second game directly. Now I wouldn't recommend it, because the first game is as much as an experience as the second, but I do suggest buying it on sale and not full price, considering it's expensive for the limited content it offers.

Now for the final part: The gameplay! If you like this kind of game and especially if you liked Shadow of Mordor, you'll defo like this one, it has everything SoM had and so much more!
A lil' bit of RPG to spice things up: You have 6 pieces of gear (bow/dagger/blade/mantle/armor/ring) divided in 4 tiers (normal/rare/epic/legendary), and you can add gems to them, a bit like in Diablo 3.
Items have your level, you can level them up a bit doing some challenges, legendaries can be leveled up to 60 (max level) if you want to keep them throughout your progression.
The nemesis system has been improved, you can now assault fortresses with your armies, fights are epic! Your armies can have special "assets" like archers, graugs, banners... Drakes that you can ride... If you want to know how Daenerys feels, now you can, and it's awesome!
The skills, you have about everything you had in the first opus, and more!
Now each skill has upgrades (up to 3), the only thing bugging me is that you can only have one upgrade for a skill at a time, so the domination upgrade, or the elf-shot upgrade for the drain, not both :( but well it forces you to adapt a bit your build to your gameplay and to the situation, it's a good thing.
Multiplayers: There's next to nothing, but the small things present are nice. You can avenge another player by killing the orc that killed him, or defend/assault a fortress online. Both of these things get you nice rewards too!
To finish, I'd like to say a word about the microtransactions: If you don't like them, you can just ignore them, and you can still farm all the legendaries and have them all, you can even have gold coins doing daily challenges to buy chests without putting in money, so for those that don't like that, ignore. I haven't bought any coins, and have about 25 legendaries on the 60/70 available, and most of them are not really useful anyway so no big deal.
However, for those who like to speed up their progress, they can, and the game can be even more profitable in the meantime, meaning more reasons to have a Shadow of Mordor 3, while doing absolutely no harm to those who won't use them, it's a win-win!
Serisously though, microtransactions can be bad in multiplayers game because they can dig a gap between paying-users and free-users, but in a solo game, where you won't even feel it if you don't want to, what's the harm ?

KSP is wonderful, unique, difficult, confusing, elating and all manner of other things bundled up into a deep and long-lasting package.
The core of the game is all about building space-rockets, and flying them to the furthest reaches of the Kerbal solar system. Sounds fun eh! Just be aware that this is not some arcade-game were you can just shoot oversized fire-crackers into space. KSP is a full-blown space-program simulation.
The upshot of this is that building rockets that really work is hard. If you want to succeed at KSP, you're going to have to spend a lot of time and effort getting to grips with how the simulation works, and in the process you're going to have to learn at least the very basic aspects of physics and even rocket-science that underpin this game.
Sound daunting? It is, and in many ways that is the beauty of this game. At first you'll fail and fail hard. You'll build rockets that have no business being in the air, let alone venturing into space. You'll loose Kerbins to the deep void as you run out of fuel or otherwise mess up.
But, spend some time reading the community guides, watching some YouTube vidoes on the principles of flight and you'll start to get the hang of things. You'll manage to launch a rocket into stable orbit and return it to Kerbin. Next you'll find yourself landing on one of the two moons that orbit Kerbin. And then from there, the challenges grow.
The one down-side to this game is that it really does not contain the information needed to teach you how to play it. You cannot just 'wing it' when it comes to building rockets. In order to get past the most crude stages possible, you're either going to have to already be well trained in physics at degree level, or you're going to have to venture outside of the game and find the information you need to calculate the all important variables you're going to need to build successful rockets.
Do I recommend this game? Yes, provided you're up for spending some serious time and effort getting to grips with it. There is nothing else quite like it, and you can learn a lot of interesting real-world physics while learning to play this. It's not, however, a game that will appeal to those looking for more instant fun.

What can I say, been playing FSX ever since it came out. Awesome for anyone with an interest in flying.
Now, since coming to Steam, there have been a few, but not many updates from the original game. Main features are Steamworks integration, which brings online flying to anyone who wants it. In the old days you would have to play around with VATSIM and specific modules to get an online connection, which if you want to fly as accurate as possible is still available, but for the more casual gamer/pilot is a doddle. Works perfectly!
Also, there has been a DirectX 11 test system introduced into the graphics options, which not only improved framerates on my GTX660Ti, but also made the scenery look better. Only issue I had here was with the CamSIm aircraft, whos landing gear doesnt appear in DX11 mode, but that isnt a problem with the game, just older addon freeware aircraft, although out of the many I've tested this one is the only issue.
Also, from what I've tested, 99.9% of previous addons still work brilliantly. I use many of the UK2000 airports from my old FSX copy and they work fine in DX11 mode, along with the POSKY 73s, 74s,, 75s, 76s A330s and A340s, alongside the old iFDG A320 series for FS2004. Alongside these are many other various aircraft which I have loved to fly again.
Only issue I've seen is with some of the new DLC loaded alongside on Steam. As some of these are just a single aircraft with a saved set of flight plans for a ridiculous amount. Many packages like these can be found on sites like
and
which will still be compatible from the original FSX and work fine in FSX Steam Edition.
All is all, still highly recommend this game for anyone with a passing interest in flying or higher.
Also, get a decent joystick or flight yoke if you can. I use a Saitek X45. If you do invest, ensure you have both a Rudder and Throttle controls.

When I heard about Alpha Protocol, I had two thoughts. One was that an espionage action-RPG was one of the best ideas for a video game I'd heard. Alpha Protocol delivers on that. The story is a pretty damned good espionage potboiler. It could almost be a lost installment of the Bourne series. That the story is pretty damned good isn't all that surprising given it's an Obsidian production. These are the people who did KotOR II and Fallout: New Vegas. True to form, expect outstanding writing, difficult choices in terms of what the "right" thing to do is, witty dialogue and bold characterization.
Of course, Obsidian has another, less positive reputation, and that's for delivering unfinished, buggy games with as much cut content as what's actually in the game. Unlike KotOR II and New Vegas, there's no real modding community that I could find dedicated to restoring cut content (if, indeed, it was even accessible). Reading about Alpha Protocol I braced for the game to bug out frequently and to have plot holes I could drive a Mack truck through due to cut content. Honestly? I was pleasantly surprised. Maybe I'm just unperceptive, but after one minor bug in the early going and one crash to desktop, the game played smoothly. There was one instance where the game triggered a flag that I had done something that I hadn't, which got brought up in the story as a plot point a few times later on. And...that's it. For Obsidian, that's shockingly solid. And as mentioned above, the story was satisfying. I'm sure there were things that were cut, but for what it's worth the story didn't have the trainwreck feel of the end of the (pre-restoration) KotOR II.
The gameplay is fun. One way to think of the game is to think of it as an espionage Mass Effect. Another way, one I think is an even better comparison, is that it is more of a spiritual ancestor of Deus Ex: Human Revolution than the previous Deus Ex games were. There's definitely no "right" way to play the game and build your character though you can make the game much harder if you generalize OR specialize too much. Playing a stealth-oriented character is tough in the early going but once you start to unlock higher powers it's almost game-breaking...except against the mostly-unskippable boss fights. Also similar to Human Revolution, if you've only been focusing on non-offensive powers, the boss battles can be ball-bustingly hard.
I've heard Alpha Protocol talked about as a "flawed gem", which is pretyt much how ALL Obsidian games are regarded. On the bell curve of what Obsidian games are usually like, I found Alpha Protocol to have a stable build, a complete story and good if not MGS great levels of stealth-action gameplay. If you like action RPGs and want to play in a fresh and different setting, you'd do well by this in my opinion.

This really isn't a team based tactics game.  It's a resource management game, and you'll never have enough.  The game ramps up its difficulty pretty fast, and the higher alarm levels are just stupid.  The fact that you have to unlock things isn't a bonus, it's a negative.   Once you do run through a few missions, you'll max all of your stats (which you buy with cash from safes), and after that, there's really no point in money.  The game will then just start putting more and more armor on the guards that it sends at you, making all of your previous things obsolete, but not giving you enough new items to compensate.  It won't matter that you have +3 armor piercing when the guards have 8 armor.
Unless you tweak the settings so that your guards stay knocked out for +99 turns, they'll just keep standing up, and the alram level will just keep rising, with an unlimited number of new guards being brough into the level.  This makes it seem like you should be rushing the levels, but you really can't.  There are stupid "tricks" the game throws at you where it will just reveal the location of your team members, wherever you're hidden, simply because it can.
The more I play this, the less fun I have with it.

tl;dr: This game is terribly drawn out and buggy.
There are 90 stages (as opposed to the usual Emily 60) which means that both the plot and the gimmicks are streched thin. Pre/post gameplay scenes are often about characters exchanging all of 4-5 sentences before another stage interrupts them, including dramatic confrontations that really could do without breaks. There's only a dozen or so characters, and some of them don't even rate any role in the plot.
The level gimmicks are repeated over and over, exactly the same - move a box, find all the scattered tools, shoo-away an interloper. Had fun? Good, because you'll repeat the exact same action another 5 times or so.
I have no idea why the game is buggy enough that both Angela and the customers occasionally milling around one on spot, unwilling to go anywhere. The same company made dozens of games with the same basic gameplay, why aren't these kinks smoothed out by now?
...
The basic gameplay is as addictive as ever, though Miracle Max trivializes every stage you use him in, and the game encourages you to grind (replay levels) to be able to afford all the upgrades.
The plot is appropriately insane (and it's interesting to see outright bad guys in this game series, instead of the usual sitcom camraderie) but suffers from being split into too many levels.

An excellent stealth centered, turn based roguelike game where each choice matters. The game does not joke about you having odds stacked against you in a direct firefight, instead you must use sneaky tactics to get around complex you infiltrated, get the objective and get out ASAP. Truly managed to captivate the hit and run tactic used by small agencies.
However, speed as well as being undetected is the key. You will not remain undeteced forever as the security level increases over time, moreso if you are caught. Invisible Inc strikes a nice balance between having to be fast and stealthy, a quality that gives a healthy game
Your squad is also accompanied by a powerful AI, that playes a major role in your success by being able to manipulate facility devices to serve you instead but beware, they are protected and sometimes you need to think about your resource allocation
I also highly recommend getting the DLC, contigeancy plan. It adds a bunch of items and characters to make the game more varied, opening up even more strategies and interesting synergies. It's only 4€ if bought in a bundle and well worth the small price
The downside of this game however is  that if you are not familiar with stealth or strategy games, then Invisible inc can be quite difficult to pick up and learn as the tutorial is quite honestly lacking finer important details which you will discover as you play. Thus I recommend starting up from the easiest difficulty (it still provides a decent challenge) and move up until you hit the hardest difficulties, which is what the game balance is centered around and what defines the true invisible inc experience
As a final word: Try to save knockouts and kills until the last moment where you absolutely need to do so and use the corpse drag option to prevent guards from waking up

I like what the game tryed to do. A look back in time to another generation of gaming.
Presentation:
Let me put this straight, you get what you ask for. The game in itself is not a grand game full of pretty graphic achivments and amazing and inuvative gameplay, it`s a throwback to another era of gaming and the game tells you that right form the begining.
The look sound and overall plot is really oldschool, and it would properly work better for me, if I was growing up in the oldschool era, but I didn`t. Instead I get to see another era of gaming, which I didn`t complain about. The game overall was a positive experince.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is very Mario-esk and you jump on enemyes to kill them. You pick up a lot of fireball spells, in order to have extra hits just like Mario. The fireball spells are all basiclly the same, with only some bouncing to really set them apart.

The platforming which is the main focus of the game, is done rather well and I only had issues with it few times throughout the game. One of the bigger issues were the convatorbelts in the game, were you have to jump with momentum. I felt the controles were a bit off here, but when you learn the timing, you won't have much trouble with it afterwards.
Charecters:
You play as a boy, who is turned into a 8-bit charecter. It`s all in the titel.
There are really not some kind of bigger thing to the game, other than you just have to clear every area, which all have bird themed enemyes and bosses. All of the three charecters (including the main charecter) dosen`t really have any charecter traids, other than in the intro of the game. Afterwards charecters don`t really matter, but I think it`s fitting for the generation of gaming, which this game treys to potrait. In this generation charecters were not that important, the gameplay itself were mutch more in focus as in this game.
Visuels:
The game has an 8-bit style, and uses it to show very typical areas for the generation. This includes an ice level, a dessert level, a robot level etc. The visuels did not do much for me, but this game is a throwback, and everyone who should buy tihs would properly like the artstyle, since that is what the game is all about.
Sound/Music:
The soundeffects are few in this game, but again it was typicall for the era. The music is fine but nothing to write home about in my opinion. I liked some of the themes and they really set the tone of an 8-bit game.
Story/Bosses:
So the story is simple; person get`s inside a game, and now he must fight through all the levels of the game he is in. From there every level is themed after a typical level from the 8-bit era. At the end of every world a bossfight with a bird happens, and you get one step closer to the end.
Now about the end...I did acually not see it. To cmplete the game fully, you have to go trough every single level, in order to find secrets to unlock the ending. Now I did not have the patience to go through the enterie game again, in order to unlock the true ending, but maybe you have more patience than me.
Overall I fell a bit sad about never seeing the end of the game, since I kind of fell like I deserved it. I played every level of the game and yet got nothing out of it other than a screne pretty much telling me to go back.
Conclution:
8-bitboy is a fun game and an amazing trowback to another generation of gaming. If you were born in the NES era, you will properly apriciate this game far more than I did. The game is very short, but you could argue that the game is not done, untill every secret is found, so there is your long game time. Overall I found the game to be a fun experience.

Invisible Inc is an intense turn based strategy game about infiltrating corporations and staying alive. You start off with two agents (you can get more as the game progresses) who have limited resources and, quite frankly, are pretty weak. As you infiltrate facilities, you can buy new gear, augments (which are basically power ups) and programs for your AI, Incognita. For a turn based strategy, it is rather fast paced. The alarm level escalates slowly even if you aren’t spotted in your turn which adds an extra layer of pressure to the game play.
PROS:
The graphics are great. They are cartoony, but the style works perfectly with the darker, ominous, cyberpunk look of the surroundings.
It is challenging, even on the beginner difficulty. This is a pro because it is a lot more rewarding when you complete a mission that you have previously failed.
The controls are easy. It takes a while to adjust to the gameplay, but the controls are very easy to pick up and use.
There is a wide variety of gear. It is not limited to guns and tasers, there is a variety of other gadgets like adrenalin shots, distraction devices and even an EMP.
The gameplay outside the mission is engaging. You have to choose targets around the world, buy/sell items from your contact and manage your agents.
The voice actors are great. There is no shortage of dialogue in this game and it adds a lot the ste personality of some simple animations (my personal favorite is Monst3r)
As you get stronger/faster/more efficient, the guards will to. You will encounter guards with armor and augments of their own. There are even drones that you can hack.
The game is very entertaining/addicting. It’s worth the money, you will come back to the game time and time again.
CONS:
The gameplay is relatively short. There is plenty to do in the game, but once you complete beginner difficulty, the missions in experienced mode are the same except for the added difficulty. If you buy it with Contingency Plan, you won’t have this problem.
Though the worlds are randomly generated, there isn’t a huge variety of how your surroundings look. There are four very subtle changes (they vary depending what corporation you’re infiltrating) but otherwise, the setting is the same.
Fundamentally, the game is phenomenal. I would highly recommend it. Put it on your wishlist and get it when it goes on sale. It’s thoroughly entertaining and worth every penny.

Sam Lake, the writer behind this and the first two Max Payne games, has an odd sort of genius. He writes deliberately badly because that is what he knows he is good at and it works. His writing is like a good take away pizza. It isn't “good”, it doesn't claim to be “good”, it doesn't aspire to be “good” and yet by virtue of piling on far more cheese than can possibly be healthy it becomes something far better than merely “good”. Still the game is good enough that I might actually give it a second play-through on the nightmare difficulty level and I'm not sure I've done that since Max Payne 2.

The game definitely brought my back to my younger age. Playing Sam & Max and Day of The Tentacle are still big moments in my life related to videogames. I loved those games back in the day. I was a real fan of the Point and Click adventures where you had to solve riddles. But those types of games just weren't selling anymore in the last 20 years, so they completely disapeared.
Double Fine Productions decided to create a new one with Kickstarter and, of course, I gave them my money. I got to play the "Beta" version before it is officially released next week because of my donation and I am very pleased.
The graphics have it's own unique and wacky style, just like I was hoping, you still have strange characters that fill a strange world that somehow still works well together.
The story is also quite interesting and hooked me in at the beginning. Not alot, just a little, but enough to make me keep playing the game even though I was pretty tired (not from the game, just in general... I was debating going to sleep or keep playing the game). You basically have two characters, in two completely different settings, unsure of their relation to one another and for each character, you have to solve puzzles to get yourself out of a situation that is bother the character.
While the stories are completely different for both, the gameplay is pretty much the same. There isn't that much gameplay truth be told. This is a point and click adventure game (and no, not like Diablo). So what you'll be doing is talking to characters in the game which will explain the world you live in and will also subtlety tell you if they require something or not. After that, it's up to you to go and explore the world pick-up some objects and then try to use them in the "proper way". The proper way however is part of the puzzle. Co-op gameplay against hordes of dinosaurs with lots of cool sci-fi guns and vehicles sounds like a great game.
ORION: Dino Horde most definitely is not that. It sucks so bad, that I'm actually not very surprised developer Spiral Games thought it was okay to rebrand this game, and get it back on the front page on Steam, despite changing basically nothing worthwhile.
The first problem that you'll notice is that this game does not run well at all. I only run my games on a £500 laptop, but my framerate stayed at around 15 throughout the entire time I played it. Despite this, the graphics are hideous. Textures are low-resolution even on max settings, gun models are hideous, it's just not pretty to look at. On top of that, the sound design is some of the worst I've ever had the pleasure of listening to. The animation quality is awful as well, with raptors typically running at you, stopping in front of you with one leg still in the air, and slightly swinging their necks to attack. The most amusing, however is when the dinosaur corpses fall to the ground, but their leg keeps flailing back and forth, and they lie there with their tongues sticking out in some of the derpiest positions ever.
The gunplay is poor, with useless aiming down sights; the Trek13 shotgun has a slight zoom that doesn't zoom the gun model in, and a lot of the other guns aim through a sniper scope, even if it's a short-range weapon such as an SMG or an LMG.
Almost every vehicle design has been taken from another sci-fi franchise; this can include the Warthog ATV and Scorpion tank from Halo, the Timber Wolf mech from Mechwarrior, or the hover bikes from Section 8. To the game's credit, though, some of the vehicles are actually quite fun to drive around.
The game even steals the "Fight To Survive" mechanic from Borderlands. However, this mechanic is extremely infuriating, because the dinos like to run off before you can kill one, forcing you to wait there for about 15 seconds until you die so you can start over again.
It doesn't exactly help that the "Dinos Remaining" tracker doesn't seem to work, and I've sometimes still been attacked after the wave is meant to be over, so I don't have time to buy new equipment.
ORION: Dino Horde feels like it should be a mod; it's a gimmicky mess, it doesn't seem to have an original bone in its body, and every single asset it uses is done better by another game. I would recommend avoiding this title at all costs. Don't even buy it when it goes down to $3.74 in sales. There are tons of other games you can get for that money that are much better! Think about that. Your time is more valuable than you claim it is...

I'd describe Alan Wake with two words: vivid yet imaginative.
This game deals with the classic light-versus-dark theme throughout the storyline and gameplay, and yields an incredible story at the same time (the protagonist being a best-seller writer is like icing on a cake). Although it is rated as a horror game, it doesn't really put too much weight on it. I'm allergic to jump-scares, and yet I have no problem playing this game. So it's better to describe it as a "dark thriller".
As you play as Alan the writer while overcoming different obstacles, you will find new challenges and new tools to solve them along the way, which definitely helps the gameplay and freshens it up once in a while. The story itself is so compelling, you can't help but to get dragged along deeper and deeper into the unknown mysteries. It's exactly how I feel like when I read a good book: easy to pick up, but hard to put down.
Seriously, if you don't get it, you're missing out. Unless you can find me another game with a best-selling novel in it.

Alan Wake is, by definition, a psychological thriller; however, it's also much more than the typical cheap scares and unexpected noises found in many "horror" games.  From the beginning, the protagonist is uncertain of what is causing the madness in the world around him.  The game excels at story telling through player interaction and internal monologue, which is fitting because the player is a bestselling author.  The selling point of the game is undoubtedly the story, that being said, the graphics are very pleasing even for a nearly 4 year old game.  Another stand out is the sound design which does an excellent job of convincing the player that the world they are interacting with is truly "alive" with something evil.  Song choice is phenomenal, especially the credits song.  Overall the only thing that could use improvement is the lack of enemy variety.  I would like to have seen varied and unique combat situations and enemies.  Overall I give Alan Wake 9 out of 10 stars and would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys story driven games.

This is my review of Generic Open World Game 6:
Technical Stuff:
Can't turn off FXAA. Screen is blurred and messy.

Police will never attack anybody else other than you. Because "they're in the mobs pocket", which is just an excuse to say "we didn't wanna code that".
As for the story, it really misses the charm of the first two games, which told a pretty serious story with finality and interesting characters. It felt like a story that was taking place within a real world. Mafia 3 seems to have gone away with that in order to accommodate their open world "take over the districts" gameplay, making it into another generic open world game with padded content. The side characters seem over the top in a way and it just doesn't feel like a good mafia story. It's a shame, I think, because the Mafia games really are unique. I always enjoyed how you were a grunt in the mafia machine and you weren't this force to be reckoned with, with a cliche revenge story, you were just a guy trying to be somebody, and sometimes that meant doing the grunt work.
It feels like it's trying to be as appealing a game as possible, instead of the unique games that Mafia 1 and 2 were.
I don't understand how people are saying the story is "amazing". It's not a bad story, but it's nothing special, just a overdone revenge plot. Every single plot point in the game is "but how should we kill them all?". One dimensional and uninteresting characters. What do we learn about Lincoln Clay throughout the entire game? Nothing really. He's good at killing and that's about it. There's no reprecussion to any of his actions, police don't come after you, the mafia doesn't respond to you in any meaningful way other than saying "Wow he's disrupting us" in some cutscenes. Yawn.
