Achievement ♥♥♥♥♥s:
This is not an easy game to get 100% completion. While writing this review, I’m at 60% with two playthroughs and around 20 hrs. of playtime. The first Banner Saga took me around 6+ playthroughs and 90 hrs. to get all of the achievements (with poor planning), and some of them were pretty tough when doing the hard mode ones, so I imagine I have at least two more playthroughs to complete the achievements.
The Game (07/2016):
The Banner Saga series is episodic. The games end abruptly and unresolved with the second continuing the story (perhaps a third will finally finish the story?), but the story is refreshing and unique with a dark theme. Be prepared to laugh, curse, and possibly cry. While the series is story rich, unlike many other story rich games, the fighting is strategic and depending on the difficulty setting, sometimes challenging to a degree of cursing at your screen.
The Banner Saga 2 maintains the same gameplay as the first, with some minor but pleasant changes (such as giving clansmen a purpose in gathering supplies for the group and the ability to train clansmen into fighters).
Below are similar pros and cons that I reviewed for the first game…
Possible CONS:
-The game is fairly short for an RPG (my first playthrough took around 10 hrs. give or take).
-It is not an open world if that is what you are looking for—it is linear with autosaves (you cannot choose where and when to save, but you have access to each autosave if you made a mistake or want to try something different at various points in the game).
-The game has a lot of reading involved (you rarely hear a person speak, but it seemed to be more speaking than the first game). The game plays out similar to a point-and-click choices count story, but the turn-based fights in-between reading provide excellent strategic game play that typical point-and-click games do not.
With that said, many PROS to the game include:
-The Banner Saga 2 gives you the option to continue your saves from the first game!!
-The story. I love it so far largely because it feels unique and is well-done.
-The dialogue and choices are often entertaining and feel realistic for the setting (the little bit of voice acting in the game is excellent).
-The art and score are beautiful.
-The game play/turn-based fights are addictive, and the fights even get a little challenging on the normal setting (I cursed at my monitor A LOT on hard mode, but I also like the challenge).
Similar to the first Banner Saga, The Banner Saga 2 is worth multiple plays not only for achievements, but to also try out different choices as they can have a fairly large impact on the story. While I suggest people playthrough the first Banner Saga before the second (considering they are episodic), The Banner Saga 2 does a fairly good job briefly including descriptions of events from the first game for people who start with the second.
I bought this game almost at full price (10% off shortly before it was released) and it was worth it. I will buy the third game when/if it comes out, and I look forward to the day that I finally know the end to the story, damn it! :D

This is a buggy, but brilliant game.  An RTS where you can jump right into the things on the battlefield is a great concept.  Flaws abound and it has all the hallmarks of a one-man show, but... buy it.
The game itself, from a RTS standpoint, is pretty simplistic:  build a base, get resources, blow stuff up.  Victory is achieved by killing the enemy Executive.
You cannot destroy bases, so you need to defeat the enemy with strategic use of your robotic troops.
The game's performance is a little lousy; it feels like it could use more optimization in spots.  Things like bouncy wreckage kind of made me cringe; it would've been better to simply blow them up and not waste CPU on something that's not interactive.  And once large numbers of units are on the field, expect choppy framerates no matter what graphics settings you use.
Dear Game Developer, if you're reading this review, here's some frank critique:
1.  The only major advantage (and it's major) to taking control over your units is that weapons have much longer ranges than the AI will use them at.  So you can kite enemy installations to death with ease once you understand how to use your stuff as snipers and selectively kill a base.
2.  Not allowing the AI troops to kill constructors and requiring resources to be spent to initiate construction really drags play down when the AI is trying, stupidly, to rebuild things you've destroyed.  It was pretty easy to figure out how to game that system.
3.  Going to Vehicles early pretty much ends the game, because Tanks kill Soldiers and buidings with ease.  Aircraft are a real threat if the AI can get them early, but cost so many resources compared to what can kill them that it's pretty easy to defend against them.  If there were Robots that could kill Tanks at an efficient rate and a Robot type that was designed to kill tank-killing Robots (i.e., classic hard-counter RTS stuff) it'd work out better, with more uses for infantry in general.  I felt like infantry was strictly there to end the game with, once I discovered how efficient vehicles were.
4.  Piloting giant mecha sounded awesome until I realized that they were basically just weak, expensive tanks that were hit more easily.  They just never felt worth their costs.
5.  I feel pretty strongly that the player-controlled <whatever> should get either significant bonuses to defense or damage or both, so that it's not just a gimmick that players use to snipe things, but makes the player "heroic" enough to significantly turn battles around by spending precious focus-time intervening.
6.  UI problems, such as losing focus on a plant's UI when placing the endpoint, are really a drag; I shouldn't have to laboriously move my focus back and forth over the battlefield to merely push buttons in 2017.
7.  The research system should've been attached to buildings, to encourage expansion.  I ended up using minimal resources and minimal research once I figured out the Thorium system.
8.  It's not cool that your builders can't heal things, don't automatically pick up nearby resources from the ground, and are destroyed upon delivering them (without telling the player).  It's also not cool that the builders can only be targetted manually; the AI should engage them constantly.
9.  It's also not cool that buildings that have just been placed have significant amounts of hitpoints; this led to some silly stuff, where I literally blocked off Iron resources with a single soldier-bot in the center so that I could finally get a mine built.
10.  I really feel like making soldier-bots cost Iron might have been a mistake; once I had the AI pinned, it was trivial to cut off all of its resources and take the base.
11.  Why can't we tell our robots to invade a base by issuing a movement order?  Having to do this manually by taking command of a giant pile of soldiers and move them around was pretty dull.  And when I died to a corridor-gun, they didn't continue to attack it, but moved away, which was also strange.
Anyhow, I hope to see another game like this, hopefully with more attention spent on what a huge tradeoff a RTS player is making by taking direct control; in the end, in this game, it felt like a game-ending gimmick and something I used to occasionally get an unfair advantage over the AI, not something I wanted to use constantly.  If units had built faster, been able to use patrol patterns (see:  Total Annihilation for classic implementation of same) etc. to reduce the amount of micro-time spent moving my units around and if I'd had "heroic" powers when taking control, I'd probably have played a lot more in the FPS mode, which is the main selling-point; as it was, it was largely a RTS with a pretty simple concept, dumb AI and a really neat gimmick that I hope to see in your next game, with better execution.

So after playing this game for quite a while, finally beating it on the highest difficulty and trying out many possible starting combinations I've got to say - this game's a blast.
Procedurally generated stealth experience that is actually a stealth experience, not just sneaking around and sneak attacking enemies deliberately placed in their spots by a designer, tweaking the level so you can play through it in a "sneaky fashion"? Damn son, that sounds like something really neat.
In this game you will have to take risks, adapt to everchanging circumstances and even though the game's turn-based, you will constantly race against time, trying to optimize your every move because the clock is always ticking. Oh and there's no turning back - you only have a few rewinds for one save, so every mistake counts.
Hard, innovative, unique and satisfying - and I really mean every single one of these words. If you like games that are an actual challenge and you kinda like stealth games but feel like you've never actually been given an experience that could be trurly called "steath", then this game is worth checking out.
One of my all-time favourites, yet another shiny gem made by Klei; game's top notch in every one of its aspects.
Check it out, it's really amazing.
And by the way, I really recommend watching a 27min long talk called "Designing Procedural Stealth for Invisible Inc."; you can find it on Youtube. One of Klei's designers talks about their way of approaching the idea of making a stealth game that is actually very different on many levels from any other well known games from this genre.
The stuff that this guy says in it is really, really interesting and it actually made me enjoy the game even more.

This is a long, but completely honest and unbiased review, if your considering buying mountain, read this first.
First, the reviewers and reporters who made such a big fuss about this game, both good and bad, are turds. Take it for what it is, its a small time no-to-low budget game. Its not life changing, its not exactly special, its just unique because nobody else has thought of making a mountain the focus of a game before. Its not a new genre of game, its not going to cause a huge shift in the industry (damn I hope it won't, shooters will turn into an episode of the simpsons).
Yes its pretty much a screensaver like everyone claims, because its not really an interactive game, you just sit and look at it (probably why reporters made such a huge fuss about it, had to be the high point of their day...). I do hope that improvements will be made to it, I'd consider mountain to be in beta state still because its lacking some basic features like being able to start a new game. It has potential to be better then it is, but that would mean adding a few levels of interactive features. How about subtle things like affecting the weather or events that change the shape of the mountain, the plantlife, the items on it, maybe even add some animals or stick men? The simulation idea is nice but its progressing way too slowly for me, consider adding a speed switch on how fast changes take place maybe?
The people who complain about spending their one dollar, what else were you going to do with it anyway? buy a pack of chips or bottle of coke? Big freakin deal, you spent one dollar to pay for a game you can't create on your own without weeks of training, no matter how bad you think it is, at least have a little bit of respect for someone else's work.
In conclusion, Mountain is a nice start to a game that you can leave on while your busy with other things around the house, its pleasant to look at on max quality settings even if its not the sharpest textures out there, but it needs improvement and additional input from the creator to make it a great small background game. It needs something to keep you interested for more then just a few hours.

I was very happy to see, that Gamehouse finally put some of their games on Steam. "Fabulous - Angela's Fashion Fever" is a time management game, focused mainly on, well, fashion - the gameplay should be very familiar to those, who played any of "Delicious" games. Besides serving customers (which does not work very well with the game's concept, which I'll explain below), there are also additional events to complete, mouses and extra item to find, plus "designing" dress (or rather choosing one from three different options, but it was still a nice thing). It has three difficulty levels, but even the "expert" one isn't particularly hard, to be honest - I was able to complete most of the game without help (you can hire other characters to make things easier for you) and without replaying levels.
If you like time management games and do not mind the premise, I think you will enjoy it.
Graphic is great, especially for a time management game. Music is very nice and not tiring, story is surprisingly interesting
and much more developed than in most games in this genre (although most TM games from Gamehouse have a good story). I enjoyed the protagonist. Humor was nice. There are six locations and each of them feels different and plays a bit differently. I liked special events - they add extra challenge to some levels and connect with the story.
Price. I'm somewhere in the middle. I bought this game during sale, for about 9€ and I'm happy with what I got (I completed this game within 9 hours, though I will probably play a little longer to unlock all achievements). Current full price seems a bit too high, especially when compared to other TM titles available on Steam. At the same time, it's definitely one of the best, when we consider art and music quality, plus all the heart that was put into this game, to make it enjoyable and one of a kind. If this game looks like something you may enjoy, please give it a shot.
My main complaint regards game's mechanic. So after first stage (where everything works perfectly, since you are a store clerk), you start to organizing runaway shows and... you are still basically a store clerk. Angela is suppose to be a designer, but instead she helps models to do whatever they want to do (dress up, do make-up and hair, add accessories) and then... they pay her? They wait in line to give her money? For what? Aren't we the ones (or rather the studio) who should pay the models, not the other way around? This system was pretty much copied from Delicious, but running a store/restaurant isn't the same as what Angela is suppose to be doing. There are much better gameplay mechanics for a games like that - happiness or style combos, as presented in "Juliette's Fashion Empire" (which may be my favorite game among fashion TM games). I hope that sequel will have some better mechanics.
More "Delicious" games on Steam. Pretty please ♥.

Despite the high positive review % this game is criminally underplayed and I believe I can provide some insight that isn't covered in the other reviews and also address some points from the negative reviews because they may deter people that would otherwise enjoy this game and get their money's worth. That said I will be as objective as possible.
First thing, this is pure turn based strategy gameplay. The campaign and storyline is there but you need to enjoy the raw gameplay in order to appreciate this game. Despite what you've been told the 'stealth' part is completely optional; it can be as disgustingly brutal as you want it to be. My preferred end-game is to kill everything and I've found the right setup to make it extremely effective.
Winning isn't about figuring out what strategy works; they all 'work' even on the 'Expert' difficulty. The reason Expert is considered by Klei to be the intended difficulty is because it's the hardest preset that doesn't limit your options. Specifically 'Expert Plus' only discourages knocking out guards until you get EMP access but I don't expect anyone who hasn't played the game to know what I'm talking about here; just know that even the "hardest" difficulty still only limits your strategical options temporarily.
I can accept most negative opinions of some features but my major gripe is their point about the RNG. Take it from me; you do not lose because of RNG when playing on a preset difficulty (not custom settings). In most cases blaming RNG on your loss is a clear case of the Dunning-Kruger effect. You lose because you made strategical or tactical mistakes. Of course everyone makes careless mistakes from time to time and Invisible Inc acknowledges and embraces that with a number of "rewinds" that essentially legitimises save-scumming.
There is an alarm system that increments every turn, adding difficulty over time throughout each mission. Some opinions express distaste for it but I think it's great. Historically most stealth games are very easy; you can be as patient as you'd like and often killing or incapacitating people has no repercussions. If that's the requirement for stealth games then this isn't one. It's a strategy game first and foremost, and a very unique one.
Overall this game isn't easy at the higher difficulties. Beginner exists for a reason so it's ok if you can't brain. If you let it this game will teach you how to brain. Not recommended under the influence of alcohol or sleep deprived, or try anyway, whatever. Fight me in the comments, on the forums, or real life.

I came into Invisible Inc. with the feeling that I'd be playing a tactical stealth game and departed with feeling like I was playing a lighter slightly less luck based X-Com. But that is hardly a bad thing. Invisible Inc. is a very strong title about fast-moving tactical stealth, full of customization options to benefit many different types of gameplay ranging from completely silent to brutal elimination.
From the start of the campaign you're given three days to gather enough resources to mount a counterattack against a shadowy corporation (even shadowy-ier than the other four ruling the world). Every mission takes between 5 to 12 hours to reach, meaning you could do a bunch of nearby missions and get about four done in a day, or as little as two. Missions typically don't take much longer than 20 minutes in game time but are meaty enough to really get your mental muscles flexing.
At the end of every successful (or unsuccessful) campaign, you earn XP which is translated into new starting agents and upgrades, all of which promoting various playstyles. On top of that the campaigns are relatively short (four and a half hours) meaning that there's a lot of room for trying these various gadgets and gizmos with minimal downtime. Another thing I greatly enjoyed is the modifiable difficulty, beginner difficulty is easy enough to get you in but still challenging enough to test you. As of writing, I haven't yet played the other difficulty levels, but I was greatly impressed by the first so I have high hopes for the rest.
The DLC - Contigency Plan - adds an additional 48 hours to the campaign while adding a challenging mission to the middle of the game, not to mention a whole lot more stuff and challenges to overcome. If anything it feels like a warmup to Endless mode (which I'm actually excited to play, a first really) as it extends the game another 4 and a half hours while throwing harder security to deal with. Unfortunately the last mission doesn't seem to scale as well and I found it an embarrassing cakewalk to overcome where I was barely making it through the mid-campaign mission that was added. Overall I liked the additions, but also felt like the game hit its stride when you had minimal resources to work with.
So all said and done, Invisible Inc. is an incredibly strong title that also happens to be pretty cheap to boot. It surprised me, feeling like an overall enjoyable game. I'm hoping they do a little more with it, but am okay if they don't. Recommended for full price, DLC is totally optional, but synergizes well with the main game so it's up to you.

I actually thought I was going to be the one guy who didn't like this game because it was slow out of the gates, and I think the game is really geared more towards younger (teenage) gamers, but damn if I didn't end up liking it in the end. Overall, the game is a "choices matter" storytelling game similar to the Telltale games (especially Wolf Among Us), except the gimmick is that you can rewind time to redo most choices.
Pros:
+ Good story. This is the main reason to play any storytelling game, so this by itself is really enough to stop reading right here. I won't spoil anything by telling why it's a good story, but it gets more interesting as more is revealed.
+ Thematic. The story has an overall aesthetic it wants to achieve. It keeps returning to the same symbolism again and again to give a very distinct overall motif. In other words, the game has a definite character and feeling.
Cons:
- Slow starting. The first couple of chapters feel like you are living the dull, mundane life of a boring teenage nerd, and the storytelling has a tendency to be a little overly reflective and moody, but this dissipates in the later chapters.
- The rewind mechanic had a tendency to remove a lot of the tension because if you don't like how a choice turns out, you can just retry. It's the opposite of the Telltale system of giving you limited time to make a snap judgment that you may immediately regret. This also wears off in the later chapters when the story picks up.
- Some of the dialog seemed pretty unrealistic to me.
- Like the Telltale games, it feels a little like you are getting funnelled into the same final decision no matter what choices you make. Do your choices really matter in these games if only a handful of details are actually different in the end?

Alan Wake is a decent game with an amazing story full of mystery and suspense. Both the characters and the plot are engaging and it's all executed very well. The game is split up into episodes, and it flows very much like a TV show, complete with a "previously in Alan Wake" section at the beginning of each episode. Every episode ends with a song. Yes, a full song. You can skip it, but I find it's actually helps with the pacing of the game a lot. It gives you time to check your phone or stand up and go do something for a minute or two. For a game that's this intense, that short break is actually pretty useful.
The same can't be said about the rest of the game. I don't really consider it a horror game. It tries to be scary but doesn't quite achieve it for me. This is largely due to the repetitive loop of:
- walk to a new area
- 1-3 enemies appear
- shine flashlight at enemies until you can shoot them
- shoot the enemies
- search the area for items
- go to the next area
that makes the gameplay very predictable and boring. All I've seen so far is the introduction of more powerful weapons along with larger/tougher enemies, but no added depth to the flashlight mechanic, which gets old fast.
In my opinion, it's definitely worth playing once, but I don't see much replay value in it outside of going back for the hidden collectibles or trying to get all of the achievements.

Alan Wake is ambitious if nothing else. It took the makers years to make (which included many delays), and there is clear evidence throughout the game that it was originally meant to be at least semi-open world rather than sectioned into levels. Once it did come out though, it heralded a new style of narrative with chapters played like episodes of a TV show, replete with visual summaries of the previous episode at the start of each of them. That desire to experiment with narrative in the game is easily the best part, and even though it's very heavily inspired by Stephen King, it's still a very original style for gaming and will keep you playing through even the dullest gameplay portions.
And that's the main problem with Alan Wake, the gameplay. Now, that's not to say it's even that bad, it's actually pretty enjoyable and adds a lot of tension that really helps the game's atmosphere. The game even introduces new and interesting enemies for a while that keep you on your toes! But somewhere around the halfway point the game gets bored with introducing new gameplay elements, and of course shortly after that point you will too. The game really does start to drag towards the end, and if you're anything like me it will feel like a real grind to finish it and see what happens to the story. Aaaand then there's no satisfactory conclusion either. The game wants you to play the episodes that were released as DLC, but due to lukewarm reception (the game already got boring, and the DLC adds nothing while rewarding you with even less substantial story), they got cut short at just the 2. I should mention Alan Wake 2 is rumoured to be in the works, so there is that anyway.
But to cut this short, Alan Wake is absolutely fantastic for half of the game, and then falls short towards the end. Despite this, it's frankly a must play for what it does right, so I recommend it for sure.

What started off as an impulse purchase became (without exaggeration) one of the most amazing gaming experiences in my life. Alan Wake is an outstanding game that mixes elements of psychological horror, thriller and and dark fantasy. Bright Falls are a perfect setting for the story of a dark, somewhat magical, entity going after the protagonist. It also features a lot of meta-elements (like the manuscript pages the protagonist finds scattered throughout the game, which give us insight into the plot and, in some cases, the events that are about to occur or which we do not see on-screen).
As for the gaming aspect: although some might find the combat monotonous, I personally always get the cold shiver each time Alan steps into a secluded part of the forest that's bound to hide malavolent lurkers. The limited amunnition and the character's poor stamina add an extra spice to the gameplay, but the developers made sure that you are able to get to the next chekpoint even with no bullets left in the barrel (alhough it's much harder). The fights are not quite scary nor horror, as the game even hints that there are enemies inbound, but is definitely adrenaline packed and fun.
The story is well-crafted, and the narration helps bring it to life. The entire plot is a huge nod to Stephen King and a myriad of other contemporary horror writers. There are a lot of references to "The Shining," "The Twilight Zone" "The Birds," "Poltergeist" and "Lost" scattered throughout the game. The dialogues are neither superficial nor superflous, and I used to spen an extra minute or two to hear out some of the characters (who sometimes provided a crutial hint for the later story development). The division into episodes, the different songs at the end of each stage and the "Previously on Alan Wake" cutscenes help make Alan Wake feel like a TV show you don't want to miss at any cost, so you keep coming back for more.
To conclude, I beleive that this game is definitely worth both your time and your money. It's fun and has a lot of replay value, especially when you have the commentary feature that comes with the collectors edition. Recommended!

It's pretty if you like the art style, not a massive fan of it myself but you can see how people would find it beautiful. Everything is a bit sparse, very few things to interact with.
Puzzles are absurdly simple, there's a couple of odd leaps of logic as per standard but since you have such a tiny inventory and so few things to interact with it's hard to get stuck.  Given this was backed on the love of oldschool adventure gamers, this should've been way more of a focus.  Also for people who are used to exploring rooms you'll find a lot of dialog is out of place - your character is suddenly asking around about things they've not yet heard of.
The two stories are charming but shallow, old adventure games were marketed at kids but the complexity of them was what made them stick.  This has none.
It's hard to picture how DoTT had a budget of 600k, while they only managed half a game with a tiny fraction of the depth, with 3.3million
In Act 2: Puzzles go from barely existing to frustratingly vague, random and even glitched to impossibility.  They don't even make sense, the two characters need to share knowledge on several occasions through the player, there is no possible way each could get the solutions the other needs to find out for them.  For one of them there is NO way to find out the answer, you have to just rely on the fact it's not the other 3 options and the game has given you a fourth out of the blue.
A lot of the fail states are mind numbingly boring to reset - do it enough times and the game will actually step in and cut out some of the steps so it's not like they weren't aware the puzzles kinda sucked.
I'm sort of imagining this is the backlash from everyone complaining act 1 was too easy, but there's a thing called balance and this is both of the worst ends of the spectrum.
Story wraps up in record time - but still makes no sense - and then the finale is forced and anticlimactic, dialogue is much shorter, much less witty, character development is nil.  Revelations that should be earth-shattering and psyche-breaking are shrugged off in seconds. The ending not only doesn't make sense, it doesn't even solve anything.
All in all if this were a quirky bargain bin game then sure pick it up, play for a bit and then forget. As a story it's a mess that clearly wasn't planned in advance. As a promised hark back to the old school games of yore, it's a nail in their coffin.

Whenever someone asks me to describe The Banner Saga 2 to them, I always tell them "Its like XCOM + The Oregon Trail + Beards". But really its all of those things put together, then made even better. The combat is great, and improvements have been made since the last game to make it better. Different combat goals have been added, and instead of constantly wailing on my dredge opponents, I found myself targeting the big baddie to make the others run away, or frantically burrowing snow with my human characters while my two varl defended them against an unstoppable wave of enemies. I wish I saw more of the alternate goals, but overall the regular battles were still very fun. One small addition I did appreaciate is that clansmen will now forage for food, instead of in the first game where they were basically just things that consumed food and did nothing else. Your choices from the last game matter here, and your choices in this game will matter in the next. When faced with an army of dredge, sending my finest varl warriors into the fray saved dozens of lives, but cost the life of one of my best fighters. Choices like these make each playthrough of The Banner Saga feel like your own. When I played The Banner Saga 1, I found myself discussing with my friends important choices in the games, like
or
. The same happened with The Banner Saga 2, as these heavy choices still exist. While the combat and actions is great, one of my favorite parts of this game  is the story. It immerses you in a rich world where the sun has stopped, tense alliances have been created between former enemies, and towns and villages are present everywhere. There are inoccent people like Alette, who dosen't want to kill anyone, and wants this war to end in peace, and there are brutal, practical people like Bolverk, who just want to make some coin, kill some people, and not die. The game shows how these different people react to a breaking world, and in some playthroughs they change, and in some they don't. It all depends on your choices. This game series has been one of the most engaging series' I have ever experienced, and I highly recommend it. While you can go into The Banner Saga 2 without playing the first game, I
recommend this as you will be missing out of much of the weight of the story. Experience the story from end to end, as I think that was the way this game series was designed to be played.

I'll review the first for overall topics, as the sequel doesn't improve much on most of it*. Though I bought it at the very minute I had finished the previous one, I found more than one thing spoiling this new experience.
First, for some reason the character screen got me serious slowdowns, specially when hiding/ opening the promotion flag and/ or checking itens. Second, as the game guideline is decision making, it's replay value is kind of high, so it's VERY frustrating that you get a lot of bonus Renown for achievements only once, as most of them will be gone in the first playthrough**. I suspect it was a measure to prevent Load exploit as you make these decisions, but you know what? It's bad means to a bad end - as the general effect is to frustrate replay attempts.
And last but certainly not least, several characters simply vanish, and the game doesn't warn you - if you don't check the heroes screen in camp, you might not notice until the next battle (or "until it's too late"). There is one especially buggy character from the previous game, which at certain point is said to be dead, but he is there in my roster (and in almost every battle, for me) and not much later even engages conversation (an interesting one, surprisingly). But then, when his presence is crucial for the story, he vanished, and the protagonists explain his death recalling an unexisting moment (in my playthrough), unless he really died in Chapter 9 - so the further conversation was actually part of the bug. It's a known bug, it seems, and apparently not much rare, so it's surprising it's not yet fixed. I have also experienced graphical glitches in one of the final battles. Nothing dramatic, but annoying still.
I still recommend the game. Story driven as it is, it builds a lot on the previous title. The buggy character mentioned above is beautifully developed (judging by the "postmortem" conversation), so it was especially frustrating to see my efforts to protect him go to waste. Various characters may vanish at this point, supposed to join the alternate party, but the buggy one is the only one dear to the story.
* Reworked renown values to promote characters, new abilities, the Survival Mode (a game in itself, of battle after battle. Recommended to play after finishing the story, and probably deserves a review of its own), and "the plot thickens". Rook's/Alette's party is divided at certain point, and the path of the new party is the most engaging; it's lead, a highly exploitable, extremely strong fighter - and even so, the battles they face are a lot more challenging than the main party's (may be so for the absence of some strong fighters supposed to join this party - the bug hits me again).
** Speaking of achievements and challenging battles, there was a specially difficult battle in which I've unlocked 3 character achievements at once (3 kills per character. Each achievement immediatly turns in 5 Renown), but couldn't win (it's tougher than the second encounter with this foe), and as had to load, there I had 15 Renown gone forever.

I feel like this game will be better tackled if I just go point by point in a Pros and Cons list, bear with me: This review may go all over the place.
Banner Saga 2 is the sequel to Banner Saga, a very engaging strategic turn-based RPG grounded in a fantastical Viking/Norse mythos. In this game you also play two different groups in which the narrative alternates at different intervals between them; much like the first one, both are trying to flee from ruthless golem-like beings called the Dredge. It is the player's task to lead their caravaa with danger from disasters, less-than-savory characters, and unfortunate events; inner politics; and what may be a fate that is proving too difficult to avoid...
As a continuation of the Banner Saga, and having loaded up my progress from the previous game, I felt like I had returned to old friends. What this studio is exceptional at--both in BS and this one--is that the characters in these games are easily identifiable. They're real people and the small meetings and discussions you have with them as you plan the best course of action flesh them out in subtle yet satisfying ways. They all have their own motives, sense of duty, prejudices, skepticism, haughtiness, fears, worries, hidden pasts that are better left un-broached (though damn me if I don't try to find out!!), and sometimes senses of humor. In this way, choosing my characters was equally dependent on the best strategy (which I profess I'm not the best at) and who I felt a connection with.

Garry's Mod is just about the most opened ended game ever released. Hundreds of player made gamemodes, models, tools, animations and more are available with full integration for Steam Workshop. This game truly is the Source engine taken to the absolute maximum, bundling dozens of gamemodes together for you to enjoy.
Because of the unique mostly player-created models and textures, it's hard to put down if the game is graphically appealing. In general you can expect the graphics to be servicable, but weak.
Garry's Mod is designed to be a sandbox environment for you and your friends to design whatever it is you so choose. This is absolutely accomplished by this game to the highest degree. You can't technically put down what the purpose of this game is - because there isn't really one. This game gives you the tools to create whatever objective you want.
Out of game, there are no progression systems in place besides achievements and server benefits. This makes the game even more community driven then it would sound on paper, and encourages server popularity.
Servers are all dedicated community servers that host one of the hundreds of gamemodes. It's impossible to rate this as they can vary depending on the server, but you can definitely expect some top notch servers for the more popular gamemodes such as Trouble in Terrorist Town or Murder.
The business model of this game is standard with the Steam Workshop. You pay the initial price and own the game and the workshop in full. Some servers allow you to pay for benefits or cosmetics, but again, this is all up to the community.
The biggest thing to note about this game is its huge diversity of gamemodes. There is something for just about any person with a computer and Steam. I encourage anyone who purchases this game to simply try different gamemodes, it's impossible to rate every gamemode in a review like this. If you are here to simply play the gamemodes and not create, which I imagine most of you are, it's entirely just trial and error.
NOTE: THIS GAME DEPENDS ON OWNING AND INSTALLING CS:S AND HL2 FOR TTT AND MURDER
Overall, this game is a heavily community-driven game that encourages both creativity and player choice for what they wish to play.

Basically a portal maze. Levels or rooms inter-linked with one another through portals with a very brief loading time
between each. The game play consisting of walking around with a torch avoiding the occasional trap with some
freaky audio and and sometimes visual effects. There don't seem to be any monsters. If you die from a trap
it's game over and you have to start over so you have to manually save your progress from time to time. The traps can often be deactivated by pushing a box into a trip wire or sensor beam, the boxes generally being convieniently placed next to the traps.
Despite the dark look of the game and the reasonable sound effects and music the levels are far too small and simplistic
and many don't seem to differ in layout very much from one another. Many of the levels don't seem to have traps or any
challenges.
Generally from where you port into the level theres a choice of 3 or 4 directions. If theres no traps, you walk along
an often straight corridoor for literally 5 seconds to the sound of some freaky sound effects to the next
portal at the end of the corridoor. So you are spending seconds not minutes on each level even with traps, which
be fair I felt was frustrating because I just wanted to explore some big, dark, complex levels.
With bigger, more complex levels and more challenges, maybe a few monsters within, this could be a reasonable game even with the purly exploration with a torch based game play.
To be fair I didn't exactly dislike the game it's just it was far to quick and easy to complete. Stumbled upon the exit within 38 minutes of total game play even after dieing the first couple of times and learning to save progress. Played it some more to try and explore but didn't realy find that much more to it.

So I bought this game for the sole reason that all of the friends I added seem to play it often.
Because of that, I feel bad that I don't like this game more. It definitely is humorous, morbid, dark, and deliciously evil if you like games like that.
But while I do like games to be challenging, I think this one may be a bit TOO challenging.
For one, if you die, you start over at the very beginning. Every time. Even if you're at the very end.
The game somewhat makes up for this, however, in that it randomly generates a new layout every time, so that no two games are ever the same.
Still, I find it very hard to play this game without a controller. I'm thinking it would be much more fun (and easier) if one has a controller hooked up. Playing with the keyboard takes getting used to.
So if you're looking for a (very) challenging game that will make you go "WTF?!" on a regular basis, this one is for you.

PAC-MAN 256 is a thoroughly good-ish game with more than enough 'good' to make up for the '-ish'.
PAC-MAN 256 is a game based off of the Kill Screen of the original Pac-Man arcade game; a strange mess of fruit, ghosts and errant code that was impossible to beat. In this game, the Missingno-esque wall of glitchiness actively advances towards you from the bottom of the screen, and you have to endlessly make your way upwards while eating as many dots as you can. It's a neat idea, and it works. Along the way there are ghosts to avoid, Power Pellets to even the odds, cherries, strawberries, apples, oranges and melons to eat, and 21 different power-ups that are unlocked as you play.
The Power-Ups are mostly pretty cool. There's lasers and fire and icicles and traps and bombs and beams and tornados and they're unlocked in an orderly fashion that keeps the gameplay fresh. You can only choose three Power-Ups at a time to show up in the maze, but whichever one is next to be unlocked will occasionally fly down and give you a brief taste of things to come. The Power-Ups occasionally repeat though, so you'll start the game with Lasers, and later earn Optics, which are exactly the same as Lasers except they fire around corners as well, making them infinitely better. You can unlock a Tornado which chases enemies down, but later you can unlock the Twinado, which is like the Tornado, but there's two of them.
You unlock the Power-Ups by eating Pac-Dots, but you upgrade them using coins that you can earn by doing missions, which include things like 'Eat a chain of 128 Dots', 'Eat 4 Apples', 'Eat 5 Power Pellets', 'Eat 20 Ghosts', 'Kill 20 Ghosts with the Fire Power-Up', and so on. They never really go up in difficulty, but the majority revolve around eating or using a certain Power-Up, so it's a nice way to force in some variety. And your progress carries over, so you don't have to eat 20 ghosts in a single run if that's a little too challenging for you.
One of the biggest down-sides is that I've heard that this is a port of a mobile game, and I'm willing to bet that it was one of those 'Free to Play - Fee to Pay' mobile games, because grinding for coins to upgrade your Power-Ups is a nightmare. There are coins in the mazes, but they're only worth 2 or 5, which is terrible when you need to earn more than 85,000 to fully upgrade your arsenal. You get boxes of coins for completing missions, and sometimes just as random free gifts, but they contain random values of either 128, 256, 512 and 1,024. As you may expect, it's most commonly 128, with the thousand only showing up very rarely, maybe once after beating 10 missions.
That's definitely the biggest problem - the grinding. This is a good game, honestly, but it's not the kind of game I'd want to play for more than 5-6 hours. And it bugs me to know that with every Power-Up unlocked, a decent high score achieved, and all of my favourte Power-Ups fully upgraded, I would still need to spend another 20 or so hours to get the last achievement, because the game wants me to keep playing, but it doesn't know how to make me beyond making the final achievement 'Fully Upgrade Every Power-Up'.
But if the greatest crime this game commits is 'Wanting me to keep playing for a very long time', then I can sort-of forgive that. After the disappointment that was Pac-Man Championship Edition 2, this is a wholeheartedly good, if not great, Pac-Man game.

A bunch of cool ideas lost in a sea of nonsense, gameplay-wise.
Pac-Man 256 has a working, if slightly boring and occasionally inconsistent, presentation, and didn't exhibit technical problems on my machine. The problem is with the gameplay. Genre-wise, it's a mix of an arcade game with an upgrade'a'thon, and it's hard to tell which part is supposed to be the side one.
If you try to ignore the upgrade'a'thon, you end up with a rather simple game where you lead Pac-Man amongst the neverending maze, with flood of glitched out glyphs preventing you from returning too far or completely slacking off. The ghosts have some interesting, unusual behaviors, probably tied down to the fact that you are in a neverending maze and not a closed one. You can also get "dot combos" by collecting regular pellets without crossing over empty spaces. The thing is, the deciding factor on your score is what will the level generator come up with. A particular oddity is that game occasionally changes minor pellets into upgrade coins and powerups, and the way it works is that pellet disappears and a thing appears a moment later - the thing would keep up the pellet combo, but if pellet gets removed just as you were to collect it, your combo is broken. Add very random locations of powerups, ghosts, and lanes, and it really is a game of luck.
The upgrade'a'thon part hinges on additional powerups being introduced into the game. Here are the facts: you select three powerups that game will spawn randomly on the field. The power pellets are always spawned but share some mechanics with powerups, most notably that while under effect of a powerup the very same powerup will refill the duration as expected, but other ones will just refill a little of duration of current one, and you can't distibugish visually between other powerups until the current one wears off. You unlock selectable powerups by total of collected regular pellets, and you can upgrade them with upgrade coins, with first upgrade costing 16 upgrade coins and eigth one 2048 upgrade coins. The upgrade coins with value of 2 and 5 spawn rather rarely during gameplay, and there are also traditional missions granting you, randomly, 128/256/512/1024 upgrade coins on fulfillment; the game can also grant you such a reward for no apparent reason. Unlike most upgrade'a'thons with mission system that come to mind, you are only given one mission at a time.
Since regular pellets are placed at roughly same density, or even decreasing one, through the maze, there is little discouragement for dying in the first unlock system. You just grind for powerup selection. How are the upgrade coins? Not much better. Most missions involve collecting specific powerups or making use of them to kill ghosts which also implies collecting them, and there we get back into maze being rather random. The fact that you don't have a wider selection of missions at once also makes this quite annoying. They don't even get harder with time, they stay time-consuming, but that's it; you could probably fulfill all but one of them by playing the game for 20 seconds, intentionally dying, and repeating. At the same time, if you are past the last unlockable powerup and want to just get the upgrades, there is no reason at all to continue a game once you get a mission success prompt, since that's the only real way to get coins and you won't get another mission until acknowledging that one.
This would perhaps be forgivable if the new powerups actually revived the overrandomized main game. They do not.
The vast majority of unlockable powerups are based on the concept of killing ghosts. The game introduces no extra buttons compared to original Pac-Man, thus question arises if those powerups are fundamentally different from (still present here) power pellets, and the answer is, quite a few aren't; the biggest yet common difference is that ghosts don't go blue and calm, thus they can rush into you and die. Typically the reach of unlockable powerups is way better than power pellet's one, to be minimally balanced by static scoring, but there are some underpowered aversions. A few powerups don't involve killing ghosts, even less don't involve ghosts at all, some introduce actually interesting kill mechanics. Now, there isn't really much more to the game in the first place, but I think the game would be better if most of these powerups were cut and the rest were made slightly more sophisticated.
And then there are upgrades for powerups, which seem to be developed with a template: all involve exclusively increase of powerup duration and/or increase of points gained upon killing a ghost with one. There is one powerup in particular in case of which I'm pretty sure duration increase is more of a downgrade than anything. If you want something else to happen to your favorite powerup, you may find it interesting that latter half of unlocks is full of semi-clones of earlier ones, with some odd upside but usually no marked downside, and with actual usablity improvements varying. The best thing I can say about this is that you can load both into your set of three spawnable powerups, thus reducing randomness for your enjoyment of general arcade part of the game, and also for selected missions in which both powerups work.
After some time spent playing, I'm sad to report the game does not really develop compared to where it started. It's fun at the beggining, sure, but there are so much better games sold at comparable price it's not even funny.

I have never played a game where my choices impacting the game on this scale.  Who your allies are, what solutions are available, who lives and dies, even shop inventory... all of these are tied to choices made during the plot.  Conversation choices, yes, but also choices on how to complete missions - sometimes completing a mission undetected yields very valuable rewards and opens up choices for later plot points.  One different choice, or performing missions in a different order, will almost always guarantee a different outcome later on.  This is an espionage RPG done right.  The gameplay is mostly smooth with some clunky moments, particularly when it comes to gunfighting, but it's almost unnoticeable.  And while the core cast is very well developed, and most everyone has a dossier that gives their backstory, two or three characters could use some more development.  Still, the gameplay is fun, and the storyline RPG elements are flawlessly executed.

I have this on my laptop and PC. on my PC I use all Saitk gear (yoke, pedals, radio, autopilot, TPM...), Track IR, and a Thrustmaster warthog stick if I'm going to fly a diamond, airbus, or some warbird. This is all good, and the game feels great (although my CFI irl still says I use too much left rudder, and I think it's FSX's fault). On my laptop I fly with just a 360 controller, and it also works fine.
So you can really have the best of both worlds with FSX. A complete sim pit, or just an xbox controller. It's really up to your preference. If you want to hang out on the back porch and drink a few road soda's while you fly from NH to NY in a Cessna on the laptop, that'll be a good time. If you want to rip a leerjet from coast to coast with a yoke and pedals, you can do that too. It can be as high or low fidelity as you want it to be. I prefer my simpit, but on a nice afternoon I don't want to be cooped up inside, and the laptop w/ xbox controller is enough to get you into the air and back down (although the TPM control would be nice, the B and Y buttons for throttle can be tough if you don't keep an eye on the RPM's).
There are plenty of addons for the game, most of the good ones are payware. I like some Carenado products, but A2A's Cessna is right on... You can burn out the starter, foul your sparkplugs, kill the battery, flood the engine, cylinders can loose compression... quite a bit can go wrong, making it more fun.
I play this usually once a week for a few hours, especially after a day of manuevers in a real c172s! Also call your local flight school and take a real plane up for an hour. You will come home and play FSX all week long.

The potato is a starchy, tuberous crop from the perennial nightshade Solanum tuberosum L. The word "potato" may refer either to the plant itself or to the edible tuber. In the Andes, where the species is indigenous, there are some other closely related cultivated potato species. Potatoes were introduced outside the Andes region approximately four centuries ago, and have since become an integral part of much of the world's food supply. It is the world's fourth-largest food crop, following maize, wheat, and rice. The green leaves and green skins of tubers exposed to the light are toxic.
Wild potato species can be found throughout the Americas from the United States to southern Chile.The potato was originally believed to have been domesticated independently in multiple locations, but later genetic testing of the wide variety of cultivars and wild species proved a single origin for potatoes in the area of present-day southern Peru and extreme northwestern Bolivia (from a species in the Solanum brevicaule complex), where they were domesticated approximately 7,000–10,000 years ago. Following centuries of selective breeding, there are now over a thousand different types of potatoes. Over 99% of the presently cultivated potatoes worldwide descended from varieties that originated in the lowlands of south-central Chile, which have displaced formerly popular varieties from the Andes.
However, the local importance of the potato is variable and changing rapidly. It remains an essential crop in Europe (especially eastern and central Europe), where per capita production is still the highest in the world, but the most rapid expansion over the past few decades has occurred in southern and eastern Asia. As of 2007 China led the world in potato production, and nearly a third of the world's potatoes were harvested in China and India.

If I had bought Potatoman Seeks the Troof for its full price, I might have second-guessed if I should, in fact, recommend it, but at this point in its lifetime it's not a matter of discussion – if you're even remotely a fan of potato-based games, get it, you can hardly find a better way to waste at least 1-2 hours than jumpin‘ n‘ runnin‘ as a potato.
Soooo... Let's get down to it, shall we? I will try to break the game down into what's good (+) and what's bad (-) about it.
(+)
This is by far the best thing about the game – who knew that adding actual potato controls into a plattformer could make it all that much more fun? I guess, if you're a fan of using 15 hotkey mobas you won't be as enticed as I was, but as I'm not, it was perfect. Ranged enemy attacks, however, are largely annoying and really high-ranged, so jumping is not valid and dodging is often a mundane exercize of dodging around projectiles for 15+ seconds.
(+)
Story is poor, yeah, but it knows it's poor. So why not just go with the flow.
(+)
Although you'll be just avoiding 'em the same way, different areas have different enemies, and a good chunk of them are randomized.
(+/-)
They do make up a large part of endgame, and I guess it's fine, but at some point you have to ask yourself: do I want to keep restarting this?
(-)
Judge it as you will – it could be seen as an advantage in a game like this, but there certainly could've been room for more story. It's barely 1 hour long.
(-)
The story is akin to the myths of how a Potatoman  came to be. That doesn't necessarily translate to a satisfying story. Don't look for motivations in some events that happen here. Some could enjoy it, I, however, didn't.
Got 1-2 hours to kill? Get it. Looking for a good plattformer experience? Get it. Want a
potatoy game that won't require your low attention span to work on memorizing the complex twists and turns of an in-depth story? Get it. Itching for a plattformer, especially one with a unique twist (potato)? Get it.
As a part of a bundle? Yes. As a huge, 75-90% discount? Yes. Full price? I would never pay full price for a game like this, I just couldn't.  And while there are many things the devs could've done to make it THE definitive potato plattformer, they always have another shot if they decide to make a Potatoman Seeks the Troof sequel. They have my trust.

Excellent game that comes highly recommended if you enjoy either stealth games or roguelikes (or both!).
The stealth mechanics are consistent and predictable. When played carefully, the game acts almost like a puzzle game, as you manipulate guards to avoid detection. Pure stealth is complicated by the escalating security measures, which add a soft time pressure to the game; take too long, and added patrols will eventually overwhelm you.
Roguelike mechanics are present, in the form of a short campaign designed for replayability, randomized loot opportunities, and of course permanent death and loss. The game is designed to be played numerous times, with different strategies and difficulty levels; a choice of many different agents and initial programs means that you can try out different builds and techniques with each run through the game.
There are a few minor gripes. Many agents and gadgets just feel subpar compared to their alternatives. Stat breakpoints are everywhere, most obviously Anarchy 2 to unlock pickpocketing (which gives you all the loot from guards without needing to KO them, a very valuable mechanic in a game where KO'd guards will get back up and start hunting you!). The game feels less balanced the later it stretches, though the vanilla game features a time limit that'll keep the length fair.
All things considered, I'd strongly recommend the game. A few flaws are overwhelmed by a slew of positive and well-executed mechanics, plus a beautiful art style and engrossing world.

This turned out to be a weird anomaly from an unknown developer that just dropped in out of nowhere. It's hard to find anything to dislike, mostly because it's so brief, and while it's not deep, incredible or revolutionary, it harkens back to those Amanita style games that are content in being merely a short, pleasant experience with minimal gameplay elements, and that's fine by me.
The key to Windosill lies in the combination of the pleasant and absorbing animation, reminiscent of early Pixar works, and the incredibly smooth difficulty spike. They marry together for a soft, short and casual ride of discovery and intrigue which is best explained as simply pleasant.
There're no mistakes to speak of with this title, and the few things that are worth mentioning are incidental. While there may be a moment or two where you wont know how to progress, and might resort to simply repeating the same incorrect step a few times, I feel like this would have become more of a problem had the game grown longer, and as it stands the frustrating part(s) are negligible.
The main concern and criticism then, is the short length of play. Average completion time sits at less than an hour, and my second run through took me less than 10 minutes. Normally I'd dismiss this concern and state that the quality of the content and the price compensate, but it may be a genuine reason not to buy if you're on a budget or looking for something deeper. I feel it would've been very simple for the developer to add another layer of content, a difficultly mechanic, a few more levels or even something as simple as hidden collectables which would've added a reason to spend more time with the title.
Priced at £1.99/2.49€/$2.99 on Steam at the time of review, Windosill is worth looking out for, and the concerns about value for money in terms of length can be mitigated by waiting for a sale, but at $2.99 it's very worth picking up if you can let go of the play length.
Vector Park Inc. also have a number of demos
, playable directly from your browser which are well worth checking out, including the entire first half of Windosill.

I've read a lot of the reviews, both by Steam users and mainstream reviews like PCMag, PC Gamer, etc, and I think the game is phenomenal. I understand that many people don't like that DLC was offered on lauch, or the fact that there are microtransactions, but it really is a great game. The microtransactions are not required, so opt in if you want to. As for the DLC, I like that it was available right away. Think of games like Fallout 4 that were amazing, but you wished there was more...SoW is offering more up front (although it costs a chunk of change). The graphics are amazeballs and the combat system is based on teh Arkham series, so it's familiar to most players. The skill tree system is good and let's you choose your play style in the early game. The nemesis system is amazing...just wow. I had this one orc that killed me on our first encounter, and retreated and escaped on our second encounter...and he remembered both previous encounters when we met for the third time and he talked smack about it...and then came back from the dead as a "Machine" on our fourth encounter which only happened because now he was hunting me. I wish there was a little more back-story in the early game, but enough is explained through little side missions and quests (like memories, etc.).
All in all, this game definitely gets an A rating, at least for the campaign...I only say this because I haven't engaged in the multiplayer stuff yet, like nemesis revenge killings, fight pit, etc.

Alan Wake is a superb survival horror game developed by Remedy - the team who made the first two episodes of Max Payne.
You play as Alan who's lost his wife under mysterious circumstances - he needs to find out why and how she disappeared and ultimately - of course - save her.
I would not call the plot very original, however, there are some twists and also the game feels like a TV show. There are several chapters and when you start the next one you hear narration and the good old "previously on..." sentence that really makes you feel as if you were playing an interactive TV show.
The gameplay is interesting, too: Alan has an array of weapons such as pistol and shotgun but none of these work until he uses his flashlight to remove the "shadow" from his enemies. Only after that can he actually wound the bad guys with these conventional weapons. Ammo is limited and the developers hid several caches throughout the game so it is recommended that you find these. There are other collectibles, of course, just to increase the number of achievements you can attain.
Alan Wake is a beautiful game - lighting and the shadows are portrayed realistically and as both are important to the story the developers could not go wrong with them. And they didn't. Voice acting and the music score are also top notch.
Too bad the game has too very short DLCs (Signal and Writer) and it has an expansion pack, too, which gives the game some arcade-like features that were completely unnecessary.
Overall, I found Alan Wake a unique third person shooter and I can only recommend it to anybody who loves the genre.

Игра с отличным закрученным сюжетом. Всем советую поиграть!
Сюжет игры повествует о приключениях писателя Алана Уэйка, автора бестселлеров в жанре «триллера», оказавшегося в городе Брайт-Фоллс, штата Вашингтон, где оживают персонажи и события его произведений. Пытаясь разобраться в происходящем и выяснить, что случилось с его женой, Алан узнаёт много неожиданного о маленьком городке — раньше здесь жил писатель Томас Зэйн. Его жена погибла, утонув при странных обстоятельствах в озере, рядом с которым они жили, хотя она и была прекрасной пловчихой. Зэйн, ныряющий на дно озера, в один прекрасный день обнаруживает там некую плывущую чёрную массу, с которой заключает сделку. Сделка состояла в том, что Зэйн пишет рассказ, и высвобождает Тёмную Сущность со дна озера. Она же в свою очередь воскрешает его жену — Барбару Джаггер.
Барбара ожила, но это была лишь человеческая оболочка, заполненная Тёмной Сущностью. Томас осознаёт свою ошибку и вырезает Барбаре сердце, пытаясь уничтожить освобождённое им зло. Но это не останавливает Тёмную Сущность, Барбара по прежнему жива, и тогда он уходит вместе с ней под воду, но так и не достигает дна. А остров с домом исчезли, оставив жителей с новостью об ожившем вулкане под озером в 70-е. Призванный пером Алана, он приходит к нему на помощь и на краткий миг ослабляет Тёмную Сущность. Воспользовавшись этим, Уэйк в ужасе убегает из домика на острове, разбивается на машине, но выживает. Теперь ему придётся пройти сквозь океан ужаса и безумия, выжигая себе путь фонариком и встречая злобных тварей, от захваченного Тёмной Сущностью охотника и сошедших с ума федералов до завораживающего сердце торнадо.

Broken Age was originally hailed as a great comeback to Double Fine's origins, the adventure point and clicks of LucasArts.
While Broken Age certainly has good audio and visual design, the gameplay is incredibly lacking. No puzzle is really difficult, you don't really have to do anything too advanced, and I don't think you even have more than 6 items in your inventory at a time.
The locations also match this lacking gameplay. Very few locations that therefore limits the game to less characters and less depth. The locations also bother me, because although it fits the style, the art is very plain and the backgrounds are way less detailed than that of other modern point and clicks, such as the remake of Monkey Island or The Whispered World.
I know I shouldn't be whining when the game has a 2nd part in the works, but judging by how most of the $3.3+ million budget was put into this first part and how Tim Schaefer wanted to get some Early Access money to fund the second part, I can only predict that the second part will be just as disappointing.
Double Fine is capable of much better things than this. Maybe they should stick to publishers and make sure that someone that isn't a complete fanboy believes that they have a good idea.

The locales were nothing short of breath-taking, the soundtrack a professional and complete score, and an ambience that added to the polish of what promised to be a stunning piece of work!
I honestly don't remember being so captivated by a storyline before. It was dark, sinister and had that air of mystery to it that would keep you turning it's pages were it a book.
The interaction was clever, you found cut scenes perfectly interacting with clever mini game type action to move the story onward. It felt whole, it felt so, so promising!
That is why I recommend it...
But heres why I don't and most of these points boggle my mind:
The animation is bordering on terrible when you consider the polish thats put into everything else, it looks terribly dated and it actually puts you back in mind of those old game development attempts at the interactive movie.
Then comes the control system. The mouse feels weird, like it's floating in water and it takes you quite sometime to realise that the best way to make Alan move around the world is to follow an imaginary 'center' point, keeping your character from straying to his left. It's VERY disconcerting, even when your used to it and you find yourself constantly wishing it was chase camera view, or even better first person. Later when you have to fight multiple enemies you start to realise how terribly 'clunky' the whole control system feels. At one point where you have to dodge several enemies and a snow plough type truck, you find yourself swearing at the controls because it was them that made you die, because they didnt react quickly enough.
And sadly, the repetition of killing 'shadow men/items' becomes boring very, very quickly.. I wasn't even out of act 3 before I started to groan at the way the game through me into yet ANOTHER forest with a long way to travel to safety.
Alan Wake has always had great reviews and a massive following and I can see why, please don;t misunderstand.
The problem with it is it's awful control system, and clunky key press responce. (and dont forget the animation which just ruins so much of the immersion and feel)
So I do recommend this game, but be warned... It's gonna frustrate you.. Even on easy level.

Simple yet addictive. The encroaching glitch makes a lot of the classic tricks to evade ghosts much more challenging, and the single life keeps the game quick and fresh. Add in the various power-ups and the inventive way in which they assign missions to teach you to use each of them, and it's not your father's Pac Man. As someone that can typically clear boards continuously on most versions of Pac Man, this is a game where I don't find myself dying out of careless boredom and quitting before my lives are lost.
Once you start learning how each ghost functions, it becomes easier to progress. The deaths don't feel cheap, more like you kick yourself for making a mistake. The reward system is based on cumulative play, so even if you die quickly you can still accomplish something toward a goal. The game also comes with several "skins" to make the appearance of the game look different, from the original classic arcade look to Pac Mania to even versions that look nothing like Pac Man.
Possibly the last Pac Man game you'll ever need.

I thought Broken Age was really excellent. It's not the best game Tim Schafer has put out, but it's definitely one of the best. I thought it lived up to all of the hype of the Kickstarter.
The art style and visuals are fantastic throughout the game, it's a creative and original style. The game just looks beautiful in motion, the animation is fluid, the backgrounds are fantastic, characters have interesting designs, it's probably the most visually impressive game Double Fine has put out. The art style doesn't have the same genius design as Grim Fandango, but it didn't have to.
The writing and voice acting was also really great. There weren't many lines that were laugh out loud funny, but a lot of it was really amusing and clever. Pretty much every character met in the game was memorable or amusing in some way.
I thought the puzzles were really well designed. They were never really difficult, but there was only one that I had a really hard time with. I thought the game did a really good job at nudging the player in the right direction through hints and conversation. The puzzles were satisfying to solve without being too challenging. I think the accessibility of the puzzles is fantastic, considering how much was riding on this game when it comes to Kickstarters. It's satisfying for me, as a huge fan of these types of games, but I don't think it will alienate any people wishing to try Broken Age out. This is probably the game's biggest success.
The general storyline is really great, I think. The world of Broken Age is wonderfully creative. It's whimsical and charming while being really original. The premises of the stories of both of the main characters are really engaging, and I really want to know what happens to them in Act 2.
Overall, I think Broken Age has absolutely lived up to the hype surrounding it. I recommend it to anybody who enjoys video games, whether or not they've ever played a point and click adventure before.

When you first start the game figuring out the controls can be a hassle and although flying without a joystick is possible, you are going to need one if you want to be able to fly properly. However after that is all figured out, it is an amazing game to play for professionals and people who just feel like goofing around. There are fun missions for times when you dont know what to do and tutorials for newcomers You are going to eventually have to buy some payware addons to really make the game shine, but there is plenty of freeware like project opensky aircraft if you dont have the money. The game does not appear to be hard on your computer and has a really good community. The graphics are ok considering when it was made, but they could be better especially the water and there is no wingflex for the default 737 and the gear doesn't tilt in the 747 which is a realism killer. The clouds also magically fade away when you get near them and there is no volumetric effect. I would definitely recommend this. After making the move from x plane to fsx i feel that the colours look my vibrant and less gloomy, better freeware, more payware, and the wingtip vortices add a nice feel. In terms of physics, i have never flown a plane myself but the physics in airplanes feel not completely realistic but pretty good in my opinion. The touchdowns feel a bit stiff but the overall flight doesn't feel "on rails" as others say. Helicopter physics do not feel very realistic. They are too stable and easy to control. For how i like to fly though the physics suit me perfectly and i personally dont want that realism but i know others will. The atc is easy to use and great for beginners aswell. No need to go all professional and download flight plans, all you need to know is where you are leaving from and where your destination is. All in all i give this game a 7/10 by itself but if you include the vast amount of addons i give this a 9/10 Even if you think a 7/10 is a bit low my opinion is to watch and read some reviews, look at some pictures, if youve already done that then my opinion is buy the game. For total honesty, there is an 88.5 percent chance you wont regret it

Superb improvement over an already decent original. The combat is more interesting with a greater variety of both allied and enemy units and more in the way of battleground terrain and structures. The storyline is also improved over the original   and the better quality of writing is almost instantly apparent. The training tent is also not so much of a white elephant and now periodically contains training puzzles which boost reknown on completion. The somewhat boring travelling sections have also been given an overhaul and creating a good balance between fighters and clansmen is no longer just random as clansmen can now be trained into fighters at the training tent. These fighters will consume twice as much food as clansmen and clansmen will now actively scavenge making them more than just the dead weight they were previously.
It's certainly an advantage to have played the original (and the final save from your previous adventure can be imported) as continuity is maintained with regard to storyline and base mechanics. But despite this BS2 remains a better and more well rounded game than the first making it a must-buy for story driven TBS fans. The only valid reason I can see for not getting hold of BS2 is if you absolutely hated the original - and why anyone would have is beyond me.
