Pac-Man 256 is everything you could ask for in a Pac-Man game. Addicting gameplay, smart enemies, a multitude of power-ups, and the drive to rack up a high score.
The power-up and upgrade system works similarly to games like Tower Defense or Clicker Heroes, in that the more you play, the more access you have to more overpowered items and upgrades, which I think is a very cool approach to this kind of game. However this also means that if you want any chance of getting the highest score possible you will have to keep playing until you ultimately get the most broken power-ups, which will take a while because because coins are disappointingly sparse, at least when you get further into the game.
Every time you upgrade a power-up the cost for the next level up is doubled, and considering most prize boxes you get for clearing a mission or otherwise are more likely than not to give you a very small increment you don't feel a very big sense of accomplishment. By the same merit you also unlock new power-ups by collecting a certain amount of dots cumulatively during play, but you eventually reach a point where you have to collect so many dots that even when you've had a really good play session you barely make any progress with unlocking the next power-up. It's a definitive feeling of "getting less for doing more," and it makes me wish the unlock criteria was determined by a different attribute. If you plan on unlocking everything then give it time, because you're going to be in for a long journey.
Even looking past this unlock system Pac-Man 256 still holds its own exceptionally well, and it defines the word "timeless." If you love arcade games then this is something you don't want to miss out on.

A successor to Middle-earth, Shadow of Mordor, with everything turned up to eleven. I went in expecting a sequel, and that was what I got.
Combat is way more difficult than it was in SoM, and that makes it more satisfying. I played on Normal, and rarely felt the game was too easy. Building up a great army and assaulting the enemy fortress is satisfying. Defending is less so, but that's to be expected.
Stealth is fun, what with all the tools you have to destroy (and/or enslave) your foes with.
As a Tolkien fanatic, I admit that the lore is somewhat (read: vastly) different from canon, but treating this as fanfiction, it's a well-written what-if-Celebrimbor-was-a-bigger♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥AU. It is, however, a great depiction of orcish politics in my opinion.
In my experience, the game has crashed but once, and that was when I alt-tabbed in a hectic battle. Optimization is a bit sub-par, as my Nvidia 1070 cannot run textures AND shadows on Ultra at once. I had to resort to Ultra textures but High shadows, which doesn't really detract from the experience.
In conclusion, Middle-earth: Shadow of War is a successful sequel to ME:SoM.

So Alan Wake, another game I should've given a chance when it first came out and now that I completed it, I"m mad I didn't. This game is spectacular. The story had me addicted to seeing what was going to happen next, a story that goes back and forth between dreams and reality to the point where we constantly question if what we are doing or seeing is even real. What is interesting about it though is that they told it in a TV format where they broke it down into episodes. Every time you start a new episode they would do a quick recap and then you would continue the story. They also have little Twilight Zone refrences especially in TV shows you can watch that are scattered throughout the world, and they pay respect to real life authors which you can tell they got some if not all their inspiration from. Collectibles in games usually hold little value, but in Alan Wake the manuscripts that are scattered around the world give you some extra story that adds to the experience, making them interesting enough to make me want to find them, instead of just for an achievement.
Characters aren't too bad, they come and go before you get to know them, except to Barry of course, who is your best friend who causes more trouble than good, but in a funny way. The voice acting is hit and miss. Sometimes its really good other times its more robotic and lacks the context of the situation. Dialogue often overlaps each other and two people are trying to talk to you at the same time, which is a bit weird sounding.  Even though crazy supernatural things are happening, the characters seem like they see this everyday and don't seem to be in the moment.
The story isn't the only important feature of the game, the atmosphere is absolutely beautiful. There were a few times I had to stop and look at the amazing landscape that reminded me a little bit of Skyrim. Though it wasn't as open as Skyrim it didn't take away from the mass scale of it. But I do have to say that for the majority of the game you do wander around in the woods alot, which I can see some people getting bored of, I enjoyed it but I see potential for criticism.
Combat is fun for awhile, shining your flashlight (which you can upgrade from a regular flashlight to an almost blinding heavy duty lantern) to weaken enemies and then finish them with a firearm. You do get flares and flashbang grenades to aid you to create distance or even the odds. But I did feel by the end that it got repetitive, You can only flash and shoot so many enemies before you start to think "That's all I do?". Also don't get too attached to your equipement, they often find creative ways for you to lose it. Enemies usually just walk slowly toward you but they ambush you which can be difficult mainly because of the camera having a mind of its own and not being in the greatest of angles. There are only a few different enemies but I didn't find that to be bad, with the short duration of the game and the urgency of the fights I never felt like they needed more variety.
So overall I enjoyed this game and will mostly like play it again in nightmare difficulty to see what is on the manuscripts you can't get unless you play on nightmare. All the little issues don't even scratch the amazing story and atmosphere. I can't recommend this game enough, still mad I didn't play it earlier.

I had hopes with the intriguing premise, but tons of bugs (or simply poor design) completely destroys the imersion.  Once that's done, you realize there really isn't that much here to begin with.
The key problem is the game's interface.  Controls are slow, imprecise, and laggy as all hell.  Given how often the game is designed to require good timing, fast reactions, and careful item placement, this is a huge strike against it.  I'm not sure if this is just poor design or horrible quality control - when I first started the game up I wasn't even able to move due to being spawned inside the floor, and even though they've fixed this the entire screen is constantly shaking (except, occasionally, when I jump and it snaps into stability) and there's a persistent damage indicator on the screen flickering on and off with varying levels of intensity.
Unfortunately even if this were patched, it would not be enough to make Twin Sector a good or even passable game.  Frankly if you were to fix the controls, get the screen to stop shaking like my character is having a constant seizure, and speed up the response, you'd be left with a series of puzzles that are disturbingly easy.  All of the difficulty in the design comes from the fact that you're fighting against the controls, and this frankly is not acceptable these days.
As for the visuals and atmosphere, I was left sadly unimpressed.  Environments are blocky and I'm pretty sure frequently using textures ripped straight from Half Life 2, with nonsensical machinery designs that seem to mock the very idea of immersion.  It's obvious that Portal's influence is showing here in the level design, but sadly the devs didn't seem to realize that a key reason that the whimsical insanity in Portal worked was because it was in an environment intended to be a puzzle, and nothing else.  Once you left the testing chambers, the world was almost disquietingly normal.
Unfortunately there is no such conceit in Twin Sector.  This is the real world - a real world where apparently engineers felt you should design a life support generator with a computer console you can only get to if you walk up three flights of stairs, turn off 2 superflous lasers on a catwalk that seems to serve no purpose whatsoever, and then jump 20 feet straight into an open topped cage over the generator's core.  The best part was that once this was done the floor dropped out of said cage so as to let you back out into the room - making that sole console completely inaccessible.  Just a little bit of creative set design here could have fixed this.  Sprinkle in a few broken consoles, dress up the lasers a bit more to make them look like they're actually part of the reactor rather than just arbitrary obstacles, and you actually start forming a cohesive, functional world for this story to be told in.  The makers of Twin Sector obviously either didn't know how, or simply didn't care to put in the effort.

Yet another puzzle game in the style of Amanita creations, with a very distinctive surrealistic art.
The game consists of 11 levels that have the same goal: you are required to move a toy car from one side on the room to another, by interacting with different abstract objects in a certain order. The objects react differently to your clicks, they surprise you with their reactions and discovering their meanings or roles is part of the fun of solving every puzzle. Putting it all together makes use of your creative thinking and seeing the picture in full is a very satisfying feeling.
What I liked a lot about this game was the difficulty of the levels: they’re neither too simplistic, nor too challenging, just the right amount to keep you wanting to solve the puzzle by yourself while being tempted to check a guide. I personally didn’t need to check a guide and I managed to find the solution to every puzzle only after a few minutes of poking around. The solution was never obvious, but the puzzles are designed so that you’ll always figure it out.
I think that this game would fit better on a touch screen device than on PC since it consists in a lot of experimenting with objects, clicking them or dragging them, and there’s no time limit or time requirement to solve the puzzles.
Although it’s quite short (45 mins – 1h), Windosill is a wonderful and relaxing experience, and I think it’s worth the price.

The story of Twin Sector takes place in a post-apocalyptic future where the remains of mankind have been put to artificial sleep in cryogenic chambers deep under the contaminated surface of earth — until the planet becomes habitable again.
You as the player must take the role of Ashley Simms, the protagonist of Twin Sector. Suddenly awakened by the station's security A.I. system O.S.C.A.R., you face the imminent extinction of all other still sleeping survivors due to an unknown failure in the life support system. According to O.S.C.A.R., you are the only person who was able to be woken and therefore the only individual capable of saving mankind. Within the next ten hours you will need to repair the broken main generator of the subterranean bunker system in order to reestablish the station's functionality. But there are yet unknown forces trying to prevent you from succeeding at all costs!
Twin Sector is a thrilling physics-based action-adventure which allows players free interaction with their environment. Using the advantages of the powerful HAVOK®-Engine, innumerable puzzles, challenges and enemies await the players in a hostile and threatening futuristic environment. Featuring more than 15 missions alongside a thrilling story line unfolding over the course of action.

You have now a follower who will save you in times you never expected (something like a secret fan), a nemesis who will defy death and haunt you, and this is just the beginning. Let me be brief :
1)Some captains will resist your "touch" (why you little...) and you will need to kill them
2)Others will betray you when you least expected
3)Others will defy death and return
4)Others will defy your last strike and continue to fight
5)Others will stalk you and strike you. Sometimes when you take one of the artifacts scattered across the lands
6)Others will betray you for you killed their blood brother
And the list could go on...Did i even mention that the variety of orcs is ridiculously huge?
You have now, more than two regions to conquer. You have minas ithil (which becomes minas morgul), seregost, nurnen, gorgoroth (which is stunning) and cirith ungol. There are a few more which you cannot go but i suspect they are for future dlc or maybe online (which i didn't play yet).
I remember how much dissapointed i was from the first game, for i finished it in two days. I guess i did the same with this too, but i didn't for I was playing it like crazy. The game is waaaaay bigger than the first one, and way more epic. You have now the possibility to conquer forts, defend forts, upgrade your conquer forces, your defence forces etc.
The game finally is more difficult than the last one. Yes you are still OP, yes its a quick time event festival, but the enemies now are able to parry your hits, adapt your tactics (like when you jump over their shoulder) and in general the game is more challenging. I currently play it in normal. Only a god knows what happens to the nemesis difficulty. I will find out.
Game has some bugs here and there, but the most annoying one was when i encountered a captain who couldn't speak to me, and he was staring at me like an idiot, and the game couldn't continue. I've managed to override it by pushing random keys (thats pro gamers do, like me). Seems the game continued when it was forced from full screen to borderless. Idiotig bug, and i hope Monolith will fix that.
Last but not least, microtransactions and the reason why the game gave me bipolar disorder. I will try to make this as brief as possible. To create an AAA title which costs 59 euros (steam price) and then have the nerve to add microtransactions, is not bad. Its greedy. Its immoral. Thankfully, you won't need them for the main game. However when you finish the main scenario, there is another ending. That ending is about armies attacking your forts, and you need strong orcs in order to defend them. Yes you can train your own orcs, you can catch stronger (usually from the revenge missions), but it will take a lot of time to get them. Thankfully you can buy orcs from lootboxes with in game money but if you really need to finish it quickly, the game urges you to buy legendary orcs from legendary loot boxes (which they can be bought with currency bought with real money). I am pretty sure someone will be able to finish it without having to buy lootboxes, but the effort from the company to promote them is very much observable, and yes... From my point of view its immoral.

A lacklustre attempt at a profound first-person puzzler, the game falls apart on controls, puzzles and getting you to care about finishing the damn level. By the time you've been through four or five puzzles you will likely have no further desire to complete the game or even play the game.
The puzzles are interesting but hardly fun. It's so easy to make fatal mistakes, given the controls, the unforgiving fall mechanics, and the lasers. Frustration will be your constant companion, as the consequences of failure make you repeat already frustrating tasks, only with the added impetus that you Must Not Screw Up. Else you will have to do it All Over Again.
The plot, on its surface, seems compelling (and partially motivated my purchase of the game), but once you dig past that surface it's just bland, banal, and uncompelling. Many plot elements are stock-standard with absolutely no sense of inspiration or even wit. The plot utterly fails to compel you to complete the game, and the characters are nothing to write home about. Certainly they are not companions that you would draw you to spend more time with them. They don't repel, but they also don't inspire any kind of attachment to them at all.
With frustration, uncompelling gameplay, and a lacklustre plot all failing to motivate a person to play on, I strongly caution any person against buying this game at anything but the most discounted price. Even at a discount, I'd recommend you not even bother. A waste of time unless you want to see how these developers screwed up first-hand.

Alpha Protocol is an incredibly peculiar blend of unbelievably awesome and utter crap. Think of it as James Bond by way of Mass Effect. Unlike Mass Effect, however, choice actually matters. This is one of the only games I can think of that provides a genuine reactive storyline: Literally every choice in the game alters the story in a profound sense. "No two playthroughs will be alike" gets bandied about, but Alpha Protocol is one of the only times where that's actually true. As per the usual, Obsidian puts every other RPG developer to shame as far as the "RP" part goes.
Unfortunately, that's really all there is to recommend it. The production values are passable, but far from outstanding. The protagonist's voice in particular grates, and while there are options to customize your appearance, they are so limited as to not even be worth the time.
Where the game really falls flat, however, is the gameplay. The level design is dull, the shooting is weak (particularly in the early levels), and the stealth system is a joke. Easily the worst parts of the game are the boss levels, which, unless you spec a very specific way, range from near-impossible to just tedious. Unfortunately, this means that for the most part, non-combat builds will have a very, very hard time progressing past the Taipei sections.
Ultimately, whether or not Alpha Protocol is worth your money depends entirely on your patience and how much mileage you can get out of the story. I'd say it's worth at least one playthrough, as the story, while not great, is entertaining, and the reactive storytelling is a beauty to behold. However, this one is to be avoided if mediocre gameplay is a turn off. I'll recommend it, but with reservations.

What is a cool concept, namely the manipulation of yourself, and not the environment (as it is the case in other games), is ruined by several flaws.
You are the single awake person, after the few survivors of the human species have been put to cryo-sleep. You awake to the voice of a security programm that starts to guide you to save the other survivors from a catastrophe that is about to occur.
A glove allows you to pull yourself towards the environment ,or to throw objects, or push yourself away from environments.
While all of this sounds cool in theory, the relatively interesting story was ruined for me by the horrid voice-acting. The graphics are functional but not really interesting or varied and have a fairly low resolution, the field of view is extremely narrow.
It'd be fun to mess around with the glove, but as soon as you fall from a tad too high, you simply die and the game restarts you at the last checkpoint. This can mean that you have to replay the same section of the game over and over because there is such limited space for mistakes. It'd be cool if the interesting idea of pushing and pulling yourself around the environments was supported by gameplay that'd allow you to do this in quick sucession and to fall from high places. Of course this would mean the level design would've to be very different to still provide a challenge and be interesting to navigate.
All in all, I can see the potential of a game like this - the adaptation is too fundemantally flawed to be any fun for me though.

Alpha Protocol is one of the few games I would label as a jack of all trades. The game lets you live out an adventure in the life of a secret agent, providing ample opportunities to play as you see fit. The gameplay varies playthrough to playthrough, and allows you to complete a level with either heavy firepower or the more difficult and rewarding stealth approach. It falls short in that while it does provide a huge variety of ways to play the game, the parts that you do end up picking lead up to an average to mediocre third person shooter.
The storyline is very similar to Mass Effect as in you pick dialogue choices which effect the story later on. It isn't actually too bad if you enjoy the sort of over the top Bond-esque action adventure.

How can Final Fantasy Tactics include this over 20 years ago and developers still leave this out?  It would have made the tactics much more diverse.  Archers are underpowered and hobbled.  What is the point of a ranged attacker if they have to get 5 tiles from a fighter?
The ending was not as good as the first game, more of a let down really.  I was surprised that I was seeing credits, rather than more story or the next part of the quest.
All in all it is a great game, but lacks the focus and feeling of a complete episode in the series.

This is the first game I've heard deemed a "classic" that I hadn't played around the time it came out where I still ended up enjoying it. The style reminds me of if Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory was an ARPG. It definitely went for the cool Hollywood feeling over realism but it doesn't go over the top.
The characters all felt unique and learning about them and trying to persuade them to do things your way really grabbed me in a way I find hard to explain. It felt like what I said and how I approached things actually mattered.
You have your usual bunch of options on how to handle /most/ of the game. There are spots with bosses that require you to take the conventional beating-the-snot-out-of route, but for the most part you're free to sneak past people rather than knock them out or kill them. Gun selection isn't great; you've got pistols, shotguns, submachine guns, assault rifles, and aside from better/worse stats here and there they all feel mostly the same. It never bothered me that much.
Around the end the upgrades felt kind of overpowered, especially stealth. I might as well have been a ghost. I guess that's kind of the point of a high stealth stat, though, so whatever.
This being a PC port shows at times (those sniper rifles!) but I didn't notice it for the most part. A boss near the end of the game proved really difficult because the sniper rifles handle like garbage and that was practically the only way to deal with him.
There are a few bugs. One of the bosses ran into a wall and I could beat him with melee attacks while he didn't fight back. In another part Mike exploded into some otherworldly mass of polygons that would've given Lovecraft a wet dream. Again, nothing too terrible. I found these two bugs more funny than annoying.
The story isn't spectacular. It's pretty stock. You'll likely see where most of it's going if you're familiar with the genre. It held up well enough though.
I'm decently impressed, which, admittedly, is a rarity for me. 7/10, well worth the money.

Broken Age is the LucasArts style adventure game from the 90s that you've been waiting for since the 90s. Tim Schafer's masterful dialog, character development and plot structure techniques are back in full force, no longer shoved into other genres.
Act I is a pleasant experience where you are constantly seeing new areas, meeting new characters and solving relatively easy puzzles (for adventure game veterans anyways). Act 2 makes great use of those characters, even if it re-uses many of the same areas. The puzzles in the second half are much closer to the difficulty found in those 90s games, your mileage may very. Personally I had a handful of those adventure game moments where I started trying to use every item on everything until I finally figured out the solution. Expect to break out some pencil and paper for a couple of the more devious but satisfying puzzles.
The art style looks like concept art in motion and has some truly stunning moments. This is a decent sized adventure that is worth seeing through to the end. We don't get a lot of adventure games with this level of production values anymore.

Okay. This is extremely hard for me. I've been around for quite some time in the gaming field. To give you a clue, I would say the first ever game I played must have been the C64 ski. There and than I got hooked on gaming and never ever quit since. Throughout the years I met ups and downs, one-time hits, instant classics, hidden gems and terrible disappointments. As my taste in playing was forged it hit me that the deepest extent that I can get absorbed by a game always occured in turn-based strategies. I grew to love the genre, where you're lost in your own endless and twisted plottings, where nothing can hurry you and where it does not matter, if you take hours to finally give command and hit the "end turn" button. Oh and it practically doesn't raise your attention to the fact that you got aaaaancient next to younger players of today :D  As a graphic artist I used to adore certain graphic styles I have met during the years and started to collect my ideas of a turn based strategy game of my own, that would include all the neat stuff that makes a great, instant classic of the genre - graphic and gameplay wide. And there - with all the experience I gathered, all the stories I lived through, I dare say a veteran player of turn based strategies - in 2015 I meet Invisible Inc. And it blows me away. Just when I thought that there is no hope for any of the game aspects that made up the good-ol-turn-based-fun to return, the masterminds at Klei come forward with the title, that puts together everything I ever dreamed of having in a game  of this sort- and that I hoped to incorporate in my own game in the future. The individual characters with their own set appearances and stories, the nail-biting stealth action, the endless possibilities to still try and save the situation that already seems hopeless and the thrill to push ever forward, they're just all there with the most butiful artististic appearance I could have wished for. My dreamgame came true. When I said this is hard for me, I meant writing a review of my favorite_game_ever. I really have took my time before deciding on this :D
So what exactly do we have here?
This game is hard and unforgiving. No, not the hard you think now, harder! It gives you a pretty decent challenge and beeing rough-like that can be a real pain in the♥♥♥♥♥for some people. Keep that in mind.
The game guides you through a main story - with that being linear - but you have several decisions to make while you get there.
The arsenal of awesome unlockable characters is great, with them all being different in some ways, but later on you may also get new abilities and thus further develop the way you wish - or can that is.
I love the aspect of hacking with Incognita, this gives a whole new level for the action in the game.
The more time you spend on a level, the harder it will get for you to escape eventually. But wouldn't you just want to discover and loot everything you can?
What I disliked? Maybe one thing. But that's not an aspect to ruin the overall experience of it all and I'm not gonna tell here, you'll know what I mean.
I highly recommend playing through with the Contingency Plan, which doesn't dully add more missions, instead it builds into and extends the main story with countless exciting extras.
I would say even the full price is absolutely worth your money, but now you can get an exceptionally neat discount during sales. You can expect a total of around 70 hours of gameplay and replay value at its best.

Ok, so first of all Alan Wake is my favourite game of all time! But why is it so good, there are many reasons (without spoilers):
1. The story is so awesome and well written and different from normal that it keeps surprising you and sometimes you just wonder that why did they tell me all this information, to add more depth to all of the characters and places wich brings me to my next reasons.
2. Characters are all different from each other and you can see that how much they put effort for just making each character feel more real, by their looks, movement and their way of thinking cause they are all so different from each other.
3. The atmoshpere is awesome! All those little details looks awesome and the light elements are just stunning. It's really dark in the woods but the way Remedy made he light work is just so beatifull! It's so cool seeing it going trough every little holy you can find!
4. Gameplay is different than normally 3rd person games are. It's one of the best games to make that cinematic feeling from slow-motion dodges and even when you are just walking in a forest.
5.The combat is very cool feeling. First, you have to get enough light to an enemy that it's darkness wears off so you can shoot it. There are not many weapons, but the game doesn't suffer from that. There are also flares, flare guns, flash granades and 3 different flashlight to give you the upper hand.
6. The light is the most important thing in the game cause if you have light, you might survive, might. But all the reflections and the light sneeking out from the dark and saving your ♥♥♥ just when you thought you would die, it's just awesome!
7. Re-play value is great in this game cause when you beat the game you will unlock nightmare difficulty wich is harder but not so hard that you will rage quit, but it's there so that you would play the game again knowing abot all the stuff and what's gonna happen when you read the pages.
8. Graphics in this game are not perfect but very detailed and cool looking, just perfect for this world.
9. Landscape is just so awesome, sometimes you just stop in the middle of the game and just look at the most beatifull enviroment ever in games and take screenshots so that you could make that your new screensaver.
10. The game itself tooks about 13-20 hours to complete with the dcl's so it's a good lenght.
Those are the main reasons why you should buy this game, I don't recommend Alan Wake Americas Nightmare so much cause it could have been a great game but compared to the original tittle, it's just so awfull. But go buy the game before they release the new one so you could play that one too!

This game rewards strategy and skill to keep your pac-man alive. You can't just blindly move forward without considering what will be coming ahead of you. You need to treat each ghost in a different way, some you will have to bait and some you have to simply avoid.
The game gets easier as you upgrade your skills and the later skills (my favorites are the lightning and the last green laser beam) but there's no end to the game so that just means you will be surviving longer and getting better scores. Riding on the heels of the portal and the half life games(you can pick up items), here we have a game called Twin Sector. Released in 2009, by german developer Dns, and I believe published by Head Up Games. This game has/had an interesting premise;The earth has fallen to apocalypse, and is not safe yet. You play the character of Ashley Simms, who had been awakend by an AI Overseer, named oscar. Apparently, you are the only human being who has been awakend, as all the other humans have been frozen? hmmmmm, intersting plot, I may add. Believe it or not, I got the game for 99 cents here on Steam. No kidding. I am at the half way point with this one. As I said earlier, this game rides on the heels of Portal and half life, as you can pick up many items in the game, but the game itself gets tedious, really fast. You wear energy gloves in the game, which can save your life by jumping from high places. In the first part of the game, I had to carefully jump onto some pipes, and then jump down using my energy glove at full max, so I would not die, and have to restart the game. There's many puzzles in this game, which is not a bad thing, and you will have to learn to get through them, at times with Oscars Help. The puzzles are ok, but those also can get tedious. Overall, this game as I said had premise, and potential, and while I kind of like it, I can't recommend it to anyone else. I had originally played this game years ago on my Xbox 360, however, my rented copy was damaged and I could only play through the first few missions. From what I was able to experience, the game was a lot of fun, and I was very excited to try it on the PC. I completed it in ~17 hours, but be advised – my character was pretty broken, so I think you can easily extend your playtime to 20+ hours. I was very satisfied with my gameplay experience.
If you like stealth-based (or not) espionage action, third-person RPG gameplay (like the Mass Effect series), lots of choices and potential consequences, and a fluid storyline, then you will really enjoy this game. I would have loved for this title to be picked up for a sequel, as it has massive appeal and all the right gaming elements.
The aesthetics are pretty good – on maximum settings the amount of detail in the characters and background is high. You can customize Agent Thorton’s appearance using a small pool of options, even deciding whether he should wear civilian clothing or armor on each mission. The countless cutscenes seamlessly integrate dialogue/action-trees (using a wheel of options, similar to those seen in the Dragon Age and Mass Effect games), and the special effects are well-done. The music and sounds are great, adding to the intensity of each mission and making you feel like an actual spy in a high-stakes situation – in some levels the music matched the scenery so well I would pump up the volume to immerse myself even more. The story is well-written and engaging – something I especially like is how, depending on the mission order you select (you can pick missions from 3 countries), the story and gameplay experience will change accordingly. For example, you can complete all of the available missions in Rome, or you can do a few, finish some missions in Taipei, then continue the Rome mission-line. Differences in mission order will affect things like available resources (intel, handlers, etc), possible interactions/choices, and character dialogue.
The controls are fairly typical of a third-person shooter and easy to familiarize yourself with. There is a (partially) skip-able tutorial segment that is very helpful at teaching you all of the gameplay elements. The learning curve is minimal to moderate depending on your experience with third-person espionage (or shooter, depending on your preferred playstyle) games. The most difficult part of the game will probably be boss fights, since you can easily stealth (or kill) your way through a majority of the missions. In-game achievements and perks are a plenty, and you will constantly receive nice bonuses like an experience gain for picking 10 locks. These bonuses will keep you strong enough to survive most missions.
Gameplay is very fun and consists of you moving through a mission area, attempting to complete a variety of goals like “destroy an objective” or “obtain information.” Along the way, you will have to stealth (or kill) your way past different enemies and cameras. Your actions during each mission (and during dialogue scenes) will influence your relationship with any accomplices, who may each be a potential handler in your missions. Depending on your relationships, handlers will provide different bonuses. An interesting component that I really liked is how handlers will provide bonuses even if they dislike or hate you – encouraging you to really play how you want to. For example, one handler will give you +10 endurance (health), and +15 if she really likes you; on the flip-side, she will grant you a 5% reduced cooldown to your abilities if she dislikes you, and a 10% reduction if she hates you. Allies are more likely to help or forgive you if they like you, and enemies who you frustrate may make more mistakes. Each individual responds to your dialogue differently – for example, some characters may prefer a professional agent, while others like a laid-back, funny one.
Overall, the game is a lot of fun and will bring you many hours of enjoyment if you are interested in any of these genres. Even if you do not like espionage (or action), you can play on an easier difficulty and just enjoy the story, cutscenes, and dialogue/action options.
Highly recommend!
Cheers,
DJSF

Twin Sector was a fun game. However, if one were to purchase the game here are some things to know.
The game isnt as bad as many people have made it out to be. The story is interesting and the voice acting is indeed terrible, but the gameplay is fun. The levels all take place in a specific area not unlike Portal and the player uses left and rightclick to pull and push objects with gravity generating gloves. Also, the player can crouch and jump as well as pick up an object without applying force to it which could be better than having to pull or push. Walking instead of running can be utilized against turrets and allow the player to control their sound. One IMPORTANT thing to note is the player can QUICKSAVE or QUICKLOAD which is very useful if you die and do not want to start from the last checkpoint.
Using a combination of the enviroment and mechanics from many enemies including: motion sensitive turrets, homing bombs, floating orbs of doom, lasers, and much more the player can overcome obstacles and progress the story. Small tactics like using barrels to block lasers or throwing an object to hit a button become key to passing obstacles or solving puzzles. Some puzzles even have multiple solutions. The difficulty can be anywhere from easy to ridiculous depending on progress into the game. Overall I was impressed and enjoyed getting turrets to fire at each other and strafing with canisters to shield myself from lasers. The final boss was a challenge as well.
Why has this game had so many bad reviews? First off, I dont believe the game was meant to run in fullscreen mode. The screen flickered madly and I had to edit a specific file to return it to windowed again. Secondly, the voice acting is terrible! I could somewhat understand the emotionless voice of Oscar (I kind of liked it actually) but Ashley's voice did not fit at all. I couldn't give an example but once heard you do not want to hear it again. It is too cutesy and princess-like. Unfortunately, I had to listen to it all game. The cutscenes were a good length, short and sweet. They were not very interesting though. Also, I would like to mention the enviroment. Half the game the player is navigating through a dump, literally. Personally I do not mind a game that has metal interior walls the whole time but I can see it being annoying for other players. Another thing to point out- the game is ambient with little soundtrack. This allowed me to hear what was going on beyond walls, such as approaching enemies, but it may be annoying to hear silence in the background for some players.
In the end, I would not recommend this game to another. It was fun and challenging. It had a story that made me keep playing and wanting to know what happened next. Also, the game has good graphics and I enjoyed the physics.
If you are looking for some challenging puzzles based around fun mechanics then this game is for you. Just endure the voices and short-length. Also don't expect an explosive ending and DO NOT put the game in FULLSCREEN.

I bought this game for a steal and figured if it was bad, oh well, $2 down the crapper. Instead, I was surprised by the depth and complexity of this admittedly flawed gem. Other reviews have mentioned the two biggest flaws: upgraded stealth is overpowered while open combat is pretty bad, and the conversation option you choose doesn't necessarily align with what comes out of your character's mouth.
Instead, let me mention the game's two main strengths.
- The protagonist. He's a♥♥♥♥♥♥ but he's your♥♥♥♥♥♥ you can make him aggressive, sleazy, cowardly, whatever. It's a real change of pace to play a game in which the player character isn't (a) a gruff, patriotic super-soldier or (b) Our Lord and Savior.
- The choices. Too many RPGs reduce player choice to a black-and-white, good vs evil dichotomy (looking at you, Mass Effect) or have no weight because their effects are minimal or nonexistent (that's you, Elder Scrolls). In Alpha Protocal,  every single choice is morally grey; there's no copping out and always picking the Paragon option. And your choices have results: key characters live or die, and there are missions you may or may not undertake based on conversation options alone. It's a lot like the Witcher games in that regard. Hell, you can sleep with and kill every female in the game.
Lastly, Turn Up the Radio will never sound the same.

Alpha Protocol is a (really) rough gem. A game with a lot of great ideas, great 'vision' yet suffered with a troubled development that result in a lack of focus, polish, and technicality. It's one of those 'could've been significantly a lot better"  game. Every aspects of this game is well thought of but all of them comes out half-baked and leave out a lot of room for improvement. It feels more like a "prototype" or some sort. And this game is surely one of those games that I REALLY wanted to see to be remastered / reimagined, or at least the ideas should be re-created. Though the chance is close to zero,
Story (9.5/10)
The main story theme of Alpha Protocol iis actually nothing special nor original, though the story of a rogue secret-organization agent story always catch my attenttion and certainly one of the more intriguing plot point. But what make Alpha Protocol stands out is the delivery of this story. The twist, the intel / dossier, flow, and pace is decent, though again.. due to the development.. there's some.. "cringe-worthy" moment, that moment when it feel rushed or generally feels that there are something missing. But, anyway, it's still a great one. The strong point is the choice and consequences system, it's not black, it's not white. It's gray. It proves Obsidian's great attenttion of story and  character interaction (which later is more realized in FO: NV) , because I feel like that this is what makes me keep going, despite all its mechanic flaws. Yet again, and again.. troubled development.. it has dated direction and story presentation.
Gameplay (7/10)
The RPG mechanic blends nicely with the gameplay, the safehouse system with E-mail, intels, black market, armor and weapon customization  adds a little chunk of immersion. Gunplay is good, it has a big potential of nicely balanced stealth and action. Yes, "potential". It has solid gameplay, OK.. the control is clunky and annoying sometimes, cameera placement is a bit odd, but the real problem is those telepathy-equipped A.I:

Despite all the technical flaw lack of polish, and , dated in almost every aspect, what truly holds this game together is the brilliant narrative and the implementation of many great ideas in this game, though it comes out half baked and lacking focus. It could've been a lot better, it could've been expanded, it could've been a bigger, more immersive, more complex game if it has better development and production value. It was an interesting and exciting experience for sure. And Alpha Protocol is one of those game that I'm eager to see it re-created in any form through remaster, sequel, or re-created ideas, from some kind of 'prototype', 'half finished' game to a full fledged, high-production value game, because surely this game has a ton of intriguing ideas.

Its as good as FSX ever was. The main improvement is that the multiplayer is now based on Steam rather than the defunct Gamespy (nice work). Also, if you're so inclined, the Xbox 360 controller is perfectly mapped out of the box, which I'm sure must be a new addition. Dovetail have made a really good job of this.
However, off the shelf, big 'survey simulators' like this represent the core of a simulator eco system. When FSX (and versions before it) was developed, Microsoft included a world that was passable, and in places quite detailed, but not detailed enough for VFR flight, and included a collection of aircraft, no single one of which was all that realistic, but was intended to be accessible to most people with an interest in aviation.
So what you're buying here is a product that is really just the tip of the iceberg. That's confirmed by the number of other companies that spend 100% of their time making, for example JUST scenery for FSX, or JUST as perfect a representation of a 747 as you can possibly get. Microsoft or Dovetail aren't going to spend their time creating ultra-realistic content because they don't need to, they can sell FSX as a platform to other developers that do that.
That said, you get a more 'complete' product designed for the home with FSX than you do with for example X-Plane 10 (X-Plane 10 is a very different beast and again, the core of a giant industrial sized simulator). Also I believe Microsoft worked with Cessna on this one, so the Skylake can't be all that bad.
If you're into flight simulators but don't own this, there is something missing in your life.

Not bad, especially for something developed by a one person team. The concept of being able to switch between traditional RTS command and playing as a unit in first person (unlike Nuclear Dawn, you can select any unit on the battlfield to play as instantly without walking all the way from the command center) is incredibly neat, one that I personally wish more developers tried.
Don't expect something to the same polish as an RTS with a traditional development team size and hundreds of thousands of dollars budget. Some of the issues you'll encounter are:
1.) Not very intelligent units when it comes to path finding
2.) Laggy controls, particularly when 50+ units are on the battlefield at highest graphics settings
3.) Sometimes funky unit commands; for example, attack command won't order an attack on a specific structure but will send ordered units to that spot as they attack
4.) Poorly optimized user interface; selecting structures to build and projects to research is akward
5.) Doesn't give player as much information as one would expect from a traditional RTS
But, again, only one person was developing this game; tackling a mechanic that even mid-size developers won't try is a tough task for a single individual, and with that in mind this game exceeds expectations. Hopefully a lot of the issues with this game are resolved in the sequel that is currently underway.

Surprisingly delightful concoction of a cyber-espionage turn based sneak simulator where the best addictive 'one more turn' qualities of XCOM is blended with uncompromising stealth ideals of Thief.
Conscientious meticulous play is always rewarded although sometimes random elements like map layout and guard patrol patterns can and will throw your best laid plans in disarray. This encourages improvisation and is precisely why it is so satisfying to come out by the skin of your teeth when gods of the odds are stacked against you. If your agent gets caught, you will have opportunities later on to rescue them. Needless to say, agents are invaluable as later procedurally generated maps get bigger and increasingly populated with advanced security gadgets plus armoured guards.
A skilled player can manipulate guards in a myriad of ways ranging from intentional agent reveals to misdirect them from one part of the map to another, footfall distractions and enterprising use of door and security cam mechanics. There are many different synergies between Incognitas’ programs and items/character builds to discover over multiple rogue like playthroughs.
Ultimately Invisible, Inc is at its superlative best when that emergent gameplay moment hits you in the guts out of nowhere as you realise, for greater good of the Agency, that one agent whom you have grown so attached to over numerous close calls and mission triumphs will have to be left behind.

The Walking Dead: Season 2 is an episodic adventure game and a continuation of The Walking Dead, developed and published by Telltale Games, the same people behind other such great adventure games as The Wolf Among Us and Game of Thrones. The game is based on Robert Kirkman's comic book series of the same name
Although the game does not follow the same exact storyline as the comic book series, it follows the same universe as the comic book follows only seeing it in a different point of view. The story continues after the events of the first game with the player now playing Clementine from the first game
The game is split up into five episodes. The game works as a normal television series. Each length of an episode is roughly two to three hours or more long
The gameplay is very simple, you move around, selecting stuff and talking to people and using button prompts when told to. The main bulk of gameplay is through the dialogue options. What you say and what you do will effect the game in the long run. Choosing who survives and who dies, choosing who stays and who leaves is all effected by your choices
The game's graphics are nice for the most part however there are some ugly texture work here and there. The sound and music options also vary in quality. Sometimes the sound quality is really good and sometimes the sound quality is bad. I have encountered numerous amounts of glitches which seems as if Telltale Games never got round to fixing them, too many to mention in this review
The Walking Dead: Season 2 shines again in its character creation, each character is superb when it comes to their own personality and backstory and especially the final moments of the game will surely make a few people upset. The game also deals with heavy amounts of gory bloody violence which although fine with me can be a bit disturbing for some people
Telltale's The Walking Dead: Season 2 is a superb Telltale Game and the continuation of the story through The Walking Dead: Michonne and the recently announced (2016) The Walking Dead: Season Three make for a stellar Telltale series

Invisible Inc. is a difficult Turn-Based Strategy Stealth game set in a world of mega corperations. You play in short campaigns of a handful of levels made with randomly procedurely generated rooms. The goal is gaining enough money through the use of stealing artifacts, dosh or valuable data from a VIP's brain to upgrade your team of agents after the initial collapse of Invisible.
I like to think of this game as a blend of FTL: Faster Than Light, XCOM and Mark of the Ninja (a previous game developed and plublished by Klei Entertainment). Each playthrough can be completed in 1-2 sittings and the difficulty of the game makes each run a stressful but fulfilling exercise for stategy minded players.
Every turn each of the agents in play are given action points (derived from the stats of the agent; upgradable with money) to perform moves, actions with items equipped and interactions with the environment across an isometric playing field. These environmental objects must first be hacked primarily with the Incognita system, a re-purposed A.I that can break down firewalls with the spending of power which can be replenished via consoles (as you progress, items and agent abilities can also accomplish this).
There are layers of stategy with the cast of agents, the spread of item variety and the different programs to equip Incognita that make this short game replayable in alternate playstyles (hidden, sneaky with tazers, tazers and sleep syringes, full-on assault with firearms etc.) This stylish gem of a game deserves to be played by more people and the developers should be proud of how polished this Early Access game turned out.

Rating 8.5/10
Overview: Underrated RPG
The Good:
+ What really sets Alpha Protocol apart from almost every other RPG out there is that EVERY choice you make influences the story or your character in some way. The order in which you play missions, the choices you make in the game, how you speak to people...all of it has a major or minor effect in how the story and missions play out. There is no right or wrong answer, there is no good or evil, there is only your choices and the consequences that follow.
+ Character creation is identical to the first Mass Effect. As you level up you gain points to spend in a variety of categories. As you spend points in any particular category you gain passive and active abilities. You could play stealthy, guns blazing, maybe some close quarter combat, the game gives you plenty of options in how to develop your character
+ The game provides a lot of different perks depending on how you play. Pick enough locks and you will get a bonus to your lock picking skills. Get enough headshots and you gain a perk in accuracy etc. Almost everything you do in the game has some sort of perk associated with it.
+ Lots of items/weapons/armor/upgrades to further customize your character
+ Multiple endings depending on the choices you make.
+ Level design is solid, giving you multiple ways of completing certain objectives. My biggest gripe however is that the levels are a little too linear for my tastes. For a game that is all about choices I would have liked some more levels that are open ended.
+ The story and dialogue is well written and doesn't take itself too seriously given the subject matter. Obsidian wasn't afraid to have a lot of interesting characters either.
+ Surprisingly, on a technical level the graphics are very well done. Textures and characters are well detailed.
The Average
The AI can be very impressive at times. The enemies hide behind cover, duck and weave, try to flank you at times and in general act the way they are suppose to. This only highlights when enemies act completely stupid, running in the same spot, getting stuck behind cover, and in general seem to prefer being dead than alive.
Very noticeable texture load in when customizing your look or selecting weapons and armor. Some texture pop in when a level loads.
Certain bosses are very difficult to complete depending on what skills you invested in.
The game can be easily 'broken' if you invest in certain skills
The Bad
- The crouching animation is one of the worst animations I've seen in gaming
- There is an overall lack of polish in the game especially regarding the cover based shooting.
- The game can be especially frustrating in the beginning when you have very low skills and killing enemies is difficult.
Conclusion

I have completed this game many times on the xbox360 and looking at this game strictly from a RPG perspective  I think Alpha Protocol is one of the best RPG's around. One of the reasons why the game did so poorly is that most people were expecting a third person shooter with RPG elements like Mass Effect, instead Alpha Protocol is a full blown RPG that happens to be a third person shooter. As long as you realize this you will have a great time.
This is a real franchise. Big companies should search for and polish niche gems instead of puking expensive garbage.

First and foremost, this isn't a "review". I haven't finished the game. I've played the prologue and these are some simple thoughts about the game so far. Period.
1. 30 fps does NOT take anything away from the game. At all. Game plays fluid and extremely well. Not a single crash or anything going wrong with pc thus far. I've experienced NONE of the pop-in that people seem to be jumping on a bandwagon about. I'm running dual Sapphire Tri-X R9 290s in Xfire. Game runs flawlessly so far. No texture popping, no shaded horizons, no cars or people or buildings cutting into view. All looks great.
2. Again, not sure what people are griping about. Graphics look solid. Scenery is vibrant (like the South is), cars are fully detailed and throttle as well as drive well enough for a Mafia game (if you've never played a Mafia game before it's NOT GTA). Walking, running, swimming and going for cover is quick and easy. UI is nice. In game menus are snappy and contain a lot of information about things that are important. IN fact, the in-game menus are, hands down, one of the best I've seen in awhile.
3. Sound is on point. Radio stations have an eclectic array of music to be heard. All great tunes as well. Voice acting is extremely well done. Car, truck, boat sounds are all pretty much what you'd expect them to sound like. Gunplay isn't some generic sounding guns. All weapons have their own distinctive sound as you'd expect. All well done.
4. In game cinematics are extremely well done. All vibrant and full of character. In fact, some of the best voice work in a game and some of the best story driven cinematics you'll see. None of them seem to be too long. Short and to the point. Kudos on that part of the game.

One thing that grab me was the story or to be more precise, the way the story is being told. You start the game with a tutorial missions and once you complete them, you gonna be send on the field. But before that you gonna be send to forward in time during an interrogation in which you gonna hear something like "overview" of your past actions and this happens for most part of the game . After the interrogation you are send on the field where the game actually starts.
Without spoiling much( aka wont say nothing about start and end of the game) can freely say that most of the game happens in 3 cities : Rome,Moscow and Taipei . Each of the cities got its own main "questline" but you can unlock side quests if you buy intel from the black market. But have in mind ... once you leave the city you cant go back so you may try to complete it all.
In terms of actual plot ... well its pretty generic : you are betrayed, you go rogue, you have to oppose a big corporation before it start a war. During the journey you will meet different characters that may or may not help you .
Game offers decision making that often counts on your response during little chit chat and less about the action you take. But you have to be a fast thinker when comes to picking a response because the game doesnt want to break immersion. But no worries since you can response in 3 ways: professional, offensive and suave. You have to take in mind that different characters respond differently to your answers so you must be quite a talker if you want to profit with your tongue. And by profit I mean getting some bonus intel or perks . Hell, you may even skip half a mission if you know the right guy!
The game isn’t a straight line of mission after mission. Instead you are given a safehouse(hub) from which you buy and equip gear, obtain intel and start missions. You still have main missions but by doing side missions may unlock different ways to complete missions or simple perks. Now some missions are available only for some “period of time”  so you have to pick well what mission to do and when.
While you play you will gather experience points which will give you ability points that will help you upgrade your skills : Stealth , 4 weapons(Pistol, SMG , Shotgun and Assault Rifles) , Sabotage , Technical Aptitude , Toughness and Martial Arts . Now you cant max them all so you have to pick the best that suits your style. To help you out with this, the game offers you to pick 1 class out of 3... or make your own class if you pick the option Freelancer.
While upgrading your skills you will "learn" some abilities to help you out in emergencies. Though some abilities like "Shadow Operative" makes the game feel more fantasy than realistic which is a shame. But overall game gives options for different styles though at some times its punishing and makes no sense.
What is gonna be a RPG game without
Well the gear options in here is quite limited but still add some sort of depth ... maybe . Before every mission you can check your gear and gear up the way you want it with gadgets and such.
You can carry 2 weapons at once and you can customize them a bit. You can change their barrel,scope, magazine and grip. Once you are done with it its time to pick your suit. Suit can be equiped with up to 4 different modifications that can help you out. Last but not least you got your gadgets wheel which you can fill with grenades, mines, EMP, first aid and some others that I never used.  Once geared up its time to head to the battlefield .
And always be sure that you have enough ammo to start the mission without problems.
As said, combat is mainly cover-based shooter style but you can do stealth takedowns and as far as I remember one boss fight ended up with kiting a lot .
Now the shooting is a bit different than most games because you need to "focus" aka wait for your crosshair to get smaller and brighter before you make your shot. This is♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off players quite fast in early games when you dont have any upgrades in your weapon of choice skill. There arent that many big fire fights to make it a "rage-quit" material. Overall it need some time to get used to it .
Now time for the most annoying part of the game for most players. The mini games for hacking,picklocking and switching off alarms.
Now switching off alarms is fairly easy : you need to press the right switches in maze-like scheme.
Picklocking is also fairly easy: put in line the switches .
Hacking ... oh lord ... the hacking ... I wonder how many people actually quit the game because of it .
Check this image :
or a video to see what I'm talking about. In-game all numbers will be switching non-stop and your goal is to find the line of symbols that isnt moving and mark them.. with one of the 2 line of codes you are given . But be careful.. one wrong step and you gonna set the alarm on and you will need to re-do it . So you are better to put points in Sabotage if you want to manually do the hacking.
Or you can just stock up yourself with EMPs and not bother with any of those.
The game got quite some replay value, 3 endings, several approaches on different missions, unlocking missions by talking much. Its easily can keep your interest for 2-3 playthrougs. First one is always to try the soil and then you may focus on different objectives.
Nice story, neat idea and RPG elements but quite lacking gameplay elements and with possible performance issues(for which you better check the hub) .

I LOVED the last two MAFIA games and thought they were awesome. They were so because of the great story, gameplay, car driving/physics and combat. This game's release is marred because the developers had a very large oversight when they ported it from console and locked the game to 30 FPS. The patch was released on 9 Oct 16 and the quality of the game IMO has doubled (I use unlimited FPS). Rapid mouse movement when looking around is no longer slugggish and everything is much smoother. I play the game on hard with no aim assist. I will split the game into good and bad points as follows:
The Good
- Music (correct for period and a reasonable selection)
- Story is engaging and developed
- Cinematics are good and complete with period slang and profanity
- Characters feel real and legitmate with good voices and motion
- Rackets are authentic
- New Orleans looks great and it is nice to drive around the city
The Bad
- The stealth/sneak system is very basic and hardly a system
- Default key assignments could use some work ('Delete' to whistle as a distraction? Really?). This was updated in the first patch ands is much better now.
- Rapidly looking around causes stuttering due to the framerate cap. Fixed with the patch.
- Graphics look a little strange at times like in the 'Waiter' mission there is a strange halo around Lincoln. Night time in the bayou is very good however you cannot see vehicle headlights in your rear vision mirror
- Draw distance is pathetic (cars materialising 100 metres ahead while driving)
- Game world interaction is buggy. There are areas when you are swimming that you could easily walk up on land but the game blocks you and others that you could pull yourself up on to but cannot.
- Minor bug - There is a mission where you get to do boxing. The outer building doors closed before an NPC could get into the building (as he was lagging behind me) and the other NPCs talked to him through the door. Because the NPC was outside he was unable to open the inside door to progress and Lincoln is then stuck in a small room. I had to reload the checkpoint and wait for the NPC to fix this bug.
I am running the game on the highest possible settings using a GEFORCE GTX TITAN X (Pascal) with unlimited FPS and it does not even break a sweat. I did have to turn the brightness up quite a bit from what it recommends because it was just too dark on my ASUS ROG Swift monitor. Additionally I have not experienced any corrupted save files that other users have reported but in just under 70 hours of gameplay I have had multiple crashes. The majority are straight to desktop (~20) while doing general in game activities and there was no message or error or tone or anything. The other crash was a loading loop, where after I finished the second moonshine run for the Irish to increase my revenue. There was a cinematic at the distillery and afterwards it just got stuck loading forever while background noise continued. My PC specs are at the bottom of the review.
Overall the game is engaging and I enjoyed the story even if it is just at its core about revenge. The characters are well presented with depth and the cinematics feel right and do not drag on. The bad points are minor and only detract from the game a litttle because the story and characters are what make it great. However these bad points become very tiresome after 40+ hours of gameplay and have caused me to quit at least once. For example I was in the water swimming and needed to swim for miles because the game would not let Lincoln clim up to a dock or walk onto land.
I completed the game twice and managed to get all of the achievements in just these two playthoughs.
7 / 10

This game deserves to be played by absolutely everyone. If you grew up playing and loving the classic LucasArts and Sierra adventure games, this will be right up your alley. And if you didn't? Well, then you're in for a treat! The humour throughout is spot on, and I found myself smiling or laughing at nearly every turn and every conversation. The extraordinary Double Fine feeling eminates from beginning to end,  and the story will most likely captivate you and leave you guessing where it's going to head next.
Broken age is yet enother example of the amazing and peerless work that Double Fine keeps producing, and it definitely gets close to the level of quality that they have produced in the past, including their own Psychonauts as well as games from their LucasArts days like Grim Fandango and Monkey Island. The puzzles in the game never reach the absurd levels that the old classics could achieve, but I did run into a handfull of headscratchers along the playthrough. The good part was the ability to switch between the two characters if I got stuck, or wanted a change of perspective in the story, very similar to the mechanic from Day of the Tentacle.
Overall, I can't recommend this game enough, it is a masterpiece in the genre, and it's only half-done! I for one can not wait untill part 2 is ready. Judging from the absolutely amazing work Double Fine did on part 1, there's no chance in hell that part 2 will dissapoint. Mark my word.

First of all I have to say I do not care about microtransactions one way or another, They aren't my bag but they don't bother me.
This game was billed as an immersive RPG-style lord O' the rings game where you could craft totally new storylines using the nemesis system.
After 20 plus hours I can report only that is is a relatively buggy hack n slash game with constantly recycled characters, a fortress-taking mechanic which seems totally divorced form the main story (I control all of mordor and Sauron has yet to lift a finger), a totally bloated set of quests and gear system and a strong ability to make you wonder what you loved so much about Shadow of mordor.
The fortress taking and holding aspect is fun and should have been DLC for SoM, it is too easy to stack against the AI on nomal difficulty that I was able to take everything but the overlord on the first try and usually finish the whole thing after two.
The main quests totally railroad you and it seems like it doesn't matter what else you have done there isn't reallly any effect on the story.
The Orcs are fun and enjoyable but if you've already seen 3 or four with the same name after playing for 3 days they clearly didn't put much effort in.
The fights all go pretty much the same with maybe 3 or so variations: the ones I can execute, the ones I can shoot and the ones I can stomp with my beast-friends.
The interface is so overloaded and confusing I literally don't know which quests are the main quests, they all seem totally unimportant and overly important at the same time.
There are only really 4 fortresses to take in the game and after taking them I feel like I have no idea what to do next, I literally rule the land where Sauron's tower is can I just have them dismantle it? I mean I got a lot of Orcs...
I am constantly getting new gear but I literally have not ever noticed a difference other than appearance and even then not much. Most of the time I check my inventory I have like 5 or 6 upgrades wating and am just like "Hmm, guess I didn't need these that bad"
Overall, I would have been hapy if this was a 20 buck DLC for Shadow of Mordor and was just the fortresses, at 60 bucks its not worth it.

I played this for about two hours.  Its addictive, its fun, but its free on phones, and vastly inferior to Pac Man Championship Edition DX.
PAC-MAN 256 is a Pacman interpretation of Crossy Roads.  Pacman must navigate an RNG maze with ghosts with new behaviors exclusive to 256 (Pinky is still the biggest threat though.)  Behind Pacman is a wall of 8-bit glitchy cacophony that swallows everything up.  You rack up points primarily from dot combos, which max out at 256, hence the name.  Furthermore, an assortment of powerups is gradually collected for your arsenal, which replace traditional power pellets and which  you can optionally equip.
The pace is frantic and fun like Crossy Roads, but I hope you don't care about score, because 256 is basically at the mercy of RNG.  Occasionally very tight dual lanes will generate with no escape.  Your dot combos are occasionally broken by areas where the dots simply stop for no reason.  The worst offender of them all is the camera.  THE CAMERA!  IN A PAC MAN GAME!  The camera is centered around PAC man no matter what, limiting your view of whats ahead, and what awaits you when you use the side warps to stay alive.
Children will like this, I know I do, but they could get it free on their phone, and for a more finely tuned experience, CE DX is the superior alternative.

The Binding of Isaac is one video game that will never be made into a movie. It's visuals and story are vile, crude, and downright disturbing... but that doesn't prevent it from being immensely charming.
Luck plays a large part in The Binding of Isaac. Each time The Binding of Isaac is played, most of the game world, including it's items, shops, (most) boss fights, and the layout of it's levels, are randomized.
The gameplay itself is reminiscent of a "Smash T.V." style overhead shoot-em-up, with design elements heavily borrowed from the original Legend of Zelda. The player has an expandable health bar, but only one life, and any progress made (aside from unlocking items for future playthroughs) is erased upon death.
Isaac's main form of attack is to cry at his enemies, which is somewhat fitting, considering the game's initial learning curve. Even so, perseverance (and a little luck) go a long way in making The Binding of Isaac a somewhat derivative, but fun descent into madness.

I LOVED the last two MAFIA games and thought they were awesome. They were so because of the great story, gameplay, car driving/physics and combat. This game's release is marred because the developers had a very large oversight when they ported it from console and locked the game to 30 FPS. The patch was released on 9 Oct 16 and the quality of the game IMO has doubled (I use unlimited FPS). Rapid mouse movement when looking around is no longer slugggish and everything is much smoother. I play the game on hard with no aim assist. I will split the game into good and bad points as follows:
The Good
- Music (correct for period and a reasonable selection)
- Story is engaging and developed
- Cinematics are good and complete with period slang and profanity
- Characters feel real and legitmate with good voices and motion
- Rackets are authentic
- New Orleans looks great and it is nice to drive around the city
The Bad
- The stealth/sneak system is very basic and hardly a system
- Default key assignments could use some work ('Delete' to whistle as a distraction? Really?). This was updated in the first patch ands is much better now.
- Rapidly looking around causes stuttering due to the framerate cap. Fixed with the patch.
- Graphics look a little strange at times like in the 'Waiter' mission there is a strange halo around Lincoln. Night time in the bayou is very good however you cannot see vehicle headlights in your rear vision mirror
- Draw distance is pathetic (cars materialising 100 metres ahead while driving)
- Game world interaction is buggy. There are areas when you are swimming that you could easily walk up on land but the game blocks you and others that you could pull yourself up on to but cannot.
- Minor bug - There is a mission where you get to do boxing. The outer building doors closed before an NPC could get into the building (as he was lagging behind me) and the other NPCs talked to him through the door. Because the NPC was outside he was unable to open the inside door to progress and Lincoln is then stuck in a small room. I had to reload the checkpoint and wait for the NPC to fix this bug.
I am running the game on the highest possible settings using a GEFORCE GTX TITAN X (Pascal) with unlimited FPS and it does not even break a sweat. I did have to turn the brightness up quite a bit from what it recommends because it was just too dark on my ASUS ROG Swift monitor. Additionally I have not experienced any corrupted save files that other users have reported but in just under 70 hours of gameplay I have had multiple crashes. The majority are straight to desktop (~20) while doing general in game activities and there was no message or error or tone or anything. The other crash was a loading loop, where after I finished the second moonshine run for the Irish to increase my revenue. There was a cinematic at the distillery and afterwards it just got stuck loading forever while background noise continued. My PC specs are at the bottom of the review.
Overall the game is engaging and I enjoyed the story even if it is just at its core about revenge. The characters are well presented with depth and the cinematics feel right and do not drag on. The bad points are minor and only detract from the game a litttle because the story and characters are what make it great. However these bad points become very tiresome after 40+ hours of gameplay and have caused me to quit at least once. For example I was in the water swimming and needed to swim for miles because the game would not let Lincoln clim up to a dock or walk onto land.
I completed the game twice and managed to get all of the achievements in just these two playthoughs.
7 / 10

Game Play: 1st person platform puzzler. No weapons. Use gravity glove for platforming and solving puzzles. Gravity glove help in movement, jumping, and limit/prevent fall damage. Gravity glove allows you to grab or repel objects.
Map design: Very linear.
How Long To Beat It: Around 7 hours on normal
Difficulties On Normal: Everybody able to beat it on normal without much problems.
Kids Rating: No blood, no foul language. Your character can be kill but no blood involved.
Bugs: Sometime crash when using quick load.
Game Control: Standard.
Save System: Check Point and Quick Save. Using quick save is important because you do die a lot. Quick save keep frustration level at a minimum.
Option Menu: Very limited on video and audio.
Recommend Buying Price: $5 or lower for general public. $7.50 or lower for puzzle lovers.
---
It's not a bad game. A 1st person platform puzzler game similar to Portal but use gravity glove (gravity gun from Half Life 2) to help platforming and solve puzzles.
Puzzles aren't hard. On a scale of 10, 1 being the easiest and 10 the hardest. The puzzles are rank 5 and below. No puzzles are at expert or master level. If you can beat Portal you will have no problem with Twin Sector.
Platforming isn't difficult. There is no racing, timing, or trick jumps. It's straight forward. There are a lot of platforming in the game.
You will die a lot in Twin Sector. Deaths comes from bad jumps, falls, lasers, sentry bots, fire, explosions, and turrets. Frustration in the game can be kept to a minimum using quick save. Quick Save and Quick Load is your friend in Twin Sector.
The plot is similar to Portal. A crazy AI wants to kill you. It first befriend you than later on want to rip your guts out. Voice acting for the crazy AI is pretty bad. Voice acting for rest of the casts is decent.
