For the most part this game is a marked improvement over the first game. The story remains interesting and starts with a bigger cast of characters. There's more situations to lose them as well, which really adds to the tension. The character customization is significantly expanded and there's more interested items to equid. This helps make the already solid combat even more interesting.
The balance of the cost of items and levels are far better, making buying an item from the market actually a potentially good idea. The battles also are far more dynamic and interestly designed, there's a variety of gimmicks, rather than two groups fighting until everyone is dead every time.
Other mechanics were also improved to make them matter more, like how wounds persist until you rest. Also, the two main characters are actually very different, unlike Rook and Hakon, who felt both like decent people. This time you have one good protagonist and one very selfish one.
The music and graphics are as good as ever, not much to say other than they're still excellent.
There are a few problems, however. The war mechanic, which had issues in the first game, is almost totally gone, making fighters kinda pointless. Also, some choices from the first game I was excited to see fuflilled didn't get an closure. I ran into one bug twice where the character models would disapear. I could still play, but it was annoying to do so and immersion breaking. Finally, I wasn't a huge fan of the ending. Like this first it is quite abrupt and the story clearly needs a Banner Saga 3, but unlike the first I feel like there's so much more left unresolved.

Overall, it's an excellent game and I'm very happy with it. It's a little short as I finished it in about 7 hours, but it's easily worth two playthroughs. If you played the first this is totally worth picking up. Otherwise, you should really get the first game and play that, because the story is compelling.

If you enjoyed Banner Saga 1, like I did, then you'll get great enjoyment out of this.
You'll get roughly around 10 hours (completion time for me) out of the game as a whole, which is quite good, although I felt it could do with an extra 2 hours of content, which I'll come to later.
In terms of improvements; honestly, I've not noticed any. That's not a bad thing, it's just that Banner Saga is rather singular, there's only so much they can do with the game, and it is essentially as the first one was. There have been a few additions to combat (which I don't consider improvements), new abilities and such. I will say however that there is more animations for this one in terms of small cutscenes, which are done very well.
And one of the favourite aspects of Banner Saga - for me anyhow - is the music. The music is still fantastic, and very much immersive. The voice overs are also well done, and suit the characters that they are attributed to very well.
One thing I've been critical of concerning the series is its combat. To be fair, the combat is quite deep. Surprisingly so for a game like this. But I do think the series suffers because of that. Normally I love deep strategic mechanics, but here it feels really tacked on, and not needed. Combat in Banner Saga has always been a convoluted mess I found, and Banner Saga 2 doesn't really improve upon that. I also found myself becoming affected by abilities in combat from the enemy that were not blatantly obvious, although this didn't become apparent until later on when facing Dredge stonesingers and so on. As the game continued on,
I found combat to be more of a chore than a pleasure to play. I enjoyed the story and narrative, and simply felt that the combat just dragged things down. A much more simpler mechanic (but not overly simplified) would certainly benefit this game.
And now comes the bit about the length of the game. 10/11 hours is a fair amount. But considering how the game ended, I'd say it wasn't enough. This has already been brought up in the forums concerning the ending. Banner Saga 1 left on a high note (or a low note depending on your perspective). It finished at just the right time. You felt vindicated and rewarded for your efforts. You felt you played the first game to its conclusion. It really did feel like the end of a tv show, a series. A proper end.
Banner Saga 2... felt like a mid-season finale than anything else. And nobody likes mid-season finales because usually it means ending rather abruptly. That's exactly what happened here. Without going into spoilers, lets just say that certain story threads felt unfinished.
Obviously it's a setup for the next game, but that's not the point. The next game should continue from the previous game's high point. Banner Saga 2 did not reach that high point, and honestly, I was hoping to get more out of it. I was hoping for a better conclusion than the one we got.
Regardless, TBS2 is highly recommended, and I look forward to TBS3!

Windosill is a short game released in 2009 through digital distribution channels by web-artist and painter Patrick Smith (usually known as Vectorpark). Windosill's aim is to inspire in the player a child-like wonder and sense of discovery (Smith, 2009), presenting him with an interactive world made by a series of rooms that can be progressed by resolving very simple point-and-click puzzles. However, those puzzle, while being the core element of the "gameplay", are not Windosill's main interactive focus. In fact the game is much more oriented on immersing the player in its abstract world. This aim is reflected by the puzzle design that, if on one hand is very simplistic, on the other forces the player to explore the environments and to interact with every element that he can see, since the abstract nature of the game makes it practically impossible to quickly resolve the puzzles on the first try. The absence of the need for complex reasoning is also another element that helps the player focusing on enjoying the world and the experience [...]

A good stick and throttle controller

We had to wait years for the sim to be improved with out buying PrePared

That together with the great artwork and soundtrack makes it a must-buy.

Invisible Inc. plays out as a stealth-focused Shadowrun Returns with limited resources and varied methods of getting past enemies.
"Combat" in this game involves masterfully sneaking, neutralizing, and outsmarting your enemy. You CANNOT take them in a fair fight. Their armor stops sniper rounds, their aim is perfect, and their allies are varied. But they are dumb muscle, and they rely on machines too much for their own good. Problem is, you only have a limited ammount of processing power to hack their stuff. And unlike most stealth games, you cannot take your time; hacking into the system leaves a trace, and as they slowly realize what is going on they will send in more forces and their own hackers to even the playfield.
The base game feels constricted, as you never really get enough resources to smooth out a playstyle build. However, there are MANY different customizable game modes that you can play at your leisure to practice. As a stealth game in a world of shooters, you will likely lose from lack of experience. But as you learn the game, each failed campaign nets you experience points to unlock new starter characters and hacking tools to smooth out your developing playstyle.
The only real problem I had was that the proceedurally generated levels seemed... too branched out? Without any meaningful interconnections, a level could have you jump all over the place and force you to miss out on some sweet loot because you didn't have the time or resources to hack things open and get there, even if said resources were in an adjacent room with no interconnecting door.
This is a good game for varying your library.

Without the DLC, this is a relatively short game. With the DLC, it's about medium-length.
The ending may not be to everyone's taste, as it starts with a "to be continued" and then swerves. Hard,
However, Inc is so exceptionally polished that it works perfectly as a roguelike, story aside, and is the absolute culmination of the gameplay formula implemented by Shadowrun Returns. Inc's universe is not as rich as Run's, but Inc is also a tighter, more focused game that squeezes in world-building only where it's unintrusive. If you enjoyed one game, you're likely to enjoy the other.
Gameplay in Inc orbits around careful planning and risk management and shouldn't feel unfamiliar if you're used to tactical RPGs or you loved Monaco, but folks who prefer kicking down doors and going in guns blazing might be put off. The music and visual design help to culture a nicely tense atmosphere and it's easy enough to forget that you can walk away, make a sandwich, eat it, and come back all in the same five second interval of game time, but the first couple lessons the game teaches you tend to be hard ones. The kind that prematurely end a run.
Still, defeat isn't bad in Inc, as it lets you cash out your xp and get new optional unlocks for your next attempt at the campaign.

First of all I have to say I do not care about microtransactions one way or another, They aren't my bag but they don't bother me.
This game was billed as an immersive RPG-style lord O' the rings game where you could craft totally new storylines using the nemesis system.
After 20 plus hours I can report only that is is a relatively buggy hack n slash game with constantly recycled characters, a fortress-taking mechanic which seems totally divorced form the main story (I control all of mordor and Sauron has yet to lift a finger), a totally bloated set of quests and gear system and a strong ability to make you wonder what you loved so much about Shadow of mordor.
The fortress taking and holding aspect is fun and should have been DLC for SoM, it is too easy to stack against the AI on nomal difficulty that I was able to take everything but the overlord on the first try and usually finish the whole thing after two.
The main quests totally railroad you and it seems like it doesn't matter what else you have done there isn't reallly any effect on the story.
The Orcs are fun and enjoyable but if you've already seen 3 or four with the same name after playing for 3 days they clearly didn't put much effort in.
The fights all go pretty much the same with maybe 3 or so variations: the ones I can execute, the ones I can shoot and the ones I can stomp with my beast-friends.
The interface is so overloaded and confusing I literally don't know which quests are the main quests, they all seem totally unimportant and overly important at the same time.
There are only really 4 fortresses to take in the game and after taking them I feel like I have no idea what to do next, I literally rule the land where Sauron's tower is can I just have them dismantle it? I mean I got a lot of Orcs...
I am constantly getting new gear but I literally have not ever noticed a difference other than appearance and even then not much. Most of the time I check my inventory I have like 5 or 6 upgrades wating and am just like "Hmm, guess I didn't need these that bad"
Overall, I would have been hapy if this was a 20 buck DLC for Shadow of Mordor and was just the fortresses, at 60 bucks its not worth it.

I played a little of this on an android device, so when I saw it on Steam, I had to grab it.  If you're even considering it, I'd say just do it.  Whether you're an old time Pac-Manner, an 8-bit hipster, or a fan of endless runner type mobile games, I think everybody can find something to love.
First of all let's talk about the style.  This game is gorgeous.  Don't let the simple appearance fool you, there's a lot going on here!  The various visual themes means the look never has to get stale.  Graphical "glitches" come across the map in waves, forcing you forward and altering the game ahead of you.  Powerups are greeted with flashy effects and zooms.
The powerups!  There's a ton of them, and each can be leveled up with coins.  Other features new to Pac-Man are loadouts, and some limited stealth mechanics.
There's some genuine gameplay innovation going on, as well.  Ghosts are more like Agent Smiths.  The traditional ghost personalities are present, but when glitches hit the map, they might switch, or even disappear.
Is it Game of the Year?  Probably not.  But it's challenging and, if you can believe it, fun!

Pacman is a simple game.  A maze with four possible directions of travel.  Avoid the bad things, eat the dots.  Nothing to it.
But a game this simple, which relies solely on the player's ability to recognize and avoid danger by pressing one of four directions, pretty much demands responsive controls.
The controls in this game are fundamentally broken.  If you press diagonal while traveling, which is a pretty tried and true technique for changing direction at the next junction, you get random behavior.  Sometimes pacman will make the intended turn, sometimes pacman will ignore you.  Sometimes, for fun, pacman will change direction in the middle of the hallway, because why not?
If you're traveling right to left, and press up and release the joystick, pacman will remember this and turn up at the first chance, even though you've changed your mind and released the button.
You had one job.  Four directions.  Do what the player wants.
Couldn't even do that.

My review of Broken Age can be broken in two (pun!).
First, the bad: This is a very simple game that puts up only a ghost of a challenge. What's worse is that unsolicited hints come in like crazy, treating the player like a kid. I'd compare the gameplay to some of Telltale Games' easier fare (Wallace & Gromit, Back to the Future), but with the hint system on.
Secondly, the good; and there is a lot of that. This is a beautiful game. It's 2D, it animates like a flash game, but man is it the most gorgeous, eye-popping flash game out there. I've seen a lot of Lead Artist "Bagel" Stapley's work for Broken Age in documentaries, but seeing it so crisp and clear in the game does his talent justice. The animations are also very fluid and charming, despite the limited technology.
In terms of story, it was also one hand or the other. The story of Shay, the boy protagonist, feels a bit dreary and uninspired - which may be unfair considering he was trying to escape a dreary and uninspiring situation. However, playing Vella, the female protagonist was a treat through and through. Great scenes, great characters, great situations. It's like the game saved most of the great bits for this half. Broken Age Part 1 also ends in an unexpected cliffhanger that still continues to have me wonder what happened and what's going to happen next. I can't wait to play Part 2, which is a good sign that I enjoyed the game despite the few issues I had.
In short, this is a game for those who are really into story, and will forgive gameplay that is almost condescendingly easy. If that's you - it's definitely me - then I highly recommend this game.

Not to mention the phenomenal soundtrack (one of the best I've heard in awhile and one of the few that I consider worth spending $5 on). My only problem with the game is that it feels a bit bland. Sure you can build a massive superbase and rain hell with artillery and rockets but after playing ten rounds against the AI you start feeling a bit board of it all. It doesn't help that the landscape it pretty bland to look at from a bird's eye view (though the soundtrack more than makes up for it). There just isn't alot of variety in the game. This has mostly to do with the fact that the seven weapons (not counting upgrades like high energy beam to quantum beam) are pretty predictable. It's either a bullet, something that explodes, or a laser with a charge up time. The units are also very bland with a few exceptions. The buildings and turret upgrades are cool but there is still a bland pit in the game.
The game is still fun to play and these would be minor if there was the guarantee of more content on the way, but there is not. Right now Robert Hesketh is working on a sequel to the game which feels unfinished. Sure the second game sounds fun but the developer should be focused on perfecting this game before working on a sequel. Especially since the community was looking forward to a big update coming up in version 2.0. I understand if Robert Hesketh wants to expand his company and I believe he will return to this game soon after he finishes his other game but at the moment the game is bland and feels a bit dull. I will give it a thumbs up because I believe it’s worth the money but right now don’t expect to play for hours on end unless you have a freind or are really starved for an rts.

100/10 would absolutely play again.

Personally I do enjoy this game and while this game certainly does have its ups and downs, I am not here to praise or criticize this game. I am here to offer a phenomenal 4 Cheese Ravioli recipe!
Here are the ingredients you will need!
Ravioli Dough: 2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 pinch salt, 1 teaspoon olive oil, 2 eggs, 1 1/2 tablespoons water.
Ravioli Filling: 1 (8 ounce) container ricotta cheese, 1 (4 ounce) package cream cheese, softened, 1/2 cup shredded mozzarella cheese, 1/2 cup provolone cheese, shredded, 1 egg, 1 1/2 teaspoons dried parsley.
Pesto-Alfredo Cream Sauce: 2 tablespoons olive oil, 2 cloves garlic, crushed, 3 tablespoons prepared basil pesto sauce, 2 cups heavy cream, 1/4 cup grated Parmesan cheese, 1 (24 ounce) jar marinara sauce.
1. Mound the flour and salt together on a work surface and form a well. Beat the teaspoon of olive oil, 2 eggs, and water in a bowl. Pour half the egg mixture into the well. Begin mixing the egg with the flour with one hand; use your other hand to keep the flour mound steady. Add the remaining egg mixture and knead to form a dough.
2. Knead the dough until smooth, 8 to 10 minutes; add more flour if the dough is too sticky. Form the dough into a ball and wrap tightly with plastic. Refrigerate for 1 hour.
3. While the dough is resting, prepare the ravioli filling. Combine the ricotta cheese, cream cheese, mozzarella cheese, provolone cheese, egg, and parsley and mix well. Set the filling aside.
4. Heat 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a skillet over medium heat. Add the crushed garlic and pesto sauce and cook for one minute. Pour in the heavy cream, raise the heat to high, and bring the sauce to a boil. Reduce the heat and simmer for 5 minutes. Add the Parmesan cheese and stir until the cheese melts. Remove the pan from the heat and keep warm.
5. Meanwhile, in a separate saucepan, warm the marinara sauce over medium-low heat.
6. Preheat an oven to 375 degrees F (190 degrees C). Beat the egg with the tablespoon of water to make the egg wash.
7. Roll out the pasta dough into thin sheets no thicker than a nickel. To assemble the ravioli, brush the egg wash over a sheet of pasta. Drop the filling mixture on the dough by teaspoonfuls about one inch apart. Cover the filling with the top sheet of pasta, pressing out the air from around each portion of filling. Press firmly around the filling to seal. Cut into individual ravioli with a knife or pizza cutter. Seal the edges.
8. Fill a large pot with lightly salted water and bring to a rolling boil over high heat. Stir in the ravioli, and return to a boil. Cook uncovered, stirring occasionally, until the ravioli float to the top and the filling is hot, 4 to 8 minutes. Drain well.
9. Grease a baking sheet. Place the cooked ravioli on the sheet pan and bake in the preheated oven until brown, about 4 minutes.
10. To serve the ravioli, divide them among four warmed serving bowls. Drizzle the marinara sauce over the ravioli and then top with the cream sauce.

Background: I have played a few Rogue-Like games and I am an IT Guy in real life so the whole hacking/technology thing piques my interest 10 fold.  I also play and DM Shadowrun so I was in for this game 100%.
First and Foremost: It is a Rogue-like with a rich cast of characters each with unique abilities to assist them in carrying out their tasks.  They cover a wide range of play styles from CQB to straight up speed and subterfuge. That being said some characters only work well in certain game types and some seemingly not at all.  There are many guides and forums available that detail how/when/where to use Agents. It does all come down to personal preference.
Speaking of which this game plays much like Shadowrun, except your Agents all go down in 1 Hit.
Floor/Enemy Mechanics: Vision plays a huge part for both the Enemy and your Agents. Guards don't ignore Movement and there isn't a "maybe" Mechanic. They investigate every slip up. Floors have sound sensors, locked doors, automated turrets, laser beam sensors, robots that are immune to Stun, and Cameras that feedback to the enemies. It has a real nice sense of Realism.
Resources: Power is the Main Resource Utilized by Incognita for hacking, but does have other uses. One agent even uses Power to Stun Guards Multiple Times per Round.  Each agent has Equipment that can help them navigate and disable Guards. This ranges from Non-Lethal and Lethal weapons, grenades, holo projectors, cloaking devices and more.
Agent Mechanics: All Agents have Unique abilities that help you in some way to fit a play style. Some excel at Combat. Some are good at Energy Management. Others at Mobility.
Incognita Mechanics: So along with your Agents is Incognita your AI System who you interface with in the Hacking Layer of the Level. She relies on Power to hack terminals, disable sensors, and take over enemy Robots and Turrets. She also has a suite of programs that allow her to perform more advanced functions like creating sound to distract guards or to override Enemy Shielding.  However her power is not without risk. Some terminals are infected with malware that cause detriments to her abilities and to those of your agents. This can include needing more power to hack terminals, bringing extra guards onto the map and even being locked out of hacking all together.
Final Thoughts: The Level of Realism this game brings to the table makes it Challenging everytime you play on any difficulty. I find myself on Easy sometimes losing on the first level due to the Random Generation of the Level.
Also this game can be VERY UNFORGIVING. One screw up and it could be game over in mere moments. I love this. It makes me care about my Agents. This does it for me 100%.

Alpha Protocol has player growth and skills similar to Deus Ex; missions, equipment, and stealth similar to Hitman; and far reaching dialogue choices similar to Mass Effect. So how does the amalgam work together? Not bad actually.
Something novel to Alpha Protocol are the achievements, called perks. Where most games would give you a shiny meaningless badge saying "good work" after doing something interesting or noteworthy, Alpha Protocol's perks have mechanical effects. As an example, if you take enough beating without dying, you get a perk which talks about how tough you are and then gives you a bonus to your endurance (which lets you take still more of a beating).
It's easier to talk about what went wrong than what went right. What's not so good about Alpha Protocol?
The early and late story feels quite solid, but the story in some areas of the middle of the game has abrupt conclusions.
Your dialog choices must be chosen before a timer expires. It isn't always obvious what some options refer to until the speaker finishes talking, but that's when the timer expires for picking your response!
The mini-games are actually interesting, but the lock picking mini-game is highly dependent upon the sensitivity of your analog triggers and there are no settings to change the sensitivity; I have no idea how it works without a gamepad. There is one way around any mini-game which give all the same rewards, but it requires a consumable item.
The game saves using checkpoints. You can copy a checkpoint save to be loaded later, but you can never save the game yourself. Many of these checkpoints are at extremely awkward or unpredictable occasions, like when you walk into a room with a bunch of baddies and turrets. Loading at those checkpoints can be unbearable. A good number of checkpoints cause events which prevent you from going backwards. As a person who likes to clean up all the baddies before exploring for hidden goodies, the checkpoint system bit me a number of times.
For my own play through, I was accused of killing people that I had not killed. At the end of a particular mission, the statistics noted I killed nobody. However, the incident of me killing these people came up again and again. I'm not sure if it was because I destroyed some turrets or what, but that really broke immersion every time it came up.
As with all games with a large selection of narrative and gameplay decisions, there are a lot of bugs. If you don't mind games with a lot of bugs and you are looking for an interesting blend of Deus Ex, Hitman, and Mass Effect, then this game is definitely worth picking up sometime.

Okay, okay.  I really like Klei Entertainment.  However, there are pros and cons.  I will go over those.
As with other games by this developer, Invisible Inc. retains Klei's trademark fantastic art style and morbid sense of humor.  There's a lot of shenanigans you can get away with if you play the ideal way - stealth - instead of engaging every enemy you see.  This is where you'll get to see some funny scenarios, like jumping in and out of a guard's "noticed" sight range, just to mess with his head.  "What was that?"  "I thought I saw something!"  Ah...priceless.
Gameplay involves a bit of trial and error.  I don't find any of the characters to be overpowering, but with experience, you can "play the system" and do things like max out Internationale's *remote* hacking abilities, since she's the best candidate to shove hacking skill points on.  As for other mechanics, I dislike turn-based games, and don't find the rewind feature particularly helpful.  I've seen this feature in other games, and it's usefulness boils down to how badly you've messed up the situation.  While you can fix a game-ending team formation in one rewind, the 5 rewind limit will not help if you spent several turns idling to regenerate your hacking power.  Even at the easiest difficulty, I felt like I lost alot of progress.
Overall, I love this game and would recommend it just because Klei does stealth games very well (they also made Mark of the Ninja, which isn't turn-based).  Again, to get missions completed effectively, you'll need to throw a bit of paint at the wall and see what sticks.  The game is worth the challenge.

I like this game, but I cannot recommend it for a few reasons that seem small but really makes a big impact on the enjoyment of the game(at least mine).
Figuring out how to play this game is hard, you are rewarded for being careful and violence is generally punished. Killing or knocking people out makes the game harder BUT the more turns you take the harder it gets as well. This is supposed to make the game into you walking a thin line between being too aggresive and being too slow however it just ends up with you feeling like every choice you make is wrong. A lot of your decisions are also based on too little information, meaning the choices are sometimes not even possible to make based on what you see but you must roll the dice.
So what we have here is a game where it is very hard to figure out how to play, well I figured out how I wanted to play this game but I was never allowed to. All the items in this game are attainable or not based on RNG, I wanted for example to knock guards out in melee but I never got any of those tools(except the ones you start with) and not even a chance to purchase one. I see what the developers are after with this they want you to make do with what you get and adapt your playstyle depending on what the RNG gives you, its a neat concept really and it creates a great replayability.
My issue here though is this, I don't want replayability and I don't want to randomly die because the tools I got were subpar and the RNG gods sneezed in my direction. I don't want to have to restart and play through the♥♥♥♥♥♥due to that, this issue might not have been so bad by itself but together with the fact that you can't even play like you want to because gear, augments and computer abilities are all based on RNG it makes it not fun.
For people that love turn based strategic games and also love to replay games for a long time and adapting your playstyle and characters depending on what gear you get this will be your thing. Sadly I really like to make the choices about how my characters are geared out and how they fight myself so I can't recommend the game even though I liked it.

I've done some programming myself and just a single misplaced period or missing semicolon can be hard to pinpoint, and that was for a simple program. Pac-Man 256 is inspired by the Level 256 Glitch that appears in the original Pac-Man game. When one reaches level 256, the right half of the maze bugs out as a result of the game trying to spawn 256 "fruit" in the bottom right corner. Regardless of the level being impossible to complete, the maze is traversable.
In Pac-Man 256, not only will you be doing the same thing on Pac-Man, but you must escape from the Glitch at the bottom of the screen that's trying to kill you as well, all the while trying to get a good score. Each of the ghosts has its own pattern, so you'll need to memorize which ghost does what in any given situation. There are also additional features, such as a Pac-Dot chain, Ghost Chains greater than 4 ghosts, powerups that help kill off ghosts, and a leaderboard that records your top scores.
Pac-Man 256 can be brutal at times, but the replay value is worth the price. And this is unlike the mobile version of the game: Credits are removed, no advertisements, and no upgrade wait times are big perks when compared to the mobile version. If you're still unsure, give it a try on mobile if you can.

I played this game for weeks on my phone when it first came out, and I enjoyed every moment of it. Well, almost. Like any FTP game for a mobile platform, it was totally playable for free, but in order to do anything quickly or get the best content, you had to deal with in-app purchases.
Now we have the console version. It's $4.99 up front, but what that gets you is no gimmicks, no money grabs, and a whole lot of fun. The game isn't quite as exciting as Pac-Man Championship Edition, but it's still a fantastic time trying to rack up as high of a score as possible. Not only that, but now that in-app purchases are gone, powerup upgrades are instant, and coins are far easier to come by, making the grind from the mobile game much easier to deal with and much easier to enjoy.
If you're a fan of the classic maze games, I'd definitely give this game a shot. Here's also hoping for an online multiplayer patch in the future. Four players on one computer just doesn't seem like something people would do.

Potatoman Seeks the Troof is a little game that took me two minutes to download and just a few more to finish, but those were some of the most enjoyable minutes I have had with such an easy game. You have two controls: left, right, and jump. With those at your disposal, you make your way jumping and dodging various obstacles. You will soon learn that this game is not easy at all. Obstacles don't just sit, some jump, some grow, some multiply right into your path, and so on and so forth, it's enough to keep you on your toes...that is until you figure out the patterns for most of them. The aerial obstacles are a bit more difficult to navigate, which actually makes the replayability a little bit better.
Audio: 70/100 C-
The sounds, like the gameplay is simple and basic, reminiscent of the Colecovision and Atari era of gaming, both paying homage and still being a modern game. It's charming, but nothing special.
Visuals: 74/100 C-
8-Bit galore, at first. The game sports the simplest of graphics, having a ton of colors and animations here and there, but things come alive when you die, of all places, as a semi 3D, blue and red hue filters everything and spins away.
Content: 75/100 C
Like I mentioned at the start, this isn't a particularly long game, but it is one you can play at a party over and over, it's simple enough that anyone can get, has enough variety to keep it challenging and definitely something you can share with others. And I'm sure kids will have more fun with this game than they will with Flappy Bird.
Design: 75/100 C
When dealing with the limited movements it really isn't hard to screw up and while they're not perfect, they are solid and do what they need to do. Sometimes there is some detection issues, but then again, that could just be me as well.
Performance: 80/100 B-
Potatoman plays very well on my PC and probably works very well on the mobile platforms as well. It isn't processor heavy at all and doesn't have the common issues higher end games.
Verdict: 76/100 C+

The Banner Saga 2 is, without a doubt, a magnificent game to behold.  The sequel to 2014's 'The Banner Saga', this is a strategy-RPG that picks up directly after that game's ending, and continues on with Stoic's epic Norse-inspired fantasy story.
Once again, you have a caravan that you guide through the world in a very 'Oregon Trail'-esque journey, where events stop you along the way and either prompt decisions which affect you and your people or prompt battle.
When you enter battle, the game enters a tile-based strategy mode where you move your units along the outlined area and choose to attack or use special commands.
While there is a recap you can follow from the main menu, to experience this fantastic journey fully, you MUST play the original game.  For veterans of that title, you can pull your finished game save points and load them in here, along with all of the choices you made from the previous chapters.  From there on, you can expect more of the same.  Stoic has added new characters and abilities, and while there is a bit too much hand-holding for the first chapter, from then on everything truly seems to matter.  They've also gone above and beyond their previous efforts, including many more gorgeous animations and larger fullscale art pieces for us to enjoy.
If you like epic fantasy, if you like strategy RPGs, or even if you're just a lover of fine art and moving symphonies, this is a great game to check out.

"Is This Game Worth It's Price Tag?" is the question I'm guessing that you are asking..
My answer.. If you love Pac-Man, if you loved the old school Pac-Man then "YES!" is my answer to you.
Obviously, if you are looking for an FPS shooter or a deep story drive RPG, then you need to look elsewhere, lol.. just sayin'
I streamed the game when it first launched on Steam after purchasing it myself...  You can that hour long stream right HERE:
This game has the same look and feel of the Frogger inspired mobile game called "Crossy Road" a free android and iOS application made by the same developers Hipster Whale.  They've done an excellent job at making this PC PC-Man job in my eyes, and it feels and plays much, much better then many of the lazy mobile ports of games I've played before.
I like the gameplay and the ability to progress and level up all the different "power-ups" available in the game such as the tornado ghost killer and the giant pac-man.  Definitely makes it more fun.  The glitchy numbers mass which I call "the matrix" that works it's way up the maze and makes you have to continually keep on the move is a cool element as well.
I gave the game a solid 85% score considering it's $5 USD price tag on Steam here.  It seems to have good value, it is fun, and the controls, while basic WASD or arrow key controls are all you use are very responsive and fluid.
Thing's I'd love to see added..
- Online multiplayer modes with perhaps the ability to sabatage other online opponents with mines, bombs, blobs of glue to make them slow, etc might be fun.
- A Global online high score list in addition to the current ability to see Steam friends high scores.
- Boss battles as you progress might be an interesing addition, like touch a glowing boss in the maze to go to a special "boss battle room" where you can use your chose power-ups to try and defeat a giant boss.. something like that anyhow.
- Anything that fits this game that could add replayability like the boss battle idea above, but maybe also adding options functionality to give players the choice of turning such options off or on would be nice as well.
Still, for $5 you can't go too wrong.. especially if you enjoy Pac-Man games or the classics.  There are NO MICROTRANSACTIONS for anyone wondering.

so i just beat broken age.
it took me roughly three hours to do so.
i think i liked the game?  the voice casting and acting was excellent, and the story itself was pretty interesting. I switched back and forth between shay and vella after they reached major points in their respective stories, so for sure saw the ending coming from preeeettttyyy far off. theres a lot of good points but i also have like, i guess, some issues.  lets discuss.
artistically this game is amazing. every area you go to is beautifully rendered and the characters actually have a nice highlight layer that respects lights located throughout the level, so even though its technically 2D they still feel like they navigate a 3D world in a way that is subtle and convincing.  all the characters had a great feel, and each area you went to had a clear artistic theme that worked well and created a good identity for the individual characters and the world itself.  Each village Vella visited had a great sense of fashion that reflected their purpose in the world, and in Shay’s case he just had a whole bunch of amazing everything friends to hang out with.  That being said there are a few places where i noticed the assets looks pixelated and improperly rezzed, but it was infrequent and it was never an object that was important to the story.
the sounds design was great.  the music was very well done, and the variety of voice actors was pretty impressive and full of wonderful and recognizable people who really did an awesome job of selling their characters.
The characters were also great. Shay’s friends were are hilarious and the way they interacted with him when on and off duty was entertaining.  The people in Vella’s world were also pretty interesting, although they all blindly love Mog Chothra which would get old if not for it being an integral part of the story, so i guess i don’t mind? It kinda bugged me that all the female characters in Shellmound were super ditzy and shallow though.  This could have been subverted by making one of the temple guards a dude, as their shallow nature ends up being a gag, but all the girls who were offered to mog chothra and the two temple guards kinda just blend together.
the gameplay was pretty standard point and click stuff, and the puzzles themselves were rarely very challenging. to be fair i’ve played point and click adventures for like, my entire life as a gamer, so these things are kinda second nature to me. there were some design choices that were a little strange - like the snake. why is the snake there? it is a dead end and misleading. there was no reason to get past the snake, and as far as i coudl tell, no way to get past the snake. why is there a snake?
the story itself was pretty interesting, and how the two stories come together is pretty obvious, but i cant fault the game for not surprising me with it’s plot twists.  Shay’s story is interesting because it all happens in a very small scale - he explores the ship to do a thing.  Vella, on the other hand, goes on this big winding adventure around her world (but really only like 3 locations).  Her story seems like a race against time, while shay’s seems far more casual and meandering.
overall though my biggest complaint is in the story.  it took me three hours to beat the game, and at the end of those three hours the story gets interesting.  the whole game is building up to this specific point (which again, is pretty easy to see coming if you like, you know, know how stories work) and when it finally happens the game ends. imagine, dear reader, that you are watching star wars, and just as luke gets on board the millenium falcon the credits roll.  Technically, yeah, you know luke is like off on an adventure, and leia needs to be rescued but NOPE. you’ll find out about it later.
I know that tim put out an apology for making the game too long and how he wanted to release SOMETHING because its been what, 2 years since the kickstarter? and so the game was split in two parts so we can play half now and half later.  but to me, this felt like maybe 1/3? speaking from my other P&C adventure experience: telltale games released a new season of sam and max every 2 years. each contain 5 episodes that take roughly 3 hours on the first play through - about the same size and substance as part 1 of broken age. they also cost the same amount of money. for 5 episodes released every month, instead of 2 released i guess like 6 months apart? they haven’t really been clear on when more is coming.
i know each studio has its own way of creating games and i’m not trying to say double fine should have made me more game, but i just feel like in 2 years and with 3 million dollars i was going to get something a little more substantial.
broken age is pretty good. it didn’t blow me away, but i enjoyed playing it. i look forward to part 2, whenever that gets finished  but like, if i am being honest, i enjoyed it more for the art and acting than i did for the game parts. the old lucas arts adventure games were challenging and engaging and really shaped my sense of humor and love for adventurous stories. the dig and monkey island will be with me the rest of my life because they impacted me in a big way.  act 1 of broken age is not memorable or impactful in the same way.  so i’m looking forward to episode 2. because episode 1 is great, but pretty forgettable.

Put simply, the game has a great art style, interesting narrative (albeit, somewhat derivative of recent works) and doesn't often play the humour just for silliness sake. That is to say, the humour is present, but not in your face or overly slapstick. The issue appears with the puzzles. Unfortunately, whilst the point and click puzzler is a cult favourite, the actual style of puzzle is very important. My experience of Broken Age is to unfortunately use puzzles that aren't so much requiring of intelligence, but knowing a specific set of steps, one mistep of which puts you back to square one. Those are the most laborious, because it doesn't require the player to "reason it out", it requires them to know a precise sequence, or learn it by trial and error. Not great fun, and has frustrated me a few times in a playthrough.
Still, overall positive impression, but I'd only recommend it to fans of the genre.

I backed this game over two years ago. I have always loved Double Fine's games and like most people, it was a gamble to shell out the money on something that could be bad... Needless to say, I'm more than happy with the results, so far! The game is beautiful and the story is really exciting. Though short, the promise of a future update will make me hungry for more.
As for game-play, the point-and-click adventure stays very true to its name and manages to weave an exciting tale with interesting characters. I've spent hours doing nothing just to hear dialogue! The puzzles were fun, though a tad easy for my tastes. I would have been a bit more happy with the game if the puzzles were a bit harder to crack. As for the graphics, the design of the game was well put together and stands out beautifully against most others out there. However, I encountered quite a few graphical glitches in cutscenes, which I felt like were quite annoying to deal with.
Overall, this game is a solid 8.7-9.4. The game is very much in need of more polish, with perhaps more care into the cutscenes to prevent visual glitches, and more sound effects to emphasize certain important actions. But the story and characters ring true to Double Fine's standard.
Buy this game. It is worth every penny. Since it's being released in stages, I have no doubt that the team will look at reviews and address the major concerns in the second act. Meaning this next part is going to be even better! ... I hope. Either or, it's a wonderful experience and I don't remember the last time a game has made me gasp for excitement.

This has the potential to be an awesome game.  What you can play of it is rather enjoyable.  As far as alpha's go, it's great.  But the developer seems to think it's full release.  And is working on Executive Assault 2.  So, I don't forsee a significant amount of development happening on this, especially considering the patch release history prior to working on EA2.
That said, I will probably purchase EA2.  From what I read it's a single individual who makes the full game, which makes this kind of an incredible project, and if that game gets more developed than this, I'll very likely recommend it.
Pros: Exellent customization system, good (though limited) base building, slightly innovative win system (assassinate the enemy commander or powerplant, which can only be accomplished with bots that can fit inside the facility).
Cons: Lots of bugs.  On par with late alpha/early beta release.  I've been playing this multiplayer with my cousin and a few friends.  About 1 out of 3 games ends with one of our systems hanging. Usually to the point alt-F4 or Ctrl-Alt-Del do not respond. Occasionally a game ends with irreparable de-sync.  During game play, terrain clipping can be an issue.  Dev has patched that fairly well.  Currently the most serious terrain clipping issue is if you pull multiple asteroids down onto the same location, resources will be unrecoverable, and units will fall through the map there.  Units/research which is useless until further content is developed (like the Hackbot. which can hack through doors. unless they get the 2nd door upgrade.  On the official wiki, it looks like there was more content planned for it, but never developed).
Balance issues: the most egregious being that with 4500 metal you can use connecting corridors to make it so no one can enter your base. Preventing assassination of your commander or powerplant.  Which is nice to mess around testing robot builds, but it means any pvp is on the honour system and you have to choose not make yourself invulnerable to the AI.  Another issue is unit balance.  If you don't build tanks, you will likely lose.  There's several different weapons you can research (lasers, plasma, rockets, ballistics...) but I can't quite determine if there's a rock-paper-scissors making one thing more effective than another.  Lasers seem good vs bots and weak against tanks. And Plasma is weak vs tanks. And rockets are strong verses your own units and buildings (friendly fire). But nothing really seems to be particularly good against tanks.  Overwhelming force seems to be the only thing.  A minor complaint would be the research system.  You can speed it up a little (up to 2x speed), but that's it (unless you're in single player where you can set research to take 3 seconds per tech).  Meaning it'll take about an hour to have a fully upgraded unit (bot with full armour and a weapon and secondary ability OR upgraded tank OR upgraded aircraft).  It's a minor complaint, and could be fixed if the game were likely to get more than an update every 6 months, but unlikely to change as things stand.  Wouldn't be so bad if you could effectively counter tanks by researching a weapon system that may be ineffective vs a different unit type, but as it is, you start a research path, and either it works, or the enemy counters it and you've wasted 20 minutes.
Overall, I enjoy it for messing around since I already paid for it, but I would recommend anyone looking at it consider waiting for executive assault 2 to come out.  In the mean time, there's always Forged Alliance.

An immersive game which pays homage to great horror/mystery works, most notably the Twin Peaks television series and Stephen King's writing (especially The Shining), to both of which Alan Wake makes numerous references. To be honest, this game has so much in common with Twin Peaks, the only reason I can think of they didn't just call it "Twin Peaks - The Game" is copyright issues.
Though most fights get quite repetitive after some time, it's the story that really got me going - the game also pays attention to little details that most people would miss in a hurried playthrough.
What annoyed me more than fighting undead lumberjacks for the gazillionth time though was the blatant product placement of real brands, which I believe doesn't belong in a game like this. But apart from that, I have no complaints.
All in all a great game by video game designer Sami Järvi, who already gave us the exceptionally intense Max Payne franchise.
If you're a fan of both horror/mystery fiction and a Max Payne-esque protagonist, this game is definitely for you.

So I have more hours logged in Banner Saga Factions then any other game in my GOG or Steam library. So when Banner Sage 1 was finally released I was obviously excited to play it. And play it I did... with some varying degrees of disappointment. The combat wasn't as engaging as Factions since the AI wasn't quite as sharp as a human opponent; the rogue-like elements felt tacked on and inconsequential; the story interesting albeit bleak, depressing and full of spelling mistakes; the artwork and music brilliant.
So I finished The Banner Saga happy that it wasn't a p.o.s. but feeling as though it could have been so much more.  Fast forward to The Banner Saga 2 and Stoic has gotten much, much closer to what I had hoped for in the first one with this second chapter. The story is far more exciting, tense and intriguing then the first. The artwork maintains its brilliance.  The combat is far more layered now with items to bolster stats, secondary traits for characters, more units to bring to battle, more varied landscape to travel through and some great traveling events to provide intrigue and replay-ability. It took me 20 hours to play through the first time on Hard and it was worth every penny.
If I were to quibble about anything it would be that the ending is a bit anti-climatic which is far from unheard of in great games (Baldur's Gate I anyone?) and that the caravan management component still doesn't quite feel as though it carries sufficient weight to be of interest. I'm not sure how they can improve the latter but I hope they can. I have finished The Banner Saga 2 and am already looking forward to the 3rd one!

EDIT: The game has now been updated to include the new framerate options. When playing with the 60 or unlimited framerate options I recommend using vsync as the screen tearing at this point in time can be pretty bad. I'll continue to update my review as I play and hopefully I can work towards a recommendation once I play more.
Let's get the obvious out of the way. Yes the game is locked to 30fps but the developer has said they will be releasing an update with 30, 60, and unlocked fps options. They still don't get a free pass on launching it this way but at least they're not ignoring our complaints to fix it as fast as possible.
With that being said, the only other major complaint I have with the visuals is that the game seems to be rendered at a much lower resolution than what you choose to natively display it as. I can't prove this fact but with how incredibly blurry the game is, even at higher resolutions (4k) It seems to be this way and I don't know if this can be improved or not.
Lack of visual options for user adjustment is a downside as everything ranges from low-high instead of giving us PC gamers what we are generally used to in terms of visual options.
I should suggest that while other people have experienced crashes on a much higher scale, I have only crashed once so far so I have been lucky it seems.
On to the good stuff:
-the game has a superb atmosphere that really captures the heart of the time the game takes place. And not just visually but the way people interact with you, cops always being supicious of you/etc really adds to the realism of the time.

This game has some major graphical issues. The low FPS is really noticeable and is only tolerable because I run a G-Sync monitor. I tested the game with G-Sync turned off and it is basically unplayable and definitely wouldn't be suitable for anyone that suffers from epilepsy or motion sickness when playing games.
The graphics are extremely blurry at default settings and look nothing like the Steam screenshots. I had to turn Shadows and AA to low and turn off movement blur to remove some of the blurriness. The worst point is how the game crashes entering or exiting a cutscene. It has crashed three times within an hour and that is after updating to the latest Nvidia game ready driver.
The texture maps used in this game are a very poor resolution and I hope they release a high resolution texture pack to clean up the textures. I am puzzled that the game takes up 44GB's of hard drive space. I hope there are some high res textures hiding in there somewhere.
The above is a real shame as the voice acting and motion capture are superb. The little I have seen of the city looks great except it is difficult to see due to the indistinct graphics. I've decided to stop playing Mafia III and wait until the first major patch is released as I do not want to exceed my 2 hour refund time limit.
I really hope they fix all the issues with the game soon before I am forced to request a Steam refund. A damn shame as I was looking forward to this game. The devs need to release the PC performance patch as soon as possible. There is a gem of a game here but it is currently hiding behind a very botched PC release.
Post FPS patch note:
So post FPS patch the game runs really well. On my system (shown on the left) I get 70-80 fps. The shadow effects during the day are really weird and big blocks of shade move across the landscape.  The reflections on cars alternate between dark to full reflection depending on how you look at the car. The transition is very jarring though.
On first load after the patch it said my saved game was corrupt and it forced me to restart the game from scratch. I wonder if this happened to anyone else. Not much else to say as I am now only 3 hours in. I turned on simulation mode for driving and it feels much better. The gun play is a lot more enjoyable now that the fps is higher.
Mafia III definitely needs a high resolution texture pack. I don't hate it but it would improve the look of the game immensely.
Post 10 hour played mark:
Overall though even with the framerate improvements you can't escape the fact that outside of the cutscenes there isn't that much to do in the game. There are the same sequence of mission events repeated over and over again. There is a shameful lack of variety of things to do in the open world. It almost seems like Hangar 13 ran out of time to work on the game and were forced to release it incomplete.
As it stands I cannot honestly recommend this game. The question is will the devs add gameplay to the game or will they simply move on to their next project and abandon it. Damn first No Man's Sky and now this.
Oh and one final point - please give us a damned high resolution texture pack.

Once every lifetime or so, a game comes along that defines an entire generation of people.  It may not be the most popular game or even the most well-made (though this one is).  But it is a game whose vitality--whose culture and mission--is guided by the spirit of the times.  A game that is of the same soul as its rapidly-evolving player-base.
This game is a leather-skinned, ten-tonne, befanged zeitgeist of the 2010s; it is filled to the brim with content, but as empty as the Dadaists who hurriedly cranked it out.  A work of passion?  Absolutely not.  It was an accident.  A beautiful, remarkable accident: Like life itself.  It was a market-savvy cynical heap of a game, desperately trying to hitch a ride on the bandwagon of dino-themed entertainment.  The game ressurected Michael Crichton--may he rest in peace--for the express purpose of tearing down everything that he could have been, in addition to everything he already was, and replace his memory with a plastic artifice and the lowest possible form of American consumerism.
This is why you need this game.  Not because it's good, but because it's the most important game of this--of any--decade.  This is the game that defines the 2010s better than any other; in all its flaws and successes.  And it could not have come sooner.
In this game, you take on the role of Captain Henk Mercer, an intrepid planet-hopping paleontologist-slash-warlord with a heart of solid dino dung.  You are tasked with killing every dinosaur that every existed, to protect future generations of hyperreligious Galactic Federal Citizens from the complexities of an increasingly secular, science-based culture which would become distracted from its faith by the presence of ancestral lizard bones.  With a ragtag team of up to 17 other cyber soldiers (your fellow players), you must defeat hordes of enemy dinos (specifically, all pterodactyls) using four different unique guns.  The guns depicted in this goddamn game have essentially never been made before.  They defy any description: But imagine a rocket launcher that has acquired sapience, knows its enemies' fears and hopes, and concludes to murder them anyway.  That's generally how ♥♥♥♥ing sweet the guns are.  But--again--only playing the game can imbue you with the visceral knowledge of how the guns work, because it's 100% feel and 0% logic.  The game proves that there is no logic greater than raw emotion and, in proving this truth, the dinosaurs have finally killed Nietzsche; God is alive, and He is you.  Read on.
The game is among the first FPS games to utilize a "healer type" class: A player whose sole purpose is to increase the Hit Points (or HP) of the other players, should they suffer Dino Damage (or DD) during the game's progress. Keeping your healer class alive becomes essential and difficult, because there are T-rexes.  Think about it: Prehistory's greatest fighting machine.  And instead of having a gun, you've got a splint and some rubbing alcohol.  But it's okay: Captain Mercer is--by the game creators' own admission--so overpowered that no dinosaur will stand a chance.  The other 21-or-so players who are working alongside Captain Mercer are basically there to server his every perverse whim, while contributing little else.  In many cases, these "whims" are a rich tapestry of scatological sex acts that would make the Marquis de Sade blush.  Make sure you are playing this game with a mature, open-minded party.
My one complaint with this game is that it deviates from Robert T. Bakker's important vision of the dinosaur.  The dinosaur's cladistic roots indicate a shared ancestry among lizards, birds, and even early mammals.  It's fair to say that all modern birds are, in fact, dinosaurs.  Science has shown this time and again, however--to this day--anyone working in the burgeoning field of Dino-themed FPS games neglects to promote these new scientific discoveries.  When you're standing on the shoulders of intellectual giants, and those giants are standing on the shoulders of sweet-as-hell stegosaurs and♥♥♥♥♥♥ you need to learn how to ♥♥♥♥ing act like it.  Show scientific progress a little respect, and maybe put some feathers and talons and beaks and♥♥♥♥♥♥in there.  Is that so much to ask?  Jesus.

So Alpha Protocol isn't great in many aspects:

Leveling your character up, sneaking, conversing, exploring and finding hidden objectives and loot in the levels, having consequenses for your actions, this game is something unique to be experienced but just don't go in to this with any high hopes and try to appreciate it for what it tried to do, that's all I can say.

Invisible, Inc. is a turn-based stealth strategy game with roguelike elements.
You control a team of up to four operatives through a number of procedurally generated levels. There are several different mission types with different objectives and rewards.
The core gameplay is excellent and you are pretty much forced to rely on stealth as lethal weapons are rare and weapon reloads are expensive. A single hit will kill any of your characters and the game is rather unforgiving with your mistakes. Luckily you get a limited number of rewinds to fix your errors.
In addition to your operatives, you also control Incognita, an advanced artificial intelligence. Incognita can provide combat support by hacking various devices such as safes, turrets and enemy drones. This adds a nice second layer to the battles.
While the gameplay itself is great, there are some design decisions that I'm not really a fan of. Most importantly, you are given a strict 72 in-game hour limit for the campaign. This only leaves you time for a pretty limited number of missions to improve your team and to prepare for the final mission.
The game could have also used some more variation with the levels as they start to look rather repetitive after a while.
Despite these flaws Invisible, Inc. is still a good game and I'd recommend it to any fans of stealth or turn-based games.
The Contingency Plan DLC pack adds new items, agents and two extra days to the campaign. Overall I think the DLC is a good addition and I definitely enjoy the longer campaign more.
The good:
- Smooth UI
- Gorgeous art style
- Interesting game mechanics
- Fun gameplay
- Good variety of agents, items, and programs
The bad:
- Repetitive levels
- Difficulty varies a lot
- Fixed time limit in the campaign

I've spent more time playing this $40 indie game than the next 10 games in my Steam library combined.  Some nerds will complain that it oversimplifies physics, but Kerbal Space Program simulates the important stuff accurately enough that even NASA has endorsed it as an entry-level school educational program for learning the basics about things like orbital mechanics, asteroid interception, and other space stuff.
Build space stations, build science colonies on and around other planets, build asteroid refueling depots, build ludicrous 1000-part atmospheric jets, or build elegant 50-part recreations of Apollo 11.  The possibilities in KSP are almost endless, especially if you start using mods.
A high-end CPU is required in order to simulate the complex physics involved in hundreds of ship components interacting in real-time.  You'll want at least a relatively modern desktop Intel i3 or i5 in order to run it well.  Entry-level and midrange laptop users will likely have a hard time running KSP without slowdowns.  On the plus side, it's not very demanding on your GPU, so just about any graphics card will run it fine.
Squad, KSP's developer, is an indie studio and this comes with a lot of obligatory jank.  There are many long-standing bugs, quirks, and limitations that can be mostly worked around once you know about them, but the first time you encounter them they might be a real headache.  The most recent versions of KSP have had a strong focus on bugfixing though, and hopefully Squad will continue to maintain this in the future.
KSP has a rather steep learning curve.  Without consulting guides, it will likely take tens of hours before your first successful orbit, and much longer before you'll have a hope of tackling more challenging objectives like landing on other planets.  Fortunately even failure is almost always fun in KSP.  This is a game with legs - it's not your typical $60 AAA title where you have a tightly-scripted 5-10 hour campaign and then never play it again.
There's been some controversy lately about Squad's development practices, with a number of high-profile developers recently leaving the project, so the years of continuous development KSP's been through might be at an end.  This is worrying, though a good portion of the game's userbase has actually expressed a measure of relief that the game's frequent updates slowing or ending altogether might mean mods will stop bring broken so frequently.  I think KSP still has lots of untapped potential and it's sold millions of copies, so I'm hopeful that the people at Squad who write the checks will start properly compensating the developers responsible for its continuing success and continue expanding the game's scope in line with their promises.
Even if 1.2 is the last version we get, it's still a great product.  There's lots of possible things I dream of doing in KSP that I still lack the skill to achieve.  Maybe after another 300 hours.

There are few games that hit a sweet spot with me like this one has. PAC-MAN 256 Is a port of a free to play mobile game developed by Hipster Whale, the talented studio behind the very addictive Crossy Road.
This particular PAC-MAN title is based around the infamous level 256 glitch in the 1980’s classic, PAC-MAN. The glitch occurred when the player makes it to level 256, where the right-hand side of the screen would turn in to a jumble of letters and numbers.
This is a very unique take on the PAC-MAN formula where you will be challenged to continuously move upwards in a never ending battle with the maze, ghosts, power-ups and the infamous level 256 glitch that is following behind.
The aim of the game, like most PAC-MAN and arcade titles is to chase the highest score possible. There are many ways to increase the score multiplier as such as eating many ghosts in quick succession, as you would expect from a PAC-MAN title. The core mechanics that you would expect from a PAC-MAN game are here and they work well, controlling PAC-MAN feels as tight and responsive as ever.
Hipster Whale evolve some of the original core PAC-MAN gameplay elements; collecting 256 pac-dots in a row will erupt 256 pac-dot chain that explodes the screen in celebration all while eliminating all ghosts on the screen. I found myself obsessively attempting to earn the 256 pac-dot chain as it was both satisfying and rewarding.
Each ghost has their own idiosyncrasies where for example, the pink ghost will chase PAC-MAN if you appear in its line of sight, the orange ghost will continuously move down the screen while the blue ghost will always hug a maze wall and move in a counter-clockwise rotation. Learning how each ghost works is imperative to your success in PAC-MAN 256.
Unlike previous titles in the series, PAC-MAN 256 features an array of power-ups that add new elements of fun, tactics and hilarity as you see a large PAC-MAN stomping around the maze squishing ghosts like a out of control bulldozer.
Power-ups can be that can be upgraded using coins that are earned within the game and not purchased with real money, unlike the mobile counterpart. Upgrading a power-up will make it more powerful; for example, leveling up the Laser power-up will allow the laser to last longer, giving PAC-MAN more protection from those ever pesky ghosts. As well as earning them in game, you will be rewarded with free coin gifts at random intervals after several runs through the game. This makes this version of the game far more generous with the coins than the original mobile game.
On top of the generousness of the in-game currency; upgrade times have been significantly reduced from the mobile game. Within PAC-MAN 256 on mobile devices, it would take anywhere from a few seconds to a few hours to upgrade the power ups. In the PC version of the game, these updates happen instantaneously.
The audio should be commended as it sticks to the classic and iconic PAC-MAN sounds and music that PAC-MAN fans have come to love over the years. It does not feel outdated and in fact feels right at home in this zany take on the franchise.
A local multiplayer mode is also featured in the game where up to 4 players can share the same screen in a frenzy to earn the highest score. Unfortunately, no online multiplayer is available.
As expected, there is not much in the way of graphics options however the game can be played in both windowed and fullscreen with a range of different screen resolutions available to chose from. In-game effects can also be turned on or off.
A option to change the skin of each maze is available and this provided me with many extra hours of enjoyment as I waka-waka’d my way through a office, garden, classic 80’s PAC-MAN and even Crossy Road.
At £3.99, this game includes no micro-transactions, no advertisements and comes with all add-ons that were available for purchase in the games mobile version.  If you have any interest in PAC-MAN or are just looking for a quick and fun time killer, I would need to recommend you check out PAC-MAN 256 and its unique take on the classic yellow  icon.

An immersive game which pays homage to great horror/mystery works, most notably the Twin Peaks television series and Stephen King's writing (especially The Shining), to both of which Alan Wake makes numerous references. To be honest, this game has so much in common with Twin Peaks, the only reason I can think of they didn't just call it "Twin Peaks - The Game" is copyright issues.
Though most fights get quite repetitive after some time, it's the story that really got me going - the game also pays attention to little details that most people would miss in a hurried playthrough.
What annoyed me more than fighting undead lumberjacks for the gazillionth time though was the blatant product placement of real brands, which I believe doesn't belong in a game like this. But apart from that, I have no complaints.

I don't plan on buying any gold for lootboxes, the ones bought with the game's own currency are good enough. Anything you want from them can be aquired without spending any additional money, they apparently even have weekly challenges you can do to aquire free lootboxes.
Dozens of other Singleplayer games already have microtransactions so one more won't change a thing, it's been around for over a decade, usually in games from Japan. I've played some and they usually have "packs" you can buy that give all sort of things, usually stuff you can get in-game but give you a boost at the start. And most of those were traditional turn based RPGs. The things I usually bought were quest characters from other games. The starter packs they gave for free always contained more items than I'd ever need so never saw the need to buy anything else, but some people don't like "grinding". Most of the time the only reason you need to grind is because you've completed the story quests too quickly and aren't prepared for the next one. Some games will give the option of a "Story" mode that allows you to play the game with minimal grinding. This game doesn't have one because the Nemesis system is what creates most of the story. I actually restarted my own game because I had rushed ahead with the story too quickly and wanted to see more of the unique missions that come up in Minas Ithil before you get your own orcs.
There are always pros and cons, two sides to every story and nothing will ever change that, someone will always find something to hate about anything. Most people actually playing this game seem to be enjoying it. Sure there are some bugs they need to fix but I have no doubt those will be fixed soon. I've done some programming myself and just a single misplaced period or missing semicolon can be hard to pinpoint, and that was for a simple program. Add all the systems they use in these games together and it creates a nightmare to sort out some problems. I do not envy what they have to go through, I dropped out of programming after seeing some things, I'm more design focused anyway.

Pros:
-Pretty much everything that was good about the first installment.
-Great story
-Animation and beautiful art
-Soundtrack and even more voice acting plus cut scenes this time, all very atmospheric
-Gameplay, battles are satisfying and strategies reasonably deep. Addition of new abilities and buffs improve even further on the original.
Cons:
-The game commits a few sins that its predecessors didn't have by presenting you with a few rather vague choices that result in horrible actions by your main character. Now I'm not talking unseen CONSEQUENCES, those happened in Banner Saga 1 and were reasonable and exciting because your abilitiy to choose the right path was limited by how little your character knew. I'm talking about you being presented with choices, choosing the one that seems like the best one and your character going and doing something you would never want them to. For example, it's like if you had a choice:
"You're at your friend's house, he's cooking apple pie, do you want some?"
You answer "no" and the game tells you, "you burn down the house and slaughter your friend's family in their beds, now safe in the knowledge that you will never be forced to eat apple pie."
It's not necessarily a massive black mark against the game since this kind of thing is present in a lot of games, especially Mass Effect, so we should be used to it now. It's just a shame that it's present here when Banner Saga 1 didn't have that issue.
-Similarly, the game tends to remove characters from you by having them arbitrarily killed, flip allegiance, go off on their own mission or just simply disappear. This can be very very annoying if you invested a lot in that character and they were an integral part of your strategy. It would actually be nail-bitingly exciting if these characters died in the field because you failed to protect them, but no, the game just wisks them off into the void. Also, you don't get the items you equipped them with back. Sucks to be you.
-Lastly, while the story is good, Banner Saga 1 felt complete, like The Matrix. Banner Saga 2 is very much The Matrix Reloaded (remember the absolute final scenes of that film?) and just as satisfying at the end, i.e. not at all, due to the massive unspoken 'TO BE CONTINUED' hanging over it. On one hand it means we'll get another game (yay) on the other, sucky ending (boo).

Reflecting on the game as a game, I really like the non-interactive nature of it. Everything is inevitable and unchangeable, but to me that's exactly what it should be. I was kind of disappointed to find out you can avert annihilation, affect time and the weather, and now move stuff around. I can (and do) play the game as if these things weren't availalble, but I think it would be truer to its original ideal if there was literally nothing you could do to influence things. Of course, the fact that the instructions lie about the existence of controls shows that my interpretation of what it 'should' be is incorrect...
Appreciate it for what it is, and don't expect any more from it than what you are told.

The devs need to release the PC performance patch as soon as possible. There is a gem of a game here but it is currently hiding behind a very botched PC release.
Post FPS patch note:
So post FPS patch the game runs really well. On my system (shown on the left) I get 70-80 fps. The shadow effects during the day are really weird and big blocks of shade move across the landscape.  The reflections on cars alternate between dark to full reflection depending on how you look at the car. The transition is very jarring though.
On first load after the patch it said my saved game was corrupt and it forced me to restart the game from scratch. I wonder if this happened to anyone else. Not much else to say as I am now only 3 hours in. I turned on simulation mode for driving and it feels much better. The gun play is a lot more enjoyable now that the fps is higher.
Mafia III definitely needs a high resolution texture pack. I don't hate it but it would improve the look of the game immensely.
Post 10 hour played mark:
Overall though even with the framerate improvements you can't escape the fact that outside of the cutscenes there isn't that much to do in the game. There are the same sequence of mission events repeated over and over again. There is a shameful lack of variety of things to do in the open world. It almost seems like Hangar 13 ran out of time to work on the game and were forced to release it incomplete.
As it stands I cannot honestly recommend this game. The question is will the devs add gameplay to the game or will they simply move on to their next project and abandon it. Damn first No Man's Sky and now this.
Oh and one final point - please give us a damned high resolution texture pack.

This is such an innovative game for allowing you to completely customize everything about your base and armies, and I love the first person experience. It's like command and conquer but you can actually BE your troops.
Also, the AI battles on this game can be really fun and interesting. If you wanted to play single player, I recommend this game when it's on sale.
The problem with this game is when you play multiplayer with real people.
Your whole company is based around power. Without power, you can't do anything. The only way to have enough power to actually build up your base and army is to accumulate power crystals, placed randomly throughout the map. If you don't get enough because they're too far away, you're screwed, because there IS NO WAY TO GET MORE POWER. Then, your enemies (who have more power) can and will research things faster than you, can and will build armies faster (because you don't have enough power for more than a couple iron mines), and will choose you to destroy first because you're the easiest target. Your puny defense troops that don't stand a chance against the enemy rocket launchers and riot armor will be smoked immediately and you will be killed in your office because you have no defense. Game over.
There are far too many ways that this game can give certain players advantages that allow them to wipe you out of the game, and you have absolutely no way to stop it.

Broken Age is a point-and-click adventure game that is the result of Double Fine's massively popular, record-breaking Kickstarter campaign. You alternate between controlling Shay, who is overly coddled by his spaceship's computer, and Vella, who is just about the only person who takes issue with human sacrifice in her civilization, and figure out how to help them battle injustice in their own way.
A lot of money went into this game, and it's easy to tell. The voice cast is star studded, with Elijah Wood doing an amazing job as Shay, and all-around great voice acting otherwise. The art has a beautiful, painted style. The orchestral music is definitely enjoyable.
As for the gameplay, well, it's a point-and-click adventure game. Some of the puzzles are tricky, but I never got completely stuck. The interface is pretty easy to use. All in all, it's a standard adventure game with modern design sensibilities.
The story is pretty interesting, and the game did a pretty good job of holding my interest. Act I is short, however, and at the moment, Act I is the whole game. It took me about five hours to beat. I really loved the humor, and Broken Age is full of it.
Overall, I'd definitely recommend Broken Age to just about anyone, and I'm definitely glad I backed it. The only real issue is the price, especially since this game is short. If this game looks interesting to you, then Broken Age will probably be worth the price.
